decisions.title: DAP transport, lifecycle, and capability profile
decisions.gist: Choose the exact Debug Adapter Protocol contract editors may rely on when they launch or attach Jet's native debugger.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-DBG1=A makes `jet debug <file>` the one public debugger entry; editors launch that path. D-DBG2 requires Jet-only frames by default and raw generated frames only through explicit expert opt-in. D-DBG3 fixes one debugger vocabulary and behavior across terminal/editor: step, next, continue, finish, break, print, locals, backtrace, Jet source/caret, and owned diagnostics. D-OBS2 makes the versioned `<file>.jetmap` JSON sidecar the authoritative Jet-to-generated mapping. This ballot defines only the DAP projection and does not reopen those laws.

Current `crates/jet-debug/src/Dap.rs` is an unverified minimum. It accepts launch and attach but both merely spawn the prebuilt binary; advertises one hard-coded main thread; has no evaluate, exception, pause, restart, cancellation, timeout, true attach, task, or protocol-state law; never deletes old backend breakpoints; can acknowledge failures; and reports exit code zero. No editor integration test exists. The winning option replaces that behavior; compatibility with the unverified wire draft is not promised.

Common transport law. Adapter is `jet debug --dap <file.jet>` over stdin/stdout. Stdout contains only DAP frames: ASCII `Content-Length: <decimal>\r\n\r\n`, then exactly that many UTF-8 JSON bytes; length counts bytes, not scalars. Header names are ASCII case-insensitive, duplicate/missing/invalid Content-Length rejects the frame, unknown headers are ignored, body must be one JSON object, and a configurable implementation ceiling defaults to 16 MiB. Stderr is empty after DAP mode begins; adapter/debuggee text travels only through output events. Every message seq is a positive integer unique for that sender during the session. Client gaps/out-of-order arrival are accepted when request correlation remains unambiguous; duplicate/nonpositive seq rejects. Adapter seq starts at 1 and increases monotonically by one. request_seq copies the exact client request seq. Every accepted request receives exactly one response, including cancellation and errors. Unknown request fields are ignored for DAP forward compatibility; missing/wrong required fields reject. Malformed framing/JSON before a request id exists emits one stderr startup failure and exits 1; afterward it emits a structured protocol error when correlation is possible, then terminates only if stream synchronization is lost. No TCP listener, socket discovery, reverse request, telemetry, or remote transport ships under this decision. Initialize negotiation is exact: adapterID must be `jet`; linesStartAt1 and columnsStartAt1 default true when omitted and may be true or false; pathFormat must be `path` or the request fails as unsupported. Client-origin line/column values are converted at the protocol boundary only; all columns denote UTF-16 code-unit offsets, never UTF-8 bytes or Unicode scalars. Every returned Source uses a local canonical path (never URI), and every returned line/column uses the client's negotiated zero/one origin. supportsVariablePaging and supportsVariableType reflect A/B true and C false; supportsANSIStyling is true only when both client and adapter negotiate it. The response contains only capability names defined by the vendored DAP schema; there is no `supportsAttachRequest` or `supportsPauseRequest` field—attach is selected by accepting/rejecting the attach request, and pause is a base request handled by the option profile.

Common lifecycle. States are Start, Initialized, Configuring, Stopped, Running, Terminated. Only initialize is legal in Start. Its successful response enters Initialized and emits no event yet. Exactly one launch selects the target; A also accepts true attach, while B/C reject attach with jet.unsupported. A successful target request selects the target and enters Configuring; its successful response is followed by exactly one initialized event. The adapter rejects a second target request. Configuration accepts setBreakpoints and setExceptionBreakpoints in any order and ends with configurationDone. Launch/attach may prepare the target but cannot run user code before configurationDone. configurationDone starts or attaches and emits process, thread-started facts, then stopped(entry) when stopOnEntry is true; otherwise it runs until a real stop/exit. Requests requiring suspension reject with `notStopped` while Running. Continue/next/stepIn/stepOut respond before resumption, invalidate all frame/scope/variable references, and later emit stopped or exited+terminated. Pause is the only client request that turns Running into Stopped without a breakpoint. Terminate kills the debuggee, then emits exited with the real resulting code/signal projection and terminated. Disconnect ends adapter ownership: launched targets default terminateDebuggee=true; attached targets default false; the explicit standard argument overrides. EOF behaves as disconnect with those defaults.

Launch contract. launch arguments are exactly standard noDebug=false plus Jet fields `{args:[String]=[],cwd:WorkspacePath=project root,env:{Text:Text}={},stopOnEntry:Bool=true,showRawFrames:Bool=false}`; the source program is the CLI `<file.jet>` and cannot be replaced by a second path in JSON. cwd must remain inside the loaded workspace unless the separately ratified authority policy permits more. Environment overrides are explicit; no shell parsing occurs. Restart reuses the original launch arguments, rebuilds through the same debug pipeline, preserves source breakpoints/exception filters, invalidates every object id, and starts a new process. A source change is picked up by restart, never hot-swapped into a paused native process.

True local attach contract for A; B/C reject attach as unsupported. A's attach arguments are exactly `{processId:Int,program:WorkspacePath,map:WorkspacePath,showRawFrames:Bool=false}`. Attach authority is atomic here: processId must name a live local process with the same effective OS user as the adapter, and the OS debugger/process-control check must succeed before any stop. program and map must be canonical local paths inside the loaded workspace or its verified build directory; symlink/reparse resolution may not escape. program identifies the process executable and map identifies the matching D-OBS2 sidecar. The adapter verifies executable build id, source hashes, map schema, architecture, and process image before stopping or instrumenting the target. The adapter verifies PID reuse immediately before attach; any user/control/path/build-id/source/map/architecture/process-image mismatch rejects before sending an attach/stop command and leaves the process unchanged. Attach never compiles or launches. Restart is unsupported for attach. terminate is available but explicit; disconnect defaults to detach/continue. Remote host/port, container PID translation, core dumps, and attach by process name are not advertised.

Breakpoints. setBreakpoints is full replacement for one canonical Jet Source: omitted/empty list removes every prior breakpoint for that source from both adapter and backend. Each SourceBreakpoint may carry line, optional column, condition, hitCondition, or logMessage when the selected option advertises it. A verified breakpoint maps to an exact stoppable Jet span from `.jetmap`; it never silently moves to another line. Unmappable requests return verified=false with Jet-owned message and no backend breakpoint. IDs remain stable within the session for the same canonical source/span/condition tuple; changed/removed backend facts emit breakpoint changed/removed events. Response order matches request order. Duplicate requests collapse to one backend site but keep response entries. A stopped breakpoint event includes hitBreakpointIds. Conditions and logpoint interpolation use the same read-only evaluate subset; invalid forms make that breakpoint unverified. hitCondition accepts positive decimal N only and stops on the Nth and later hits when written `>=N`, or exactly N for bare N; no hidden expression language.

Full suspended-data profile for A/B; C supplies only its stated main-thread/flat-locals subset. In A/B, threads returns every live Jet task plus the main execution context with stable positive ids for the session; names are `main` or `task <Jet-id> (<state>)`. Foreign/runtime helper threads are hidden unless showRawFrames is true, when they appear as `[raw] thread <backend-id>`. thread started/exited events track changes. V1 native control is all-stop: every stopped event sets allThreadsStopped=true; continue/step resumes all tasks, and singleThread requests reject as unsupported. stackTrace honors threadId,startFrame,levels; returns only Jet-mapped frames by default, innermost first, with canonical local Source path, negotiated-origin line/UTF-16 column, totalFrames, and stable frame ids valid only for that stop generation. scopes returns Arguments and Locals plus Captures when present. variables supports nested children, start/count paging, namedVariables/indexedVariables, Jet names/types/values, and cycle-safe references. Values are safe summaries under D-OBS law; no address, generated Rust name, allocator internals, or secret-marked value leaks by default.

Evaluate for A/B. evaluate is available only while Stopped and supports contexts hover, watch, and repl through one read-only Jet expression evaluator. Allowed forms are literals, local/argument names, field access, indexing/get, pure operators, and calls already proven pure with no authority/effect; no assignment, move, mutation, allocation with observable identity, IO, task control, FFI, unsafe, panic, or arbitrary debugger command. It runs against a snapshot with a fixed 100000-step and 50 ms wall budget, whichever arrives first, and never resumes the debuggee. Result and child variables use ordinary Jet rendering. Terminal `print` lowers to this same evaluator. setVariable/setExpression remain unsupported because mutation is not in D-DBG3. C rejects evaluate.

Exceptions for A/B. setExceptionBreakpoints replaces filters. Filters are `panic` (default always), `error` (uncaught `T ? E` reaching run boundary), `signal` (fatal platform signal), and `all` (union); caught propagated errors do not stop under error. A stop emits reason exception, threadId, text in Jet terms, and exceptionInfo returns stable exceptionId, breakMode, description, Jet stack details, and no raw backend text. Existing E3001/E3002 rendering remains the source for panic/error facts. Unsupported platform exceptions become signal with sanitized name/code. C rejects exception requests and still reports a fatal exit truthfully.

Pause, cancellation, timeouts, and output. A/B implement the base pause request plus capability-gated cancel, progress, and launch restart; C rejects all four. pause interrupts the selected running process and reports reason pause at the first Jet-mapped frame; generated glue is stepped transparently until a Jet frame or a 5-second mapping timeout. cancel is best-effort for launch, attach, restart, stackTrace, variables, and evaluate; the original request still receives success or message `cancelled`. Launch/attach/restart use progress events and a 120-second adapter-operation timeout; paused inspection requests use 30 seconds; evaluate keeps its smaller budget. Continue itself has no program-runtime timeout. Timeout returns structured failure, restores the last safe stopped/detached state when possible, and never silently kills an attached process. Every option emits debuggee bytes as ordered stdout/stderr output events without ANSI unless client and adapter both negotiate styling; adapter notices use console, never telemetry. Output is drained before each stopped/exited event. exited carries the real process exit code; fatal signal uses 128+signal where the platform defines it and includes a preceding exception stop when configured. terminated follows exited for a finished process and may occur without exited only when adapter ownership ends but an attached process continues.

Errors and unsupported requests. Failed responses use success=false, command, message from `cancelled`, `notStopped`, or stable Jet DAP ids `jet.invalidState`, `jet.invalidArguments`, `jet.unsupported`, `jet.unavailable`, `jet.timeout`, `jet.staleReference`, `jet.mapMismatch`, and ErrorResponse.body.error `{id:Int,format:Text,showUser:Bool,variables?}`. Numeric ids are 22031..22038 in that order. Format is Jet-owned plain copy; backend/rustc/lldb text may appear only after laundering and never contains generated paths by default. Unsupported requests receive jet.unsupported and list the supported alternative; they are never acknowledged as empty success. Advertised capabilities exactly equal implemented behavior. Explicitly false/absent unless a later ballot adds them: function/data/instruction breakpoints, setVariable/setExpression, goto, restartFrame, reverse execution, disassembly, memory read/write, modules/loadedSources/source retrieval, completions, terminateThreads, and runInTerminal/startDebugging reverse requests.

Raw-frame projection. showRawFrames defaults false on launch and A's attach and is the D-DBG2 expert opt-in. False means no generated Rust source/name/path, helper frame/thread, backend value, or lldb text crosses DAP. True appends raw frames after mapped Jet frames, marks frame name `[raw] <backend-name>` and presentationHint `subtle`, supplies generated source only when it is a local debug artifact, and exposes raw helper threads/values under a separate Raw scope. It never changes stepping, breakpoints, evaluate semantics, or exception ownership. Client cannot toggle it mid-session; restart may change it. B supports launch raw frames; C does not advertise raw DAP frames.

Conformance. Implementation vendors the official Microsoft DAP JSON schema revision/hash used for release, records it in source, and runs generated request/response shape tests without importing a compiler dependency. A protocol model test covers every legal/illegal state transition, object-reference lifetime, sequence correlation, replacement breakpoint, cancellation, timeout, malformed frame, and unsupported request. Real acceptance drives unmodified current stable VS Code and Zed clients through clean-installed Jet extensions against launch; the extension offers an attach configuration only under A, and A additionally proves true attach in every client that exposes that configuration. Real LLDB-backed tests cover multiple Jet tasks, nested variables, conditions/logpoints, evaluate denial, panic/error/signal, pause, restart, output ordering, nonzero exit, detach, and raw-frame gating for each advertised option. Supported-host CI may not skip for missing backend; unsupported hosts report a declared matrix result. Captured client/server transcripts are scrubbed of machine paths and golden-tested.

Beginner pass: press Debug, stop on Jet source, inspect values, continue; no DAP/backend vocabulary or generated Rust appears. Expert pass: args/cwd/env, true local attach under A, conditions/hit counts/logpoints under A/B, task stacks, read-only evaluation, exception filters, pause/restart/cancel, raw frames under A/B, progress, and exact process outcomes are explicit. Hybrid pass: terminal and editors use one compiled target, map, evaluator, breakpoint engine, task model, exception facts, and Jet-owned errors; DAP is a projection, not a second debugger.
decisions.story: Noor presses Debug in a fresh Jet project, stops in a task, inspects a nested value, evaluates a safe expression, pauses a runaway loop, then restarts with new arguments. Later she attaches to a locally running service without relaunching it. VS Code and Zed must see the same Jet files, frames, tasks, exceptions, output, and exit status; an unsupported button must fail clearly instead of pretending it worked.
decisions.inWild:
// Editor starts one adapter process:
jet debug --dap src/main.jet

// DAP session:
initialize -> launch -> initialized
setBreakpoints + setExceptionBreakpoints -> configurationDone
stopped(entry) -> threads -> stackTrace -> scopes -> variables
evaluate -> next -> pause -> continue -> exited -> terminated
decisions.detail:
Recommend A. It ships the full daily-driver capability set — verified local attach, conditional and hit-count breakpoints, logpoints, task-aware stacks, read-only evaluate, panic/error/signal filters, pause, restart, cancellation/progress/timeouts, and exact output/exit — behind one Jet-owned projection, with every unsupported advanced feature (memory read/write, reverse execution, mutation) reported truthfully false rather than faked. B rejects attach and leaves an existing service undebuggable; C leaves editor buttons that routinely fail.

Tier compatibility (D-CANVAS-DEBUG-UX1). The capability axis here — full / launch-only / minimal — is independent of which engine executes the program. Per the ratified tier-aware direction, one DAP contract fronts both backends: a native lldb/DAP session for compiled runs (`jet run` / release binary) and the in-tier session under `jet dev`. The same transport, lifecycle, breakpoint engine, evaluator, task model, exception facts, and Jet-owned errors project from either engine; only the underlying stop spans, values, and taken path come from the engine actually running, and the status chip always names it. Facts that exist solely for a compiled OS process — true `attach` to a live PID, a real OS exit code or `128+signal` — belong to the native backend; the in-tier session is launch-model and projects the same lifecycle with the running tier's equivalents, never simulating a step or value. This ballot fixes the wire contract; the engine selection is D-CANVAS-DEBUG-UX1's, and A's projection is what both engines speak.

options.name: Full local daily-driver profile
options.detail: Recommended. Ship every common-law capability: launch, verified true local attach, source breakpoints with conditions/hit counts/logpoints, task-aware stacks, nested variables, read-only evaluate, panic/error/signal filters, pause, launch restart, cancellation/progress/timeouts, exact output/exit, and D-DBG2 raw-frame opt-in. Unsupported advanced memory/reverse/mutation features are truthfully false. This meets the card's full native/editor bar through one Jet debugger model.

options.name: Launch-only focused profile
options.detail: Keep the same transport, lifecycle truth, task-aware inspection, source breakpoints, evaluate, exceptions, pause, restart, cancel, output/exit, and raw-frame law, but reject attach with jet.unsupported. Editors always build and launch through `jet debug --dap`; existing services require terminal/native tools outside Jet. Smaller authority surface, but misses the explicit attach workflow expected from a daily-driver debugger.

options.name: Minimal stepping bridge
options.detail: Standardize only launch, unconditional source breakpoints, one main thread, Jet stack/locals, continue/next/stepIn/stepOut, output, disconnect, and exit. No attach, tasks, evaluate, exceptions, pause, restart, cancellation, conditions, or raw DAP frames. This resembles current code with truthful failures and tests, but editor buttons routinely fail and native-only task/error workflows remain below modern debugger parity.

comparisons.note: DAP requires capability-advertised optional requests, one response per request, replacement setBreakpoints semantics, invalidated object references after resume, and initialized/configurationDone ordering. A implements a strict local subset rather than claiming the whole protocol.
comparisons.code:
initialize -> launch|attach -> initialized
setBreakpoints* -> configurationDone
stopped -> threads -> stackTrace -> scopes -> variables

comparisons.note: CodeLLDB provides launch/attach, conditions, expressions, exceptions, tasks/threads, and raw native inspection. A matches daily workflow breadth while translating the default view into Jet terms.
Delve exposes goroutines as debugger execution contexts and keeps language-aware stacks/variables above a native engine. A similarly projects Jet tasks, not helper threads, as the beginner model.

A modern built-in debugger supports launch/attach, conditional/log breakpoints, watches, exceptions, pause/restart, and exact console output. A makes that interaction baseline available without importing JavaScript's runtime model.

decisions.title: Native debugger backends, provisioning, and supported hosts
decisions.gist: Choose which native debugger Jet supports on each host and who installs and locates it.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-DBG1 fixes `jet debug <file>` as the sole public entry. D-DBG2 hides generated/backend frames unless `--raw-frames` is explicit. D-DBG3 fixes one terminal/editor command model and Jet-owned output. D-OBS2 makes the versioned `.jetmap` authoritative. This ballot does not reopen those laws or D-DBG-DAP1's still-open protocol contract. It decides the external native tool, supported host matrix, provisioning, discovery, and missing-tool behavior.

Current truth is narrower than the product claim. `Source/Debug/Inferior.rs` shells out to the first `lldb` on PATH and parses LLDB text. `Inferior::available` checks only whether `lldb --version` exits successfully; it does not parse a version, bind one executable for the session, or reject a fake/incompatible binary. `Source/Debug/Native.rs` names Linux/macOS phase 1 and says Windows/gdb are follow-ups. The Nix dev shell includes unversioned `pkgs.lldb`, while installed Jet has no provisioning contract. The real native test in `tests/debug.rs` skips when rustc or lldb is missing, so a clean CI image can pass without exercising native debugging. The sidequest records one live LLDB 21.1.8 run, not a supported version range or cross-platform matrix.

Common backend contract. Jet owns compilation, `.jetmap`, breakpoint mapping, value sanitation, command semantics, diagnostics, and DAP projection. External debuggers are private process-control engines; their names, frames, generated paths, and errors remain hidden unless D-DBG2 raw frames are enabled. Jet resolves one executable before building or stopping a process, canonicalizes it, opens it without a shell, records its path/version/vendor/hash in verbose and JSON audit output, and uses that same executable for the full session. A changed or vanished executable aborts before launch/attach. User init files, plugins, aliases, and environment command injection are disabled. Backend output is parsed as untrusted bounded input; malformed or unsupported output becomes a Jet-owned error, never a panic or false success.

Version floors are compatibility floors, not floating preferences. Upstream LLVM LLDB must be 18.1.0 or newer within a Jet-tested major range recorded by each Jet release. Apple LLDB must come from Xcode Command Line Tools 16.0 or newer within the Jet release's tested Xcode range; Apple and upstream LLDB version numbers are not compared. Windows CDB must be Debugging Tools for Windows 10.0.26100.0 or newer within the tested Windows SDK range. Jet parses the real vendor/version banner, runs a harmless capability probe, then rejects wrong vendor, older version, unsupported architecture, or a backend outside the release's tested-major manifest. Newer untested releases are rejected even through an expert override; upgrade Jet or select a backend inside the release's tested range. D-DBG2 `--raw-frames` changes presentation only and never weakens backend compatibility checks.

Supported native hosts are Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, and Windows MSVC x86_64/arm64. Linux uses upstream LLDB; macOS uses Apple LLDB because its signing, entitlements, and platform runtime integration are host facilities; Windows uses CDB because it is the supported Windows-native process/PDB engine. Host architecture and debuggee architecture must match for v1 native launch/attach. Linux musl, Android, iOS device debugging, 32-bit targets, FreeBSD/other Unix, cross-host debugging, containers without host process authority, remote targets, and core/minidump sessions are unsupported under this ballot. Unsupported hosts never probe random debugger names.

Managed realization is not PATH installation and never requires a project manifest. Each Jet release carries the authoritative signed debugger-tool manifest. On Linux, Option A asks Jetpack to realize the manifest's exact upstream LLDB package into the per-user hangar; the Nix provider records nixpkgs revision, derivation, output hash, executable hash, and version, while the ratified no-Nix provider must produce the same locked tool identity when it ships. On macOS, Jet never treats `/usr/bin/lldb` as the backend. It opens `/usr/bin/xcode-select` and `/usr/bin/xcrun` from the sealed system volume, clears ambient `DEVELOPER_DIR`, obtains the selected developer root with `xcode-select -p`, then runs `/usr/bin/xcrun --sdk macosx --find lldb` with `DEVELOPER_DIR` set to that exact root. The result must be a canonical executable inside that root and from Xcode Command Line Tools 16.0 or newer. Jet captures root and executable file identities and rechecks both immediately before spawn; selection/shim/target drift aborts before debuggee launch. Missing CLT produces `xcode-select --install`, which Jet never runs silently.

Windows installation under A is one explicit privileged transaction. The Jet release manifest pins an exact supported Windows SDK 10.0.26100 servicing version, immutable final Microsoft HTTPS installer URL, byte length, SHA-256, and expected Authenticode publisher/chain policy. Jet downloads to a create-new user cache file, enforces HTTPS with no credential forwarding, bounds bytes, hashes before execution, verifies an intact timestamped Authenticode signature whose leaf subject is Microsoft Corporation and whose chain terminates in the Windows trusted Microsoft root policy, then rechecks file identity/hash immediately before launch. Redirect targets, version, hash, or signature drift reject. `jet doctor --fix` previews network origin, exact SDK version, download size/hash, system-wide Debugging Tools write, elevation, Microsoft license link/acceptance, and no-reboot policy; only an interactive confirmation launches `winsdksetup.exe /features OptionId.WindowsDesktopDebuggers /quiet /norestart`. Exit 0 is success; 3010 is success with reboot required and Jet reports it without rebooting; every other exit, including cancellation, is failure with sanitized installer-log location. Noninteractive, DAP/editor, offline cache miss, or declined consent never downloads/elevates. After success Jet independently discovers CDB, verifies SDK version/vendor/architecture/capabilities, and does not trust installer exit alone. B/C never install anything.

`JET_DEBUG_BACKEND` is an expert executable override, not workspace configuration. It must be an absolute path supplied in the adapter's inherited host environment before startup; DAP launch `env`, project files, workspace editor settings, tasks, and debuggee children cannot set or change it. Terminal and DAP/editor use the same resolver; a trusted user-level editor process may inherit the variable, but no DAP request field carries it. Jet resolves every symlink/reparse point once to a canonical regular executable, then requires target and every writable parent to be owned by the current user, root/system, or Windows TrustedInstaller/Administrators and not writable by any less-trusted principal; network shares, relative paths, alternate data streams, setuid/setgid files, and world/group-writable Unix or permissive Windows ACL paths reject. It records canonical path, file id, owner/ACL or mode, size, mtime, SHA-256, vendor/version, and capability probe, then reopens no-follow and rechecks them immediately before every backend spawn. Override never bypasses supported vendor/version/host checks and appears in authority preview/audit.

Discovery is option-scoped. A resolves: trusted `JET_DEBUG_BACKEND`, then Option A's release-manifest realization/platform installation; it never falls through to PATH. B resolves: trusted override, then fixed verified platform installation roots/registries only—Linux `/usr/bin/lldb` from the host package database, macOS through the exact xcrun law above, Windows CDB through the installed SDK registry and canonical kit root; it never downloads, realizes, or searches PATH. C resolves only the trusted override and PATH in deterministic PATH order; every candidate still passes the same vendor/version/architecture/capability checks. C's CI must install an exact backend version, export its absolute bin directory, assert the resolved canonical path/hash/version, and run every native acceptance test; missing or different PATH backend fails rather than skips. Offline mode never changes order or admits a candidate; under A it permits only an already-realized manifest object.

No-tool and unsupported-host behavior is one semantic fallback, not two debugger commands. Programs covered by the shipped interpreter backend debug immediately and do not resolve a native tool. Diagnostics and I4 are exact. Reserve E2205 for a supported host with no usable backend. What: `native debugger <tool> <floor> is unavailable on <host>-<arch>`. Why: `this program needs native debugging because it uses <feature>; <candidate summary>` where summary is exactly `no candidate was installed`, `the candidate is older than <floor>`, `the candidate is outside Jet <jet-version>'s tested range <range>`, or `the candidate failed <vendor|architecture|capability|trust> verification`. Fix is option-specific and byte-stable. A: Linux `run jet doctor --fix to realize <tool-id>, then run jet doctor`; macOS `run xcode-select --install, then run jet doctor`; Windows `run jet doctor --fix, approve Windows SDK Debugging Tools <version>, then run jet doctor`. B: Linux `install upstream lldb <range> through the host package database, then run jet doctor`; macOS uses the same xcode-select copy; Windows `install Windows SDK Debugging Tools <version> at a Windows Kits system root, then run jet doctor`. C: Linux/Windows `install <tool> <range> on PATH, then run jet doctor`; macOS uses the same xcode-select copy and PATH must resolve its xcrun-selected target. Diagnostics may summarize a rejected candidate by basename, vendor, version, and reason only; they never print a full candidate path, PATH value, foreign directory list, installer URL, or environment value. Reserve E2206 only outside the host matrix. What: `native debugging is unsupported on <host>-<arch>`. Why: `Jet <jet-version> supports native debugging on linux-{x86_64,aarch64}, macos-{x86_64,arm64}, and windows-msvc-{x86_64,arm64}`. Fix: `build and run without source stepping, or debug on a supported host with the same target architecture`. Both exit 1 before compile/launch, never print raw backend output or foreign full paths, and DAP projects DAP1's selected unavailable/unsupported response. Before emission: diagnostics.md What/Why/Fix, `jet explain`, terminal fixtures and exact snapshots for every Why/Fix variant and host, JSON schema/goldens, DAP goldens, color/NO_COLOR, redaction, and exit-code tests. E2203 remains only the interpreter boundary and points to native resolution, not a future milestone.

Clean acceptance is mandatory. Linux x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, and Windows x86_64/arm64 CI each start from a fresh base image. A provisions only through its release-manifest/system contract; B's image setup installs the exact verified system package before Jet runs; C's setup installs one exact version, exports one exact PATH directory, and asserts canonical path/hash/version before tests. Every row runs a real native session covering C FFI, tasks, `#Unsafe`, native Core IO, break/step/next/finish, locals/backtrace, panic, nonzero exit, output separation, raw-frame gating, and `.jetmap` mismatch. Each supported row tests exact floor, one version below floor, current selected version, poisoned PATH, spaces/non-ASCII paths, absent tool, and option-relevant offline cache hit/miss. No supported-host test may skip because a backend is missing; setup/resolution failure fails the job. Unsupported rows assert E2206. Packaging tests prove release archives contain no debugger binaries/libraries. A additionally proves Linux hangar closure plus macOS CLT/Windows SDK discovery from a new user profile; B proves fixed system discovery; C proves PATH order and poisoning resistance. DAP/editor acceptance remains gated by D-DBG-DAP1.

Beginner pass: `jet debug` either opens a Jet source session or gives one exact platform install action; no LLDB/CDB choice is required. Expert pass: absolute override, locked identity, offline behavior, hashes, tested version range, backend audit output, raw frames, and supported matrix are explicit. Hybrid pass: interpreter and native engines remain private implementations behind one `jet debug`, one `.jetmap`, one command vocabulary, and one error model. No editor-only provisioning path or second debugger CLI exists.
decisions.story: Maya installs Jet on a new Linux laptop, presses Debug on a program that calls C and starts tasks, then opens the same repository on a Mac and a Windows workstation. She should not need to know which system debugger Jet drives, edit PATH, or discover that CI silently skipped every native test. Her teammate Arun needs to pin or override the backend for a locked-down build image and inspect the exact tool identity used.

breakpoint hit  server.jet:24  in serve()
(jet) locals
request = Request.{ method: "GET", path: "/health" }

$ jet doctor
native debugger  ready  lldb 18.1.8  /home/maya/.jet/hangar/.../bin/lldb

decisions.detail:
Recommend A. Each host gets its maintained platform process and debug-info engine — locked upstream LLDB on Linux, Apple LLDB on macOS, CDB on Windows — with recorded tool identity and real native CI on every supported row, all behind one Jet-facing debugger. B leaves install, licensing, and updates to the OS administrator; C leaves two identical Jet installs behaving differently until the user repairs PATH, with no release-pinned default.

Tier compatibility (D-CANVAS-DEBUG-UX1). This ballot already carries the tier split: programs covered by the shipped interpreter backend debug immediately and never resolve a native tool (the E2203 interpreter boundary), and a native tool is resolved only when the program actually needs a native process. That matches the ratified tier-aware direction — native session for compiled runs, in-tier session under `jet dev`, one `jet debug` command, one `.jetmap`, one command vocabulary, one error model, the engine always named on screen. The provisioning axis chosen here — managed / verified-system / user-PATH — governs only how the native tool is obtained and never touches the interpreter tier, so the beginner's `jet dev` session works regardless of which option wins.

options.name: Managed platform-native backends
options.detail: Recommended. Linux uses locked upstream LLDB >=18.1.0, macOS uses Apple LLDB from Xcode CLT >=16.0, and Windows uses CDB from Windows Debugging Tools >=10.0.26100. Jetpack realizes or verifies each tool, Jet records exact identity, and A never searches or falls through to PATH. Every supported CI row executes real native sessions. This gives each host its maintained process/debug-info engine while preserving one Jet-facing debugger.

Error [E2205]: native debugger cdb 10.0.26100.0 is unavailable on windows-msvc-x86_64
 Why: this program needs native debugging because it uses C FFI; no candidate was installed
 Fix: run jet doctor --fix, approve Windows SDK Debugging Tools 10.0.26100.0, then run jet doctor

options.name: Verified system installations
options.detail: Support A's platform-native matrix and checks, but Jetpack never downloads or realizes a debugger. Linux uses the compatible LLDB registered by the host package database, macOS uses Xcode CLT through the pinned xcrun resolution law, and Windows uses CDB from an already-installed Windows SDK kit root. Fixed system discovery avoids ambient PATH while leaving installation, licensing, and updates to the OS administrator. Clean CI preinstalls exact tools and still runs every native test without skips.

 Why: this program needs native debugging because it uses C FFI; no candidate was installed
 Fix: install Windows SDK Debugging Tools 10.0.26100.0 at a Windows Kits system root, then run jet doctor

options.name: User-managed tools on PATH
options.detail: Support the same full Linux/macOS/Windows backend and version matrix as A, but never realize or verify a system installation through Jetpack. Users install LLDB, Xcode CLT, or Windows Debugging Tools and place the compatible executable on PATH; CI does the same explicitly and still runs every real acceptance test without skips. This avoids managed tool state, but identical Jet installs can differ until the user repairs PATH and there is no release-pinned default.

 Why: this program needs native debugging because it uses C FFI; no candidate was installed
 Fix: install upstream lldb 18.1.0 through Jet's tested release maximum on PATH, then run jet doctor

decisions.title: Debugger execution, attach, and workspace authority
decisions.gist: Choose what a debug session may build, run, inspect, inherit, and attach to.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-DBG1 keeps `jet debug <file>` as the one public debugger entry. D-DBG2 keeps generated/backend state hidden unless `--raw-frames` is explicit. D-DBG3 fixes terminal/editor command meaning, and D-OBS2 makes the versioned `.jetmap` the source-map authority. I1/I2/I3 still apply. AUTH1 owns debugger-session authority; live D-DBG-DAP1 may only project this law. DAP true attach activates only if both decisions permit it. D-DBG-NATIVE1 is live, open, and unratified: interpreter launch may use AUTH1 now, but every LLDB, native attach, formatter, tool discovery, and tool identity clause below stays dormant unless and until the owner ratifies a NATIVE1 outcome whose discovery and identity law matches this ballot.

Common ceiling. Debug never broadens compiler, build, runtime, package, filesystem, network, process, `#Unsafe`, FFI, or secret authority. Compilation uses the normal front end/build graph and existing declared grants. Debuggee children inherit this session ceiling or less; spawn/exec cannot recover stripped environment, cwd access, debugger handles, control channels, attach rights, or descriptors. Debug control descriptors are close-on-exec and never inherited.

Paths are capabilities. Source, workspace, cwd, executable, map, toolchain, audit root, and backend artifacts are opened component-by-component without following symlinks/reparse points outside allowed roots. Capture post-open canonical identity and recheck immediately before effect. Replacement invalidates consent. A/C cwd stays inside the loaded project; B may grant one explicit external cwd. Relative debuggee arguments remain bytes, not adapter-resolved paths.

Exact backend argument encoding. Debuggee invocation uses direct OS argv/environment APIs: no shell, response file, startup file, or interpolation. POSIX argv/env values reject NUL; environment names also reject `=`. Windows values are exact UTF-16 and reject NUL or unpaired surrogates; environment names also reject `=`. PID syntax is positive ASCII decimal with no sign or whitespace. Workspace/client bytes reach LLDB only through structured APIs. LLDB command text may contain internal constant commands only; if an operation lacks a structured API, Jet reports E2244 and does not offer it. Hostile spaces, quotes, backslashes, CR/LF, Unicode, leading dashes, and control bytes must round-trip exactly in positive tests or reject before launch in negative tests.

Backend initialization is closed. Disable user/system/project init, plugin/script/formatter discovery, executable/source/cwd/home/environment/debug-symbol auto-load, Python imports, command files, target hooks, and stop hooks. Conditional on matching NATIVE1 law, Jet may load only compiler-toolchain-shipped native formatter files after no-follow open, owner/mode check, manifest path+hash verification, and byte recheck. A formatter has debugger-equivalent access to all stopped-process memory and backend state; containment therefore gives the backend empty secret environment, no network, read-only verified toolchain/target/map/source handles, private-temp-only writes, and no extraneous handles. Formatter output is tainted and passes the same redactor as raw memory before UI/DAP/audit. A/C never load workspace scripts. B may grant one no-follow/hash-pinned script only if NATIVE1 explicitly permits it; preview states that it can read and modify target memory, and containment/redaction still apply.

Exact environment baseline. On POSIX, inherit only existing parent values named `PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `LANG`, `TZ`, plus names matching `LC_[A-Z0-9_]+`; absent names remain absent. On Windows, inherit only existing `SystemRoot`, `WINDIR`, `COMSPEC`, `PATHEXT`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `USERPROFILE`, and `PATH`; absent names remain absent. Adding a baseline name needs a new AUTH decision. Additional names come only from CLI `--env NAME` or DAP `env`; every requested DAP environment name is classified automatically by provenance and built-in patterns before preview. AUTH1 adds no `secretEnvNames` launch field: DAP1's exact launch schema remains unchanged unless a later atomic DAP amendment ratifies one. No workspace file grants names implicitly. Secret names come from vault provenance, `@Redact`, built-in ASCII-case-insensitive globs `*TOKEN*`, `*SECRET*`, `*PASSWORD*`, `*CREDENTIAL*`, `*COOKIE*`, `*AUTH*`, `*_KEY`, `KEY_*`, `*_PASS`, `PASS_*`. Glob grammar has only `*` meaning zero-or-more ASCII bytes: no `?`, classes, escapes, locale, or Unicode folding; classify after ASCII uppercase. Client/workspace configuration may add patterns but never remove built-ins. Secrets require exact per-session grants, values never render or log.

Fail-closed raw projection. Vault, `@Redact`, secret environment, and derived values retain taint through expressions, copies, aggregates, formatter summaries, and DAP projections. Even with `--raw-frames`, a value is shown only when provenance proves it nonsecret. Unknown provenance, raw memory, pointer walks, mixed backend summaries, and unproven formatter output render `[redacted]` with no child reference. Arbitrary debugger memory read/write is unsupported. Backend text is data and never re-evaluated.

Atomic local attach. Attach never compiles or launches. Before control, acquire a non-reusable held target identity: Linux pidfd plus opened executable, Windows process/debug handle, macOS audit-token/start identity plus task/process handle, or an OS-equivalent stable handle. Verify positive PID, live local process, same effective user/session, OS permission, canonical image, architecture, Jet build id, exact toolchain, D-OBS2 map schema/hash, source hashes, workspace/build-root confinement, and no traced/setuid/protected/system target against that held identity; attach/control must use it without reopening the numeric PID. If an OS cannot prove identity before attach, the only fallback is attach-and-stop, issue no breakpoint, memory read/write, evaluate, continue, or other control, then verify through the held post-attach identity; any mismatch/error immediately detaches and continues. Preview/audit states this temporary stop, never claims untouched attach. Only successful proof permits control. Disconnect defaults detach+continue; terminating an attached process is separate. Name/wildcard/container/core/kernel/service/different-user/elevated attach is forbidden.

Amendment to DAP1. AUTH1 is the stronger authority law and explicitly supersedes two D-DBG-DAP1 clauses if both ratify. First, DAP1's claim that attach mismatch always rejects before sending any stop command is replaced by AUTH1's held-identity rule: platforms with atomic pre-attach proof remain no-stop; a platform lacking it may use the disclosed attach-and-stop proof fallback, with no control before proof and immediate detach+continue on failure. DAP attach preview, audit, progress, and errors must state `proofMode:"pre-attach"` or `proofMode:"temporary-stop"`; it may never claim the latter left the process untouched. Second, DAP1/D-DBG2 `showRawFrames` does not authorize raw memory/value disclosure. It may reveal only generated frame/thread names and local generated artifact locations plus values whose provenance proves nonsecret. Raw memory, pointer walks, mixed summaries, unknown provenance, formatter output without proof, allocator internals, and secret-derived children stay `[redacted]` with no VariablesReference. Memory read/write remains unsupported. Any DAP implementation or capability test must use this amended projection.

Remote is disabled in A, B, and C. Reject host/port/socket/SSH/container targets and never listen on TCP. A future dedicated D-DBG-REMOTE1 ballot must ratify endpoint authentication, transport, agent identity, secret handling, and remote source/build/map proof before any remote flag or DAP capability exists. AUTH1 grants none.

Consent token and human gesture. Canonical redacted AuthorityPreview bytes include operation, identities/hashes, cwd, environment-name set, secret grants, formatter set, child policy, attach proof mode, and audit request; PreviewHash is SHA-256 of those bytes. Approval issuance is outside DAP stdio. Jet creates one private, inherited-handle control endpoint scoped to the editor extension host and authenticates its local peer before showing consent: Unix uses a create-new mode-0600 AF_UNIX socket plus SO_PEERCRED/getpeereid uid+pid and executable identity; Windows uses a current-user-only named pipe plus ImpersonateNamedPipeClient token SID, session id, pid, and signed executable identity; macOS additionally binds the peer audit token and code-signing designated requirement. Jet authenticates only the editor host process and OS session; a shared extension-host process cannot prove which co-resident extension sent bytes, so AUTH never claims extension identity or trusts an extension hash. The peer must be the expected signed/hash-pinned VS Code or Zed host in the same logged-in user/session with the verified OS parent chain. Unknown, changed, cross-user, remote, headless, or merely stdio-connected peers cannot open the broker. A co-resident extension may at most cause Jet's native preview to appear; it cannot approve, alter, obscure, or pre-answer that Jet-owned UI.

Approval exists only after the authenticated editor host asks Jet to display the canonical preview in a Jet-owned OS window, separate from extension webviews and attached to the authenticated host window and the logged-in human performs a fresh pointer click or non-synthetic Enter/Space key event while that modal is foreground. Editor-supplied “approved” JSON, DAP requests, accessibility automation, IPC replay, launch configuration, workspace trust, and stdin bytes are never gestures. Jet's broker verifies OS foreground/session event provenance where the platform exposes it; where it cannot, editor approval is unsupported and the user must approve in a Jet TTY. TTY approval requires an actual terminal, controlling-tty/session ownership matching Jet, and a fresh y/Enter read from /dev/tty or Windows console input—not redirected stdin. Successful approval issues an in-memory, single-use token bound to PreviewHash, authenticated host process identity, OS window/session, Jet process nonce, operation, and five-minute expiry. DAP approval is a pending-request state, not a launch field or retry. On an otherwise valid launch/attach needing approval, the adapter keeps the original request open, enters AwaitingAuthority under Initialized, emits progressStart plus one console output carrying E2240 and PreviewHash, and performs no build/run/attach effect. Only cancel and disconnect are accepted for that pending request; other target/control requests fail jet.invalidState. The authenticated broker performs the gesture out-of-band, delivers approval over its private control endpoint, and the adapter atomically validates and consumes the token immediately before the first effect. No DAP message carries, mints, echoes, or resubmits a token; a stdio client knowing PreviewHash cannot approve itself. After consumption the original request continues through AUTH validation, receives its one ordinary launch/attach response, and follows DAP1 configuration ordering. Denial, modal close, broker loss, cancel, disconnect, or five-minute expiry produces one failure response for the original request using DAP cancelled (user denial/cancel) or unavailable with E2240 (expiry/broker loss), then returns to Initialized with zero effects. Token never enters argv, environment, source, DAP transcript, audit, or logs. Wrong peer/window/session/hash/nonce/op or replay is rejected and invalidates the pending approval. Terminal EOF/N/no/cancel exits successfully with zero effects. Restart reuses approval only for exact PreviewHash and same authenticated host/session; otherwise it enters AwaitingAuthority again.

Audit export. Exact CLI form is `jet debug <file> --audit <filename>`. Filename is one ASCII component matching `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,58}\.json`. Fixed destination is `.jet/debug/audit`; reject separators, `..`, absolute paths, alternate streams, trailing dot/space, reserved device names, non-ASCII, and existing destinations. Open verified owner-controlled root no-follow; create a random same-directory temp with create-new and mode 0600/current-user-only ACL; write canonical JSON, fsync file, atomically install with no-replace, then fsync directory. On failure remove only Jet's own temp. Ledger includes redacted authority facts, hashes, consent/revocation, denials, attach held identity/proof mode, and formatter hashes; never values, memory, expressions, transcripts, command lines, tokens, or secret bytes.

Diagnostics are byte-pinned:
E2240 What: `debug operation needs authority approval`. Why: `the pending <launch|attach|restart> request would build, run, or control a process using the authority shown in preview <hash>`. Fix: `approve that exact pending preview in Jet's window and wait for the original request to continue, or cancel to make no changes`.
E2241 What: `debug environment name <name> is not granted`. Why: `the launch requested <ordinary|secret> environment name <name>, but the approved preview does not contain it`. Fix: `add <name> explicitly to the debug environment request and approve the new preview, or remove it from the launch`.
E2242 What: `debug path is outside workspace authority`. Why: `<source|cwd|program|map|toolchain|audit> resolves outside the approved root <workspace-relative-root-label>`. Fix: `choose a path inside the approved workspace/build root; an external cwd requires the ratified expert grant and a new preview`.
E2243 What: `debug attach target is not authorized`. Why variants: `the process identity changed before control`; `the process is not a same-session, same-user local Jet target`; `the process build, map, source, architecture, or protection state does not match the approved target`; `this AUTH outcome does not permit attach`. Fix: `choose the process again and approve its new verified identity, or launch it through jet debug <file>`.
E2244 What: `debug backend component is unavailable or untrusted`. Why variants: `the requested operation has no structured backend API`; `formatter or script identity changed after preview`; `the component failed toolchain manifest, ownership, mode, containment, or hash verification`. Fix: `use the supported Jet debugger operation or restore the verified Jet toolchain component, then start a new session`.
E2245 What: `remote debugging is not authorized`. Why: `AUTH1 permits local launch and conditional local attach only; no D-DBG-REMOTE1 outcome has granted remote process control`. Fix: `debug a local Jet program; remote debugging remains unavailable until a dedicated remote decision is ratified`.
Each exact What/Why/Fix variant has diagnostics.md and jet explain text, terminal plain/TTY/NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR snapshots, JSON schema/goldens, DAP error goldens, VS Code/Zed rendering, exit assertions, redaction fixtures, and source/argument spans where applicable. Denials never include values, approval tokens, full foreign paths, backend text, or process command lines. Cancellation is not an error.

Beginner pass: one concrete preview appears only when authority changes, then the chosen program runs with minimal environment and no debugger discovery. Expert pass: exact cwd/env/secret/child/attach/backend/audit facts are inspectable; B adds explicit external cwd, full-environment, and one formatter-script grants but no remote authority. Hybrid pass: terminal and DAP share one preview hash, token, redactor, and ledger.
decisions.story: Noor opens a downloaded service in an editor and presses Debug. The project has build hooks, her shell contains production tokens, and another same-user process is running nearby. She needs the selected Jet program to behave like a real local run without letting the workspace silently execute debugger scripts, inherit unrelated secrets, escape through paths, or attach to the wrong process after PID reuse. When she deliberately attaches to her own service, the adapter must prove it is the exact Jet build she selected before stopping it.
decisions.inWild:
# First local launch: editor shows Jet's authority preview before starting.
Debug src/server.jet
  build: normal Jet build policy
  run: src/server.jet
  cwd: /work/acme
  environment: 5 ordinary names; 0 secret names
  children: inherit this session ceiling
[Start debug session] [Cancel]

# Explicit local attach from the process picker.
Attach PID 4182 — /work/acme/.jet/build/server
  same user · matching build/map/source · local only
[Attach] [Cancel]
decisions.detail:
Recommend A. First launch or attach and every material authority change shows one concrete redacted preview; consent is session-scoped, workspace-confined, local-only, environment-minimal, secret-explicit, and same-user-attach with full identity proof, with no durable blanket trust and no nagging on unchanged restarts. B adds explicit expert grants — one external cwd, the full parent environment, one verified backend script — through the same single mechanism and preview; C forbids attach entirely and so cannot debug an already-running service.

Tier compatibility (D-CANVAS-DEBUG-UX1). AUTH1 already separates the tiers: interpreter-backed launch may use this authority law now, while every native-tool, attach, and formatter clause stays dormant until NATIVE1 ratifies a matching outcome. One preview hash, one token, one redactor, and one ledger cover both the in-tier session under `jet dev` and the native session for compiled runs. Attach authority is a compiled-process capability; the in-tier session is launch-model, so under `jet dev` the attach-proof machinery simply does not arise. This is the authority projection behind the ratified tier-aware direction — one mechanism, two honest backends — not a second policy per engine.

options.name: Session-scoped workspace authority
options.detail: Recommended. First launch/attach and every material authority change gets one concrete preview. Consent is session-scoped, workspace-confined, local-only, environment-minimal, secret-explicit, no-init, and same-user attach with full identity proof. Ordinary unchanged restarts do not nag. This gives beginners a safe Debug button and experts an exact audit without durable blanket trust.

#   env        PATH, HOME, LANG, TMPDIR
#   secrets    none

#   children   same ceiling
# Start? [y/N]

# Editor/DAP attach picker invokes the same preview:
# Attach PID 4182 (/work/acme/.jet/build/server)? [y/N]

options.name: Expert grantable authority
options.detail: Keep A's fail-closed substrate, but allow explicit per-session grants for one external cwd, the full parent environment, and one verified backend script if matching NATIVE1 law permits it. Every expansion is separately previewed, redacted, non-durable, and audited. Remote remains disabled pending D-DBG-REMOTE1. This gives expert reach through explicit opt-in while preserving one authority mechanism.

options.name: Workspace launch only
options.detail: Permit only workspace-confined launch with A's minimal environment, pinned backend, child ceiling, redaction, and preview. Reject all attach, external cwd, inherited secret environment, workspace formatter scripts, and remote targets. Smallest authority surface, but cannot satisfy DAP1's true-attach option or debug an already-running local service.

Same-user identity alone is insufficient: OS policy, protected targets, PID reuse, and image drift matter. A requires OS permission plus start/image/build/map revalidation before the first stop.

decisions.title: VS Code and Zed debugger discovery and launch experience
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet debugging appears and starts in VS Code and Zed.
decisions.explainer:
Scope and inherited law. Ratified D-DBG1 makes `jet debug <file>` the only public debugger command. D-DBG2 keeps generated/backend frames hidden unless raw frames are explicitly enabled. D-DBG3 fixes debugger command meaning. D-OBS2 owns `.jetmap`. Live open D-DBG-DAP1 owns wire behavior and capabilities; D-DBG-AUTH1 is live, open, and unratified; it owns the proposed consent, path, environment, secret, attach-proof, and workspace-authority law but grants nothing until the owner chooses an outcome. D-DBG-DIAG1 is absent from Tower; its /tmp artifact is a draft only. EDITOR1 cannot ship authority- or diagnostic-dependent integration until AUTH1 and DIAG1 are both ratified compatibly. AUTH1 would own consent, paths, environment, secrets, attach proof, and workspace authority; live open, unratified D-DBG-NATIVE1 owns native backend support, discovery, identity, and diagnostics. EDITOR1 chooses editor discovery and launch UX only. It cannot widen any other outcome. Native launch/attach UI remains dormant until DAP1, AUTH1, and NATIVE1 ratify compatible support; interpreter-backed launch can ship independently. If DAP1 or AUTH1 rejects attach, editors do not register, generate, suggest, or accept an attach configuration.

Current clean audit. `editors/vscode/package.json` activates on Jet language and contributes language, grammar, LSP settings, and Run/Test commands only; it has no `contributes.debuggers`, debug configuration provider, adapter descriptor, Debug command, initial configuration, or editor acceptance test. Its executable discovery is explicit `jet.languageServerPath`, then compiler-workspace `target/debug/jet`, then PATH. `editors/zed/extension.toml` and its WASM register Jet language and `jet lsp` only; they have no debug-adapter registration or debug scenarios. Existing VSIX/WASM files are build artifacts, not proof of debugger behavior.

One executable, one adapter. Every enabled editor integration resolves one Jet driver executable and invoke it directly with argv `["debug","--dap",<canonical-program>]`; no terminal text, shell, task wrapper, backend command, or alternate adapter binary. The source program is the CLI argument, matching DAP1; editor launch JSON cannot send a second conflicting program. The adapter receives launch/attach fields through DAP after initialization. The editor never discovers LLDB, CDB, formatters, or toolchains. When a selected program requires native debugging, the launched Jet driver alone applies the ratified NATIVE1 discovery/tool-identity law; until that law is ratified, the editor must not claim native availability or implement its own fallback. Interpreter/native selection remains Jet's existing one-command boundary.

Jet driver discovery is deterministic and shared by LSP, Run, Test, and Debug. VS Code setting `jet.executablePath` and Zed's standard per-language binary override are the only explicit overrides; each must resolve to an absolute regular executable. Otherwise a compiler-development workspace identified by verified Jet repository markers may use its canonical `target/debug/jet`; otherwise resolve `jet` through the editor host's direct executable lookup. No recursive workspace search, downloaded binary, sibling extension, task, shell profile, or debugger-backend PATH search. The extension runs `jet --version --json` once, requires the compatible CLI/editor protocol version, caches identity for that window, and rechecks file identity before each spawn. Missing/incompatible Jet gets one Jet-owned action: install/update Jet or set the executable override. Existing `jet.languageServerPath` is read only as a migration input: if set and `jet.executablePath` is empty, show the resolved value and offer an explicit one-click settings migration; never silently copy or keep two active discovery laws.

Option-scoped VS Code registration. Under A, The extension contributes debugger `type:"jet"`, label `Jet Debugger`, language `jet`, and configuration attributes for request `launch` plus conditional `attach`. It contributes `Jet: Debug Current File`, `Jet: Debug Package Entry`, and—only when attach is ratified—`Jet: Attach to Local Jet Process`. A dynamic DebugConfigurationProvider supplies no-config launch and schema validation; a DebugAdapterDescriptorFactory returns the direct Jet executable/argv above. Initial configurations are named `Jet: Debug current file` and `Jet: Debug package entry`; attach is added only under compatible ratification. F5 with an active runnable Jet file chooses it. Package entry resolution never invents a public command. The extension invokes the private, versioned editor bridge directly. Exact argv is `["__editor","debug-targets","--schema","jet.editor.debug-targets/v1","--anchor",<canonical active file or workspace root>,"--auth-handle",<inherited handle number>]`. This private spelling is ratified only as extension/compiler protocol, omitted from help/completions/manpages, and never executes user code. Before spawn, the installed hash-recorded extension creates a private non-inheritable-by-default local socket pair/Windows anonymous pipe, marks exactly the child endpoint inheritable, generates 32 random bytes from the OS CSPRNG, and writes `{schema:"jet.editor.bridge-auth/v1",nonce:<64 lowercase hex>,editorPid:<decimal>,expiresAt:<monotonic now+10s>}` to that endpoint after spawn. `--auth-handle` names only that inherited endpoint; no nonce appears in argv/env/files. Jet does not trust any extension-asserted hash. The signed Jet release manifest separately pins editor product id, publisher/code-signing identity, extension id+version, distribution archive SHA-256, canonical unpacked-tree SHA-256, required component SHA-256+byte length, and allowed parent-chain shape. VS Code components are at least `package.json`, `extension.js`, grammar/config/schema assets; Zed components are `extension.toml`, `extension.wasm`, language config, grammar, and debug schema when B enables it. Archive hash never stands in for installed bytes. Canonical tree hash is SHA-256 over sorted records for every regular installed file: ASCII `jet.extension-tree/v1\\0`, relative path encoded UTF-8 NFC with `/` separators and u32-LE length, executable bit byte 0/1, file byte length u64 LE, and file SHA-256; reject non-UTF-8 paths, symlinks, duplicate normalized paths, devices, and files absent from the signed manifest. Jet walks the OS process parent chain from direct child to extension host to signed VS Code/Zed executable, checks same user/session and OS code-signing identity where available, then receives no-follow read-only handles for the installed extension manifest and executable JS/WASM over the private channel (SCM_RIGHTS on Unix; DuplicateHandle from the authenticated parent on Windows), hashes bytes and lengths from those handles, enumerates installed files no-follow to recompute the canonical tree hash, and requires archive-recorded manifest identity, every component hash, and installed-tree hash to match the signed release manifest. Linux packages without OS signing must match the release-manifest executable hash. Jet then verifies nonce length/hex, expiry, single read, and EOF and closes every handle before target enumeration. Missing, redirected, replayed, inherited-by-grandchild, wrong-parent, expired, or trailing data rejects E2236. This authenticates the private bridge only; it cannot approve AUTH. Stdout is exactly one UTF-8 JSON object `{"schema":"jet.editor.debug-targets/v1","workspace":<canonical path>,"targets":[{"id":"sha256:<64 lowercase hex>","label":String,"program":<canonical .jet path>,"packageRoot":<canonical path>,"source":"active-file"|"package-entry"}]}`; stderr is empty on success and diagnostics use the shared editor protocol on failure. Target id is SHA-256 over tagged binary bytes, not ambiguous JSON. Input is ASCII `jet.debug-target/v1\0`, then each identity length-prefixed with a little-endian u32: POSIX identity is tag 0x01 + `st_dev` u64 LE + `st_ino` u64 LE; Windows identity is tag 0x02 + volume serial u64 LE + FILE_ID_128's 16 bytes; absent package root is tag 0x00. For a package target append tag 0x03 + SHA-256 of the exact no-follow-opened `pkg.jet` bytes + SHA-256 of canonical selected-entry bytes `{"schema":"jet.package-entry/v1","entry":<workspace-relative UTF-8 NFC path>}` with keys in that order and no whitespace; standalone targets append tag 0x04. Append workspace-relative program path as UTF-8 NFC with `/` separators, length-prefixed u32. Non-UTF-8 paths reject E2236. Any file-id, package manifest byte, canonical entry declaration, package root, or relative path change changes id. Targets are sorted by id. Zero targets produces E2236/no runnable file; one launches; multiple always show a picker. Generated config persists canonical `program`, never id; every launch reopens/canonicalizes program and re-resolves package membership, so stale ids cannot redirect execution. The extension never guesses `main.jet`, parses `pkg.jet`, or scans files. Schema/version mismatch is E2236 and no fallback.

Conditional Zed registration. The released baseline is Zed Rust extension API `zed_extension_api = "0.7.0"`. Its exact contract is `extension.toml` section `[debug_adapters.Jet]` with `schema_path = "debug_adapter_schemas/Jet.json"`, plus Extension methods `get_dap_binary`, `dap_request_kind`, and `dap_config_to_scenario`; A does not register any Zed adapter, locator, schema, or scenario under API 0.7.0 because its trust/auth requirements are not realizable. B may register the stated adapter only if a separately ratified AUTH outcome provides an editor-independent OS broker that authenticates Zed without a trust API; otherwise B also disables Zed. A future Zed-capable outcome may use `dap_locator_create_scenario` only after a pinned released API supplies the missing trust fact. `get_dap_binary` returns command=<resolved Jet executable>, arguments=[`debug`,`--dap`,<canonical program>], empty added env, cwd=<authorized cwd>, stdio connection, and the launch/conditional-attach request args. The extension never downloads Jet. The only Zed adapter override is the standard `dap.Jet.binary`, received as `user_provided_debug_adapter_path`, and it is treated as `jet.executablePath`; `dap.Jet.args` is rejected because adapter argv is fixed.

Exact `.zed/debug.json` is an array. Jet entries accept `{"adapter":"Jet","label":String,"request":"launch","program":String,"args":[String],"cwd":String,"env":{String:String},"stopOnEntry":Bool,"showRawFrames":Bool}`; conditional attach replaces launch fields with positive `processId`, `program`, `map`, and optional `showRawFrames`. Example: `[{"adapter":"Jet","label":"Jet: API","request":"launch","program":"$ZED_WORKTREE_ROOT/src/api.jet","args":["--port","8080"],"cwd":"$ZED_WORKTREE_ROOT","env":{"LOG_LEVEL":"debug"},"stopOnEntry":false,"showRawFrames":false}]`. Unknown fields reject through the shipped schema. Zed's `dap.Jet.binary` overrides only the Jet driver; it never names LLDB/CDB.

Zed 0.7.0 exposes DAP registration but no extension API that proves workspace trusted/restricted state or authenticates a Jet-owned approval window. Therefore, while AUTH1 remains open/unratified, Zed integration is planning only; if the owner ratifies AUTH1 with its current broker law, Zed 0.7.0 cannot satisfy A's automatic locator or AUTH editor-token path: A registers no Zed debug adapter, Debug item, locator, scenario, schema, or debug command until a released Zed API provides both facts. A may expose only non-debug `Jet: Debugger Status` command/language status text explaining the pinned API prerequisite; it cannot start Jet or resemble a launch action. Clean-install acceptance must fail before claiming Zed support if any Debug UI item appears. Explicit `.zed/debug.json` under B is also unsupported if AUTH requires that missing trust signal. C may expose a terminal command only when Zed itself labels it a user-confirmed task; it is never called integrated debugging. A later released API version may replace 0.7.0 only after the ballot contract, version, and acceptance are updated; “current stable” alone is not a version pin.

Option boundaries. A registers contextual/no-config providers, package-target bridge calls, and ordinary Debug-button behavior in VS Code only; Zed is explicitly disabled and excluded from A acceptance until a pinned released trust/auth API exists. B registers the adapter and schema in VS Code and may do so in Zed only if the ratified editor-independent AUTH broker proves signed Zed identity and human approval without extension trust state; otherwise Zed is disabled. B it never calls the target bridge automatically and launches solely from an explicit `launch.json` or `.zed/debug.json`. C registers no debugger, adapter, provider, locator, schema, initial configuration, breakpoint integration, or acceptance claim; its commands are terminal wrappers around public `jet debug <file>` and cannot present editor stacks/variables. Common acceptance language applies only to behavior each option claims.

Configuration law. Editor configuration is a projection onto DAP1/AUTH1, not a second policy. No editor schema contains a separate secret-name field: AUTH classifies every requested `env` name and derives any secret grant inside the authenticated approval broker. Secret classification, secret-name grants, and approval tokens are never transported in DAP JSON, launch files, `.zed/debug.json`, or adapter argv. Launch accepts `type:"jet"`, `request:"launch"`, `name`, `program`, `args:[String]`, `cwd`, `env:{String:String}`, `stopOnEntry:Bool`, and `showRawFrames:Bool`; defaults are active/resolved program, empty args, package/workspace root cwd, empty explicit env, true, and false. Unknown Jet fields fail with the editor's schema error; no shell-string args. `program` must be one canonical local `.jet` file accepted by the Jet driver. Attach, only if ratified, accepts `type`, `request:"attach"`, `name`, positive integer `processId`, canonical `program`, canonical `map`, and `showRawFrames`; process picker results come from a Jet-owned, authority-filtered query and display redacted PID/image/build identity, never arbitrary OS command lines. Editor variables such as workspace folder are expanded by the client once, then Jet canonicalizes and authorizes the result. Any authority-sensitive field change creates a new AUTH preview hash.

Option-scoped beginner law. Only A provides zero-config launch. On trusted VS Code workspaces, gutter breakpoints and the ordinary editor Debug action work without checked-in configuration. The active runnable Jet file wins; package entry is the explicit second action, never a hidden replacement. A generated initial configuration is an editable suggestion, not required state. Defaults expose no raw frames, secret inheritance, external cwd, attach, backend script, or remote authority. The first material launch still displays AUTH1's redacted authority preview and uses its preview-hash-bound approval token; editor workspace trust is not approval. Cancel, EOF, denial, or editor disconnect before token consumption causes zero build/run/attach effects.

Workspace trust. In an untrusted/restricted workspace, every enabled integration provides syntax coloring and read-only language metadata but do not start Jet, LSP, Run, Test, package metadata, debug adapter, process picker, or executable probes against workspace paths. Debug commands explain that editor workspace trust is required. Granting editor trust merely allows Jet to start; it does not grant AUTH1 authority, environment, secrets, scripts, attach, native backend, or remote access. Checked-in launch/scenario configuration is data and receives the same schema, canonicalization, preview, and redaction as interactive launch. Extension logs never contain environment values, secret names when policy redacts them, approval tokens, raw values, backend output, or foreign command lines.

Editor diagnostic contract. E2236 remains a draft DIAG1 allocation, not live law until D-DBG-DIAG1 ratifies; EDITOR cannot emit it early. Exact What is `Jet debug configuration is invalid`. Each failure chooses one byte-pinned Why/Fix pair: Why `field <field> <constraint>`; Fix `correct <field> in the editor's Jet debug configuration`. Why `no runnable Jet file is active`; Fix `open a runnable .jet file or choose Jet: Debug package entry`. Why `package entry selection is ambiguous: <workspace-relative entries>`; Fix `choose one package entry explicitly`. Why `Jet extension protocol <editor-version> is incompatible with Jet <jet-version>`; Fix `update Jet and the Jet editor extension to compatible versions`. Why `the private editor bridge could not authenticate the installed extension`; Fix `reinstall the Jet extension and restart the editor, then retry`. Why `target path cannot be represented by jet.editor.debug-targets/v1`; Fix `move the Jet source to a UTF-8 path, then retry`. Every pair gets diagnostics.md, jet explain, plain/TTY/JSON/DAP/editor snapshots, exact exit, redaction, and hostile field/path fixtures under I4. Until DIAG1 ratifies, the feature is blocked rather than borrowing another code.

Diagnostics and UX truth. Adapter launch failures surface the structured Jet/DAP diagnostic and one relevant action; extensions do not rewrite backend/rustc text or infer success from process creation. Status UI distinguishes interpreter session, native session, unavailable native backend, authority approval needed, and unsupported attach. Capability-driven UI hides unsupported actions; it never advertises a grayed feature as shipped. Restart, disconnect, terminate, breakpoint, variables, evaluate, output, and attach semantics come only from DAP1. All editor strings say Jet, Jet source, and Jet Debugger; generated Rust and DAP jargon stay out of beginner surfaces.

Option-scoped clean-install acceptance. A proves the full zero-config matrix below in VS Code and proves Zed 0.7.0 has no Jet adapter/button/locator and shows one unsupported-version explanation. B proves VS Code adapter/schema/explicit-config launch and no zero-config provider; Zed runs the same explicit-config matrix only when the independent AUTH broker prerequisite is ratified and proved, otherwise B proves Zed disabled. C proves command/task wrappers and asserts no debugger registration, F5 integration, stacks, or variables. Test released, unpacked artifacts—not source-only mocks—on fresh user profiles with no settings, launch files, scenarios, cached server, PATH pollution, or prior Jet extension. Install the pinned supported VS Code release and Zed 0.7.0 host plus a release Jet executable, open (1) one standalone `.jet` file and (2) a package whose path, file, args, and cwd include spaces and non-ASCII. In every client claimed by the selected option prove extension activation and shared executable identity. Only A/VS Code proves ordinary Debug with zero config; B proves explicit configuration only; disabled Zed rows prove no registration or execution. Claimed integrated rows prove: breakpoint binding on exact Jet line; stop/step/continue; Jet stack/locals; ordered stdout/stderr; nonzero exit; cancel before approval causes zero effects; workspace-untrusted suppression; malformed config rejection; missing/incompatible Jet repair; and no generated/backend leakage. Conditional native rows use the exact NATIVE1 clean-host matrix and cannot skip a supported host for a missing backend. Conditional attach rows prove the Jet-owned picker, identity preview, true attach, detach+continue, and mismatch rejection. Capture scrubbed editor/DAP transcripts and UI screenshots; fail on console errors, hidden fallback, shell spawn, stale packaged artifact, or capability mismatch. The VSIX is rebuilt, installed, and hash-recorded. A's disabled Zed row installs the released WASM/manifest, invokes only `Jet: Debugger Status`, and proves it contains no debug registration or Debug item; B hash-records a Zed debugger artifact only when its AUTH prerequisite is met.

Beginner pass: in A's supported VS Code release, install extension, open Jet file, set breakpoint, press Debug; Zed truthfully says integrated Jet debugging is unavailable rather than presenting a broken path. no configuration, adapter choice, backend choice, or package knowledge. Expert pass: file/package selection, argv, cwd, explicit environment names and broker-derived secret classification, raw frames, executable override, exact identity, audit, and conditional verified attach are available through standard editor configuration. Hybrid pass: every enabled editor entrypoint resolves one Jet driver and project the same DAP, AUTH, NATIVE, map, diagnostics, and debugger model; editor convenience never becomes a second execution path.
decisions.story: Maya installs the Jet extension, opens a new `hello.jet`, adds a breakpoint, and presses the editor's ordinary Debug button. She expects Jet to choose that file, stop on Jet source, and show Jet values without first learning DAP or writing configuration. Later, her teammate Arun needs package arguments, a staging cwd, selected environment names, raw frames, and—if attach is ratified—a verified local process attach, all without the editor inventing a second debugger path or silently trusting the workspace.

decisions.detail:
Recommend A. VS Code gets a real zero-config Jet debugger — active-file and package discovery plus expert launch and conditional-attach configuration — while Zed integration is truthfully disabled under API 0.7.0 until a pinned released trust/auth API can satisfy AUTH, rather than shipping a button that looks live but cannot prove workspace trust or approval identity. B requires checked-in configuration in every editor; C never connects editor breakpoints, stacks, or variables at all.

Tier compatibility (D-CANVAS-DEBUG-UX1). EDITOR1 already names the engine: its status UI distinguishes interpreter session, native session, unavailable native backend, authority-approval-needed, and unsupported attach, and interpreter-backed launch ships independently of the native path. That matches the ratified tier-aware direction — one Jet driver resolves and projects the same DAP, AUTH, NATIVE, map, and diagnostic model whether the run is compiled (native session) or under `jet dev` (in-tier session), and editor convenience never becomes a second execution path. The editor-UX axis chosen here — zero-config / explicit-config / commands-only — is independent of which engine tier is running underneath.
