whyNot.reason: Its nixpkgs source identity is complete, but the snapshot no longer anchors a current repository environment. It adds no stronger evaluator or build guarantee than the recommended source.
Its migration coverage is useful, but the nixpkgs NAR hash is missing. It begins with one more unresolved identity while retaining the same platform build requirements.

recommendation.tradeoff: The chosen nixpkgs snapshot was selected for Jet's development environment, not specifically for evaluator coverage. Corpus rows remain separately reviewed, and no row runs until exact Nix build identities exist.

decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, commit `tests/fixtures/nix-compat/oracle.json` with Nix version 2.34.8, annotated tag object `b6769c588f60b3e762f73d3a8cf60294df078ccd`, peeled source commit `f3f1c3c5b8ad91850e0f7c590cf177f7ab022024`, selected nixpkgs revision, and nixpkgs NAR hash. Record each supported oracle system explicitly. For every system, build through one declared recipe and record the complete install-output NAR hash plus the exact invoked executable NAR hash. Null, absent, unknown-system, or mismatched hashes must fail before fixture generation, snapshot update, expected-byte acceptance, or parity claims. Prove a tag-name match, tag-object match, or source-commit match alone cannot pass the build gate. Prove ordinary root `flake.lock` updates cannot mutate the oracle manifest. Differential CI must verify the executable hash before invocation and the build hash before accepting results. A future Nix source, build recipe, platform build, or nixpkgs re-pin requires a green proposed corpus and a new owner amendment. If C wins, its nixpkgs NAR hash must also be populated before any corpus row can run.

decisions.title: How Packages relate in a monorepo
decisions.gist: Decide whether a monorepo Package refers to independent member Packages or contains recursive Package definitions.
decisions.lesson: A Package is the complete checked unit defined by its nearest `package.jet`. A member reference points from a monorepo root to another Package. Depth cap 1 means a member Package cannot list members. This decision controls only Package membership. Config composition, source imports, and repository layout remain separate.
decisions.story: Mara keeps an API and billing tool in one repository. The root must name both without letting billing define another hidden Package tree that changes discovery and lock identity.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's enterprise monorepo uses one root `members:` list. A nested member is rejected with a diagnostic naming both `package.jet` files and telling the user to lift the inner references.

options.name: Flat member references
options.detail: The root lists member Packages by reference. Members cannot have members, and a single Package needs no membership field.
options.code:
members: find("./packages")

$ jet check
Error: member package `packages/api/package.jet` lists members from `packages/api/modules/package.jet`
 What: root `package.jet` references `packages/api/package.jet`, which also has a `members:` field
 Why: package membership has depth cap 1; members cannot have members
 Fix: remove the inner `members:` field and lift its references into root `package.jet`

options.name: Recursive Packages
options.detail: Every Package may contain more Packages through `members:`. Discovery and lock identity follow the full tree.

options.name: Workspace root plus Packages
options.detail: A separate Workspace type owns Package membership. Individual Packages never have `members:`.

options.name: Named sub-units
options.detail: The root contains differently named sub-units instead of member Packages.

recommendation.why: Flat references keep one Package noun, one membership boundary, and one deterministic depth rule while supporting monorepos.

whyNot.reason: Recursive membership makes discovery, identity, and diagnostics depend on an unbounded Package tree.
A Workspace type restores the second root noun the Package choice removed.
A renamed sub-unit creates another distribution concept beside Package.

recommendation.tradeoff: Large monorepos must list every member from the root instead of grouping them through nested Package membership.

decisions.title: Commands for Package growth and reversal
decisions.gist: Choose the commands that extract Package facts and reverse a recorded extraction.
decisions.lesson: A split moves or extracts facts without changing the checked Package graph. A fold reverses a split through Jet's private provenance ledger. Both commands preview before writing, refuse unsafe boundaries, and preserve the graph fingerprint. This decision names the two commands; D-ECO-SPLITPOLICY1 separately decides whether split may create a Config from inline facts.
decisions.story: Maya's development environment outgrows `package.jet`. She extracts it, reviews the new Config, then restores the original file after a teammate asks for the earlier layout.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses the same verbs for extracting an environment, a flat member Package, and a System-to-Fleet host map. Reversal always names the generated member file and consumes the recorded split ledger.

options.name: jet split and jet fold
options.detail: Use one extraction verb and one explicit reversal verb for every supported Package tier.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Created package/env.jet.
package graph unchanged: sha256:39df…
Reverse with: jet fold package/env.jet

options.name: jet split with reverse flag
options.detail: Use `jet split` for extraction and `jet split --reverse` for reversal.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Created package/env.jet.

$ jet split --reverse package/env.jet
Restored package.jet.

options.name: Intent-specific verbs
options.detail: Use different verbs for environments, member Packages, and Fleets.
options.code:
$ jet extract-env
$ jet extract-package billing
$ jet make-fleet halcyon
$ jet restore package/env.jet

recommendation.why: One split/fold pair applies to every graph-preserving extraction and keeps reversal visible as its own operation.

whyNot.reason: A reverse flag hides a distinct destructive direction behind the extraction command.
Tier-specific verbs create several mechanisms for the same graph-preserving refactor.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users must learn that fold is source-layout reversal, not graph aggregation or runtime behavior.

decisions.title: Fleet rollout command
decisions.gist: Choose the command for planning, staging, observing, and rolling back a Fleet rollout.
decisions.lesson: A Fleet maps host names to System Outputs plus rollout policy. Deployment builds and verifies generations, activates hosts by cohort, observes health, and rolls back according to that policy. This decision names the top-level intent. It does not change the Fleet schema or per-host activation proof.
decisions.story: Rin rolls a production Fleet through one canary and one later host. The command must read clearly in an interactive prompt, CI, and audit logs.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's beginner path runs `jet deploy prod`. Expert flags stage without activation, choose a cohort, set concurrency, emit JSON, or roll back one host without changing Fleet declarations.

options.name: jet deploy
options.detail: Use the standard deployment verb at the top level.
options.code:
$ jet deploy prod
Plan fleet `prod`
  hosts: web1, web2
  canary: web1
  then: web2
  failure: rollback changed host and stop
Push this plan? [y/N]

options.name: jet fleet push
options.detail: Group Fleet operations under a fleet noun and use push for rollout.
options.code:
$ jet fleet push prod
Plan fleet `prod`
Push this plan? [y/N]

options.name: jet os push
options.detail: Keep rollout under the JetOS command group.
options.code:
$ jet os push prod
Plan fleet `prod`
Push this plan? [y/N]

options.name: jet push
options.detail: Use the shortest top-level verb.
options.code:
$ jet push prod
Plan fleet `prod`
Push this plan? [y/N]

recommendation.why: Deploy is the established word for staged rollout and leaves push available for transfer operations.

whyNot.reason: Fleet grouping adds a noun before the primary user intent and keeps the ambiguous push verb.
OS grouping hides that one deployment spans Fleet policy, packages, services, and remote targets.
Bare push does not state whether Jet transfers source, artifacts, or activates hosts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Deploy becomes a top-level Jet command and must route to Fleet rollout without conflicting with package publication.

decisions.title: Reserved Package source-file law
decisions.gist: Decide whether one reserved `package.jet` replaces permanent package, environment, workspace, and OS role files.
decisions.lesson: A script remains complete without any reserved file. When a Package root exists, its reserved filename can supply the expected `Package` type so top-level fields construct it directly. This bare-fields root and inferred construction reuse already-ratified D-DOTCTOR2; they do not create another constructor syntax. Configs may move to discovered `.jet` files, and a leading underscore disables a discovered file. Generated state remains under `.jet/`.
decisions.story: Maya grows a script into a Package, then adds an environment and a System. She needs one place to find the Package root without learning four permanent authority files.
decisions.inWild: The proposal replaces `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and JetOS `config.jet`. During one migration epoch, `jet init --check` previews a reversible fold and `jet init --restore-role-files` restores byte-identical originals.

options.name: One package.jet
options.detail: Use `package.jet` as the sole reserved ecosystem file. Other `.jet` files contribute Configs.
options.code:
// package.jet
systems: .{ halcyon: .System.{ packages: [cli] } }

$ jet os plan halcyon
Plan: halcyon
No machine changed.

$ jet check
Warning [L1320]: this Package uses four retired ecosystem filenames
 What: `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and `config.jet` describe one Package
 Why: `package.jet` is now the one reserved ecosystem source file
 Fix: run `jet init --check`, review the fold, then run `jet init`

options.name: Keep role files
options.detail: Keep `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and `config.jet` as permanent authorities.
options.code:
pkg.jet
env.jet
workspace.jet
config.jet

$ jet explain services.db.port
services.db.port = 5432
winning role file: env.jet

options.name: No reserved file
options.detail: Require users to select an arbitrary Package root file when one cannot be inferred.
options.code:
$ jet --package config/root.jet build
Built Package.

$ jet build
No Package root selected.

recommendation.why: One root file makes later file growth organizational, removes competing identities, and leaves the single-file script path ceremony-free.

whyNot.reason: Permanent role files preserve several authorities and require provenance to explain which file identity won.
The first multi-file Package adds permanent root-selection ceremony to normal commands.

recommendation.tradeoff: One migration epoch must teach and reversibly fold four previously ratified filenames.

decisions.title: Closed v1 Output kind set
decisions.gist: Decide whether v1 has one closed Output kind set spanning packages and JetOS results.
decisions.lesson: An Output is a named typed projection from one Package graph. A closed kind set lets selection, inspection, proof, defaults, and lifecycle commands check every case. The proposed kinds are Library, Executable, Service, Check, Environment, Image, Bundle, System, and Fleet. Adding another kind would require a later owner decision.
decisions.story: Maya's Package produces a library, command, release check, image, System, and Fleet. Tooling must know which outputs are runnable, testable, enterable, deployable, and publishable without interpreting plugin strings.
decisions.inWild: The proposal declares all nine kinds beside each other and rejects `.Wheel.{}` with a diagnostic pointing to Bundle or a future ratified kind.

options.name: Nine closed kinds
options.detail: Use Library, Executable, Service, Check, Environment, Image, Bundle, System, and Fleet as the closed v1 set.

options.name: Package-only closure
options.detail: Keep package result kinds closed while System and Fleet use separate root node types.

options.name: Extensible text kinds
options.detail: Allow plugins to introduce arbitrary Output kind strings and payloads.

recommendation.why: One closed capability model makes build, selection, inspection, proof, and defaults exhaustive from Package through Fleet.

whyNot.reason: System and Fleet would split selection, inspection, and lifecycle rules from the Output model.
Arbitrary strings prevent exhaustive tools and precise beginner diagnostics.

recommendation.tradeoff: A genuinely new output kind requires an owner decision instead of a local plugin string.

decisions.title: Default build profile for everyday commands
decisions.gist: Which build profile the everyday commands (jet run, jet dev, jet build) use by default.
decisions.lesson:
Today the unnamed Default profile optimizes: opt-level 2, thin-LTO, and strip (Source/main.rs). Every `jet run`, `jet dev`, and `jet build` pays optimizer time, even a first hello-world run.

R8 says the default leans toward speed, but that speed is the runtime binary's, not the compile. In the edit-run loop, compile time is the speed a beginner actually feels.

D-BUILDPROFILE1 stays intact: profiles are still selected by explicit flag, never ambient env. This ballot only changes what the unnamed Default profile contains; `--release` remains the optimized profile.
decisions.story: Sam is learning Jet and runs `jet run hello.jet` after almost every edit. Each run waits on the optimizer before printing one line, so the loop feels sluggish from the first program.

options.name: Fast-codegen default, optimize behind --release
options.detail: The unnamed Default profile becomes opt-level 0, codegen-units 256, no LTO. `--release` selects the optimized, thin-LTO, stripped profile that is the default today.
options.code:
# Today (optimized default): the edit-run loop pays the optimizer each time
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~450 ms   (illustrative)

# Option A: opt-level 0, codegen-units 256, no LTO
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~150 ms   (illustrative)

# Shipping build — one flag, fully optimized + thin-LTO + strip
$ jet build --release hello.jet
$ ./hello              # same fast binary today's default produced

options.name: Split by command: run/dev fast, build optimized
options.detail: `jet run` and `jet dev` compile at opt-level 0; `jet build` keeps the optimized profile. An explicit `--profile`/`--release` flag overrides either command's default.
options.code:
# Option B: the command decides the profile
$ jet run hello.jet    # fast: opt-level 0         ~150 ms (illustrative)
$ jet dev  hello.jet   # fast: opt-level 0         ~150 ms (illustrative)
$ jet build hello.jet  # optimized: -O + thin-LTO  ~450 ms (illustrative)

# Override either way with an explicit profile flag
$ jet build --profile=debug hello.jet   # fast build of a build artifact
$ jet run   --release       hello.jet   # optimized one-off run

options.name: Keep optimized-everywhere default (status quo)
options.detail: Every everyday command keeps opt-level 2, thin-LTO, and strip. Fast compiles stay opt-in behind `--profile=debug`.
options.code:
# Option C: every everyday command optimizes (today's behavior)
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~450 ms   (illustrative)
$ jet build hello.jet
$ ./hello              # ~450 ms build; fast small binary

# Fast compile only if you remember the opt-in flag
$ jet run --profile=debug hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~150 ms   (illustrative)

comparisons.note: `cargo build` is unoptimized debug by default; `cargo build --release` opts into optimization. Jet's Default profile is the opposite today, optimizing on every build.
comparisons.code:
cargo build            # debug, fast compile
cargo build --release  # optimized

comparisons.note: `zig build` produces a Debug binary by default; `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast` is the opt-in. Fast iterate, explicit ship.
`go build` has no user-picked optimize/debug split. It is fast by default, with no separate optimized build command in the everyday loop.

recommendation.why: A makes the loop beginners run hundreds of times a day instant, and keeps the optimized binary one keystroke away as `--release`.

whyNot.reason: Two profiles by command means `jet run` and `jet build` of one file can produce different binaries, so a bug seen under one may vanish under the other.
The common path stays slow: every first `jet run` pays optimizer time the beginner never asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A default binaries run slower than today's until `--release`. Everyday commands exist for iterating, not shipping, so compile speed is the right default there.

decisions.title: Backend for the explicit fast AOT debug profile
decisions.gist: D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B already guarantees `jet build --profile=debug` as a fast on-disk AOT artifact. Choose whether rustc or Cranelift emits that existing profile; this does not add a third lens or change any command default.
decisions.lesson: Jet has one compiler core and two feature-identical lenses. The JIT lens runs `jet run` and `jet dev` quickly. The AOT lens emits binaries: `jet build` is optimized by default, while the ratified `jet build --profile=debug` asks for a fast unoptimized artifact. A profile controls optimization intent inside the AOT lens; it is not another feature tier. This ballot chooses only the debug-profile backend. Both choices consume the same sema-approved executable TIR, preserve every feature, and face R12 differential tests.
decisions.explainer: The current transpile path sends even debug-profile output through generated Rust and rustc at opt-level 0. Cranelift already serves the JIT lens and can also emit native objects on supported targets. Using it for debug-profile AOT avoids rustc re-parsing and re-verifying proven TIR, but requires native object/link/debug-info parity and a truthful target fallback. Keeping rustc is the smaller backend set but retains that redundant work. `jet run`, `jet dev`, plain `jet build`, `--profile=debug`, and `--release` keep their ratified meanings whichever backend wins.
decisions.story: Priya uses the JIT loop while editing. CI then needs a real unoptimized binary to run packaging, debugger, and deploy-shape smoke tests, so it invokes the existing debug profile. Priya wants the artifact quickly, with the same behavior and diagnostics as the optimized build, and an audit that names the backend used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet                     # JIT lens
$ jet build app.jet                   # optimized AOT
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet   # fast AOT artifact; this ballot chooses its backend
$ jet run --release app.jet           # explicit optimized override

$ jet explain build app.jet
profile   debug
lens      AOT
backend   cranelift | rustc-opt0
parity    executable TIR / R12
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: ordinary run/dev/build defaults stay unchanged; no backend choice is required. Expert pass: the explicit profile selects optimization intent, and build explain/audit output names backend, target support, fallback reason, timings, cache identity, and parity evidence. Backend availability may affect latency, never supported features or program behavior.

options.name: rustc opt-level 0 emits fast AOT
options.detail: Keep Cranelift JIT-only. `jet build --profile=debug` uses the current generated-Rust path with rustc optimization disabled. One native AOT backend covers every target and debug-info path, but rustc still parses and verifies code the Jet front end already proved.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet
# checked Jet -> executable TIR -> generated Rust -> rustc opt-level 0 -> app
$ jet explain build app.jet
lens AOT; profile debug; backend rustc-opt0

options.name: Cranelift emits fast AOT
options.detail: Recommended. On supported targets, lower the same executable TIR through Cranelift to object code and link the debug-profile binary without generated Rust/rustc. Unsupported targets fall back to rustc opt-level 0 and report that fact; they do not lose features or silently switch optimization intent. Optimized AOT remains the existing ship backend.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet
# checked Jet -> executable TIR -> Cranelift object -> app
$ jet explain build app.jet
lens AOT; profile debug; backend cranelift
# unsupported target: backend rustc-opt0; reason shown

comparisons.note: Rust uses Cranelift for faster debug codegen while LLVM remains the optimized release backend. Option B applies that backend split inside Jet's single AOT lens and existing debug/release profiles.
comparisons.code:
cargo +nightly cg_clif build   # debug
cargo build --release          # LLVM

comparisons.note: Zig uses a fast native backend for debug artifacts and an optimizing backend for release. The artifact purpose stays explicit; backend choice does not create a second language.

Go owns direct object emission, so a real binary does not require a second compiler to re-check source. Option B gives Jet's explicit debug artifact that property while retaining optimized AOT for shipping.

recommendation.why: B spends the existing Cranelift investment on the one fast on-disk artifact D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 already guarantees. It removes redundant rustc work where optimization is intentionally disabled while preserving one front end, one executable TIR, two lenses, and full feature parity.

whyNot.reason: A is sound and universal, but every debug artifact still pays generated-Rust parsing and rustc verification after Jet sema has already proved the program.

recommendation.tradeoff: B adds object/link/debug-info conformance work and per-target support accounting. Unsupported targets use the truthful rustc-opt0 fallback until their Cranelift object path passes the same R12 and native evidence gates.

decisions.comment: Owner question q4mspet2 answered with measured numbers: jet check 0.007s vs ~12s rustc path; Cranelift debug AOT lands at about check-plus-link time. His universality point about option A is preserved: B falls back to A's exact rustc-opt0 path on unsupported targets and names the fallback in jet explain build.

decisions.title: Epoch boundary for package sandbox proof
decisions.gist: Decide whether real Linux, macOS, and Windows package sandbox proof remains an Epoch 4 exit requirement or moves with JP3 to Epoch 8.
decisions.lesson:
A build sandbox is an operating-system boundary around package recipes. It limits files, processes, devices, and network access even when a recipe is hostile. A policy record saying ‘sandboxed’ is not proof; the child process must actually enter the boundary.

Epoch 4’s package-manager plan currently requires that proof before Jetpack claims full Nix replacement parity. On July 12, JP3 moved to Epoch 8 so Epoch 4 could finish package behavior first. Several live Epoch 4 cards still depend on JP3, so the board now contains two incompatible exit laws.

This choice does not change safe defaults or permit false labels. It decides which epoch owns the proof and which product claim Epoch 4 may make. Beginners still run one command. Experts still see the exact sandbox class, denied authority, platform, worker, and audit evidence.
decisions.story: Maya runs a third-party package recipe on a new laptop. Jetpack resolves, caches, and builds it correctly, but the platform sandbox has not passed hostile-system proof. Release notes must say whether Epoch 4 is incomplete or whether sandbox parity belongs to the later portability gate.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack build image-tools
Plan: image-tools#4.1
  source: locked sha256:20f1…
  cache: verified miss
  sandbox: linux namespace, passed
Built sha256:91b8…

$ jetpack inspect dossier image-tools
Package behavior: verified
Sandbox proof: Linux passed; macOS and Windows pending #398

options.name: Full parity stays in Epoch 4
options.detail: Restore #398 to Epoch 4. Keep #395, #399, #422, #427, #429, #432, and #656 in Epoch 4 with their current functional plans and sandbox-dependent hostile acceptance criteria. Replace each card's temporary D-JPK-EPOCHBOUNDARY1 blocker with a direct #398 blocker. Keep #433's exit criterion at all 21 Epoch 4 lanes and keep its full package-manager and isolation parity product claim gated on #398 plus the other 20 lanes.
options.technical: Board mutations after ratification: set #398 epoch=E4; for #395/#399/#422/#427/#429/#432/#656 preserve their E4 plans and criteria, remove blocker D-JPK-EPOCHBOUNDARY1, and add direct blocker c0zqnb18 (#398); preserve #433's all-21-lanes criterion and full-parity claim. #398 must prove real Linux, macOS, and Windows child confinement, syscall-level offline behavior, hostile recipes, crash cleanup, and accurate platform capability reporting. Model-only or detection-only status closes nothing.
options.code:
Epoch 4 exit:
  #398 sandbox matrix: passed
  #395 #399 #422 #427 #429 #432 #656: passed
  all 21 lanes: passed

Claim: full Jetpack package-manager and isolation parity

options.name: Functional Epoch 4, sandbox proof in Epoch 8
options.detail:
Keep #398 in Epoch 8. Keep #395, #399, #422, #427, #429, #432, and #656 in Epoch 4 for functional behavior.

#395 keeps cache/NAR behavior in E4. Its sandboxed local-fallback proof moves to #398.

#399 keeps no-installed-Nix behavior in E4. Hostile isolation and the full-replacement claim move to #398.

#422 keeps remote execution in E4 and reports each worker's actual sandbox class. Hostile cross-platform worker confinement moves to #398.

#427 keeps hook authority and finite actions in E4. Hostile hook confinement moves to #398.

#429 keeps reproducibility bound to the reported sandbox class in E4. Cross-platform sandbox proof moves to #398.

#432 keeps finite staging in E4. Hostile stage confinement moves to #398.

#656 keeps per-user paths and the transient broker in E4. Hostile cross-platform ephemeral-builder confinement moves to #398.

#433 becomes a 20-lane functional exit. Full hostile isolation and complete Nix-replacement claims wait for #398 in Epoch 8.
options.technical:
After ratification, leave #398 in Epoch 8.

On #395, #399, #422, #427, #429, #432, and #656, remove D-JPK-EPOCHBOUNDARY1. Add no #398 blocker. Keep functional E4 steps. Move only named sandbox-dependent proof to #398 without duplicate implementation.

Every E4 action reports its actual sandbox class. Fallback never prints `sandboxed`.

Revise #433 to require 20 functional lanes and limit its product claim. #398 owns hostile Linux, macOS, and Windows proof plus the later full-parity claim.
options.code:
Epoch 4 exit:
  20 functional lanes: passed
  sandbox class: reported honestly
  isolation parity: pending #398 / Epoch 8

Claim: functional Jetpack package management
Not claimed: full hostile isolation or complete Nix replacement parity

comparisons.note: Nix treats sandboxing as part of build trust, while platform support and policy vary. Jet must distinguish functional compatibility from proven isolation when the platform matrix is incomplete.
comparisons.code: build succeeds != hostile recipe is confined

recommendation.why: B follows the latest recorded epoch assignment and makes every affected plan, criterion, blocker, and product claim truthful. Epoch 4 can close one functional package graph while each command reports the sandbox class actually enforced. #398 in Epoch 8 remains the sole proof gate for complete cross-platform hostile isolation.

whyNot.reason: A reverses the recorded July 12 epoch assignment and makes #398 plus all 21 lanes prerequisites for the Epoch 4 full-parity claim.

recommendation.tradeoff: Epoch 4 closes 20 functional lanes and must limit product language. Full hostile isolation and complete Nix-replacement claims remain unavailable until #398 passes in Epoch 8.

decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, update #398's epoch exactly as selected. For #395, #399, #422, #427, #429, #432, and #656, apply the selected blocker, plan, and criterion consequences; no card may retain D-JPK-EPOCHBOUNDARY1 as a blocker. Update #433's lane count and product-claim criterion exactly as selected. Read back all nine cards and verify no sandbox-dependent E4 criterion or full-parity claim contradicts the chosen boundary.

decisions.title: One compiler, two lenses
decisions.outcome: One compiler core, two lenses. JIT lens = rapid dev work people love in python/typescript; AOT lens = highly optimized ship binary at the cost of longer build time. Same compiler core prevents drift: there should NEVER be a difference in supported features/functionality between JIT and AOT.
decisions.comment: One compiler core, two lenses. JIT lens = rapid dev work people love in python/typescript; AOT lens = highly optimized ship binary at the cost of longer build time. Same compiler core prevents drift: there should NEVER be a difference in supported features/functionality between JIT and AOT.

decisions.title: jetos first-boot welcome: where the driver and codec offer appears
decisions.gist: Where the jetos first-boot driver and codec offer appears: a dedicated Studio welcome view, an inline state on the existing control center, or a terminal flow.
decisions.lesson: The detect-and-apply backend is ungated and ships now. It reads the scanned `hardware.<host>` facts, lists driver and codec candidates, and writes accepted offers as a reviewable `config.jet` diff through the existing declarative-apply path. D-JOS-FIRSTBOOT1=D already ratified that first boot opens Studio as the control center. This ballot decides only where the beginner driver and codec offer is surfaced.
decisions.story: Priya installs jetos on a laptop with an Nvidia GPU and needs the proprietary driver plus media codecs. She boots for the first time and has never seen jetos before. The question is what greets her, and where she accepts the driver and codec offers.
decisions.inWild: The hardware scan (card #326) finds `nvidia` and reports missing codecs. Accepting an offer writes a reviewable diff into the host `config.jet`. A second boot with unchanged hardware shows nothing new.

options.name: Dedicated first-boot welcome view
options.detail: A new Studio view appears once at first boot. It steps through each detected driver and codec offer, then a Finish action deep-links into the normal control-center settings. It never renders again after the offers are resolved.
options.code:
First boot: Studio opens the Welcome view (shown once):

  Welcome to jetos
  Detected hardware needs setup:

  [1/2] Nvidia GPU
        Proprietary driver available.   [ Install ]  [ Skip ]
  [2/2] Media codecs
        H.264 / AAC not installed.      [ Install ]  [ Skip ]

  Finish -> opens the control center.

After Finish, the Welcome view never appears again.

options.name: Inline state on the control center
options.detail: No new view. The ratified control center renders a dismissible offer panel at the top of its normal host/generation/proof home until the offers are accepted or dismissed. This is the same surface a returning user already sees.
options.code:
First boot: Studio opens the control center (the normal home):

  Host: laptop   Generation 1   Source: config.jet   Proof: ok

  +-- Detected hardware (dismiss) ----------------------+
  | Nvidia GPU: proprietary driver     [ Install ]      |
  | Media codecs: H.264 / AAC missing  [ Install ]      |
  +----------------------------------------------------+

  (rest of the control center below)

Once installed or dismissed, the panel is gone. A second boot
with unchanged hardware shows no panel.

options.name: Terminal welcome flow
options.detail: The offer runs as a terminal flow. A first-boot notice on the control center points to `jetos welcome`. The Studio control center renders its ratified home unchanged, with no driver-offer element. A GUI offer can follow in a later ballot.
options.code:
First boot: Studio control center opens unchanged.
A one-line notice: "Run `jetos welcome` to set up detected hardware."

$ jetos welcome
Detected hardware:
  Nvidia GPU     proprietary driver available
  Media codecs   H.264 / AAC not installed

Install proprietary Nvidia driver? [y/N] y
Install media codecs? [y/N] y
Writing config.jet diff... review with `jetos diff`, apply staged.

comparisons.note: Mint ships a separate Welcome app and a standalone Driver Manager window. That is two surfaces for one first-run job, and users miss the Driver Manager because it is not on the path they already walk.
comparisons.code:
Welcome app  ->  (user closes it)
Driver Manager  ->  separate window, often never opened

recommendation.why: B puts the offer on the control center that D-JOS-FIRSTBOOT1=D already opens at first boot. Priya sees driver and codec offers on the surface she lands on, accepts with one click, and learns no second view.

whyNot.reason: Adds a Studio view that renders only at first boot and never again. It is a permanent surface for a one-time event, and it splits driver settings between the wizard and the control center.
Hides the beginner offer behind a terminal command. A first-time GUI user may never learn the proprietary driver or codecs are available, which misses the out-of-box goal.

recommendation.tradeoff: B shows offers inline on the home, so a laptop with several detected devices shows a longer home until Priya acts or dismisses. The panel must collapse cleanly once resolved.

decisions.title: Computed module fields: dependency and effect law
decisions.gist: Choose whether computed module fields may depend on other fields and whether locked file or network reads belong in their default evaluation.
decisions.lesson:
A computed module field is a configuration value produced by an expression during planning. Jet already evaluates many field expressions through its shared compile-time interpreter. Literals, conditionals, and pure helper calls work today. This ballot does not invent another evaluator or another field spelling.

Pure evaluation means the answer depends only on declared values and pure code. A dependency graph records which field needs which other field. Jet can evaluate that graph in dependency order. A loop such as `name` needing `label` while `label` needs `name` has no first value, so planning must reject it and print the full loop.

Tier 1 operations read external inputs reproducibly. Examples are embedding a file or fetching content with a required hash. The lock records those exact inputs. Tier 2 operations read ambient state such as an environment variable or unpinned network response. They remain forbidden in module fields under every option.

The choice matters because module files are read as declarations. Beginners need ordinary values and pure helpers to work without build-policy ceremony. Experts need deterministic ordering, exact provenance, and a clear boundary between configuration evaluation and the separate `fn build` authority model.

comptime and `fn build` are different tools; the computed-field law sits on top of comptime, not build. comptime (S26, D-CTEFFECT1) is pure value evaluation: a fuel-limited interpreter runs type-checked Core code and lowers results to constant data, with no authority and no types created. Its only external reads are Tier-1 locked operations (`embed_file`, `find`, `fetch(url, sha256:)`) recorded in `.jet/lock`. comptime values feed constants, markers, and module fields with no ceremony.

`fn build(b: BuildContext)` (D-BUILDENTRY1, D-BUILDACTION1) is a build-time action runner: it registers targets, declares capability-gated cached actions, runs processes, and emits artifacts under `.jet/generated/`. Both are kept. Merging them would give every constant expression filesystem and process authority, or strip build actions of their capability gate, breaking safe-by-default (I1). Module fields evaluate through comptime; build authority stays behind the explicit `BuildContext` grant.
decisions.story: Mara declares one development environment. Its label, prompt, and banner share a computed release name. She wants one source value, clear cycle errors, and no surprising host reads when CI evaluates the same file.

options.name: Pure dependency graph
options.detail: Fields may use any Tier-0 pure expression, top-level immutable compile-time values, pure helper call graphs, and other fields in the same module. Jet evaluates dependencies in deterministic order. A cycle fails before a plan exists and names the complete chain. Tier-1 and Tier-2 reads are rejected.
options.technical: Reuse jet-env-model ModuleEval and jet-comptime. Build a field dependency graph after front-end name/type/purity validation. Evaluate each node once in topological order, using source order to break independent ties. No field gains BuildContext, #Impure, filesystem, network, environment, clock, or randomness authority. Allocate and snapshot exact cycle and forbidden-tier diagnostics before implementation.
options.code:
comptime release = "1.4.0"
module env.dev {
  label: "ledger " + release
  prompt: label + " > "
}

$ jet env
label: ledger 1.4.0
prompt: ledger 1.4.0 >

module env.bad { a: b, b: a }
Error: module fields form a cycle: `a -> b -> a`
 Why: each field needs another field before either has a value
 Fix: remove one dependency or compute both from one top-level `comptime` value

options.name: Independent pure fields
options.detail: Fields may use Tier-0 expressions, top-level immutable compile-time values, and pure helper calls, but cannot name another field. Each field evaluates independently, so module-field cycles cannot exist. Shared values must be lifted to a top-level `comptime` binding.
options.technical: Reuse the current per-field evaluator with a validated top-level immutable environment. Reject a field name during expression resolution. Tier-1 and Tier-2 remain forbidden. `fn build` authority stays separate.
options.code:
comptime release = "1.4.0"
module env.dev {
  label: "ledger " + release
  prompt: label + " > "
}
Error: module field `prompt` cannot read sibling field `label`
 Why: each field evaluates independently
 Fix: compute the shared text in a top-level `comptime` value

options.name: Graph plus locked reads
options.detail: Everything in A also permits Tier-1 file discovery, embedding, and hash-pinned fetches. Every external input is recorded in the unified lock and reproduced offline. Tier-2 ambient reads remain forbidden.
options.technical: Field identity and plan provenance include the exact Tier-1 operation, normalized declared path or URL, content digest, lock schema, and dependency graph. Missing or changed locked inputs fail closed under --locked/offline. No Tier-1 operation falls through to host state or fn-build grants.

comparisons.note: Nix lets configuration values depend on other values, but filesystem and import effects can be less obvious at the use site.
Cargo manifests keep fields independent and literal-like; shared computation usually moves into a separate build script.

recommendation.why: A completes the owner's pure-computed direction with one existing interpreter. Shared field dependencies stay natural for beginners, while experts receive deterministic graph order and exact cycle evidence without granting host authority.

whyNot.reason: It makes harmless field reuse indirect. Users must lift values out of the module solely to avoid a dependency graph the planner can prove safely.
It mixes pure declarations with external input authority. Locked reads remain available through explicit build and input surfaces without widening every module field.

recommendation.tradeoff: A field name becomes part of other fields' dependency graph, so renaming it can break those dependents. That coupling is acceptable because it is explicit, checked, and reported before any plan runs.

decisions.comment: Owner question q7b6hkv9 answered: comptime is the pure value calculator, fn build is the authorized effect runner; both stay (I1). C loses nothing on safety and nothing on effort; it loses on I8: D-CTIO1 comptime bindings already deliver locked reads to fields through one binding line, so C would scatter external-input provenance across every field for one line of convenience.

decisions.title: Name the NixOS comparison migration command
decisions.gist: Choose the explicit `jet os` command that may reach the migration-only NixOS backend.
decisions.lesson:
`jet os import` translates existing NixOS source into Jet configuration. The migration comparison backend has a different job: after import, it builds a clearly labeled NixOS guest and captures boot proof for comparison. `jet os proof` remains native-jetos proof; comparison artifacts live only under the migration output.

Only `jet os migrate compare-nixos` may enter `nixos_backend`. Native plan, build, switch, image, and proof dispatch must reject that backend before work. Existing `--out` and `--json` controls remain canonical. Offline mode succeeds only with every locked input present. The choice below decides whether successful comparison always includes boot proof or may stop after building.
decisions.story: Mara imports a laptop configuration, builds native jetos, then creates one NixOS comparison guest. She reads its separate receipt and boot proof without mistaking it for a native generation.
decisions.inWild:
jet os import ~/nixos --host laptop --write --out ./migrated
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare --json

options.name: Build and boot-prove every comparison
options.detail: The command builds the NixOS guest, boots it, verifies guest identity, and then publishes artifacts. There is no successful unproved comparison state.
options.technical: Success atomically publishes `<out>/nixos/laptop/system.qcow2`, `proof.json`, and `receipt.json`, prints all three paths, and exits 0. Missing locked offline input prints `migration comparison unavailable offline: <input>` and exits 2. Any native command attempting this backend prints `NixOS backend is migration-only; use jet os migrate compare-nixos` and exits 2.
options.code:
$ jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare
built NixOS comparison: ./compare/nixos/laptop/system.qcow2
boot proof: ./compare/nixos/laptop/proof.json
receipt: ./compare/nixos/laptop/receipt.json
$ echo $?
0

options.name: Build by default, prove with --proof
options.detail: The command publishes a labeled comparison guest after building. `--proof` boots it and adds proof before success.
options.technical: Build-only success publishes the image and receipt with `proofState: not-run`. `--proof` publishes all three A artifacts. Offline and forbidden-backend errors match A.
options.code:
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare --proof --json

options.name: Plan by default, build with --write
options.detail: The default prints the comparison plan. `--write` builds and automatically boot-proves before publication.
options.technical: Plan exits 0 without artifact paths. `--write` has A success and error behavior.
options.code:
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare
jet os migrate compare-nixos laptop --out ./compare --write --json

comparisons.note: Legacy comparison is named explicitly and stored apart from production verification.

recommendation.why: A comparison guest is useful only when it actually boots and proves its NixOS identity. Automatic proof prevents a built file from being mistaken for verified comparison evidence.

whyNot.reason: A successful unproved image creates a weaker state that users can mistake for comparison evidence.
The dedicated compare command already states intent; an additional write gate duplicates the existing migration boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every successful comparison includes a guest boot. That is acceptable because boot behavior is the fact this oracle exists to compare.

decisions.title: Fix the `jet os image --format` values
decisions.gist: Add `--format` to `jet os image` and choose its stable native-image value vocabulary.
decisions.lesson:
`jet os image` currently has no public `--format` selector. This decision adds one for native operating-system artifacts. D-JPK-IMAGE1 remains separate: `jet image` builds OCI layouts and does not gain these values.

Each format packages one already-built system generation. Bare `jet os image <host>` keeps ISO as the default. A successful command atomically changes an artifact from `staged` to `built` only after format validation and proof. Cross-architecture requests must produce matching kernel, initrd, firmware, and boot metadata or fail before staging. No aliases or hidden normalization are included in any option.
decisions.story: Inez uses one router generation for an installer ISO, a VM disk, an SD card, and a netboot tree. Each artifact has the same source and closure identity.
decisions.inWild: jet os image router --format sd --arch aarch64 --out ./images

options.name: iso | qcow | raw | sd | netboot
options.detail: Short stable media names cover installer, VM, disk, card, and network boot. Bare image defaults to `iso`. No other spelling is accepted.
options.technical: Success prints artifact and proof paths and exits 0. Proof JSON records `state: built`, canonical format, architecture, source, generation, closure, tools, hash, and boot result. An incomplete directory remains `state: staged`, is not published, and exits 1. Unsupported architecture prints `image format <format> cannot build <arch>: missing matching <asset>` and exits 2.
options.code:
$ jet os image router --format sd --arch aarch64 --out ./images
built sd image: ./images/jetos-router-sd.img
proof: ./images/jetos-router-sd.proof.json
$ echo $?
0

options.name: iso | qcow2 | raw | sdcard | pxe
options.detail: Use ecosystem-specific names. The values are longer and mix file-format, medium, and protocol vocabulary.
options.technical: Default, state transition, architecture errors, artifacts, proof, and exits match A. Only these exact values parse.
options.code:
jet os image router --format sdcard
jet os image router --format pxe

options.name: installer | vm | disk | card | network
options.detail: Use purpose names instead of artifact names. This reads naturally but hides whether the VM artifact is QCOW or another format.
options.technical: `vm` fixes QCOW and `disk` fixes raw. All proof and error behavior matches A.
options.code:
jet os image router --format card
jet os image router --format network

comparisons.note: The file format is commonly called qcow2, while a short CLI value can remain canonical if diagnostics teach it.

recommendation.why: The values are compact, technically exact, and stable across local and automated use. They map directly to artifact and proof identities without aliases.

whyNot.reason: The vocabulary mixes implementation names and delivery concepts while making common values longer.
Purpose names conceal the actual artifact format that automation must consume.

recommendation.tradeoff: `qcow` is shorter than the common file extension `qcow2`. That is acceptable because help and artifact paths show the exact output while the public value stays concise.

decisions.title: Set generation retention and automatic-upgrade policy
decisions.gist: Choose exact lifecycle fields and whether automatic upgrades are enabled by default.
decisions.lesson:
`packages.generations.*` selects protected system-generation roots. E7 plans and explains those roots; the shared E4 Hangar collector deletes only unprotected objects. `deploy.autoUpgrade.*` schedules the existing native sequence: `jet os build`, `jet os proof`, then `jet os switch`. This ballot does not add an update command.

An enabled schedule persists while the user is logged out through the platform user scheduler. No Jet privileged daemon remains resident. Build and proof run without privilege; switch requests one-shot activation authority. Privilege failure leaves the built candidate current-proof intact and the live generation unchanged. Offline input gaps, stale proof, failed health, and rollback each produce explicit receipts and terminal output.
decisions.story: Sam keeps ten rollback generations on a laptop. An operator uses the same fields for a weekly proved update window, without installing a privileged updater daemon.

options.name: Visible retention, automatic upgrade off
options.detail: Init writes all fields into the system module with `enable: false`. Experts turn on the same schedule; it continues while logged out.
options.technical: Plan output lists every kept and collectible generation with reason, scheduled next run, offline input state, candidate, proof fingerprint, activation authority, health window, and rollback target. Missing offline input prints `auto-upgrade: no change; locked input unavailable offline: <input>` and exits 0 with a no-change receipt. Privilege denial exits 2 and retains the candidate. Stale proof refuses switch with exit 2. Failed health rolls back, prints both generation names, writes rollback receipt, and exits 1.

options.name: Security scope enabled weekly
options.detail: Init enables a logged-out weekly security schedule. All other fields and failure behavior match A.
options.technical: `deploy.autoUpgrade.scope: .Security` requires locked provider security classification. Unknown classification becomes offline-style no-change, never a broad upgrade.

options.name: Retention fields only
options.detail: The system module owns retention, but scheduling remains external. Operators invoke existing build, proof, and switch commands.
options.technical: Generation plan and Hangar behavior match A. No `deploy.autoUpgrade.*` fields or scheduler receipts exist.

comparisons.note: A user timer starts a short-lived job and does not require a resident privileged service.

recommendation.why: Retention and update intent stay fully visible, while unattended system mutation remains opt-in. The same fields give experts schedules, offline behavior, proof, health, and rollback control.

whyNot.reason: Default unattended activation changes a machine without the owner first choosing that policy.
Removing source scheduling forces durable system intent into external automation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Beginners must enable automatic updates themselves. That is acceptable because init and Studio can present the choice without silently activating it.

decisions.title: Name the native service journal command
decisions.gist: Choose whether runtime journals use `jet os logs` or a nested service command.
decisions.lesson:
Native service journals differ from `jet dev` output and Jetpack build logs. One JetOS journal backend owns storage, permission checks, generation identity, unit normalization, time filtering, follow mode, remote transport, and JSON rows.

A bare unit like `web` normalizes to `web.service`; an explicit suffix such as `backup.timer` remains unchanged. Without `--host`, the selected local `system.<host>` is used. `--host prod-1` must resolve a declared fleet host and its ratified local authority binding before transport. Remote rows use the same schema as local rows. The examples below are product-copy requirements, not invented diagnostic codes. Card #329 must allocate any missing registered codes in `diagnostics.md` and add UI snapshots before implementation.
decisions.story: Noah sees a failed web-service health check, reads its current-generation journal, follows the restart, then exports identical rows from a remote host as JSON.
decisions.inWild:
jet os logs web --since 10m
jet os logs web --host prod-1 --generation current --follow --json

options.name: jet os logs <unit>
options.detail: The unit is positional and normalizes to a systemd unit. Expert filters extend the same local or authorized remote query.
options.technical: Each JSON line is `{"host":String,"generation":String,"unit":String,"at":String,"cursor":String,"stream":String,"level":String,"message":String}`. Normal completion exits 0. Unknown unit, denied journal access, unknown host, and stale generation exit 2. Remote connection failure or follow disconnect prints the last cursor and exits 1. Card #329 owns code registration plus diagnostics.md and UI snapshots for any message lacking an exact existing code.
options.code:
$ jet os logs web --generation g42
jet os logs: unknown unit `web`; resolved `web.service` is not present in generation `g42`

$ jet os logs web --host prod-1
jet os logs: access denied for `web.service` on host `prod-1`; check the local host authority binding

$ jet os logs web --host prod-1 --follow
jet os logs: host `prod-1` became unavailable; resume with cursor `s=42`

options.name: jet os service logs <unit>
options.detail: A service namespace owns the same normalization, authority, schema, errors, resume cursor, and exits.
options.technical: Behavior and exact product copy are identical to A after dispatch. Card #329 owns missing diagnostic registration and snapshots.
options.code: jet os service logs web --host prod-1 --follow --json

options.name: jet os logs --unit <name>
options.detail: The unit is explicit as a flag. Omitting it queries every authorized unit in the selected generation.
options.technical: Schema, authority, normalization, exact product copy, cursor, and exits match A. Whole-generation access uses the same permission boundary.
options.code:
jet os logs --unit web --since 10m
jet os logs --generation current --json

comparisons.note: `journalctl -u` queries the same journal by unit; Jet can make the unit positional for its common path.

recommendation.why: The canonical `jet os` boundary distinguishes runtime journals, and the positional unit keeps the beginner path direct. Expert filters remain on one backend and schema.

whyNot.reason: A service namespace adds ceremony before any other service subcommands are ratified.
A required flag burdens the dominant one-unit query and invites accidental whole-journal reads.

recommendation.tradeoff: The command reserves `jet os logs` for service journals rather than all OS logs. That is acceptable because boot and proof facts already have `jet os proof`.

decisions.title: Protect live system accounts during declarative removal
decisions.gist: Choose how `users.<name>` absence revokes login while preserving or deliberately disposing of home data.
decisions.lesson:
`users.<name>` describes a live system account. It is distinct from portable `user.<name>` profiles. When a live account disappears from merged configuration, JetOS may revoke login and preserve the home automatically. Any archive or destruction intent lives in the separate `users.removals` tombstone collection; the removed `users.sam` declaration does not coexist with a nested removal field.

A tombstone binds name, expected user ID, expected home, action, reason, source revision, and live fingerprint. It remains in source until an action receipt exists. The generation ledger retains UID reservation and home disposition after source cleanup. Repeated switches are idempotent. Noninteractive activation cannot invent confirmation. Archive and destruction require current backup proof; stale identity, missing proof, or changed home refuses action.
decisions.story: Ari removes a contractor from the system. Login stops on the next switch, but the home remains until an explicit reviewed archive or destruction action completes.

options.name: Absence locks and preserves; tombstones govern disposal
options.detail: Removing `users.sam` locks login and preserves its home and UID reservation. `users.removals["sam"]` is needed only to preserve explicitly, archive, or destroy with audit facts.
options.technical: `.PreserveHome` needs identity facts and reason. `.Archive` additionally needs destination and current backup proof. `.DestroyHome` needs current backup proof and reason. Plan prints account, UID, home, action, backup proof, repeat state, and rollback limit. Stale identity or backup exits 2. Archive/destruction failure exits 1 with live data unchanged. Success writes action and UID-tombstone receipts; repeated switch exits 0 no-change.

options.name: A tombstone is required before declaration removal
options.detail: Removing `users.sam` without a matching `users.removals` row is a plan error. The row chooses preserve, archive, or destroy.
options.technical: Lifetime, UID reservation, stale checks, backup proof, repeat behavior, receipts, and exits match A.
options.code: users.removals: ["sam": [expectedUid: 1004, expectedHome: "/home/sam", action: .PreserveHome, reason: "contract ended"]]

options.name: Absence locks and creates an archive-required tombstone
options.detail: Removing the declaration locks login immediately and creates a pending durable tombstone. Later noninteractive switches refuse until source supplies archive proof.
options.technical: The generated pending state cannot archive or destroy. Source must adopt it with exact identity and backup fields.
options.code:
plan: lock sam; preserve /home/sam; create pending removal receipt
fix: add users.removals["sam"] with archive proof

comparisons.note: Locking an account and deleting its home are separate operations because their recovery properties differ.

recommendation.why: Login authority is revoked immediately while data and UID ownership remain safe. A separate source tombstone provides one audited path for preserve, archive, or destruction without reviving the removed account declaration.

whyNot.reason: Requiring a source tombstone before absence delays immediate login revocation when the owner removes a user declaration.
A generated pending tombstone creates split truth: source says the account is gone while durable semantic removal intent exists only in generated state.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preserved homes and UID reservations remain until an explicit tombstone action is reviewed. That is acceptable because storage and later cleanup are recoverable, while premature identity reuse or deletion is not.

decisions.title: Place and govern declared `/etc` files
decisions.gist: Choose the exact source home and managed-by-default law for `/etc` entries.
decisions.lesson:
No ratified source namespace currently owns arbitrary `/etc` entries, so this ballot chooses one. Entries live inside a complete `module system.<host>` options map. Each entry has a relative path, ownership, mode as a decimal integer, and exactly one content input: inline `contents`, project `source`, or mutable `seed`.

Managed entries use contents or source and are backed by the immutable generation. `/etc/<path>` is a JetOS-owned symlink to that backing file. Mutable entries use seed, are copied once to `/var/lib/jetos/etc/<entry>`, and `/etc/<path>` links there.

Managed and mutable paths cannot overlap by equality or ancestry. Removing a managed entry deletes only its owned link. Removing a mutable entry preserves backing data unless a later decision governs deletion. The samples require exact product copy. Card #401 must allocate missing diagnostic codes, register them in `diagnostics.md`, and add UI snapshots.
decisions.story: Lee manages SSH configuration exactly from source, while one upstream daemon must retain a live-edited state file under `/etc`.

options.name: filesystem.etc map
options.detail: Named entries live under the full-word filesystem family. Managed is default; mutable requires `mutable: true` and seed.
options.technical: `contents`, `source`, and `seed` are mutually exclusive. Seed requires mutable; contents/source reject mutable. Absolute, parent, NUL, duplicate, symlink-escape, file-directory overlap, managed-mutable ancestry overlap, unknown user/group, invalid mode, and stale mutable fingerprints fail during plan. Plan prints backing path, link target, action, ownership, seed fingerprint, drift, and rollback. Card #401 owns missing diagnostic registration and snapshots.
options.code:
module system.laptop {
  options: [
    filesystem.etc: [
      sshd: [path: "ssh/sshd_config", source: ./sshd_config, mode: 384, user: "root", group: "root"],
    ],
  ]
}

jet os plan: `/etc/ssh` overlaps `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`
  `filesystem.etc.sshDir` owns the directory path
  `filesystem.etc.sshd` owns the file path
fix: keep one owner or move one path

jet os plan: mutable `/etc/database/state` changed since this plan
  expected seed fingerprint: sha256:old
  live fingerprint: sha256:new
fix: review the live file and run `jet os plan` again

options.name: system.files.etc map
options.detail: The identical entry law lives under a system-files family. The path repeats both files and etc.
options.technical: All exclusivity, backing, link, deletion, exact product copy, diagnostics, plan, drift, and rollback behavior matches A.
options.code: module system.laptop { options: [system.files.etc: [sshd: [path: "ssh/sshd_config", source: ./sshd_config, mode: 384, user: "root", group: "root"]]] }

options.name: etc map
options.detail: A short top-level map owns the identical law. It adds a new root beside full-word system namespaces.
options.technical: All behavior and diagnostic discipline matches A.
options.code: module system.laptop { options: [etc: [sshd: [path: "ssh/sshd_config", source: ./sshd_config, mode: 384, user: "root", group: "root"]]] }

comparisons.note: Declared `/etc` entries are generation-managed by default; mutable service state normally lives elsewhere.

recommendation.why: The full-word filesystem family states the domain clearly and keeps managed files reproducible. Explicit mutable entries retain expert compatibility with complete drift evidence.

whyNot.reason: The repeated `files.etc` path adds words without adding a semantic boundary.
A new short root conflicts with the established full-word namespace direction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each entry needs a semantic name and a path. That is acceptable because stable names improve merge provenance while paths remain exact filesystem facts.

decisions.title: Choose what happens when two packages in one profile provide the same file path
decisions.gist: When two packages in one profile both provide the same file path, decide how Jet resolves the clash.
decisions.lesson:
A profile (`profile.<name>`) merges several packages into one file tree. `jet profile`, JetOS system builds, and user environments all merge with the same engine (D-JPK-PROFILE1=D), so whatever this ballot decides applies to all three.

Most overlaps are harmless. If two packages install byte-identical files at the same path, Jet keeps one copy automatically, no conflict. If two packages both provide a folder at the same path, Jet merges the folders, no conflict. Only a genuine clash needs a decision.

One kind of clash has no winner to pick. If one package has a file at a path and another has a folder or a different symlink target there, the build always fails. The shapes do not match, so no selection fixes it.

This ballot is about the other kind of clash: two packages provide different files at the same exact path. Someone has to pick which one wins.
decisions.story: Priya builds a workstation profile that includes two code editors. Both editors install a program at `bin/editor`. She wants to keep both editors for their other files, but only one program can live at that exact path. She wants a clear error naming both editors, and one line she can add to her profile to say which one wins.

options.name: Exact-path provider map
options.detail: If two packages provide different files at the same path, the build fails and names both packages. Priya adds one line to a `collisions` list saying which package wins that exact path. If either package's file later changes, the old pick stops working and Jet makes her look at the new files before picking again. Identical files and merged folders never need a line.
options.technical: Plan output lists path, type, every candidate package identity and content hash, identical/directory status, chosen provider, staleness, and downstream views. A successful build repeats the locked row. A missing pick, a stale pick, a file/directory mismatch, or a conflicting symlink target exits with code 2. Identical files and merged directories need no `collisions` entry. Card #425 owns diagnostic code registration and snapshot tests.
options.code:
module profile.workstation {
  packages: [packages.helix, packages.compatEditors]
  collisions: [
    "bin/editor": packages.helix,
  ]
}

profile collision at `bin/editor` needs a provider
  packages.helix: sha256:aaa
  packages.compatEditors: sha256:bbb
fix: add `"bin/editor": packages.helix` to `collisions`

profile collision selection for `bin/editor` is stale
  selected packages.helix: expected sha256:aaa, locked sha256:ccc
fix: run `jet profile plan workstation` and review the new contenders

profile path `share/icons` is both a file and a directory
  packages.iconBlob: file
  packages.desktopTheme: directory
fix: remove, rename, or adapt one package; a provider selection cannot change path type

options.name: Fail and require package output renaming
options.detail: There is no `collisions` list. If two packages provide different files at the same path, Priya cannot pick a winner. She must drop one editor, or rebuild one editor's package so its program installs under a different path.
options.technical: Identical-file and merged-directory rules match option A, same product copy, same diagnostic discipline. A package adapter that renames output paths shows up as a normal package in build results, with no path-specific override step.

options.name: First package wins each exact path
options.detail: The order packages appear in the list decides every clash automatically. The first package listed always wins, silently, with no error and no line to add. Reordering the list changes which editor's `bin/editor` ends up installed.
options.technical: Identical-file, directory, file/directory-mismatch, symlink, staleness, plan, receipt, and diagnostic rules match option A. Changing package list order changes which package wins and changes the build's identity, with no recorded reason.

comparisons.note: Nix profiles pick a winner using one priority number attached to a whole package. Jet's map is narrower: it names a winner for one specific file, not the whole package.

recommendation.why: One line records the decision once, in the profile file, and it applies the same way for a `jet profile`, a JetOS system, or a user environment. A later package upgrade forces Priya to look at the pick again instead of silently keeping a stale choice.

whyNot.reason: Dropping or rebuilding a whole package is more work than naming a winner for the one file that actually clashes.
List order changes easily by accident, so a silent order-based pick is not a real, reviewed decision.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every genuine file clash needs one line in `collisions`. That cost is fair, because each clash changes which program the profile actually installs.

decisions.comment: Owner question q69bs9wc answered: ballot reworked in place in plain language (two editors both installing bin/editor). A records each real clash as one reviewed line, applies identically across jet profile, JetOS, and user environments, and refuses stale picks after upgrades.

decisions.title: Should typed project budgets cover compile latency?
decisions.gist: Decide whether Jet projects may enforce cold, unchanged, and representative-edit compile latency, and how each measured workload gets an exact identity.
decisions.lesson:
Compile latency is workload-relative. A cold build, an unchanged rebuild, and a one-file edit exercise different cache paths. A number without source, cache, compiler, target, profile, linker, and host identity cannot be compared safely.

Jet already measures its product compiler in #666. #241 enforces project performance facts, but its closed metric and provider set has no compile workload. Extending that public typed vocabulary requires this decision.
decisions.explainer: All options preserve zero-ceremony defaults. No project receives a compile budget unless its author declares one. Any measurement uses #241's canonical evaluator, pinned baselines, reports, diagnostics, and CI behavior. The choice is whether project-level compile regressions are enforceable and whether representative edits are first-class.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a large Jet service. A harmless generic helper change doubles every developer rebuild, while runtime benchmarks remain green. Mina wants CI to catch that regression with enough provenance to reproduce it.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: no new ceremony or measurement occurs by default. Expert pass: declared probes pin the source tree, edit, cache state, toolchain, target, profile, backend, linker, host, warmups, samples, and phase breakdown.

options.name: Internal Jet SLOs only
options.detail: Keep compile latency entirely in #666's compiler corpus. Projects cannot declare or enforce their own compile-time regressions through performance budgets.
options.code:
$ jet budget check
# Runtime, size, and existing compiler-fact budgets only.
# Compile latency remains a Jet compiler product gate in #666.

options.name: Fixed compile scenarios
options.detail: Add typed Clean and NoChange compiler probes. They are reproducible, but they cannot model the representative edit loop that developers feel most often.
options.code:
Budget.{
    name: "clean-compile",
    scope: .Target("cli"),
    metric: .CompileTime(.P95),
    provider: .CompilerProbe(.Clean),
    comparison: .RelativeTo("ci/linux-x64"),
    limit: .RegressionAtMost(5pct),
}

Budget.{
    name: "no-change-compile",
    scope: .Target("cli"),
    metric: .CompileTime(.P95),
    provider: .CompilerProbe(.NoChange),
    comparison: .RelativeTo("ci/linux-x64"),
    limit: .RegressionAtMost(5pct),
}

options.name: Typed compile workloads
options.detail: Add one CompilerProbe provider with Clean, NoChange, and named Edit workload values. The edit value records a deterministic source patch instead of guessing from timestamps.

comparisons.note: The checked compiler corpus protects Jet's compiler as a product. It does not let one application preserve its own representative edit latency.
comparisons.code:
cold / warm / incremental JIT and AOT corpus
parse / sema / TIR / backend / link timings

comparisons.note: The mined video shows why one total is insufficient. Generics, state machines, linker choice, libc, allocator, profile, and cache state can each dominate.
comparisons.code:
same source + different profile/cache/environment
=> different cause, different useful fix

recommendation.why: C serves both facets with one existing budget mechanism. Beginners pay nothing; experts can prevent the real edit-loop regression, not only clean or unchanged build regressions.

whyNot.reason: A protects Jet's compiler average but gives application teams no enforceable guard for project-specific generic, derive, or module-graph cliffs.
B measures two useful endpoints yet omits the representative edit path where incremental invalidation failures appear.

recommendation.tradeoff: C adds public metric, provider, workload, and edit identity types. Their closed typed form keeps cache state and source changes auditable instead of relying on ambient files or timestamps.

decisions.checkInstructions: Before deciding, compare the beginner default, expert workload identity, cache-key completeness, and whether each option can catch a one-file incremental regression without flaky ambient state.

decisions.title: Default program entry is run.jet
decisions.outcome: Jet’s canonical default program entry file is run.jet, matching the jet run command and fn run entry method. Scaffolding, bare project resolution, and onboarding use run.jet by default; explicit file targets remain available.
decisions.comment: Jet’s canonical default program entry file is run.jet, matching the jet run command and fn run entry method. Scaffolding, bare project resolution, and onboarding use run.jet by default; explicit file targets remain available.

decisions.title: Client TLS trust, credentials, and version policy
decisions.gist: Choose how one immutable ClientConfig accepts custom trust, client credentials, and TLS version bounds.
decisions.lesson:
A TLS client authenticates a server through trusted certificate authorities, called roots. System roots cover public websites. Private services may add their own roots or deliberately trust only a private set.

Mutual TLS also authenticates the client. The client sends a certificate chain and proves possession of its private key. That key is secret, while root and certificate data are public.

Version bounds limit protocol negotiation to a closed range such as TLS 1.2 through TLS 1.3. These inputs should become a valid immutable configuration before a socket is consumed. The handshake still performs server-name verification and never exposes an insecure-verifier switch.
decisions.story: Priya connects a hospital service to a private gateway. The gateway uses a private root, requires a client certificate, and permits only TLS 1.3.
decisions.inWild:
roots := tls.RootCertificates.from_pem(ca_pem)?
identity := tls.ClientIdentity.from_pem(cert_chain_pem, private_key_pem)?
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_trust(.CustomOnly(roots))
    .with_client_identity(identity)
    .with_version_bounds(min: .Tls13, max: .Tls13)
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
decisions.detail: Fixed law remains unchanged: ClientConfig.default(), with_alpn([String]), and tls.client(stream, server_name:, config:, deadline:) are already ratified. Every option preserves built-in certificate and server-name verification. No option permits an insecure verifier. RootCertificates and ClientIdentity are opaque validated values. TlsVersion is closed to supported protocol versions. Invalid PEM, an empty root set, an unusable key, a mismatched certificate/key, an empty ALPN item, or min above max rejects before consuming the TcpStream.

options.name: Validated typed inputs
options.detail: Parse roots and client identity into opaque validated values, then add them through an immutable builder. Trust mode explicitly distinguishes system roots, system plus custom roots, and custom-only roots. Version bounds validate when added.
options.technical: RootCertificates.from_pem([U8]) validates one or more certificate blocks. ClientIdentity.from_pem(cert_chain: [U8], private_key: [U8]) validates the ordered chain, supported key encoding, and certificate/key match; its internal key storage is zeroized on drop. ClientConfig.with_trust accepts .System, .SystemPlus(RootCertificates), or .CustomOnly(RootCertificates). with_client_identity accepts ClientIdentity. with_version_bounds accepts closed TlsVersion values .Tls12 and .Tls13 and rejects min > max. Builder calls return ClientConfig ? IOError and never retain a partially valid value.
options.code:
roots := tls.RootCertificates.from_pem(ca_pem)?
identity := tls.ClientIdentity.from_pem(chain_pem, key_pem)?
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_trust(.SystemPlus(roots))?
    .with_client_identity(identity)?
    .with_version_bounds(min: .Tls12, max: .Tls13)?
    .with_alpn(["h2", "http/1.1"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?

options.name: Raw configuration data
options.detail: Store PEM bytes and version fields directly in ClientConfig. Validate the complete record only when tls.client begins the handshake. The configuration is easy to serialize, but malformed credentials survive until a live connection attempt.
options.technical: ClientConfig carries trust mode plus root_pem, certificate_chain_pem, private_key_pem, min_version, max_version, and ALPN strings as ordinary data. tls.client validates all fields before consuming or registering the transport. Secret key bytes remain redacted from Show, Debug, diagnostics, and audit output.
options.code:
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_raw_credentials(.{
        trust: .SystemPlusPem(ca_pem),
        certificate_chain_pem: chain_pem,
        private_key_pem: key_pem,
        min_version: .Tls12,
        max_version: .Tls13,
    })?
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?

options.name: Platform credential references
options.detail: ClientConfig names roots and client identities stored by the operating system. Jet receives no private-key bytes. This fits managed hosts, but containers, tests, and portable private PKI need platform provisioning first.
options.technical: TlsCredentialRef is an opaque platform reference. ClientConfig.with_trust_ref selects a platform root bundle or custom trust store. with_client_identity_ref selects a certificate and non-exportable key. Missing, ambiguous, inaccessible, or unsupported references fail before transport consumption. Version bounds remain closed typed values on ClientConfig.
options.code:
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_trust_ref(tls.CredentialRef.system("hospital-roots"))?
    .with_client_identity_ref(tls.CredentialRef.system("gateway-client"))?
    .with_version_bounds(min: .Tls13, max: .Tls13)?
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?

comparisons.note: tls.Config groups roots, client certificates, ALPN, and version bounds. RootCAs replaces the default pool unless callers build from system roots explicitly.
comparisons.code: cfg := &tls.Config{RootCAs: roots, Certificates: []tls.Certificate{id}, MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13, NextProtos: []string{"h2"}}

comparisons.note: ClientConfig is built through states that require roots and client-auth choice before use. Protocol versions and ALPN are configuration facts.
TrustManager and KeyManager separate server trust from client identity, usually through platform key stores. Protocol bounds are configured on each socket or engine.

recommendation.why: A makes invalid trust and credential material ordinary typed errors before networking starts. It supports public roots, private PKI, mutual TLS, hermetic tests, and explicit version policy through one immutable configuration.

whyNot.reason: B keeps malformed certificates and keys inside an apparently usable configuration until a connection attempt, weakening the boundary between configuration and live I/O.
C protects non-exportable keys well, but makes portable services and tests depend on host-specific credential provisioning. It cannot be Jet's only cross-platform expert surface.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts private-key bytes when constructing ClientIdentity. Jet must copy them into redacted, zeroized storage, while platform-only deployments may still need a later credential-reference constructor.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify that every option preserves system-root defaults, server-name verification, ALPN's ratified [String] shape, immutable config reuse, pre-consumption validation, secret redaction, and one IOError tree.

decisions.title: Verified TLS peer identity evidence
decisions.gist: Choose what verified certificate evidence a TlsStream retains for expert inspection.
decisions.lesson:
A successful TLS handshake proves that the server certificate matches the requested name and chains to the configured roots. Applications sometimes need evidence beyond success, such as certificate fingerprints, issuer data, or the complete chain.
