Certificate bytes are public, but retaining them affects audit capability and memory. A compact summary answers common policy questions. A full immutable snapshot also supports pinning reports, compliance records, and protocol-specific certificate processing.

Inspection must never replace built-in verification. The observer sees evidence only after normal certificate and server-name checks succeed. It cannot approve a failed peer or alter the handshake.
decisions.story: Elena operates a payment client. She records the verified leaf fingerprint and issuer, then investigates a rotation by comparing the complete chain without parsing log text.
decisions.inWild:
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
peer := secure.peer_identity()
print(peer.verified_server_name)
print(peer.leaf.spki_sha256)
for certificate in peer.certificate_chain {
    audit(certificate.der)
}
decisions.detail: The TlsStream return shape and tls.client spelling remain fixed. Evidence is available only after a verified handshake. Certificate objects expose exact DER bytes plus stable derived facts; human-readable subject and issuer text is audit display, never identity control. Private keys and session secrets are never exposed. Renegotiation is unavailable, so a stored snapshot cannot become stale.

options.name: Full immutable peer snapshot
options.detail: TlsStream retains one PeerIdentity snapshot with the verified server name and ordered certificate chain. Each certificate exposes exact DER and stable fingerprints. Experts can derive summaries without losing evidence.
options.technical: peer_identity() returns an immutable PeerIdentity. Fields are verified_server_name: String, leaf: TlsCertificate, and certificate_chain: [TlsCertificate] in wire order. TlsCertificate exposes der: [U8], sha256: [U8], spki_sha256: [U8], dns_names: [String], valid_from_unix_ms: Int, valid_until_unix_ms: Int, subject: String, and issuer: String. Only DER and hashes are stable control data; rendered names are audit text.
options.code:
peer := secure.peer_identity()
require(peer.verified_server_name == host)
require(peer.leaf.spki_sha256 == expected_spki)
audit_chain(peer.certificate_chain.map((cert) => cert.der))

options.name: Compact verified summary
options.detail: TlsStream retains only the verified name, leaf fingerprints, names, issuer, and validity window. This covers routine policy checks while omitting the raw chain needed for independent audit or future derivations.
options.technical: peer_identity() returns PeerIdentitySummary with verified_server_name, leaf_sha256, leaf_spki_sha256, dns_names, valid_from_unix_ms, valid_until_unix_ms, subject, and issuer. Intermediate certificates and raw DER are discarded after verification. Strings remain audit text; hashes are stable bytes.
options.code:
peer := secure.peer_identity()
require(peer.leaf_spki_sha256 == expected_spki)
print("verified {peer.verified_server_name} until {peer.valid_until_unix_ms}")
// complete chain bytes are unavailable

options.name: Post-verification observer
options.detail: ClientConfig accepts an observer called once with the verified chain during the handshake. TlsStream retains no certificate evidence. Callers choose what to copy, but observation becomes callback state rather than a simple stream query.
options.technical: with_peer_observer receives a non-fallible observer of borrowed PeerIdentityView after built-in verification succeeds and before tls.client returns. The observer cannot reject, replace roots, or alter verification. Borrowed certificate bytes become invalid when the callback returns; retained evidence requires an explicit copy.
options.code:
audit := PeerAudit.new()
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_peer_observer((peer) => audit.record(peer.leaf.spki_sha256.copy()))
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
require(audit.last_spki_sha256() == expected_spki)

comparisons.note: ConnectionState exposes verified chains, peer certificates, and the negotiated server name after the handshake.
ClientConnection exposes peer_certificates as the certificate chain presented by the peer after verification.
SSLSession returns peer certificates and principals after a verified handshake. Callers inspect them outside the trust decision.

recommendation.why: A preserves the actual verified evidence once and keeps inspection separate from verification. It serves simple fingerprint policy and deeper audits without callbacks or message parsing.

whyNot.reason: B answers common checks but permanently discards intermediate certificates and exact DER, preventing independent audit and later derivation from the verified chain.
C avoids retained evidence, but forces ordinary inspection through callback capture and mutable state. It also makes evidence lifetime harder to explain and test.

recommendation.tradeoff: A retains one public certificate chain for the stream lifetime. Long-lived connections therefore keep more memory than a summary-only design, bounded by the verified handshake chain.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify built-in trust and server-name checks always run first; evidence is immutable; no private key or session secret appears; DER and hashes are stable; display strings are not control-flow law.

decisions.title: Advanced TLS close-notify and truncation law
decisions.gist: Choose how experts half-close TLS writes and prove whether the peer ended the stream cleanly.
decisions.lesson:
TLS has a close-notify alert for ending encrypted application data. Sending it says this side will write no more. Receiving the peer alert proves the peer ended cleanly rather than the transport disappearing mid-record.

The two directions are independent. A request protocol may finish writing, send close-notify, and continue reading a response. A plain close can instead send the alert and release the transport without waiting for the peer.

A raw TCP end without peer close-notify is a truncation failure, not clean end-of-stream. Deadlines and cancellation still bound every wait. Repeated close operations remain harmless under the ratified stream law.
decisions.story: Mateo uploads a signed archive, closes only the request direction, and keeps reading the server receipt. He must reject an abrupt TCP end as truncated TLS.
decisions.detail: Existing close() remains fixed: it sends and flushes local close-notify, closes the transport, and is idempotent. This ballot chooses the additional expert surface and peer-EOF law. Every option uses the same ambient, inherited, or explicit earliest deadline and returns the shared IOError variants. No option treats raw transport EOF as successful TLS EOF.

options.name: Directional write close
options.detail: Add close_write(deadline:) to send and flush close-notify while leaving reads open. Later writes return Closed. Reads return empty bytes only after peer close-notify; abrupt transport EOF returns Protocol truncation.
options.technical: close_write(deadline: Duration) is idempotent, observes the earliest active deadline, and completes only after the alert is flushed and the transport write half is shut down. It does not consume unread peer application data. read continues normally. A verified peer close-notify makes the next exhausted read return []; EOF without that alert returns IOError.Protocol with operation Read and a TLS truncation cause. close delegates to local alert flush when needed, then releases the handle without waiting for the peer.
options.code:
secure.write_all(request)?
secure.close_write(deadline: 2.seconds)?
reply := []
loop {
    chunk := secure.read(64.kib)?
    if chunk.is_empty() { break } // peer close-notify observed
    reply.extend(chunk)
}
secure.close()?

options.name: One bidirectional graceful close
options.detail: Add close_gracefully(deadline:) to send close-notify and wait for the peer alert before releasing the transport. It proves clean closure in one call, but cannot safely discard unread application data.
options.technical: close_gracefully sends and flushes local close-notify, then drives TLS until peer close-notify. If peer application data arrives before the alert, it returns IOError.Protocol rather than buffering or discarding that data. Timeout and cancellation leave the handle closing; a later close may release it. Existing close remains the non-waiting idempotent release path.
options.code:
secure.write_all(request)?
read_complete_response(&secure)?
secure.close_gracefully(deadline: 2.seconds)?
// error if unread application bytes arrive before peer close-notify

options.name: Configuration-selected close policy
options.detail: ClientConfig chooses whether close waits for peer close-notify. Call sites keep using close(), but the same method can release immediately or block according to distant configuration.
options.technical: ClientConfig.with_close_policy accepts .SendOnly or .WaitForPeer(deadline). close always sends and flushes local close-notify. Under WaitForPeer it waits for the peer alert and rejects intervening unread application data. Raw EOF is always Protocol truncation. The policy is immutable and shared by every stream created from the config.
options.code:
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_close_policy(.WaitForPeer(2.seconds))
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
read_complete_response(&secure)?
secure.close()? // waits because config selected it

comparisons.note: CloseWrite sends TLS close-notify while keeping reads available. ConnectionState and read errors distinguish protocol state from ordinary use.
send_close_notify queues the alert. Callers continue driving connection I/O and decide whether to wait for the peer alert.
unwrap performs the TLS shutdown exchange and returns the underlying socket. It may block while waiting for the peer.

recommendation.why: A models TLS shutdown's directional nature directly. It supports request-half-close protocols, preserves unread response data, and makes clean peer EOF versus truncation part of normal Reader behavior.

whyNot.reason: B is convenient only after all response data is already drained. Before then it must reject, discard, or buffer application bytes, so it cannot replace directional shutdown.
C hides whether close waits behind shared configuration. The same source call can gain blocking behavior unrelated to the stream's visible lifecycle.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives experts one additional lifecycle method. Callers that require mutual clean shutdown must close writes, continue reading until empty bytes, then call the existing idempotent close.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify partial alert writes, readiness, cancellation, deadlines, repeated calls, post-close writes, response reads after close_write, peer close-notify, abrupt EOF truncation, and existing close behavior across AOT and dev.

decisions.title: D-LENS-RUN1: jet run = JIT lens, jet build = AOT lens
decisions.outcome: One compiler core. JIT and AOT are lenses only over the same front end and executable TIR — never parallel feature implementations and never a supported-feature gap between lenses. jet run uses the JIT lens; jet build uses the AOT lens. Missing JIT coverage is a compiler defect, not a user fallback to AOT.
decisions.comment: One compiler core. JIT and AOT are lenses only over the same front end and executable TIR — never parallel feature implementations and never a supported-feature gap between lenses. jet run uses the JIT lens; jet build uses the AOT lens. Missing JIT coverage is a compiler defect, not a user fallback to AOT.

decisions.title: Canvas scope: logic graphs only, or a full visual app builder
decisions.gist: Whether Canvas grows a drag-and-drop app designer beside its logic graphs, and where that designer lives.
decisions.lesson:
Canvas today is a visual editor for Jet logic. Programs appear as node graphs in the style of Unreal Engine's Blueprint, and every visual edit is a source-code transaction, so the graph and the text never drift apart.

RAD (rapid application development) is a different kind of visual tool. In Delphi, Lazarus, or classic Visual Basic you drag a button onto a window, set its label in a property panel, then double-click it. The tool generates the click handler and drops you inside it. App, layout, and code stay one thing.

That loop built the largest hobbyist and small-business software wave in history, and Lazarus keeps devoted users today because no modern tool matches it. Meanwhile Blueprint owns the logic-graph half and its vendor is stepping away from it, which leaves both halves contested.

Jet already has the pieces. The reactive UI kit (signals, renderer, styles, widgets) is the runtime a designer would target. The source-transaction engine is what keeps a visual edit honest. The question is whether Canvas points those pieces at a design surface, and if so, whether inside Canvas or as a separate tool.

The current Canvas roadmap (milestones M2 through M6) is unaffected in every option: nothing here reorders shipped commitments.
decisions.story: Sam, the game-jam hobbyist from the persona audit, wants a settings screen: two sliders and a start button. In Lazarus he would have it in three minutes without reading layout docs. In Jet today he hand-writes widget code, and the visual editor he already uses for logic cannot help him.

options.name: One editor, two surfaces
options.detail: Canvas grows a design surface — component palette, property inspector, callback generation — beside the logic graph, both writing through the same source-transaction engine. Double-clicking a button's handler opens that code as graph or text. You build an app and its logic in one tool. The cost: Canvas's scope grows well past logic editing, and the design surface competes for the same product attention.
options.technical: Design surface targets the reactive UI kit. Widgets and properties are source constructs, layout edits are ordinary transactions on the same file set. Staged strictly after the current M-arc, as its own milestone series.

options.name: Separate designer product
options.detail: A distinct app-designer tool shares the source-transaction engine but ships and evolves apart from Canvas. Canvas stays a focused logic editor. Each tool stays simple on its own. The cost: the double-click-into-your-callback loop now crosses a product boundary, and users juggle two editors for one app.
options.technical: Same engine and file truth, separate front end and roadmap. Cross-tool jump protocol required for designer-to-logic navigation.
options.code:
$ jet design app.jet    # designer: windows, widgets, properties
$ jet canvas app.jet    # canvas: the logic behind them
# double-click Start in the designer -> switches app to canvas

options.name: Stay Blueprint-only
options.detail: Canvas remains a logic editor. UI building stays code plus the reactive kit, and a designer is reconsidered after Canvas M6 ships. Full focus on finishing the committed arc. The cost: the beginner who is best served by drag-and-drop building — Jet's own headline persona — keeps hand-writing layout code for at least an epoch.
options.technical: No change. A future reconsideration would start from this ballot's record.

comparisons.note: Form designer plus double-click-into-callback is the loyalty loop that still holds users decades later.
The mass-market proof that drag-and-drop plus callbacks onboards non-programmers at scale.
Owns the logic-graph half only, and its vendor is stepping away — the opening Canvas already targets.
A design surface detached from logic editing. The round-trip pain of that split is the anti-pattern to avoid.

recommendation.why: The source-transaction engine is the hard-won asset, and pointing it at a design surface makes Canvas the only tool where visual UI building, visual logic, and text are the same file. That is the Lazarus loyalty loop without the code-generation drift that killed most RAD tools.

whyNot.reason: The double-click-into-your-callback jump defines the RAD loop, and option B routes it across a product boundary. Two front ends over one engine also split design attention permanently.
Drag-and-drop building serves the beginner facet better than any feature on the board, and deferring it concedes that ground for an epoch while the market gap is open.

recommendation.tradeoff: Canvas's mission grows from logic editor to app builder, and that larger mission is permanent. Accepted by staging the design surface strictly after the current M-arc, so no shipped commitment moves.

decisions.title: Language tooling packs for jet env
decisions.gist: How a beginner turns on a full language toolchain in a Jet env.
decisions.lesson:
A language pack is a named preset that pulls the tools people expect for one language.

Think of it as a shopping list the tool fills for you. For Rust that list usually means the compiler, the package tool, the language server, and the formatter.

Without packs, you name every package yourself. That is precise, but beginners must know the whole list.

With packs, one short enable line fills the common tools. Experts still need a way to pin versions and add or remove tools.

The stakes are beginner speed versus expert control, and whether Jet grows a second way to declare packages.
decisions.story: Maya opens a Jet repo to write a small Rust service. She wants cargo and rust-analyzer in one step, like devenv languages.rust.enable, without pasting a twelve-package list.

options.name: Typed language packs on env
options.detail: Beginners enable a language with one typed field. Packs expand into ordinary packages. Experts can still list packages and pin versions. One mechanism underneath.
options.technical: Add languages: map on env modules. Each Lang record has enable, optional version/channel, and optional extra packages. Expansion is pure data into the existing package realize path. No second resolver.

options.name: Explicit packages only
options.detail: Keep today’s model. Docs and jet add helpers teach the lists. No languages field. Beginners paste or generate package lists.
options.technical: No new env syntax. Rely on packages: and overlays. Helpers may print suggested package sets but do not invent a pack type.

options.name: Packs as recipes only, no env field
options.detail: Ship recipe macros or jet add --lang rust that write packages: for you. No lasting languages: field in env modules.
options.technical: Scaffolding writes ordinary packages into env.jet. Re-running the helper can drift from hand edits unless merge rules are defined.
options.code:
$ jet env add-lang rust
# rewrites env.jet packages: [..., rustc, cargo, rust-analyzer, ...]

options.name: Packs plus mandatory explicit confirm
options.detail: languages.enable only prints the package set and refuses until the user pastes it. Maximum explicitness; high ceremony.
options.technical: Enable is a doctor/suggest step, not realize. Conflicts with beginner magic defaults.
options.code:
$ jet env
error: languages.rust.enable needs packages: [rustc, cargo, ...] — paste to confirm

comparisons.note: languages.rust.enable bundles toolchain and helpers with version/channel options.
Usually lists packages by hand in devShell.buildInputs.

recommendation.why: Packs give beginners one clear enable line while still expanding into the same package realize path experts already use.

whyNot.reason: Forces every beginner to memorize toolchain package sets that devenv already proved people want as one toggle.
Scaffold rewrite fights hand edits and hides the live declaration readers expect in env.jet.
Adds ceremony without removing the need for a pack definition, so beginners still stall.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must maintain pack definitions per language. That cost is accepted to keep the beginner path short without a second package system.

decisions.title: Workflow profiles for jet env
decisions.gist: Whether Jet envs get named workflow profiles beyond env.dev / env.test overlays.
decisions.lesson:
A workflow profile is a named slice of an environment you turn on for a job.

Example slices: backend databases, frontend node tooling, or CI-only browsers.

Jet already has role overlays such as env.dev and env.test. Those cover common intents.

Devenv also adds named profiles you combine with flags, and profiles that auto-apply from hostname or username.

Auto profiles save typing. They can also surprise someone on a shared machine if a hostname flips services on.

The choice is how much profile power Jet adds on top of today’s overlays.
decisions.story: Sam maintains a monorepo. On the laptop they want frontend tools. On the CI host they want browsers and stricter env vars. They do not want three separate repos.

options.name: Overlays only
options.detail: Keep env.dev / env.test / env.build. Compose with imports. No named profiles and no hostname or user auto-apply.
options.technical: No new profile syntax. Monorepo uses imports:find and workspace.jet. CI selects jet env test explicitly.
options.code:
$ jet env dev
$ jet env test

options.name: Named profiles with extends, manual only
options.detail: Add named profiles you pass on the CLI. Profiles can extend each other. No hostname or user auto-apply.
options.technical: profiles: on env modules; jet env --profile frontend. Merge law reuses module merge + priority. Auto host/user profiles omitted.
options.code: $ jet env --profile backend --profile testing

options.name: Named profiles plus hostname/user auto
options.detail: Everything in B, plus profiles that activate from hostname or username like devenv. Maximum convenience; more surprise risk.
options.technical: profiles.hostname / profiles.user auto-merge with documented priority. Must show what activated in jet env info.
options.code:
$ jet env
# also applied: hostname.ci-server, user.sam

options.name: Imports-only composition, no profile noun
options.detail: Teach folder imports as the only compose tool. Avoid the word profile to prevent clash with package profiles.
options.technical: Deepen imports for remote locked env modules. Package profiles (D-JPK-PROFILE*) stay a separate concept.
options.code:
imports: find("./frontend")
imports: find("./backend")

comparisons.note: profiles with extends, --profile flags, and hostname/user auto activation.
env role overlays and imports:find without named workflow profiles.

recommendation.why: Named manual profiles cover monorepo and CI slices without surprising auto activation from hostname or username.

whyNot.reason: Overlays alone force awkward env names for every cross-cutting slice a monorepo needs.
Hostname and user auto-apply can enable services without an explicit command, which is a trust hazard on shared machines.
Imports help structure folders but do not give a first-class switch for temporary slices like testing browsers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must teach profile as a workflow idea beside package profiles. Clear CLI naming and docs must keep the two concepts apart.

decisions.title: Beginner Jet env vs expert flake-parts
decisions.gist: Whether experts can use flake-parts while beginners keep a simple Jet env default.
decisions.lesson:
flake-parts is a Nix toolkit for splitting a project into reusable flake modules.

People use it to assemble languages, services, and shells from small pieces instead of one big file.

Jet already aims for one easy default: typed env modules that just work.

The dual-facet rule says beginners get magic defaults, and experts get explicit control of the same outcomes.

So the question is not whether Jet copies flake-parts as the only UI. It is whether the expert facet may opt into flake-parts composition and interop beside that default.
decisions.story: Alex wants new teammates on jet env with no Nix module homework. Riley maintains a large monorepo already split with flake-parts and needs Jet to consume and extend that graph without a rewrite.

options.name: Dual-facet: Jet default + expert flake-parts
options.detail: Beginners use typed env.* only. Experts can consume and compose flake-parts flakes through an explicit expert path. Same lock and realize engine underneath.
options.technical: Default: env modules + imports:find. Expert: U16/#783 bridge understands flake-parts module flakes; optional emit/import of flake-parts-compatible shards. No beginner requirement to touch flake-parts. I8 preserved: one realize path, two entry surfaces.
options.code:
$ jet env
# beginner repo → env.dev

$ jet env
# flake-parts repo → bridge activates modules; jet env info notes flake-parts

options.name: Jet env only — no flake-parts
options.detail: Experts rewrite flake-parts setups into Jet modules. Bridge may read plain flakes but not flake-parts module composition as a supported expert product.
options.technical: Keep U16 best-effort flake translate. Document flake-parts as unsupported; users flatten manually.
options.code:
$ jet bridge flake
# L0204 / unsupported: flake-parts modules — flatten into env.*

options.name: flake-parts as primary UX
options.detail: Teach flake-parts first. Jet env becomes a thin skin over module flakes. Beginners must learn Nix module composition.
options.technical: Inverts beginner default. Conflicts with epoch-4 vision of typed env without a second language.
options.code:
$ jet env
# requires flake-parts modules even for hello-world

options.name: Emit-only flake-parts, no consume
options.detail: Jet can generate flake-parts shards for Nix neighbors, but cannot activate an existing flake-parts monorepo as a first-class expert path.
options.technical: One-way bridge. Riley's existing repo still needs a rewrite to be consumed.
options.code:
$ jet bridge flake --emit-parts
# writes modules/; cannot jet env an upstream flake-parts tree

comparisons.note: Simple devenv.nix default; flake-parts users often embed devenv as a module inside a larger flake.
Dual-facet: beginner magic defaults; expert explicit control of the same mechanism.
comparisons.code:
module env.dev { ... }  // default
// expert flake-parts via bridge/opt-in

recommendation.why: Keeps the easy Jet env path for beginners while giving experts a real flake-parts consume and compose path on the same lock and realize engine.

whyNot.reason: Forces experts to abandon working flake-parts monorepos even though the owner asked for that expert path.
Makes Nix module composition the default and burdens beginners.
Only helps Jet export outward; it does not load the expert repos people already have.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must maintain flake-parts interop tests and docs. That cost is accepted so the expert facet is real, not a slogan.

decisions.comment: Jet has its own package/module system that should already support single file vs flake parts style devenvs -> ensure alignment with those existing paradigms

decisions.title: One typed contract for user literal prefixes
decisions.gist: Choose one typed literal contract that gives users simple prefixes and library authors full checked control.
decisions.lesson:
A literal prefix turns source text into a value while the compiler checks the program. For example, `sql"..."` can produce a checked `Sql` value.

The compiler must keep text parts and typed holes separate. If it joins them first, the library loses injection safety and accurate source locations.

Beginners should only see the useful prefix. Library authors need explicit control over its name, accepted holes, errors, and generated value.

Jet already has typed text and comptime builders. The choice is how one type claims a prefix without adding macros or another interpolation engine.
decisions.story: Iris uses `sql"..."` in an application. Her database library checks syntax at compile time and keeps each value hole parameterized. Its author can inspect every lowering rule.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: lowercase name inference can collide, tag functions can grant syntax by accident, and joined strings can reopen injection bugs. The winner must reject collisions, preserve hole spans and types, run only at comptime, and use the existing typed-text engine. `Sql.raw` remains the sole audited raw escape under D-TYPEDTEXT1.

options.name: Type-owned contract with beginner shorthand and expert policy
options.detail: A result type derives one `Literal` contract. Users type only the prefix. Authors may accept the unambiguous lowercase default or set an explicit spelling and hole policy. Built-in and user prefixes use one typed-text path. Collisions and unsupported holes fail at the source span.
options.technical: The registry key is the explicit prefix or an unambiguous lowercase type name. The builder receives immutable text segments, typed hole facts, and spans. It returns only its owning type or a registered `LiteralError`. It cannot perform runtime effects or introduce grammar.

options.name: Any comptime tag function
options.detail: Any matching comptime function becomes a prefix. This is concise for authors and exposes functions directly. It also makes syntax capability depend on naming, permits accidental collisions, and leaves result ownership unclear.

options.name: Closed Core prefixes plus expected-type elaboration
options.detail: Only Core owns prefixes. Existing SQL typed text still follows D-TYPEDTEXT1 expected-type elaboration. User libraries cannot add safe domain prefixes, so their custom domains use ordinary constructors without typed holes.

comparisons.note: Tagged templates preserve text and values, but tags run at runtime and ownership follows an ordinary function binding.
Procedural macros offer deep control, but they add a separate token and macro system with macro-specific errors.
comparisons.code: sql!("select * from users where id = {}", id)

recommendation.why: A gives application users one clean prefix while giving authors explicit ownership, policy, errors, and inspection on Jet's existing typed-text path.

whyNot.reason: Function naming grants syntax implicitly and cannot make ownership or collisions clear.
A closed built-in set blocks safe domain literals from user libraries.

recommendation.tradeoff: Library authors must declare a contract and resolve prefix collisions. This visible work protects every simple call site.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, reserve E0358 with the exact what, why, and fix shown here. Bind the prefix registry to Syntax coverage. Prove collisions, typed holes, spans, comptime-only execution, AOT/JIT parity, inspection, and the existing raw escape.

decisions.title: First-party MCP surface with typed defaults and protocol control
decisions.gist: Choose one MCP client and server API that starts simple and exposes full protocol, transport, version, and authorization control.
decisions.lesson:
Model Context Protocol, or MCP, lets clients discover and call tools, resources, and prompts. JSON-RPC is the request and reply envelope that names each operation. JSON Schema describes the allowed input and output data.

A codec converts typed Jet values to exact protocol messages. A transport carries those messages through standard input and output or HTTP. Authorization decides which remote identity may use each operation. An interceptor is an expert hook around message handling.

MCP revisions can change lifecycle rules. Stable `2025-11-25` uses initialization and can use HTTP sessions. The `2026-07-28` release candidate uses a stateless core and extensions.

A beginner should register a typed function and serve it. An expert needs version policy, transports, authorization, cancellation, progress, extensions, raw messages, and audit facts. One protocol core can serve both depths.
decisions.story: Noor serves one repository search function over stdio. The same binary later serves remote clients with OAuth, strict version policy, custom limits, and complete redacted traces.
decisions.inWild:
use core.mcp as mcp

server :: mcp.server("repo-tools")
  .tool("search", search)
server.serve(.Stdio)?

remote :: server.with(McpPolicy.{
  versions: .StableAnd(["2026-07-28"])
  auth: repo_oauth
  limits: strict_limits
})
remote.serve(.Http("127.0.0.1:8443"))?
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: the original lesson treated `2025-11-25` as timeless and made the builder sound closed. As of 2026-07-25, it is stable while `2026-07-28` is a release candidate with breaking lifecycle changes. The winner must use per-revision codecs, stable-by-default negotiation, explicit preview opt-in, bounded schema work, no token passthrough, and one low-level peer beneath the builders.

options.name: Layered typed SDK over one protocol core
options.detail: Typed builders register ordinary functions and cover the common client or server path. Experts use the same public codec, peer, transport, authorization, extension, and interceptor types. Stable revisions negotiate by default. Preview revisions require explicit policy until final.
options.technical: One revision registry owns messages and lifecycle laws. `2025-11-25` keeps session behavior. `2026-07-28` uses its stateless codec when enabled. Schema depth, message size, validation time, deadlines, redirects, origins, tokens, and extension sets are bounded and audited.

options.name: Compiler-discovered MCP markers
options.detail: Markers make registration short and permit generated tables. They also add MCP-specific syntax, hide registry order and policy, and burden functions that applications may call normally.

options.name: Low-level protocol package only
options.detail: Applications get codecs, messages, and transports without builders. Experts get full control, but every project must rebuild schema registration, validation, lifecycle, auth, cleanup, and typed dispatch.

comparisons.note: The stable revision uses initialization, negotiated capabilities, sessions, and Streamable HTTP.
The candidate uses per-request protocol facts, stateless HTTP, discovery, and extensions. It requires a separate revision codec.
Generated services give strong typed calls. MCP also needs runtime discovery and revision-aware JSON schemas.

recommendation.why: A makes the first tool small while preserving every protocol and security control through the same revisioned core and unified grant graph.

whyNot.reason: Markers create syntax and hide policy that an explicit registry can show.
A low-level package alone makes every application rebuild unsafe and inconsistent SDK machinery.

recommendation.tradeoff: Revision negotiation can expose an explicit incompatibility instead of silently adapting unlike lifecycle rules. Preview revisions also require an explicit opt-in.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, test each revision as a separate wire profile. Prove stable defaults, preview opt-in, downgrade refusal, schema bounds, transport cleanup, authorization isolation, redacted traces, unified grants, and `jet inspect dossier` facts.

decisions.title: One authority model for agent command execution
decisions.gist: Choose one process authority model with a safe workspace default and exact expert grants, plans, isolation, and receipts.
decisions.lesson:
An agent can choose commands, so its plan is untrusted input. A familiar command name does not make execution safe.

Authority is the exact set of files, hosts, secrets, programs, devices, and resources a command may use. Isolation enforces that set.

Beginners need one safe workspace command that denies ambient credentials and network access. Experts need exact grants, limits, backend facts, dry-run plans, and machine-readable receipts.

Jet already has `core.process`, native isolation, and one trust graph. The choice is whether agent execution deepens those mechanisms or forks them.
decisions.story: Sam lets an agent run tests. The easy path reads the repository and writes only an isolated build area. A release job later grants one host and one signing key by name.
decisions.inWild:
// beginner-safe workspace policy
result :: process.cmd(["cargo", "test"])
  .under(ProcessAuthority.workspace("."))
  .run()?

// expert expansion on the same policy
release :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network([Host.https("registry.example.com")])
  .secret([SecretRef.signing("release")])
  .limits(strict_limits)
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a policy object is only useful if defaults deny ambient authority and every host enforces it. Plans can lie if resolution changes after review. Receipts can leak secrets. The winner must bind executable identity, policy, inputs, and backend into one launch transaction. Unsupported enforcement fails before spawn.

options.name: Safe workspace defaults plus exact core.process authority
options.detail: `ProcessSpec` accepts one authority object. The workspace constructor gives a useful read-only repository and private build area with network, home, secrets, devices, and inherited handles denied. Experts widen exact rights on the same object. CLI and MCP tools use the same engine.
options.technical: Resolve executable identity before review and bind it into launch. The plan and receipt share a policy digest. Native enforcement comes from #398. Denied attempts, descendants, limits, outputs, and redaction facts use the D-WD1 grant graph and D-WD2 dossier.
options.code:
// beginner
jet self exec --workspace . -- cargo test

// expert
policy :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network([Host.https("registry.example.com")])
  .executable([locked.cosign])
print(process.cmd(args).under(policy).plan())

options.name: Separate agent executor
options.detail: A dedicated executor can use agent terms and strict defaults. It duplicates command, child, signal, stream, cancellation, and isolation semantics. The two process systems can then disagree.
options.code:
agent.exec(Command.{ args, authority })?

// ordinary process and agent process now have separate lifecycle laws

options.name: CLI-only sandbox
options.detail: External agents get a safe command, but Jet programs and first-party SDKs cannot use the authority types. Libraries must shell out or launch unrestricted children.
options.code:
jet self exec --workspace . --write src,tests -- cargo test

// no equivalent typed ProcessSpec policy

comparisons.note: Deno grants scoped runtime permissions. Jet also needs executable identity, build authority, process-tree control, plans, and final receipts.
Bazel actions declare inputs and outputs for isolation and caching. Agent work also needs interactive plans and revocable trust.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one safe command and experts exact control without splitting process lifecycle, isolation, grants, or audit facts.

whyNot.reason: A second executor duplicates the most safety-sensitive process semantics.
CLI-only protection leaves Jet programs and SDKs outside the authority boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: `core.process` gains a substantial authority surface. The common constructor keeps that detail outside beginner code.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove no ambient authority, time-of-check binding, and fail-closed hosts. Also prove full-tree cleanup, redacted receipts, denied-attempt facts, shared digests, D-WD1 integration, and API/CLI parity.

decisions.title: One flake-class graph for Jet environments
decisions.gist: Choose one easy Jet environment graph with full expert input, lock, follows, output, and foreign projection control.
decisions.lesson:
A reproducible source graph names external inputs, pins exact revisions, connects shared inputs, and exposes outputs. A lock records the resolved identity.

A follows edge makes two sources share one dependency. This avoids hidden duplicate package worlds and keeps overlays aligned.

Beginners need a small `sources` list and one automatic lock. Experts need named nodes, follows edges, output selection, graph queries, merge facts, and loss-accounted foreign projection.

Jet already has sources, outputs, environment modules, and `.jet/lock`. Ratified flake-parts support also requires expert composition without making Nix the beginner language.
decisions.story: Mina pins nixpkgs and a Rust overlay with two short entries. Riley imports a flake-parts monorepo, inspects every follows edge, and exports a compatible view.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a bridge-only design loses graph intent, a separate flake block creates two locks, and best-effort translation can hide semantic loss. The winner must keep one graph and lock, honor D-ENV-FLAKEPARTS1, report every projection loss, preserve source provenance, and reject ambiguous follows edges.

options.name: Progressive Jet graph with loss-accounted foreign projections
options.detail: Beginners list sources and use automatic exact locking. Experts add typed follows edges, output projections, provider mappings, merge policy, and flake-parts composition in the same graph. Import and export use that graph and produce exact loss reports.
options.technical: `.jet/lock` remains sole identity. Every foreign node maps to a source, follows edge, output, or explicit unsupported fact. Imported arbitrary Nix functions remain in the native compatibility evaluator. They never become opaque native Jet values.

options.name: Separate flake compatibility block
options.detail: Nix users get familiar inputs, outputs, and follows. Jet projects then own two graph vocabularies and must define which lock, source, output, and policy wins.
options.code:
flake: { inputs: { ... }, outputs: fn(inputs) { ... } }
env: { packages: [flake.outputs.rust] }

options.name: Resolved-package bridge only
options.detail: Jet keeps a small native graph and imports final packages from an external evaluator. This cannot preserve follows, output structure, lock reasons, module composition, or round-trip intent.
options.code:
packages: import_flake(".").packages

// graph identity and follows edges are hidden

comparisons.note: Inputs, follows, outputs, and `flake.lock` form one reproducible graph with a functional output layer.
flake-parts composes that graph from modules. D-ENV-FLAKEPARTS1 requires an expert Jet path over the same realization engine.

recommendation.why: A keeps the beginner graph small while giving experts full graph, lock, projection, and flake-parts control through one realization path.

whyNot.reason: A second graph duplicates identity, locking, policy, and outputs.
Resolved packages alone discard graph intent and cannot support honest round trips.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some Nix functions remain evaluator-backed and cannot become ordinary typed Jet values. Their boundaries and projection losses stay explicit.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove one lock, exact follows, and flake-parts use. Prove round trips for representable graph facts. Also prove exact loss reports for evaluator-backed constructs, merge facts, containment, and stable graph and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: One typed environment lifecycle with simple defaults and expert policy
decisions.gist: Choose one lifecycle planner for enter tasks, dotenv, unset rules, default reload, clean-shell checks, trust, and the existing expert hook.
decisions.lesson:
Environment lifecycle actions run when a developer enters or reloads a project environment. They can change files, variables, and services.

A dotenv file supplies named environment values. An unset rule removes an inherited name. Reload evaluates source changes again. A check tests the environment from a clean shell.

A cloned repository must not run code or read secrets silently. Jet therefore needs a plan, typed effects, trust grants, and exact change detection before lifecycle work runs.

Beginners need short fields such as `dotenv` and `checks`. Experts need key allowlists, secret treatment, ordering, reload triggers, cache policy, failure policy, and audit output. One planner can use `#Task`, D-ECO7's hook, and the unified grant graph.
decisions.story: Tess lists `.env`, one setup task, and one check. Reload works by default. A sensitive repo expands key, secret, timing, and failure policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: shell strings bypass effects, magic names hide execution, dotenv can import secrets, reload can loop, and a denied hook can leave partial state. Binding owner law requires a first-run prompt with a hash allowlist. Background re-evaluation is on by default and applies at the next prompt. `jet env test` proves a clean shell. The winner must use D-WD1 grants, keep D-ECO7 as the sole arbitrary hook, and publish reload and rollback facts.

options.name: Typed lifecycle fields over one task and grant planner
options.detail: Simple lists cover dotenv files, unset names, enter tasks, and checks. Reload is on by default and applies a background plan at the next prompt. Experts expand key, secret, ordering, reload, cache, and failure policy. An unseen or denied D-ECO7 hook is skipped, and the shell still opens.
options.technical: The planner resolves data changes first, then granted task or hook nodes, then checks. It binds source digests and effects before execution. Hook grants stay scoped per role module and bind the plan hash. Reload coalesces changes and rejects cycles. `jet env test` starts clean. Failure reports exact retained state.

options.name: Embedded shell hooks
options.detail: Existing shell scripts fit directly and experts control their shell. Jet loses typed effects, portable behavior, structured plans, key tracking, and consistent rollback.
options.code:
enterShell: "source .env && ./scripts/setup.sh"
enterTest: "test -f .env"

options.name: Reserved lifecycle function names
options.detail: Authors write ordinary Jet functions with little configuration. Renaming or importing a function can silently change lifecycle behavior, and the module does not show execution order.
options.code:
fn enter() #Fs { ... }
fn enter_test() #Fs { ... }

comparisons.note: Directory entry can load environment code after trust. Jet also needs typed effects, tasks, checks, and structured reload facts.
devenv provides enter hooks, dotenv, tests, and reload behavior through Nix and shell fields.

recommendation.why: A keeps common entry short and gives experts exact lifecycle, trust, secret, reload, failure, and audit control through one ordered plan.

whyNot.reason: Shell strings bypass Jet's type, effect, trust, and rollback facts.
Reserved names hide wiring and make ordinary refactors change behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: First use can show a trust prompt. Default background reload waits until the next shell prompt before it changes the active environment.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove per-role-module hook grants, plan-hash binding, and denied-hook shell entry. Prove default reload at the next prompt and clean-shell `jet env test`. Also prove plan order, dotenv allowlists, redaction, task effects, cycles, retained-state facts, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: One Service record from simple command to full dev topology
decisions.gist: Choose one Service record with useful defaults and full expert readiness, recovery, watch, resource, dependency, and audit control.
decisions.lesson:
A development service is a long-running process with logs and cleanup. Readiness tells dependents when the service can accept work.

Restart and watch policies control recovery and reload. Ports, sockets, and dependency edges describe resources and start order.

Beginners need a service with only a command. Experts need exact probes, restart budgets, backoff, watch rules, shutdown stages, ports, sockets, dependencies, and receipts.

Jet already has one `Service` record, one service CLI, safe process-tree authority, and ordinary task calls for finite work. The choice is whether that one record grows by progressive disclosure.
decisions.story: Owen starts an API from one `run` field. His full stack later adds database readiness, a migration task, restart limits, file watches, reserved ports, and exact shutdown policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: process start is not application readiness. Restart loops can burn resources, watch events can storm, dependency edges can cycle, and port checks can race. The winner must distinguish start from readiness and reserve resources before release. It must bound retries, detect cycles, and honor D-JPK-SERVICEAUTH1 before background spawn.

options.name: Progressive Service record over one supervised graph
options.detail: A `run` field creates a foreground-capable service with safe cleanup and no claimed application readiness. Experts add typed probes, bounded restart, watch, ports, sockets, order, shutdown, and logs. Finite migrations stay ordinary `#Task` calls attached as explicit dependencies.
options.technical: The service planner owns resource reservation, acyclic order, generation identity, readiness transitions, restart budgets, watch debounce, and receipts. Background start uses D-JPK-SERVICEAUTH1 and fails before spawn when safe authority is unavailable.

options.name: Separate ProcessGraph record
options.detail: A graph can model tasks and services uniformly. It duplicates service identity, process ownership, logs, readiness, cancellation, resource claims, and CLI state beside `Service`.
options.code: ProcessGraph.{ nodes: [db, migrate, api], edges: [...] }

options.name: Delegate advanced topology to process-compose
options.detail: Projects gain a mature external supervisor. Advanced behavior then depends on another binary, configuration language, lifecycle, lock, diagnostics, and authority model.
options.code: jet os services export --format process-compose | process-compose up

comparisons.note: It combines dependencies, readiness, restarts, logs, and process supervision in a separate configuration system.
systemd distinguishes process state, readiness, restart policy, resources, and ordering. Jet needs portable typed versions for development.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one command field and experts a complete supervised topology without duplicating service identity, lifecycle, authority, or inspection.

whyNot.reason: A second graph repeats the same service and process facts.
External delegation makes core behavior depend on another configuration and authority stack.

recommendation.tradeoff: The Service type becomes broad. Closed typed policy records and short defaults keep that breadth out of basic declarations.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove start versus readiness, bounded retries, backoff, debounce, resource reservation, and cycle errors. Also prove task and service order, tree cleanup, D-JPK-SERVICEAUTH1 failure, plans, logs, receipts, and dossier facts.

decisions.title: Task metadata with zero-ceremony defaults and exact expert execution
decisions.gist: Choose one `#Task` signature that stays bare and exposes packages, paths, skip rules, cache, authority, resources, and outputs when needed.
decisions.lesson:
A task is an ordinary Jet function exposed to project tooling. D-JPK-TASKRUN1 already makes `#Task fn` the one task identity.

Simple tasks should run with the current environment, project directory, and no hidden cache promise. No metadata is required.

Experts need task-local packages, a working directory, declared inputs and outputs, cache policy, authority, limits, and execution facts. Tooling needs those facts before the body runs.

D-MARKSIG1 gives markers one ordinary call grammar. The choice is whether `#Task` uses that grammar or duplicates task identity in another map.
decisions.story: Rae marks `book` with bare `#Task` and runs it. CI later adds mdbook, inputs, outputs, a platform skip rule, cache, and authority.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: automatic caching can return false results, and runtime provisioning hides the plan. Output globs can capture secrets. Unchecked skip rules can hide required work. The winner must keep bare tasks uncached, use D-MARKSIG1, show skip reasons, and bind facts before execution. Dynamic undeclared access must fail or disable promotion.

options.name: Progressive typed metadata on the existing #Task marker
options.detail: Bare `#Task` stays the beginner form and runs honestly without reusable caching. Experts add closed typed arguments for packages, cwd, inputs, outputs, skip, cache, authority, and limits. Task calls remain the only dependency edges.
options.technical: Metadata uses D-MARKSIG1. Cache keys bind function identity, arguments, locked packages, declared inputs, policy, platform, and compiler. Skip uses typed host or platform facts and reports its reason. Undeclared access fails in strict cached mode. Dynamic tasks may select `.Off`.

options.name: Separate task configuration map
options.detail: The marker stays tiny and a central map can review all tasks. Names, functions, dependencies, arguments, and metadata can drift between two sources of truth.
options.code: tasks: { book: { fn: book, packages: [pkg.mdbook], cwd: "docs" } }

options.name: Provision only inside task bodies
options.detail: Authors use ordinary code for every unusual case. The planner cannot know packages, cwd, inputs, outputs, cache safety, or authority until execution has started.

comparisons.note: Declared actions give strong cache facts, but require a separate build language and explicit metadata for every action.
Recipes are easy to write, but their shell bodies hide inputs, outputs, packages, effects, and portable cache rules.

recommendation.why: A preserves the one-line task while giving experts and tooling exact execution, cache, package, authority, and output facts on the same identity.

whyNot.reason: A separate map duplicates task identity and can drift from the function.
Runtime-only setup hides every fact needed for planning and safe caching.

recommendation.tradeoff: `#Task` gains a broad typed signature. Beginners keep bare `#Task`, and experts reveal only fields they need.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, bind D-MARKSIG1 and keep bare tasks uncached. Prove typed skip reasons, cache keys, undeclared-access errors, output containment, secret exclusion, task-local packages, cwd, authority, limits, dependency calls, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: One managed file graph with safe shorthand and exact sync policy
decisions.gist: Choose one typed file graph for simple managed links and expert seed, copy, generation, permissions, secrets, drift, and conflict control.
decisions.lesson:
Environment files include tool configuration, seed data, generated text, and links to locked content. Jet must know who owns each destination.

A symlink follows its managed source. A seed writes only when the destination is absent. A copy replaces managed output after review.

Beginners need a short map with a safe default. Experts need mode, permissions, secret treatment, generation, conflict policy, atomic updates, drift checks, and exact diffs.

Typed values and ordinary Jet functions can generate content. A separate template language is not required. One file graph can plan and audit every write.
decisions.story: Kai links one tool file with a short map entry. A local settings file uses seed mode, while a generated secret file requires strict permissions and redacted diffs.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: implicit overwrite can destroy local work, and symlink targets can escape the project. Generated content can leak secrets. Seed drift can become invisible, and templates add injection rules. The winner must stop on unmanaged conflicts, use atomic replacement, redact sensitive diffs, bind source hashes, and show exact ownership.

options.name: Progressive typed files map with plan-before-apply
options.detail: A bare value means a managed symlink to immutable content and never overwrites an unmanaged destination. Experts expand the entry with Seed or Copy mode, permissions, sensitivity, generation, and conflict policy. `jet env sync` plans, confirms, applies atomically, and audits drift.
options.technical: Every entry has destination, source digest, mode, ownership, sensitivity, and last applied state. Relative destinations cannot escape their root. Sensitive bytes never enter logs or world-readable stores. Dynamic sources return typed text or bytes before planning.

options.name: Lifecycle tasks only
options.detail: Ordinary filesystem code can express every case. Plans cannot know destinations, ownership, overwrite rules, sensitivity, or drift before the task runs.
options.code:
on_enter: [seed_files]
#Task fn seed_files() #Fs { ... }

options.name: Separate template manifest
options.detail: A template system makes text generation convenient and reviewable. It adds another interpolation language, escaping law, secret path, and ownership model beside Jet values.
options.code: generated_files: { ".env": template("env.tpl", values) }

comparisons.note: Typed declarations manage files and links with source ownership. Jet also needs project sync, seed behavior, and unified trust facts.
chezmoi handles templates, secrets, diffs, and apply workflows through a separate configuration product.

recommendation.why: A makes the common link short and gives experts exact write, generation, secret, conflict, drift, and audit control through one file graph.

whyNot.reason: Imperative tasks hide ownership and overwrite policy until execution.
A template manifest adds a second interpolation and secret-rendering system.

recommendation.tradeoff: An unmanaged ownership conflict stops synchronization and requires a user choice. Jet never guesses which file may be replaced.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove safe shorthand, conflict refusal, and Symlink, Seed, and Copy semantics. Also prove atomic recovery, path containment, permissions, redaction, source hashes, generated values, drift, plan confirmation, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: OCI images as one projection of the environment and image graphs
decisions.gist: Choose one existing image record with a simple environment source and full expert entrypoint, platform, layer, security, and provenance control.
decisions.lesson:
An environment graph already knows packages, variables, files, tasks, services, and locked sources. An Open Container Initiative, or OCI, image packages a filesystem and runtime settings.

A layer is one immutable filesystem change. An entrypoint is the first program the image starts. Provenance records the inputs, builder, and policy that made the image.

Not every environment fact belongs in an image. Host hooks, local secrets, mutable sockets, and unsupported services must fail or require an explicit replacement.

Beginners need `from: env.dev` and a useful shell image. Experts need service selection, platforms, users, layers, ports, health, entrypoints, secret rules, cache, and provenance. Jet can extend its existing image record.
decisions.story: Uma creates a development shell image with one source line. Her CI image later selects the API service, non-root user, two platforms, health probe, and exact layer policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: environment projection can copy secrets, activation hooks, host paths, impure outputs, or mutable state into layers. A second container record would split locks and publishing. The winner must classify every fact and refuse non-projectable state. It must use a non-root default, exclude secrets, show the projection plan, and preserve D-JPK-REMOTE1 for remote builds.

options.name: Progressive environment projection in the existing image record
options.detail: `from: env.dev` creates a locked shell image with safe non-root defaults. Experts select services, platforms, users, entrypoints, layers, ports, health, cache, and signatures on the same record. Host-only facts fail with a specific projection error.
options.technical: Projection records included, transformed, omitted, and rejected facts. Secrets use runtime mounts or references and never layers. Hangar owns content, cache, signing, archive, and publish. `.jet/lock` owns exact inputs and platforms. Remote builders use only prior D-JPK-REMOTE1 host bindings and grants.

options.name: Separate container environment records
options.detail: Container users get a focused namespace with its own layers, commands, ports, build, and publish fields. It duplicates image identity, locks, Hangar, provenance, and lifecycle.
options.code: container.api { environment: env.dev, command: api.run }

options.name: CLI-only environment projection
options.detail: One command creates ad hoc images without source changes. The image contract, service selection, platform policy, and security choices disappear from reviewable source.
options.code: jet os image build --env dev --services api

comparisons.note: OCI standardizes image content and runtime configuration. It does not define how a development environment becomes that image.
Nix can build layered images from a package closure. Jet also projects typed services, files, policy, and provenance.

recommendation.why: A makes a shell image one line and gives experts full OCI, security, platform, and provenance control without splitting Jet's image machinery.

whyNot.reason: A container namespace duplicates image identity, locking, storage, signing, and publishing.
CLI-only flags hide the image contract from source review and reproducible builds.

recommendation.tradeoff: A host-only or secret-bearing environment fact stops projection until the user replaces or omits it explicitly.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove shell defaults, service entrypoints, non-root policy, fact classes, secret exclusion, and host-only rejection. Also prove platform locks, deterministic layers, D-JPK-REMOTE1 bindings, Hangar reuse, signatures, publishing, plans, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: Optional environment integrations through Jet-native typed modules
decisions.gist: Choose how simple presets and exact expert controls for platforms, certificates, hosts, and agents fit the existing module and grant systems.
decisions.lesson:
Optional integrations combine packages, variables, files, licenses, secrets, permissions, and host capabilities. Android and Apple toolchains are examples.

A beginner wants one named preset with safe locked defaults. An expert needs exact SDK versions, targets, paths, license decisions, certificates, host mappings, agent tools, and failure policy.

Adding top-level fields for every product would make the environment record grow forever. Raw recipes avoid that growth but lose validation and shared planning.

Jet already has typed modules, imports, packages, files, tasks, providers, and grants. First-party integration modules can compose those facts without creating another mechanism.
decisions.story: Devon imports an Android preset and gets a locked supported SDK. A mobile release environment expands versions, Apple targets, certificates, host aliases, and Codex MCP servers with exact grants.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: closed top-level domains can become a second package system, and direct devenv mirroring freezes foreign names. Generic recipes hide licenses, secrets, host support, and grants. The winner must use typed modules, lower to existing facts, support two depths, and import foreign configs with exact loss reports.

options.name: First-party typed integration modules over existing facts
options.detail: Beginners import a named module with locked safe defaults. Experts pass typed versions, targets, paths, licenses, certificates, hosts, agent tools, and policy. Each module lowers to existing package, file, task, provider, host-check, secret, and grant facts.
options.technical: Integration modules have no private resolver, lock, effect, or activation engine. Their public outputs are typed graph facts. Foreign devenv modules import into canonical editable Jet modules with TODO diagnostics for every unsupported fact.

options.name: Mirror devenv module roots
options.detail: Migration is direct and existing users recognize names. Jet inherits another product's taxonomy, enable flags, nesting, defaults, and compatibility burden as public law.

options.name: Packages and lifecycle tasks only
options.detail: Projects assemble each integration from packages and lifecycle tasks without a curated preset. Beginners repeat fragile recipes, while planning cannot validate licenses, host support, certificates, or agent authority.
options.code:
packages: [pkg.android_sdk]
on_enter: [configure_android]

comparisons.note: devenv offers many named modules with enable flags and nested options. Jet can import them without adopting their taxonomy.
Typed modules compose options and defaults. Jet's modules also lower to one package, task, file, and grant graph.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners curated presets and experts exact integration control while preserving one module, package, file, task, host, lock, and grant mechanism.

whyNot.reason: A direct mirror turns foreign organization and enable flags into permanent Jet law.
Recipes alone cannot provide shared validation, planning, diagnostics, or safe defaults.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only first-party integration schemas receive preset guarantees and tailored diagnostics. Unusual tools use ordinary module composition with less specific guidance.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove beginner presets, expert parameters, module composition, one lock, license checks, and host failures. Also prove certificate and secret handling, agent grants, devenv loss reports, TODO diagnostics, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: Views with more than one possible owner
decisions.gist: Choose how one safe view can refer to several possible owners.
decisions.lesson:
A view reads or edits storage that another value owns. Provenance is the compiler record that links the view to that owner. Jet uses this record to stop the owner from moving while the view is live.

Current Jet requires one fixed owner path for each returned view. This works for `first(values)`, because the result always points into `values`. It rejects `longer(left, right)`, because the result can point into either input.

Rust describes this relation with lifetime parameters. Jet can keep those details hidden, but sema still needs an exact relation. The same issue appears when a list, enum, callback, or trait value carries views from several owners.
decisions.story: Mira writes a zero-copy protocol parser. Each packet contains many text fields that point into one of two receive buffers. Copying every field defeats the parser design.

options.name: One hidden set of possible owners
options.detail: Keep `View<T>` unchanged. Sema records a bounded set of possible owner paths and keeps every possible owner live. Containers and callbacks carry the same hidden relation.
options.technical: Public API metadata records source unions and their projections. All return paths must fit the declared union. Dynamic dispatch must publish one compatible union contract.

options.name: Explicit owner relation syntax
options.detail: Make expert APIs state owner relations in source. This gives full control, but it adds lifetime-like notation that every caller and library author must learn.
options.technical: The exact proposed form is `View<T from left | right>`. Generic relations use named owner parameters. Sema checks the written relation and publishes it.

options.name: Borrow only through callbacks
options.detail: Do not return a multi-owner view. A function receives a callback and calls it while the selected owner is known. This stays safe but makes composition and storage harder.
options.technical: The callback cannot return or store the view. It gives dynamic selection without extending public provenance metadata.

options.name: Keep one stable owner
options.detail: Keep the current rule. Programs copy data, use one fixed owner, or use Shared and Pool handles. This preserves a small model but leaves safe Rust programs inexpressible.
options.technical: E2305 and E2307 continue to reject source unions, view containers, view-returning function values, and open trait dispatch.

comparisons.note: A shared lifetime can link one result to either input. Containers and traits can also carry lifetime parameters.
comparisons.code: fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str

comparisons.note: Borrowing features use compiler-managed lifetime dependencies and aim to hide most explicit lifetime notation.
comparisons.code: // compiler tracks that a borrowed result depends on its input

recommendation.why: It closes the Rust capability gap while keeping Jet source free of lifetime notation. It also extends the existing provenance graph instead of adding another memory model.

whyNot.reason: It exposes compiler bookkeeping in routine APIs and makes the beginner surface harder to read.
It cannot support ordinary collections, returned parsers, or trait-backed lending APIs.
It keeps confirmed safe Rust patterns impossible without copying or changing the data model.

recommendation.tradeoff: Sema and API metadata become more complex because each live view can keep several possible owners stable.

decisions.title: Runtime proof for disjoint mutable views
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet safely edits several runtime-selected parts at once.
decisions.lesson:
Two write views are safe when they cannot reach the same storage. Jet proves different fields and constant ranges at compile time. It treats runtime indices and ranges as overlapping because their values are unknown during compilation.

A checked split can prove separation at runtime before any write starts. For example, splitting at index `mid` makes a left range below `mid` and a right range at or above `mid`. A multi-index check can reject duplicate indices before it returns write views.

Rust puts these proofs in trusted collection methods. Jet must choose whether the proof belongs in named methods, ordinary range syntax, or only unsafe code.
decisions.story: Andre updates two bodies in a physics world. Their indices come from collision detection. He needs direct mutable access to both bodies without cloning or serializing every update.
decisions.detail: `edit_disjoint`, `get_disjoint_write`, and `split_write` are three entry points into one proof mechanism. The closure form is the beginner default. Explicit views and the special split give experts direct control. All checks finish before any mutation. Failures use one typed bounds-or-overlap error. Ordinary range expressions never hide a runtime loan check.

options.name: Scoped edits and explicit views over one checked proof
options.detail: Beginners call `edit_disjoint` with targets and a closure. Jet checks all bounds and overlap before the closure starts. It lends each view, then releases every loan automatically. Experts use `get_disjoint_write` or `split_write` when views must cross helper calls. Ordinary ranges remain compile-time checked and never gain hidden runtime failure.
options.technical: All forms lower to one sema-visible disjointness proof for one owner. The runtime normalizes requested regions and completes every check before it creates any view. Slice splits need one bounds check. Index and key sets reject duplicates. The explicit form returns tracked `ViewMut` values under existing loan rules. Lending mutable iterators reuse the same proof and expose one element loan at a time.

options.name: Runtime checks on ordinary ranges
options.detail: Let ordinary dynamic write ranges coexist. Jet inserts one overlap check when sema cannot prove separation. This is concise, but a static-looking loan can now fail at runtime.
options.technical: Sema groups dynamic write windows by owner. It emits bounds and pairwise overlap checks before it creates any mutable reference.

options.name: Compile-time proof only
options.detail: Keep current behavior. Users rewrite algorithms around one write view, copy values, or use fixed ranges. The model stays simple but dynamic safe algorithms remain blocked.
options.technical: Dynamic projections always overlap. No standard API can mint several runtime-proven write views.

options.name: Unsafe split primitives
options.detail: Expose raw split operations only inside `#Unsafe`. Experts can proceed, but every caller must audit bounds and overlap manually.
options.technical: No safe API certifies disjointness. A raw pointer or unchecked view constructor carries the proof obligation.

comparisons.note: Slices use `split_at_mut`. Maps use `get_disjoint_mut`. Trusted methods check the relation and return safe mutable references.
Slices are simple pointer-length values. The programmer carries more alias responsibility, especially across mutable slices.
comparisons.code:
const left = values[0..mid];
const right = values[mid..];

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one short scoped call and gives experts retained views and a specialized split. Every form uses one visible proof rule. Ordinary place syntax stays predictable.

whyNot.reason: B hides runtime failure and overlap cost inside ordinary-looking loans.
C blocks safe dynamic updates and lending mutable iterators.
D repeats a standard collection proof in every unsafe caller.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds three method shapes. Clear staging must teach the closure first, then explicit views and the specialized split.

hybrid.synthesis: A combines automatic scoped loans with explicit expert views over one checked proof. It keeps ordinary ranges compile-time-only.

harvest.aspect: Named methods make checks and cost visible.
harvest.use: Keep all runtime proof behind the checked-disjoint method family.

harvest.aspect: Short multi-target code improves everyday ergonomics.
harvest.use: Put the short form in `edit_disjoint`, not ordinary range syntax.

harvest.aspect: Ordinary place syntax stays statically predictable.
harvest.use: Keep compile-time rejection when no checked method is present.

harvest.aspect: Experts need direct control over view lifetime and proof cost.
harvest.use: Give safe explicit views and specialized splits before unsafe primitives.

decisions.title: Borrowed captures in a taskgroup
decisions.gist: Choose which stack borrows taskgroup children may use.
decisions.lesson:
A detached task can outlive the function that created it. It must own its captured data. A scoped taskgroup is different because the group joins every child before the scope ends.

That join can make stack borrowing safe. Read-only data can be shared by many children. Mutable data needs exclusive or proven disjoint access for each child. The owner cannot move until all children finish.

Jet currently applies detached-task capture rules to taskgroups. The choice is whether taskgroups remain ownership-only or use their scope to admit safe borrows.
decisions.story: Leah loads a large image and runs four filters over separate bands. The group joins before the function returns. Copying the image or wrapping it in Shared adds needless cost.

options.name: Reads and proven disjoint writes
options.detail: Keep the current `g.task` spelling. Let children borrow reads freely and borrow writes only when sema proves disjoint places. The group owns every loan.
options.technical: Loans start before child launch and end after join or group cleanup. Cancellation, panic, return, and error paths join before owner invalidation.

options.name: Read borrows only
options.detail: Let children read borrowed data, but require ownership or Shared for every write. This closes common analysis cases with a smaller race proof.
options.technical: All borrowed captures are shared views. Mutable captures remain E1101, even when ranges are statically disjoint.

options.name: Separate borrowed-task spelling
options.detail: Keep `g.task` ownership-only. Add `g.borrow` for scoped reads and proven disjoint writes. The boundary is explicit, but users must choose between two task forms.
options.technical: `g.borrow` handles cannot detach or enter channels. Its result cannot contain a view that escapes the group.

options.name: Keep ownership-only groups
options.detail: Keep current rules. Every child owns, copies, channels, or uses Shared. The task model stays uniform but ignores the group's lifetime guarantee.
options.technical: Taskgroups continue to change cancellation and join behavior only. E1101 and E1102 remain identical to `tasks.spawn`.

comparisons.note: `std::thread::scope` lets scoped threads borrow non-static data because all threads join before the scope returns.
Task groups use structured lifetimes, but strict concurrency rules still restrict unsafe shared mutation.

recommendation.why: It uses the guarantee taskgroup already provides and reaches Rust scoped-thread capability without another task spelling.

whyNot.reason: It still forces copies or locks for parallel updates that sema can prove disjoint.
It creates two scoped child mechanisms with the same lifetime and cancellation behavior.
It keeps a confirmed expressiveness gap and wastes the group's join guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: Sema must track loans across scheduler edges and prove every exceptional group exit joins before storage changes.

decisions.title: Safe address-stable values
decisions.gist: Choose how safe code prevents an address-sensitive value from moving.
decisions.lesson:
Most values remain valid when moved to another address. A self-referential value is different because one field points into another field. An intrusive collection can also keep pointers between nodes.

A pin contract starts an address-sensitive state. Safe code can still read or edit the value, but it cannot move or replace the pinned storage. Unsafe construction may rely on this promise.

Rust exposes `Pin`. Jet has stable allocator storage and raw pointers, but it has no reusable source-level contract. The choice must cover stack values, caller storage, arenas, cleanup, and safe library boundaries.
decisions.story: Noah writes a zero-allocation event loop. Each operation stores links into a caller-owned queue. The library needs one audited constructor and safe use everywhere else.

options.name: Borrowed Pin<T> contract
options.detail: Add `mem.pin(&place) -> Pin<T>`. The pin is a tracked write view that blocks movement and replacement. Libraries accept or return `Pin<T>` where address stability matters.
options.technical: Pin provenance reuses the owner graph. Structural field projection is declared by the type implementation. Dropping the final pin ends the no-move loan.

options.name: Owned Stable<T> handle
options.detail: Move the value into stable storage and return a copyable handle. The handle can move, but the value cannot. Storage can use heap, arena, or Fixed backing.
options.technical: The owner is the stable allocation, not the local handle. Self-reference starts only after placement. Deallocation waits for all safe views and links.

options.name: Pinned type marker
options.detail: Mark a whole type as non-movable after construction. This is visible at the declaration, but it adds a new language marker and can burden values that are not yet address-sensitive.
options.technical: `#Pinned` suppresses ordinary movement after initialization. APIs use views to access the value. Construction and projection rules become type-level law.

options.name: Keep allocator and unsafe workarounds
options.detail: Use Pool IDs, arena views, Shared handles, or raw pointers. These solve many designs, but no common contract lets safe code rely on address stability.
options.technical: Each library owns its representation and unsafe proof. Sema does not prevent movement for an address-sensitive user type.

comparisons.note: `Pin<Ptr>` prevents safe code from moving an address-sensitive pointee and supports self-referential futures and intrusive collections.
comparisons.code: fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>)
