comparisons.note: Libraries often rely on heap addresses and conventions. The type system does not provide one standard no-move contract.

recommendation.why: It gives zero-allocation parity and reuses Jet's existing place, loan, and provenance model. The pin lasts only as long as the address-sensitive use.

whyNot.reason: It changes representation and can require storage indirection where Rust can pin an existing place.
It adds syntax and makes the whole type non-movable before address sensitivity starts.
It cannot support reusable safe APIs whose implementation depends on a no-move promise.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pinned APIs add an expert type and stricter projection rules that library authors must state and audit.

decisions.title: Stack-local interior mutability
decisions.gist: Choose how read-only code updates private local state safely.
decisions.lesson:
Interior mutability means a type can change private state through a read-only reference. A cache is a common example: the object looks unchanged to callers, but it saves a computed result inside.

The type must still enforce the reader-writer rule. A simple cell moves or copies values without lending a reference. A borrow cell checks active read and write guards at runtime. These local types must not cross tasks without synchronization.

Jet can use `Shared<T>` today, but that adds a copyable synchronized handle and lock even when one thread owns the object.
decisions.story: Iris builds a syntax tree with a lazy line index. Read methods fill the cache on first use. The tree stays local and never needs an Arc or operating-system lock.

options.name: One local Cell<T> family
options.detail: Add one non-sendable `Cell<T>`. Value methods handle get, set, replace, and initialization. Read, edit, and guard methods provide runtime-checked borrowed access.
options.technical: The runtime borrow state permits many readers or one writer. Guards carry view provenance. Sema rejects every task, channel, Shared, and parallel crossing.
options.code:
cache :: Cell<[Int]?>.new(None)
cache.set(Val(offsets))
value :: cache.read(lines => lines.len())
guard :: cache.guard_edit()?

options.name: Separate Cell and BorrowCell types
options.detail: Use `Cell<T>` for replace-style access and `BorrowCell<T>` for runtime guards. Each type has a smaller rule, but users must choose and migrate between two containers.
options.technical: `Cell<T>` never returns a view. `BorrowCell<T>` returns tracked read and write guards and checks conflicts at runtime.
options.code:
hits :: Cell<Int>.new(0)
cache :: BorrowCell<Map<Key, Value>>.new(Map.new())
cache.edit(map => map.insert(key, value))

options.name: Shared<T> only
options.detail: Keep one shared-mutation type for local and cross-task use. This is simple to teach, but local caches pay synchronization and shared-ownership costs.
options.technical: No local dynamic-borrow primitive is added. `Shared<T>` remains Arc plus a read-write lock.
options.code:
cache :: Shared.new(Map<Key, Value>.new())
cache.edit(map => map.insert(key, value))

options.name: Implicit mutation in read methods
options.detail: Let private fields change in a read method when they do not affect public equality. This looks easy but hides mutation and needs a new compiler rule for logical state.
options.technical: The compiler would classify fields as observational or cached. This creates a second mutability rule outside explicit capability types.

comparisons.note: `Cell<T>` uses replace-style access. `RefCell<T>` checks borrowed reads and writes at runtime. Both are not Sync.
Reference types and property wrappers can hide mutation, but exclusivity and thread safety depend on the chosen wrapper.

recommendation.why: One explicit local type keeps the beginner model small and gives experts both cheap value operations and checked borrowed access.

whyNot.reason: It creates two closely related local mutation containers and forces an early choice that one type can avoid.
It keeps needless shared ownership and synchronization in single-threaded code.
It hides real mutation and adds a second field-level capability system.

recommendation.tradeoff: One type has a wider method set, so documentation must separate value access from guard access clearly.

decisions.title: Expert guards and waiting for Shared<T>
decisions.gist: Choose how experts hold and wait on Shared access.
decisions.lesson:
`Shared.read` and `Shared.edit` lock one value for one closure. This short scope prevents many deadlocks and makes release automatic.

Some protocols need a lock across several helper calls. Others wait until a protected condition changes. A correct wait must register interest and release the write lock as one atomic action. It reacquires the lock before it checks the condition again.

A guard is an owned lock token. Safe cleanup releases it on return, error, panic, or cancellation. Jet must keep short closures as the default while choosing an expert form.
decisions.story: Sam builds a bounded work queue. A producer must wait while the queue is full. The wait must not miss the consumer signal between checking the size and sleeping.
decisions.inWild:
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

options.name: Explicit Shared guards and Condition
options.detail: Keep `read` and `edit` unchanged. Add expert `guard_read`, `guard_edit`, and `Condition`. Guards can map, split, and wait with automatic cleanup.
options.technical: A wait atomically registers, releases, parks, reacquires, and rechecks. Cancellation unregisters before guard release. Lock-order receipts cover nested guards.
options.code:
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

options.name: Closure-only wait methods
options.detail: Do not expose guards. Add `edit_when` and notification methods that keep the whole protocol inside one closure. This is safer but cannot span helper APIs.
options.technical: The runtime owns registration, release, park, reacquire, predicate checks, and edit execution. User code never receives a lock token.

options.name: Raw lock type family
options.detail: Expose Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, and their guards. This matches common systems APIs but creates several overlapping shared-state mechanisms.
options.technical: Users select lock types and control ordering. `#Transact` remains separate. Sema tracks guard cleanup but cannot prevent every protocol deadlock.
options.code:
lock :: Mutex.new(queue)
ready :: Condvar.new()
guard :: lock.lock()
ready.wait(&guard, q => q.len() < limit)?

options.name: Keep short closures and channels
options.detail: Keep current Shared access. Rewrite wait protocols as channels, task loops, or transactions. This avoids guards but makes some state protocols indirect.
options.technical: No guard or condition surface is added. Shared locks remain scoped to one closure call.

comparisons.note: Mutex and RwLock return guards. Condvar waits release and reacquire a Mutex guard while callers loop on the predicate.
comparisons.code: let mut q = cv.wait_while(q, |q| q.len() == limit)?;

comparisons.note: Mutex and Cond expose manual lock protocols. Channels often give a clearer ownership design, but shared conditions still exist.

recommendation.why: It preserves Jet's short safe default and adds the control needed for established lock and condition protocols through one Shared family.

whyNot.reason: It cannot pass guarded access through helper layers or support protocols that need several guarded operations.
It duplicates Shared and #Transact with several lower-level public lock families.
It keeps direct condition and guard protocols needlessly awkward or unavailable.

recommendation.tradeoff: Expert guards can create longer lock scopes, so diagnostics and lock-order audit output become required.

decisions.title: D-CONST-RETIRE1 — retire keyword const
decisions.outcome: User-facing `const` is retired. The only module immutable binding keyword is `comptime` (S57). `#Persist` is a marker on a binding that preserves that binding across jet-dev reloads; it is not tied to a `const` keyword. `#Static`/`#Inline` attach to `comptime` bindings. Writing `const` gets a teaching diagnostic pointing at `comptime`.
decisions.comment: User-facing `const` is retired. The only module immutable binding keyword is `comptime` (S57). `#Persist` is a marker on a binding that preserves that binding across jet-dev reloads; it is not tied to a `const` keyword. `#Static`/`#Inline` attach to `comptime` bindings. Writing `const` gets a teaching diagnostic pointing at `comptime`.

decisions.title: D-PERSIST-BARE1 — Persist marks a bare binding
decisions.outcome: #Persist is a marker on a bare module binding (name :: / name :=), not on comptime. Example: `#Persist counter := 0`. Keyword const remains retired in favor of comptime for former const cases; Persist does not use the comptime keyword form.
decisions.comment: #Persist is a marker on a bare module binding (name :: / name :=), not on comptime. Example: `#Persist counter := 0`. Keyword const remains retired in favor of comptime for former const cases; Persist does not use the comptime keyword form.

decisions.title: Waiting for many tasks at once
decisions.gist: Decide whether waiting for many task handles needs anything new at all.
decisions.lesson:
`tasks.spawn(() => work())` starts a task and hands back a `Task<T>` handle. `handle.wait()` blocks until that task finishes and consumes the handle. Dropping a handle without waiting warns with L1101, because the program could end first.

Eight spawns therefore leave eight handles and eight waits, one line each. That is the paste this card started from.

Jet already ships a shorter way. Inside `taskgroup g { … }`, `g.task => work()` starts a child the group owns. Every child still running when the block ends is joined before the block returns. No handle can be forgotten.

The group also takes lists. `g.all([t1, t2])` waits for all of them and fails fast, `g.race` keeps the first success, and `g.any` keeps the first finisher.

So two ways to wait for many tasks already exist. Under I8, a third has to earn its place rather than simply read a little shorter.

Decide this after D-EACH1, because one option here is written with the fenced line that ballot decides.
decisions.story: Nate's shared transaction demo pastes eight `.wait()` lines. He wants them gone. He does not want a second mechanism doing what taskgroups already do.
decisions.inWild:
// examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet, today
t1 :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
// … seven more spawns …
t1.wait()
t2.wait()
t3.wait()
t4.wait()
t5.wait()
t6.wait()
t7.wait()
t8.wait()
from_bal :: from.read(a => a.balance)
decisions.detail: Reframes the original card question. The original framing assumed multi-wait was unsolved and proposed a `tasks.join_all` helper. Structured concurrency (D-TASKSCOPE1, D-CONCCOMB1, verified 2026-06-30) already joins every child at scope exit and already offers `g.all` for a list of handles.

options.name: Use the taskgroup that already exists
options.detail: Add nothing. Rewrite the demo so the group owns the tasks and joins them at the closing brace. The eight waits disappear, and a forgotten handle becomes impossible rather than merely warned about.
options.technical: No language or library change. Rewrites `examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet` to a `taskgroup` with a `loop` body, keeping the `#Transact` point of the example intact. Golden output is unchanged. The card then closes on the fan-out reach ballots alone.

options.name: Expand the wait line
options.detail: Keep the named handles and let one fenced line stand for the eight waits, the same way the eight spawns collapse. No new library call, and the same shape works for any repeated line.
options.technical: Needs D-EACH1 to ratify line expansion. Each copy is a real `tN.wait()` statement, so each handle is consumed by its own call and L1101 stays satisfied. No list is built and no ownership mark is needed.
options.code:
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :> :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :>.wait()

options.name: Add `tasks.join_all(handles)`
options.detail: A plain named call that waits for a whole list of handles. It reads clearly, works without a group, and needs no operator knowledge at all.
options.technical: New library surface on `core.tasks`: `join_all([Task<T>]) => [T]`, waiting in list order and consuming each handle. Overlaps `g.all`, which already does this inside a group, so the docs must say plainly when each one is right.
options.code:
work :: () => transfer(from, to, 100)
handles :: /* eight spawned tasks in a list */
tasks.join_all(^handles)

options.name: Add both the fan-out wait and `join_all`
options.detail: Ship the operator form for short expressions and the named call for readability. Authors pick per site. Most convenience, and four ways in total to wait for many tasks.
options.technical: Union of B and C on top of the two group forms. Needs an explicit house style in the docs and examples, or the four forms drift apart across the codebase.
options.code:
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :>.wait()
// or
tasks.join_all(^handles)

comparisons.note: A task group awaits its children at the end of the scope. There is no separate join-all call for loose handles.
Handles are loose, so a join-all helper is genuinely needed. The standard library leaves it to a loop or a crate.
No handles at all. A wait group counts the outstanding work, which is easy to get wrong by one.
comparisons.code: wg.Add(8); go func(){ defer wg.Done(); work() }(); wg.Wait()

recommendation.why: The demo is the whole evidence for a multi-wait feature, and a taskgroup already covers it while removing the forgotten-handle failure mode. Nothing new has to be taught, tested, or kept working.

whyNot.reason: Reads well and needs no new library call, but keeps eight named handles that the group model exists to retire.
Adds a second list-shaped join beside `g.all` for the same job, which is the duplication I8 forbids.
Leaves four ways to wait for many tasks, so the codebase drifts and beginners cannot tell which one is meant.

recommendation.tradeoff: Loose handles outside a group keep their one wait per line. That is accepted: the group is the shape Jet already teaches, and it is the shape that cannot leak a task.

decisions.title: Fenced names: one written line that stands for several
decisions.gist: Decide whether one fenced line may stand in for several near-identical lines.
decisions.lesson:
Some code repeats a line only to change one name. Eight spawns that differ by a handle name. Eight waits that differ the same way. The reader learns nothing from lines two through eight.

A fence on the changing part says: write the line once, and run it once per entry.

`<: t1, t2 :> :: tasks.spawn(work)` stands for two lines, `t1 :: tasks.spawn(work)` and `t2 :: tasks.spawn(work)`. Sixteen lines become two.

This is not a list and not a loop. Nothing is gathered up and nothing is returned. The line is written out several times, top to bottom, and each copy runs in full before the next one starts.

Because each copy is a real line, everything in it runs again. Two spawns are two calls, not one call reused. That is the point for tasks, and it is worth knowing for anything expensive.

Jet already has a mark that looks related and means the opposite. `[a, b, c] :: result` splits one value into three names. A fence runs the line three times. The marks have to stay far apart in the eye.

The fan-out operator `double.[1, 2, 3]` is a third, separate thing: one expression that yields a list of results. It is untouched by this ballot.
decisions.story: Nate is looking at `examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet`. Sixteen of its twenty-nine body lines are the same spawn and the same wait, eight times each. He wants to trade a little width for that much height.
decisions.detail:
Collision review, checked against the lexer and the shipped grammar.

LEXER. `<` scans as `<<=`, `<<`, `<=`, `<`; `>` as `>>=`, `>>`, `>=`, `>`; `:` as `::`, `:=`, `:`. Adding `<:` and `:>` as longest-match digraphs takes no existing pair, because no expression or type may begin with `:`, and none may begin with `>`. No existing program changes meaning. The marks are never used between two values, so `a <: b` is not grammatical and cannot be misread as a comparison.

NEAREST NEIGHBOUR. `[a, b, c] :: result` (S76 destructuring) and `(sender, receiver) :: tasks.channel()` (D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1) both split one value across names. A fenced target runs the line once per name. This is the one real confusion risk, and it is why the round brackets Nate first sketched are the wrong marks: `<: … :>` cannot be mistaken for either.

LINE BREAKS. `Terminators.rs` inserts a synthetic `Semi` after a line-ending token, with no bracket-depth tracking. `:>` must join `suppresses_terminator` so a fence closing at the start of a line does not cut the statement. Neither mark may join `ends_statement`.

WHERE A FENCE MAY SIT. In a binding target, and anywhere inside an expression statement — an argument, a receiver, a field value. Not in an `if`, `loop`, or `switch` header, and not in an item declaration, in this pass.

DIAGNOSTICS. Empty fence; duplicate name in one fence; entry counts that disagree between two fences in one statement; a fence in a rejected position; a fenced target that would bind the same name twice. Each needs a code and a UI snapshot (I4).

SPANS. Every expanded copy must carry a span pointing at both the original line and its entry, so an error on the fifth copy names `t5` and underlines the right mark. This is the standard cost of expansion and it decides whether the feature is pleasant or hateful in practice.

FORMATTER. Emission plus a `fmt` stability test, and a wrapping rule for a fence too wide for the line.

ALREADY RATIFIED NEARBY. D-FANOUT3=C ships `tasks.join_all(handles)`, which takes a list. Fenced names are not a list, so the two answers to the demo do not compose: either eight names and eight expanded waits, or a list of handles and one join call. S75 `f.[a, b, c]` keeps building lists, and `taskgroup` keeps owning concurrent work.

options.name: The fence expands the line, and several fences step together
options.detail: A statement holding fences is written out once per entry, in order. When a line carries more than one fence, they advance together, so the first copy takes every first entry. Counts that disagree are rejected.
options.technical: Parser-level expansion into N statements before checking. Entries are ordinary expressions, or names when the fence is a binding target. Lock-step gives paired declaration for free, and a plain count-mismatch error when the columns disagree. No list is built and no type is introduced.
options.code:
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :> :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :>.wait()

// two fences advance together
<: north, south :> :: load(<: "north.json", "south.json" :>)

// and anywhere else in the line
report("Q3 results", <: north, south, east :>, Level.Summary)

options.name: The fence expands the line, one fence per statement
options.detail: The same expansion, with a hard limit of one fence per line. Nothing pairs up, so nothing can be miscounted, and the reader never has to check two columns against each other.
options.technical: Same expansion machinery, with a second fence rejected outright. Paired declaration needs two statements instead of one. Removes the count-mismatch error and the mental work behind it.
options.code:
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :> :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
<: t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7, t8 :>.wait()

// paired declaration needs the values in a list instead
paths :: ["north.json", "south.json"]
<: north, south :> :: load(paths[<: 0, 1 :>])  // rejected: second fence

options.name: Expansion, plus numbered names from a range
options.detail: Everything in option A, and a range writes the numbered names for you. Eight handles cost four characters instead of thirty-two, at both the spawn and the wait.
options.technical: `<: t1..t8 :>` in a binding target generates `t1` through `t8`. The names exist only after expansion, so a plain text search for `t5` finds nothing, and jump-to-definition must be taught to look through the range. Ranges are rejected outside binding targets.
options.code:
<: t1..t8 :> :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
<: t1..t8 :>.wait()

// searching the file for `t5` returns no match

options.name: The fence is an expression that yields a list
options.detail: The marks build one value rather than several lines. The line runs once, gathers the results, and hands back a list. Good for mapping, and it cannot declare eight names or run eight statements.
options.technical: The expression reading of the same marks: `f(<: a, b :>)` yields `[R#2]`. Needs a reach rule for how far the repeat grows, once-only evaluation of unmarked parts, and a failure law. Overlaps S75, which already builds a list from written items.

options.name: Add nothing; use what is already here
options.detail: A loop covers repeated statements, a taskgroup covers this demo without naming a handle, and the ratified `tasks.join_all` covers the waiting. Nothing new to learn, and pasted lines stay wherever a loop does not fit.
options.technical: No language change. Uses D-FANOUT3=C for the waiting half and either S75 or a loop for the spawning half. Cases that genuinely need eight distinct names keep their eight lines.
options.code:
// with a list of handles and the ratified join helper
work :: () => transfer(from, to, 100)
handles :: tasks.spawn.[work, work, work, work, work, work, work, work]
tasks.join_all(^handles)

comparisons.note: Repetition inside a macro does exactly this job, but only after you define and name a macro for it.
The preprocessor expands text before the compiler sees it. Powerful, and famous for errors that point at lines nobody wrote.
Filling a formula down writes a real row each time. Nothing is gathered up unless a later formula asks for the range.

recommendation.why: It removes the pasted lines without inventing a value, a type, or a reach rule. The line means what it looks like: itself, written out once per entry. Lock-step comes free and makes paired declaration read as one line.

whyNot.reason: Bans the paired case that reads best, and buys only the removal of one count-mismatch error the compiler can state plainly.
Saves the most typing and hides the names from search and from jump-to-definition, which is a poor trade in a language that wants tooling to be first class.
Solves a different problem. It maps values to a list, cannot declare the eight names, and overlaps the fan-out operator that already builds lists.
Right for this demo, since the ratified join helper takes a list, and wrong for the general case, because a loop cannot declare eight separate names.

recommendation.tradeoff: Expansion means the compiler reports errors on lines the author never wrote, so every copy must carry a span naming both the original line and its entry. Get that wrong and the feature is worse than the paste it replaces.

decisions.title: Names for the expert terminal surface
decisions.gist: What the expert terminal controls are called, and how many new public names ship.
decisions.lesson:
A program that starts another program normally talks through pipes. A pipe is a plain byte channel. It carries output, and nothing else.

Some programs refuse to behave on a pipe. A debugger, a shell, and a password prompt all check whether they are attached to a terminal. On a pipe they turn off colour, drop their prompt, or refuse to read a password at all.

A pseudo-terminal fixes this. It is a fake terminal supplied by the operating system. The child believes a person is typing at a real screen. Unix calls this a PTY. Windows calls it a ConPTY.

Once a terminal exists, three kinds of detail matter. Size is columns and rows, because programs redraw when it changes. Mode says whether the operating system pre-processes keys or hands them over untouched. Raw mode is the untouched kind. An editor needs it to see a single arrow key.

The third kind is the host report. Call it the capability report, or host facts for short. It answers: can this machine give me a terminal at all? Can I resize it? Can I enter raw mode? A stripped container may have no terminal. So the program asks first, then adapts, rather than failing halfway.

Host facts are not settings you choose. They are answers the machine gives back. That is why their shape may differ from the types you use when you set size and mode.

Jet already ratified the beginner half. Writing `.terminal()` asks for safe portable defaults, and that ships today. The ratified text also sketched the expert half with names like `TerminalPolicy`, `mode`, `size`, and `capabilities()`.

It did not say what those names attach to. It never named the type holding columns and rows. It never named the mode that is not raw. It never named what `capabilities()` hands back, nor the terminal handle on the started child.

Those are user-typeable names, so Jet requires the owner to ratify them before code exists. This ballot chooses how many such names ship and what shape they take.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a test runner that drives a debugger. On a pipe the debugger prints no prompt, so her runner hangs waiting for text that never comes. She wants a terminal, raw key handling, and a size she sets herself. She also runs the same suite inside a stripped container, where no terminal exists, and she needs that to fail clearly rather than hang again.
decisions.detail: Owner follow-up: "facts" means the host capability report from `capabilities()`, not a second settings object. Exploration needs a short ask-then-adapt path. Safety needs typed controls on the request side. Option D below keeps growing reports without a breaking struct change, and uses named fact keys so ordinary typos fail at compile time.

options.name: A named type for each idea
options.detail: Every concept gets its own public name. Size, mode, the support report, and the child's terminal handle are four separate named types. Each one can be searched for, jumped to, and documented on its own page. This is the largest number of new names, and the most that a reader must learn before writing expert code.
options.technical: Ships `TerminalSize.{ cols: Int, rows: Int }`, `TerminalMode` with variants `.Raw` and `.Cooked`, `TerminalReport` returned by `capabilities()`, and `TerminalSession` as the handle on `ProcessChild`. Four Syntax.rs entries with decision ids. Field names are fixed by the type, so a wrong field is a compile error naming the type.
options.code:
size :: TerminalSize.{ cols: 120, rows: 40 }

plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{ size, mode: .Cooked })

report : TerminalReport :: plan.capabilities()
print(report.resize)      // true

child :: plan.spawn()?
session : TerminalSession :: child.terminal
session.resize(TerminalSize.{ cols: 80, rows: 24 })

options.name: One policy record carries everything
options.detail: Only `TerminalPolicy` is public. Columns and rows sit directly on it as ordinary numbers, so no size type exists. The support report comes back as another `TerminalPolicy` describing what the host would actually grant. Fewer names to learn, but the same type means two different things depending on where it appears.
options.technical: `TerminalPolicy.{ cols: Int, rows: Int, mode: TerminalMode, ... }`. `capabilities()` returns `TerminalPolicy` holding granted values rather than requested ones. `ProcessChild.terminal` is typed as the child itself, with resize and mode methods hung directly on `ProcessChild`. One new type plus the mode enum.
options.code:
plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{ cols: 120, rows: 40, mode: .Cooked })

// same type coming back, now meaning "what you would get"
granted :: plan.capabilities()
if granted.cols == 0 { return Err("no terminal here") }

child :: plan.spawn()?
child.resize(80, 24)

options.name: Borrow the shapes Core already has
options.detail: Jet already ships types for a width-and-height pair and for reporting what a host supports. This option reuses them instead of minting terminal-only twins. Only the mode needs a new name. The smallest addition to the language, at the cost of types whose names never say the word terminal.
options.technical: Size reuses Core's existing two-field extent type; `capabilities()` reuses the existing host-facts record used elsewhere in Core, keyed by fact name. `ProcessChild.terminal` is an existing stream handle. One new public name, `TerminalMode`. Requires an audit that the reused types are a genuine fit and not a coincidence of shape.
options.code:
plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{ size: Extent.{ 120, 40 }, mode: .Cooked })

report :: plan.capabilities()          // the same record kind used by core.os
if !report.has("terminal") { return Err("no terminal here") }

child :: plan.spawn()?
child.terminal.resize(Extent.{ 80, 24 })

options.name: Typed controls, keyed host report with named facts
options.detail: The things you set are named types, because a wrong field should fail while writing. The things you read back are a host report that can grow. Known facts use named keys such as `TerminalFact.terminal`, so a typo on a known fact fails to compile. Preview facts may use a string form with a nearest-key diagnostic. This keeps strong typing on everyday paths and still lets a new host answer appear without a breaking type change.
options.technical: Ships `TerminalSize`, `TerminalMode`, `TerminalSession`, and `TerminalFact` key constants. `capabilities()` returns a keyed report. `report.has(TerminalFact.resize)` is compile-checked. `report.has("preview_x")` stays open for growth. Documented keys get Syntax.rs entries. String typos suggest the nearest known key.

options.name: Typed stable report plus open preview bag
options.detail: Controls stay named types. The host report also has typed fields for the stable answers every backend must give today: terminal present, resize, raw mode. A separate preview bag holds experimental answers. Everyday exploration uses field access with full type checking. New stable fields still need a release that extends the public type.
options.technical: `TerminalReport.{ terminal: Bool, resize: Bool, raw: Bool, preview: FactBag }`. Stable fields are required. Preview keys are strings with nearest-key diagnostics. More names than D, and each new stable fact is a type change.
options.code:
plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{
    size: TerminalSize.{ cols: 120, rows: 40 },
    mode: .Cooked
  })

report :: plan.capabilities()
if !report.terminal { return Err("no terminal here") }
print(report.resize)
print(report.preview.has("future_fact"))

child :: plan.spawn()?
child.terminal.resize(TerminalSize.{ cols: 80, rows: 24 })

comparisons.note: The standard library exposes raw file descriptors and leaves naming to the caller. Size is an unnamed four-number packed struct. Readers must know the layout by heart.
comparisons.code:
import pty, struct, fcntl, termios
pid, fd = pty.fork()
fcntl.ioctl(fd, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, struct.pack("HHHH", 40, 120, 0, 0))

comparisons.note: portable-pty names every concept, including a size struct with named fields and pixel dimensions most callers ignore.
node-pty takes a plain options object. Columns and rows are loose fields, and a misspelled key silently falls back to a default.
comparisons.code:
const p = pty.spawn("lldb", [app], { cols: 120, rows: 40 });
p.resize(80, 24);

comparisons.note: creack/pty names the size type but keeps mode as raw operating-system flags, so callers reach for a second package to turn raw mode on.

recommendation.why: D keeps request-side mistakes compile-time hard, keeps ask-then-adapt exploration short, and lets host answers grow without breaking everyday code. Named fact keys remove the old string-typo trap on the known set.

whyNot.reason: A fixed report type makes every new host answer a breaking change to a public type. Callers still read answers by name rather than destructure them.
One type meaning both the request and the grant reads wrong at the call site. Using `granted.cols == 0` as "no terminal" is a sentinel, which Jet avoids elsewhere.
Reuse is right only when the shapes mean the same thing. A terminal size is characters, not pixels or generic extent.
E wins on typed everyday fields, but every new stable host answer becomes a public type change. D gives the same safety on known facts through named keys without that churn.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preview facts still use strings, so a typo there reads as absent. That is limited to experimental keys. Known keys stay named constants. Docs and a nearest-key diagnostic cover the preview path.

decisions.title: Names for the process authority surface
decisions.gist: What the authority, plan, and receipt types are called, and how the CLI spells the same grants.
decisions.lesson:
An agent or a Jet program can start another program. That child may read files, talk on the network, or use secrets. Authority is the exact set of rights the child is allowed to use.

Jet already chose the model. Authority sits on the ordinary process API. Beginners get one safe workspace default. Experts widen exact grants. A dry-run plan shows what would happen. A final receipt records what did happen.

The model ballot sketched names such as `ProcessAuthority`, `Host`, `SecretRef`, `.under(policy)`, `.plan()`, and `jet self exec --workspace`. It did not lock the full public name set.

It never named the plan type, the receipt type, or the grant builders as Syntax-backed spellings. It never said whether network grants take a `Host` type or plain strings. It never fixed how the CLI mirrors the typed API.

Those are user-typeable names and flags. This ballot chooses the public spelling before code lands.
decisions.story: Sam lets an agent run tests in a workspace. Later a release job grants one registry host and one signing key by name. Sam wants the typed API and the CLI to use the same words, so a reviewed plan matches the command that ships.
decisions.detail: Follow-on to D-AGENT-EXEC1=A, same pattern as D-PROCESS-SESSION2 after D-PROCESS-SESSION1. Mechanism is fixed. This ballot locks names only.

options.name: Named types for authority, plan, receipt, host, and secret
options.detail: Every major idea gets its own public name. `ProcessAuthority` holds grants. `ProcessPlan` and `ProcessReceipt` are distinct types. Network and secret grants use `Host` and `SecretRef`. The CLI mirrors the same words as flags. Readers can jump to each type. This is the largest name set.
options.technical: Ships `ProcessAuthority`, `ProcessPlan`, `ProcessReceipt`, `Host`, and `SecretRef` with Syntax.rs decision ids where user-typeable. `.under`, `.plan`, `.run` stay methods. CLI: `--workspace`, `--write`, `--network`, `--secret`, `--executable`, `--limits`.
options.code:
policy :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network([Host.https("registry.example.com")])
  .secret([SecretRef.signing("release")])

plan : ProcessPlan :: process.cmd(args).under(policy).plan()
receipt : ProcessReceipt :: process.cmd(args).under(policy).run()?

// jet self exec --workspace . --write dist \
//   --network https://registry.example.com -- cargo test

options.name: Authority type only; plan and receipt stay plain data
options.detail: `ProcessAuthority` is the one new named type. Plan and receipt are ordinary records or strings you print. Hosts and secrets are plain strings on the grant methods. Fewer names to learn. Weaker jump-to-definition on plan and receipt fields.
options.technical: One Syntax-backed type: `ProcessAuthority`. `.plan()` returns a structured but unnamed record. `.run()` returns a receipt record. CLI flags still mirror grant verbs.
options.code:
policy :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network(["https://registry.example.com"])

print(process.cmd(args).under(policy).plan())
receipt :: process.cmd(args).under(policy).run()?
print(receipt.digest)

// jet self exec --workspace . --write dist -- cargo test

options.name: Reuse existing process config names
options.detail: Fold grants into types Jet already has for process limits and environment. No `ProcessAuthority` name. Experts extend the existing process config record. Smallest addition, but authority and ordinary config blur together at the call site.
options.technical: Extend current `ProcessSpec` config/limits records with grant fields. No new authority type. CLI keeps today's process flags plus grant flags without a parallel type vocabulary.
options.code:
child :: process.cmd(args)
  .limits(limits)
  .grants(.{ workspace: ".", write: ["dist"] })
  .spawn()?

// no ProcessAuthority in source

options.name: Typed authority; stringly CLI
options.detail: The Jet API gets the full named types from option A. The CLI stays a thin stringly wrapper with fewer curated flags. Experts script the typed API for exact grants. Beginners still get `--workspace`. The two surfaces can drift unless docs bind them.
options.technical: `ProcessAuthority`, `ProcessPlan`, `ProcessReceipt`, `Host`, `SecretRef` in Jet. CLI guarantees only `--workspace` parity; other grants documented as Jet-first.

comparisons.note: Permissions use explicit allow flags. There is no separate plan type; denial is runtime.
CLI flags name each grant. There is no typed twin inside ordinary application code.
Config and credentials use several file formats. Authority is not one typed process object.
comparisons.code: # cargo config and credential providers are separate surfaces

recommendation.why: A makes the typed API and the CLI speak the same words. Plan and receipt stay searchable types, which matters when agents review a dry-run before launch.

whyNot.reason: Plain strings for hosts and secrets lose checked construction, and unnamed plan or receipt types hide fields from ordinary navigation.
Mixing authority with ordinary process config hides the trust boundary the feature exists to show.
A stringly CLI breaks the ratified API and CLI parity rule from D-AGENT-EXEC1.

recommendation.tradeoff: More public names ship on day one. The workspace constructor still hides that list from beginner call sites.

decisions.title: How a pinned type declares field projection
decisions.gist: How library authors mark which fields stay pinned when you pin the whole value.
decisions.lesson:
Some values must not move in memory once they become address-sensitive. A pin is Jet's promise that safe code will not move or replace that storage while the pin is live.

Jet already chose the contract. You write `mem.pin(&place)` and get a `Pin<T>`. Safe callers can read or edit through the pin. They cannot move the place.

Real libraries often need a field, not only the whole value. An intrusive list node may pin the node and still hand out a pinned link field. That is projection: reaching a field without ending the no-move promise.

The model ballot said projection is declared by the type implementation. It did not say how authors write that declaration. It did not say whether every field projects, or only marked fields, or none until unsafe code builds a field pin.

This ballot chooses the author-facing spelling for safe field projection under `Pin`.
decisions.story: Noah builds a zero-allocation event queue. Each node is pinned in caller storage. The queue needs a pinned `next` field view without letting callers move the node. He needs one clear way to mark that field in the type.
decisions.detail: Follow-on to D-PIN1=A. `Pin` and `mem.pin` stay. This ballot only locks projection declaration.

options.name: Mark pin-projected fields on the type
options.detail: Authors mark each field that may be reached as `Pin`. Unmarked fields are not safely reachable through a pin, or are reachable only as ordinary views when the rules allow. The marks make the contract visible in the type. Readers see which links are address-sensitive.
options.technical: Field attribute or field-level pin marker registered in Syntax.rs under this decision. Sema allows `Pin` projection only to marked structural fields. Unmarked field access through `Pin` is a typed error with a fix that names the mark.

options.name: Project every field by default
options.detail: Once a value is pinned, every field is reachable under the same no-move promise. Authors write no marks. Easy to start. Easy to project a field that should never have been address-sensitive, unless a second opt-out mark exists.
options.technical: Default structural projection for all fields of a pinned place. Optional `#UnpinField` or similar opt-out if needed. Larger safe surface; libraries must audit every field.
options.code:
struct Node {
  next: PinLink<Node>?,
  payload: Event
}

pinned :: mem.pin(&node)
link :: pinned.next       // ok
data :: pinned.payload    // also ok by default

options.name: No safe field projection
options.detail: Safe code pins only whole values. Field-level pins stay inside `#Unsafe` constructors that libraries expose as safe APIs. The beginner pin surface stays tiny. Intrusive structures need more unsafe inside the library boundary.
options.technical: Sema rejects field access that would reborrow `Pin<T>` as `Pin<Field>`. Libraries mint field pins only in audited `#Unsafe` blocks and return safe handles.

options.name: Projection methods written by the author
options.detail: No field marks and no default projection. Authors implement methods such as `fn next(self: Pin<Node>) -> Pin<Link>`. Control is exact. Every pinned structure needs boilerplate methods, and forgotten methods block callers.
options.technical: Sema treats projection as ordinary methods on `Pin<T>`. No structural field sugar through `Pin`. Method return types carry pin provenance.

comparisons.note: pin-project macros generate safe projections from field marks. Manual projection is unsafe.
comparisons.code:
#[pin_project]
struct Node { #[pin] next: Link, payload: Event }

comparisons.note: No standard pin projection. Libraries keep addresses stable by convention and documentation.
comparisons.code: auto* next = &node.next; // caller must not move node

recommendation.why: A keeps whole-value `mem.pin` simple and makes address-sensitive fields visible on the type. Callers get safe field pins without a second projection style.

whyNot.reason: Default projection treats every field as address-sensitive and hides the real risk surface.
It pushes routine intrusive patterns back into unsafe code that Pin exists to wrap once.
Method-only projection repeats the same boilerplate on every type and still needs a convention for which methods are structural.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must mark projected fields. That is accepted because unmarked fields fail closed with a clear diagnostic.

decisions.title: Names for Shared guards and conditions
decisions.gist: What the long-lived Shared lock token and wait object are called, and how you build them.
decisions.lesson:
Shared values use a lock so many tasks can take turns. The beginner path locks for one short closure. The lock releases when the closure ends.

Some protocols need the lock across several helper calls. A guard is the owned token that means the lock is still held. When the guard is dropped, the lock releases.

Some protocols also wait until a condition becomes true. One example is "the queue is not full." A correct wait must release the lock, sleep, wake, and take the lock again. It must not miss the signal.

Jet already chose expert guards and a condition object. Short closures stay the default. The model ballot sketched `guard_edit`, `guard.wait(...)`, and `Condition` with `notify_one`.

It did not lock whether the guard type is named. It did not lock where `Condition` lives or how you construct one. It did not lock whether wait hangs on the guard, on the condition, or on Shared.

Those names decide what beginners never see and what experts type every day.
decisions.story: Sam builds a bounded work queue on `Shared`. Producers must wait while the queue is full. Sam wants one spelling he can teach in a short expert note, without inventing a second lock family.
decisions.inWild:
queue :: Shared.new(WorkQueue.new())
space_ready :: /* how do you build the wait object? */

guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

// open: Condition.new vs Shared.condition vs other
// open: is `guard` a named SharedGuard type?
decisions.detail: Follow-on to D-SHAREDGUARD1=A. Beginner `read`/`edit` stay unchanged. This ballot locks expert names and constructors.

options.name: Named SharedGuard plus Condition.new
options.detail: `guard_read` and `guard_edit` return a named `SharedGuard`. Waiting uses a separate `Condition` you construct with `Condition.new()`. Wait is a method on the guard. Notify methods sit on the condition. The roles stay obvious: guard holds the lock, condition wakes waiters.
options.technical: Public types `SharedGuard` and `Condition`. `guard.wait(cond, pred)` atomically releases and reacquires. `Condition.notify_one` / `notify_all`. Syntax.rs entries for both type names.
options.code:
space_ready :: Condition.new()
guard : SharedGuard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

options.name: Condition is created from Shared
options.detail: Guards stay as today. You build a condition from the shared value, such as `queue.condition()`, so the wait object is visibly tied to that lock. Fewer free-floating conditions. Harder to share one condition across several Shared values on purpose.
options.technical: `Shared.condition()` returns `Condition` bound to that Shared's lock identity. Guard type may stay unnamed. Wait remains on the guard or on Shared with a guard argument.
options.code:
space_ready :: queue.condition()
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

options.name: No Condition type; wait methods on Shared
options.detail: Do not ship a `Condition` name. Experts call `guard.wait_until(pred)`. Notification uses `queue.notify_one()`. One fewer type. Wait and notify must still agree on an internal wait queue.
options.technical: Wait queues live inside Shared. APIs: `guard.wait_until(pred)` and `Shared.notify_one` / `notify_all`. No public `Condition` type.
options.code:
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait_until(q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
queue.notify_one()

options.name: Match Rust MutexGuard and Condvar names
options.detail: Use familiar systems names: mutex-style guards and `Condvar`. Experts from Rust feel at home. Jet would then teach two vocabularies: Shared for beginners and Mutex or Condvar words for experts.
options.technical: Alias or rename expert surface toward `Condvar` and guard names that read like mutex guards, while beginner methods stay `read`/`edit` on Shared.
options.code:
space_ready :: Condvar.new()
guard :: queue.lock_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
space_ready.notify_one()

comparisons.note: Mutex guards are named. Condvar is a separate type. Wait takes the guard and returns it.
comparisons.code: let mut g = cv.wait_while(g, |q| q.len() == limit)?;

comparisons.note: sync.Cond binds to a locker. Notify methods sit on Cond.
threading.Condition wraps a lock and owns wait/notify.
comparisons.code:
with cond:
    while full:
        cond.wait()
    cond.notify()

recommendation.why: A keeps Shared as the one beginner lock type, gives experts a named guard they can pass, and keeps Condition as the ordinary wait object without renaming the whole model after Mutex.

whyNot.reason: Binding Condition construction to one Shared value blocks common multi-lock wake patterns without adding power for the common queue case.
Hiding Condition inside Shared makes notify targets less explicit and harder to share across related structures.
Rust Mutex/Condvar words split the teaching surface after Jet already chose Shared as the public name.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two expert type names ship beside Shared. Short closures still hide them from beginners.

decisions.title: Preferred multi-line branch spelling
decisions.gist: Multi-line branches should prefer arm tables over braced if and else.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has one branch keyword: if. A branch chooses which arm runs.

An arm table lists heads and bodies. The first true or matching head wins. You write if { head -> body } or if subject == { head -> body }.

A classic braced form looks like other C-family languages: if cond { … } else { … }. It means the same two-arm choice.

This decision picks the house style for multi-line code. It does not add a second keyword.
decisions.story: Maya lists directory entries. She writes a multi-line if and else with braces. She wants the same shape the docs teach for three or more arms.

options.name: Arm table is the house style
options.detail: Docs, examples, and lints push arm tables for multi-line branches. Braced classic stays legal but secondary.

options.name: Both forms stay equal
options.detail: No preference lint. Braced classic and arm tables stay first-class forever.

options.name: Braced classic stays the beginner default
options.detail: Arm tables are taught as advanced. Beginner docs keep braced if and else.

comparisons.note: if/else and match are different keywords.
One keyword; arm tables are the multi-branch model.

recommendation.why: One ontology for two or more arms. Matches S68 and the dir_entry intent.

whyNot.reason: Equal forms hide which shape Jet wants people to learn.
Keeps a second beginner costume for the same mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: Beginners learn arrow arms earlier when a branch spans lines.

decisions.title: One-line short if stays first-class
decisions.gist: When a two-arm branch fits one line, keep the short if form.
decisions.lesson:
A short effect form writes the condition and the statement on one line. Example: if n > 5 print("big") else print("small").

A short value form uses arrows on one line. Example: m :: if a > b -> a else -> b.

Arm tables stay available. This decision only sets when the short form needs no lint.
decisions.story: Leo clamps a score in one line. He does not want a four-line table for a tiny choice.

options.name: One-line forms stay preferred when they fit
options.detail: No lint when the whole branch is one simple source line.
options.code: if n > 5 print("big") else print("small")

options.name: Always prefer arm tables
options.detail: Even tiny two-arm choices should use if { … }.

options.name: Width-based only
options.detail: Lint and fmt use column width, not author line breaks.
options.code: if n > 5 print("big") else print("small")

comparisons.note: One-line guards stay common for tiny branches.

recommendation.why: Keeps short scripts dense. Arm tables cover multi-line clarity.

whyNot.reason: Forces ceremony on the smallest branches.
Fights author line breaks already used by the formatter law.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings remain. The lint must check layout, not only AST shape.

decisions.title: Fate of else if chains
decisions.gist: Decide whether else if stays quiet, gets a lint, or retires.
decisions.lesson:
else if chains another test after a failed if. Many languages teach this as the main multi-test form.

Jet already has ordered arm tables for the same job. S68 says else if stays legal, but docs should not teach it as the normal form.

This decision picks how hard the tools push people off else if.
decisions.story: Priya ports a status classifier with four else if arms. She wants to know if Jet will warn or break that code.

options.name: Keep legal; lint toward arm table
options.detail: Soft warning. Code still runs. Fix points at the arm-table spelling.

options.name: Keep legal; no lint
options.detail: Only docs discourage else if. Tools stay silent.

options.name: Retire with a migration diagnostic
options.detail: else if becomes an error with a clear fix to an arm table.
options.code: Error: use an arm table instead of else if

comparisons.note: else if remains legal; rarely prefer it.

recommendation.why: Finishes S68 teaching without a hard break for existing code.

whyNot.reason: Leaves a second multi-test costume without tool pressure.
Breaks ports and old examples in one step.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dual spellings remain until codebases migrate.

decisions.title: Prefer-arm-table lint triggers
decisions.gist: Pick exact warning cases for braced if and else if.
decisions.lesson:
A lint warns. It does not stop the build by default.

This lint teaches the preferred branch spelling. It must skip forms we still want, such as a one-line short if.

A fixit can rewrite code later. That is a separate choice from when to warn.
decisions.story: Chris runs jet check on an old module full of braced if and else. He needs a predictable warning rule, not surprise rewrites.

options.name: Warn multi-line braced if/else and any else if
options.detail: Skip one-line adjacent and one-line value forms. Warn only.
options.code: Warning: prefer if { ready -> start() else -> wait() }

options.name: Warn only else if chains
options.detail: Two-arm braced if and else stay quiet.
options.code: Warning only when else if appears

options.name: Warn plus machine fixit
options.detail: Same triggers as A, and tools can rewrite to an arm table.
options.code: Warning + autofix to if { … }

comparisons.note: Style lint with snapshot tests.
comparisons.code: prefer += instead of repeating the left side

recommendation.why: Matches the preferred multi-line house style without shipping rewrite risk first.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the common two-arm braced form untaught.
Fixit can wait until the warn rule is stable.

recommendation.tradeoff: Old examples may warn until updated.

decisions.title: Value if follows the same preference law
decisions.gist: Value branches use the same one-line versus arm-table preference.
decisions.lesson:
An effect if runs statements. A value if yields a value.

Both are the same branch mechanism. Only the result differs.

This decision asks whether value forms share the house style with effect forms.
decisions.story: Ana picks a display string with a value if. She wants one rule, not a special style for expressions.

options.name: Same preference matrix for effect and value
options.detail: One teaching story. One-line value forms stay fine when they fit.

options.name: Value braced arrows stay freer
options.detail: Expression style can keep braced value branches without the same lint.

options.name: Value multi-arm must use tables
options.detail: Stricter than effect form for multi-arm values.

recommendation.why: Effect versus value is only whether the branch yields. The ontology stays one.

whyNot.reason: Splits house style by expression versus statement.
Adds a stricter costume without a new meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some value braces in examples may get the same lint.

decisions.title: May formatter rewrite branch shape?
decisions.gist: Decide whether jet fmt may turn braced if into an arm table.
decisions.lesson:
The formatter reprints code in one style. Jet law keeps author intent for many shapes. It does not treat format as a full rewrite engine.

Changing braced if into an arm table changes the written mechanism costume. A lint or fixit can do that on purpose.

This decision sets the formatter boundary for branches only.
decisions.story: Sam hits save and expects spaces and indents to settle. Sam does not want silent rewrites of every if into a table.

options.name: Fmt never changes mechanism; lint only
options.detail: Formatter keeps braced if as braced if. Preference stays in lint and docs.
options.code: jet fmt  # still braced if/else

options.name: Fmt may rewrite when the lint would fire
options.detail: Lossless rewrites to arm tables become part of format.
options.code: jet fmt  # becomes if { ready -> start() else -> wait() }

options.name: Fmt only normalizes within one shape
options.detail: Spaces, arrows, and indent settle. No If to table rewrite. Matches today.

comparisons.note: Author intent preserved; not AST-canonical.

recommendation.why: Keeps format honest. Shape change belongs to lint or fixit, not silent save.

whyNot.reason: Almost the same as C; C also locks within-shape cleanup.
Turns format into a migrator and fights author-intent law.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preferred style still needs lint or manual edits.

decisions.title: Example corpus after the prefer lint
decisions.gist: Choose how hard examples must match the new branch house style.
decisions.lesson:
Jet examples are executable specs. Readers copy them.

After a prefer lint lands, the corpus can move with it, stay grandfathered, or silence the lint in-tree.

This decision sets that bar for feature examples.
decisions.story: The docs owner opens basics examples after the lint ships. They need a clear pass or allow-list rule.
decisions.inWild:
examples/features/basics/if_universal.jet
examples/features/io/dir_entry.jet

options.name: All feature examples must pass the lint
options.detail: Strong teaching. Corpus matches house style.
options.code: examples/** pass prefer-arm-table lint

options.name: Only branch basics and new code
options.detail: Softer landing. Legacy examples can wait.
options.code: update if_universal + new files first

options.name: No example churn; allow in tree
options.detail: Lint exists for users; repo examples may warn or allow.
options.code: allow(prefer_arm_table) in examples

recommendation.why: Examples teach the ontology. They should show the preferred form.

whyNot.reason: Leaves mixed costumes in the feature corpus.
Undercuts the lint as a teaching tool.

recommendation.tradeoff: One-time example pass across touched features.

decisions.title: One semantic IR for branches
decisions.gist: Choose whether classic if stays a separate AST node or desugars into arm-table IR.
decisions.lesson:
Users type if. Inside the compiler, Jet today has two shapes. Stmt::If is a nested then and else tree. Stmt::Switch is a flat arm list used for tables.

Both mean ordered choice. Dual nodes force duplicate walks in sema, ownership, and codegen helpers.

This decision picks the internal law. User spelling can still include short if forms.
decisions.story: A codegen engineer adds a new branch optimization. They must special-case If and Switch or forget one path.

options.name: Keep dual AST; share helpers
options.detail: Least churn. Document that both mean one mechanism.
options.technical: Stmt::If and Stmt::Switch remain. Shared lower/check helpers.
options.code:
check_if(…)
check_switch(…)

options.name: Early-desugar classic if into arm-table IR
options.detail: Parser may build If. A desugar pass makes one arm-table IR for sema and codegen.
options.technical: Classic two-arm becomes arms + optional else. Spans preserved for diagnostics.
options.code:
if ready start() else wait()
# IR: arms [ready->start, else->wait]

options.name: Single AST node from the parser
options.detail: Parser always builds the arm-table node. One IR from parse through sema and codegen. No desugar pass to maintain. Same runtime forms as B once lowering runs. Up-front cost is parser, formatter, and IDE churn.
options.technical: Stmt::If goes away or becomes sugar only at parse. Spans attach to arms directly. Classic one-line if still parses; it builds the same arm list.

recommendation.why: You asked to spend more up front for a better long-term path. Option C removes a permanent dual-shape seam. Runtime speed still comes from the ratified classifier on D-BRANCH-CODEGEN1, not from parse shape.

whyNot.reason: Keeps two IR shapes forever. Every new branch opt can miss one path.
Reaches the same middle-end IR, but leaves a desugar layer that can drift from the parser over time.

recommendation.tradeoff: Larger first parser and formatter pass. No extra runtime win versus a correct B desugar.

decisions.title: Branch lowering classifier and machine forms
decisions.gist: Lock how Jet picks select, match, tables, or compare chains for each arm table.
decisions.lesson:
On modern optimizers, source if and match often become the same machine code for equality cases. Timing wins come from the right shape: branchless select, data table, jump table, or ordered compares.

A classifier labels each arm table. Then codegen emits the best safe form.

Classes include two-way bool, enum patterns, dense ints, sparse ints, ordered predicates, and mixed heads.
decisions.story: Remy ships a hot protocol demux. Random dense codes want a table. A biased Ok path wants a predicted compare. One blunt always-match rule loses on the biased path.

options.name: Codify today only
options.detail: Enum and Result or Option pattern tables become match. Everything else stays an if-chain.
options.technical: Matches current lower_enum_match / fallible / guard_switch paths.
options.code:
enum table -> Rust match
bool table -> if/else chain

options.name: Full classifier; best form per class
options.detail: Bool2 may select. Enum uses match. Dense ints use data or jump tables. Sparse uses search or hash. Ordered stays compares. Mixed falls back safely. Bind subject once. Avoid needless clone.
options.technical: Classes: C-BOOL2, C-ENUM, C-DENSE-INT, C-SPARSE-INT, C-ORDERED, C-MIXED. PGO weights later.
options.code:
dense value arms -> static table load
ordered guards -> compare chain
enum payloads -> match

options.name: Always if-chain
options.detail: Simplest codegen. Never rely on match or tables.
options.code: all branches -> if/else if

comparisons.note: Dense equality often becomes a table load; jump tables can lose when one arm dominates.
match helps the backend see a switch; if chains often optimize to the same code.

recommendation.why: This is the path to beat careful C and Rust on dispatch: classify, then emit the winning machine form.

whyNot.reason: Leaves dense int and select wins on the table.
Gives up match and table shapes on purpose.

recommendation.tradeoff: More lowering cases to test and bench. Syntax stays one if.

decisions.title: One spelling for domain text and byte patterns
decisions.gist: How writers mark SQL, HTML, shell commands, and byte patterns so each recipe stays explicit.
decisions.lesson:
Some quoted text is not a normal string. It is a recipe in another language.

SQL recipes become checked queries. HTML recipes escape inserts. Shell recipes become argv lists. Byte recipes match bit fields in a buffer.

A typed head names the language. The body is the recipe. Example: SQL.{"select id={id}"} builds a query. [U8].{"{len:U16be}{rest:...}"} matches bytes.

Plain quotes alone stay for ordinary String values and for text-match convenience. Runtime String values still cannot fill a SQL, HTML, or Sh slot.

The choice is whether Jet also keeps short prefixes and silent rewrites, or whether the typed head is the only spelling.
decisions.story: Nate reviews safety examples and sees sql"…", html"…", Sh.{"…"}, and b"…" side by side. He wants one intentional shape so a typo cannot pick the wrong language.

options.name: Typed head only
options.detail: Domain text uses only Type.{"…"} plus Type.raw. Byte patterns use only [U8].{"…"}. Kill sql"/html"/sh" and silent rewrite of bare quotes into those types. Keep plain quotes for String and for text-pattern convenience. Optional String.{"…"} matches the same text pattern.
options.technical: Amends D-TYPEDTEXT1/2 and D-BINPAT1. Supersedes D-LITERAL-PREFIX1 prefix surface. Sema elaborates typed-text only from typed-literal heads. Bare String into SQL/HTML/Sh remains E0149. Lexer BinStr and hardcoded typed-text prefixes retire.

options.name: Typed head plus silent expected-type rewrite
options.detail: Keep Type.{"…"} as the clear form. Also let a bare quote elaborate when the slot already expects SQL, HTML, or Sh. Kill only the lowercase prefixes. Call sites stay shorter when a parameter is already typed.
options.technical: Keeps D-TYPEDTEXT1 expected-type path. Removes D-TYPEDTEXT2 prefixes. Byte patterns still move to [U8].{"…"}.

options.name: Keep prefixes as sugar
options.detail: Document Type.{"…"} as preferred, but keep sql"/html"/sh" and silent rewrite. Clean example drift only. Byte patterns stay b"…" or switch alone.
options.technical: Status quo for typed text. Optional D-BINPAT1 spelling change only.
options.code:
q :: sql"select * from t where id = {id}" page :: html"

{name}

" cmd :: sh"echo {name}"

options.name: Type-owned prefixes via derive
options.detail: Honor D-LITERAL-PREFIX1. Libraries own prefixes like sql" through a derive contract. Typed heads remain available. Hardcoded parser list goes away by becoming type-owned.
options.technical: Implements ratified D-LITERAL-PREFIX1=A. Opposite of removing prefixes.

comparisons.note: b"…" builds a byte string value. Jet's old b"…" was a pattern mode, not a value.
s"…", f"…", and raw"…" are prefix languages. Jet is choosing typed heads instead of growing that prefix set.
comparisons.code: val q = sql"select * from t where id = $id"

comparisons.note: Sh examples already prefer Sh.{"…"}. SQL/HTML examples still show prefixes. That split is the inconsistency this ballot closes.

recommendation.why: One head names one language. Writers see the type at the recipe. Typos and silent quote rewrites cannot pick SQL, HTML, Sh, or byte-match by accident.

whyNot.reason: Bare quotes at typed call sites still look like String while meaning another language.
Leaves the three spellings and the sql"/b" visual family that caused the review.
Expands prefixes after the owner asked for fewer hidden spellings and more Type.{"…"}.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bindings and untyped slots must write the typed head. Call sites lose bare-quote sugar into SQL, HTML, and Sh.

decisions.title: Code-as-argument spelling: explicit () => blocks
decisions.gist: How a caller passes a multiline code block into a function argument.
decisions.lesson:
A function can take another function as an input. The caller often writes that input at the call site as a short block of code.

The clear spelling is an explicit lambda inside the call's parentheses: `twice(() => { … })`. The block may hold many statements. You can pass several such lambdas in one call, mixed with ordinary values.

An older sugar (D-TRAILBLOCK1) let a bare `{ … }` trail after the call, or even after a bare name with no parentheses. That form only covers one final zero-arg slot, and `twice { … }` can look like a keyword instead of a call.

This decision picks the spelling Jet keeps.
decisions.story: Nate wants helpers like `twice` to take a multiline body as a normal argument. The call must read as a function call. He wrote the shape he wants: `twice(() => { print("HI"); print("Hello") })` with each statement on its own line.

options.name: Require () => inside the call; drop trailing { } sugar
options.detail: Code arguments use `() => { … }` inside the parentheses. Multiline bodies are normal. Multiple code arguments are ordinary comma-separated args. Trailing bare `{ }` after a call is rejected with a teaching fix that shows the `() =>` form.
options.technical: Amend D-TRAILBLOCK1: remove trailing-block attach in postfix parse/format. Keep zero-param `() =>` lambdas as CallArg values. Retarget E0334/E0335 to teach `callee(() => { … })`. Migrate examples and UI goldens.

options.name: Keep trailing sugar only after visible ()
options.detail: Still allow `name() { … }` and `name(args) { … }` for one final block. Reject bare `name { … }`. Teach `() =>` for multi-block and non-final callbacks.
options.technical: Narrow D-TRAILBLOCK1: trailing block requires a prior `()` argument list. Formatter never emits bare `name { … }`.

options.name: Keep D-TRAILBLOCK1 unchanged
options.detail: Bare `twice { … }` stays legal. Multi-block APIs already use `() =>` inside parentheses. Docs change only.
options.technical: No parser change.

options.name: Allow bare { } inside parentheses as a lambda
options.detail: Treat `{ … }` in value position as a zero-arg lambda so `f({ … }, { … })` works without `() =>`. Quieter, more ambiguous.
options.technical: New primary/block-literal form; resolve vs statement blocks and struct literals.

comparisons.note: Arrow functions are ordinary values inside call parentheses, including multiline bodies.
Trailing closure exists for one final block; multiple closures use the parenthesized form.

recommendation.why: A matches the owner's stated shape: a normal call with an explicit `() =>` multiline body. It stays honest when more than one code argument is needed, and it stops helpers from reading like keywords.

whyNot.reason: Keeping trailing sugar still special-cases one final block and splits the teaching story from the owner's required `() =>` form.
Bare `twice { … }` is the keyword look the owner rejected.
Bare `{ }` as a value hides that the argument is a function, and `() =>` already gives the clear multiline form.

recommendation.tradeoff: One-block UI calls get a little longer (`button("Save", () => { … })` instead of `button("Save") { … }`). That cost buys one spelling for every code argument.

decisions.title: Default auto-derive with reject and override?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet turns useful built-in traits on by default, and how experts turn them off or replace them.
decisions.lesson:
A derive is a compiler-written implementation of a common trait for a type.

Traits like Printable, Equatable, and Debug describe everyday behavior: show a value, compare two values, or dump a value for debugging. For many structs and enums, the safe default is obvious: walk the fields and do the field-wise thing.

Jet already auto-derives some of these when every field qualifies, and a hand-written impl can replace that default. Less clear: can users reject automatic behavior for a type or package? Should auto-derive be the normal beginner path for every useful built-in trait that qualifies?

This decision picks the default policy and the expert escape hatches. One mechanism should cover magic for beginners, reject for control, and override for custom behavior.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game save format. Most types should print and compare for free. One secret type must not auto-print. Another needs a custom Debug layout. Sam wants defaults on, with clear reject and override paths — not a wall of markers on every type.

options.name: Default-on for qualifying types; reject + override
options.detail: Whenever fields qualify, Jet auto-derives the useful built-in traits. Experts reject auto-derive for a type or package, or override with a hand impl. Beginners write almost nothing.
options.technical: Extend S55 / D-MARK-DEBUG1: keep silent auto for Printable/Equatable/Debug (and any later ratified auto family) when fields qualify. Add an explicit reject spelling (type or package scope). Hand impl remains the override. Reject beats auto; override beats both for that trait.

options.name: Keep today's S55: auto when fields qualify; override only
options.detail: No new reject surface. Auto-derive stays for Printable, Equatable, and Debug when fields qualify. Hand impl still overrides. Types that must opt out use awkward workarounds.
options.technical: No law change beyond clarifying docs. No #NoAuto / package deny. Secret-like types rely on #Redact, non-qualifying fields, or never printing.

options.name: Opt-in markers for every derive
options.detail: Nothing auto-derives. Each type lists the traits it wants. Experts get full visibility. Beginners pay ceremony on almost every type.
options.technical: Reverse S55 / D-MARK-DEBUG1 auto policy. Restore explicit derive markers for Printable/Equatable/Debug. Hand impl still allowed.
options.code:
#Printable
#Equatable
#Debug
struct Player {
    name: String
    score: Int
}

options.name: Package flag off by default; per-type opt-in
options.detail: A package or build flag disables auto-derive globally. Types then opt in one by one. Good for strict codebases; bad for the common beginner package.
options.technical: Introduce package/project auto-derive policy defaulting to off or requiring an enable flag. Per-type markers restore derives. Conflicts with beginner-default philosophy unless the flag defaults on.

options.name: Default-on, package kill-switch, type reject, type override
options.detail: Same beginner default as A, plus a package-level switch that turns auto-derive off for that package. Types can still reject or override one by one.
options.technical: A plus package policy (default on). Package off makes auto-derive opt-in inside that package only. Type reject and hand override still work. One mechanism, three scopes.

comparisons.note: Opt-in #[derive(...)]; no silent auto for user types. High ceremony, high visibility.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Player { name: String, score: i32 }

comparisons.note: Many protocols synthesize members when fields allow; you can write your own implementation to override.
data class generates equals/toString/copy by default; you can override members.
comparisons.code: data class Player(val name: String, val score: Int)

recommendation.why: Beginners get free derives for the common case. Experts can kill auto-derive for a whole package, reject it on one type, or replace it with a hand impl. That matches Jet's two-facet design without a second mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Stops short of a package kill-switch that strict codebases will ask for anyway.
Leaves no clean reject path; secret or intentional non-print types stay awkward.
Pushes beginner ceremony onto every type for the most likely case.
Makes the rare strict package the default, so ordinary projects pay opt-in tax.

recommendation.tradeoff: We must design a small reject spelling and a package policy knob. That is acceptable because both sit on the existing derive mechanism rather than inventing a parallel one.

decisions.title: Should quantity and unit values print with their units?
decisions.gist: Choose what print and Display show for values that carry units or physical dimensions.
decisions.lesson:
A quantity is a number plus a unit the compiler understands.

Jet already checks unit families and physical dimensions. You can write 12meter, divide by 3second, and get a speed. Wrong mixes become clear errors. At runtime the unit metadata erases, so the machine cost stays a plain number.

Printing is the last mile. If print shows only 12, the human loses the unit the compiler just protected. People expect 12 meter, 4 meter/second, or 766 px in logs, demos, and UI text unless they asked for a bare number.

This decision picks the default print and Display behavior for unit and quantity values, and how experts override it.
decisions.story: Riley demos dimensional algebra in a physics toy. The math works. print(recovered) shows a bare number, so the demo fails to teach what was recovered. Riley also draws UI sizes in px and wants 766 px in debug output without hand formatting every value.

options.name: Default Display includes units; override allowed
options.detail: print and Display show value plus unit text for quantities and unit-family values. Derived dimensions print in a readable form such as meter/second. A hand Display overrides.
options.technical: Auto Display/Printable for Quantity and #UnitFamily generated types formats magnitude + canonical unit spelling. Compound dimensions use a normalized product/quotient form. Explicit Display wins. Bare numeric extraction stays available via existing numeric APIs.

options.name: Keep bare numeric print; format helpers only
options.detail: print stays a bare number. Users call helpers or write Display when they want units. Dimension checking stays; presentation is manual.
options.technical: No auto unit-aware Display. Document format helpers if added later. Examples keep string labels beside prints.

options.name: Debug shows units; Display stays bare
options.detail: Everyday print stays numeric. Debug and {value#Debug} show units for developers. User-facing Display must be written when units matter in product text.
options.technical: Auto Debug for quantity/unit types includes unit spelling. Display/Printable remain numeric or absent until explicit. Interpolation {} follows Display rules.

options.name: Units on print, with style controls
options.detail: Default print includes units. Call sites or type attributes can pick short names, long names, or bare numbers without writing a full Display impl.
options.technical: Default like A, plus formatting policy (symbol vs name vs bare) via attribute or format syntax. Still one Display mechanism underneath; styles select rendering.

options.name: Require explicit Display for every unit type
options.detail: No auto unit printing. Authors of each #UnitFamily must define Display. Maximum control; maximum ceremony for demos and science code.
options.technical: Do not auto-implement Display/Printable for unit/quantity types. Missing Display is an error at print sites.

comparisons.note: Units erase at runtime; printing is still a plain number unless you format yourself.
comparisons.code:
let d = 12.0<m>
printfn "%A" d  // numeric unless custom

comparisons.note: Printing includes units by default; very pragmatism-friendly for science workloads.
Lengths are authored and shown with unit suffixes (px, rem). Bare numbers feel wrong in UI work.

recommendation.why: The compiler already knows the unit. Showing it on print finishes the feature people hire quantities for, in science demos and UI sizes alike. Experts still override Display when they need custom text.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the last mile broken; every call site re-attaches knowledge the type already has.
Hides units from the everyday print path beginners actually use.
Useful later, but style knobs can extend A; they need not block the default.
Forces ceremony onto every unit family for the most likely demo and log case.

recommendation.tradeoff: We must pick readable default spellings for compound dimensions. That is acceptable because one Display path serves beginners, and overrides cover special cases.

decisions.comment: A but add the explicit controls to modify style like in option D

decisions.title: Typed JSON on the HTTP client and server
decisions.gist: How a program sends and receives JSON over HTTP without hand glue.
decisions.lesson:
JSON is the text format most web services speak. A program that calls a service gets JSON text back and must turn it into typed values. A program that serves an API must turn typed values into JSON text and label the response with a content type header.

Jet already has both halves separately. `#Codable` on a struct gives typed encode and decode. The HTTP client can fetch text, and the server can return text. The missing piece is the join: today a user reads the body as text with a size limit, then calls the JSON decoder as a second step. On the server, a user builds a JSON string by hand and sets the header by hand.

This decision picks where the join lives. It can be explicit helper methods on requests and responses, a content-type driven automatic decode, or no join at all with the two-step pattern documented. The stakes are daily: calling a JSON API into structs is likely the single most common network job a Jet user will do.
