decisions.story: Ana's team encodes review status with tags, connection lifecycle with states, and file access with effect rows. A new teammate asks her the difference between a tag and a state. She starts explaining and realizes the honest answer is the keyword plus which marker consumes it. Four lessons for one idea, and her editor completes none of the names in any of them.

options.name: Facts are enums
options.detail: States, taint kinds, and declared effect leaves become enum declarations that markers consume at compile time. Enum groups already give trees, subtree matching, exhaustiveness, and payloads — facts reuse all of it. One classification mechanism for runtime and compile time; erasure is just what happens when only markers consume the enum. The tag keyword stays for flat one-off qualifiers or retires into the same story.
options.technical: Reuses D-TAG1 machinery. #State/#Transition/#Tainted/#Caps argument positions resolve against enum declarations. Ballot language amends S26-adjacent text explicitly (facts classify values and erase; they never select types or drive dispatch). User taint kinds remain gated on the deferred IFC decision — a kind with no sink checks nothing.

options.name: Tree-bodied tags
options.detail: The tag keyword grows an optional tree body and becomes the one fact declarator. Tags, states, taint kinds, and effect leaves all declare with tag; markers consume them. Runtime enums stay purely runtime. This keeps the compile-time plane visually distinct, at the cost of a third tree-classification syntax next to enums and enum groups.
options.technical: Amends D-QUAL2's ratified "exactly two qualifier kinds" text (trait / tag) to give tag a tree body. New parse form; same consumption sites as option A. Retirement terms for `state` as a separate keyword must ship in the same ruling or the spelling count goes up, not down.

options.name: Internal unification only
options.detail: Ship layer one — one registry, one matching algorithm, one reflection surface — and keep all four user spellings as they are. Users see better errors and reflection but still learn four mechanisms. Every per-mechanism improvement (state namespaces, effect declarations) still lands, each in its own shape.
options.technical: No surface change, no D-QUAL2 or S26 contact. The follow-on ballots (D-STATE-NS1, D-EFFECT-DECL1, D-TAG-STRICT1) each define their own naming and resolution rules independently.

comparisons.note: DataKinds promotes ordinary data declarations to compile-time labels — the direct precedent for option A: one declaration form serving runtime values and erased type-level facts.
comparisons.code:
data ConnState = Fresh | Open | Closed   -- one declaration
query :: Conn 'Open -> Query -> IO Rows  -- promoted to a compile-time fact

comparisons.note: String-literal unions get used as erased fact labels (branding, state unions) precisely because they reuse the ordinary type vocabulary. No second mechanism was added; users unified it themselves.
comparisons.code:
type ConnState = "fresh" | "open" | "closed";
type Open<T> = T & { readonly state: "open" };

comparisons.note: The counterexample: typestate is hand-rolled with marker structs plus PhantomData — two mechanisms and real ceremony, widely cited as expert-only.

recommendation.why: Facts-are-enums retires spellings instead of adding one. Enum groups already own trees, subtree matching, and exhaustiveness under ratified law, and the effect-matching rule already points at them. Every fact name becomes an ordinary lookup, so completion, did-you-mean, and reflection arrive without new machinery.

whyNot.reason: A tree-bodied tag is a third tree-classification syntax beside enums and enum groups. It also forces the D-QUAL2 amendment while still needing retirement terms for state — more ruling for less unification.
Users keep learning four mechanisms for one idea, and each follow-on ballot designs its naming rules against a future this ballot declined to pick.

recommendation.tradeoff: The enum keyword now serves runtime variants and erased facts, and the spec must teach the difference: a fact enum is one that only markers consume. That is one new sentence in the enum lesson, accepted to avoid a whole new declaration kind.

decisions.title: TaskGroup becomes a nameable parameter type
decisions.gist: Whether a taskgroup handle can be passed to helper functions, and under what capture rule that stays safe.
decisions.lesson:
Structured concurrency is Jet's model for parallel work: a `taskgroup g { ... }` block owns every task spawned inside it and joins them all before the block exits. No orphan threads, no leaked work. Inside the block, `g.task => expr` spawns a child and `g.all(handles)` collects results.

Today the group handle `g` is locked to its block. You cannot write a helper `fn fan_out(g: TaskGroup, xs: [Int])` — the type name does not exist (E0119), and spawning outside the block is its own error (E1110). Any fan-out pattern must be written inline, again, in every function that needs it.

Why the lock exists: safety without lifetimes. A spawned task may capture variables. If it captures a view (a borrow) of a local, the task must not outlive that local — and Jet v1 has no lifetimes to track that across calls. The lexical rule solves it structurally: the task cannot outlive the block, the block cannot outlive the enclosing function, so view captures of that function's locals are safe. Pass `g` into a helper and the trick breaks: a task could view-capture the helper's locals and outlive its frame.

The fix candidates therefore differ in how they close that hole. The main proposal: passing a group is allowed, and spawns through a parameter group require owned captures — the closure must move or copy what it uses (`~x`), never borrow. Owned data cannot dangle. Jet already applies exactly this discipline to detached tasks.
decisions.story: Tomas writes a crawler. Fetch-all-and-collect appears in six functions. In any other language he would extract `fn fetch_all(g, urls)`. In Jet the helper cannot exist: TaskGroup is not a type he can write. He copies the same eleven-line taskgroup block six times, and the six copies drift apart within a sprint.

options.name: Nameable parameter + owned captures for non-local spawns
options.detail: TaskGroup becomes a type you can write in parameter position. A helper may spawn through it, with one rule: spawns through a parameter group must own their captures — move or copy, never a view. Spawns inside the group's own block keep today's freedom. The group value still cannot be stored in a struct or returned; it flows down the call stack only.
options.technical: Extends D-DETACH1's owned-captures discipline to non-local spawns. TaskGroup is second-class: legal in parameter position, illegal in struct fields, returns, and closures that escape. Escape checking stays lexical per frame — no interprocedural analysis needed because owned captures cannot dangle. E1110 copy updates to teach the parameter path.

options.name: Keep the lexical lock
options.detail: No change. Fan-out stays inline in every function that needs it. The safety story stays maximally simple — one rule, no capture-mode distinction — and the duplication cost lands on every concurrent codebase. TaskGroup keeps appearing in error copy as a type that does not exist.
options.technical: Status quo. The E0119/E1110 pair remains the answer to helper extraction. Diagnostics honesty fix (copy stops naming TaskGroup as a type) can land regardless.

options.name: First-class TaskGroup values
options.detail: The group becomes an ordinary value: storable in structs, returnable, capturable. Maximum flexibility — and the structured guarantee quietly dies, because a stored group outlives its block and every safety argument with it. This is the unstructured-concurrency door Jet deliberately did not build.
options.technical: Requires lifetime tracking or reference counting for group handles, plus join semantics for groups that escape their scope. Conflicts with v1's no-stored-references model (C1) and with the structured-concurrency ruling that tasks join at scope exit.

comparisons.note: Nurseries pass into helpers as a core idiom — the pattern option A enables. Trio leans on garbage collection for capture safety; Jet substitutes the owned-captures rule.
TaskGroup is scoped to withTaskGroup and non-escaping — you may pass it down but never store it. The same second-class shape option A proposes.
CoroutineScope flows through receivers into helpers; storing scopes is possible and is the community's top-cited source of leaked jobs — the option C warning.
comparisons.code: fun CoroutineScope.fanOut(xs: List<Int>) = xs.map { async { it * 2 } }

recommendation.why: Fan-out helpers are a day-one pattern in every concurrent codebase. The owned-captures rule keeps the safety argument airtight without lifetimes: owned data cannot dangle, and the discipline already exists for detached tasks. Structured concurrency's guarantee — the block joins everything — survives untouched.

whyNot.reason: Inline-only taskgroups force the same block to be copied into every function that fans out, and the copies drift. The error copy also keeps naming a type the language refuses to admit exists.
Storable groups outlive their block, which un-structures structured concurrency and needs the lifetime machinery v1 rejected.

recommendation.tradeoff: Helpers cannot view-capture their own locals into spawned tasks; some code must copy or move data it would rather borrow. That is the price of keeping capture safety local to each frame.

decisions.title: Ranges become values: one Range type in core
decisions.gist: Whether 1..10 becomes a value you can store, pass, and return — and if so, one range type or two.
decisions.lesson:
A range names a band of integers: `1..10` (inclusive end) or `1..<10` (exclusive end). Jet uses ranges in exactly five places: loop sources, arm heads in match-style dispatch, slices, view arguments, and distinct-type constraints like `distinct Int(0..10)`.

In all five, the range is syntax — a shape the parser recognizes in that spot. It is not a value. There is no `Range` type. You cannot write `band :: 1..10`, put ranges in a list, return one from a function, or accept one as a parameter. A pagination API that wants "rows 40 to 60" takes two integers. A histogram that wants buckets takes pairs. The concept exists in the language; the value does not.

Making ranges values is old, proven ground — most modern languages did it. The design questions are small but real. One type or two? Rust has separate types for every inclusivity combination, and its users cite the range-type zoo as a wart. One type that carries its own end-exclusivity is simpler.

Which element types? The five current positions are integer positions, so Int-only matches today's language. And one honest asymmetry: `distinct Int(0..10)` consumes its range at type-declaration time. A runtime range value cannot flow into a type declaration — that would be value-dependent types, a different language. The literal-only rule there stays.

Performance does not change either way: loops over ranges keep compiling to plain jumps. Whether the surface calls it a value is a surface fact, not a codegen fact.
decisions.story: Lena builds a log dashboard. Latency buckets: 0–10ms, 10–100ms, 100ms and up. She wants `buckets :: [0..<10, 10..<100]` and a function that takes a band and counts hits. Neither line has a type that can exist. She ships `[(0, 10), (10, 100)]` with a comment explaining which end is exclusive, and the comment is wrong within a month.

options.name: One Range type; the value carries its exclusivity
options.detail: Core gains one nominal Range over Int. Both spellings construct it; an inclusive and an exclusive range are the same type with different end behavior. Fields and methods: .start, .end, .contains(x). Every current range position keeps working unchanged and also accepts a Range value where a value can appear. The distinct-constraint position stays literal-only, stated in the spec.
options.technical: Range { start: Int, end: Int, inclusive: Bool } semantics (representation is core's choice). Loop/slice/view positions accept literals as today plus Range-typed values; lowering specializes identically — no iterator object, no allocation. Arm heads accept range literals as today; Range values in arm heads are a later question, not this ballot. Int-only in v1.

options.name: Two types: Range and RangeExclusive
options.detail: Each spelling gets its own nominal type, so the inclusivity is visible in signatures. APIs must pick one or accept both, generic code needs two paths, and users learn which functions take which. This is Rust's shape, and Rust's users name it as a pain point.
options.technical: Range (inclusive) and RangeExclusive as separate core types; .contains on both; conversions between them. Every API taking a band either doubles its signature or picks a canonical one and forces conversions at call sites.

options.name: Stay syntax-only
options.detail: No Range type. The five positions keep working; bands-as-data stay inexpressible; APIs keep taking integer pairs with meaning by convention. Zero new surface, and the one concept the language clearly already has keeps not being a value.
options.technical: Status quo. S22/S72 and D-RANGE-EXCL1 unchanged.
options.code:
fn page(rows: Rows, lo: Int, hi: Int) => Rows { ... }
// call sites forever: page(rows, 40, 60) — is 60 in or out? read the docs

comparisons.note: IntRange is one value type; downTo and until construct variants of the same concept. The closest match to option A, widely liked.
Range, RangeInclusive, RangeTo, RangeFrom, RangeFull — the option B endpoint. Powerful, and the proliferation is a documented ergonomic complaint.
comparisons.code:
fn page(rows: &Rows, band: std::ops::Range<usize>) -> Rows { ... }
// callers with an inclusive range must convert: (40..=60) doesn't fit

comparisons.note: Two types (Range, ClosedRange) with protocol glue to accept both — the middle path, at the cost of protocol machinery Jet does not want to spend here.
comparisons.code: func page(_ rows: Rows, _ band: some RangeExpression<Int>) -> Rows { ... }

recommendation.why: One type makes ranges data with one lesson: 1..10 is a value like any literal, wherever a value can go. The inclusivity travels inside the value, so APIs take one Range and every call site reads correctly without conversions.

whyNot.reason: Two types double every band-taking signature or force conversions at call sites — the documented Rust pain, imported for no gain a .contains check does not already give.
The language keeps a concept it refuses to hand to users; integer-pair APIs keep encoding exclusivity in comments that go stale.

recommendation.tradeoff: One stated asymmetry remains: distinct Int(0..10) stays a literal-only position, because a runtime range flowing into a type declaration is value-dependent typing. The spec says this in one sentence.

decisions.title: Optional effect-leaf declarations kill typo leaves
decisions.gist: Whether effect names like FS.Read can be declared, so a typo like FS.Raed becomes an error instead of a new permission.
decisions.lesson:
Effects are Jet's answer to "what can this function touch?". A function's effect row — `=[FS.Read, Net]=>` — lists its capabilities. Callers see it, package budgets cap it, and `#Grant` scopes authorize it.

Effect names form a tree. The roots are a fixed set of ten (FS, Net, Env, and so on) — a small vocabulary beginners can hold in their head, and that closure is ratified and right. Below a root, names are dotted paths: `FS.Read`, `Net.HTTP.Get`. Matching uses the tree: a grant of `FS` covers `FS.Read`.

Here is the gap: leaves are never declared anywhere. Any dotted path under a legal root is accepted. Write `=[FS.Raed]=>` and the compiler mints a brand-new effect on the spot. No error, no warning. Now your function claims a capability nothing grants, or worse, a package budget that meant to cap `FS.Read` fails to cover the misspelled twin. Effect names are a security surface, and today they are compared as raw strings.

The language already reserved the fix: the `effect` keyword exists in the syntax registry, reserved and unused. Leaf declarations would make effect names resolvable — real names with did-you-mean — without touching the closed roots or the tree matching.

The design choice is strictness. Mandatory declarations would break the lightweight idiom of inventing an app-local leaf on the fly. Optional declarations with a per-root rule split the difference: once any leaf is declared under a root, that root becomes checked; untouched roots keep today's freedom.
decisions.story: Rui's team caps their web service's package budget: file access is read-only, `FS.Read`. A teammate adds a cache module and types `=[FS.Raed]=>` in a helper. It compiles — a new leaf now exists. Code review misses one vowel. The budget that was supposed to be the backstop never matches the misspelled name, and the mistake surfaces months later in an audit.

options.name: Optional declarations; a declared root becomes checked
options.detail: New declaration form: effect FS.Read. Once any leaf is declared under a root in a package's view, undeclared leaves under that root are resolution errors with did-you-mean. Roots nobody declared under keep today's mint-on-use freedom. The prelude declares the stdlib's own leaves, so every user gets typo protection on the common roots from day one, having written nothing.
options.technical: Mints the reserved effect keyword (D-EFF4/5 slot). Declarations are package-scoped facts; the checked/unchecked flag is per root per package view (own + dependencies' declared leaves). pkg.jet budgets and #Caps/#Grant arguments resolve against the same names. Tree matching unchanged.

options.name: Mandatory declarations for every leaf
options.detail: Every dotted leaf must be declared before use, everywhere. Maximum typo protection and a complete effect inventory per package. The cost: the invent-a-leaf-inline idiom dies, and every quick script with a custom effect writes a declaration first. The beginner path gains a ceremony step the closed roots were designed to avoid.
options.technical: Same declaration form as A; no per-root freedom. Undeclared leaf anywhere is an error. Requires the prelude to be complete for stdlib leaves before landing, or every existing program breaks at once.

options.name: Status quo: freeform leaves
options.detail: No declarations. Leaves keep minting on use. The docs warn about typos, budgets keep comparing strings, and the effect keyword stays reserved for a future that never gets scheduled. Zero new surface; the security-surface string matching stays.
options.technical: No change. The FS.Raed class of bug remains unfindable by the compiler.
options.code:
fn warm_cache(path: String) =[FS.Raed]=> Bool { ... }
// compiles forever; the budget backstop silently does not apply

comparisons.note: Permissions are strings on the command line; a typo in --allow-net silently over- or under-grants. The cautionary tale for option C on a real security surface.
comparisons.code: deno run --allow-net=api.exmaple.com app.ts   # typo: grant never matches

comparisons.note: Capabilities are handles minted by the host, not strings — misspelling one is impossible by construction. The direction option A moves toward while keeping Jet's readable names.
comparisons.code: // wasi: fd = preopened directory handle; there is no name to misspell

recommendation.why: Optional declarations put typo checking exactly where names carry authority, and the prelude makes the protection free for the roots everyone uses. The one-line app-local leaf survives, so the lightweight idiom and the security backstop stop being enemies.

whyNot.reason: Mandatory declarations tax every quick script and kill the inline leaf idiom, buying little beyond option A once the prelude covers the stdlib roots.
Effect names gate real authority, and string-matched authority with silent minting is how the FS.Raed bug ships and hides for months.

recommendation.tradeoff: The per-root rule has a mixed moment: the first declaration under a root flips that root to checked for the package. A team adding its first declaration must therefore declare the leaves it already uses. The error's fix text lists them.

decisions.title: Marker/trait name-collision law, and the two worst renames
decisions.gist: One naming law so markers and traits stop sharing names by accident — and whether to rename the two worst offenders now.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has two Pascal-case vocabularies that meet in user code. Traits are contracts: `Comparable`, `Printable`. Markers are `#` rules: `#Comparable`, `#Codable`, `#Task`. Some markers *are* trait requests — `#Comparable` on a struct derives the `Comparable` trait, and user derives already work exactly this way (`derive T.Wire` defines it, `#Wire` applies it). For those, sharing the name is correct: the marker is the trait, applied.

The trouble is the names that collide by accident. "Tag" means three unrelated things today. It is the `tag` keyword (erased qualifiers), serde's `#Tag("type")` (the discriminant field a serialized enum writes), and the spec's own name for nested enum groups. `#Task` marks a scheduled entry-point function, while `Task<T>` is the concurrency handle — same word, unrelated machinery, both near any async code. When one word means three things, error messages, docs, and searches all degrade at once.

A naming law fixes the future: a marker that derives trait X is spelled `#X`, and a marker that is not a derive may not take a trait's name. Cheap, permanent, and it turns the marker/trait relationship from a coincidence into a rule the spec can state in one line.

The remaining question is the past: whether to rename serde's `#Tag` and the scheduled `#Task` now. Greenfield policy makes renames ordinary errors with fix text, not migrations — the cost is real but small, and it only shrinks with time in one direction.
decisions.story: Noor searches the docs for "tag" to understand a serialization error. She gets the tag keyword page, the enum-groups section, and the serde marker — three unrelated mechanisms wearing one name. The error she is chasing involves exactly one of them, and nothing in the word tells her which.

options.name: Law + rename the two offenders
options.detail: Adopt the naming law for all future markers. Rename serde's #Tag to #Discriminant (the standard term for the variant field) and the scheduled #Task to #Job (a scheduled unit of work, distinct from the Task handle). Old spellings error with fix text pointing at the new name. "Tag" shrinks to two meanings, and the remaining pair (tag keyword, spec prose for enum groups) is a docs cleanup, not surface.
options.technical: Registry renames with retirement rows (E-code teaching the new spelling). Spec prose for D-TAG1 groups switches to "variant groups" in the same pass. The law lands in the marker-authoring section of the spec and as a registry lint.

options.name: Law only; keep today's names
options.detail: The naming law prevents every future collision, and the three-way "tag" overload plus #Task/Task stay as grandfathered exceptions the docs must forever disambiguate. No respell cost now; the two worst offenders remain the two worst offenders permanently, and each new user meets them.
options.technical: Spec law + registry lint only. Docs add disambiguation boxes to the tag keyword page and the scheduling page.

options.name: No law, no renames
options.detail: Names stay first-come, first-served. Nothing breaks, nothing improves, and the collision count grows with every rule added — each future marker author re-argues naming from scratch in review.
options.technical: Status quo.
options.code:
// next year, plausibly:
#Stream fn ingest() { ... }   // and Stream<T> gains its own #Task problem

comparisons.note: serde contains the same concept inside its own namespace — #[serde(tag = "type")] — so 'tag' never collides with a language keyword. Jet's flat marker plane has no namespace to hide in, which is why the law matters more here.
Annotations live in packages; two @Task annotations coexist by import path. The namespacing Jet chose not to have is exactly what a naming law substitutes for.
comparisons.code:
import org.quartz.Task;    // vs
import myapp.Task;         // collision resolved by package, not by law

recommendation.why: The law costs one spec line and prevents every future collision; the two renames retire the only overloads bad enough that new users meet them in week one. Greenfield policy makes the respell ordinary errors with fix text, and that price only grows if deferred.

whyNot.reason: Grandfathering the two worst offenders means every future reader of docs, errors, and search results pays the disambiguation tax the law was written to end.
Without the law, each new rule re-fights naming in review, and the collision count only goes up.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing examples, snapshots, and docs that use #Tag and #Task respell now. Two retirement diagnostics join the registry and stay for an epoch.

decisions.title: One tag mechanism: checking behavior chosen in the declaration
decisions.gist: Whether tags and taints become one mechanism where each tag declares what the compiler enforces.
decisions.lesson:
A tag is a label the compiler attaches to a value and erases at runtime. It costs nothing when the program runs. It exists only to catch mistakes while you write.

Jet ships two label mechanisms that look alike and behave differently. A value tag like `#Reviewed String` is documentation: the compiler checks nothing. A taint like `#Tainted(Pii)` is enforced: the compiler follows the value through the program and blocks it at dangerous places (sinks) such as queries and logs.

These are two polarities of one idea. A taint is a negative fact: this value may be dangerous. The check forbids it at sinks. The only way to clear it is an audited function marked `#Sanitizer` — the door out. A strict positive fact says: this value passed X, such as review or validation. The check requires it at marked positions. The only way to gain it would be an audited blessing function — the door in.

Same engine, mirrored. One polarity forbids reaching a place while the label is present. The other requires the label before entering a place. Both erase. Both have exactly one audited door, and reviewers can grep for the doors.

One fact model is already ratified law (D-FACTMODEL1 = A): tags, states, taint kinds, and effect leaves share one registry and one matching rule. Flat `tag` stays for one-off qualifiers; tree-shaped facts declare as enums. This ballot decides the remaining user-facing axis: does each tag declare its own checking behavior, so tags and taints live under one banner? And where does that choice live — the declaration, or the call site?
decisions.story: Maya reads Jet's security chapter. She learns `#Tainted` is enforced, and assumes `#Reviewed` is too — same spelling, same look. She writes `fn publish(desc: #Reviewed String)`. A teammate passes raw form input; it compiles; unreviewed text ships. One mechanism that states what each tag enforces would have made her signature true — or made her declare the mode she needed.
decisions.detail: Raised from owner question q8jh0b7a. Supersedes D-TAG-STRICT1: strict tags become one mode of this mechanism instead of a standalone feature. Builds on ratified D-FACTMODEL1 = A; nothing here reopens the facts-are-enums ruling.

options.name: One banner: each tag declares its checking mode
options.detail:
Every tag picks its behavior where it is declared. Plain (the default) is documentation: erases, checks nothing — today's tags, unchanged and free. Strict is a positive fact: untagged values cannot enter tagged positions; the one way in is that tag's blessing door. Taint is a negative fact: it spreads through derived values and cannot reach its declared sinks; the one way out is that tag's sanitizer door.

The built-in taint kinds (Input, PII, Secret, Credential) become prelude tag declarations in taint mode, so #Tainted stops being a special case. Every signature becomes self-describing.
options.technical: Mode spelling on the declaration (working: `tag Reviewed strict`; `tag Pii taint(sinks: DB, Exec, Net, Log)`). Doors are one mirrored marker pair: #Blesses(Tag) adds the fact by contract; #Sanitizer(Tag) removes it by contract. Amends D-TAINT1/D-TAINT2 spelling only — lattice, dataflow spread, sink set, and E0721 carry over verbatim as taint-mode semantics; source marking respells #Tainted(Pii) expr → #Pii expr. Fact enums under D-FACTMODEL1=A carry the same modes for tree-shaped facts. User-declared sinks stay gated on the deferred IFC ruling — a taint with no live sink checks nothing. Depends on card #1289 (undeclared tags error). I7 rows: mode keywords, #Blesses.

options.name: One model in the spec; ratified spellings stay
options.detail: The spec teaches one fact model with two polarities, and strict tags land with their blessing door. But the taint family keeps its ratified spelling: #Tainted(Kind) to mark, #Sanitizer to clear, kinds staying a closed built-in set. No shipped surface respells. The cost: the false rhyme survives — #Reviewed and #Tainted still look alike while behaving differently, and the taint kinds stay outside the tag namespace users can extend.
options.technical: D-TAG-STRICT1 option A lands as designed (strict declarations + #Blesses). D-TAINT1/D-TAINT2 untouched. The unification is documentation plus the already-ratified internal fact registry from D-FACTMODEL1 layer one.

options.name: Checking chosen at call sites, not declarations
options.detail: The declaration stays neutral; each use site opts into checking — for example, a strictness sigil on the parameter. Maximum flexibility, but the guarantee becomes local: the same #Reviewed String is checked in one signature and decoration in another. A reader can never trust a tag without inspecting every site that touches it, which is today's problem with more machinery. Security properties that hold only where someone remembered to ask are the properties that fail.
options.technical: Per-position opt-in (working: `#Reviewed! String`). Requires flow checking to activate per position; provenance questions (does a blessed value satisfy an unchecked position and vice versa) multiply. No amendment to D-TAINT1 — taint cannot be call-site optional without breaking E0721 guarantees.

comparisons.note: One annotation mechanism hosts many checkers; each qualifier declares its own flow rules — tainting, nullness, units. The direct precedent for checking behavior living in the declaration, under one banner.
comparisons.code:
void run(@Untainted String query) { ... }
// one mechanism; the qualifier's checker decides what is enforced

comparisons.note: Taint mode is the negative polarity with an audited door out: the only way from tainted to trusted is an explicit, greppable untaint operation.
comparisons.code: my ($clean) = $input =~ /^([\w.-]+)$/;   # the one blessed door out of taint

comparisons.note: Branded types are the positive polarity hand-rolled at massive scale: an erased brand with a blessing function as the door in. Proof of demand for checked positive facts.
comparisons.code:
type Reviewed = string & { readonly __brand: "reviewed" };
function approve(s: string): Reviewed { moderate(s); return s as Reviewed; }

recommendation.why: One mechanism replaces two that shared a spelling plane but not a meaning. The declaration states what each tag enforces, so every signature reads true. The taint machinery is untouched — it becomes the taint mode's engine instead of a parallel special case, and the audited-door pattern becomes one mirrored rule instead of two lessons.

whyNot.reason: It fixes positive facts but preserves the false rhyme this card exists to kill, and the taint kinds stay a closed special case outside the namespace users can extend.
Call-site opt-in makes every guarantee local: the same tag checks in one signature and decorates in another, so no reader can trust any tag anywhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: The ratified #Tainted(Kind) surface respells to prelude taint-mode tags, and the tag lesson grows a modes section. Accepted: that one lesson replaces two whole mechanisms' lessons, and D-TAINT1/D-TAINT2 semantics carry over verbatim under the new spelling.

decisions.comment: But we need to reevaluate ALL the syntax/wording/casing. We still need all caps acronyms and pascal case, I dont like the blesses wording, and the formatting/syntax you have for tag keyword then taint as a function type thing after the name is ugly and incoherent with jet syntax. Propose a  full ballot to ensure the best syntax/surface possible that maintains coherence with jet

decisions.title: Distributed compare if + Void-or-value tables
decisions.gist: How multi-arm if tables compare a subject and produce a value.
decisions.lesson:
An if table picks one arm. Today Jet writes if subject == { value -> body }. The == is a marker that means each arm head is compared to the subject.

You often want other comparisons too. Writing if n < { 16 -> 0 32 -> 1 } should mean n < 16, then n < 32, without repeating n each time. That is a distributed compare: the operator before the brace applies to every bare arm value.

A bar | joins several values for the same arm (a union). And and or (&& and ||) add extra true or false checks on that arm.

The same table should work as a statement or as a value. When arms give values of one type, the if expression has that type. When arms only do work, the type is Void.
decisions.story: Nate is writing a browser hex color helper. He wants return if n < { 16 -> 0 ... } and return if n == { 0 -> "0" ... } in the same style as statement tables, and he needs that shape to compile for the web target.

options.name: All comparisons distribute; tables yield Void or a value
options.detail: Any comparison can sit before the brace. A bare arm value becomes subject OP value. Bar joins those with or. And and or combine extra checks. The same spelling works in expressions. Web must emit value if.
options.technical: Amend D-IF3/D-MATCHARM2/S68. Marker ops: == != < > <= >=. arm_atom_to_cond(subject, value, op). Drop E0328. parse_if_expr accepts subject OP { value-arms }. Desugar to Expr::If chain. Pattern heads remain ==-only.

options.name: Keep == only; rewrite with full predicates
options.detail: No new marker ops. Writers repeat the subject on every arm as a full boolean. Expression dispatch stays blocked.

options.name: Distribute comparisons only in statements
options.detail: Allow if n < { … } as a statement, but keep expression position on subjectless or two-arm forms only.

comparisons.note: case / when uses ===; no distributed < table.
when can be an expression; comparisons are written in full on each branch.

recommendation.why: One table spelling for statements and values matches how people already write == dispatch, and distributed compares remove repeated subjects without a second mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Forces repeated subjects and leaves the showcase expression form illegal.
Splits statement and expression surfaces, so return if n < { … } still fails.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must learn that bar always means or of subject OP atom, including for !=, which is rarely useful with multiple alternates.

decisions.title: Tags v2: one checked tag mechanism — struct-bodied deny/from, #Scrub doors
decisions.gist: Whether tags become one checked mechanism: a struct-shaped declaration with deny and from lines, scrub functions as the only way off, and no plain or strict modes.
decisions.lesson:
A tag is a label the compiler attaches to a value and erases before the program runs. It costs nothing at runtime. It exists to stop mistakes while you write.

In v2, every tag checks, and every tag has the same behavior. A tag starts where a value is born. It follows the value through every derived value — interpolation, math, struct fields. It stops the value at the effects the tag denies. An effect is Jet's word for what a function does to the outside world: DB, Net, Log. Functions already declare them (`=[DB]=>`).

The declaration is struct-shaped, like Jet's policy bodies. `deny:` lists the effects a tagged value must not reach. It is required — a tag that denies nothing checks nothing. `from:` lists origins whose outputs are born tagged, such as network reads. It is optional. For single spots, you put the tag marker directly on a field, a return type, or an expression.

One function kind removes a tag: a scrub, written `#Scrub(Tag) fn`. Scrubs are the audit points. One search for `#Scrub` finds every place a program cleans a tagged value.

The earlier ratified design had three modes: plain (checks nothing), strict (proof required), and taint (danger tracked). The boil-down with the owner found: plain tags look enforced and are not — a trap. Strict cases either become a tag stopped at an effect, or they are contracts and typestate, which Jet already has. So one mode remains, and the mode axis leaves the surface.

Word picks, made by the owner: the mechanism is called tags. The stopping rule is `deny` (firewall wording). The cleaning door is `scrub` — the word Jet's own diagnostic copy already uses.
decisions.story: Maya reads Jet's security chapter. She learns `#Tainted` is enforced, and assumes `#Reviewed` is too — same spelling, same look. She writes `fn publish(desc: #Reviewed String)`. A teammate passes raw form input; it compiles; unreviewed text ships. V2 exists so that every tag she can write is a tag the compiler enforces, under one rule she learns once.
decisions.detail: Third surface proposal for the tag unification, designed with the owner in chat on 2026-07-28 (two earlier option sets rejected). Option A amends D-TAG-UNIFY1=A: the plain and strict modes retire; one checked mechanism remains. Constants per D-CASING1: tag names are PascalCase with acronyms in caps (PII, SQL, GDPR); markers PascalCase. Prelude tags: Input, PII, Secret, Credential, written as ordinary tag declarations. `#Tainted` and `#Sanitizer` retire with greenfield teaching errors pointing at the tag marker and `#Scrub`. Diagnostic copy moves from 'sink' to 'denied at' wording (E0721/E0722 respell).

options.name: V2 complete: struct-bodied tags with deny and from, #Scrub doors
options.detail:
One mechanism. A tag declares as a small struct body: `deny:` (required) lists the effects a tagged value must not reach; `from:` (optional) lists origins whose outputs are born tagged. Retail sources use the marker directly on a field, return type, or expression. `#Scrub(Tag) fn` is the one way to remove a tag, and the one grep for audits.

The beginner writes nothing and keeps full protection: the prelude tags carry the common sources and denials. The expert reads the prelude as ordinary code and writes new tags in the same three-line shape. Old strict-tag cases become a tag plus an effect on the guarded call; pure proof cases route to contracts and typestate.
options.technical: Grammar: `tag Name { … }` with fields `deny: [EffectLeaf, …]` (required, nonempty) and `from: [EffectLeaf | path, …]` (optional). Entries resolve by ordinary name lookup against effect leaves (D-FACTMODEL1=A, user-declarable) and module/function paths; typos get did-you-mean. Spread: dataflow propagation as D-TAINT1; derivation keeps the tag; only a matching `#Scrub` removes it. `#Scrub(Tag)` validates the signature consumes the tagged type. Empty or missing `deny:` is a teaching error. I7 rows: tag body fields `deny`/`from`, `#Scrub`. Retires: plain tags (bare `tag Name` errors with the fix), strict mode/D-TAG-STRICT1 routing, `#Tainted`, `#Sanitizer`. E0721/E0722 semantics carry over with 'denied at' copy. Existing plain-tag examples migrate or retire (greenfield).

options.name: V2 without from: retail sources only
options.detail:
The same mechanism, but no `from:` line. Every source is marked by hand: a marker on a field, a return type, or an expression. The declaration body carries `deny:` alone.

The gain is a smaller surface with one way to mark a source. The loss is the unmarked-origin hole: a value from the database or the network is clean unless someone remembered the marker. Stored attacks ride exactly that gap, and the prelude cannot express 'everything off the network is untrusted' as code.
options.technical: As A minus the `from` field; `from:` stays a reserved body field name for a future ballot. Prelude source coverage moves into compiler magic instead of readable declarations.

options.name: V2 plus plain tags: deny becomes optional
options.detail:
The same mechanism, but a tag may omit `deny:` and become documentation — the ratified plain mode survives. Teams get free labels for intent (`#Internal String`) without designing enforcement first.

The cost is the trap this whole redesign started from: a label that looks exactly like an enforced tag and checks nothing. Two behaviors return under one look, and the reader must open the declaration to know which one they have.
options.technical: As A with `deny:` optional; an empty body declares a plain tag. Keeps D-TAG-UNIFY1's plain mode; existing plain-tag examples stay valid. Lint (not error) offered for plain tags in parameter position.

comparisons.note: Every piece of v2 reuses a shipped shape: struct-style bodies with named fields (policy surface), effect leaves as the deny targets, and markers on declarations. The scrub word is already in Jet's own E0722 fix text: 'Scrub the credential before logging.'

The original enforced-taint language: input values are tainted and blocked at dangerous operations. But any regex capture launders, so audits cannot find the cleaning points. Named #Scrub doors exist to fix exactly this.
Taint qualifiers as annotations, with a named, greppable annotation as the cleaning point — the audit property v2 keeps, without the annotation burden on every intermediate function.
comparisons.code:
@Untainted String query;
@SuppressWarnings("tainting")  // the audited, greppable door

recommendation.why: One mechanism with one behavior ends the false rhyme for good: every tag a user can write is a tag the compiler enforces. The beginner writes nothing and keeps injection, secret, and PII protection. The expert writes a three-line struct body in a shape Jet already uses, and one grep for #Scrub is the whole audit surface. `from:` closes the unmarked-origin hole and lets the prelude ship as readable code.

whyNot.reason: Dropping `from:` reopens the stored-attack gap: values from the database or network arrive clean unless a human remembered a marker, and the prelude goes back to being magic prose.
Plain tags recreate the trap that started this redesign — a label that looks enforced and checks nothing — to save a feature a comment already provides.

recommendation.tradeoff: A amends D-TAG-UNIFY1=A: plain and strict modes retire, and pure proof cases must route to contracts, typestate, or distinct types. Requirement-style tags get negative names (Unreviewed, Untrusted). Accepted: that is the price of one mechanism with one rule, and the positive cases already have checked homes.

decisions.title: Whole-number literals beside a fixed-width integer
decisions.gist: Whether writing 1 next to a 32-bit number is allowed, or needs its type spelled.
decisions.lesson:
A whole number in Jet is normally an `Int`, which is 64 bits wide. For hardware, file formats, and foreign libraries, Jet also offers a fixed-width menu: `I8`, `I16`, `I32`, `U8`, and the rest. A `U8` holds 0 to 255. An `I32` holds about minus two billion to plus two billion.

These are separate types on purpose. Mixing widths by accident is how programs lose data or wrap around silently. Jet keeps them apart, and conversion is always spelled out.

Now the wrinkle. When you type the numeral `1` in your source, it has no width yet. It is just a number the compiler can see. The compiler must decide what type to give it. That decision is called literal typing.

Jet already makes that decision in one place. If a function takes an `I32` and you call it with `2`, the call compiles. The numeral takes the width the function asked for.

But in arithmetic it does not. Here is the whole problem:

    fn increment(x: I32) => I32 { return x + 1 }

That line is rejected today. The message says `+` cannot combine `I32` and `Int`. The workaround is to write the width on the numeral: `x + I32.{ 1 }`.

So the same numeral is fine as an argument and rejected as an operand. This ballot decides whether that gap closes, and which way.

One thing must not change either way. Jet arithmetic stops the program on overflow at every width, and a value never narrows behind your back. Any option here has to leave that alone.

One more piece of today's behaviour matters for the options below. Two different named widths never mix either. `I32 + I16` is refused, even though every `I16` value fits in an `I32` with nothing lost.
decisions.story:
Priya is writing a driver for a temperature sensor. The chip reports readings as `I32` counts, and her calibration step adds a one-count offset. She writes `raw + 1` and the compiler refuses it. She tries `I32.from_int(1)` and now holds a fallible result to unwrap, for a constant she typed herself.

She has written three spellings of the number one and shipped nothing. A test in this repository, `cffi_named_pure_callback_has_stable_c_symbol`, is written the way Priya expected and fails for the same reason.

options.name: A numeral takes the width of what it sits beside
options.detail: `x + 1` compiles when `x` is an `I32`, and the `1` becomes an `I32`. This is the rule Jet already uses for arguments, now used for operators too. A numeral too large for the width is a compile error naming the width and the limit. Nothing else about the fixed-width menu changes: two named widths still never mix, and no value ever narrows on its own.
options.technical: Expected-type propagation extends from call arguments into binary operand positions. When exactly one side is an untyped integer literal and the other has a concrete integer type, the literal takes that type. The range check runs at compile time against the destination width and reports E0135-class out-of-range. Two concretely typed operands of different widths remain E0109. D-NUMOPS1 trap-on-overflow and S42 separation are untouched, because only compile-time-known literals participate.

options.name: Keep the rule; teach it in the error
options.detail: Nothing about the language changes. `x + 1` stays an error, and the fix text stops saying "make both sides the same type" and starts showing the exact line to type: `x + I32.{ 1 }`. The repository test that assumes otherwise is corrected to spell the width. You always read a numeral's type off the numeral itself.
options.technical: Copy-only change in the E0109 handler: when one operand is an untyped integer literal and the other has a concrete width, render a fix that reproduces the literal in typed-head form. Registered fix text plus UI snapshot per I4. The cffi fixture is rewritten to `x + I32.{ 1 }`.

options.name: Narrow types do their arithmetic at full width
options.detail: Fixed-width values widen to `Int` whenever they take part in arithmetic, and the result narrows back when it is stored somewhere with a declared width. `x + 1` compiles because both sides are `Int` by then. This is how C and Java behave, so it will feel familiar. The cost is that overflow is no longer caught at the width you declared, only where the result lands.
options.technical: Integer promotion on every arithmetic operator: operands below platform Int width widen to Int, the operation runs at Int, and assignment or return into a narrower declared type performs a checked narrowing. This contradicts D-NUMOPS1's trap-at-every-width rule, which would need an explicit amendment. Intermediate results no longer wrap or trap at the declared width.
options.code:
fn increment(x: I32) => I32 { return x + 1 }        // ok, computed at Int width

byte :: U8.{ 200 }
sum: U8 :: byte + 100                                // 300 computed, then trapped at the store
mid :: byte + 100 - 100                              // ok: intermediate 300 never trapped

options.name: Keep the rule; let the tools write the width for you
options.detail: The language keeps its current rule, and the tooling removes the typing. A lint flags a bare numeral beside a fixed-width value, and the formatter and the editor fix rewrite it to `I32.{ 1 }` on save. You type what you meant and the file ends up spelling the width. Every source file still reads with the width visible on the numeral.
options.technical: B's diagnostic plus a machine-applicable fix. The lint fires on an untyped literal operand facing a concrete integer type, and the rewrite inserts the typed head with the same numeral. The formatter applies it only when the literal fits the target width; otherwise the error stands. No sema or lowering change.

options.name: Give the numeral its smallest type, then widen it losslessly
options.detail:
The numeral `1` becomes the narrowest type that holds it, and then widens to the other side when nothing can be lost. `x + 1` works when `x` is an `I32`, because a small unsigned number fits an `I32` exactly.

The catch is that "smallest" cannot be decided without looking at the other side anyway. The narrowest type for `1` is an unsigned byte, and an unsigned byte does not fit in an `I8`. So `x + 1` would be refused when `x` is an `I8`, which is the plainest case there is.

The second catch is the value that does not fit. When `x` is a `U8` and you write `x + 300`, the numeral becomes a 16-bit number, `x` widens to meet it, and the sum is 16 bits wide. The mistake is accepted and the expression quietly changes width.
options.technical: Literal gets the minimal-width type containing its value, then implicit lossless widening applies to the operator. Signedness makes minimal-width ill-defined without the destination: min(1) = U8, and U8 does not widen to I8 or I16-signed-narrow cases cleanly, so a signed destination narrower than the promoted literal is rejected. Out-of-destination-range literals promote the whole expression rather than erroring, deferring the diagnostic to the store and losing the declared width as the trap point.
options.code:
fn increment(x: I32) => I32 { return x + 1 }   // ok: 1 is a byte, widens to I32

fn tick(x: I8) => I8 { return x + 1 }          // refused: a byte does not fit I8

byte :: U8.{ 200 }
sum :: byte + 300                              // accepted, and sum is 16 bits wide
out: U8 :: sum                                 // the error lands here, not at the 300

options.name: Lossless widening is implicit everywhere, numerals included
options.detail:
Any whole number, written or stored, moves on its own into a wider type that holds every one of its values. `x + 1` works. So does `I32 + I16`, giving an `I32`. Nothing ever narrows on its own, and a mix with no common wider type, such as `U8` with `I8`, is still refused.

This answers the whole family of complaints, not just the numeral one, and it removes the conversion ceremony from cases that provably cannot lose anything.

Two costs. The separation of named widths in S42 is deliberate, and this ends it. And floats would then disagree with whole numbers: mixing `F32` with `Float` stays a compile error under the ratified float rule, so the two halves of the numeric menu would follow opposite laws.
options.technical: Implicit widening coercion on integer types ordered by value-set containment: In widens to Im when every value of In is representable in Im. Applies to literals via the same rule after minimal-width assignment. Expression type is the join; no common supertype is E0109. Amends S42 separation. Puts D-FLOATW1 under pressure, since F32-with-Float remains explicit under the ratified float rule, and the two would need reconciling in the spec.

comparisons.note: An integer literal takes the type of its neighbour, and an out-of-range literal is a compile error. This is option A.
comparisons.code:
fn increment(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 }   // 1 is an i32
let b: u8 = 200 + 100;                  // error: literal out of range

comparisons.note: Narrow types widen to int for arithmetic and narrow back on assignment. This is option C, including the silent wrap.
comparisons.code:
unsigned char b = 200;
unsigned char s = b + 100;   /* 300 computed as int, then wraps to 44 */

comparisons.note: An untyped constant takes the type it is used at, but two named types never mix, even at the same width.
comparisons.code:
var x int32 = 5
x = x + 1        // ok, 1 is untyped
var y int = 1
x = x + y        // error: mismatched types

comparisons.note: Closest to today's Jet: strict named widths, but literals are typed by context, so the arithmetic case still works.

recommendation.why: Jet already gives a bare numeral the width the context asks for when it is a call argument. Option A applies that same rule to operators, so one law covers both places instead of two.

whyNot.reason: It teaches a rule the language does not actually hold. `increment(2)` compiles and `x + 2` does not, and better wording cannot explain that difference to a beginner.
Arithmetic would stop trapping at the width the programmer declared, which contradicts the ratified trap-on-overflow rule and hides the exact class of bug the fixed-width menu exists to expose.
It leaves the same inconsistency as B and adds a tool that edits the source. A beginner who reads the rewritten line still cannot say why the argument form needed no rewrite.
The narrowest type for a numeral cannot be picked without looking at the other side, so it refuses the plain `I8` case and it accepts an out-of-range numeral by widening the whole expression.
It ends the deliberate separation of named widths and leaves whole numbers and floats under opposite laws, since mixing F32 with Float stays explicit under the ratified float rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: A numeral's type now depends on what sits beside it, so a line read in isolation says less about itself. That is already true of arguments, so the language gains one rule instead of a second exception. A also leaves `I32 + I16` refused, which option F would fix.

decisions.title: Name of the reserved namespace for the language's own declarations
decisions.gist: What to call the built-in namespace that holds the compiler's own type declarations.
decisions.lesson:
A namespace is a labelled drawer for names. Jet already has `core.files`, `core.net`, and their siblings. You open one with a line like `use core.files as fs`. The label is part of what a person types and reads. It stays with the language for as long as the language lasts.

This ballot needs a new drawer, and it is unusual. Everything in it is written by the compiler, not by a person.

Here is why it appeared. Jet has markers, the `#Name` annotations you attach to code. Many take arguments, such as `#Rule(target: Track)`. Today the type of that argument exists only inside the compiler. You can see `Track` in an error message but you cannot name it, complete it, or look it up. Card #1293 fixes that by declaring those fourteen argument types as ordinary enums, generated from the compiler's own registry, so that errors, hovers, documentation, and reflection all read one source.

Those declarations need somewhere to live. Two neighbouring rulings send more into the same place. Card #1292 moves the physical dimensions out of a compiler table and into ordinary declarations. Card #1294 turns states, taint kinds, and effect leaves into enums. So the drawer is likely to hold the language's own declarations in general, not only marker arguments.

The name matters because it appears in error messages, in completion lists, in documentation, and in any `use` line an expert writes to reach inside. Picking it once, before the first release, avoids a rename later.
decisions.story:
Marco is reading an error that says his marker argument must be a `Track`. He wants to know what values a `Track` can take. He types the name into his editor, gets nothing, and searches the standard library index, which does not list it.

After #1293 lands, the answer is a real declaration he can open, and the path to it is whatever this ballot decides. Marco reads that path every time an error sends him to one of these types, which is often.

options.name: core.lang
options.detail: The drawer for everything the language declares about itself: marker argument types now, dimensions and fact enums as their cards land. The word is short, is already the convention in several large ecosystems, and does not promise anything narrower than what will end up inside. A reader who sees `core.lang.Track` can guess it is the language's own vocabulary.
options.technical: Reserved path `core.lang`, generated from `Policy::APPLIED_RULES` signatures with a drift-guard test. Open for the prelude declarations from D-DIMENSION-OPEN1 and D-FACTMODEL1 without a second reservation. I7 rows cover the path and the generated enum names.
options.code:
use core.lang as lang

t :: lang.Track.Backend
m :: lang.Maturity.Stable

// later cards land in the same drawer:
d :: lang.Length          // from the open-dimension work

options.name: core.marker
options.detail: The drawer says exactly what is in it today: the argument types that markers take. Someone who reads an error about a marker argument and then sees `core.marker.Track` needs no explanation at all. The cost is that the neighbouring work does not fit. Dimensions and fact enums are not marker arguments, so they need a second drawer or an awkward home.
options.technical: Reserved path `core.marker`, same generation and drift guard as A. D-DIMENSION-OPEN1 prelude dimensions and D-FACTMODEL1 fact enums would need their own reserved path, so this option accepts two reservations instead of one.
options.code:
use core.marker as mk

t :: mk.Track.Backend
m :: mk.Maturity.Stable

// dimensions would need somewhere else:
d :: core.units.Length

options.name: core.spec
options.detail: The drawer holds the parts of the specification that are written as code rather than prose: what a track is, what a maturity level is, what the base dimensions are. It reads as authoritative, and it invites the reader to treat the contents as law they can open and read. The risk is confusion with a test specification, which is a common meaning of the word.
options.technical: Reserved path `core.spec`, same generation and drift guard as A. Scope identical to A. The naming risk is collision with the ordinary software meaning of "spec" as a test or an interface description, which appears in Jet's own docs.
options.code:
use core.spec as spec

t :: spec.Track.Backend
m :: spec.Maturity.Stable
d :: spec.Length

options.name: core.panel
options.detail: The instrument panel: the fixed set of dials and switches the aircraft itself provides, as opposed to the cargo you load. It matches the aviation vocabulary the project uses elsewhere and it reads as a place you consult rather than a place you extend. The cost is that a newcomer cannot guess the contents from the word without being told the metaphor once.
options.technical: Reserved path `core.panel`, same generation and drift guard as A. Scope identical to A. Discoverability rests on documentation and on error messages naming the full path, since the word carries no ecosystem convention.
options.code:
use core.panel as panel

t :: panel.Track.Backend
m :: panel.Maturity.Stable
d :: panel.Length

options.name: No namespace: the names sit in the prelude
options.detail: `Track` and `Maturity` are simply in scope, like `Int` and `String`, with no path and no import. The shortest thing to read and to type. The cost is fourteen more names competing with whatever a user wants to call their own types, growing as the neighbouring cards add dimensions and fact enums.
options.technical: Declarations join the ordinary prelude scope with no reserved path. Every added name is a potential shadowing conflict with user code, and the set grows with D-DIMENSION-OPEN1 and D-FACTMODEL1. Shadowing rules and a reserved-name policy would have to be decided as part of this option.
options.code:
t :: Track.Backend
m :: Maturity.Stable
d :: Length

// a user type of the same name now has to be renamed:
struct Track { … }        // conflict

comparisons.note: `java.lang` holds the language's own types and is the one package imported for you. The word has carried this meaning for thirty years.
comparisons.code:
// no import needed
String s = "hi";   // java.lang.String

comparisons.note: `std::marker` holds language-level marker traits, so the narrower word also has an ecosystem precedent.
`System.Runtime.CompilerServices` holds compiler-generated declarations, and is widely cited as a name that tells a reader nothing useful.

recommendation.why: Two ratified rulings on neighbouring cards already send prelude dimensions and fact enums into this same drawer. `core.lang` is the only candidate whose word covers all three without stretching, so one reservation serves the whole epoch.

whyNot.reason: Dimensions and fact enums are not marker arguments, so this name forces a second reserved namespace within the same epoch and splits one idea across two paths.
"Spec" already means a test or an interface description in Jet's own documentation, so the path would collide with an established meaning on first read.
The word carries no meaning until someone explains the metaphor, and this path appears mostly in error messages, where a reader has no room to learn one.
It adds fourteen names to the global scope now and more as the neighbouring cards land, so ordinary words like `Track` and `Length` stop being available to user code.

recommendation.tradeoff: `core.lang` says less about the contents than `core.marker` does today, so a first-time reader learns what is inside by opening it. That is accepted because the contents will outgrow any narrower word within this epoch.

decisions.title: Lossless widening covers floats too (amends D-FLOATW1)
decisions.outcome: Implicit lossless widening covers floats as well as whole numbers. An F32 moves on its own into Float, exactly as a narrow whole number moves into a wider whole number; nothing ever narrows on its own. This amends D-FLOATW1, which today makes mixing F32 and Float a compile error with a convert fix-it. Owner words (2026-07-28): "Ok, again we want beginner magic out of the box and full expert control. So let's go with option f but for both int and floats". With D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F this is the ruled surface: one widening law across the whole numeric menu.
decisions.comment: Implicit lossless widening covers floats as well as whole numbers. An F32 moves on its own into Float, exactly as a narrow whole number moves into a wider whole number; nothing ever narrows on its own. This amends D-FLOATW1, which today makes mixing F32 and Float a compile error with a convert fix-it. Owner words (2026-07-28): "Ok, again we want beginner magic out of the box and full expert control. So let's go with option f but for both int and floats". With D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F this is the ruled surface: one widening law across the whole numeric menu.

decisions.title: Does automatic widening cross between whole numbers and decimals
decisions.gist: Whether a whole number can meet a decimal number without you writing a conversion.
decisions.lesson:
You have just ruled that a number widens on its own whenever nothing can be lost. A 16-bit whole number becomes a 32-bit one by itself. An `F32` becomes a `Float` by itself. Nothing ever narrows on its own.

That rule was written about whole numbers meeting whole numbers, and decimals meeting decimals. It does not say what happens when the two kinds meet, and the rule as stated answers that question by accident. Here is why.

A `Float` is a 64-bit decimal. It can hold every 32-bit whole number exactly, all four billion of them. So under a strict reading of "widens when nothing is lost", an `I32` would move into a `Float` on its own.

But `Int`, the everyday whole number, is 64 bits. A 64-bit decimal cannot hold every 64-bit whole number exactly. Above about nine thousand million million, values start rounding. So `Int` would not move into `Float`.

That is the awkward part. Read strictly, the rule gives the automatic conversion to `I32`, which is an expert's type for hardware and foreign libraries, and refuses it to `Int`, which is what every beginner writes. The magic would land on the wrong side.

So this needs a deliberate pick rather than a strict reading. There is also a separate and much smaller case worth noticing: a bare numeral. When you write `price * 3`, the `3` you typed has no kind yet, so letting it become a decimal costs nothing and converts nothing you stored.

One more thing matters, because this is the ground where MATLAB and Python are strong. Both let a whole number meet a decimal with no ceremony at all. Both pay for it in the same place: above the exact range, the value quietly rounds and nothing tells you. Jet can take the convenience without taking the silence, because it already stops the program on whole-number overflow rather than wrapping.
decisions.story:
Ana is pricing an order. She writes `total :: price * 3` where `price` is a decimal, and the compiler tells her to write `3.0` instead. She fixes it and moves on, slightly puzzled, since she meant three either way.

Later she writes `total :: price * quantity`, where `quantity` is a whole number she read from a form. Same message. This time the fix is a real decision, because a whole number and a decimal are genuinely different things and she has to say which she wants.

options.name: Strict reading: cross whenever nothing is lost
options.detail:
One law, applied without exception. A whole number moves into a decimal whenever every one of its values is held exactly. `I32` and everything narrower crosses into `Float`. `Int` does not, because a 64-bit decimal cannot hold every 64-bit whole number.

The law is easy to state and never loses a value. The cost is where the magic lands. The expert's `I32` gets it and the beginner's `Int` does not, which is the opposite of what we are aiming for.
options.technical: Containment ordering extended across the integer and float families. Lossless pairs: I8, I16, I32, U8, U16, U32 into Float; I8, I16, U8, U16 into F32. Lossy and therefore refused: I64, U64, Int into Float; I32, U32 into F32, since F32 is exact only to 2^24. Expression type is the join. Error copy must explain why the narrower type crossed and the default did not.

options.name: Widening stays inside its own kind
options.detail:
Whole numbers widen among whole numbers. Decimals widen among decimals. Crossing between the two is always something you write. One sentence, no exceptions, no cases to remember.

The cost is that the smallest version of the friction stays. Writing `price * 3` is still refused and still asks you for `3.0`, even though the numeral you typed has no kind and converting it loses nothing.
options.technical: Containment ordering applies within the integer family and within the float family only. Cross-kind requires the destination-owned conversion, Float.from_int and its siblings, per D-SHAPE-CONVERT1. The current E0109 cross-kind copy stays as it is, including the "write 2.0 instead of 2" fix line.
options.code:
counts :: I32.{ 1000 }
scale :: 2.5
out :: counts * scale                    // refused
out2 :: Float.from_i32(counts) * scale   // what you write

price :: 19.99
with_fee :: price * 3                    // refused: write 3.0
with_fee2 :: price * 3.0                 // what you write

options.name: Every whole number crosses into a decimal
options.detail:
Any whole number meets any decimal, `Int` included, and the result is a decimal. This is what C, Java, and JavaScript do, so it will feel like arithmetic simply working. The beginner never meets the wall.

The cost is real and it is the kind Jet exists to prevent. Above about nine thousand million million, a whole number quietly loses its exact value on the way into a decimal. That range holds account identifiers, database keys, nanosecond timestamps, and currency held in the smallest unit.
options.technical: Implicit conversion from every integer type to the float type of the other operand. I64, U64, and Int into Float round beyond 2^53, and I32 into F32 rounds beyond 2^24. No diagnostic is possible at the conversion site, because whether a given value rounds is a runtime fact. This is a deliberate exception to the no-silent-loss posture and must be stated as one in the spec.
options.code:
id :: 9007199254740993        // an Int, exact
rate :: 1.0
out :: id * rate              // ok, and out is 9007199254740992.0

// the last digit is gone, and nothing warned you

price :: 19.99
with_fee :: price * 3         // ok
total :: price * quantity     // ok for any whole number

options.name: Numerals cross; stored values do not
options.detail:
A numeral you type takes whichever kind the other side is, so `price * 3` works and means what you wrote. A value you stored as a whole number still needs an explicit conversion to become a decimal.

This puts the magic exactly where nothing is at stake. A numeral has no kind until it is used, so giving it one converts nothing and can lose nothing you were holding. A stored whole number is a thing you chose, and turning it into a decimal stays a decision you write down.
options.technical: Within-kind containment widening as in B, plus untyped numeric literals resolving against the expected type across both families. A literal is checked at compile time for exact representability at the destination, so an out-of-range or inexact literal is a compile error rather than a rounded value. Stored values keep D-SHAPE-CONVERT1's destination-owned conversion. This is the same context rule the ratified numeral ruling already uses.
options.code:
price :: 19.99
with_fee :: price * 3         // ok, 3 is a decimal here

small :: F32.{ 1.5 }
out :: small + 2              // ok, 2 is an F32 here

n :: 5                        // a stored Int
bad :: price * n              // refused: write Float.from_int(n)

counts :: I32.{ 1000 }
bad2 :: counts * price        // refused: it is stored, so you say so

options.name: Everything crosses, and a cross that cannot be proved exact is checked
options.detail:
Any whole number meets any decimal, `Int` included, so the ordinary line works with nothing written. Where the compiler can prove the value survives, as with an `I32` into a `Float`, the conversion is free and nothing is checked.

Where it cannot, as with a 64-bit whole number, the conversion is checked as it happens and stops the program if the value would not survive. You get the convenience of MATLAB and Python, and you never lose an identifier in silence.

Experts opt out per operation, the same way they already opt out of overflow trapping.
options.technical: Cross-kind implicit conversion for every integer and float pair. The compiler proves exactness statically where the source value set is contained in the destination: I8, I16, I32, U8, U16, U32 into Float, and I8, I16, U8, U16 into F32 emit no check. The remaining pairs emit a round-trip check on conversion and trap on mismatch, reusing the D-NUMOPS1 trap path and its per-operation escapes. Numerals keep their compile-time exactness check and never emit a runtime check.
options.code:
counts :: I32.{ 1000 }
scale :: 2.5
out :: counts * scale         // free, an I32 fits a Float exactly

price :: 19.99
qty :: 5
total :: price * qty          // works, and qty is checked as it converts

id :: 9007199254740993        // an Int past the exact range
bad :: id * 1.0               // stops here, instead of quietly dropping a digit

// expert escape, the same shape as the overflow escapes:
fast :: price * approx(qty)   // no check, loss accepted on purpose

comparisons.note: A whole number meets a decimal with no ceremony, and the result is a decimal. Above the exact range the value rounds and nothing is reported.
comparisons.code:
>>> 9007199254740993 + 1.0
9007199254740992.0        # a digit is gone, no warning

>>> 9007199254740993 == 9007199254740992.0
False                     # comparison is exact; only arithmetic loses

comparisons.note: Everything is a double unless you say otherwise. An integer meeting a scalar double takes the integer type, rounds, and saturates. Two different integer classes are an error.
comparisons.code:
>> int8(5) * 2.5
ans = 13            % int8: computed as 12.5, rounded, silently

>> int8(127) + int8(1)
ans = 127           % saturates instead of trapping

>> int8(1) + int16(1)
Error: Integers can only be combined with integers of the same class

comparisons.note: The array world moved toward weak literals in 2024. A written numeral takes the array type, an out-of-range numeral is an error, and stored values promote by a fixed table.
comparisons.code:
>>> np.int8(1) + 1
np.int8(2)                # the numeral is weak, no promotion

>>> np.uint8(1) + 300
OverflowError             # out of range for the dtype

>>> np.int64(1) + np.float32(1)
np.float64(2.0)           # stored values promote to hold both

comparisons.note: Every whole number converts into a decimal on its own, and the loss above the exact range is silent. This is option C.
comparisons.code:
long id = 9007199254740993L;
double d = id;   /* becomes 9007199254740992.0, no warning */

comparisons.note: None of them cross on their own. All three type a written numeral from context, which is option D.

recommendation.why: It is the only option that matches MATLAB and Python for convenience and then beats them where they lose. The ordinary line works with nothing written, and a value that cannot survive the crossing stops the program instead of rounding in silence.

whyNot.reason: It hands the automatic conversion to `I32`, an expert type for hardware and foreign code, and refuses it to `Int`, which is what a beginner writes. The magic lands on the wrong side.
It leaves the smallest and most common friction in place. `price * 3` still asks you to retype the numeral, and `price * quantity` still needs a conversion written out.
This is exactly what MATLAB and Python already do, including the silent rounding above the exact range. Copying it means matching them rather than beating them.
It is safe and it is simple, but it still refuses `price * quantity`, which is the line a MATLAB or Python user writes without thinking about it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A crossing from a 64-bit whole number carries a check and can stop the program. That is the same bargain overflow trapping already makes, and the check is provably unnecessary for `I32` and narrower, so it never appears on those paths.

decisions.title: Package auto-derive switch and type opt-in spelling
decisions.gist: Choose where packages disable auto-derive and how a type turns one trait back on.
decisions.lesson:
An auto-derive is a compiler-written trait implementation. Jet already writes Printable, Equatable, and Debug implementations when every field supports the trait. This default removes routine code from ordinary types.

D-AUTODERIVE1=E fixes the behavior. Auto-derive is on by default. A package can turn it off. A type can reject one automatic trait. A hand-written implementation always wins.

A package manifest stores settings that apply to every source file in that package. A local opt-in restores selected traits for one type after the package switch disables automatic derives.

The remaining choice is syntax, not behavior. The package setting must be easy to find and must not look like package identity. The type spelling must name selected traits clearly.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game-save library. Most projects want free printing and equality. This audited package lists every generated trait. Sam still wants selected records to derive all three built-ins. Secret types use hand-written Debug output.

options.name: Policy block with direct trait markers
options.detail: Put auto_derive in the existing policy block. A type opts in with each trait's own marker. The spelling follows Jet's marker and trait naming law.
options.technical: Use policy: .{ auto_derive: false }. The default is true. Add active type-site rows for Printable, Equatable, and Debug. This narrowly amends D-MARK-DEBUG1 because package-off gives #Debug a required job. #[Printable, Equatable, Debug] records explicit derives. #NoAuto(Trait) rejects only silent auto. A direct opt-in and #NoAuto for the same trait produce a diagnostic. A hand-written impl wins over package policy, opt-in, and reject.

options.name: Payload field with one Auto marker
options.detail: Put auto_derive beside package identity. Use one #Auto marker with a trait list. The local spelling is compact, but it hides the direct trait relationship.
options.technical: Use payload: .{ auto_derive: false }. Add #Auto(Printable, Equatable, Debug) as one type-site rule with a closed built-in trait list. Keep #Debug retired. #NoAuto remains the inverse control. Repeating one trait in both lists produces a diagnostic. A hand-written impl wins over both lists.

options.name: Derives block with body opt-ins
options.detail: Give derive policy its own manifest block. Each type lists opt-ins inside its body. This separates policy, but it adds a manifest section and hides type facts.
options.technical: Use derives: .{ auto_derive: false }. Restore derive Printable;, derive Equatable;, and derive Debug; as explicit built-in requests. These lines remain valid when auto-derive is on. This amends the retired Debug body spelling. #NoAuto continues to control silent auto. A hand-written impl wins.

options.name: Policy block with signed trait markers
options.detail: Put auto_derive in the policy block. A bare trait opts in. A trait with ! opts out. One marker list can mix both choices.
options.technical: Use policy: .{ auto_derive: true|false }. A single reject is #!Printable. A mixed list is #[!Debug, !Equatable, Printable]. Missing traits follow the package default. Positive traits request generation when fields qualify. Negative traits reject only automatic generation. A hand-written impl wins over package policy and either sign. This option amends D-AUTODERIVE1=E by replacing #NoAuto(Trait) with the signed form.

comparisons.note: Rust has no silent derive for user types. Each type names generated traits directly. Package-wide compiler policy uses separate manifest sections.
Swift names a protocol directly on the type. The compiler writes the implementation when fields qualify. A hand-written implementation replaces synthesis.
A data class gets equality and text output automatically. A type can override generated members. Kotlin has no package switch for this behavior.

recommendation.why: The policy block already holds package-wide compiler rules. Signed trait markers use one list for opt-in and opt-out. The same type stays explicit across package defaults.

whyNot.reason: #NoAuto adds a separate negative marker beside direct positive trait markers. Signed names express both directions through one existing marker list.
Payload describes package identity and compatibility. Compiler generation policy has a different job. #Auto also weakens the direct link between a trait and its marker.
A new derives block creates another manifest category for one Boolean setting. Body lines also hide important type facts below the declaration header.
