recommendation.tradeoff: This adds ! to applied-rule names and replaces the ratified #NoAuto spelling. The polarity matches effect rejection, but tooling must parse and show the sign.

decisions.title: Name a structural derived dimension
decisions.gist: How ordinary Jet source gives a standard name to a dimension made from other dimensions.
decisions.lesson:
A base dimension is one independent axis, such as Mass, Length, or Time. A derived dimension combines those axes. Force is Mass times Length divided by Time twice.

Jet can calculate that structure when values multiply and divide. The result has a safe type even when nobody names it.

D-DIMENSION-OPEN1 also requires standard derived units such as newton and joule in ordinary Jet source. A unit suffix needs a declared family member. The current ruled spelling can only mint a new independent axis, so it cannot honestly declare newton as Force.

This choice adds the missing claim. The claim must preserve the structural identity. It must not create a second Force axis or hide a compiler table.
decisions.explainer:
Owner question (2026-07-30): how do mixed units such as pound-force and newton stay exact and fast, and what ships by default?

Precision comes from one coherent anchor, not pairwise conversion tables. Under A, a derived family's base member is coherent: exactly 1 of the product of its base dimensions' base units. So 1 newton = 1 kilogram*meter/second/second by construction. Every other unit of that dimension is an exact arbitrary-precision rational scale from that anchor (ratified D-QUANTITY-DECL1). Nearly every standard unit is defined exactly against SI: the pound is exactly 0.45359237 kg and standard gravity is exactly 9.80665 m/s^2, so 1 pound-force = 4.4482216152605 newton exactly. Any conversion between two units of one dimension is a single ratio of two exact rationals, folded at compile time. Implicit conversion happens only when exact; anything lossy requires the explicit rounded form (ratified D-UNIT-CONV1). A value therefore rounds at most once, and only when the program asks.

Speed: dimensions and units erase after sema. A conversion is one runtime multiply (plus one add for affine units such as celsius) against a compile-time constant. Same-unit arithmetic costs zero.

Coverage is a prelude duty already ratified in D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D and applies regardless of this ballot's outcome: all seven SI base dimensions; every SI named derived unit (hertz, newton, pascal, joule, watt, coulomb, volt, farad, ohm, siemens, weber, tesla, henry, lumen, lux, becquerel, gray, sievert, katal, radian, steradian, degree Celsius); the SI prefix ladder; accepted non-SI units (litre, tonne, minute, hour, day, degree, electronvolt, dalton, astronomical unit, bar, mmHg); and customary units with exact defined scales (inch, foot, yard, mile, ounce, pound, pound-force, psi, gallon, mph). Electronics is fully covered: ampere is a base dimension; volt, ohm, farad, henry, siemens, weber, tesla, and coulomb are coherent derived families. This ballot only decides the spelling that lets ordinary Jet source declare those derived families.
decisions.story: Maya writes a mechanics simulator. She wants `4newton` to match the type of `4kg * 1meter / 1second / 1second` without compiler magic.

options.name: Dimension expression in the family header
options.detail: A derived family states its structure beside its name. Its base member is coherent: exactly one of the product of the base dimensions' base units. Every other member, including foreign units like pound-force, is an exact rational scale from that anchor. Members then use the existing unit-family scale and offset rules. Base families keep the short `dimension` flag.
options.technical: Extend the existing `#UnitFamily` marker with a `dimension:` expression over declared dimension names and `*` or `/`. Sema normalizes the expression to the same open exponent map used by value arithmetic. The base member is pinned coherent (1 newton = 1 kilogram*meter/second/second), so structurally computed quantities and named members share one exact scale spine. Non-coherent units (pound-force, psi) are ordinary scaled members; every conversion is one exact rational ratio folded at compile time per D-QUANTITY-DECL1 and D-UNIT-CONV1. Cycles, unknown names, affine factors, and zero or overflowing exponents are errors.

options.name: A member gives the structural witness
options.detail: The base member states one exact unit equation. Jet gets the family dimension and scale from that equation. Other members remain relative to the base.
options.technical: Extend unit-member metadata with one `equals:` quantity expression on the canonical base member. Sema evaluates only exact unit products and ratios at compile time. The family receives the witness dimension and scale. Cycles and affine witness units are errors.

options.name: Ordinary named quantity functions
options.detail: The prelude defines functions that build structural quantities. No family claims the dimension. Users write multiplication with the named function instead of a numeric suffix.
options.technical: Add no derived-family grammar. Prelude functions return the inferred structural Quantity type from ordinary value arithmetic. Base unit suffixes stay available. Derived names are values, not UnitFamily members, so formatting uses base-unit products.

comparisons.note: A derived unit names an equation over existing measures. The compiler keeps the normalized structure.
comparisons.code:
[<Measure>] type kg
[<Measure>] type m
[<Measure>] type s
[<Measure>] type N = kg m / s^2

comparisons.note: A named derived dimension is an alias for a normalized equation. Units then attach scales to that dimension.

recommendation.why: The family header owns family identity, so it is the clearest place to state that Force is an existing structure. Base and derived units keep one mechanism. Pinning the base member coherent gives one exact scale spine, so mixed units such as pound-force convert by a single exact ratio.

whyNot.reason: It hides a type-level fact inside one value member and makes readers derive family identity from a scale witness.
It loses the `4newton` unit literal and makes standard derived units feel unlike the base units.

recommendation.tradeoff: The marker gains a small compile-time dimension-expression grammar. It reuses existing names and arithmetic marks, and sema erases the result before runtime.

decisions.title: Represent standard unit scales that are not exact rationals
decisions.gist: How Jet ships degrees, daltons, and conventional mmHg honestly without weakening the exact-rational unit spine.
decisions.lesson:
Most standard unit conversions are exact rational numbers. One inch is exactly 0.0254 metre. One pound-force is exactly 4.4482216152605 newton. Jet can reduce those ratios at compile time.

Three required cases need more provenance. A degree is exactly pi/180 radian. That definition is exact, but pi is irrational, not a rational number. A dalton is one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom's mass. Its value in kilograms is measured, and the current BIPM/CODATA value carries uncertainty. Millimetre of mercury is convention-sensitive: NIST distinguishes a conventional coefficient from a physical mercury column and does not present plain mmHg as one timeless exact definition.

The 2026 BIPM SI Brochure states 1 degree = pi/180 radian and 1 dalton = 1.66053906892(52)e-27 kilogram. CODATA reports relative uncertainty 3.1e-10 for the dalton-to-kilogram value. Sources: https://doi.org/10.59161/AUEZ1291, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/JPCRD2022CODATA.pdf, and https://www.nist.gov/pml/special-publication-811/nist-guide-si-appendix-b-conversion-factors/nist-guide-si-appendix-b8.

Calling these plain exact rationals would be false or ambiguous. Omitting them would break the ratified full standard battery. This choice adds the smallest honest representation.
decisions.story: Leila mixes telescope angles in degrees with a simulation in radians, compares molecular masses in daltons with a balance model in kilograms, and imports a clinical pressure in mmHg. She needs all three conversions, and she needs Jet to distinguish exact definitions, measured values, and named conventions.
decisions.inWild:
angle :: 90degree
phase :: angle.to<Radian>()

mass :: 12dalton
kg_mass :: mass.to<Kilogram>()

pressure :: 120mmHg
// Angle is exact-by-definition through pi.
// Mass is measured. Pressure names a published convention.

options.name: Typed scale provenance; measured crossings stay explicit
options.detail: Unit declarations have four honest scale classes: exact rational, exact symbolic, conventional, and measured. Degrees use an exact symbolic pi ratio. Daltons use a versioned central value, uncertainty, and source. Conventional mmHg names its published coefficient and source instead of pretending to be a physical mercury column. Rational and symbolic definitions keep the ordinary conversion path. A measured crossing must use the existing explicit rounded conversion form, whose audit output names the value, uncertainty, and source.
options.technical: Extend the unit scale fact from one rational to a tagged value: Rational(num, den), SymbolicPi(num, den), Conventional(decimal, source_id), or Measured(decimal, standard_uncertainty, source_id). SymbolicPi is folded once at the destination numeric precision; it is exact-by-definition even though a finite numeric result rounds. Measured facts are never labeled exact and never enter implicit conversion. Conventional facts retain their named standard and provenance. The prelude pins BIPM, CODATA, and NIST editions. API facts and diagnostics preserve every tag and source. Same-unit arithmetic stays zero-cost; a conversion remains one multiply.

options.name: Typed provenance; measured crossings are automatic
options.detail: Use the same four scale classes, but a measured unit converts automatically through its current central value. Audit output still exposes the uncertainty and source. This is the smoothest beginner experience, but ordinary arithmetic can silently depend on a measured constant that may change with a later CODATA edition.
options.technical: Same representation as A. The type checker admits Measured in implicit conversion and codegen multiplies by the pinned central value. The result type does not carry uncertainty because Jet has no uncertainty-propagating quantity in this card.

options.name: Exact scales only; defer the exceptional units
options.detail: Keep rational scales only. Ship all unambiguous exactly defined rational units now, but omit degree, arcminute, arcsecond, dalton, and mmHg until a later constants or uncertainty system exists.
options.technical: No representation change. This preserves the current exact law but violates the ratified requirement that the default prelude include every listed standard unit.
options.code: // degree, dalton, and mmHg are unavailable in this release

options.name: Freeze decimal approximations as rationals
options.detail: Write long decimal approximations for pi/180, the dalton conversion, and mmHg, then treat those finite decimals as exact rational scales. It is simple and fast, but it makes a false precision claim, hides the dalton's measurement uncertainty, and erases the mmHg convention.
options.technical: No new fact shape. The prelude stores finite decimals as rational numerators and denominators. Diagnostics and audit output cannot distinguish definitions, approximations, and measurements.

comparisons.note: The current authoritative table writes angular scales with pi and writes the dalton with parenthesized uncertainty. It does not present either as an exact decimal ratio.
CODATA versions measured constants and publishes the value, standard uncertainty, relative uncertainty, and source edition together.
comparisons.code: dalton: central value + standard uncertainty + CODATA edition

recommendation.why: A keeps the batteries, the precision claim, and the audit trail. Exact definitions stay convenient and fast. Measured crossings remain available but cannot masquerade as exact arithmetic.

whyNot.reason: It silently inserts a measured central value into ordinary arithmetic without carrying uncertainty.
It breaks the owner's full standard-unit requirement.
It labels approximations and measurements as exact, which is unacceptable for scientific work.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dalton-to-kilogram conversion has explicit rounding ceremony. The diagnostic can show the exact fix and the pinned BIPM/CODATA provenance.

decisions.title: Widening where several branches produce one value
decisions.gist: Whether a value built from two branches of different number widths takes the wider one, or is refused.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has one default whole-number type, `Int`, plus a sized menu for experts: `I8`, `U8`, `I32`, `U64`, and friends. The number in the name is how many bits of storage a value gets. A `U8` holds 0 through 255. An `Int` holds every whole number up to about nine quintillion.

Widening means moving a value into a type that holds every value the old type could hold. Moving 200 out of a `U8` into an `Int` cannot lose anything, so Jet does it silently. Moving the other direction could lose data, so Jet never does it on its own.

The ratified rule D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F applies that idea in four places: operators, arguments, returns, and assignments. The same rule also gives a written numeral its smallest fitting type first. So the expression `40 + 2` is a `U8`, because 42 fits in one byte.

A join is a fifth place, and the rule never named it. A join happens when one value has more than one producer. In `answer :: if ready -> 40 + 2 else -> 0` there are two producers. The first is a `U8`. The second is a plain `Int`.

Today Jet compares the two branch types for exact equality. It sees `U8` beside `Int` and reports E0124. Nothing was lost and no value was in danger, so the refusal reads as a compiler bug to whoever wrote four ordinary numerals.

The same arithmetic is accepted one line earlier, as a binding or an argument, because those places already follow the widening rule. This decision picks the rule that joins follow.
decisions.story: Priya writes firmware dashboards in Jet. She reads a byte from a sensor register, then picks a retry budget with `budget :: if aggressive -> 8 + 8 else -> 0`. Jet refuses it and tells her the branches produce `U8` and `Int`. She never asked for a byte anywhere; she typed four plain numbers. Her fix is to spell a width she does not care about, in code that had no sized types in it.

options.name: One join law wherever a value has several producers
options.detail: Every place a single value comes from more than one producer follows the widening rule already used by operators. That covers `if` and `switch` value branches, loop values, and the elements of a list. One side widens to the other. Jet never invents a third type and never narrows. Priya's `backoff` becomes an `Int`, because a byte fits in one.
options.technical: Branch and element joins call the same value-set containment join as binary operators: `Type::numeric_join`, one step, no least-upper-bound search. E0124 stays for pairs with no containment, such as `U8` beside `I8`. List element joins reuse the same call, so `[byte, 300]` yields `[U16]` instead of an error. No narrowing path is added.
options.code:
backoff :: if register > 200 -> 40 + 2 else -> 0   // Int
sizes   :: [U8.{1}, 300]                          // [U16]
mixed   :: if flag -> U8.{1} else -> I8.{1}       // still E0124: neither holds the other

options.name: Control-flow branches only
options.detail: `if` and `switch` value branches and loop values widen; collection literals keep exact matching. Priya's code compiles. A list holding a byte beside 300 still fails, so the rule has to be learned twice: once for branches, once for collections.
options.technical: Join applied in `infer_if_value`, `infer_switch_value`, and yielding-loop item typing only. `infer_list_lit` keeps exact-equality element checking and its current E0074/E0124 paths.
options.code:
backoff :: if register > 200 -> 40 + 2 else -> 0   // Int
sizes   :: [U8.{1}, 300]                          // refused: element types differ

options.name: Exact match stays, with a teaching error
options.detail: Branch types must be identical. Priya keeps her error, but the message names the wider type and offers the exact edit that fixes it. The sized menu stays strictly separated once a value has several producers, which is easy to state and easy to predict.
options.technical: E0124 keeps exact equality. The fix line gains the computed widening target and a suggested edit, for example annotating the narrow branch or wrapping it in the destination constructor. No inference change.

options.name: A numeral with no sized neighbour stays Int
options.detail: Drop the smallest-fitting-type step when nothing sized sits beside the numeral. `40 + 2` becomes an `Int`, so Priya's two branches already agree and no join rule is needed. The cost is that a numeral no longer arrives pre-sized, so a byte-typed destination must be reached through the surrounding context instead.
options.technical: `minimal_integer_literal_type` narrows only with a fixed-width peer; with no peer both operands stay `Int`. The expected-type channel must then thread destination width into literal arithmetic, or `accept_u8(1 + 2)` regresses to E0112 since `Int` does not widen to `U8`.

comparisons.note: Branches must already have one type; there is no implicit widening, so the programmer writes a cast.
The conditional operator applies the usual arithmetic conversions, so the result silently takes the wider type.
comparisons.code:
unsigned char b = 200;
int r = flag ? b + 1 : 0;   /* both arms promote to int */

comparisons.note: Literals have no fixed type until the whole expression is solved, so both branches settle on one type together.
comparisons.code:
let b: UInt8 = 200
let r = flag ? Int(b) + 1 : 0   // conversion is explicit; literals adapt

comparisons.note: Branches produce a union of both types, which is a third type Jet deliberately refuses to invent.
comparisons.code: const r = flag ? small : big;   // type is `Small | Big`

recommendation.why: A value with two producers asks the same question as an operator with two operands. One law answers both, so nobody has to learn where the sized menu stops mixing. Priya's numerals stay numerals, and the widening she gets can never lose a value.

whyNot.reason: A list holding a byte beside 300 still fails, so the same pair is legal in a branch and illegal one line later in a list.
It keeps a refusal the writer cannot act on without naming a width their code never mentioned, in the beginner-facing form of `if`.
It reopens the ratified smallest-fitting-type step, and `accept_u8(1 + 2)` compiles today only because that step exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: A branch result becomes width-sensitive: adding a branch can widen the whole value's type. That is acceptable because a widening never loses a value and never reaches for a third type.

decisions.title: Who guarantees the working memory the compiler needs for nested code
decisions.gist: What happens when a deeply nested program runs the compiler out of its scratch memory.
decisions.lesson:
A running program keeps a stack: a block of memory where each active function call parks its local values. Every call pushes a frame; every return pops one. The block has a fixed size, chosen when the thread starts.

On Linux the first thread of a process gets about 8 megabytes. A thread created later gets 2 megabytes by default. Nothing warns you which one you are on.

Compilers walk nested code by calling themselves. A list inside a call inside an `if` inside a lambda becomes one nested chain of calls, so nesting in the source turns into depth on the stack. Each of Jet's checking frames is large, because it carries types, spans, and scope maps.

When the frames no longer fit, the operating system stops the process immediately. There is no error to catch and no diagnostic to print. The output is one line: `fatal runtime error: stack overflow`. That is a crash, not a refusal.

Jet hits this today. The `jet` binary survives because it checks on the process's first thread, with 8 megabytes. Calling `jet::compile` from a 2-megabyte worker thread aborts on a ten-line program. Our own test suite trips it, and one test file already sets a bigger stack by hand to dodge it.

That matters beyond tests. An editor server, a build server, or any embedder calls the compiler from a pool thread. Jet promises that every refusal is a diagnostic with a code and a fix. A crash keeps that promise only by luck, depending on which thread called in.
decisions.story: Marcus runs a build server that embeds the Jet compiler and answers requests on a thread pool. One generated file with deeply nested data takes the whole server process down. His log shows a single line about a stack overflow: no file, no line, no error code, and no way to tell the user what to fix. Locally the same file compiles, because his terminal runs the compiler on the process's first thread.

options.name: The compiler owns its stack and names a depth limit
options.detail: `jet::compile` runs the checking passes on a thread it creates itself, with a stack large enough for realistic code. Past a published nesting limit it stops and reports an ordinary diagnostic naming the limit. Every caller is safe without configuring anything, and absurdly nested input gets a product error instead of a crash.
options.technical: The public entry points spawn one worker with an explicit stack size (32 MiB) and join it, so callers keep the current synchronous signature. Sema and the TIR evaluator keep a depth counter beside the existing fuel counter and emit a registered diagnostic past the limit, with a UI snapshot. The limit is documented in docs/spec/diagnostics.md and chosen to sit well inside the reserved stack.

options.name: Grow the stack on demand
options.detail: The recursive passes check how much room is left before descending, and add a fresh chunk of memory when it runs low. Depth is then bounded by available memory rather than a fixed reservation, so no realistic program is refused and no memory is reserved up front.
options.technical: Adds a stack-probing dependency (the `stacker` crate, as rustc uses) or a hand-rolled equivalent, called at each recursive entry in sema, TIR lowering, and the evaluator. Requires a new external dependency in a compiler seam crate, which I6 gates on owner approval. Missed call sites still crash, so coverage must be audited.

options.name: Publish a depth limit and refuse past it
options.detail: Keep whatever stack the caller happens to have, and count nesting instead. Past a conservative published limit the compiler reports a diagnostic. The limit must be low enough to be safe on a 2-megabyte thread, so some legal deeply nested code is refused on every platform to protect the smallest case.
options.technical: Depth counter and registered diagnostic as in A, with the limit derived from the 2 MiB worst case rather than a reserved stack. No thread spawning, no new dependency. Frame sizes then become a hard product constraint: any frame growth lowers the limit users see.
options.code:
// same diagnostic as A, but the ceiling is much lower
// Error [E0xxx]: this code nests 70 levels deep; the limit is 64

options.name: Callers configure the stack
options.detail: Document that the compiler needs a large stack, and let each caller arrange it. Our test harness and any embedder set the size themselves. Nothing changes inside the compiler, and a caller who misses the note gets today's crash.
options.technical: Document a minimum thread stack in docs/spec/architecture.md; set RUST_MIN_STACK in the test harness and spawn sized threads in the CLI, LSP, and build paths. The failure stays an abort with no diagnostic, and the contract lives only in prose.
options.code:
# test harness and embedders opt in by hand
RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 cargo test

std::thread::Builder::new()
    .stack_size(32 * 1024 * 1024)
    .spawn(|| jet::compile(source))?;

comparisons.note: Runs the compiler on a spawned thread with a large explicit stack, and additionally grows the stack on deep recursion.
comparisons.code:
// rustc_interface: spawn with an 8 MiB (or RUST_MIN_STACK) stack, then
// ensure_sufficient_stack(|| ...) around deeply recursive work

comparisons.note: Reserves a large stack and enforces a published bracket-depth limit, reporting a normal compiler error past it.
comparisons.code:
// error: bracket nesting level exceeded maximum of 256
//   note: use -fbracket-depth=N to increase maximum nesting level

comparisons.note: Counts recursion instead of trusting the stack, and raises a catchable error at a documented limit.
comparisons.code:
>>> sys.setrecursionlimit(3000)
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

comparisons.note: Goroutine stacks start tiny and grow automatically, so depth is bounded by memory, and a runaway hits a documented 1 GB ceiling.

recommendation.why: It makes the guarantee the compiler's own promise instead of the caller's homework, so Marcus's server, the editor, and the test suite are all safe by default. Nested input past the limit becomes a diagnostic with a code and a fix, which is what every other refusal in Jet already is.

whyNot.reason: It needs a new external dependency inside a compiler seam crate, and one missed recursive call site still aborts the process.
Sizing the limit for a 2-megabyte thread refuses code that fits comfortably everywhere else, and every frame that grows lowers it again.
It leaves a crash reachable from any caller who never reads the note, and prose cannot enforce a memory contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each compile pays one thread spawn and reserves address space it usually will not touch. That is acceptable because the reservation is virtual until used, and one spawn is invisible next to checking a program.

decisions.title: Fence spelling and expression entries
decisions.outcome: Respell the D-EACH1 fence as symmetric $[ ... ]$ (open $[, close ]$). Expression-position fences accept arbitrary expression entries separated by top-level commas; binding fences still require plain names. Statement fanout semantics unchanged: one statement copy per entry, lock-step across fences.
decisions.comment: Respell the D-EACH1 fence as symmetric $[ ... ]$ (open $[, close ]$). Expression-position fences accept arbitrary expression entries separated by top-level commas; binding fences still require plain names. Statement fanout semantics unchanged: one statement copy per entry, lock-step across fences.

decisions.title: Variadic newline print
decisions.outcome: print and eprint accept one or more arguments; each argument renders on its own line (print(a, b) == print(a); print(b)). Single-line composition stays with interpolation.
decisions.comment: print and eprint accept one or more arguments; each argument renders on its own line (print(a, b) == print(a); print(b)). Single-line composition stays with interpolation.

decisions.title: Task group helper set
decisions.outcome: Ship the full ergonomic group set: tasks.spawn_group(n, fn) => [Task<T>] plus list methods join_all/wait_all (consume), detach_all (consume), cancel_all, pause_all, resume_all (borrow). Beginner magic first: handles.cancel_all() must work without writing a loop.
decisions.comment: Ship the full ergonomic group set: tasks.spawn_group(n, fn) => [Task<T>] plus list methods join_all/wait_all (consume), detach_all (consume), cancel_all, pause_all, resume_all (borrow). Beginner magic first: handles.cancel_all() must work without writing a loop.

decisions.title: Remove S75 fan-out operator
decisions.outcome: Remove (not deprecate) the S75 fan-out operator f.[a, b, c] and its E0961/E0962 diagnostics. Keep S76 [T#N] fixed-size lists and their typed literal heads.
decisions.comment: Remove (not deprecate) the S75 fan-out operator f.[a, b, c] and its E0961/E0962 diagnostics. Keep S76 [T#N] fixed-size lists and their typed literal heads.

decisions.title: Labeling a loop that produces no value
decisions.gist: How to name a pure-effect loop so `break(name)` and `next(name)` can target it.
decisions.lesson:
When loops nest, `break` and `next` normally act on the innermost one. To act on an outer loop instead, that loop needs a name: `break(outer)` exits the loop named `outer`.

Today a loop gets its name from binding syntax. Writing `found :: loop { … }` does two jobs at once: it declares that the loop's break payload lands in `found`, and it makes `found` a target for `break` and `next`. When the loop produces a value, this is elegant — the name of the destination is the name of the loop.

The wrinkle appears with loops that produce nothing. A logging sweep or a retry driver is pure effect; it has no value to bind. To label it today you must still write `sweep :: loop { … }`, which binds the empty value Void to `sweep`. The binding is harmless but dishonest: it looks like data flow and is really only a control label.

The question is whether that dishonesty matters enough to give loops a second way to get a name, or whether one slightly awkward spelling is better than two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Marco writes a crawler: an outer loop over sites, an inner loop over pages. When a site returns a rate-limit error he wants `next(sites)` — skip to the next site. His outer loop returns nothing, so to name it he writes `sites :: loop site; queue { … }` and now has a binding `sites` that holds Void forever. His reviewer asks what `sites` stores. The honest answer is: nothing, it exists only so `next` can aim at it.

options.name: Keep binding-as-label, accept the Void binding
options.detail: No change. A labeled effect loop binds Void to its name. One mechanism covers both value loops and labels; the cost is an occasional binding that exists only for control. The compiler already accepts it and the unused Void value is inert.
options.technical: No grammar or sema change. Optionally suppress unused-binding lints for Void-typed loop bindings that are used as control targets.

options.name: Head label only: loop(name)
options.detail: A loop is named in its head, mirroring how exits already target: `loop(sites) site; queue { … }`. The binding form stops being a control target — `found :: loop` still binds the payload, but `break(found)` no longer resolves to it; you would write `found :: loop(search) { break(search, -1) }`. One naming mechanism, but value loops that want a targeted break now carry both a binding and a label.
options.technical: Grammar: optional `( name )` immediately after KW_LOOP. Loop names move to a control-label namespace; D-LOOPLABEL3's binding-name targeting is retired.

options.name: Both: binding names value loops, head label for effect loops
options.detail: Value loops keep the elegant `found :: loop { break(found, -1) }`. Effect loops gain `loop(sites) …` so nobody binds Void as a label. Every loop has exactly one natural spelling, but the language now has two labeling mechanisms and style guides must say when each applies.
options.code:
found :: loop { break(found, -1) }   // value loop: binding is the label
loop(sites) site; queue {             // effect loop: head label
    next(sites)
}
options.technical: Both mechanisms feed one label namespace; a loop with both a binding and a head label is an error to keep targeting unambiguous.

comparisons.note: Python has no labeled break at all. Breaking out of nested loops requires a flag variable, an exception, or refactoring into a function — a long-standing, frequently-cited pain point. Any of these options beats it.
Rust labels at the head with a lifetime-style tick: `'outer: for … { break 'outer; }`. Labels live in their own namespace and never pretend to be bindings.
JavaScript uses statement labels (`sites: for (…)`), also purely in a label namespace. They work but read as an obscure corner because nothing else in the language uses labels.

recommendation.why: One mechanism stays one mechanism. The Void binding is rare, inert, and two characters of noise; both alternatives buy honesty in that rare case by adding a second naming plane that every reader must then learn. Naming the destination and the loop with one word is also a genuinely good idea — it reads as 'exit toward found' — and both alternatives weaken it.

whyNot.reason: It taxes the common elegant case (value loops with targeted breaks now need a binding plus a separate label) to fix the rare awkward one.
Two labeling spellings for one concept is exactly the surface split I8 forbids, and every style discussion about which to use costs more than the Void binding ever did.

recommendation.tradeoff: Labeled pure-effect loops keep binding Void to a name that is only a control target. That is accepted as the cheapest honest price for a single naming mechanism; a lint exemption keeps the binding quiet.

decisions.title: One loop header shape carries two different meanings
decisions.gist: Whether the three-slot loop header keeps two meanings, loses one, or is redesigned so one shape always means one thing.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has one loop keyword. The header is what sits between `loop` and the body, and semicolons separate its parts.

Start from what repetition is. Every loop has a driver: run forever, run while a test holds, or run once per item that a source hands you. Jet spells these `loop { … }`, `loop n > 0 …`, and `loop i; 0..10 …`.

The C-style counter — `loop i := 0; i < n; i++` — is not a fourth driver. It is a test-driven loop plus two conveniences. The counter variable lives only inside the loop, and the advance runs on every path back to the test.

Now the shape problem. A surface is honest when one shape always means one thing. Today the three-slot header has two readings: binding; source; stride — or init; test; advance. Slot two flips between data and a test. Slot three flips between a count and an action. Only the `:=` in slot one says which reading applies.

People read code by silhouette first and tokens second. Two constructs with one silhouette and two meanings interfere, the way false-friend words do across languages. A two-character token is too small a cue to flip the meaning of a whole line.

One more asymmetry hides in the logic of `next`, the skip-to-the-following-pass word. In a counter loop, `next` runs the advance and then retests, so the increment cannot be skipped. In a bare test loop, `next` only retests. Any option that removes the counter form must say what protects that edge.

The choice: which header design gives one shape one meaning, keeps counters expressible, and protects the `next` edge.
decisions.story: Priya learned Jet from the examples and reads `loop i; 0..10; 2` correctly: walk the range by twos. A teammate writes `loop size := 1; size < budget; size *= 2`. The same silhouette now means start, test, advance, and Priya misreads slot three as a stride. Later the teammate rewrites it as a bare test loop, puts `next` above the doubling line, and ships a loop that spins forever. Both failures trace back to the same header design.

options.name: Keep both dialects, unchanged
options.detail: Nothing changes. Readers keep telling the families apart by spotting `:=` in slot one. Programmers arriving from C, Go, or JavaScript keep a familiar one-line counter, and the `next` edge stays safe. The cost is permanent: every reader of every three-slot header pays the which-dialect check, and the misreading Priya hit stays writable forever.
options.code:
loop i := 0; i < n; i++ draw(i)       // counter dialect
loop chunk; chunks; 4 upload(chunk)    // source dialect, same silhouette
options.technical: No change. Parser keeps disambiguating on ColonEq in the first clause (Parser/Statements/control.rs).

options.name: Retire the counter form; visible state plus a test loop
options.detail: Three slots always mean binding; source; stride. Counters with irregular advance move their state above the loop and advance in the body. Every program stays expressible and the state becomes visible. Two honest costs the old ballot hid: the variable now leaks into the enclosing scope, and `next` no longer runs the advance — the skip-the-doubling spin from the in-the-wild example becomes writable.
options.technical: Remove the init;test;advance parse. A teaching diagnostic on `loop name := …` shows the rewrite. Migration of existing code is mechanical.

options.name: Keep the advance, drop the init slot: loop test; advance
options.detail: The header keeps only what belongs to the loop: its driver test and its continuation action. Starting state was always just a binding, so it moves above the loop. `next` still runs the advance first, so the spin bug stays impossible. Costs: the variable leaks into the enclosing scope, and two-slot headers still carry two readings — a name starts a source loop, an expression starts a test loop — so the dialect split shrinks but survives.
options.technical: Grammar: `loop expr ; assignment` when the first clause is not a bare name list. A test that is only a Bool variable needs parentheses or a comparison, or it parses as a source binding. The advance clause runs on body completion and on `next`.

options.name: One meaning for three slots: binding; source; step rule
options.detail: The counter dissolves into data. Slot three accepts a whole number — today's every-Nth stride — or a step rule like `s => s * 2` that computes the next value from the current one, with a range giving the start and the stop bound. Counting, striding, and irregular growth all read in one dialect, one line. The binding stays loop-scoped, and `next` means advance-the-source everywhere. Counters juggling several variables, or tests that are not range bounds, use the visible-state rewrite from option B.
options.code:
loop size; 1..<budget; s => s * 2 probe(size)   // start 1, stop at budget, doubling
loop i; 0..10; 2 audit(i)                        // stride unchanged
loop chunk; chunks; 4 upload(chunk)              // every 4th chunk
options.technical: A step-rule stride is legal only on range sources: the range supplies start and stop test; the rule supplies the advance. Int strides keep today's index-stride law over any source. The counter form retires with a teaching diagnostic. Pointer-chase loops (`node = node.next`) get a Core generated-sequence (Swift's sequence(first:next:) shape); name settled at implementation. Yield arrows keep working since this stays a source loop.

options.name: Keep both, split the silhouettes: parenthesized counter head
options.detail: The counter form survives but must wear parentheses: `loop (i := 0; i < n; i++)`. The paren group reads as one machine-with-state unit; bare slots always mean binding; source; stride. The interference dies at a glance because the shapes differ before any token is read, and the `next` edge stays safe. Cost: the language keeps two loop dialects forever, the counter gains ceremony, and semicolons mean statement-separation inside the parens but slot-separation outside.
options.technical: Grammar: KW_LOOP `(` init `;` test `;` advance `)` body. `loop(` is unclaimed surface after D-LOOPLABEL4=A. Old bare counter headers get a teaching diagnostic pointing at the paren form.

comparisons.note: No C-style loop; `range` covers regular counters. Irregular ones fall to `while` with a manual advance, and `continue` above the advance line spins — exactly the hazard option B imports.
comparisons.code:
size = 1
while size < budget:
    if not ready(): continue   # spins: size never doubles
    probe(size)
    size *= 2

comparisons.note: Removed the C-style for loop in Swift 3. `stride(from:to:by:)` and `sequence(first:next:)` cover counters and generated sequences — option D's shape, shipped at scale and considered an uncontroversial cleanup.
comparisons.code: for size in sequence(first: 1, next: { $0 * 2 < budget ? $0 * 2 : nil }) { probe(size) }

comparisons.note: Keeps the advance co-located with the loop in a visually distinct continuation slot, so `continue` cannot skip it — the direction options C and E take.

One `for` keyword carrying both dialects, disambiguated by header shape — option A shipped. Its spec needs three separate header forms explained, and Jet's current ambiguity is inherited from this design.
comparisons.code:
for i := 0; i < n; i *= 2 { }
for _, v := range items { }

recommendation.why: One shape keeps one meaning across every loop: binding, source, step. The counter concept dissolves into data, so the advance is a visible named rule at the header instead of hidden mutation in a body. `next` keeps a single law — advance the source — so the spin bug cannot be written. The binding stays loop-scoped. And it beats Python on Python's turf: exponential growth stays one line with no mutable state.

whyNot.reason: Two meanings stay behind one silhouette, cued by a two-character token. The which-dialect reading tax lands on every reader of every three-slot header, forever.
The cheapest surface, but it trades a reading trap for a runtime trap: `next` above the advance now spins forever, and the counter leaks into the enclosing scope.
It protects the `next` edge but still leaves two readings for one slot shape, and a plain Bool-variable test collides with a source binding, needing a parse tiebreak nobody will remember.
It kills the interference but signs Jet up for two loop dialects permanently, plus ceremony, with semicolons meaning different things inside and outside the parens.

recommendation.tradeoff: Slot three becomes two-typed — a count or a step rule — and counters that juggle several variables or non-range tests lose their one-line spelling and take the visible-state rewrite. Accepted: those loops are rare, stay fully expressible, and every remaining header reads in one dialect.

decisions.title: Two ways to map: eager loop-yield vs lazy adapters
decisions.gist: Whether Jet keeps eager loop comprehensions and lazy method pipelines side by side, and how the split is taught.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has two spellings for 'transform every item'. The loop form, `doubled :: loop v; values -> v * 2`, runs immediately and produces a complete List. The method form, `values.map(v => v * 2)`, produces a lazy pipeline: nothing runs until something pulls from it, for example `.to_list()` or a fold.

Eager means the work happens at the line where you wrote it, and you hold real data afterward. Lazy means the pipeline is a recipe; work happens later, possibly fused with more steps, possibly never. Lazy pipelines avoid building throwaway middle lists when you chain several steps.

Both behaviors are useful. The concern is that nothing in the spelling says which is which. A reader sees `map` and, if they come from Python, expects a list; they get a pipeline object. A reader who writes a loop-yield inside a hot path materializes a full List where a lazy chain would have avoided it.

The question is not whether both should exist — they serve different jobs — but whether the current split is discoverable enough, and whether anything should change in spelling, defaults, or teaching.
decisions.story: Ana ports a Python script. She writes `evens :: values.map(v => v * 2)` and then `print(evens)`, expecting a list like Python's comprehensions give her. She gets a pipeline value, not data. Her fix is `.to_list()`, but nothing told her at the `map` call; she found out at the print. Meanwhile her teammate Ken writes a loop-yield over ten million rows, chains three more transformations after it, and builds four full lists where a lazy chain would build one.

options.name: Keep the split, document it as the plane boundary
options.detail: Loop-yield is the beginner plane: eager, immediate, holds data. Adapters are the expert plane: lazy, fusable, allocation-free until pulled. Nothing changes in the language; the spec and docs state the rule in one sentence so the split is a teachable boundary instead of folklore.
options.technical: No compiler change. Spec section under S19/D-COMPREHENSION1 states the eager/lazy boundary; hover docs on adapters say 'lazy — pull with .to_list(), fold, or a loop'.

options.name: Make adapters eager; opt into laziness with .lazy()
options.detail: `values.map(f)` returns a List, matching what Python-trained users expect everywhere. Chained pipelines that should not build middle lists opt in: `values.lazy().map(f).filter(g).to_list()`. Beginners never meet a pipeline object uninvited; experts type one extra word. Cost: innocent-looking chains like `xs.map(f).filter(g)` now build a full middle list unless the author remembered `.lazy()`.
options.code:
evens :: values.map(v => v * 2)        // a real List now
hot :: readings.lazy()
    .map(r => r.celsius)
    .filter(c => c > 30)
    .to_list()                          // one pass, no middle lists
options.technical: Adapter methods on List/Set/Map return collections; `.lazy()` enters the pipeline plane where current adapter semantics apply. Iterator sources (files, channels) stay lazy — eagerness applies only to in-memory collections.

options.name: Keep the split, add a boundary lint
options.detail: Semantics unchanged. A lint fires exactly where the confusion bites. Using a pipeline value where a List is expected teaches `.to_list()`. Materializing a loop-yield only to chain more adapters onto it teaches starting the pipeline at the source. Legal code that is plausibly intended stays quiet.
options.technical: Two lint sites in sema: pipeline-typed value reaching a List-typed or Printable sink; loop-yield binding whose only use is a single adapter chain.

comparisons.note: Python splits the same way: comprehensions are eager, `map()`/generators are lazy. It is a known stumbling block — `map` returning a non-list surprises learners — and comprehensions won the culture war precisely because they hand back real data.
comparisons.code:
evens = [v * 2 for v in values]   # eager, everyone's default
evens = map(lambda v: v * 2, values)  # lazy iterator, surprises

comparisons.note: Rust is lazy-only with explicit collection: `.iter().map(f).collect()`. Nobody is surprised because there is no eager spelling to contrast with — but every beginner must learn `.collect()` on day one.

Kotlin made collection operators eager and gave laziness its own entry word, `asSequence()`. This is option B's shape, shipped at scale; the middle-list cost on long eager chains is real and documented.
comparisons.code:
val evens = values.map { it * 2 }          // eager List
val hot = readings.asSequence()
    .map { it.celsius }.filter { it > 30 }.toList()

recommendation.why: Beating Python for its own users means the obvious spelling hands back data, everywhere, with no pipeline object arriving uninvited. Eager `map` plus an explicit `.lazy()` entry word gives beginners Python's comfort. Experts get a single visible switch for fused, allocation-free chains — clearer control than semantics that depend on which of two spellings was used. The loop-yield and eager adapters then agree with each other, and laziness becomes something you can point at in the code.

whyNot.reason: Documentation cannot fix a surprise that arrives at runtime distance from its cause; the reader meets the pipeline object long after the `map` call that created it.
A lint at the sink still teaches after the surprise exists, and its second half polices style on legal code, which erodes trust in lints.

recommendation.tradeoff: Chained eager adapters build intermediate collections unless the author writes `.lazy()`. That is accepted: the cost is visible and local, Kotlin demonstrates it works at scale, and hot paths get one obvious word to reach for.

decisions.title: What type a numeral takes when nothing typed sits beside it
decisions.gist: Whether plain numbers with no other type around them keep the default whole-number type or shrink to their smallest fit.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's default whole-number type is `Int`. It holds every whole number up to about nine quintillion. Experts can also name an exact size. A `U8` holds 0 through 255. A `U32` holds 0 through about four billion.

Say a written number sits next to a sized value. The ratified rule D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F gives that numeral its smallest fitting type first. Then it widens one side to the other, if nothing can be lost. That is what makes `byte + 1` work when `byte` is a `U8`.

The rule as implemented applies that first step even when there is nothing sized to fit. So in `1000000 * 1000000` each numeral shrinks to a 32-bit unsigned number, because a million fits there. Both sides are then 32-bit, so the product is 32-bit too.

Jet traps on overflow at every width, by ratified design. A million times a million is a trillion, which no 32-bit number holds. The program stops. At compile time it stops the build.

The same first step turns `0 - 17` into unsigned-byte subtraction, because `0` and `17` both fit in a byte. Unsigned bytes cannot hold minus seventeen, so that traps too.

Both expressions are ordinary arithmetic with no sized type anywhere in the source. Today they fail. This decision picks what a numeral means when nothing beside it asks for a size.
decisions.story: Tomas checks a throughput budget in a build script: `comptime budget = 1000000 * 1000000`. The build stops with a compile-time overflow, naming a 32-bit range he never wrote. He tries `0 - 17` in the next line and that stops too. Nothing in his file mentions a fixed width; both are plain numbers, and both would be fine in a pocket calculator.

options.name: A numeral with no sized neighbour is an Int
options.detail: The smallest-fit step only runs when something sized sits beside the numeral, which is the case it was designed for. With no sized neighbour, numerals keep the default `Int`. Tomas gets a trillion and minus seventeen. `byte + 1` still works, because `byte` is the neighbour that asks for a byte.
options.technical: `minimal_integer_literal_type` narrows only when the peer operand resolves to a fixed-width integer; with no peer both operands stay `Int`. Amends D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F's "after minimal-width assignment" clause to "after minimal-width assignment against a typed peer". Destination-driven cases keep working through the expected-type channel: a `U8` parameter or annotation still pushes `U8` into the literals.
options.code:
budget :: 1000000 * 1000000   // Int, 1000000000000
offset :: 0 - 17              // Int, -17

fn tick(byte: U8) => U8 { return byte + 1 }   // unchanged
fn take_u8(value: U8) {}
take_u8(1 + 2)                // still U8: the parameter asks for it

options.name: Keep smallest-fit, and size the result to the value
options.detail: Numerals still shrink, but a numeral-only expression is folded at compile time and typed by its *result*, not its inputs. A trillion becomes a 64-bit number; minus seventeen becomes signed. Nothing traps, and small constants stay small, which matters for packed data and hardware registers.
options.technical: Constant-fold integer expressions whose leaves are all bare numerals, then assign the minimal type containing the folded result (signed when negative). Requires the fold to run before type assignment in sema, and a rule for what happens when a folded constant meets a sized peer later in the expression tree.
options.code:
budget :: 1000000 * 1000000   // folds to 1000000000000, takes I64
offset :: 0 - 17              // folds to -17, takes I8
mask   :: 255 & 15            // folds to 15, takes U8

options.name: Keep today's rule and refuse instead of trapping
options.detail: Numerals keep shrinking. An expression the compiler can prove overflows its own inferred width becomes a compile error naming that width and value, not a run-time trap. Tomas still cannot write his multiplication, but he learns exactly which width was chosen and why.
options.technical: Constant-evaluate numeral-only integer expressions during checking and report a registered diagnostic naming the inferred width, the computed value, and the containing range, with a fix-it that annotates a wider type. The trap stays for values that are not compile-time known.

options.name: Numerals are always Int; sized types are reached only by conversion
options.detail: Drop smallest-fit entirely. Every numeral is an `Int`, and a sized value comes from its own constructor. Simplest rule in the language, and the beginner never meets a width. The cost falls on expert code: `byte + 1` needs the numeral spelled as a byte.
options.technical: Remove literal narrowing; `Int` never widens to a narrower type, so mixed expressions with sized operands need an explicit constructor or conversion. Reverts the part of D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F that closed the original `x + 1` complaint, so that ergonomics loss returns.

comparisons.note: An unsuffixed integer literal defaults to `i32` when nothing constrains it, and constant overflow is a deny-by-default compile error.
comparisons.code:
let x = 1000000 * 1000000;   // error: this arithmetic operation will overflow
let y = 0 - 17;              // fine: both are i32

comparisons.note: Untyped constants are arbitrary precision until they need a type, so a constant product cannot overflow on the way.
comparisons.code: const budget = 1000000 * 1000000   // exact; only assignment to a sized type can fail

comparisons.note: Literals default to `Int` (64-bit) unless context asks otherwise, and overflow traps at run time.
comparisons.code:
let budget = 1_000_000 * 1_000_000   // Int, fine
let offset = 0 - 17                  // Int, -17

comparisons.note: Integer promotion pulls small operands up to `int` before arithmetic, so byte-sized inputs never do byte-sized math.
comparisons.code:
unsigned char a = 0, b = 17;
int d = a - b;   /* -17: both promote to int first */

recommendation.why: It fixes the broken case by narrowing the rule to the case it was written for: a numeral takes a size from a neighbour that has one. With no neighbour there is nothing to match, and the language default is the honest answer. Tomas's arithmetic works and expert `byte + 1` is untouched.

whyNot.reason: It types an expression by its answer, so the same numerals mean different widths depending on the arithmetic around them, and folding has to precede checking.
It turns ordinary arithmetic into a compile error and asks the writer to annotate around a width the compiler invented.
It reopens the `x + 1` complaint that D-INTLIT-WIDTH1 was ratified to close, and puts conversion ceremony back into every expert expression.

recommendation.tradeoff: A numeral-only expression is `Int`-wide even when its values are tiny, so packed or register-sized code must name its width in the destination. That is acceptable because the destination is exactly where a width belongs.

decisions.title: Mandatory braces for control-flow bodies
decisions.gist: Whether every if/else/loop body must be wrapped in { }, and whether the formatter collapses short bodies onto one line.
decisions.lesson:
A body is the code a control statement runs when its condition holds. Jet today allows two spellings for a one-statement body. You can write braces: `if n < 0 { return 0 }`. Or you can write the statement adjacent, with no braces: `if n < 0 return 0`.

The adjacent form saves four characters. Its cost is that the body's boundary is invisible. The reader must infer where the guarded code ends. Editors and merge tools must infer it too.

This failure has a famous name: Apple's goto-fail bug. A duplicated line after a braceless `if` shipped inside TLS verification, because nothing marked where the body ended. Jet's own repository holds a live specimen today: a stray closing brace beside a braceless guard in git_diff_review.jet. The parser reports that failure 21 lines away from its cause.

Mandatory braces mean the compiler rejects the adjacent form everywhere. The formatter then owns compactness instead: any single-statement body that fits the 100-column width is printed on one line, braces included. So `if n < 0 { return 0 }` stays exactly one line. The change trades four characters per guard for one body shape, machine-checkable boundaries, and a formatter that makes the compact spelling automatic.
decisions.story: Nate is reviewing a contributor's patch to a CLI adapter. The diff shows `if root_name != "before" panic(...)}` — a stray brace after a braceless guard. The build fails 21 lines below the real mistake, and he spends ten minutes finding it. He asks why a guarded body has no visible boundary in the first place.

options.name: Mandatory braces + fmt collapses fitting one-liners
options.detail: The adjacent form becomes an error with a teaching diagnostic, and fmt auto-fixes it by wrapping braces. fmt also canonically prints any single-statement control body on one line when it fits 100 columns. Writers lose nothing vertically; every body gains a visible boundary; formatted style is uniform with zero judgment calls.
options.technical: Retire D-IFGUARD1's adjacent spelling and the adjacent loop body. New diagnostic (registered code, what/why/fix, UI snapshot) for an unbraced body; `jet fmt` rewrites source form to braced. S44 amendment: single-statement if/else/loop bodies use collapse-if-fits (canonical), replacing author-choice preservation for those bodies. Arrow arm bodies (`->`) are expression arms and keep their existing rules.

options.name: Mandatory braces, fmt preserves the author's line choice
options.detail: Same brace rule as A, but fmt keeps a body one-line or multi-line exactly as the author wrote it (current S44 behavior). Authors keep control of vertical shape. The cost is two coexisting printed styles for identical code, and review debates about which to use.
options.technical: Brace enforcement and diagnostic identical to A. S44 unchanged: a single-simple-statement one-line body stays one-line only if authored that way; multi-line stays multi-line.

options.name: Keep the adjacent form (status quo)
options.detail: No grammar change. The adjacent guard remains the compact spelling and the brace form remains legal. Existing code is untouched. The boundary-invisibility failure class stays open, including the goto-fail pattern the repo has already reproduced once.
options.technical: No change to D-IFGUARD1 or S44. Optionally add a lint recommending braces around adjacent bodies that sit next to closing braces.
options.code:
if n < 0 return 0                    // stays legal
if index == 0 root_name = piece else pieces.push(piece)

comparisons.note: Braces are mandatory on every if/for body; gofmt owns layout. The rule is widely credited with eliminating dangling-body bugs, and nobody writes a linter for it because the compiler is the linter.
Braces mandatory; rustfmt always expands bodies to multiple lines, so guard-heavy code pays 3 lines per guard. Jet's collapse-if-fits keeps the safety without that vertical tax.
Optional braces produced the Apple goto-fail TLS vulnerability: a duplicated statement after a braceless if silently escaped the condition.

recommendation.why: One body shape with a visible machine-checked boundary removes the stray-brace failure class the repo has already hit, while collapse-if-fits keeps every current guard exactly one line, four characters wider.

whyNot.reason: Preserving author line choice keeps two printed styles for identical code, so files drift and reviews relitigate layout; A's canonical collapse makes the compact form automatic instead of optional.
The adjacent form's invisible boundary already produced a live parse bug in this repo, and it is the goto-fail shape. A lint would still ship two spellings of one body.

recommendation.tradeoff: Adjacent one-line if/else pairs get 8 characters wider, and the formatter overrides author intent on body layout for single-statement control bodies. Accepted because uniform output is the point of a zero-config formatter.

decisions.title: Loop header clause separator: comma or semicolon
decisions.gist: Which symbol separates the clauses of a multi-part loop header, and how the two-name iteration form is spelled under that choice.
decisions.lesson:
A loop header can carry several clauses that do different jobs. Take `loop i := 0; i < 3; i += 1 { }`. The first clause binds a counter. The second is the test rerun before each pass. The third advances the counter after each pass.

Today those clauses are separated by semicolons (D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1). This is the only place a Jet author types a semicolon. Everywhere else commas separate things: call arguments, struct fields, bound names.

That last form is the crux. In `loop key, value; map` the comma groups two names being bound, and the semicolon splits the name group from the source. If commas also separated clauses, `loop a, b, c` could mean two names iterating one source, or one name with a source and a stride. The parser could not tell without type information, which Jet forbids.

So switching to commas requires a respelling of the name group, such as parentheses: `loop (key, value), map`. The reward is one meaning per symbol across the language: comma always separates header clauses and list items, and the semicolon is freed to mean only a statement boundary. That matters if one-line bodies with `;` inside braces are adopted later. A semicolon header would then mix two semicolon meanings on one line; a comma header keeps them apart.
decisions.story: Nate is teaching a friend Jet. She writes `loop i := 0; i < 3; i += 1 { sum += i; print(sum) }` from an example and asks why the same symbol splits the header clauses and the body statements. He has no answer except history: C spelled for-loops that way in 1972.

options.name: Comma clauses, parenthesized name group
options.detail: Commas separate header clauses. Multi-name binding wraps its names in parentheses, matching how grouped things look everywhere else. Every header is unambiguous at parse time, and the semicolon disappears from loop headers entirely.
options.technical: Clauses split on depth-0 commas; Jet expressions have no top-level comma so this is unambiguous. Two-name form becomes `loop (key, value), source`. S19 and D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 amended; old `;` headers get a teaching diagnostic plus fmt auto-fix. All loop examples, goldens, and formatter emission updated.

options.name: Comma clauses, bare names with a shape rule
options.detail: Commas separate clauses and the two-name form stays bare: `loop key, value, map`. A shape rule decides the reading: when every clause before the last is a lone name, they are bindings. Saves the parentheses but the rule is invisible, and `loop a, b, c` reads two ways to a human even when the parser has picked one.
options.technical: Grammar rule: N leading clauses that are bare identifiers followed by one expression clause parse as an N-name binding over that source. A bare-name source variable (`loop x, xs, 2`) collides with three-clause counted form when `xs` is also a lone name; needs a tie-break and a diagnostic explaining it.

options.name: Keep semicolon clauses (status quo)
options.detail: No change. Semicolons keep separating header clauses, commas keep grouping bound names, and the C-family muscle memory for counted loops keeps working. The semicolon stays a header-only symbol, and any future one-line body semicolon shares a line with it.
options.technical: No grammar, formatter, or migration work. D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 stands as ratified.

comparisons.note: Both spell counted loops with semicolon clauses; Go dropped the parens but kept the semicolons. This is the muscle memory option C preserves.
No clause headers at all — iteration is always over an object, and tuple unpacking uses bare commas: the same bare-comma binding Jet's two-name form copies today.
Removed the C-style for(;;) loop entirely in Swift 3, arguing the semicolon header was the language's least consistent corner. Iteration and while cover the same ground.
comparisons.code:
for i in stride(from: 0, to: 10, by: 2) {
}

recommendation.why: One meaning per symbol across the whole language: comma separates clauses and list items, semicolon means only a statement boundary. The parenthesized name group keeps every header unambiguous to both the parser and a human reader.

whyNot.reason: The bare-name shape rule makes `loop a, b, c` two-faced: readers must run the disambiguation rule in their head, and a rename can silently change which form a header is.
Keeps the language's only author-typed semicolon as a header-only special case, and collides with body semicolons on one-line loops if those are adopted.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two-name iteration gains a pair of parentheses, and every C-family newcomer must unlearn `for(;;)` muscle memory once. Accepted for symbol-level consistency across the surface.

decisions.title: How a pinned field is marked
decisions.gist: How an author marks the fields of a type that must keep their address.
decisions.lesson:
Most values in a program can be moved. Copying a value to a new place and forgetting the old one is normal and cheap. A few values cannot survive that. A node in a linked list may hold the address of its neighbour. A parser may hold the address of a byte inside its own buffer. If the value moves, those stored addresses now point at the old place, which no longer holds what they expect. Reading through one is a bug that no test reliably catches.

Jet's answer is a pin. Pinning a value promises that it will not move while the pin is alive. D-PIN1=A ratified the entry point: mem.pin(&place) hands back a Pin<T>, a tracked write view, and the promise ends when the last pin goes away.

A whole-value promise is not enough on its own. An intrusive list needs to reach a node's next link and get a pin back, not an ordinary view, because that link is itself address-sensitive. Handing out an ordinary view would let a caller move the thing the promise was protecting. Reaching a field of a pinned value and keeping the promise is called projection.

D-PIN2=A ratified that the author decides, field by field, which fields carry the promise. Unmarked fields are ordinary. This ballot settles the one thing that ruling left open: what the mark looks like when you type it.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a scheduler. Each task is a node in an intrusive list, so every task holds a link to the next one. She marks that link field, so reaching it through a pin gives her another pin. The task name and priority stay ordinary data. When a colleague reads the type later, the difference has to be obvious. Getting it wrong is the difference between a working scheduler and a crash under load.

options.name: The field's type carries the mark
options.detail: The field is declared as Pin<T>. There is no separate marker. A reader sees the promise in the type, in the same place every other fact about the field already lives, and the name is the one D-PIN1=A already ratified. A field that is not address-sensitive stays an ordinary type and needs no thought.
options.technical: Projection is decided by the declared field type. Reaching a Pin<T> field through a pinned value yields Pin<T>; reaching any other field yields an ordinary view under the existing rules. Nothing new enters Syntax.rs beyond the Pin type name.

options.name: A field attribute
options.detail: The field keeps its ordinary type and gains a marker. The promise reads as something the containing type says about the field, not as something the field is. The same Node type can then be pinned in one struct and ordinary in another.
options.technical: Adds one user-typeable marker to Syntax.rs. Projection consults the marker list on the struct rather than the field type, so a type used in both pinned and unpinned positions needs no wrapper.

options.name: One pinned block in the type
options.detail: Every address-sensitive field is named together in one place. A reader learns the whole contract of the type from a single short block. That matters most when a type has many fields and only two are links.
options.technical: Adds one user-typeable keyword to Syntax.rs and a second place a reader must consult to know what a field means. Field declarations no longer carry the fact themselves.

comparisons.note: Rust has no field mark at all. Projection is hand-written per field, usually behind a macro, and forgetting one silently blocks callers.
No contract exists. Address stability is a comment, and every container documents its own invalidation rules.
comparisons.code: // callers must not move Task while queued

recommendation.why: The fact lives where a reader already looks for facts about a field, and it costs no new syntax. Jet already ratified Pin<T> as the name for this promise, so a Pin<Node> field reads as the same idea in a second position rather than a second idea. It also fails safe: an author who forgets the mark gets an ordinary field and a diagnostic at the projection site, not a silent ordinary view where a pin was needed.

whyNot.reason: Splits one promise across two spellings. The same fact would be a type in one position and a marker in another, and it adds a marker to a surface the beginner pass wants to keep small.
Moves the fact away from the field it describes. A reader scanning the fields learns nothing, and the block drifts out of date as fields are added.

recommendation.tradeoff: A type used both pinned and unpinned needs the wrapper at each pinned position rather than one marker. That is the honest cost of putting the promise in the type, and it is the cost that keeps one name for one idea.

decisions.title: Expert spelling for declared view provenance
decisions.gist: How an expert writes down which inputs a view may borrow from.
decisions.lesson:
A view is a lightweight window into memory that another value owns. The owner is the value that really holds the data. Provenance is the compiler's record linking each view to its possible owners. While a view is live, Jet freezes every possible owner: none may move, resize, or be dropped.

Jet infers provenance silently (ratified as D-MEMPROVENANCE2 option A). Sema reads each function body and records which inputs a returned view can come from. A view that might come from either of two inputs gets both recorded — a source union. Rust states the same relation with lifetime annotations such as `'a`. Jet bans that notation, and inference took its place.

Inference has a blind spot: it states what a body does today, never what an author promises. Three walls follow. A library's borrow contract shifts silently whenever a body is edited — a breaking change no signature shows. A callback type has no body to read, so callers of a view-returning callback freeze every non-scalar argument. A trait object's method has no single body either, so a view-returning call through it is refused outright (error E2305).

The fix is a declaration: the author names which sources a view may borrow from. Sema checks every return path against the declaration and teaches on escape. Callers rely on the declared set, trait implementations are held to their trait's declaration, and open dispatch becomes checkable. The same spelling covers view parameters, aggregate slots, and static storage. Inference stays the default; a beginner never writes any of this. This ballot picks the spelling.
decisions.story: Mira ships the zero-copy parser from D-MEMPROVENANCE2 as a library. Callers depend on which buffer each view borrows from, but that fact is inferred from her bodies. Any refactor silently changes her public contract and breaks downstream builds. Her next feature is pluggable decoders behind a trait, and every view-returning decoder call dies with E2305. In Rust both are one lifetime annotation. Jet gives her no spelling at all.
decisions.detail:
Relation to the ratified record: D-MEMPROVENANCE2=A stays law. Inference remains the only thing a beginner sees; the hidden relation machinery is unchanged. That ratification rejected mandatory owner notation in routine APIs. This ballot adds only the opt-in declared form option A left without a spelling. Undeclared code behaves exactly as today.

Parity checklist — every borrow relation safe Rust can state, and its home here. Returned borrows and source unions: a declaration on the return. Borrow-carrying structs and enums (Rust `struct Foo<'a>`): per-slot declarations at the signatures that produce or accept them; type definitions never carry owner parameters. Outlives relations between inputs (Rust `'b: 'a`): two slots declared against one shared source. Lending traits, trait objects, and lending iterators (Rust GATs): a declaration on the trait method that binds every implementation. Higher-rank callbacks (Rust `for<'a>`): a declaration on the function type's own named parameters. Static storage (Rust `'static`): a static path as a source. Owned-only generics (Rust `T: 'static` bounds): already covered by owned and sendable facts (E1102); no new syntax.

Out of scope exactly as in safe Rust: self-referential values route to Pin (D-PIN1) and Pool/Id, and variance stays internal to sema, never user-facing.

options.name: Trailing `from` clause — on results, parameters, traits, and function types
options.detail: One word, four placements, one rule: a `from` clause after a type names the sources its views may borrow from. Results declare contracts where callers read them. View parameters declare required sources, which spells Rust's outlives relations. Trait clauses bind every implementation, so trait objects lend. Function-type clauses make callbacks precise. Beginners still write nothing.
options.technical: Grammar: `from src (| src)*` after a return type, a view-typed parameter's type, a trait-method return, or a function type's return. src = parameter name, `self`, or `static.<path>`, each with optional field/index/range projections. Per-slot form for aggregates: `from (text: primary, meta: fallback)`, keyed by output path; a bare clause binds every view slot in the type. Checking: each return path's inferred sources must be a subset of the declaration; declaring wider than the body is legal and reserves evolution room; a violation reports the offending return with a fix-it. Parameter clauses are call-boundary requirements: the argument must derive from the named source — sharing one source name across slots expresses Rust's `'b: 'a`. Trait clauses bind impls after receiver substitution and retire E2305 for declared methods, including lending-iterator shapes (Rust GATs). Function-type clauses quantify per call (Rust `for<'a>`). Type definitions never carry owner parameters; relations attach at signatures. API digests publish declared relations flagged `declared`; changing one stays a breaking provenance change.

options.name: Lender-marked parameters — `from` as a parameter prefix
options.detail: Instead of describing the result, mark the inputs that lend: any view in the result may borrow from any `from`-marked parameter. It is the shortest spelling and can never drift out of sync with the parameter list. But one mark serves every output slot, so per-slot relations, parameter requirements, and static sources have no home.
options.technical: Prefix `from` on parameter declarations, on `self`, and on function-type parameters. The declared relation for every view slot in the result is the union of the marked parameters. No per-slot form, no parameter-to-parameter requirement, no static sources — those cases fall back to inference or stay rejected. Checking and publication law otherwise identical to option A.

options.name: Type-attached `from` — the clause lives inside the view type
options.detail: The relation travels with the type itself: `View<str from left | right>`. Nested lists, options, tuples, and function types need no extra rule, because the fact sits wherever the type is spelled. The cost: the most-read line of an API carries the machinery, deep nesting repeats it, and named view-holding structs still need signature-level declarations anyway.
options.technical: Type grammar gains `View<T from srcs>` and `ViewMut<T from srcs>`, legal anywhere a type is written, including function types and aggregate element positions. Named structs and enums do not carry owner parameters; signatures producing or accepting them still need slot declarations, so this form is a superset of option A's grammar only for anonymous positions. Checking and publication law identical to option A.

options.name: Path-keyed `from` block — one table after the signature
options.detail: Every declaration lives in one block after the signature, keyed by output path — nothing inline, ever. Multi-slot APIs read like a table, and every function states its whole borrow story in one place. Simple cases pay one extra line, and the contract sits apart from the return type it governs.
options.technical: `from { <path>: src (| src)*, ... }` after the signature. `result` names the whole return, `result.text` one slot, a parameter name states a call-boundary requirement, `static.<path>` a static source. Trait methods and function types take the same block; function types inline it after their return type. Checking and publication law identical to option A.

comparisons.note: One lifetime variable links a result to its inputs; traits, closures, and structs carry the same variables. Fully general, and the single most-cited learning cliff in the language.
The origin of a returned reference is named in the return type by parameter name — no abstract variable in the common case.
comparisons.code: fn choose(a: String, b: String) -> ref [a, b] String

comparisons.note: Lifetime-dependency attributes on nonescapable returns name the source value; inference covers the common cases.

recommendation.why: One English word in four placements covers the entire safe-Rust lifetime surface. Returns, aggregate slots, parameter requirements, statics, lending traits, and callbacks all use the same clause. The common case stays one short clause on the exact line callers read. It is the only option that is both complete and lightest where reading actually happens.

whyNot.reason: One mark for all outputs cannot state per-slot relations, parameter requirements, or static sources — parity with Rust fails exactly where the hard programs live.
The relation inflates every nested type and the most-read API line, and named view-holding structs still need signature clauses — so the type-position form buys nothing the trailing clause lacks.
Forcing a block on every declaration turns the common single-source case into two lines of ceremony and moves the contract away from the return type it governs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Opted-in signatures grow a trailing clause, and a second provenance vocabulary now exists beside silent inference — readers must learn that a missing clause means inferred, never none.

decisions.title: Writing many members that share one prefix
decisions.gist: How you list several names that all hang off the same thing.
decisions.lesson:
A prefix is the part before the dot. In `default.git`, `default` is the prefix and `git` is the member. Jet code reads members off a prefix constantly: a package source, a module, a settings group.

When you want many members from one prefix, you repeat the prefix. Ten packages from `default` means typing `default` ten times. The repetition carries no information, and a typo in one of the ten is easy to miss.

A spread is a shorthand that writes the prefix once and the members once each. The compiler expands it back to the long form before anything else runs, so it is a typing convenience, not a new runtime idea.
