Jet used to have a similar-looking operator called fan-out, spelled `f.[a, b, c]`. That one meant something different: it CALLED `f` on each entry, producing `[f(a), f(b), f(c)]`. The owner removed it. jetpack's config files happened to use the same brackets, but they meant member spread, never calls. So the bracket spelling is now free, and the meaning jetpack needs has never actually been decided.

One detail matters for every option below. When a spread sits inside a list, it should flatten into that list rather than nest a list inside it. `[default.[a, b], mine.c]` should mean three packages, not a two-item list beside one package.
decisions.story: Nate keeps this repository's development shell in `env.jet`. It pins nineteen packages, every one of them from the `default` nixpkgs source. He also writes host configurations that pull packages, services, and user settings from the same few sources. He wants to name the source once per group, not once per line, and he asked for that spreading back specifically for jetpack.
decisions.inWild:
// env.jet — this repository's own development shell, after the removal.
module env.dev {
    sources: { default: github@NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable }
    packages: [
        default.cargo,
        default.clippy,
        default.rustc,
        default.gcc,
        default.clang,
        default.lld,
        default.nodejs_22,
        default.nixfmt,
        default.ripgrep,
        default.jq,
        default.gh,
        default.fd,
        default.bashInteractive,
        default.zsh,
        default.fish,
        default.util-linux,
        default.wasm-tools,
        default.tree-sitter,
        default.pkg-config,
    ]
    prompt: "jet"
}

// The word `default` appears nineteen times and says nothing nineteen times.

options.name: Bracket member spread, everywhere in Jet
options.detail: Write the prefix, a dot, then the members in brackets. It works in any Jet code, not only config files. Inside a list it flattens, so you can mix spreads and single members freely. You gain one short mechanism that reads the same wherever prefixes repeat. You lose the ability to ever reuse this bracket spelling for anything else.
options.technical: Sigil `.[` reuses the slot freed by D-VERDICT-1324-1. Entries are plain member names only, never expressions or calls; a non-ident entry is a registered sema error. Desugars in sema before type inference: in list position it splices into the surrounding `ListLit`, elsewhere it produces a fixed-size `[T#N]` list (S76). No TIR, codegen, or engine work, so tier parity is structural.

options.name: Grouped map in the config data
options.detail: No new operator. The config fields that take a list also accept a map from prefix to members. The grouping lives in the data shape you already write. You gain a spelling that needs no language change and reads clearly in settings files. You lose the shorthand everywhere outside jetpack, and each field that wants it must opt in.
options.technical: `packages`, `services`, and peer fields gain a second accepted shape: `{ prefix: [name, …] }`, merged into the same `Pkg` list the flat form produces. Implemented in `jet-pkg-model` and `jet-env-model` only. No Syntax.rs entry, no parser change, no I7 decision beyond this one.

options.name: Prefix block
options.detail: Open a block that names the prefix once. Inside it, bare names resolve against that prefix. It covers packages, services, and options with one construct instead of one spread per list. You gain the most saving on large config files. You lose local clarity: a bare name inside the block means something different from the same name outside it.
options.technical: New keyword-led block `with <path> { … }`, a user-typeable keyword needing its own Syntax.rs entry (I7). Name resolution inside the block tries the prefix first, then the enclosing scope, which introduces a shadowing rule the language does not have today. Sema rewrites the block away before inference.

options.name: Write every prefix out
options.detail: No shorthand at all. Every member carries its own prefix, which is what the repository does right now. You gain a surface with nothing extra to learn and no expansion rule to reason about. You lose exactly what was asked for: the prefix keeps repeating on every line of every package list.
options.technical: The state after D-VERDICT-1324-1 with the callers migrated. `Merge::parse_package_list` already handles the flat `source.name` form, so nothing is built and nothing is removed.
options.code:
packages: [
    default.cargo,
    default.clippy,
    default.rustc,
    default.ripgrep,
    default.jq,
    default.fd,
]

comparisons.note: The language jetpack's package sources come from spells this with a prefix block, the model option C follows.
comparisons.code: with pkgs; [ cargo clippy rustc ripgrep ]

comparisons.note: Names the prefix once at import, then uses bare members. The saving is real, and so is the loss of provenance at the use site.
comparisons.code: from validators import length, charset, entropy

comparisons.note: Braces after a path expand to several members of that path. Closest in shape to option A, though it applies to imports rather than values.

recommendation.why: It is the spelling already written in this repository's `env.jet` and every jetpack fixture, so the owner's existing files become correct again rather than being rewritten twice. One mechanism serves config files and ordinary Jet code, and the sigil is free because the call fan-out that held it is gone.

whyNot.reason: It helps only the jetpack fields that opt in, so ordinary Jet code keeps repeating prefixes and the language gains nothing.
A bare name inside the block means something different from the same name outside it, which hides where a value came from at the place you read it.
It is the state the owner just asked to change, and it makes a nineteen-package list say `default` nineteen times.

recommendation.tradeoff: The `.[ ]` brackets are spent for good, so no later feature can claim them. That is acceptable because the one feature that held them was removed by owner ruling, and no other pending surface wants that sigil.

decisions.title: Jet as guest: #Import / #Export parity for the native library edge
decisions.gist: Whether Jet's foreign edge uses matching Import and Export spellings so both directions read as one system.
decisions.lesson:
Jet talks to other languages over the C ABI: a shared calling convention for scalars, strings, and C-layout records. Crossing that edge has two directions.

Import means a Jet program calls a function that already lives in a foreign library. Export means a foreign program calls a function that lives in Jet. Same phone line, opposite ends.

Today only import exists. The everyday overlay spelling is `#Extern module c.<lib>`. Generated caches live under `.jet/bindings/`. Call sites use `use c.<lib>`. A separate fourth tier, `#FFI(c)`, pastes a foreign body inside a Jet function — that is not how you consume a library.

Maximum parity means the two directions share names, shape, type law, and on-disk layout. The natural twin words are Import and Export. This ballot picks how far that twinning goes, including whether today's `#Extern` becomes `#Import`.
decisions.story: Priya rewrites a pricing kernel in Jet inside a Java host. Her Jet code still imports libc and a Go helper with the existing binders. She wants `#Import` and `#Export` to feel like one dial turned two ways — not `#Extern` in, something else out.

options.name: Exact twins: #Import(c) / #Export(c) (retire #Extern)
options.detail: One marker family for both directions. #Import(c) declares a foreign symbol Jet will call. #Export(c) offers a Jet function foreign code will call. Same C-safe type law, same expert args for symbol and ABI. #Extern is renamed to #Import (module form: #Import module c.<lib>). Generated inbound caches stay under .jet/bindings/; outbound products land under .jet/exports/ with a re-import #Bindgen so use c.<lib> round-trips. #FFI(c) stays the inline-body escape — not the library Import path. Beginners learn two words that face each other.
options.technical: Amends S59 / D-FFI-UNIFY1 overlay spelling: #Extern module → #Import module; per-function foreign decls may use #Import(c) fn … = "sym". #Export(c) fn … { body } lowers to non-mangled extern "C". Emit .jet/exports/c/<lib>.{h,a|so|dylib|dll} plus .jet/bindings/c/<lib>.jet #Bindgen for round-trip. Teaching diagnostic maps #Extern → #Import. #Bindgen remains compiler-only in generated caches (E3207). #FFI(c|cpp) unchanged as the inline fourth tier.

options.name: Module twins only: #Import module / #Export module
options.detail: Parity at the module keyword, not on each function. #Import module c.<lib> replaces #Extern module. #Export module c.<lib> lists what this package offers out. Function bodies stay unmarked on the export side. Same trees and type law as A. You get matching words at the module level, but reading a function no longer shows it has foreign callers, and renames need a second edit in the export module.
options.technical: S59 overlay rename only: #Extern module → #Import module. New #Export module c.<lib> { fn price(...) => Int; } resolves bodies by name from package modules. No #Import(c)/#Export(c) function markers. Same emit layout as A.

options.name: Keep #Extern; add only #Export(c)
options.detail: Leave the ratified import spelling alone. Export gets #Export(c) without renaming Import. Directions work, but the words do not match: Extern in, Export out. That is the asymmetry this question is pushing against. Smaller syntax churn; weaker everyday rhyme.
options.technical: No S59 rename. New #Export(c) marker + .jet/exports/ emit + round-trip #Bindgen only. #Extern module and #FFI(c) unchanged.

options.name: Mirror #FFI instead: #Export(c) as reverse of #FFI(c)
options.detail: Treat #FFI(c) as the import-side twin. That marker pastes a foreign body into Jet; #Export(c) would offer a Jet body out. The rhyme is real at the inline-body tier, but it is the wrong tier for library migration. Everyday import is use c.<lib> and #Extern/#Import modules, not #FFI. Teams would learn Export against a rare escape hatch instead of against the normal Import path.

comparisons.note: Import overlay is #Extern, not #Import. Generated caches are #Bindgen under .jet/bindings/. No export twin yet.
Export uses //export; import of C uses import "C". Words differ, but both sit on the function. Jet can do better with literal Import/Export twins.
comparisons.code:
//export price
func price(cents int64) int64 { return cents / 100 }

comparisons.note: import and export are exact spelling twins for opposite directions of the same module edge — the parity target here.
comparisons.code:
import { strlen } from "./libc";
export function price(cents: number): number { ... }

recommendation.why: Option A gives the parity you asked for: the same word family on both ends of the C edge. #Import(c) brings a foreign symbol in; #Export(c) sends a Jet symbol out. Renaming #Extern to #Import finishes the rhyme instead of papering over it. #FFI(c) stays the rare inline-body escape, not the Import twin.

whyNot.reason: Module-only twins match keywords but hide foreign callers at the function, so everyday reading and renames stay split across two places.
Keeping #Extern while adding #Export leaves the exact asymmetry you called out: two directions, mismatched words.
Pairing Export with #FFI mirrors the wrong import tier — inline foreign bodies, not the library Import path migration teams live in.

recommendation.tradeoff: Renaming #Extern to #Import is a clean break on ratified S59 spelling, with a teaching diagnostic for the old word. That churn buys a durable Import/Export rhyme instead of a permanent Extern/Export mismatch.

decisions.title: Where the C compiler behind jet cc comes from
decisions.gist: Whether jet cc ships a C compiler inside Jet, fetches one through Jet's package store, borrows the host's, or is not built.
decisions.lesson:
A C toolchain is the compiler, linker, and standard C library headers needed to turn C source into a program. Cross-compiling means building on one machine for a different kind of machine. The set of target headers and libraries is called a sysroot.

Zig proved a language can win users through its toolchain before its syntax. The zig cc command is a full C compiler that behaves the same on every machine and targets any platform out of the box. Teams adopt it just to build their existing C code, and meet the language later.

Jet today uses whatever clang and cc the host machine happens to have. That works, but every machine behaves differently, and cross-compiling depends on what the user installed. A jet cc that always works identically would be Jet's front door into every C and C++ estate.

This ballot picks how jet cc obtains its compiler. The choice sets the first-run experience, the install size everyone pays, whether two machines produce identical builds, and whether the wedge exists at all.
decisions.story: Marcus maintains a C codebase with a Makefile that predates him. His CI cross-builds four platforms with four fragile container images. He hears one tool can replace all four with CC=jet cc. If the first try works identically on his laptop and in CI, Jet has a champion inside his company.
decisions.inWild:
# unmodified upstream project, cross-built from an x86 Linux laptop:
$ CC="jet cc -target aarch64-linux-gnu" make
$ CC="jet cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu" make

# CI runs the same two lines and produces byte-identical artifacts.

options.name: Bundle clang, lld, and sysroots inside the Jet install
options.detail: Every Jet install carries a complete C compiler and target sysroots, the way Zig does. jet cc works instantly and offline on a fresh machine. Every user pays the download and disk weight even if they never compile C, and the C toolchain can only update when Jet itself ships a release.
options.code:
$ curl -L jet.dev/install | sh   # one large download, everything inside
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello         # works offline immediately

options.name: Jetpack store provisions a pinned toolchain on first use
options.detail: jet cc looks and behaves exactly like option A, but the compiler and sysroots arrive through Jet's own package store the first time they are needed. Every machine gets the identical pinned toolchain, so builds reproduce everywhere. Air-gapped sites preload it with the store's offline bundles. The base Jet install stays small.
options.technical: Toolchain and per-target sysroots become ordinary content-addressed store packages, riding the same provisioning that already fetches nixpkgs C dependencies (CFFI.rs). Offline staging uses the #957 bundle lanes. Keeps compiler seams dependency-free (I6) and one provisioning mechanism (I8).
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
  fetching toolchain clang-19.1 (pinned)...   # first use only
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello                     # instant from then on

options.name: Wrap the host toolchain only
options.detail: jet cc translates flags and shells out to whatever clang or gcc the machine has. Nothing to download. Two machines can produce different binaries from the same source, cross-compiling works only if the host happens to have the right pieces, and works-on-my-machine failures return.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
  # uses /usr/bin/cc — whatever version this machine has
$ ssh ci 'jet cc hello.c -o hello'
  # different cc, different binary, maybe different bugs

options.name: No jet cc
options.detail: C compilation stays internal to Jet's FFI bridges. C estates get call-in interop but no reason to adopt Jet's toolchain first. The adoption wedge this program exists for is abandoned.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c
  error: unknown command "cc"

comparisons.note: Bundles clang, lld, and multiple libcs in one tarball; instant and offline, at the cost of a large install for everyone.
Store-provisioned pinned toolchains; byte-reproducible builds, first use fetches from a cache.
comparisons.code: $ nix develop  # brings the exact pinned gcc/clang

comparisons.note: Downloads toolchains and targets on demand; small base install, per-target additions.

recommendation.why: The experience matches the Zig model from the second invocation onward, and the first invocation is one visible, pinned fetch. Every machine gets bit-identical toolchains — the reproducibility story enterprises audit for. The base install stays small for users who never compile C, and toolchain updates ship on their own schedule. It reuses the store that already provisions C dependencies, keeping one mechanism and the compiler seam dependency-free.

whyNot.reason: Every Jet user pays hundreds of megabytes for a C compiler most never invoke, and a clang security fix must wait for a Jet release.
Host toolchains differ per machine, so the one promise that wins C estates — identical builds everywhere — is broken on day one.
Forfeits the toolchain-first adoption path entirely; C teams get nothing to adopt before the language.

recommendation.tradeoff: The very first jet cc on a fresh machine needs the network or a preloaded offline bundle. Fully air-gapped sites must stage the toolchain bundle in advance.

decisions.title: Migration tier map: which languages get source importers
decisions.gist: Which foreign languages get automatic source conversion into Jet, and which get an explicit call-in-only verdict.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has three ways to meet a foreign codebase. A binder lets Jet call the foreign code where it stands. An overlay replaces one foreign library with a Jet package that must prove identical behavior first. An importer converts foreign source files into editable Jet source with TODO markers, so the team maintains Jet from then on.

The importer contract is already ratified (D-MIGRATE-SRC1): jet import must produce honest, editable Jet, verified by differential tests against the original. Python is the first proof. No other language has a ruling yet.

Conversion quality depends on the source language. Managed languages such as Java or TypeScript have garbage collection and no pointer arithmetic, so their meaning maps cleanly onto Jet's safe surface. C++ has templates, preprocessor macros, and undefined behavior. Faithful conversion of C++ tends to produce machine-shaped output no human wants to maintain.

This ballot decides the wave: which languages get importers, and which get a stated binder-or-overlay-only verdict. Enterprise teams then know the transition story for every pile of code they own.
decisions.story: Elena is an engineering director with 2.3 million lines of Java and 400k lines of C++. Her board approved a five-year modernization. She will only pick Jet if she can show a credible, named path for both piles — even if the two paths differ.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet import java services/pricing/src/main/java
  wrote 214 files under pricing-jet/ (37 TODO markers)
  differential: 1,892/1,892 behavior tests match

$ jet import cpp engine/
  error: C++ has no source importer.
  fix: call it in place instead — use cpp.engine

options.name: Importers for Java, C#, TypeScript/JavaScript, Go, Python; binder-plus-overlay verdict for C and C++
options.detail: The five importer languages cover most enterprise line counts, and each converts into Jet a human would keep. C and C++ get an honest, documented verdict: coexist through the binder, replace module by module by hand, with overlays proving each replacement. No language is left without a named story.
options.code:
$ jet import java src/     # editable Jet + TODOs
$ jet import csharp src/   # editable Jet + TODOs
$ jet import cpp src/
  error: C++ has no source importer.
  fix: use cpp.engine — coexist, then replace by module

options.name: Importers only for scripting languages (TypeScript/JavaScript, Python)
options.detail: Dynamic scripting code converts most cleanly, so only those importers ship. Java, C#, Go, and C++ teams get binders only. The largest enterprise estates — Java and C# — have no conversion story, so a director like Elena cannot present a full modernization plan built on Jet.
options.code:
$ jet import ts web/       # works
$ jet import java src/
  error: Java has no source importer.

options.name: Importers for everything, including a C++ subset
options.detail: Every language gets an importer, with C++ limited to a defined subset. The C++ output would be machine-shaped where templates, macros, or undefined behavior appear, breaking the ratified promise that imported code is editable Jet a team can own. First impressions in the hardest estates would be of generated sludge.

options.name: Stop at Python; every other language is binder-only
options.detail: Only the already-planned Python importer ships. All other languages coexist through binders indefinitely. One scripting importer cannot carry an enterprise migration story; it reads as a demo, not a path, and the tier map this program promises never exists.
options.code:
$ jet import py scripts/   # works
$ jet import java src/
  error: Java has no source importer.

comparisons.note: Won the Java world with a one-click Java-to-Kotlin converter producing idiomatic, editable output — conversion quality drove adoption.
comparisons.code: // IntelliJ: Code > Convert Java File to Kotlin File

comparisons.note: Won JavaScript by making every .js file already-valid input — migration was per-file and gradual.
Transpiles C to Rust but the output is unsafe, machine-shaped Rust that teams struggle to own — the cautionary case for option C.

recommendation.why: It gives every enterprise estate a named, truthful story. The five importer languages convert into Jet a human would keep, which is what makes conversion feel magical rather than burdensome. C++ gets honesty instead of silence: coexist through the binder, replace by hand behind overlay proof. Elena can put the whole plan on one slide.

whyNot.reason: Java and C# are the largest enterprise estates; leaving them binder-only concedes exactly the market this program targets.
A C++ importer would emit unreadable machine-shaped Jet, violating the ratified editable-output contract and poisoning first impressions in the hardest estates.
One scripting importer cannot carry an enterprise migration story; it reads as a demo, not a path.

recommendation.tradeoff: C++ teams are told plainly that conversion is manual behind the binder, and the five importer tracks land over time rather than all at once — some estates wait for theirs.

decisions.title: How Jet libraries reach foreign package registries
decisions.gist: How a Jet library gets published so Python, Node, JVM, and .NET developers can install it with the tools they already use.
decisions.lesson:
Every language ecosystem has a package registry and an install command. Python has pip, Node has npm, the JVM has Maven, and C# has NuGet. Developers only adopt what arrives through those doors.

A compiled language can hide inside those packages. Rust took this road: many popular Python and Node packages are Rust inside, installed as ordinary wheels and npm modules. Users never learn Rust exists; they just get faster libraries. The authors, meanwhile, chose Rust for the core. That is how a language wins share invisibly.

For Jet this means: once a Jet library exports a native C surface, glue code can wrap it for any host. The wrapper becomes a wheel, an npm module, a JAR, or a NuGet package. Each ecosystem has fiddly rules — platform tags, binary loading, version matrices — that decide whether the consumer's install just works.

This ballot picks who produces that wrapper: the Jet toolchain itself, a scaffold each team maintains, or the community.
decisions.story: Sam maintains an open-source data library written in Jet. A Python data scientist finds it on a benchmark page. If she can type pip install and use it within the same minute, Sam gains a user and Jet gains a beachhead inside her company.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet publish --to pypi
  built fastpricer-1.4.0-cp3-abi3-manylinux_x86_64.whl
  uploaded to pypi.org

# the consumer, who has never heard of Jet:
$ pip install fastpricer
>>> import fastpricer   # just works

options.name: First-party jet publish --to <registry>
options.detail: One command builds the ecosystem-correct artifact — wheel, npm module with native glue, JAR with library loading, NuGet package — straight from the same typed export surface the compiler already checks. The glue can never drift from the library. Publishing becomes a one-command habit, so far more Jet ships into foreign registries.
options.technical: Packaging generators consume the D-ADOPT-GUEST1 export facts: Python abi3 wheels with manylinux/musllinux tags, Node N-API prebuilds, JVM JNI loader JARs, NuGet runtimes/ layout. Registry credentials follow each ecosystem's standard auth.
options.code:
$ jet publish --to pypi
$ jet publish --to npm
$ jet publish --to maven
  # artifact + glue generated from the export surface, then uploaded

options.name: Scaffold generators the team maintains
options.detail: Jet generates a starter packaging project once, and the team owns it afterward. Every team re-solves the same platform-matrix and binary-loading problems alone. The scaffold drifts from the export surface with every release, so consumers hit broken installs that Jet's reputation pays for.
options.code:
$ jet new binding-python
  wrote python-pkg/  (yours to maintain from now on)
# six months later: export surface changed, wheel builds stale glue

options.name: Community-owned; Jet ships only the C export
options.detail: Jet's job ends at the .so and header. Whether wheels or npm modules exist depends on volunteers per ecosystem. The invisible-adoption channel opens years late or never, and install quality varies wildly between ecosystems.
options.code:
$ pip install fastpricer
  ERROR: No matching distribution found
  # nobody wrapped it for PyPI yet

comparisons.note: One command turned Rust-inside-Python into the normal case; PyO3 wheels made Rust invisible to pip users.
Prebuilt N-API binaries per platform; npm consumers never see a compiler.
Generates Kotlin, Swift, and Python bindings from one interface definition — one source of truth for many hosts.

recommendation.why: The whole value is that a foreign developer's first minute is flawless: install, import, run. Only compiler-owned packaging keeps the glue permanently in sync with the exported types, so that first minute never breaks. One-command publishing also multiplies how many Jet authors actually ship to foreign registries.

whyNot.reason: Scaffolds rot: every release risks glue drift, and every author re-learns platform tags and binary-loading rules alone, with consumers paying for the mistakes.
Rust needed maturin before Rust-inside-Python became normal; shipping only a header outsources the decisive channel to chance.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet's toolchain owns four ecosystems' packaging rules, and when those ecosystems change their rules, publishing correctness depends on Jet updating promptly.

decisions.title: Command spelling for Jet's C compiler front end
decisions.gist: What the user types to invoke Jet's C compiler: a jet subcommand, a single-word program, both as one mechanism, or a namespaced command.
decisions.lesson:
Jet will ship a built-in C compiler front end (ratified D-ADOPT-CC1=B). Build systems find a C compiler through the CC variable or an explicit compiler path. Whatever spelling Jet picks becomes the string pasted into Makefiles, CMake caches, and CI files across every estate the wedge targets.

There is one practical trap. CC usually holds a single program name. A value with a space, like "jet cc", works in plain make but confuses some tools. Those tools treat the whole string as one file name, cannot find a program by that name, and abort. Zig users hit exactly this with CC="zig cc" and work around it with tiny wrapper scripts in every affected repository.

The spelling therefore decides the first five minutes of adoption on legacy build systems. This ballot picks it.
decisions.story: Marcus, from the toolchain card, pastes CC="jet cc" into his CMake invocation. CMake stores it as a single compiler path, finds no program literally named "jet cc", and aborts. His first five minutes with Jet become a workaround hunt instead of a build.
decisions.inWild:
$ CC="jet cc" make
  # works — make splits the words

$ cmake -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="jet cc" ..
  CMake Error: Could not find compiler "jet cc"
  # the space is treated as part of one program name

options.name: jet cc / jet c++ subcommands plus jet-cc / jet-c++ alias binaries
options.detail: One mechanism with two spellings. Humans and docs use the subcommand, matching the zig habit and keeping one front door under jet help. Tools that require a bare program name get the installed single-word alias, so CC=jet-cc pastes safely into every build system on the first try. The alias simply re-enters the subcommand — same code path, same behavior, forever.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello        # humans, docs, muscle memory
$ CC=jet-cc cmake ..              # single word — every tool accepts it
# jet-cc re-executes 'jet cc' — one mechanism, two spellings

options.name: Subcommands only: jet cc / jet c++
options.detail: The cleanest single spelling and the exact zig shape. Every space-hostile tool then needs a user-written wrapper script, so the worst first-run experience lands on precisely the legacy build systems this wedge exists to win.
options.code:
$ jet cc hello.c -o hello
$ cat > cc-wrap.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
exec jet cc "$@"
EOF
# every affected repo re-invents this wrapper

options.name: Standalone binaries only: jetcc / jetc++
options.detail: A single word everywhere, so CC always pastes safely. But the compiler leaves Jet's front door. jet help does not list it, typing jet cc gets an error, and the product surface splits into a second command family.
options.code:
$ jetcc hello.c -o hello
$ jet cc hello.c
  error: unknown command "cc"   # muscle memory from zig breaks

options.name: Namespaced: jet toolchain cc
options.detail: Explicit and greppable, and it groups future toolchain verbs under one noun. Three words in CC fail in even more tools than two, and the ceremony reads as policy jargon to the beginner pass. Drop-in adoption is defeated at the paste.
options.code:
$ CC="jet toolchain cc" make
  # breaks wherever two words already broke, plus more

comparisons.note: Subcommand only; CC="zig cc" breakage is a recurring community issue solved per-project with wrapper scripts.
comparisons.code: $ CC="zig cc" cmake ..   # fails in tools that want one word

comparisons.note: A standalone single-word binary designed to be dropped into CC — the paste-safe pattern option A's alias copies.
Everything is a go subcommand; go tool namespaces the long tail — precedent for option D's grouping.

recommendation.why: Drop-in adoption is the entire point of jet cc, so the spelling must survive every legacy tool's CC handling on the first paste. The subcommand keeps one front door and matches zig muscle memory; the single-word alias makes CC=jet-cc safe everywhere. Both spell one mechanism, which I8 permits as flexible spelling of a single canonical path.

whyNot.reason: Space-hostile tools greet exactly the target audience with a failure, and every affected repo hand-writes the wrapper Jet declined to ship.
The compiler leaves the jet front door: jet help discovery and zig-trained muscle memory both miss it, splitting the product surface.
Three words in CC fail in more tools than two, and the ceremony burdens the beginner paste for no safety gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings of one tool must stay behavior-identical forever, and installers must manage the extra alias binaries on PATH.

decisions.title: Interpolation debug-label shorthand
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets a one-character way to print a variable's name and its value together while debugging.
decisions.lesson:
String interpolation lets you drop a value into text: print("total is {total}") prints the value of total inside the sentence.

While debugging, people rarely write sentences. They want a quick dump that shows which variable they printed and what it held, like: total = 42. Today that takes typing the name twice — print("total = {total}"). The two copies drift apart: rename the variable or tweak the expression, and the label silently lies.

A debug-label shorthand makes the compiler write the label for you. You mark the interpolation hole, and Jet prints the expression's own source text, an equals sign, then the value. One keystroke replaces the duplicated name, and the label can never go stale.

Jet already has one interpolation add-on rail: selectors, spelled with a hash inside the braces. {price#Fixed(2)} formats a number with two decimals; {value#Debug} shows a value's developer-facing form. Selectors change how a value renders. A debug label is different: it adds new text (the name) rather than reformatting the value. The options below differ on whether the label rides that existing rail or gets its own tiny mark.
decisions.story: Priya is a data analyst three weeks into Jet, chasing a wrong total through a pricing script. She peppers the code with print lines. Every line means typing each variable's name twice, and yesterday a stale label sent her down the wrong path for an hour: the print said discount but the hole actually held surcharge. She wants the label to come from the code itself, for free.

options.name: Trailing equals: {expr=}
options.detail: A single equals sign at the end of the hole prints the expression text, then ' = ', then the value. It is the cheapest possible spelling at the exact moment users want zero friction. Python programmers already know it. The cost: interpolation gains a second modifier mark besides the hash selector rail.
options.technical: Renders expression source text verbatim, then " = ", then the value through the same Display path as a bare hole. Composes with selectors: {x=#Fixed(2)} labels then formats. Registered in Syntax.rs under I7; misuse (empty hole, pattern position) gets one diagnostic with snapshot.
options.code:
print("{base=}")            // base = 104.5
print("{order.tier_rate()=}") // order.tier_rate() = 0.15
print("{discount=#Fixed(2)}") // discount = 15.68

options.name: Selector spelling: {expr#Label}
options.detail: The label rides the existing hash-selector rail next to #Debug and #Fixed. Nothing new to learn beyond one more selector name, and the error listing valid selectors makes it discoverable. The cost: seven extra characters per debug line, and the rail's meaning blurs — every other selector reformats the value, while this one injects new text.
options.technical: One more row in the selector registry; unknown-selector diagnostic E0914 already lists the valid set. Same rendering law as option A.
options.code:
print("{base#Label}")      // base = 104.5
print("{discount#Label}")  // discount = 15.68

options.name: Decline: keep typing the name
options.detail: No new surface. Users keep writing print("x = {x}"). The language stays one mark smaller, but the duplicated-label papercut and its stale-label bug stay forever, felt most by beginners who debug with prints the most.
options.code: print("base = {base}")   // fine until someone renames base

comparisons.note: f-strings added the trailing-equals form in 3.8; it is now the most-taught debug idiom in the language.
dbg!(x) prints file, line, expression text, and value — a macro rather than an interpolation mark.

recommendation.why: A debug shorthand only earns its keep if it is nearly free to type. One trailing character wins that test, and the largest beginner population arrives already knowing this exact spelling from Python.

whyNot.reason: Seven extra characters at the highest-frequency debug moment, and it bends the selector rail: every other selector reformats a value, this one injects new text.
Keeps the duplicated name and the stale-label bug this decision exists to remove; the papercut lands hardest on beginners.

recommendation.tradeoff: Interpolation gains a second modifier mark besides the hash rail. It is one fixed character with one meaning, ratified in Syntax.rs, and it composes with selectors instead of competing with them.

decisions.title: Map spelling: keep [K: V] or move to a comma-style form
decisions.gist: Whether the map type keeps its bracket-and-colon spelling, [K: V], or changes to look more like other comma-separated generic types.
decisions.lesson:
A map stores key-to-value pairs, like a phone book from names to numbers. Jet spells the map type [K: V] — for example [String: Int] — and a map value ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]. Lists use the matching sugar [T], as in [Int].

Jet uses two punctuation marks around collections, each with one job. The comma separates items in every sequence: list elements, call arguments, and also the entries of a map. The colon pairs a name or key with its value. That pairing colon appears in type annotations (x: Int), named tuples ((x: 1, y: 2)), struct literals (Point.{ x: 1 }), and each map entry ("ana": 31).

Inside a map literal both marks appear on their usual duty: colons pair, commas separate. The place the spelling can look odd is the type position. Named generics such as Lru<K, V> take comma-separated angle-bracket parameters, while the map sugar writes [K: V] with a colon. This ballot decides whether that colon is a win (the type mirrors the literal) or a loss (it breaks the comma rule of other generics).

One more fact matters: the compiler is never confused, but a reader can be, in two places. First, trait bounds also put a bracket list after a colon — <T: [Hash, Eq]> means 'T constrained by these traits', which looks like an annotation with a map type (x: [String: Int]) but pairs nothing. Second, map keys are expressions, so [limit: 3] means 'key = the value of variable limit'. The same word-colon-value shape in parens or braces — (limit: 3), Point.{ limit: 3 } — declares a field named limit instead.
decisions.story: Nate, the language owner, is reading an audit report that quotes the cache type Lru<K, V> in one sentence and the map type [K: V] in the next. The two spellings carry the same two type parameters with different punctuation. He flags that maps look inconsistent with everything else that separates with commas, and asks for the choice to be put on the board.

options.name: Keep [K: V] (status quo)
options.detail: The type keeps mirroring the literal: you write ["ana": 31] daily, so the type [String: Int] reads as 'a map shaped like that'. The colon stays on its one job — pairing — and entries stay comma-separated like everything else. The angle-bracket difference against Lru<K, V> remains, accepted as the price of the sugar.
options.technical: No change. D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A, S38, S64 stand as ratified.
options.code:
ages: [String: Int] = ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]
empty :: [String: Int].{}

options.name: Retire the sugar: Map<K, V>
options.detail: The map type becomes an ordinary named generic, punctuated exactly like Lru<K, V>. Every generic type now reads one way. The loss: the type stops mirroring the literal (which keeps its colons), and the everyday collection gets a heavier name that beginners must discover instead of a shape they already type.
options.technical: Amends D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A and S64; [T] list sugar would stand alone. Migration sweep across examples, tests, docs, and formatter.
options.code:
ages: Map<String, Int> = ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]
empty :: Map<String, Int>.new()

options.name: Comma type form: [K, V]
options.detail: The type swaps its colon for a comma so brackets always separate with commas. But [Int, String] now reads like a list of two different things, not a pairing. The type also stops matching the literal: the same key-value relationship gets a colon in values and a comma in types.
options.technical: Amends D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A and S64; grammar must disambiguate from any future heterogeneous-list spelling. Literal S38 unchanged.
options.code: ages: [String, Int] = ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]  // type comma, literal colon

options.name: Comma everywhere: positional pair literals
options.detail: Both type and literal drop the colon: ["ana", 31, "bo", 27] alternates keys and values by position. It is the only option that fully removes the colon. The cost is that nothing marks which item is a key, so one missing element silently shifts every later pair.
options.technical: Amends S38, S64, D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A. Odd-length literals need a new diagnostic; nested pairs become visually ambiguous.

comparisons.note: Type and literal both use the colon pair — exactly Jet's current design.
Type and literal disagree: the type hint separates with a comma while the literal pairs with colons.
No literal and no sugar; the named generic is precise but heavy for the everyday case.

recommendation.why: The colon is not a separator — it is Jet's one pairing mark, used identically in annotations, named tuples, struct literals, and map entries. Entries already separate with commas. The current spelling follows both rails at once, and the type mirrors the literal users type daily.

whyNot.reason: Loses the lightweight sugar that parallels [T] lists, and the type stops mirroring the literal — Python's exact mismatch, which its own users cite as confusing.
[K, V] reads as a two-item list, and the same key-value relationship would be punctuated one way in types and another in values.
Positional pairs hide which item is the key; one dropped element silently shifts every later pair — the exact bug class the colon prevents.

recommendation.tradeoff: Maps keep a bracket sugar that other named collections like Lru and Deque do not get. That asymmetry is accepted because lists and maps are the two everyday collections and earn their shorthand.

decisions.title: Name of the bounded cache collection
decisions.gist: What Jet calls its built-in size-limited cache, currently named Lru.
decisions.lesson:
A cache keeps recent results of expensive work so the program can reuse them instead of recomputing. A useful cache must be size-limited, or it grows forever. When a full cache gets a new entry, an old one must go. Choosing which one to drop is called eviction.

Jet's Core library ships one such collection today. It evicts the entry that has gone unused for the longest time. The classic computer-science name for that rule is Least Recently Used, shortened to LRU. Jet currently names the whole type after the rule: Lru<K, V>.

That name tells an expert the eviction rule instantly. It tells a beginner nothing: it is an unexpanded acronym, and nothing in it says 'cache'. Jet's naming law elsewhere favors plain words — membership is has, storage is add. The question is whether this type's name should say what it is (a cache) or how it evicts (LRU), and in which words.
decisions.story: Sam is building his first Jet web scraper and wants to avoid re-fetching pages. He searches the Core docs for 'cache' and finds nothing by that name. The type he needed was sitting in the collections table the whole time, labeled Lru — three letters he has never seen before and does not think to click.

options.name: Cache<K, V>
options.detail: The plain word. A beginner searching for a cache finds a type called Cache. Jet ships one cache mechanism, so the plain name is unambiguous today. The eviction rule moves to the doc line: 'a size-limited map that forgets the least recently used entry when full.' Other eviction rules, if ever ratified, become constructors on this one type. No new type names would appear.
options.technical: Rename in jet-foundation Collections, comptime dispatch, and the D-COLLBREADTH1 row; method law (has_key, add, add_new) unchanged. Future policies as constructors: Cache.new(cap) stays least-recently-used; a hypothetical Cache.by_frequency(cap) would be a later ballot.
options.code:
cache :: Cache.new(256)
page :: cache.get(url) ?? fetch(url)

options.name: RecentCache<K, V>
options.detail: Says both what it is and roughly how it evicts, in plain words, no acronym. The cost: the compound reads oddly — it is not a 'recent cache', it is a cache that keeps recent entries — and beginners searching 'cache' must still scan past the modifier.
options.code: cache :: RecentCache.new(256)

options.name: LruCache<K, V>
options.detail: The industry compound: Android and Rust's ecosystem both ship an LruCache. Experts recognize it on sight, and 'Cache' is now in the name for searchers. The confusing part the owner flagged — the unexpanded acronym — stays, and stays first.
options.code: cache :: LruCache.new(256)

options.name: Keep Lru<K, V>
options.detail: No change, no migration. The shortest spelling for people who already know the term, and the name is honest about the eviction rule. Fails the beginner test outright: it cannot be explained without first expanding an acronym.
options.code: cache :: Lru.new(256)

comparisons.note: Ships the compound LruCache — option C's exact precedent.
The dominant crate is named lru with type LruCache; std ships no cache at all.
comparisons.code: let mut cache: LruCache<String, Page> = LruCache::new(cap);

comparisons.note: Hides the acronym behind a decorator use-site; most users say 'cache' and never learn what LRU means.

recommendation.why: A beginner's search word is 'cache', and Jet ships exactly one cache, so the plain word is both findable and unambiguous. It matches the existing naming law that picked has and add over jargon. The eviction rule is one doc sentence away for experts.

whyNot.reason: The compound misreads — the cache is not recent, its entries are — and it still buries the search word behind a modifier.
Keeps the unexpanded acronym the owner flagged, and puts it first, where a beginner's eye lands.
The name cannot be explained to a beginner without expanding an acronym; the owner already judged it confusing.

recommendation.tradeoff: The name stops stating its eviction policy. Accepted: policy is a doc-line detail for experts, and a second policy, if ever ratified, arrives as a constructor on the same type rather than a competing name.

decisions.title: Stable identity for UI nodes across re-renders
decisions.gist: How a UI node keeps the same identity when the tree is rebuilt on each render.
decisions.lesson:
A UI tree is a picture of the screen right now. Many backends rebuild that picture on every update. Click handlers hang on real screen objects (DOM nodes, GTK widgets). If the picture is new but the identity is lost, the click dies or the handler is attached twice.

Identity is the answer to: which screen object is the same logical button as last time? One common answer is the path in the tree (first child of the root row, and so on). Another answer is an explicit key the author writes on the node. A third answer mixes both: use the path by default, and let a key override when the author moves nodes around.

Jet's DOM runtime already stores painted boxes by render path in jetDomBoxRegistry. GTK already has an on_click that takes a numeric id. The portable on_click design must pick one identity rule that every backend can honor, so a button keeps its handler after a redraw.
decisions.story: Maya ships a counter button on the web demo. Each click updates a signal and re-renders the tree. After the second click the button looks fine, but the handler is gone — or worse, every click fires three times because each render added another listener.

options.name: Render path is identity
options.detail: The path in the tree names the node. No extra key in beginner code. Moving a node to a new path is a new node. Authors who reorder lists can get surprising remounts.
options.technical: Keep jetDomBoxRegistry keyed by render path. Portable on_click attaches by path. GTK maps path (or a derived stable i64) into its existing id. No new syntax.

options.name: Explicit key on every interactive node
options.detail: Authors always write a key for nodes with handlers. Reorders keep the handler. Beginners must learn a key before their first click works well. Forgetting a key is an error or a silent path fallback — either costs ceremony.
options.technical: New optional or required key field on interactive UI nodes. Registry keys by author key. Duplicate keys are a diagnostic.
options.code:
ui.button("Save", key: "save", on_click: () => save())
// Reorder siblings; handler stays on key "save".

options.name: Path by default; optional key override
options.detail: Simple screens need no key. Lists and reorders opt into a key. One mechanism, two spellings of identity. Cost: authors must know when the default path is not enough.
options.technical: Registry key = author key if present, else render path. Duplicate keys diagnostic. Matches common React-style practice without requiring keys everywhere.
options.code:
ui.button("Save", on_click: () => save())
ui.for(items, (item) =>
  ui.button(item.name, key: item.id, on_click: () => open(item.id))
)

options.name: Backend-local identity; no portable rule
options.detail: Each backend keeps its own rule. Portable on_click cannot promise the same remount behavior. Authors debug web and GTK separately. Breaks the point of one portable handler.
options.technical: Document divergence. Rejected by I8 / D-WEB-CLICK-OWN1 destination B unless owner accepts non-portable remounts.

comparisons.note: Reconciles by position; keys opt in for lists.
Element identity follows Element tree; keys preserve State across moves.
comparisons.code:
ElevatedButton(onPressed: save, child: Text('Save'))
ListView(children: items.map((i) =>
  ElevatedButton(key: ValueKey(i.id), onPressed: () => open(i.id), ...)).toList())

recommendation.why: Beginners keep zero ceremony. List and reorder cases get an explicit key without a second click mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Reordered lists remount by path and surprise authors who did not ask for that.
Forces a key on every click before a beginner needs list identity.
Gives up portable click lifetime, which this card exists to deliver.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must learn when to add a key. That cost is paid only when path identity is wrong, not on the first button.

decisions.title: How a browser click reaches Jet handler code
decisions.gist: How a DOM click reaches Jet handler code with production speed, safety, and expert control.
decisions.lesson:
Jet UI must win on the web the same way it wins on the desktop. A button click starts in the browser. The handler runs as Jet code inside WebAssembly.

That crossing must be fast enough for dense UIs: editors, games, trading boards, and design tools. It must be safe when a node unmounts mid-click. Authors must write almost nothing for the common case.

Stable node identity is already decided (path by default, optional key). This ballot picks the pipe under that identity: how JavaScript names the Jet handler and when the handler runs.

Beginner magic means on_click on the node just works. Expert control means you can opt into ordered scheduling, filters, and batching without a second event system.
decisions.story: Priya ships a collaborative editor with thousands of interactive nodes. A Save click must hit the Jet handler in microseconds. A list reorder must not call a freed handler. Experts on her team also need clicks ordered with animation frames. A demo-only bind will not carry that product.

options.name: Handler-id table only
options.detail: Each on_click gets a numeric slot. JavaScript calls one wasm export with that id. Fast and clear. No built-in path to ordered batching with the rest of the UI scheduler.
options.technical: DomRuntime listener → jet_ui_dispatch(id, event). Unmount clears the slot. Matches GTK id-shaped handlers.
options.code:
element.addEventListener("click", () => wasm.jet_ui_dispatch(id, ev))
// missing slot → no-op

options.name: Raw closure handle only
options.detail: JavaScript holds an opaque wasm callable. Direct, but easy to leave stale after remount. Weak audit story for a market-facing runtime.
options.technical: externref / callable export. Drop must clear listener and handle together.
options.code: element.addEventListener("click", (ev) => wasmCb(normalize(ev)))

options.name: Selector bind (web.on) only
options.detail: Portable on_click is sugar over CSS selectors. Fragile under dense trees. Not acceptable as the long-term web channel for a language that aims to replace everything.
options.technical: Generated selectors; collisions on duplicates.
options.code:
ui.button("Save", on_click: () => save())
// lowers to web.on("#jet-el-12", "click", …)

options.name: Queue-only dispatch
options.detail: Every click is enqueued and drained later. Great for ordering. Adds latency and machinery to the default button path.
options.technical: JS posts {kind, nodeId}; Jet scheduler invokes handlers.
options.code:
queue.push({ kind: "click", target: nodeId })
// drain loop runs on_click later

options.name: Node-keyed slots by default; expert scheduler opt-in
options.detail: Default path: O(1) dispatch by stable node identity into a handler slot table. Unmount clears the slot. Beginners only write on_click. Experts opt the same handlers into the shared UI event scheduler for ordering, coalescing, and frame alignment — one mechanism, two strengths.
options.technical: Hot path: jet_ui_dispatch(node_or_handler_id, event) sync. Slot free on unmount/remount. Expert: ui.events.schedule / backend policy routes selected events through the shared drain without a second author-facing API. Never selector identity. Full I9 meaning across web and native backends that share the slot model.

comparisons.note: Synthetic events + delegation; production apps still need stable identity and careful unmount.
Events become messages on a queue — strong ordering, always async relative to the DOM callback.
Closures need explicit drop; stale handles are a real class of bugs.

recommendation.why: E is built for real products: microsecond default clicks, safe unmount, zero beginner ceremony, and expert scheduling without a second event system. It matches Jet's beginner-magic / expert-control law and the already-ratified stable node identity.

whyNot.reason: Fast table alone leaves experts without a first-class ordered path.
Opaque handles are the stale-handle footgun at scale.
Selector identity will not dominate dense, dynamic UIs.
Queue-only taxes every click with latency the default path does not need.

recommendation.tradeoff: The runtime must implement both the hot slot path and the opt-in scheduler route cleanly. That cost buys one author-facing model that can win demos and trading floors.

hybrid.synthesis: E keeps A's O(1) table as the default and harvests D's queue only where experts ask for ordered drain.

harvest.aspect: Numeric/slot dispatch is simple and fast.
harvest.use: Default hot path.

harvest.aspect: Queued drain gives ordering and batching.
harvest.use: Expert opt-in on the same handlers.

harvest.aspect: Author spelling stays on_click on the node.
harvest.use: Keep the portable spelling; drop selector identity.

decisions.title: Which UI events every backend must support
decisions.gist: Which events portable UI nodes support, and what a backend does when it cannot produce one.
decisions.lesson:
A click is not the only UI event. Hover, focus, text input, and key repeat exist on some devices and not on others. A terminal UI may have enter and focus-like selection. It may never have hover. A phone may have tap and long-press.

Portable handlers need a declared set. For each event outside a backend's power, the language needs a rule: error at build time, ignore at run time, or map to a cousin event. Without that rule, authors write on_hover and only find the gap on the device that lacks it.
decisions.story: Priya writes on_click and on_hover for a toolbar. It feels great in the browser. On the terminal backend the hover handler never runs, and she thinks her logic is wrong. She needs a clear rule up front.

options.name: Small core only: click (and submit-like activate)
options.detail: Every backend must support click/activate. Other events stay backend-specific modules (web.on, gtk.…). Portable code stays honest. Authors leave the portable layer for rich events.
options.technical: Portable node fields: on_click (and maybe on_activate). Hover/focus/key are not portable fields. Document backend modules for the rest.
options.code:
ui.button("Go", on_click: () => go())
// hover stays: web.on(sel, "mouseenter", ...)

options.name: Wide portable set; missing events are compile errors
options.detail: Authors can write many on_* fields. Building for a backend that cannot produce one fails with a teaching diagnostic. Safest. Forces ifdef-like splits or feature gates per target.
options.technical: Sema checks target backend capability matrix. Unsupported handler → diagnostic with snapshot.
options.code:
ui.button("Go", on_hover: () => hint())
// jet build --target terminal → error: hover not supported on terminal

options.name: Wide portable set; missing events no-op at runtime
options.detail: Same spelling everywhere. Unsupported handlers never fire. Easy to write once. Easy to ship a dead hover on terminal with no warning.
options.technical: Backend registers only capabilities it has. Others attach as no-ops. Optional runtime warning under a debug flag.
options.code:
ui.button("Go", on_hover: () => hint())
// terminal: builds clean; hint() never runs

options.name: Core click plus capability traits per backend
options.detail: Portable core is click. Rich events live behind explicit backend capability traits or target packages the author imports. Expert control stays visible. Beginners see one click path.
options.technical: on_click on ui.*. Hover etc. require importing ui.web or a Hoverable capability in scope. I8: one click mechanism; extras are opt-in modules.
options.code:
use ui.web.hover
ui.button("Go", on_click: () => go(), on_hover: () => hint())

comparisons.note: Gesture detectors vary by platform; some no-op or are absent on desktop vs mobile.
Modifiers apply widely; unsupported ones degrade per platform.
comparisons.code:
Button("Go", action: go)
  .onHover { hovering in showHint(hovering) }

recommendation.why: Keeps portable click small and safe, and makes richer events an explicit opt-in instead of a silent or noisy surprise.

whyNot.reason: Pushes all non-click events back into ad hoc web.on-style binds forever.
Forces target splits early for common hover/focus experiments.
Silent no-ops hide bugs when a backend cannot produce the event.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors import a capability module for rich events. That ceremony protects the beginner default.

decisions.title: Map merge when both sides share a key
decisions.gist: When two maps merge and share a key, which value wins.
decisions.lesson:
A map stores keys with values. Merge builds one map from two. When both sides share a key, Jet needs one clear conflict rule.

Beginners should overlay configs with no ceremony. Experts sometimes need a per-key choice. One method can do both: a default rule for the common case, and an optional callback when you need control.
decisions.story: Devon merges default settings with user settings. Both maps have theme. If the wrong side wins, dark mode vanishes after every load. Later Devon also merges inventory counts and must add quantities on clash instead of picking one side.

options.name: Right wins only
options.detail: merge always keeps the right map on overlap. Simple overlays work. No per-key control on the same call.
options.technical: Map.merge(self, other) copies self then other; duplicates take other. Full I9 Prelude.
options.code: defaults.merge(user)  // theme = dark

options.name: Left wins only
options.detail: First map keeps its values. Feels like fill-in blanks. Opposite of common overlay order.
options.technical: Duplicates keep self.
options.code: defaults.merge(user)  // theme = light

options.name: Error on conflict
options.detail: Overlap is always an error. Safe for strict joins. Painful for normal config overlays.
options.technical: Result or runtime error on duplicate keys.
options.code: defaults.merge(user)  // error: key theme on both

options.name: Callback always required
options.detail: Every merge takes a conflict function. Maximum control. Beginners must pass a lambda for basic overlays.
options.technical: merge(other, (k, a, b) => …) with no defaulted form.
options.code: defaults.merge(user, (_k, _a, b) => b)

options.name: One merge: right-wins default, optional conflict callback
options.detail: defaults.merge(user) overlays with right wins — beginner magic, no ceremony. Experts pass an optional conflict callback on the same method for per-key control. One name, one idea, two strengths.
options.technical: Map.merge(self, other, conflict: ((K, V, V) => V)? = None). Absent/None → right wins. Present → callback result. Label conflict: at call site. Full I9 in Prelude. No second method name.

comparisons.note: dict | is right-wins with no callback.
Map.merge/3 optional conflict function — closest to E.
comparisons.code: Map.merge(defaults, user, fn _k, _a, b -> b end)

comparisons.note: extend is right-wins; custom combine is manual.

recommendation.why: E is one mechanism: beginners get right-wins overlays with zero extra args; experts pass an optional callback for per-key policy. That is beginner magic plus expert control without splitting the surface.

whyNot.reason: Right-wins alone leaves experts without a first-class per-key path.
Reverses usual overlay order and invites silent wrong themes.
Punishes normal override merges that are not errors.
Forces a callback on every simple overlay.

recommendation.tradeoff: The signature grows one optional labeled argument. That is the cost of keeping a single merge name for both audiences.

hybrid.synthesis: E is A for the default path and D when the callback is supplied — one signature, not two methods.

harvest.use: Default when conflict is omitted.
Optional conflict: argument on the same merge.

decisions.title: When pause stops a task on each engine
decisions.gist: When does pause stop a task, and must every Jet engine use the same rule?
decisions.lesson:
Jet can run one program on more than one engine. Ahead-of-time and just-in-time engines run compiled code. The interpreter steps a slower form on some fallback paths.

Pause means: this task should stop soon. Cancel means: this task should stop and must not resume.

A wait point is a place where the task already yields. Examples are sleep, channel receive, and similar waits.

If engines pause at different times, the same source lies about its meaning. Jet forbids that drift.

Beginners need one rule that just works. Experts sometimes need a stronger pause that can stop a tight loop. This ballot also keeps one shared text form for paused and cancel flags.
decisions.story: Nia calls pause on a pool of workers while she debugs. She expects the same stop rule on every engine. She also wants a strong pause mode when she hunts a hot loop that never waits.

options.name: Wait-point pause on every engine
options.detail: Every engine pauses only at the next wait. A tight loop with no wait keeps running. One shared rule. No strong pause for hot loops.
options.technical: Document cooperative pause as the only law. Unify the trace string in Prelude.

options.name: Different pause strength per engine
options.detail: Compiled engines may stop sooner. The interpreter stays wait-only. Honest about today. Breaks one meaning across engines.
options.technical: Needs an owner carve-out from execution-tier parity. Trace string can still be shared.
options.code:
// JIT may stop earlier
// interpreter only at waits

options.name: Forced stop on every engine
options.detail: Pause always stops soon, even in a tight loop. Best for some debuggers. Costs interrupt checks on every engine all the time.
options.technical: Interrupt or signal checks on AOT, JIT, and interpreter.
options.code:
tasks.pause_all(workers)
// even while true { n = n + 1 } stops soon

options.name: Fix the text only; leave pause timing open
options.detail: Only share the paused and cancel text form now. Pause timing stays as today until a later card. Smallest change. Leaves the stop rule unclear.
options.technical: One Prelude formatter. No pause behavior change.
options.code: print(task)  // both engines call the same formatter

options.name: Same wait-point default; optional strong pause
options.detail: Default: every engine pauses at the next wait. One beginner rule. Experts pass an optional strong mode that also checks in tight loops. The paused and cancel text always comes from one shared formatter.
options.technical: Default cooperative wait-point law on all tiers (I9). Optional labeled mode on pause APIs, e.g. mode: .WaitPoints | .CheckLoops, default .WaitPoints. Strong mode adds portable yield or back-edge checks on every engine — never engine-specific timing. Trace flags only via Prelude.

comparisons.note: Cancel is seen at wait or call points. A tight loop can delay it.
comparisons.code: // check ctx when you Read, Wait, or select

comparisons.note: Cancel is cooperative at await points.

recommendation.why: E gives beginners one pause rule that matches on every engine. Experts get a stronger mode when they ask. The text form stays shared. That is magic for the common case and control for hard debug work.

whyNot.reason: Wait-only with no expert mode leaves hot-loop debug weak.
Different stop times per engine break one program meaning.
Forced checks on every pause tax the default fast path.
Leaves the pause rule unclear after this card.

recommendation.tradeoff: Strong mode needs portable interrupt or yield checks on every engine. Default pause stays cheap and cooperative.

hybrid.synthesis: E uses A's shared wait-point default and borrows C's strong stop only behind an explicit expert mode.

harvest.use: Default beginner path.
Optional strong mode.
Always ship with E.

decisions.title: One spelling for field defaults
decisions.gist: Should struct fields use the same = default spelling as function parameters, retiring #Default?
decisions.lesson:
A default is a value used when the caller or input leaves something out.

Jet already has defaults in two places. Function parameters use name: Type = value. The caller may skip that argument.

Struct fields use a different marker today: #Default(value). That fills a missing key when decoding JSON or when a CLI flag is absent.

Two spellings for the same idea force people to remember which form belongs on a field. Markers also compete for attention on crowded fields that already need docs, rename, env, and similar tags.

This choice decides whether fields keep the marker, switch to = like parameters, and whether writing Type.{ name: "web" } may omit other fields that declare defaults.
decisions.story: Maya ships a small HTTP tool. She wants port to default to 3000 on the CLI struct and the same default when her config JSON omits port. She also wants Config.{ name: "api" } in tests without restating every field. Today she writes #Default(3000) on the field and still fills every field in source literals. She asks why the language uses a second spelling for the same idea.

options.name: Keep the split
options.detail: Fields keep #Default for wire and CLI absence. Parameters keep =. Source literals still require every field. No migration. Marker congestion stays.
options.technical: Preserves D-SERDE5 and D-CLIFLAG1 as written. S61 remains call-site only. Construction omission stays illegal (E0303).

options.name: Fields use = for absence only
options.detail: Replace #Default(expr) with field: T = expr for decode and CLI absence. Retire the #Default marker. Source Type.{ … } still requires every field unless you write a constructor function.
options.technical: Amend D-SERDE5 / D-CLIFLAG1: field = is the absence default. Migrate examples and diagnostics. Construction law unchanged. Free Default marker name in Policy/Syntax.

options.name: Fields use = for absence and construction
options.detail: Same as B, and omitted fields in Type.{ … } fill from their = defaults. One spelling covers params, wire, CLI, and partial construction. Biggest beginner win; largest migration.
options.technical: Amend D-SERDE5 / D-CLIFLAG1 / construction (E0303). Field = is compile-time constant like today's #Default. Required fields remain those without =. Partial literals legal when every omitted field has =.

options.name: Allow both spellings
options.detail: Accept #Default(expr) and field = as synonyms forever. Softens migration but keeps two ways to say one thing and does not free the marker.
options.technical: Violates I8 preference for one mechanism. Docs and fmt must pick a canon anyway. Marker name stays reserved.

comparisons.note: Data/class fields commonly use = for construction defaults in one spelling.
comparisons.code:
data class Serve(val port: Int = 3000)
// Serve(name = "api") fills port

comparisons.note: No field =. serde uses attributes; Default trait is a separate mechanism — closer to today's Jet split.
Params use =; fields use #Default; construction does not fill from #Default.
comparisons.code:
fn f(x: Int = 0) {}
struct S { #Default(0) x: Int }

recommendation.why: Owner wants one short spelling and a freed marker. C makes field = mean the same idea everywhere a value can be omitted — call site, wire, CLI, and source construction — which matches how beginners already read =.

whyNot.reason: Keeps the confusing split and the marker congestion the owner called out.
Fixes spelling for wire/CLI but still forces full literals in source, so the everyday Type.{ … } story stays incomplete.
Two spellings forever; does not free #Default; fights I8.

recommendation.tradeoff: C is a breaking syntax migration across serde, CLI, and construction, with a large example and diagnostic update. That cost buys one mechanism and an empty marker slot for more important tags.

decisions.title: Collapse every fitting braced block
decisions.gist: Should jet fmt put any braced block that fits the line width onto one line, not only control bodies?
decisions.lesson:
jet fmt rewrites Jet source into a canonical layout so projects do not argue about spacing.

Card #1335 already made braces mandatory for if/else/loop bodies and told fmt to collapse a single-statement control body when it fits the width.

Other braces still keep authored multiline shape: match arms, function bodies, and marker blocks such as #Unsafe("…") { … }.

This choice is whether "fits means one line" becomes the rule for every brace pair, or stays limited to control bodies.
decisions.story: Rio runs jet fmt before every commit. A one-line #Impure("probe") { … } block keeps getting expanded across three lines, while a matching if body collapses. They want one predictable rule: if the contents fit, the braces stay on one line.

options.name: Control bodies only (status quo)
options.detail: Keep #1335. Only if/else/loop single-statement bodies collapse. Arms, functions, and marker blocks keep authored layout.
options.technical: No amendment beyond D-IFBRACE / #1335 collapse-if-fits for control bodies.
options.code:
if ok { print("ready") }          // collapses
#Impure("x") {\n  work()\n}       // stays multiline if authored that way

options.name: Every fitting braced block collapses
options.detail: Any { … } whose contents fit the width budget becomes one line: controls, arms, function bodies, marker regions. Comments or over-width contents keep multiline. Nested blocks collapse inside-out.
options.technical: Amend fmt law after #1335. Re-bless snapshots/goldens. Width budget unchanged (S44 / 100-col).

options.name: Collapse list with opt-outs
options.detail: Collapse controls, arms, and marker blocks, but never collapse multi-statement function bodies even when they fit. More special cases to learn.
options.technical: Partial extension of #1335 with an fn-body exception. Extra fmt classification.
options.code:
#Impure("x") { work() }    // collapses
fn run() {\n  print("hi")\n} // stays broken even if it fits

comparisons.note: Uses width heuristics; does not force every small block onto one line the same way.
Already collapses fitting single-statement control bodies only.

recommendation.why: Owner asked for one rule: if it fits, it is one line, including marker blocks. B matches that without a special-case menu.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the inconsistency that motivated the card.
Adds another exception beginners must memorize.

recommendation.tradeoff: Large snapshot and golden churn when fmt rewrites the corpus. That is accepted to get a uniform brace rule.

decisions.title: BuildContext defaults for CLI and effect knobs
decisions.gist: How a project sets default build flags and effect grants once inside fn build.
decisions.lesson:
A build flag is a switch you pass on the command line. Examples are --release, --profile=debug, and --allow-exec. Effect grants are the yes-you-may switches for risky build steps such as running a process or reading the network.

Today those switches are typed again on every jet build line, or they live in package files that this card does not own. Many projects want one shared default: set the knobs once, then run a plain jet build.

fn build(b: BuildContext) is Jet's build-time entry. BuildContext is the typed toolbox that fn build uses to register targets and actions. This ballot picks whether BuildContext also carries project defaults for ordinary CLI and effect knobs. It also picks which knobs it may set, and what happens when you pass a flag on the command line.

The rule must stay Jet-facing. It must not leak rustc flags. Explicit command-line intent should stay stronger than a project default unless you pick a lock option on purpose.
decisions.story: Omar maintains a tools package. Every CI job repeats jet build --release --allow-exec --allow-fs. He wants those defaults declared once beside fn run, then a plain jet build in scripts. He still needs a one-off jet build --profile=debug to win over the project default when he debugs.

options.name: Typed default methods; CLI always wins
options.detail: BuildContext gains small methods such as default_profile and default_allow. Beginners set defaults in fn build. Any matching flag on the command line overrides the default. Effect grants still name each effect. No way to lock out CLI.
options.technical: Add BuildContext methods for profile/release-class knobs and for default --allow-* grants that apply when CLI omits them. Merge order: batteries/command defaults, then fn build defaults, then explicit CLI (CLI highest). Does not amend D-BUILDFLAGS1's per-effect naming. I2: Jet knobs only.

options.name: One defaults record; CLI always wins
options.detail: One call passes a BuildDefaults record for profile and allows. Same override rule as A: CLI wins. Slightly more ceremony than methods. Easy to extend with new fields later.
options.technical: b.defaults(BuildDefaults.{ profile: .Release, allow: [.Exec, .FS] }). Same merge order as A. Missing fields mean no default for that knob.

options.name: Defaults plus optional CLI lock
options.detail: Same defaults as A or B, plus an expert lock that rejects conflicting CLI flags. Strong for sealed CI images. Easy to surprise a developer who passes --profile=debug and gets an error.
options.technical: b.default_profile(.Release, lock: true) or defaults(..., lock_cli: true). Locked knobs: CLI match ok; CLI conflict is a diagnostic. Unlocked knobs keep CLI-wins.

options.name: Profile defaults only; effects stay CLI/pkg
options.detail: BuildContext may set profile/release defaults. Effect grants stay on --allow-* and package grants (D-BUILDFLAGS1). Smaller surface. Omar still repeats allow flags in CI.
options.technical: Methods or record for Build profile knobs only. No default_allow on BuildContext. Effect path unchanged.
options.code:
b.default_profile(.Release)
$ jet build --allow-exec --allow-fs

options.name: No BuildContext defaults
options.detail: Keep defaults in CLI and package files only. Rejects the owner ask for this card. Avoids a second defaults channel next to package profiles.
options.technical: Close or re-scope #1370. No new BuildContext default APIs.
options.code:
// no b.default_* 
$ jet build --release --allow-exec --allow-fs

comparisons.note: Shared flag tables set once; tools reuse them without retyping every switch.
comparisons.code: // conceptual: shared flags struct applied to multiple targets

comparisons.note: Permissions are explicit --allow-* flags; projects often wrap them in tasks rather than locking them in code.
Profile defaults live in Cargo.toml; CLI --release still selects the release profile.

recommendation.why: A matches the owner ask: BuildContext methods, shared defaults beside fn build, and explicit CLI still wins. Typed methods stay small and Jet-facing without a lock footgun.

whyNot.reason: A record works, but methods match how BuildContext already adds targets and stay shorter for the common case.
CLI lock fights the stated rule that explicit CLI overrides still win, and it surprises local debug flags.
Leaves effect grants as repeated CI noise, which is half of the pain this card names.
Rejects the BuildContext defaults the owner asked to track on this card.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must learn a few default_* methods. That cost buys one place for shared knobs without sealing out CLI overrides.

decisions.title: Portable on_click identity, dispatch, and event set
decisions.gist: How portable on_click names widgets, reaches Jet from the host, and which events every backend must honor.
decisions.lesson: A UI backend paints a tree of nodes. Click handlers need a stable node id across re-renders. They also need a channel from the host into Jet code. A closed event list keeps missing events honest. Portable on_click is one method on every backend. Backends that cannot produce an event leave that handler unbound.
decisions.story: Maya ships a counter demo for web and desktop. She wants one `app.on_click(btn, …)` line. Today web uses `web.on("#btn", "click", …)` while GTK uses widget ids — she cannot teach one story.
decisions.inWild: ui_web_click.jet still binds with web.on while ui_native_linux.jet uses on_click. Without identity and dispatch law, a portable respell either breaks re-render or invents a second click API.

options.name: DOM-only: CSS selectors + JS bridge forever
options.detail: Keep web.on selectors as the web identity; GTK keeps integer ids. Document the split. Fast for web, no portable surface.
options.technical: No shared on_click. Rejects D-WEB-CLICK-OWN1=D destination B.
options.code: web.on("#btn", "click", ev => count.set(count.get() + 1))

options.name: Stable node id + host callback table + closed Click set
options.detail: Every backend node carries a stable i64 id across reconcile. Hosts call into a registered Jet callback table by that id. The portable set is Click (and later Focus/Input as separate cards). A backend that cannot emit Click leaves on_click unbound and documents it — never fakes clicks.
options.technical: Identity: JetUiNode.id assigned at construction, preserved on reconcile match (same key path as GTK). Dispatch: host → extern "C"/wasm import → look up id → invoke Fn(). Event set v1: Click only on on_click; unknown host events ignored. Terminal/null backends: on_click registers but never fires unless the backend can produce Click.
options.code:
app.on_click(btn, () => count.set(count.get() + 1))
// same on GtkBackend, web backend, and future mobile

options.name: String keys everywhere, free-form event names
