options.detail: Identity is an author string; events are arbitrary strings. Maximum flexibility. Typo-prone; breaks I8 closed surfaces.
options.code: app.on("save-btn", "click", …)

options.name: Hybrid: B identity/dispatch + Click-only v1 + explicit unsupported
options.detail: Same as B, and each backend publishes which portable events it supports. Unsupported on_click on a headless null backend is a documented no-op with a debug trace, not a type error — beginners keep one API; experts query capability.
options.technical: Harvest A’s honesty about host limits and C’s desire for discoverability without free-form strings. Capability query is optional follow-up; v1 law is B plus no-op semantics for unsupported backends.
options.code:
backend.on_click(btn, handler)  // Click only
// Terminal without pointer: register succeeds; handler never runs

comparisons.note: Stable keys across reconcile; synthetic events.
Widget pointers / ids for signal connect.
addEventListener + element identity.

recommendation.why: D keeps one portable on_click (D-WEB-CLICK-OWN1=B destination), stable ids, and a closed Click set while staying honest when a backend cannot fire.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the web/desktop fork that the parent ruling already rejected.
Almost complete; D only adds explicit unsupported/no-op honesty for headless backends.
Free-form strings fight I8 and turn typos into runtime misses.

recommendation.tradeoff: Headless demos that call on_click will compile but never fire until the backend can produce Click — that must be documented in the example.

hybrid.synthesis: D is B’s identity and dispatch with A’s honesty about host limits, without C’s open strings.

harvest.use: Unsupported backend = no-op, not a fake event.
Core portable law.
Closed enum + docs, not free-form names.

decisions.title: Shared-in-Shared cycles: reject or execute
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet rejects cyclic Shared payloads at compile time or executes them with full tier parity and a free-or-leak proof.
decisions.lesson:
Shared<T> is Jet's synchronized shared handle. A value of type Shared<T> can be passed into many places at once. Each place can read or edit the same T under the Shared contract.

A cycle appears when T itself contains Shared<T>, or Shared of something that eventually points back. Example: struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }. Two nodes can each hold the other. Reference counting alone cannot free that pair: each handle keeps the other alive.

Terms: Shared-in-Shared means a Shared field whose payload type contains Shared again. A cycle is a live graph of Shared handles that points back to itself. Free means the last reachable handle ends and storage is released. Leak means storage stays after the program dropped every named handle.

Mental model: either the type system forbids building that cycle, or the runtime must define how cycles die (for example a weak link, or a collector that finds unreachable cycles).

Tiny example:

struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }
a :: Shared(Node.{ next: Absent })
b :: Shared(Node.{ next: Present(a) })
a.edit(n => { n.next = Present(b) })

Stakes: without a clear rule, beginners can build graphs that never free, and experts cannot audit ownership. #1353 proved sema accepts the type today while neither default jet run nor AOT executes the constructing function cleanly.
decisions.story: Mira ships a graph editor. Each node holds Shared handles to neighbors. On Linux CI, jet run --release hits an ICE. On her laptop, default jet run says the function is unsupported. She cannot tell whether closing the last window frees the graph or leaks it. She needs either a clear compile error naming the cycle, or a working Shared cycle story with a free-or-leak measurement she can trust.

options.name: Reject Shared-in-Shared / cyclic Shared at sema
options.detail: Sema diagnoses Shared fields whose payload can form a Shared cycle. Construction that would close a cycle is a named diagnostic with what/why/fix and a UI snapshot. Beginners never build an un-freeable graph by accident. Experts who need graphs use an explicit non-Shared edge or a later weak-handle design under a different card.
options.technical: Add a structural check on type definitions and Shared constructors: if a Shared payload's type graph can reach Shared of a type that reaches back, emit a registered diagnostic (new E-code). Keep I9: every tier refuses the same programs. No interpreter/JIT special case. Docs name the rule; example shows the diagnostic.
options.code:
struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }
// error: Shared cycle in Node.next — use an explicit weak edge or a non-Shared id

options.name: Full I9 execute Shared cycles + free-or-leak measurement
options.detail: Make Shared-in-Shared constructible and runnable on AOT, default jet run, and interpreter ambient with one Prelude meaning. Ship a proof that either frees the cycle when last external roots drop, or documents a deliberate leak with a measurable test. Weak references may be part of the mechanism if needed for free.
options.technical: Close the Items.rs / quick-run gaps for Shared-bearing recursive types. Define cycle lifetime in Prelude (collector, weak back-edge, or owned break). Prove free vs leak with an example golden and a runtime measurement. I9 required end to end.

options.name: Both now: beginner-safe Shared + expert cycles on this card
options.detail: One Shared mechanism (I8). Beginner path never builds an immortal graph by accident: either construction that would cycle needs an explicit expert form, or cycles free when external roots drop — with a clear diagnostic if the beginner form is wrong. Expert path ships in the same delivery: intentional Shared graphs (weak back-edges or equivalent), full I9 on AOT / jet run / interpreter, and a free-or-leak proof. No follow-on card for the expert surface. No parking in jit_gaps.
options.technical: Implement reject-or-require-opt-in for the accidental beginner cycle, plus the expert cycle/weak API, Prelude free-or-leak law, I9 adapters only, example+golden, and a free-or-leak measurement test — all acceptance for this card.
options.code:
struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }  // beginner: clear diagnostic or free-safe
struct Node { next: Shared.Weak<Node>? } // expert: intentional cycle, frees — ships here

options.name: Leave constructible; document ICE/unsupported as known gap
options.detail: Keep today's sema acceptance. Document that constructing Shared cycles may ICE or hit quick-run unsupported. Do not add a diagnostic or an execution path on this card.
options.technical: Docs-only. Violates I2 spirit (rustc/ICE as user path) and I9 (tiers disagree). Not a product outcome.
options.code: // status quo from #1353 — not recommended

comparisons.note: Rc/Arc cycles need Weak to free. Strong-only cycles leak until the process exits.
comparisons.code: struct Node { next: Option<Rc<RefCell<Node>>> } // leaks without Weak

comparisons.note: Class cycles need weak/unowned for ARC to free.
comparisons.code: class Node { weak var next: Node? }

comparisons.note: GC collects pointer cycles; no Shared handle distinction.

recommendation.why: Matches the owner rule: beginner magic and full expert control in one delivery. C (revised) keeps Shared one mechanism, stops accidental leaks for beginners, and ships expert cycle graphs now with I9 and free-or-leak proof — not a later card.

whyNot.reason: Reject-only gives beginner safety but denies expert graphs entirely. Owner wants expert control out of the box.
Execute-all as the silent default risks beginner immortal graphs unless free law is perfect; revised C keeps beginner default safe and still ships B's expert power now.
Documenting ICE/unsupported violates I2 spirit and leaves both facets unfinished.

recommendation.tradeoff: This card's scope grows: reject/opt-in beginner path plus expert cycle API, I9, and free-or-leak proof all close together. That is the point — no deferred expert half.

hybrid.synthesis: Harvest A's beginner non-leak default and B's full execute/I9/free-or-leak expert path into one option that ships both now.

harvest.aspect: Beginners never accidentally immortalize a graph.
harvest.use: Default/diagnostic path for ordinary Shared.

harvest.aspect: Intentional cycles run on every tier with free-or-leak proof.
harvest.use: Expert Shared cycle/weak surface on this card.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A/B/C/D. Guidance already recorded: both beginner magic and full expert control now — no later. Recommended revised C. After ratify: implement the whole dual surface on this card (I9 + free-or-leak); do not split expert to a follow-on.

decisions.title: What LTS cadence and support window does Jet promise at GA?
decisions.gist: Choose how often Jet names an LTS compiler line and how long it receives active and maintenance fixes after 1.0 GA.
decisions.lesson:
An LTS line is a specific compiler release family, such as 1.4.x, that keeps receiving selected fixes after newer feature releases exist. Cadence answers how often a new LTS starts. The support window answers when fixes stop. Active support normally includes security, critical correctness, supported-host, and toolchain fixes. Maintenance support is narrower: security and severe data-loss or compiler-correctness fixes.

Jet editions are separate. An edition controls source compatibility. An LTS line controls how long one compiler family is serviced. D-REL4 already forbids a pre-GA LTS and says the window is set at GA. This ballot supplies that missing promise.
decisions.story: Mina's company qualifies a Jet compiler for a regulated product. Qualification takes three months, so she cannot move to every feature release. She needs the next baseline date, the security-fix window, and the number of overlapping LTS lines. She also needs to know when an upgrade project must begin.
decisions.inWild:
Example if Jet 1.0 GA ships in October 2027:

line       starts       active until   maintenance until
1.0 LTS    Oct 2027     Oct 2028       Oct 2030
next LTS   Oct 2028     Oct 2029       Oct 2031

`jet --version --support` and the signed release manifest name the line, phase, exact end date, supported editions, hosts, and replacement LTS. The public calendar lists dates at least twelve months ahead.

options.name: Annual LTS, 36 months total
options.detail: Make 1.0 GA the first LTS. Start one successor LTS every twelve months in the same published month. Give each line twelve months of active support and twenty-four months of maintenance, for three years total and at most three overlapping LTS lines. Current non-LTS releases remain available, but the latest stable plus every live LTS receives applicable security fixes. Publish exact dates, phases, supported editions and hosts, and the replacement line.
options.technical: Active: security, critical compiler/runtime correctness, supported-host/toolchain breakage, and severe performance regressions; no new language behavior. Maintenance: security plus critical data-loss, memory-safety, type-safety, or miscompilation fixes. Patch releases preserve D-REL1. An LTS keeps the editions and target matrix it advertised; dropping either before EOL needs the existing security/safety exception process and a migration notice. Calendar changes require at least six months' notice and cannot shorten an existing line.
options.code:
Jet 1.0.x LTS
active:      2027-10-01 .. 2028-09-30
maintenance: 2028-10-01 .. 2030-09-30
replacement: Jet 1.4.x LTS (example; exact SemVer chosen by shipped release)

options.name: Annual LTS, 24 months total
options.detail: Start an LTS every twelve months, with twelve months active and twelve months maintenance. At most two LTS lines overlap. This gives enterprises a predictable yearly baseline while reducing the age of code Jet must patch.
options.technical: Use the same active and maintenance definitions as A, but end support after two years. Publish exact dates and never shorten a live line. Customers that qualify slowly must begin migration within the first LTS year to keep overlap with the replacement.

options.name: Biennial LTS, 48 months total
options.detail: Start one LTS every twenty-four months. Give it twenty-four months active and twenty-four months maintenance, for four years total and at most two overlapping lines. Enterprises upgrade less often, but each baseline waits longer for a successor and carries an older compiler, Core, host, and toolchain contract.
options.technical: Use the same fix classes and no-shortening rule as A. The longer active phase accepts supported-host and toolchain compatibility fixes for two years. Feature releases between LTS lines are not promoted later; the next scheduled line is cut from then-current stable after its release gates pass.

comparisons.note: Node's official policy promotes even-numbered major lines to LTS and gives them twelve months of Active LTS plus eighteen months of Maintenance. Its public schedule records exact transition and end dates. https://github.com/nodejs/Release

Go supports each major release until two newer major releases exist and issues minor revisions for critical problems, including security problems. This is simple, but it ties the time window to release cadence instead of fixed enterprise dates. https://go.dev/doc/devel/release
comparisons.code: support Go N until Go N+2 ships

comparisons.note: Rust ships stable every six weeks and officially supports the newest stable release, so each version's support is about six weeks. That fast train is useful for current users but is not an enterprise LTS promise. https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html
comparisons.code: stable every six weeks; previous stable reaches EOL

recommendation.why: A gives adopters a predictable yearly qualification target and a full two-year migration overlap after the replacement LTS starts. Three years is long enough for regulated and air-gapped estates without binding Jet to four-year-old host and toolchain assumptions. It also keeps editions separate from servicing, so source compatibility does not depend on choosing an old compiler forever.

whyNot.reason: Two years leaves only one year of overlap after the replacement starts. A slow qualification or skipped annual cycle can put an enterprise against EOL before its replacement is approved.
Four years improves stability but makes Jet promise old hosts, toolchains, runtime dependencies, and security backports for too long at GA, while a two-year cadence delays a fresh qualified baseline.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must service up to three LTS lines at once and publish backport eligibility clearly. The fixed three-year promise is worth that bounded cost because the adoption pack explicitly targets enterprises that qualify toolchains slowly.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, record the relative policy in release-policy.md. When the GA month is fixed, publish the first dated calendar and signed support metadata without reopening this cadence decision.

decisions.title: Authorize the Nix evaluator product boundary
decisions.gist: Should Jet evaluate supported Nix flakes as normal Jet environment inputs now?
decisions.lesson:
A Nix flake is a project description that names inputs, such as nixpkgs, and outputs, such as packages or development shells. A lock file records the exact revision of each input. Jet can read a small set of these facts without running Nix, or it can evaluate a supported Nix surface and turn the result into Jet's typed environment graph.

A private boundary is an internal reader. It can inspect a value and reject it, but users cannot depend on its result. A product evaluator is part of Jet's normal behavior. It must return typed packages, services, locks, and errors. It must use one identity and one graph across `jet env sync`, development mode, and other execution paths.

This choice does not require Jet to support every Nix expression. The evaluator can support a bounded surface and report unsupported facts. The result must keep the exact Nix 2.34.8 identity and exact input revisions. It must never expose an opaque Nix value or silently call a second resolver.

Design checks: the beginner path stays `env.*` and needs no Nix knowledge. The expert path can import a flake without creating a second environment model. The hybrid path uses the same typed graph for native Jet declarations and supported flake facts. Adversarial checks reject missing tools, malformed input, unsupported expressions, resource overuse, and unrepresentable results with clear errors. Improvement checks keep provenance, lock identity, and audit output visible.
decisions.story: Nate uses flake-parts for a development shell. He wants `jet env sync` to produce the same package graph on every machine, while a malformed or unsupported Nix expression must fail with a typed Jet error.
decisions.inWild:
```sh
$ jet env sync
resolved flake input nixpkgs at 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
resolved devShell packages: ripgrep, rustc

$ jet env sync --offline
error: the locked flake graph needs an evaluator result that is not present
```
decisions.detail: The decision controls whether the existing native Nix boundary becomes a supported product path. It does not decide the syntax of native `env.*` declarations or permit arbitrary Nix values in Jet.

options.name: Native typed evaluator
options.detail: Make the native evaluator part of Jet's product path. Users get one typed graph for native modules and supported flakes. Unsupported facts stay visible as errors. The cost is a bounded compatibility surface instead of full Nix behavior.
options.technical: The evaluator is the sole semantic owner for the supported Nix surface. It returns typed graph facts, applies fixed resource limits, records evaluator identity, and reports every unsupported projection. AOT, development, and interpreter adapters consume the same result.
options.code:
```text
jet env sync
  -> typed FlakeGraph + EnvironmentFacts
  -> .jet/lock records evaluator identity and exact revisions
  -> E1256/L0204 on unavailable or unrepresentable facts
```

options.name: External Nix evaluator
options.detail: Run the pinned Nix 2.34.8 executable as the product evaluator. This supports more Nix expressions, but every machine needs the executable and its process policy becomes part of Jet behavior.
options.technical: The bridge must verify the tool version, bound input and output, serialize a typed result, retain provenance, and reject facts that Jet cannot represent. This changes the ratified native-evaluator architecture.
options.code:
```text
$ jet env sync
error: Nix 2.34.8 is required on PATH
fix: install the pinned Nix evaluator or use a native env.* declaration
```

options.name: Keep the private boundary
options.detail: Keep the current reader private and defer product evaluation. Native `env.*` declarations remain supported, while foreign flakes fail honestly or use an explicit bridge. This keeps the boundary safe but leaves the flake product path incomplete.
options.technical: No opaque evaluator value becomes public. The one-graph flake-parts criteria and the native product-evaluator law remain open until a later owner decision.
options.code:
```text
$ jet env sync
error: foreign flake evaluation is not available in the Jet product path
fix: declare the environment in env.* or run `jet bridge flake`
```

comparisons.note: Cargo turns a manifest and lock file into typed package and dependency data. Jet should give supported flake inputs the same stable identity, while keeping unsupported Nix facts explicit.
Nix evaluates arbitrary expressions with Nix semantics. Option A supports a named Jet-owned subset and does not pretend that every Nix value is a Jet fact.

recommendation.why: Option A follows the ratified native evaluator law and gives supported flakes one typed graph. It keeps the beginner path small and keeps expert provenance, locks, and errors visible.

whyNot.reason: Option B makes an external executable part of ordinary Jet semantics and changes the ratified architecture.
Option C keeps the safe private seam but leaves the promised flake-parts and product-evaluator behavior incomplete.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option A accepts a bounded supported Nix surface. Jet must maintain clear unsupported-fact errors and differential proof for each supported fact.

decisions.title: How does a compiled row policy bind to every DB path?
decisions.gist: Choose the public authority that carries a compiled row policy and user identity through query, mutation, and live-query paths.
decisions.lesson: D-DBPOLICY1=A makes a row policy a typed, compiled predicate. That predicate is not safe until each database operation receives the policy and the user identity. A plain DBConnection currently has no policy context. An unbound query, mutation, or live query could bypass the rule. The binding must be explicit or must have a lifetime rule that prevents cross-request leakage.
decisions.story: Maya serves two users from one process. Both users call the same repository. A query must return only rows allowed by the compiled policy. An update and a live query must apply the same rule. If the policy lives in hidden global state, one request must never reuse another request's identity.
decisions.inWild:
policy := db.policy("tasks", "owner == user")
scoped := conn.with_policy(policy, user)
scoped.query("select * from tasks", binds)
scoped.execute("update tasks set done = true", binds)
scoped.live("select * from tasks", binds)

options.name: Explicit policy scope
options.detail: Add one policy-bound DB scope. The scope carries the compiled policy and user identity. Query, query_one, execute, transaction, and live-query methods accept only that scope. The ordinary connection cannot run row-scoped operations.
options.technical: The scope is an owned capability. It contains a DBConnection, a JetRowPolicy, and a validated user identity. Prelude applies the predicate to returned rows and write targets. Sema rejects a policy-protected path that uses an unscoped connection. The same scope is passed to AOT, JIT, interpreter, and live adapters.
options.code:
scoped := conn.with_policy(policy, user)
scoped.query(sql, binds)
scoped.execute(sql, binds)
scoped.live(sql, binds)

options.name: Request policy context
options.detail: Bind the policy and user to an explicit request or task context. DB methods read that context while the request runs. Context creation and cleanup become mandatory at every boundary.
options.technical: The runtime owns a scoped context guard. A missing context fails closed. Nested requests must save and restore the prior context. All query, mutation, transaction, and live paths read the same Prelude context.

options.name: Typed repository binding
options.detail: Attach the policy to a typed repository or table handle. Only the repository exposes row-scoped query, mutation, and live methods.
options.technical: The repository carries the row type, table identity, compiled policy, and user identity. Sema can reject a repository whose policy table does not match the row type. This adds schema and repository machinery to the DB surface.
options.code:
tasks := db.repository<Task>(conn, policy, user)
tasks.query()
tasks.update(id, patch)
tasks.live()

comparisons.note: The database session carries policy identity. This is compact, but a pooled session must reset identity on every checkout.
An owned handle can carry authority without a process-global variable. The type of the handle makes the boundary visible at each call site.

recommendation.why: A makes the authority visible and local. A DB scope cannot silently cross a request unless the caller moves it. One scope can cover query, mutation, transaction, and live-query paths without adding a hidden runtime context or a second repository model.

whyNot.reason: A context is shorter at call sites, but hidden state can leak across pooled work, nested requests, or live subscriptions. The cleanup rule also becomes part of every adapter.
A typed repository gives strong schema checks, but it adds a second public abstraction before Jet has a ratified repository surface. It also duplicates the scope authority.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one explicit scope value and a small amount of call-site ceremony. That cost buys visible authority, fail-closed missing policy handling, and one enforcement seam for every DB path.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, implement the selected binding for query, query_one, execute, transaction, and live-query paths. Do not close #1160 or its closeout cards until bypass and cross-request tests pass on AOT and default jet run.

decisions.title: How does durable service authority carry receipts and retention?
decisions.gist: Choose the public authority that carries delivery receipts, retention, and transaction truth through durable service paths.
decisions.lesson: D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1=D gives Jet bounded mailboxes and at-least-once retry with idempotency, but a boolean success result is not a durable receipt. A production caller must know whether a message was accepted, retained, dead-lettered, or rejected. Retention and transaction boundaries must be explicit; hidden global state cannot safely cross restarts or requests.
decisions.story: Nora submits an order while the worker is restarting. She needs a typed answer that distinguishes accepted-and-retained from mailbox-full, duplicate, dead-lettered, and unavailable. A retry must reuse the same authority without creating a second delivery.
decisions.inWild:
runtime := services.runtime(store, retention: time.hours(24))
receipt := runtime.send(order_endpoint, order, key: order.id)?
match receipt {
    .Accepted(id) -> audit(id)
    .Duplicate(id) -> continue
    .Retained(id, until) -> schedule_retry(id, until)
    .Rejected(reason) -> report(reason)
}
decisions.detail: The chosen model must define receipt identity, accepted versus retained state, duplicate replay, dead-letter ownership, retention expiry, durable commit ordering, transaction grouping, crash recovery, and the behavior of a retry after a generation handoff. It must use the existing service runtime and Prelude seam; it must not add actor syntax or a second scheduler.

options.name: Explicit durable authority scope
options.detail: Create one owned service authority scope carrying the durable store, retention policy, and transaction boundary. Send and retry return a typed receipt from that scope; the ordinary in-memory tree remains the bounded local path.
options.technical: The scope contains the service tree, durable store capability, retention facts, and generation authority. Commit order is store record then receipt; a crash before the receipt leaves a retryable idempotency record. Receipts are stable by idempotency key and report Accepted, Duplicate, Retained, DeadLettered, Rejected, or Unavailable. AOT, JIT, interpreter, and live adapters call the same Prelude functions.
options.code:
authority := services.authority(tree, durable_store, retention: .Hours(24))
receipt := authority.send(endpoint, message, key)?
retry := authority.retry(receipt.id)?

options.name: Hidden request delivery context
options.detail: Put the durable store and retention policy in the current task or request context. Existing send calls infer the authority and return a compact status.
options.technical: Every task boundary must install and restore the context. Missing context fails closed. Nested calls, pooled workers, and live subscriptions must preserve the correct authority without ambient leakage.

options.name: External queue adapter
options.detail: Keep the core service tree in-memory and require each application to integrate its own queue or database for durable receipts.
options.technical: The adapter owns commit order, retry, retention, and receipt schema outside the one service Prelude. Jet can type the adapter boundary but cannot prove one delivery law across providers.
options.code:
queue := app_queue.connect(config)?
queue.publish(order, key: order.id)?

comparisons.note: A producer acknowledgment identifies durable broker acceptance, but retention and transaction scope remain explicit broker facts.
An owned capability carries authority without process-global state and makes the commit boundary visible at the call site.

recommendation.why: A makes the durability authority explicit and gives every retry one stable receipt and idempotency seam. It preserves the current simple tree for beginner in-memory services while making durable behavior auditable and tier-parity-safe.

whyNot.reason: Hidden context reduces call-site noise, but pooled tasks, nested requests, and live subscriptions create cross-request leakage risks and make authority hard to audit.
An external adapter can ship sooner, but it fragments receipt, retention, and transaction semantics and leaves the first-party service card without one production law.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one explicit authority value and a durable store capability. That ceremony buys stable receipts, fail-closed missing authority, and one shared implementation across all execution tiers.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, implement the selected authority through durable send, retry, dead-letter, retention, generation handoff, and transaction paths. Do not close #1148 or #444 until duplicate, crash, retention, and cross-tier receipt tests pass on AOT and default jet run.

decisions.title: How is an ordinary safe compute kernel declared and proved?
decisions.gist: Choose the public representation for compiler-proved ordinary kernels before execution, while keeping raw device code behind #Unsafe.
decisions.lesson: D-COMPUTE-KERNEL1=D says an ordinary Jet kernel is safe only when sema proves bounds, alias and race freedom, captures, barrier uniformity, and control flow. Raw device code remains an audited #Unsafe escape with a typed boundary contract. The current raw contract descriptor records requirements but is not a proof of an ordinary kernel; the public surface must not imply otherwise.
decisions.story: Eli writes a tiled matrix kernel. He wants the compiler to reject an out-of-bounds index, a shared write race, or a divergent barrier before any backend runs. An expert later needs a vendor-specific raw kernel, but that path must carry an audit reason and explicit boundary proof.
decisions.detail: The decision must define kernel declaration spelling, index and shape proof inputs, alias and capture rules, barrier uniformity, effect and placement facts, rejection diagnostics, backend lowering, and the exact boundary between compiler-proved ordinary code and raw #Unsafe code. It must preserve one Prelude semantic law and differential CPU evidence.

options.name: Existing safe functions with compiler kernel lowering
options.detail: Keep ordinary Jet function syntax. A function becomes a kernel only through a checked compute call or compiler-known context; sema emits a typed proof record and codegen lowers the same body.
options.technical: No new user keyword is added. The owning sema pass proves shape/index bounds, non-aliasing, captures, race freedom, barrier uniformity, and control flow before TIR. The proof record is attached to the typed kernel call and every backend consumes it; raw vendor code still requires #Unsafe and a boundary contract.
options.code:
compute.launch(add, grid: shape, args: [a, b])?
// ordinary `add` is accepted only when sema can produce the kernel proof

options.name: Explicit kernel declaration
options.detail: Add a dedicated kernel declaration or marker so authors and tools can see the parallel boundary directly in source.
options.technical: The marker is a new owner-controlled syntax surface. Sema checks the same proof obligations as A, records a stable proof identity, and rejects ordinary function calls that bypass the declaration's effects or placement contract.

options.name: Raw kernels only
options.detail: Do not expose a new safe ordinary-kernel surface in this epoch. All device kernels use #Unsafe with a typed contract and explicit differential tests.
options.technical: This keeps the public language small but leaves safe accelerator work unavailable. The raw contract cannot claim compiler proof; each invocation must surface the audit reason, target, bounds, alias, race, barrier, and CPU-oracle evidence.

comparisons.note: Safe parallel APIs derive freedom from ownership and structured iteration instead of exposing a raw thread contract.
Vendor kernels expose thread indices and barriers directly; safety depends on external review and runtime discipline.

recommendation.why: A preserves the existing beginner surface and makes the compiler own the complete safety proof at the call site. It avoids a second kernel syntax while still allowing explicit expert raw code under #Unsafe.

whyNot.reason: A visible marker improves discoverability, but it adds a new user-typeable syntax choice and another declaration surface before the existing proof seam is exhausted.
Raw-only kernels keep implementation narrow but make safe ordinary kernels impossible and weaken the beginner promise for compute.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires sema to recognize a checked launch context and persist proof facts through TIR, but it adds no syntax and keeps one safe mechanism for ordinary code.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, implement only the selected public surface and its sema proof record. Keep raw device code #Unsafe-gated, reject unproved safe kernels, and prove AOT/default jet run parity plus CPU differential behavior.
decisions.comment: You can incorporate parts of a that improve robustness and feature richness, but I think for now having the marker is a good idea

decisions.title: How should service state receive its storage authority?
decisions.gist: Choose the explicit typed handle that gives a service its durable state store.
decisions.lesson:
A service can keep state in memory, but that state disappears when the process stops. A snapshot saves one complete state image. An event log saves changes and rebuilds state by replaying them.

Both choices need a named place for bytes and a rule for interpreting them. That named capability is the storage authority. Injection means the service receives it as an input instead of finding a process-global file or database.

A schema identifies the format. A version or migration rule explains how older data becomes current. The commit point is when a change becomes durable. Corrupt or newer data must refuse startup with recovery guidance. This ballot chooses the public shape for those facts.
decisions.story: Maya runs two copies of an order service during a deploy. She needs each copy to open the same approved store, reject corrupt or newer state before serving requests, and commit one snapshot or event atomically. A hidden file lookup would make the result depend on the process that happens to run it.
decisions.inWild:
store := state.store("orders", root: data_dir)?
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.snapshot(tree, store, schema: "orders.v1")?
services.start(tree)?
services.commit_snapshot(tree, order_state)?

options.name: Explicit state authority on the adapter
options.detail: Pass one typed store handle and schema to the Snapshot or EventLog adapter. The tree keeps the authority, validates it before start, and uses it for every commit and recovery read. Beginners see one explicit setup value; experts can inspect the store, schema, and migration facts.
options.technical: The adapter owns a StateAuthority containing the injected store capability, adapter kind, schema id, schema version, and migration/recovery policy. Empty has no authority. Snapshot commits one complete record. EventLog appends one event record. Reads and writes use one Prelude authority across AOT, default dev, interpreter, and applicable web targets. No ambient path or process-global state is permitted.
options.code:
store := state.store("orders", root: data_dir)?
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.snapshot(tree, store, schema: "orders.v1")?
services.start(tree)?
services.commit_snapshot(tree, order_state)?

options.name: Create a state handle, then attach it
options.detail: Build a typed Snapshot or EventLog handle first, then attach that handle to the service tree. This makes state reusable across trees, but it creates a second setup object and makes ownership and lifecycle less obvious at the beginner call site.
options.technical: The handle carries store, adapter kind, schema, and migration facts. The attach operation consumes or shares the handle under an explicit ownership rule. Every tree operation validates that the handle belongs to the tree authority and has not been attached twice.
options.code:
state := state.snapshot(store, schema: "orders.v1")?
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.use_state(tree, state)?
services.start(tree)?

options.name: Keep adapter markers and inject storage at start
options.detail: Declare Snapshot or EventLog on the tree, then pass a store only when starting it. This keeps declaration short, but the adapter's schema and storage authority are separated from the state operations and are easier to mismatch.
options.technical: The tree records adapter kind and schema. The start operation injects the authority and performs recovery. Commit and append use the stored start-time authority. A missing or incompatible authority refuses start before workers run.
options.code:
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.set_state_snapshot(tree, schema: "orders.v1")?
services.start(tree, store: store)?
services.commit_snapshot(tree, order_state)?

comparisons.note: A type often receives a reader or database connection as an argument. The value makes the resource boundary visible and testable.
A supervised process owns its state, while durable state is supplied by an explicit persistence strategy rather than an accidental global.

recommendation.why: A keeps adapter meaning and storage authority together at the only place that can enforce them. It makes the commit and recovery boundary visible without introducing a separate handle lifecycle or a start-time mismatch.

whyNot.reason: A reusable handle can help advanced composition, but it adds another public object and ownership rule before Jet needs that flexibility.
Start-time injection is explicit, but it separates the adapter's schema from its store and makes later state operations depend on hidden start configuration.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds a small setup value at the adapter declaration. That cost buys one inspectable authority, one schema boundary, and one place to reject corrupt or incompatible state before startup.

decisions.title: Core source authority and intrinsic kernel boundary
decisions.gist: Choose whether normal Jet source or compiler templates define Core behavior.
decisions.lesson: Jet's Core library supplies common features such as text, files, tasks, and math. Most Core behavior now comes from snippets stored inside the compiler. The open choice is whether that behavior should stay there, move into normal Jet files, or ship as one complete bundle. Every option must keep offline builds, small output, correct caches, and the same results in every execution mode.
decisions.story: Luna updates a Core text function. She needs the compiler dossier to name the checked source, reachable packages, kernel calls, and cache identity used by every execution tier.
decisions.inWild:
use core.text
use core.compute

fn report(xs: [Int]) -> String {
    total := core.compute.sum(xs)
    core.text.format("total={total}")
}

$ jet build --offline --dossier
frontend: parser -> sema -> TIR
compile core.text: ordinary Jet package
compile core.compute: ordinary Jet package
emit Core: reachable packages only
kernel: 3 audited ABI calls
cache identity: semantic-source sha256:7f4e...a91c

$ jet run
total=6
decisions.detail:
Base — The revised first draft gives one short paragraph of neutral context, then leaves definitions and exact rules to the options. It presents three complete choices with realistic build output and a provisional recommendation.

Boil-the-ocean — The review tested direct source builds, compiler templates, eager bundles, precompiled artifacts, generated fallbacks, and dynamic runtime libraries. It kept three choices that change source authority or reachability, and folded cache tactics into those choices.

Hybrid — The review kept A as the source law, borrowed B's pinned offline delivery and strict compiler boundary, and borrowed C's reusable package artifacts without eager linking. It added the audited kernel, content identity, and differential tier checks to A.

Cooperative — The review strengthened every option on its own terms. B now gets reachable template emission and strong fingerprints, while C gets ordinary source, one bundle identity, and simple offline delivery.

Adversarial — The review attacked A for bootstrap cycles, kernel growth, stale caches, and tier drift. It added a narrow kernel rule, source-bound cache identity, reachable closure proof, and shared Prelude conformance; A still best meets UL3, R10, and I9.

options.name: Ordinary Core packages plus a minimal kernel
options.detail: Normal Jet source defines Core behavior. Jet checks that source through the normal front end, emits only reachable packages and helpers, and keeps only unexpressible operations in a small audited kernel. Users gain inspectable source, exact cache identity, and one meaning across all tiers. The pinned toolchain must carry source and verified package metadata for offline builds.
options.technical: Core source follows parser -> sema -> TIR -> Prelude. Reachable closure controls package and kernel emission. Cache identity covers semantic source, dependencies, toolchain, target, mode, and instances. AOT, dev, interpreter, and web adapters call the same Prelude functions. Differential tests compare every accelerated backend with the canonical Jet path.
options.code:
use core.text
use core.compute

fn total_text(xs: [Int]) -> String {
    n := core.compute.sum(xs)
    core.text.format("total={n}")
}

$ jet build --offline --dossier
core.text      ordinary Jet package      reachable
core.compute   ordinary Jet package      reachable
kernel         3 audited ABI calls
cache          semantic-source sha256:7f4e...a91c

$ jet run
total=6

options.name: Compiler templates with strong fingerprints
options.detail: Compiler templates remain the only broad Core authority. Jet emits only templates for reachable helpers and fingerprints every template, compiler, target, and dependency input. Users gain pinned offline delivery and one compiler-controlled source location. They lose normal Jet source checks, package inspection, and direct Core testing through the front end.
options.technical: Sema records reachable helper identities. Codegen selects matching templates and binds the complete template closure into cache identity. AOT, dev, and interpreter still call shared Prelude functions, but broad behavior remains stored inside compiler code rather than ordinary packages.
options.code:
use core.text

$ jet build --offline --dossier
core.text authority: compiler template
emit: reachable text helpers only
cache: template+compiler sha256:3b19...d044
source check: compiler build, not Core package sema

$ jet run
hello from template-backed Core

options.name: Ordinary source with an eager Core bundle
options.detail: Normal Jet source defines Core behavior, but the pinned toolchain builds and links one complete Core bundle. Users gain inspectable source, one bundle identity, and simple offline delivery. Every program pays for unused Core packages in build work, artifacts, and caches.
options.technical: The toolchain compiles the full Core source graph into one versioned bundle. Cache identity covers the complete bundle. All tiers share that bundle's Prelude meaning, but the build does not use the program's reachable package closure.
options.code:
use core.text

$ jet build --offline --dossier
source authority: ordinary Core packages
compile: core.text core.compute core.db core.net ...
emit: complete Core bundle
cache: full-bundle sha256:91ab...e602

$ jet run
hello
// compute, db, and net were unused but still linked

comparisons.note: Rust stores much of its standard library as normal source. A small set of intrinsics and language items remains compiler-owned, which keeps the special boundary narrow.
Swift uses source-backed library code with narrow compiler builtins and runtime calls. The broad library does not need to live inside compiler templates.

recommendation.why: A is the only option that combines normal source checks, R10 reachable emission, source-bound cache identity, and I9 tier parity. It also makes UL3's minimal kernel boundary visible and auditable.

whyNot.reason: B can emit reachable helpers and reject stale output, but broad Core behavior still bypasses normal Jet package checks. A fingerprint proves identity; it does not make templates inspectable Core source.
C gives Core a normal source authority, but it builds and links packages that the program cannot reach. That breaks R10 and expands artifacts and caches without changing program meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: Offline toolchains carry reachable Core source and verified package metadata instead of one opaque compiler blob. Jet accepts that visible provenance to keep source, cache, and tier meaning aligned.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep ordinary source as the authority, then use B's pinned delivery and C's reusable package artifacts without keeping broad templates or linking unused packages.

harvest.aspect: Pinned offline delivery and strict compiler fingerprints.
harvest.use: Apply them to the minimal kernel and every semantic source input.

harvest.aspect: Reusable package artifacts from one source version.
harvest.use: Cache them separately, then link only the reachable closure.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A, B, or C. The full review still recommends A. A requires ordinary Core source, a minimal audited intrinsic/ABI kernel, reachable package and helper emission, complete semantic cache identity, and shared Prelude behavior across every applicable tier.

decisions.title: Full and short ballot contract
decisions.gist: Choose how Tower enforces complete short ballots and reviewed full ballots.
decisions.lesson: Tower's current Learn this first rule asks for a long lesson, so ballots can bury the decision under definitions. The open choice is how much review Tower should require before a ballot reaches you. Every ballot will use /simple and start with a short paragraph that gives only the context needed to compare its options.
decisions.story: Nate opens a difficult architecture ballot. He wants a clear lesson, strong alternatives, visible review evidence, and a recommendation that already survived several different attacks.
decisions.inWild:
$ tower decision add --file cache-policy.json --by sol
ballot profile: full
base            complete
boil-the-ocean  recorded
hybrid          recorded
cooperative     recorded
adversarial     recorded
recommendation  B

$ tower decision add --file naming.json --by sol
ballot profile: short
owner request: "Make this a short ballot."
base: complete
reviews: skipped by owner request
decisions.detail:
Base — The revised first draft makes Learn this first a short orientation, not a glossary or tutorial. It still defines full and short profiles, owner authorization, review order, summaries, colors, and final recommendation proof.

Boil-the-ocean — The review tested guidance-only rules, hard CLI gates, separate commands, profile fields, automatic review agents, and one universal full format. It kept three choices that change enforcement or owner control and removed duplicate command spellings.

Hybrid — The review combines flexible draft creation with strict ready-state checks. It also joins short context, structured review data, fixed UI order, and skill instructions without creating a second ballot system.

Cooperative — The review strengthens guidance-only mode with clear skills and makes all-full mode consistent and predictable. It strengthens the recommendation with explicit owner authorization, one-paragraph context, legacy safety, and accessibility rules.

Adversarial — The review attacks long lessons, context that is too thin, fake review evidence, old ballot breakage, and color-only meaning. It adds a one-paragraph cap, /simple for every field, a required owner quote for short mode, unchanged ratified history, labels and icons, and full-path tests.

options.name: Enforced profiles with visible review records
options.detail: Tower stores full or short as an explicit profile. Every field uses /simple, and Learn this first gives context in one short paragraph at most. Full is the default and requires the complete base plus all ordered review summaries before ready state. Short requires a recorded owner request and the complete base. Users gain durable process, visible reasoning, and one clear interface. Drafts stay open while work is incomplete.
options.technical: Add ballotMode: full|short. The lesson accepts one paragraph at most; the skill targets a few sentences, and the CLI keeps its plain-language limits. Full stores reviewPasses in fixed base, boilOcean, hybrid, cooperative, adversarial order. Each entry contains a one-to-two-sentence summary. Short stores shortAuthorizedBy with the owner's words and rejects reviewPasses. addDecision and update --ready enforce the contract for new or edited open ballots. Ratified history stays valid. Focus Mode renders labeled color blocks: slate, violet, cyan, green, orange, then blue recommendation and muted-red rejections. Text and icons preserve meaning without color.

options.name: Skill guidance without a CLI gate
options.detail: Tower skills tell agents to use /simple, keep Learn this first short, and run the ordered reviews. The data model and ready-state gate stay unchanged. Users gain fast adoption and flexible prose. They cannot tell whether every review ran, and later agents can omit the process without an error.
options.technical: Update tower-ballot and tower skills only. Store optional summaries in detail, hybrid, or recommendation fields. Do not add ballotMode, owner authorization, reviewPasses, lesson validation, or dedicated Focus Mode sections.
options.code:
# tower-ballot skill
1. Write one short Learn this first paragraph.
2. Write the complete base.
3. Run boil-the-ocean.
4. Run hybrid.
5. Run cooperative.
6. Run adversarial.

$ tower decision add --file ballot.json --by sol
# CLI accepts long lessons or missing review evidence

options.name: Require full review for every ballot
options.detail: Tower requires short context, the complete base, and all four reviews for every ready ballot. Users gain one strict path and never need profile authorization. They lose the owner-requested short path for small, clear decisions and must record reviews even when the owner asked for a short ballot.
options.technical: Add one-paragraph lesson validation and require reviewPasses for every narrative decision. Do not add ballotMode or shortAuthorizedBy. Drafts remain exempt. Ratified history remains valid.

comparisons.note: A pull request can require named checks before merge. Tower can use the same model: drafts stay flexible, while ready ballots must show required review evidence.
comparisons.code:
required checks: scope, tests, security, review
merge: blocked until every check reports

comparisons.note: An architecture decision record keeps context, options, and reasons. Tower adds ordered challenge passes so the owner can see how the recommendation improved before the verdict.
comparisons.code:
status: proposed
context: ...
options: A | B | C
decision: B
consequences: ...

recommendation.why: A makes the owner's requested order and evidence part of Tower's ready-state contract. It keeps short ballots owner-controlled, gives every ballot clear prose, and shows how full review improved the recommendation.

whyNot.reason: B can produce excellent ballots when every agent follows the skill, but Tower cannot detect a skipped pass or an unauthorized short ballot. The process would drift again.
C gives strong and consistent review, but it removes the short profile that the owner specifically requested. Small decisions would carry review records even when the owner chose less ceremony.

recommendation.tradeoff: New and edited open ballots must carry explicit profile data, and full ballots carry five short stage summaries. That extra visible record is the cost of a durable review contract.

hybrid.synthesis: Use flexible drafts from B, strict ready-state evidence from C, and an owner-authorized short profile so one Tower mechanism serves both decision sizes.

harvest.aspect: Draft authors need room to work before every field exists.
harvest.use: Keep --draft exempt until decision update --ready.

harvest.aspect: A single strict full path prevents review drift.
harvest.use: Make full the default and gate all five stage summaries.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A, B, or C. The full review recommends A. If A wins, update schema and CLI validation first. Learn this first must use /simple, contain one paragraph at most, and explain only the situation needed to compare options. Every other ballot field also uses /simple. Then update the ordered UI, accessible colors, skills, docs, targeted tests, and independent review. Do not change ratified history.

decisions.title: Accept #1376 — Make Now count ballots and color done count blue

decisions.title: How decode reports accumulated validation failures
decisions.gist: Choose how decode exposes several validation failures without breaking typed decode.
decisions.lesson: Jet validation checks every rule and collects every failure so one bad input can show all useful fixes at once. A decoded value first passes shape checks, then its type rules run. Decode currently returns one DecodeError with one path and one reason. Validation returns a list of FieldError values, with one field and reason per failure. DecodeError explains why wire data cannot become a value. FieldError explains why a value is unacceptable. This choice defines the boundary between those two reports.
decisions.story: Mira decodes an incoming account request. The shape is valid, but the email, age, and country rules all fail. She wants one response with all three field fixes, while existing codecs and callers must keep their typed Decode contract.

options.name: Keep DecodeError and carry all failures
options.detail: Run validation automatically. If it fails, return the existing DecodeError type with a deterministic validation path and a structured reason containing every FieldError. Existing callers keep compiling, and clients can still receive all field fixes. The tradeoff is that callers must use the validation rendering instead of matching a native list.
options.technical: The generated decoder calls Type.validate after construction. It maps Err([FieldError]) to DecodeError with path `validation` and a canonical list encoding in reason. Shape errors keep their existing path and reason.
options.code:
account := body.decode<Account>() ? DecodeError
// Err { path: "validation", reason: "email: use an email address; age: must be an adult; country: is required" }

options.name: Change decode to return FieldError lists
options.detail: Make decode return the accumulated list directly. This gives the cleanest validation API, but changes the Decode trait, format adapters, generated implementations, and existing callers that match DecodeError. The migration is a language-wide compatibility break.
options.technical: The canonical Decode result becomes Result<T, [FieldError]> or a new common error union. Every built-in and user codec must implement the same result contract before the change ships.
options.code:
account := body.decode<Account>() ? [FieldError]
// Err [{ path: "email", reason: "use an email address" }, ...]

options.name: Add a separate validated decoder
options.detail: Keep decode shape-compatible and add a validated entry point that returns FieldError lists. This gives native list matching, but creates two ways to decode and makes the ratified automatic behavior depend on which method the caller remembers.
options.technical: `decode<T>()` remains shape-only; `decode_validated<T>()` performs Type.validate and returns the accumulated list. The extra API becomes a second mechanism unless the owner explicitly accepts it as a compatibility bridge.
options.code:
account := body.decode_validated<Account>() ? [FieldError]
// Err [{ path: "email", reason: "use an email address" }, ...]

comparisons.note: Serde separates structural deserialize errors from application validation, so projects choose their own validation layer. Jet's ratified law asks the compiler to connect the two.
Zod returns a structured issue list for one parse operation, which is close to Jet's accumulated FieldError goal.
comparisons.code:
const result = Account.safeParse(input);
// result.error.issues contains every field issue

recommendation.why: It ships automatic validation now, preserves the existing Decode ABI, and still returns every field failure in one deterministic result.

whyNot.reason: It breaks the existing Decode contract across every format and user codec.
It leaves automatic validation dependent on a second API and duplicates the decode path.

recommendation.tradeoff: Decode callers inspect a structured reason or a validation-specific helper instead of matching a native FieldError list. That compatibility cost is accepted to keep one Decode mechanism.

reviewPasses.base: Kept the existing DecodeError contract visible while preserving accumulated field failures.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Compared compatibility, native list results, and a parallel API. No fourth contract was needed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Used the existing error envelope with a structured validation payload instead of adding a second decoder.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened each option with a concrete caller result and stated its migration cost.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Checked malformed wire data, several rule failures, and old Decode callers. Option A keeps shape errors distinct.

decisions.comment: Greenfield ruling: choose B. The canonical Decode result is Result<T, [FieldError]>. Fix every in-repo codec, generated implementation, adapter, caller, test, example, and document in the same change. Do not use a new common error union or keep any bridge, alias, fallback, compatibility flag, or second decode API.

decisions.title: Typed provider boundary for raw compute kernels
decisions.gist: Choose how a provider creates the proof needed to launch raw kernel code.
decisions.lesson: A raw kernel is device code that Jet cannot inspect as ordinary safe Jet. It may read or write memory, use a device address space, or synchronize threads. A reason such as ‘vendor shuffle’ records intent. It does not prove those facts. A boundary proof is an opaque value created by a trusted provider after checking kernel metadata. The safe Core API accepts it only inside #Unsafe. Sema carries its type into TIR. The backend records the launch and reference evidence.
decisions.story: Ari has a CUDA stencil that uses a warp shuffle. The ordinary Jet kernel subset rejects the intrinsic, so Ari needs one audited raw launch. Ari wants the compiler to reject a missing or forged memory and barrier proof before the kernel reaches the device.
decisions.inWild:
contract :: cuda.raw_contract(
    shape: launch.shape,
    address_space: .Global,
    reads: [x],
    writes: [y],
    barriers: .Uniform,
    differential: reference)
#Unsafe("warp shuffle; mask complete") {
    raw :: compute.raw_kernel(cuda_source, contract) ?? panic("raw kernel failed")
}

options.name: Provider-issued opaque token
options.detail: A typed provider factory checks the launch metadata and returns an opaque contract. Safe Jet cannot forge or edit it. This keeps provider knowledge at the provider boundary and gives sema one clear proof origin.
options.technical: The Core signature accepts RawKernelContract only when the value carries provider provenance. TIR stores the opaque proof and its differential receipt. The launch remains inside #Unsafe and strict profiles reject a missing reference.

options.name: Typed boundary record
options.detail: Jet exposes a normal typed boundary record with shape, address-space, read/write, effect, barrier, and reference fields. Sema checks the record at the call. Experts can inspect it, but every caller must fill the full contract.
options.technical: The record is immutable and validated before launch. Core raw_kernel accepts only the checked record type. The record schema becomes a public compatibility contract for every provider.

options.name: Provider launch capability
options.detail: The provider owns a typed launch capability rather than handing Core a contract value. Core calls the capability inside #Unsafe. This isolates ABI details, but sema and audit tools see less of the kernel boundary.
options.technical: A provider capability implements the raw launch protocol and returns a receipt containing the checked boundary and differential identity. Core does not accept a general raw source plus contract pair.

comparisons.note: The compiler accepts many launches while the programmer owns bounds, address spaces, races, and barriers. Jet moves the common proof to sema and keeps raw escape explicit.
A typed wrapper can restrict the safe call surface while the provider owns the unsafe ABI. The wrapper still needs a real capability, not a string label.

recommendation.why: An opaque provider-issued token preserves the ratified raw #Unsafe tier without making Core pretend it can prove vendor code. Sema can require provenance, TIR can carry the proof, and the backend can emit a real receipt.

whyNot.reason: A public record makes proof fields look like user claims and turns the boundary schema into a second safety mechanism that every provider must duplicate.
A provider-owned launcher hides the exact boundary from the common sema and audit path, weakening the evidence required by D-COMPUTE-KERNEL1.

recommendation.tradeoff: Providers must implement the typed factory and provenance bridge before their raw kernels can launch. The current legacy reason-and-arity helper therefore fails closed until that bridge exists.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an opaque provider token, a public boundary record, and a provider launch capability. It recommended the opaque token because the proof origin stays clear.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a Core-created token, a compiler-only raw tier, and no first-party raw API. Those choices cannot prove vendor facts or would contradict the ratified raw tier, so the provider capability remains distinct.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested wrapping the opaque token in a provider launch capability. It kept the provider factory from option A and the explicit launch receipt from option C, without hiding the token from sema and audit.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the public record with immutable fields and full validation, and the capability with a checked boundary receipt. Both remain useful, but neither gives the common Core path as much proof visibility as option A.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked forged values, stale provider proofs, missing differential references, and provider ABI drift. Requiring opaque provenance, #Unsafe, TIR carriage, and fail-closed launch repairs those risks while keeping option A recommended.

decisions.title: Which surface should expose compiler-owned type facts?
decisions.gist: Choose the focused spelling for layout and future small compiler facts. Full reflection stays explicit in every option.
decisions.lesson: This is a surface decision, not a data-model decision. Every option returns the same typed `LayoutInfo` and uses the same target-layout engine. The choice is how code asks for a focused compiler fact without making metaprogramming noisy, hidden, or collision-prone.
decisions.explainer: Voting for any option also ratifies the shared inner API: `.kind`, `.size`, `.alignment`, `.stride`, `.target`, `.guarantee`, `.source`, `.fields`, and typed field selection with `[.field]`. Known fields never become strings. The focused path is exactly the `reflect().layout` object, not a second mechanism.
decisions.story: Mira binds `Packet` to C. She wants one readable compile-time check for size and one rename-safe field offset. Later, a tool author needs every field and marker. Mira should get easy magic. The tool author should get an explicit, extensible reflection root. Both must read the same facts.
decisions.detail: Exact byte facts exist only for layouts and targets Jet guarantees. Plain layout returns unknown optional physical facts. Every answer names its target, guarantee, and source rule. Completion, hover, go-to-definition, diagnostics, CLI text, and JSON are part of this decision.

options.name: Compiler dunder member
options.detail: Write `T.__layout` for the focused view and `T.reflect()` for the full model. Jet owns every `__*` declaration. User code may read only documented compiler members, and completion shows them in a visible Compiler facts group.
options.technical: This amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 from access-forbidden to declaration-reserved. Unknown dunders fail; users and libraries cannot define them. `T.__layout` is a compiler-provided projection of `T.reflect().layout`.
options.code:
size :: Packet.__layout.size
alignment :: Packet.__layout.alignment
offset :: Packet.__layout[.count].offset

meta :: Packet.reflect()
fields :: meta.layout.fields

options.name: Single meta sigil member
options.detail: Write `T.$layout` for the focused view and `T.reflect()` for the full model. `$` means a compiler-known value at this member position. Existing `$name` remains the splice of a user-known compile-time binding.
options.technical: This broadens D-CTMARKER1 into one known-value law. Prefix `$name` materializes a known binding; member `T.$name` selects a documented compiler-known fact. Users cannot declare `$` members. Completion shows them in a visible Compiler facts group.
options.code:
size :: Packet.$layout.size
alignment :: Packet.$layout.alignment
offset :: Packet.$layout[.count].offset

meta :: Packet.reflect()
fields :: meta.layout.fields

options.name: Explicit reflection only
options.detail: Add no focused magic member. Every caller writes `T.reflect().layout`; tools keep the returned object when they need several facts. This preserves the current dunder and dollar rules unchanged.
options.technical: No new token role or reserved reference surface is needed. `reflect()` remains an ordinary compiler-provided method in the user member plane. Its layout projection has the same type and tooling contract as A and B.
options.code:
layout :: Packet.reflect().layout
size :: layout.size
alignment :: layout.alignment
offset :: layout[.count].offset

meta :: Packet.reflect()
fields :: meta.layout.fields

comparisons.note: Closest to A in ownership. Python reserves documented dunder names for the system, but layout is fragmented across `ctypes.sizeof`, `alignment`, and field descriptors. A keeps the ownership signal and groups the facts.

Closest to B in visual signaling. Zig marks compiler built-ins with `@`, but exposes a flat catalog and uses a string for field offsets. B puts the sigil after the inspected type and keeps field identity typed.
Closest to C in explicit grouping. Swift uses a generic `MemoryLayout<T>` namespace and typed key paths. C is shorter because the inspected type comes first and the field selector is contextual.
No option copies Rust's fragmented surface. Rust separates size, alignment, and offset and adds turbofish or a macro. All Jet options return one typed object instead.

recommendation.why: B is shortest, visually explicit, and coherent with Jet's existing compile-time `$` signal. `Packet.$layout` reads as a compiler-known fact, while `Packet.reflect()` remains the obvious expert root. It avoids underscore noise and prevents collision with user members.

whyNot.reason: A has strong precedent and preserves `$` as splice-only, but leading dunders are visually heavier and many developers expect tools to hide them. Jet can fix discovery, but cannot remove that learned friction.
C is architecturally clean, but it makes a common focused check spell the whole metaprogramming path. Beginners pay expert ceremony even when they need one compiler fact.

recommendation.tradeoff: B widens a ratified sigil law and needs `T.$name` member grammar. The compiler-fact catalog must stay small and closed, or `$` becomes a flat magic namespace.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared the user's dunder idea, a single-sigil member, and explicit reflection only. Every option now shares one typed fact model and one full reflection root.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested `@`, `#`, `?`, `!`, `^`, `~`, `%`, free functions, static namespaces, scalar magic fields, and CLI-only access. Existing sigils conflict, new sigils lack meaning, and flat queries fragment one fact set.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass keeps focused access for the common fact and `reflect()` for expert enumeration. It rejects aliases: the focused member must be an exact projection of the full object, not a second API.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gives dunder visible completion and gives reflection-only callers a short local binding. It gives the sigil option one precise known-value law instead of calling it mere punctuation.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested name collisions, hidden completion, unknown fields, rename, targets, plain layout, columnar layout, strings, and catalog growth. B wins only if `$` members stay compiler-owned, documented, grouped, and few.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A, B, or C. Voting for any option also chooses the shared typed selector and tooling contract described above.

decisions.title: How should Jet calls spell generic type arguments?
decisions.gist: Choose one rule for every generic call. Inference stays the normal path in both options.
decisions.lesson: A generic function can often infer its type arguments from inputs or the expected result. Some calls have no such evidence, and expert code sometimes needs to pin the choice locally. This decision chooses whether Jet permits that explicit call-site escape everywhere or never permits it.
decisions.explainer: This ballot resolves a real contradiction. S45 first chose inference-only calls. D-SERDE6 later authorized `call<T>(...)` for every generic call, but a later summary described `decode<T>` as an exception. The winning verdict supersedes every conflicting clause. Jet will have no API-specific exception.
decisions.story: Noor writes a generic parser. Most callers write `parse(text)` because inputs and expected results identify the type. In a pipeline with no useful expected type, Noor wants either one local type argument or a separate annotated binding. Both can work. Jet needs one predictable rule across free functions, namespaced calls, and methods.
decisions.detail: Option A keeps inference as the default and allows explicit `<...>` after any named or member callee. Option B removes call-site arguments everywhere, including decode. Neither option changes generic declarations or generic types such as `fn id<T>` and `Box<Int>`.

options.name: Infer by default; allow explicit arguments
options.detail: Normal calls omit type arguments. Any generic free function, namespaced function, or method may add `<T>` when inference lacks evidence or local clarity matters. Jet uses `call<T>(...)`, never Rust's `call::<T>(...)`.
options.technical: A balanced `<...>` is a call argument list only when it is adjacent to the callee and immediately followed by the call parentheses. The formatter emits `call<T>(...)`. Spaced `a < B > (c)` remains comparison syntax. Arity and bounds fail in sema with what, why, and fix text.
options.code:
values := empty<Int>()
row := json.decode<Row>(text) ?? panic("bad row")
page := query.fetch<Page<User>>()

// Still preferred when inference is clear:
copy := identity(value)

options.name: Inference-only calls
options.detail: No call may carry type arguments. Inputs and expected result types must determine every generic parameter. Underconstrained code adds a result annotation or uses a type-owned API. Existing `decode<T>` calls migrate with no compatibility spelling.
options.technical: The parser always reads `<` after a value as comparison syntax. Sema diagnoses missing inference evidence and suggests an exact binding annotation. APIs whose main purpose is to create or inspect a type should prefer a type-owned shape.
options.code:
values: [Int] :: empty()
row: Row :: json.decode(text) ?? panic("bad row")
page: Page<User> :: query.fetch()

// Type-owned redesign when that reads better:
row := Row.decode(text) ?? panic("bad row")

comparisons.note: Closest to A. Kotlin normally infers function type arguments but permits explicit arguments when needed.
comparisons.code:
val box = emptyBox<Int>()
val copy = identity(value)

comparisons.note: Closest to A. C# documents both `Swap<int>(...)` and the shorter inferred call.
comparisons.code:
Swap<int>(ref a, ref b);
Swap(ref a, ref b);

comparisons.note: Closest to B. Generic function calls infer their arguments; callers use contextual types or a different API shape when inference is insufficient.
Closest to A, but Rust often needs the extra `::` separator. Jet can keep explicit control without copying that punctuation.
comparisons.code:
let values = Vec::<i32>::new();
let item = parse::<Item>(text);

recommendation.why: A gives beginners the shortest call through inference and gives experts a precise local override. Kotlin and C# show that optional explicit arguments can stay uncommon without becoming confusing. One general rule is cleaner than a decode-only exception.

whyNot.reason: B makes ordinary calls clean, but it forces distant result annotations or API redesign when a generic parameter has no input evidence. That removes useful expert control without improving the common call.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one parser ambiguity around `<` and comparison. Jet must make adjacency, formatting, completion, and diagnostics exact so the escape never makes ordinary expressions surprising.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared general optional arguments with a complete inference-only rule. It rejected any API-specific exception because one call grammar must apply everywhere.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Rust turbofish, keyword arguments, brackets, type-owned factories, and result annotations. None beats plain `<T>` as an optional local override while keeping inferred calls unchanged.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested explicit arguments only for result-only parameters or selected Core APIs. It rejected that split because users would need to memorize which generic calls permit the same syntax.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gives inference-only code exact expected-type inference and useful fixes. It gives optional-explicit code the same clean default, so the comparison turns only on the expert escape.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested nested `>>`, methods, bad arity, failed bounds, comparisons, formatter stability, and misleading decode precedent. Option A survives only with a strict adjacency and diagnostic contract.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A or B. The verdict will become canonical S33 and will explicitly supersede conflicting S45, D-SERDE6, parser comments, examples, and summaries.

decisions.title: Argument labels and parameter contracts
decisions.gist: Choose how calls bind names and require clear arguments.
decisions.lesson: Jet labels now check spelling at one fixed position. They cannot skip defaults or reorder arguments. This makes policy-heavy APIs longer than Python and prevents label-only safety contracts.
decisions.story: Maya opens a service connection. She wants a five-second timeout but accepts every other safe default. The call should name only the changed policy.
decisions.inWild: client :: connect("db.internal", timeout: 5, tls: true)?

options.name: Named binding with parameter zones
options.detail: A written label binds by name and can skip defaults. `/` ends positional-only parameters. `*` starts label-only parameters. Unmarked parameters accept either form. A public label defaults to the local parameter name; `timeout seconds: Int` keeps public label timeout while local code uses seconds.
options.technical: Sema builds one parameter map before type checking and rejects unknown, repeated, missing, forbidden, or unlabeled-after-labeled arguments. Supplied expressions run left to right. Unbound defaults then run at call time in declaration order and may use earlier bound parameters. Public labels and zones are callable type identity; function types reuse parameter grammar. Local names and default bodies are not identity. Inferred function values retain defaults; annotated values expose only defaults written in their type. Public-label changes break callers; local-only renames do not when an external label stays stable.
options.code:
fn connect(host: String, /, *, timeout seconds: Int = 30, tls: Bool = true) => Client ? ConnectError
client :: connect("db.internal", tls: true, timeout: 5)?

forced: fn(*, force: Bool) => Void = save
forced(force: true)
// forced(true) is rejected

options.name: Named binding without zones
options.detail: A written label binds by name and can skip defaults. Every parameter still accepts positional calls. This keeps declarations small but cannot require labels or protect positional compatibility.
options.technical: The binder maps labels to parameter names. There is no label-only or positional-only declaration. Public labels are part of callable type identity and function types spell them with the same parameter grammar. Renaming any public parameter remains a source change for labeled callers.
options.code:
fn connect(host: String, timeout: Int = 30, tls: Bool = true) => Client ? ConnectError

client :: connect("db.internal", tls: true)?
legacy :: connect("db.internal", 30, true)?

options.name: Mandatory external label contracts
options.detail: Each declaration writes a public label or `_` for positional use, even when public and local names match. The rule is explicit per parameter but adds text to ordinary declarations.
options.technical: This follows a strict Swift-style external and internal name split. A public label binds by name. `_` forbids a label. Every parameter and function type declares its public call contract separately; no label is inferred from the local name. Public labels are part of callable type identity.
options.code:
fn connect(_ host: String, timeout seconds: Int = 30, tls enabled: Bool = true) => Client ? ConnectError

client :: connect("db.internal", timeout: 5, tls: true)?

options.name: Keep fixed positional binding
options.detail: Labels remain optional spelling checks at fixed positions. Existing calls stay unchanged. APIs still cannot skip an earlier default or require a policy label.
options.technical: S61 stays unchanged. Labels never reorder. Only trailing defaults can be omitted. Function types keep erasing labels because labels remain positional spelling checks rather than a call contract.
options.code: client :: connect("db.internal", EncodingLimits.safe(), 5, true)?
