recommendation.why: It reuses the bare-member rule dispatch arms already ratified, so the language grows a home, not a mechanism. At 11 tokens it beats Python by 4 on the corpus's most common transform, and the body keeps inline `?`, `next`, and `break`.

whyNot.reason: It mints a contextual pronoun that collides with user names, repeats at every read, and still costs two tokens more than the bare member.
It leaves the most common transform at parity, never ahead, and keeps four spellings of a binding the body reads once.

recommendation.tradeoff: Scalar items have no member to read, so scalar transforms keep a named binding. The sentence-form win applies to record sources, which dominate the measured corpus.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a bare-member subject, a Kotlin-style `it`, and requiring bindings. It recommended the bare member because dispatch arms already teach that exact rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Scala's underscore and Swift's positional names. Both mint a new sigil family that reads as nothing, so they folded into option B as the named-pronoun representative.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested shipping A and B together. Two spellings for one subject violate the one-form rule, and `it` adds nothing the named binding does not already give scalars.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its natural scalar story and C with its zero-rule clarity. B's scalar win is real and is recorded in A's tradeoff honestly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack found scalar sources, nested subject shadowing, and collisions with expected-type static shorthand. The repairs: scalars name bindings, nesting requires names, and inside bindingless bodies the subject always owns bare members.

decisions.title: Bare-member shorthand for one-parameter callable arguments
decisions.gist: Choose whether `.member` may stand for a one-parameter lambda at a call site.
decisions.lesson: Jet's method-chain pipeline costs 33 tokens on the task Python's comprehension does in 15, because every step writes a full lambda to read one member. This ballot decides whether a bare member chain may stand for that lambda when the expected argument is a one-parameter callable. The same desugar is proposed for bindingless loops in D-LOOP-SUBJECT1; this ballot owns the call-site half on its own.
decisions.story: Mina keeps the pipeline style for a long transformation because each stage reads separately. Every stage needs a whole lambda whose body is one member read, and the ceremony triples the cost of her Python original.

options.name: Member chains
options.detail: Where the expected argument is a one-parameter callable, a bare member chain stands for that lambda, including method calls along the chain. The pipeline drops from 33 tokens to 15. Anything beyond a member chain still writes the lambda.
options.technical: The rule fires only when the expected parameter type is known and is a one-parameter callable. The shorthand is a member chain on the parameter: fields, methods, and their arguments. Operators, literals, and multi-parameter callables are excluded; write the lambda. Function types have no static members, so the expected-type static shorthand (D-SHAPE3a) cannot collide here.
options.code:
names :: users.filter(.active).map(.name)
shouting :: users.map(.name.to_upper())
oldest :: users.max_by(.age)

total :: orders.fold(0, fn (sum: Int, o: Order) => Int = sum + o.total)
// Two parameters: the shorthand never applies.

options.name: Single member only
options.detail: The shorthand allows exactly one bare member: `.name` works, `.name.to_upper()` does not. The rule is smaller to state, but the lambda returns the moment a chain grows one link, and readers must learn where the cliff is.
options.technical: Same expected-type rule as option A, restricted to one field or one zero-argument method. Any longer chain is an error that teaches the full lambda.

options.name: No shorthand
options.detail: Arguments always write full lambdas. One spelling for callables everywhere, nothing contextual to resolve. The pipeline stays at 33 tokens, half again dearer than TypeScript on the same task.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: names :: users.filter(fn (u: User) => Bool = u.active).map(fn (u: User) => String = u.name)

comparisons.note: Key paths pass a member read where a function is expected. Adopted widely because pipelines are mostly member reads.
The implicit `it` shortens the lambda but keeps a pronoun at every read.
Method references pass an existing accessor by name. The double colon adds ceremony Jet's dot form avoids.

recommendation.why: Pipelines are mostly member reads, and the shorthand removes exactly that ceremony: 33 tokens fall to 15, under TypeScript's 22. It reuses the bare-member atom Jet already owns instead of minting a key-path sigil.

whyNot.reason: Half the measured pipeline steps call a method on the member, so the cliff lands in the middle of real code and the rule's value halves.
The audit's most-written style stays Jet's dearest spelling, and the pipeline keeps losing to every measured peer.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bare `.member` gains a second contextual meaning: static shorthand under a non-callable expected type, lambda under a callable one. The two contexts cannot overlap, and sema owns one diagnostic for the unknown-type case.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared member chains, a single-member form, and no shorthand. It recommended chains because measured pipelines are member reads with occasional method calls.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Swift key-path sigils, Scala underscores, and bound method references. Each mints a new sigil or duplicates the dot form, so all folded into the three options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed this desugar and D-LOOP-SUBJECT1 are one rule in two homes. The ballots stay separate so each home is judged on its own evidence.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C with its uniform-spelling clarity and B with its smaller rule. Both stand, and both leave the pipeline losing to TypeScript.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack targeted inference: generic adapters may not know the parameter type mid-inference, so the rule fires only on a known expected type, and the diagnostic teaches the lambda. Operators like `!.active` stay excluded.

decisions.title: Comprehension guard spelling in the loop head
decisions.gist: Choose how a yielding loop head spells its item filter.
decisions.lesson: A yielding loop can keep or skip items with an `if` guard in its head. Today the guard parses only without a comma, while every other head clause uses commas (D-LOOP-COMMA1). The natural comma spelling misparses as a stride and fails with an unrelated error about value `if` branches. The guard form is Jet's cheapest collection transform, and it beats Python when people can find it. Zero examples show it today.
decisions.story: Mina converts a Python script to Jet. Commas separate every loop clause she has seen, so she writes the guard with a comma. The compiler answers with an error about `if` branches needing values. The working spelling appears nowhere in the docs, so she gives up and writes a method chain that costs more than her Python original.

options.name: Comma-less guard stays canonical
options.detail: Keep the shipped spelling: the guard follows the source with no comma. Add the missing docs, examples, and a teaching diagnostic for the comma spelling. This is the cheapest form at 14 tokens, one under Python. The cost is a head with two separation laws: commas everywhere, except before the guard.
options.technical: No grammar change. The parser adds one lookahead so `, if` in a yielding head produces a teaching diagnostic naming the comma-less form, instead of parsing a stride. Formatter output is already stable for the shipped form.

options.name: Guard is a comma clause
options.detail: The guard becomes an ordinary comma-separated head clause, so one law covers the whole head. The natural spelling works on the first try. It costs one comma token, landing at 15, level with Python. The formatter rewrites the old comma-less spelling.
options.technical: In a yielding head, `, if` always begins a guard clause and never a stride. A stride expression may not begin with a value `if` unless parenthesized; measured strides are numeric, so the loss is theoretical. One guard per head; combine conditions with `&&`. The formatter canonicalizes the comma-less form to the comma form.
options.code:
names :: loop u, users, if u.active -> u.name   // canonical, 15 tokens
evens :: loop n, nums, if n % 2 == 0 -> n * n
pairs :: loop (key, value), scores, if value > 0 -> key

options.name: Retire the header guard
options.detail: Remove the guard from the head. Filtering uses `next` in the body, the same skip word every loop already has. The head grammar shrinks, but the common filtered transform grows to about 19 tokens and loses to Python by 4.
options.technical: The parser removes the head guard production. Existing guard code migrates to a body `if` with `next`. No new token.

comparisons.note: The guard trails the source with no separator. It is the most used transform surface in the measured corpus.
comparisons.code: names = [u.name for u in users if u.active]

comparisons.note: Commas separate generators and guards alike inside a comprehension. This is the precedent for one separator law.
comparisons.code: names = [name u | u <- users, active u]

comparisons.note: No comprehension exists; filtering rides a method chain with a closure per step.
comparisons.code: let names: Vec<_> = users.iter().filter(|u| u.active).map(|u| u.name.clone()).collect();

recommendation.why: Commas separate the positional clauses whose meaning comes from position; the guard announces itself with a keyword, exactly like the yield arrow that already takes no comma. The shipped form is the consistent one, and at 14 tokens it beats Python outright.

whyNot.reason: The comma before a self-announcing keyword is redundant punctuation, and its uniformity claim fails because the yield arrow already attaches without one.
It retires Jet's cheapest transform, drops the common case to 19 tokens, and loses to Python by 4.

recommendation.tradeoff: The natural first guess with a comma stays an error. A precise teaching diagnostic that says remove the comma closes that gap at first compile.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared the shipped comma-less guard, a comma guard clause, and retiring the guard. It recommended the comma clause because one law should govern the head.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a Python-style guard after the yield expression, a `where` keyword, and filtering only through fallback-next. Each reorders or duplicates an existing mechanism, so all folded into the three options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested accepting both spellings at once. Two canonical spellings for one clause violate the one-form rule, so the loser becomes a teaching diagnostic either way.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with zero migration and a one-token lead, and C with the smallest grammar and a uniform body-skip story. B kept its first-guess advantage.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The owner challenged the comma's benefit, and the attack confirmed the uniformity claim fails: the yield arrow already attaches without a comma, so the head is positional commas plus keyword-marked trailers. The recommendation moved to A; both options still need the same stride carve-out for a head-position value if.

decisions.title: Jet library reuse and linking model
decisions.gist: How Jet reuses compiled dependencies, and whether Jet ships its own dynamic libraries.
decisions.lesson: Rust ships every dependency as source, and each project compiles all of it again. Clean builds are slow and binaries are large. Rust also has no fixed binary layout, called an application binary interface or ABI, between compiler versions. Compiled Rust libraries therefore cannot be shared safely. Jet already plans a Nix-style package store with binary caches. This choice decides how Jet reuses compiled dependency work, and whether Jet ever promises a stable binary layout of its own.
decisions.story: Priya runs three Jet services that share twelve packages. Every clean build today would compile all twelve from source, in each service, on every continuous-integration run. She wants the second build to reuse the work the first build already did. She also asks whether her team can ship a plugin as a compiled Jet library.
decisions.inWild:
# pkg.jet
Package.{
  name: "flightdeck",
  deps: .{ http: "2.1", json: "1.4", metrics: "0.9" },
}

$ jet build
  http 2.1, json 1.4, metrics 0.9: restored from cache (0.2s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

options.name: Sealed package objects
options.detail: Each dependency compiles once into a sealed object keyed on the exact compiler version, target, and profile. Later builds restore it from the local or shared cache instead of recompiling. A compiler upgrade simply rebuilds once. You never think about it; builds just get faster.
options.technical: Per-package compile actions lower into the ratified jetpack action IR (E4-JP2). Identity covers package sources, dependency artifact digests, compiler identity, target, and profile. Artifacts link statically. Generic function bodies travel as typed IR inside the artifact and instantiate at the use site. Sema and diagnostics always run; no cache path bypasses them.
options.code:
$ jet build          # first build on this machine
  http 2.1: compile (1.8s)
  json 1.4: compile (1.1s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

$ jet build          # second build, or a teammate via shared cache
  http 2.1, json 1.4: restored from cache (0.2s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

$ jet build          # after a compiler upgrade
  cache empty for Jet 1.4.2 — rebuilding dependencies once

options.name: Sealed objects plus pinned Jet dynamic libraries
options.detail: Everything in the sealed-objects option, plus a way to build a Jet dynamic library that another Jet program loads at run time. Both sides must use the exact same compiler version. Loading a mismatched library is a checked error, not a crash. This serves plugins and game mods.
options.technical: Same artifact identity as sealed objects. The loader verifies compiler identity and package digests before mapping the library. No layout promise crosses compiler versions.
options.code:
$ jet build --emit jet-shared plugins/echo
  built target/echo.jetso (Jet 1.4.2)

# in the host program
plugin := Plugin.load("target/echo.jetso")?

# mismatched compiler version
error[E0912]: echo.jetso was built by Jet 1.4.1, this program uses Jet 1.4.2
  fix: rebuild the plugin with the same Jet version

options.name: Public stable Jet ABI
options.detail: Jet commits to a fixed binary layout and evolution rules, like Swift did in version 5. Anyone can ship a compiled Jet library, including closed-source vendors, and any later Jet compiles against it. Every future change to layout or calling rules must stay compatible forever.
options.technical: Requires a versioned layout specification, resilience rules for public types, and a frozen calling convention. Every public type pays an indirection cost unless marked frozen, following Swift's library-evolution model.
options.code:
# vendor ships a binary-only package, no source
$ jet add sensorlib --binary vendor/sensorlib.jetso

# five years later, Jet 3.0 must still load it unchanged
sensor := Sensor.open("lidar0")?

options.name: Source-only, whole-program
options.detail: Keep today's model. Every build compiles the whole program and all dependencies from source. Speed comes from the fast development loop and incremental checking only. Clean builds and continuous integration pay the full cost every time.
options.code:
$ jet build     # every clean build, every CI run
  http 2.1: compile (1.8s)
  json 1.4: compile (1.1s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

comparisons.note: Ships source only. The rich stable ABI proposal, crabi, has stayed an open experiment since 2022.
comparisons.code: cargo build   # recompiles every crate, per project

comparisons.note: Committed to a stable ABI in Swift 5. Apple ships Swift libraries with the operating system, and pays a permanent indirection cost on resilient public types.
comparisons.code: @frozen public struct Point { var x, y: Double }

comparisons.note: Binary caches substitute build results keyed on exact inputs. No ABI promise exists; identity does the work. Jet's ratified package store already follows this model.

recommendation.why: Sealed package objects remove the recompile tax on every machine and in continuous integration, using the store and cache machinery already ratified. Jet promises nothing about binary layout, so the language stays free to evolve.

whyNot.reason: No shipped Jet feature needs run-time loading of Jet libraries today, and jet dev already covers live reload. A dormant loading surface would sit untested in the product.

A public ABI freezes layout and calling rules before the language has settled, and Swift paid a permanent performance and design tax for that promise. It also conflicts with Jet's greenfield law until the owner declares a compatibility baseline.
Clean builds and continuous integration keep paying the full recompile cost that drives people away from Rust.

recommendation.tradeoff: No compiled artifact survives a compiler upgrade. Every upgrade rebuilds or re-downloads the world once. That is accepted because the rebuild is automatic and correctness never depends on layout luck.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared source-only builds, sealed cached objects, pinned dynamic libraries, and a public stable ABI. It recommended sealed objects because they cut recompilation without freezing the language.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested shipping typed intermediate code per package, per-module granularity, and caching only checker summaries. All three folded into the sealed-objects option as artifact-format details, not separate owner choices.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a partial stable ABI covering only a frozen core subset, and rejected it because public types leak the full promise. It also confirmed pinned dynamic libraries compose cleanly on top of sealed objects later.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option on its own terms: dynamic libraries best serve game mods, a stable ABI best serves closed-source vendors, and source-only stays the simplest mental model.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked cache poisoning, unreproducible outputs, and generic functions; the ratified writer-authority and repro-cache decisions answer the first two. Generic bodies travel as typed intermediate code and instantiate at use sites, so sealed objects survive.

decisions.title: In-place adoption: can jetos convert a running Linux install, and must it be reversible?
decisions.gist: Whether jetos can take over an existing Linux system in place, and whether that conversion must be undoable.
decisions.lesson: Bedrock Linux wins users by installing onto the system they already run. No reinstall, no spare disk. But its conversion is one way: the installer makes the user type "Not reversible!". jetos already has generations, activation proof, and rollback. Those tools could make an in-place conversion safe to undo. Today jetos installs only from ISO media, plus a config importer for NixOS systems.
decisions.story: Maya runs Ubuntu on her only laptop. She wants jetos, but she cannot risk a working machine or spend a weekend reinstalling. She would switch tonight if one command converted her system and one command promised to give Ubuntu back.
decisions.inWild:
# Bedrock Linux today: adoption by hijack, one way
$ sh bedrock-linux-0.7.30-x86_64.sh --hijack
* Please type "Not reversible!" to confirm: Not reversible!
* Hijack complete. Reboot to finish.

# The question for jetos: same on-ramp, but with a way back?
$ jet os takeover laptop
plan: capture current Ubuntu as generation 0, prove, then switch
$ jet os rollback 0
restored: the exact Ubuntu install from before takeover

options.name: Reversible takeover
options.detail: jetos converts the running system in place. The current install is captured as generation 0. The switch happens only after the normal activation proof passes. One rollback command restores the original system exactly. Gain: the easiest adoption path any OS offers, and safer than Bedrock's. Loss: the original system stays on disk until the user deletes it, so disk use roughly doubles at first.
options.technical: Capture: the host root becomes a preserved, bootable generation-0 entry (own kernel, initrd, and boot entry) under hangar management. Refusal: hosts whose disk layout cannot hold two bootable roots get a diagnostic, not a best-effort attempt. Proof: the same activation-proof gate as jet os switch. Rollback: restores the generation-0 boot entry and root as the default.
options.code:
$ jet os takeover laptop
checking host: disk ok, bootloader ok, space ok
capturing current system as generation 0 ("ubuntu-2026-08-04")
building jetos system for host laptop
proof: activation plan verified
switch complete — reboot into jetos, or `jet os rollback 0` any time

$ jet os rollback 0
default boot restored: generation 0 ("ubuntu-2026-08-04")

options.name: Media install and importer only (today's path)
options.detail: No in-place conversion. Users install jetos from ISO media onto a disk they choose. The importer converts an existing NixOS config for them. Gain: jetos never touches a running system, so there is no destructive surface at all. Loss: anyone whose only machine runs another distro must back up, wipe, and reinstall — the biggest group of potential users keeps the highest barrier.
options.technical: Status quo. Install surface stays the hybrid ISO installer with GPT/ESP/ext4/Limine. Migration stays config-level via the semantic importer (#415).
options.code:
$ jet os image build laptop --iso
wrote jetos-laptop.iso
# user writes USB media, backs up /home, reboots, wipes the disk,
# installs, then restores files by hand

options.name: One-way takeover (Bedrock's shape)
options.detail: Convert in place without capturing the old system. Smallest disk cost and the fastest conversion. Loss: the machine has no way back. A failed or regretted conversion means a reinstall from media. This is the exact flaw Bedrock documents about itself.
options.technical: Host root is rewritten into the jetos layout directly. No generation-0 entry exists; rollback history starts at the first jetos generation.
options.code:
$ jet os takeover laptop --no-capture
WARNING: this conversion cannot be undone
type "not reversible" to continue: not reversible
switch complete

options.name: Preview double, then media install
options.detail: jetos never converts the live disk. Instead it builds a virtual machine image of "this machine as jetos" from the imported config, so the user can try their converted system safely. Gain: zero risk to the host. Loss: the journey still ends in a full media reinstall, and a virtual preview can hide real hardware problems like Wi-Fi and graphics drivers.
options.technical: Reuses the importer plus the existing QEMU proof harness to boot a preview guest from the user's captured facts. The live disk is never written.
options.code:
$ jet os preview laptop --from-host
built preview VM from this machine's imported config
booting QEMU guest... (your apps, users, and services, as jetos)
# to adopt for real: jet os image build laptop --iso, then reinstall

comparisons.note: The hijack installer converts the running distro in place and is permanently one way. It is the project's main adoption path and its most criticized risk.
comparisons.code:
$ sh bedrock-installer.sh --hijack
* Please type "Not reversible!" to confirm:

comparisons.note: Has no official in-place conversion. The community nixos-infect script overwrites a cloud host one way, with no capture and no rollback to the old distro.
comparisons.code:
$ curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elitak/nixos-infect/... | bash
# old distro is destroyed; recovery is a provider reimage

recommendation.why: A reversible takeover turns machinery jetos already owns — generations, activation proof, rollback — into the safest adoption path in the field. It reaches people on their only machine, which is most people, and it keeps the rollback promise that defines jetos.

whyNot.reason: Media-only keeps the highest barrier for the largest group: people with one machine and no spare disk stay locked out.
A one-way conversion breaks the rollback promise and risks a working machine, repeating the exact flaw Bedrock documents about itself.
A preview still ends in a wipe-and-reinstall, so the adoption barrier it was meant to remove stays in place.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generation 0 keeps the old system on disk, roughly doubling use until the user deletes it. Hosts with layouts that cannot hold two bootable roots are refused and must use media install.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reversible takeover, media-only, one-way takeover, and a virtual preview. It recommended reversible takeover because it opens the largest adoption path without breaking the rollback promise.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested dual-boot side-install, a container trial, and a persistent live-USB trial. All three fold into media install or the preview option because none converts the running system.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined preview with takeover: the takeover flow can boot a preview guest from the same generation-0 capture before switching. This strengthened option A instead of adding a fifth option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened media-only with the importer story and gave one-way takeover an explicit consent gate. Media-only still excludes single-machine users; one-way still cannot restore the host.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the capture with encrypted disks, unusual bootloaders, low disk space, and secrets inside the preserved root. Option A now refuses unsupported layouts with a diagnostic and documents what generation 0 contains, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Runtime provenance: how a user asks what put a file, command, or process on their system
decisions.gist: Which surface answers "what package, source, and generation put this file, command, or process here?"
decisions.lesson: On Bedrock Linux every file and process has an owner the user can query with one command, brl which. Reviewers single it out as what makes a mixed system understandable. jetos builds systems from two package universes — native hangar packages and imported Nix package closures — across generations. Studio already shows where a config value came from. Nothing yet answers the runtime side: who put this binary here, from which package, in which generation.
decisions.story: Ravi finds an unfamiliar binary on his PATH after a desktop swap. On Debian he would run dpkg -S. On jetos he wants one command that names the package, the universe it came from, and the generation that introduced it — before he decides whether to worry.
decisions.inWild:
$ which weird-tool
/run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool

# the question this ballot decides the spelling of:
$ <surface> /run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool
weird-tool 1.4.2 — package tools.weird-tool (hangar, native)
introduced: generation 41 ("desktop swap to niri", 2026-08-01)
declared by: system.laptop -> services.desktop.extras

options.name: Extend jet info
options.detail: jet info already answers "what is this?" for packages, and the owner ratified extending jet search and jet info for options search rather than minting a new verb. Teach jet info to accept files, commands, paths, and process IDs too. Gain: one question surface for everything, in the terminal and in scripts. Loss: jet info's help must stay simple while it learns three new target kinds.
options.technical: One provenance resolver maps artifact -> package -> universe (native or compat root) -> generation -> declaring option path. jet info and Studio both render that resolver's answer. Unowned targets (user files, runtime-created files) answer "not owned by any package" honestly.
options.code:
$ jet info weird-tool
$ jet info /run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool
$ jet info --pid 4312
weird-tool 1.4.2 — package tools.weird-tool (hangar, native)
introduced: generation 41 ("desktop swap to niri")
declared by: system.laptop -> services.desktop.extras

$ jet info ~/notes.txt
not owned by any package (user file in /home)

options.name: New verb: jet os which
options.detail: Mirror Bedrock's brl which as a dedicated jetos verb. Gain: a short, discoverable command whose name states the question. Loss: it mints a second lookup surface beside jet info, so users must learn which verb answers which kind of "what is this?" question.
options.technical: Same resolver as option A behind a separate verb under jet os. jet info keeps its package-only scope.
options.code:
$ jet os which weird-tool
tools.weird-tool (hangar, native), generation 41
$ jet os which --pid 4312
tools.weird-tool via service desktop-extras.service
$ jet info tools.weird-tool   # still needed for the full package view

options.name: Studio-only drill-down
options.detail: Provenance stays a Studio feature: click any installed file, app, or service to see its package, universe, and generation. No terminal surface. Gain: no new command-line spelling to ratify or document. Loss: scripts, remote shells, and terminal-first users get no answer at all, and the beginner in a broken graphical session loses the tool exactly when they need it.
options.technical: The resolver ships inside Studio's projection layer only. The CLI exposes nothing.
options.code:
# terminal user today, under option C:
$ jet info /run/current-system/sw/bin/weird-tool
error: jet info takes a package name
# answer exists only inside the Studio app

comparisons.note: brl which answers for a command, file, path, or process ID with one spelling. It is the model for the question, though Bedrock only names the providing stratum.
comparisons.code:
$ brl which apk
tut-alpine
$ brl which 1
debian

comparisons.note: dpkg -S and pacman -Qo map a file to its owning package, but say nothing about when it arrived or what configuration asked for it.
comparisons.code:
$ dpkg -S /usr/bin/vim
vim: /usr/bin/vim
$ pacman -Qo /usr/bin/vim
/usr/bin/vim is owned by vim 9.1-1

comparisons.note: Provenance exists but is expert-only: chained store queries that beginners never find.

recommendation.why: One question surface keeps the beginner story simple: point jet info at anything — a name, a file, a process — and it answers with package, universe, generation, and the declaring option. It follows the pattern the owner already ratified for options search (D-JOS-OPTIONSVERB1=B): extend jet search and jet info instead of minting verbs.

whyNot.reason: A second lookup verb splits one question across two spellings and contradicts the ratified extend-don't-mint pattern.
Studio-only leaves terminals, scripts, and remote sessions blind, and fails the user whose graphical session is the thing that broke.

recommendation.tradeoff: jet info grows file, path, and process targets, so its help text and docs must keep the plain name-lookup case front and center.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft mirrored the ratified options-search menu: extend jet info, mint a dedicated verb, or keep it Studio-only. It recommended extending jet info to keep one question surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested filesystem-level answers (ownership attributes on installed files) and a shell hook printing provenance on command-not-found. Both folded in as possible backends of the same surface, not separate owner choices.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed Studio and the command line should share one provenance resolver so both render identical facts. The ballot now names that shared resolver in every option's technical notes.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the dedicated verb with Bedrock's exact ergonomics and Studio-only with click-through from the app library. Each still narrows or splits the question surface.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked coverage with user files, runtime-created files, and files inside imported Nix closures. The surface now answers "not owned by any package" honestly and reports closure membership with its generation, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: General automatic differentiation in core.compute
decisions.gist: How Jet computes derivatives of a calculation.
decisions.lesson: A derivative tells you how much a result moves when an input moves. Machine learning fits models by following derivatives. Today core.compute can only differentiate three fixed operations: add, multiply and matmul. Anything you build from them cannot be differentiated. This choice picks the shape of the general answer, which decides what users type and how the compiler tracks the work.
decisions.story: Priya trains a small model to rank support tickets. She writes a loss from a matmul, a subtraction, a square and a sum. She asks Jet for the gradient. Today there is no call that answers, because her loss is not one of the three fixed shapes.

options.name: Function transform
options.detail: You pass a function to `grad`, `vjp` or `jvp` and get a new function back. Nothing is stored between calls, so the same code works inside tasks and runs twice with the same answer. You can take a gradient of a gradient by applying the transform again. The cost is that the value you differentiate must live in a function.
options.technical:
`grad(f)` returns a callable with the parameter contract of `f` and a Tensor result. `vjp(f)` returns value and a cotangent-consuming closure; `jvp(f)` returns value and tangent. Reverse mode records a per-call tape owned by the returned closure, so no global or thread-local state exists. The transform is a Prelude function over Jet callable values; it adds no syntax. Higher-order use nests transforms. Effect rows carry through unchanged; a differentiated function must be pure over its Tensor arguments and is rejected otherwise.

Invoking a returned function uses the `.call(…)` spelling from D-CALLVALUE1.

options.name: Explicit tape scope
options.detail: You open a tape, tell it which tensors to watch, run ordinary code, then ask the tape for a gradient. The recording is a value you can see and pass around, so there is no hidden state. The cost is three extra lines around the calculation and a tape you must not reuse after it is consumed.
options.technical: `GradTape.new()` returns an owned recorder. `tape.watch(t)` marks a leaf. Recording happens because watched tensors carry the tape identity, so unrelated tensors cost nothing. `tape.gradient(loss, [w])` walks the recorded graph in reverse and returns one Tensor per requested leaf. The tape is second-class and cannot escape its scope, which keeps recording bounded. Reuse after `gradient` is an E-coded error unless the tape was opened as persistent.
options.code:
tape :: compute.GradTape.new()
tape.watch(w)

pred :: compute.matmul(x, w)
loss :: compute.sum_axis(compute.mul(pred, pred), 0)

gw :: tape.gradient(loss, w)

// reuse without persistent is rejected
// Error [E0xxx]: this tape was already consumed

options.name: Tracked tensors
options.detail: You mark a tensor as tracked once. Every later operation on it records itself. You call `backward` on the result and read `.grad` from the tracked tensor. This is the shortest code to type and the most familiar to people coming from PyTorch. The cost is that recording is implicit and gradients pile up on the tensor until you clear them.
options.technical: `tracked(t)` returns a Tensor carrying a recorder handle. Operations propagate the handle. `backward(loss)` accumulates into each tracked leaf; `grad_of(t)` reads the accumulation. Accumulation is additive, so a training loop must call `zero_grad` between steps. The recorder lives in the tensor rather than in a scope, so lifetime follows ordinary ownership. Concurrent use across tasks requires the tensor to be exclusively owned, which sema enforces.
options.code:
w :: compute.tracked(compute.zeros([4, 1]))

pred :: compute.matmul(x, w)
loss :: compute.sum_axis(compute.mul(pred, pred), 0)

compute.backward(loss)
gw :: compute.grad_of(w)

compute.zero_grad(w)   // forgetting this silently adds to the last step

options.name: Keep one call per operation
options.detail: Nothing changes in shape. Every differentiable operation gains its own `vjp_` and `jvp_` call as it is needed. Users chain those calls by hand to differentiate anything larger. This adds no new mechanism, but a user must write the chain rule themselves for every model they build.
options.technical: The current `vjp_add`, `vjp_mul`, `vjp_matmul`, `jvp_*` and `value_and_grad_mul` set grows one entry per operation. No tape, transform or recorder exists. Composition is the caller's responsibility and is not checked. The public surface grows with the operation table and never closes, because each new operation needs two more names.
options.code:
// Priya differentiates her loss by hand
p :: compute.matmul(x, w)
d :: compute.sub(p, y)
sq :: compute.vjp_mul(d, d, compute.ones(compute.shape(d)))
back :: compute.vjp_matmul(x, w, compute.grad_a(sq))
gw :: compute.grad_b(back)
// one mistake in this chain is silent and wrong

comparisons.note: JAX transforms a function into its gradient function. The transform is pure and composes, so a second derivative is the same call applied twice.
comparisons.code:
gw = jax.grad(loss)(w, x)
hess = jax.grad(jax.grad(loss))(w, x)

comparisons.note: PyTorch marks a tensor as requiring a gradient. Operations record automatically and gradients accumulate on the tensor.
TensorFlow opens a tape scope, watches tensors, then asks the tape for the gradient.
comparisons.code:
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    tape.watch(w)
    loss = f(w)
gw = tape.gradient(loss, w)

comparisons.note: Swift used a function transform with a compiler-checked differentiable attribute, close to option A.
comparisons.code: let gw = gradient(at: w) { w in loss(w, x) }

recommendation.why: A keeps derivative work inside ordinary values with no hidden state, which matches how Jet already treats effects, ownership and tasks. The same code gives a second derivative by nesting, so the surface stays two names wide instead of growing with the operation table. Because each call owns its own recording, two tasks can differentiate at the same time without sharing anything.

whyNot.reason: B is honest about state but makes the user manage a tape that must not outlive its scope or be consumed twice. That is a new lifetime rule to teach, and it gives no benefit A does not already have.

C is the shortest to type but hides recording inside tensors and makes gradients accumulate silently. A forgotten clear step produces a wrong answer with no error, which is the failure mode Jet exists to prevent.
D never closes. The public surface grows by two names per operation and still leaves the user to apply the chain rule by hand, where one mistake is silent and wrong.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires the thing you differentiate to be a function, so a user cannot ask for the gradient of a value they already computed. They must wrap that calculation in a function first.

reviewPasses.base: Wrote the four credible shapes for a general derivative surface. Each carries a worked example over Priya's loss, including the hand-chained version option D forces.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Searched wider designs: compile-time source transforms, a dual-number type, and an overloading graph builder. Compile-time transforms hit ratified metaprogram limits, so they folded into A as an implementation choice.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested combining A with C so a user could differentiate a bare value. That reintroduced hidden accumulation and gave two ways to do one thing, so the options stayed separate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B by making the tape second-class, and C by naming the sema rule that keeps a tracked tensor exclusively owned. Gave D its fairest form: no new mechanism.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on the point that reverse mode still needs a tape. The tape can be owned by the returned closure for one call, so no global state is needed.

decisions.title: Calling a returned function value
decisions.gist: How you call a function that another call just returned.
decisions.lesson: Some calls return a function as their result. Today the only spelling to use that result at once is a second parenthesis pair, as in `grad(loss)(w, x)`. The owner review of the autodiff ballot found that shape foreign and hard to read. This choice picks one clear spelling for calling a function value that is not a plain name.
decisions.story: Priya reads a Jet tutorial that computes a gradient. The line `compute.grad(loss)(w, x)` stops her cold. She cannot tell what the second parenthesis pair belongs to, and she has never seen that shape anywhere else in Jet.

options.name: Uniform call, status quo
options.detail: Any expression followed by a parenthesis pair is a call. This is the smallest rule and matches Python, JavaScript, Rust and Swift. Docs teach the two-line form that binds the returned function to a name first. The cost is that the `)(` shape stays legal and will keep appearing in real code and tutorials.
options.technical: The parser postfix loop already produces a call-of-value node when `(` follows any expression. Nothing changes in parser, sema, formatter, or grammars. The style guide and formatter would steer toward bind-then-call.
options.code:
dloss :: compute.grad(loss)
gw :: dloss(w, x, y)

// also legal, and the shape in question
gw :: compute.grad(loss)(w, x, y)

options.name: Chained .call, ban the double parenthesis
options.detail: A call result is invoked with a chained `.call(…)`, and a parenthesis pair directly after a call is an error with a fix. `compute.grad(loss).call(w, x)` reads as the chain it is: build the gradient function, then call it. Plain names and stored fields keep the direct spelling, so `f(x)` and `w.step(4)` do not change. The cost is one extra word at a rare call site.
options.technical: Every function-typed value carries a builtin `.call(…)` member with the callee's parameter contract. The parser rejects `(` directly after a call expression with an E-coded error whose fix-it inserts `.call`. Member lookup on structs wins over the builtin, so a user field named `call` keeps its meaning. The ban covers any call result, including a `.call` result, so longer chains stay in `.call` form. Formatter, tree-sitter, tmGrammar, and LSP completion learn the member.

options.name: Dot-call sigil
options.detail: A function value is called with `.(…)`, a dot directly before the parenthesis. Elixir uses this exact shape to separate named calls from value calls. It is shorter than `.call`, but it is a sigil a reader must already know. A beginner cannot guess it, and it can read as a typo.
options.technical: A new `.(` token sequence in postfix position lowers to the same call-of-value node. Parser, formatter, both grammars, and highlighting change. The `)(` shape is rejected the same way as option B.
options.code: gw :: compute.grad(loss).(w, x, y)

options.name: Pipe operator
options.detail: A new `|>` operator feeds a value into a function from the left. It reads in data-flow order and many functional languages ship it. It is a whole new operator with language-wide reach. It only moves one argument, so multi-argument calls still need another rule, and the `)(` shape survives without a separate ban.
options.technical: `x |> f` rewrites to a call of `f` with `x` as the first argument. This adds an operator to the expression grammar and touches precedence, formatter, grammars, and docs. It does not remove the call-of-value shape on its own.
options.code:
gw :: w |> compute.grad_wrt_w(loss)   // one value pipes cleanly
// multi-argument calls still need bind-then-call or a ban like option B

comparisons.note: A proc is called with an explicit method. The direct parenthesis spelling does not exist for proc values.
Function values have a named `invoke` method, and `f(x)` is sugar for it. The explicit form is always available.
A function value is an object with a named calling method. There is no direct parenthesis call on values at all.
Function values must be called with a dot before the parenthesis, which separates them from named calls.
Any expression can be called directly, so the double parenthesis appears wherever a call returns a function.

recommendation.why: B says in one word what the second parenthesis pair only implies. The line reads as a dot chain, which is how Jet users already read everything else. The rule bans exactly the shape the owner review found foreign and changes nothing else in the language. Ruby, Kotlin and Java all ship this shape, so it carries mainstream precedent.

whyNot.reason: A keeps the `)(` shape legal, so tutorials and real code will still show it. Teaching an idiom around a confusing legal shape is weaker than removing the shape.
C replaces one cryptic shape with another. A sigil the reader must already know fails the beginner test that started this decision.
D is a language-wide operator decision far bigger than this question. It also does not remove the `)(` shape on its own, so the confusion survives.

recommendation.tradeoff: Calling a returned function costs one extra word, and function values gain a reserved member name. A user field named `call` keeps its meaning because struct member lookup wins, but that shadowing rule must be documented.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the uniform status quo, a chained `.call` method, the Elixir sigil, and a pipe operator. It recommended `.call` for readability at a rare but load-bearing call site.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested Haskell-style juxtaposition, Ruby bracket calls, and a Kotlin `invoke` name. Juxtaposition breaks the whole call grammar, brackets collide with indexing, and the name choice folded into option B.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested allowing `.call` everywhere alongside direct calls. That makes two full spellings for every call, so option B stays a targeted ban on the call-result position only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened A with a formatter hint toward bind-then-call, C with full tool support, and D with its honest data-flow reading. Each option now shows its best form.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked B with a struct field named `call`, longer call chains, and lambda results. Member lookup precedence and applying the ban to every call result repair all three, so B survives.

decisions.title: Exponent operator spelling
decisions.gist: Which spelling raises a number to a power.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no power operator today. Powers go through `math.pow` and `math.int_pow` function calls. Scientific, engineering, and data users type powers constantly, so the spelling shapes everyday code. The infix `^` currently means exclusive-or, a bitwise operation that is rare outside low-level bit work. Typing `3 ** 2` today parses as a multiply followed by a raw-pointer sigil and fails with a confusing unsafe-pointer error.
decisions.story: Maya, a mechanical engineering student, ports a beam-deflection script from MATLAB. She types `L^3` exactly the way her textbook writes it. Today Jet quietly computes an exclusive-or of two numbers instead, and her deflection results are wrong with no error at all.

options.name: Infix `^` becomes exponent; xor moves
options.detail: `^` reads as power, the way mathematics, MATLAB, Julia, R, Lua, and Excel all write it. Exclusive-or gives up the glyph and gets a new spelling in its own decision. Gain: ported formulas from math tools work unchanged, and `L^3` means what the textbook means. Loss: any existing xor code must migrate, and the glyph now has an infix meaning (power) and a prefix meaning (take).
options.technical: Infix `^` reparses as BinOp::Pow. Compound `^=` becomes power-assign. Prefix `^` (the take capability sigil, D-MEM1) is untouched; parser position disambiguates, exactly as it disambiguates xor and take today. Xor respelling is D-XORSPELL1. Precedence, associativity, and Int typing are D-EXPSEM1.
options.code:
area :: side ^ 2
volume :: side ^ 3
growth :: principal * (1.0 + rate) ^ years

options.name: Add `**`; xor keeps `^`
options.detail: The Python, JavaScript, and Ruby spelling. Gain: nothing existing moves, and Python migrants recognize it instantly. Loss: `**` exists in those languages only because C had already spent `^` on exclusive-or. Jet is free of that history and would be adopting the workaround instead of the math spelling. MATLAB, R, and Julia users must retrain their fingers.
options.technical: New token `**` plus compound `**=`. Today `3 ** 2` lexes as `*` then prefix `*`, which is never valid, so the token is free. `^` stays BinOp::BitXor.
options.code:
area :: side ** 2
volume :: side ** 3
growth :: principal * (1.0 + rate) ** years

options.name: No operator; keep `math.pow`
options.detail: Powers stay function calls. Gain: no grammar change and no xor migration. Loss: everyday formulas stay noisy, nested powers become unreadable, and both Python and MATLAB migrants hit friction on day one. This works against the goal of being the best language for scientific and data work.
options.technical: Status quo. `math.pow(Float, Float)` and `math.int_pow(Int, Int)` remain the only power surface.
options.code:
volume :: math.pow(side, 3.0)
growth :: principal * math.pow(1.0 + rate, years.to_float())

comparisons.note: The math-tool family all spell power with a caret.
The C-descended family uses double-star because C spent the caret on xor.
No power operator at all; a function call is the only spelling.

recommendation.why: Jet targets scientific, engineering, and data work, where formulas are written and read as math. `^` is the spelling every math tool and every textbook uses, and Jet has no C legacy forcing the workaround.

whyNot.reason: `**` is a historical workaround for languages that had already spent `^` on xor. Jet has no such debt, and the math-tool audience reads `^` natively.
Function calls make everyday formulas noisy and unreadable, which directly hurts the audience this language is built for.

recommendation.tradeoff: Exclusive-or must move to a new spelling and existing xor code migrates. That is acceptable because xor is rare outside expert bit work, while powers appear in everyday beginner code.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared `^`, `**`, and function-only, and recommended `^` because the target audience reads and writes formulas the math-tool way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a named infix word `pow`, superscript unicode digits, and supporting both `^` and `**`. The word is noisy in formulas, unicode is untypeable, and dual spellings violate the one-spelling rule, so none joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested `^` for floats with `**` for integers and rejected it: one operation with two spellings by type is worse than either option alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with its Python-migrant familiarity and free lexer slot, and strengthened C by noting it needs no migration at all. Both remain weaker for formula-heavy code.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on the double life of the glyph: prefix take versus infix power. The parser already runs exactly this split for xor today, and no ambiguous program exists, so the recommendation survives with the xor migration as its accepted cost.

decisions.title: Exponent semantics: grouping and integer results
decisions.gist: How power expressions group, and what type integer powers return.
decisions.lesson: Tools disagree about power expressions in two places. First, grouping: does `2^3^2` mean `2^(3^2)` (512) or `(2^3)^2` (64), and does `-3^2` mean `-(3^2)` (-9) or `(-3)^2` (9)? Second, integer results: does `2^10` stay an exact integer, and what happens on a negative exponent like `2^-1`? These choices decide whether ported formulas compute the same numbers they did at home.
decisions.story: Priya ports a statistics routine that computes `-x^2 / 2.0` inside a normal-distribution formula. In Python and MATLAB that means minus the square. If Jet groups it the other way, her probabilities silently come out positive-shifted and every downstream chart is wrong.

options.name: Math convention: right-grouping, exact integers
options.detail: `2^3^2` is 512 and `-3^2` is -9, matching Python, Julia, Ruby, and written mathematics. Integer base with a non-negative integer exponent stays an exact integer. A negative integer exponent returns a Float, the way Python does. Gain: textbook formulas and Python ports compute identical numbers. Loss: MATLAB users get 512 where MATLAB gave 64 on chained powers, a rare shape.
options.technical: Right-associative. Power binds tighter than unary minus but looser than postfix and prefix capability sigils. `Int ^ Int(>=0) -> Int`, exact under the default Int. `Int ^ Int(<0) -> Float`. Any Float operand makes the result Float.
options.code:
print(2^3^2)   // 512
print(-3^2)    // -9
print(2^10)    // 1024, exact Int
print(2^-1)    // 0.5, Float

options.name: MATLAB convention: left-grouping, float results
options.detail: `2^3^2` is 64, evaluated left to right, and `-3^2` is -9. Every power returns a Float, because MATLAB numbers are all doubles. Gain: chained powers match MATLAB exactly. Loss: `2^10` stops being an exact integer, which poisons index math and big exact arithmetic, and Python ports of chained powers change value.
options.technical: Left-associative. Power binds tighter than unary minus. Result type is always Float regardless of operand types.

options.name: Excel convention: unary minus wins
options.detail: `-3^2` is 9 because the leading minus binds tighter than the power, and chains group left. Gain: spreadsheet migrants get Excel's numbers. Loss: this contradicts written mathematics and every programming language, so textbook formulas silently compute wrong values. Included for completeness because spreadsheet users are a real audience.
options.technical: Left-associative. Unary minus binds tighter than power. Result is Float.
options.code:
print(-3^2)    // 9.0, unlike every textbook
print(2^3^2)   // 64.0

comparisons.note: Right-grouping, minus applies last, ints stay exact until a negative exponent.
Left-grouping, everything is a double.
The odd one out: a leading minus beats the power.

recommendation.why: Written mathematics and the largest migration source (Python) agree on right-grouping with minus applying last. Exact integer powers keep index math and combinatorics correct under the default Int.

whyNot.reason: Forcing every power to Float breaks exact integer arithmetic, and left-grouping matches only MATLAB against math convention and Python alike.
Excel's grouping contradicts textbooks and every programming language, so it silently corrupts ported formulas for everyone except spreadsheet migrants.

recommendation.tradeoff: MATLAB migrants who chain powers without parentheses get 512 where MATLAB gave 64. That shape is rare, and a formatter hint can suggest explicit parentheses on chained powers.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared math-convention, MATLAB, and Excel packages and recommended math convention for textbook and Python parity.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review considered requiring parentheses on any chained or minus-adjacent power, making ambiguity a compile error. It was folded into option A as a possible formatter hint rather than a hard error, to keep textbook formulas typeable.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested right-grouping with always-Float results and rejected it: exact integer powers are load-bearing for the arbitrary-precision Int direction.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by noting MATLAB parity matters for whole-script ports, and C by naming spreadsheet users as a genuine audience. Both still lose on silent number changes for the majority.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's negative-exponent rule: an Int silently becoming Float can surprise. Python behaves identically and the alternative, a runtime error, is harsher for beginners, so A survives unchanged.

decisions.title: Respell exclusive-or after `^` becomes power
decisions.gist: Where bitwise exclusive-or lives once `^` means power.
decisions.lesson: If D-EXPOP1 gives `^` to the power operator, exclusive-or needs a new home. Exclusive-or keeps a bit where exactly one input has a one bit: either, but not both. It is rare in everyday code but essential in hashing, graphics, checksums, and hardware work. The rest of the bitwise family is sigil-spelled (`&`, `|`, `<<`, `>>`) with compound assignments. On Bool, `!=` already is logical xor. Gate ops like nand and nor have operator spellings only in hardware languages and compose from these primitives.
decisions.story: Tomás writes a fast hash for a game asset cache. His inner loop xors a rolling state with each chunk. He needs a spelling that reads clearly in a dense loop body and does not tangle with the new power operator one line above.

options.name: Infix `~|` with compound `~|=`
options.detail: A new sigil built from the family it belongs to: `|` keeps a bit when either or both inputs have it; `~|` keeps a bit when either input has it, but not both. Gain: the spelling teaches itself as the exclusive variant of or, and the compound `~|=` reads unmistakably as an or-family update. Loss: no language spells xor this way, and Verilog readers arrive expecting `~|` to mean nor, since their tilde negates a result.
options.technical: New token `~|`, BinOp::BitXor in the old `^` precedence slot, compound `~|=`. Both glyphs are free in infix position today; prefix `~` (copy) is untouched. If gate operators were ever wanted, Verilog's `~&`/`~|` spellings would be unavailable, an accepted cost since gates compose from primitives.

options.name: Infix `~` with compound `~=`
options.detail: Bare tilde, the choice Lua made when its caret became power; prefix `~` stays the copy sigil, the same position-split infix-and-prefix `&` lives with. Gain: one glyph, direct precedent. Loss: bare tilde says nothing about or-ness, and C and Python readers expect it to mean complement. Worse, the compound `~=` means not-equal in Lua itself, a false friend planted in the precedent's own community.
options.technical: Infix `~` becomes BinOp::BitXor with compound `~=`. Parser position disambiguates against prefix copy. The retired `~~` connector is only a teaching diagnostic.

options.name: Infix word `xor`
options.detail: `a xor b`, the Ada, Pascal, and VHDL spelling. Gain: reads exactly as pronounced and can never be mistaken for any sigil meaning. Loss: it becomes Jet's only word-spelled binary operator, since and/or are `&&` and `||`, so the bitwise family splits into words and sigils, and there is no natural compound assignment.
options.technical: New keyword `xor` in the old `^` precedence slot. No compound spelling; write `a = a xor b`.

options.name: Method `a.xor(b)`; no operator
options.detail: Exclusive-or leaves the operator family and becomes an integer method. Gain: zero new grammar and autocomplete discoverability beside future bit helpers like rotate and popcount. Loss: xor becomes the only bitwise operation without an operator, and chained bit expressions turn into nested calls exactly where operator shape matters most.
options.technical: Fixed-signature method on all integer widths. A fuller bits toolkit can grow beside it independently of this ballot.

comparisons.note: Faced the same collision and chose bare tilde; note Lua's own `~=` means not-equal.
Word-spelled xor operator; VHDL also has nand, nor, xnor words.
Caret means xor because power has no operator there.
Tilde negates a result there, so its `~|` is nor, not xor.

recommendation.why: `~|` is the only candidate that says what it means: the exclusive variant of `|`, learnable from its own glyphs. Its compound `~|=` stays visibly an or-family update, and it avoids every false friend the bare tilde carries.

whyNot.reason: Bare tilde reads as complement to C and Python eyes, and its compound `~=` means not-equal in Lua, the very community its precedent cites.
A lone word operator splits the bitwise family's shape and loses compound assignment, a real cost in accumulator loops.
Making xor the only operator-less bitwise operation breaks family symmetry exactly where dense expressions need operator shape most.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spelling is a Jet invention, and Verilog readers must unlearn `~|` as nor. That is acceptable because the glyph pair teaches itself to everyone else, and the hardware audience overlap is far smaller than the C, Python, and Lua audiences the alternatives confuse.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a word operator, a method, and a bits-module function, recommending the word. The owner rejected that menu, prompting a family-wide audit of every logical and bitwise spelling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The audit found infix tilde and tilde-pipe both free. Bare tilde joined with Lua precedent; the owner then challenged its compound as unreadable, surfacing tilde-pipe, which self-describes as exclusive-or and joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested operator plus a discoverable method alias and rejected the alias: one operation, one spelling. It confirmed gate ops stay compositions, with the Verilog family noted for the future.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened bare tilde with its one-glyph brevity and real precedent, the word with its VHDL pedigree, and the method with bit-toolkit discoverability. Each remains weaker on family shape or false friends.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked `~|` as an unprecedented invention and via the Verilog nor reading. Novelty is mitigated by self-description, the nor collision touches the smallest audience, and no parse ambiguity exists, so `~|` survives as the recommendation.

decisions.title: Floor division operator
decisions.gist: How to spell whole-number division that rounds down.
decisions.lesson: Floor division divides and rounds toward negative infinity, so `7 /% 2` is 3 and `-7 /% 2` is -4. Python and Lua spell it `//`, but in Jet `//` starts a comment and cannot be an operator. Doc comments (`///`, S49) and doctests (D-TEST4) already work today, so the comment marker is settled and only the floor-division spelling is open. Floor division pairs with floored modulo (D-MODSEM1) so that `a == b * (a /% b) + a % b` always holds.
decisions.story: Ana lays out a photo grid. She computes `row :: index /% columns` and `col :: index % columns`. With a floor pair these are correct for every index she will ever pass, and the two spellings visibly rhyme.

options.name: `/%` with compound `/%=`
options.detail: A new two-glyph operator: divide, then the `%` reminds you it is the partner of modulo. Gain: a first-class operator for an everyday operation, visibly paired with `%`, and the spelling is free today because `a /% b` currently parses as an error. Loss: no other language uses this exact spelling, so every migrant learns it once.
options.technical: New token `/%`, BinOp slot, compound `/%=`. Works on Int and Float; floors toward negative infinity in both. Satisfies `a == b * (a /% b) + a % b` with floored `%` (D-MODSEM1). Division by zero traps like `/`.
options.code:
print(7 /% 2)    // 3
print(-7 /% 2)   // -4
print(7.5 /% 2.0) // 3.0
page := index
page /%= per_page

options.name: Infix word `div`
options.detail: `a div b`, the Pascal and SQL spelling. Gain: pronounceable and precedented. Loss: it does not visually pair with `%`, it reads as prose inside dense arithmetic, and word operators need D-XORSPELL1-style precedent to feel at home in Jet.
options.technical: New keyword `div`, same precedence as `/`. No compound spelling.
options.code:
print(7 div 2)    // 3
print(-7 div 2)   // -4

options.name: Function only: `math.floor_div`
options.detail: No operator; a named function does the job. Gain: no new grammar. Loss: an operation this common in index math, pagination, and time arithmetic deserves better than a function call, and the identity with `%` becomes invisible.
options.technical: Status quo plus a `math.floor_div` fixed signature for Int and Float.
options.code:
print(math.floor_div(7, 2))   // 3
print(math.floor_div(-7, 2))  // -4

comparisons.note: Spells it with double slash, which Jet's comments make impossible.
Word operator.
Percent-bracketed operator family.

recommendation.why: Floor division is everyday index math and deserves an operator. `/%` visibly pairs with `%`, keeps the division-family look, and the spelling is unclaimed by any current syntax.

whyNot.reason: A word operator reads as prose inside arithmetic and hides the pairing with modulo.
A function call is too heavy for an operation that appears in every pagination and grid loop.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spelling is novel, so every migrant learns it once. That is acceptable because the glyphs teach themselves: divide, in the manner of modulo.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared `/%`, the word `div`, and a function, recommending `/%` for its pairing with modulo.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested reclaiming `//` by moving comments to `#` or `--`. Both evict ratified syntax (markers, decrement) for one operator, and doc comments plus doctests already work on `///`, so reclaiming was rejected outright.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping `/%` plus a `math.floor_div` alias and rejected the alias: one operation, one spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened `div` with its Pascal and SQL pedigree and the function option with zero grammar cost. Both still hide the modulo pairing that makes the floor pair teachable.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked `/%` as line noise and probed whether `a /% b` could ever parse ambiguously today. It cannot, because `%` has no prefix form, and the noise concern fades against the pairing it buys, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Modulo semantics: `%` floored, `%%` truncated
decisions.gist: What `-7 % 2` returns, and how to spell the other remainder.
decisions.lesson: Two remainder definitions exist. Floored modulo follows the divisor's sign, so `-7 % 2` is 1; clock, index, and wrap-around math want this one. Truncated remainder follows the dividend's sign, so `-7 % 2` is -1; C, Rust, and JavaScript ship this one. Jet's `%` is truncated today, which silently breaks even/odd checks and array wrap-around on negative numbers. Python, Ruby, and Lua chose floored for exactly that reason.
decisions.story: Ben writes a music sequencer. Beat position is `tick % 16`. When the user scrubs backward past zero, ticks go negative. With truncated remainder his sequencer indexes step -1 and crashes; with floored remainder it wraps to step 15 and just keeps playing.

options.name: `%` floored, `%%` truncated
options.detail: The everyday spelling gets the answer that index, clock, and parity math want: `-7 % 2` is 1. The C-style remainder stays available as `%%` for ports and specialist code. Gain: the beginner default is the correct one for wrap-around math, matching Python. Loss: code ported from C, Rust, or JavaScript changes meaning on negative operands unless it switches to `%%`.
options.technical: `%` becomes floored on Int and Float, with `%=` following. New token `%%` is truncated remainder with `%%=`. Identity `a == b * (a /% b) + a % b` holds with floored floor division (D-FLOORDIV1). Both trap on zero divisor. Prelude jet_rem splits into jet_mod (floored) and jet_rem (truncated) per I9 across all tiers.
options.code:
print(-7 % 2)    // 1
print(-7 %% 2)   // -1
print(step(-1))  // 15, wraps correctly

options.name: Keep `%` truncated only
options.detail: Status quo, matching C, Rust, and JavaScript. Gain: no migration and C-family ports keep their meaning. Loss: the beginner default stays wrong for wrap-around and parity math on negatives, the single most reported modulo trap across languages, and Python ports silently change meaning instead.
options.technical: No change. Floored modulo would remain unspelled or become a math function.
options.code:
print(-7 % 2)    // -1
print(step(-1))  // -1, indexes out of range

options.name: `%` floored only, no `%%`
options.detail: One remainder, the floored one; truncated becomes a method for the rare port that needs it. Gain: smallest surface, one obvious spelling. Loss: C-family ports lose a direct spelling, and systems programmers reaching for hardware-native remainder get a method instead of an operator.
options.technical: `%` floored everywhere. `a.rem_trunc(b)` fixed signature covers the truncated case.
options.code:
print(-7 % 2)          // 1
print((-7).rem_trunc(2)) // -1

options.name: `%` truncated, `%%` floored
options.detail: Keep C meaning on the short spelling and add the floored one at `%%`, roughly R's arrangement. Gain: zero migration for existing Jet code and C ports. Loss: the beginner-facing default stays the trap, and the correct-for-indexing operation hides behind the longer spelling.
options.technical: `%` unchanged; new `%%` floored with `%%=`.

comparisons.note: Floored on the everyday spelling.
Truncated on the everyday spelling.
Floored, spelled with doubled percent.

recommendation.why: The short spelling should give the answer wrap-around, clock, and parity math need, which is what beginners write first. Keeping truncated at `%%` preserves an explicit spelling for C-family ports and hardware-native code.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the most famous modulo trap as the default and silently changes the meaning of Python ports.
Dropping the truncated operator entirely pushes systems code to a method for a real hardware operation.
It optimizes for existing C habits over the correctness of the beginner default, against the mission.

recommendation.tradeoff: C, Rust, and JavaScript ports change meaning on negative operands until they switch to `%%`. That is acceptable because the compiler can lint suspicious negative-capable `%` during migration, and the scientific audience mostly arrives from Python.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared four arrangements of floored and truncated remainder and recommended floored on `%` with truncated on `%%`.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Euclidean remainder (always non-negative) as a candidate meaning. For positive divisors it equals floored, and positive divisors dominate real code, so it was folded into option A's technical notes rather than added as a fifth option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested `%` floored plus a compile warning whenever a possibly-negative dividend meets `%`. The warning punished correct code, so it was cut; the migration lint in the tradeoff is one-time instead.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B and D on zero-migration grounds and C on smallest-surface grounds. Each still leaves either the default wrong or systems code underserved.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the performance cost of floored modulo over the hardware instruction and with double-glyph confusability. The cost is one branch, unmeasurable outside hot loops where `%%` remains available, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: What `Int / Int` returns
decisions.gist: Whether 7 / 2 is 3.5 or 3.
decisions.lesson: With floor division getting its own operator (D-FLOORDIV1), plain `/` no longer has to do double duty. Today Jet truncates: `7 / 2` is 3, the C behavior. Python 3 famously changed `/` to always return a float precisely because silent integer truncation was its most common beginner bug, and moved whole-number division to a dedicated operator. This decision sets what a calculator-shaped expression returns in Jet.
decisions.story: Leo, in his first week of programming, computes an average: `total / count`. With truncating division his average of 7 and 2 is 4 with no warning. His spreadsheet says 4.5. He concludes the language is broken, and he is not entirely wrong.

options.name: `/` always returns Float
options.detail: `7 / 2` is 3.5, the Python 3 and calculator answer. Whole-number division is `/%`, an explicit choice. Gain: the single most common beginner numeric bug becomes impossible, and averages, rates, and ratios are correct by default. Loss: code wanting integer division must say `/%`, and C-family ports of `/` on ints change type.
options.technical: `Int / Int -> Float`. `Int /% Int -> Int` (D-FLOORDIV1). `/=` on an Int binding whose division produces Float is a type error pointing at `/%=`. Large default-Int values may lose precision crossing to Float, exactly as Python accepts.
options.code:
print(7 / 2)     // 3.5
print(7 /% 2)    // 3
average :: scores.sum() / scores.len()   // 8.5, correct

options.name: Keep truncating `Int / Int -> Int`
options.detail: The C, Rust, Go, and Java behavior. Gain: no migration, integer expressions stay closed over Int, systems code keeps its habits. Loss: the averages bug stays the default experience for every beginner and data user, which is the audience this language is built to win.
options.technical: No change. Truncation toward zero, trap on zero divisor.
options.code:
print(7 / 2)     // 3
average :: scores.sum() / scores.len()   // 8, silently wrong as a mean

options.name: `Int / Int -> Int`, flooring
options.detail: Keep division closed over Int but round down instead of toward zero, aligning with floored `%`. Gain: internal consistency with D-MODSEM1 and no type change. Loss: `7 / 2` still is not 3.5, so the beginner trap survives, and it now differs from both C and Python at once.
options.technical: Floors toward negative infinity, making `/` and `/%` identical on Int, which duplicates one mechanism under two spellings.

comparisons.note: Changed this exact default after two decades of the truncation bug.
Truncating integer division.
Division is numeric, never silently whole.

recommendation.why: Every math tool the target audience comes from answers 3.5. With `/%` available for explicit whole-number division, keeping the truncation trap would preserve a famous bug purely for C-family nostalgia.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the beginner-hostile default that Python 3 spent a painful decade migrating away from, with the benefit of hindsight available for free.
It makes `/` and `/%` the same operation on Int, two spellings for one mechanism, while still giving the wrong average.

recommendation.tradeoff: Integer-heavy code must write `/%` to stay in Int, and enormous default-Int values lose precision when `/` produces a Float. Both are explicit and visible, unlike the silent truncation they replace.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared float-producing, truncating, and flooring division and recommended the float result for calculator correctness.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added exact-rational results as a candidate: `7 / 2` as a Rational preserving exactness. It was rejected as a new core numeric type with pervasive cost, better raised someday as its own proposal, not smuggled through an operator ballot.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested context-dependent division, Int in Int contexts and Float otherwise. Result types that depend on surrounding inference make errors non-local, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with systems-code closure over Int and C with its consistency story beside floored modulo. Neither fixes the average that is simply wrong.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on precision loss for huge arbitrary-precision Ints and on `/=` breakage. The type error on `/=` is loud and mechanical to fix, Python demonstrates the precision tradeoff is livable, so A survives.

decisions.title: Bitwise NOT: extend `!` to integers
decisions.gist: How to flip every bit of an integer.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no bitwise complement at all today. `!` works only on Bool, and `~`, the spelling C and Python use for complement, is Jet's copy sigil. Complement builds bit masks: clearing a flag is `flags & !mask`. On a Bool, `!` already flips the single bit, so extending it to flip all bits of an integer is one rule, not two. Rust ships exactly this design.
decisions.story: Rosa writes a driver for a sensor board. To clear the interrupt-enable bit she needs `status & !INTERRUPT_MASK`. Today Jet gives her no spelling for the complement at all, and she hand-writes the inverted constant, which breaks the day the register grows.

options.name: `!` flips bits on integers
options.detail: One prefix operator: on Bool it flips the truth bit, on integers it flips every bit. Gain: no new sigil, one consistent rule, and Rust proves the design works at scale. Loss: readers from C and Python expect tilde and must learn that Jet's tilde means copy, and a stray `!` on an integer is no longer caught as a type error.
options.technical: UnOp::Not extends from Bool to all integer widths as bitwise complement, matching Rust's `!`. On the default arbitrary-precision Int, complement is defined as `-x - 1`, the two's-complement identity, so it is width-independent. Fixed-width types flip their exact bits.
options.code:
print(!true)         // false
print(!0b1010)       // ...11110101 (two's-complement -11)
cleared :: status & !ENABLE

options.name: Method `x.flip_bits()`
options.detail: No operator; complement is an integer method. Gain: keeps `!` Bool-only so an integer `!` stays a type error, and the name says what happens. Loss: mask expressions read worse (`status & ENABLE.flip_bits()`), and complement becomes the only bitwise operation without an operator.
options.technical: Fixed-signature method on integer types; same `-x - 1` definition on default Int.
options.code: cleared :: status & ENABLE.flip_bits()

options.name: No complement; masks via xor
options.detail: Skip it; experts write `x xor all_ones` or precompute inverted constants. Gain: zero surface growth. Loss: every driver, protocol, and graphics programmer rebuilds a basic operation by hand, and the width of all-ones is a per-type trap.
options.technical: No change. The all-ones value differs per width, which is exactly the bug the operator prevents.
options.code: cleared :: status & (ENABLE xor 0b1111_1111)   // must match width by hand

comparisons.note: One `!` for logical and bitwise NOT, chosen deliberately over C's tilde.
Separate tilde operator for complement.

recommendation.why: Flipping bits is what `!` already does on Bool, so one rule covers both, with Rust as working precedent. No new sigil is spent, which matters in a language where tilde and caret are already claimed.

whyNot.reason: A method call in the middle of a mask expression is heavier than the operator every peer language provides.
