Hand-built all-ones masks are width traps, recreating the exact bug a complement operator exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: An accidental `!` on an integer now compiles instead of erroring. That is acceptable because the same is true in Rust and the confusion is rare, while the Bool-only rule left a real operation unspellable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared extending `!`, a named method, and no complement, recommending the extension for its one-rule consistency.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review searched for a dedicated sigil: tilde is the copy sigil, doubled `!!` reads as double negation, and inventing a new glyph fails the no-unprecedented-sigils bar. None were menu-worthy.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested operator plus method as a teaching alias and rejected the alias: one operation, one spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by naming its discoverability and its preservation of `!`-on-Int as an error, the strongest honest case against the extension.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's meaning on arbitrary-precision Int, where bit width is unbounded. The two's-complement identity `-x - 1` is total and width-free, Python defines tilde identically for its big ints, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Three-way comparison: operator or method
decisions.gist: How custom ordering is written for sorting.
decisions.lesson: A three-way comparison answers less, equal, or greater in one step. Its real job is custom sorting: define ordering once and every sort and comparison derives from it. Ruby, PHP, and C++ spell it `<=>`, the spaceship operator. The spelling is free in Jet — `a <= > b` is invalid today, so no conflict exists. The question is whether ordering deserves an operator or stays a named method, since ordinary user code compares with the six operators and rarely needs the three-way form directly.
decisions.story: Sam sorts a leaderboard by score, then by name for ties. He writes one ordering rule for his Player type and expects `sort` to use it. He touches the three-way form once, inside that rule, and never again in the rest of the program.

options.name: `compare` method returning Ordering
options.detail: Ordering is a named method and an Ordering type; no new operator. Gain: the three-way form appears exactly where it is defined and read, in ordering rules, where a named method with combinators like `then` reads better than operator chains. Loss: Ruby and PHP migrants type `<=>` and get a parse error, and dense comparator bodies carry method-call weight.
options.technical: Core `Ordering` type (Less, Equal, Greater) with `then` and `reverse`. Fixed-signature `compare` on ordered core types; user types define `compare(self, other)` and the six comparison operators plus sorting derive from it.

options.name: Spaceship operator `<=>` plus Ordering
options.detail: The Ruby and C++ spelling as a real operator, sugar over the same method. Gain: comparator bodies get shorter and migrants keep their muscle memory. Loss: an operator visible to every learner for an operation used almost only inside ordering rules, and Jet gains a three-glyph sigil whose meaning cannot be guessed from its parts.
options.technical: New token `<=>`, lexed before `<=`. Desugars to `compare`. Everything else as option A.

options.name: Neither; six operators only
options.detail: No Ordering type, no three-way form; custom sorting takes a key function or a Bool less-than rule. Gain: nothing new. Loss: tie-breaking multi-field sorts through Bool rules are error-prone boilerplate, and library authors lose the single-definition derivation that every peer language provides.
options.technical: Sorting APIs accept key extraction or a `less` predicate only.

comparisons.note: Spaceship operator returning order.
Named method plus Ordering enum with combinators; no operator.
Dropped its three-way cmp entirely; key functions dominate.

recommendation.why: Three-way comparison lives inside ordering definitions, read by library authors, not beginners. A named method with combinators covers that audience fully without spending a three-glyph operator on the everyday surface.

whyNot.reason: The operator's entire benefit is brevity inside comparator bodies, too small a payoff for a new learner-visible sigil.
Bool-rule comparators are the worst of both worlds: verbose, error-prone on ties, and without single-definition derivation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Comparator bodies stay slightly wordier than Ruby's. That is acceptable because the `then` combinator keeps multi-field ordering flat and readable, which is the case that actually matters.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared method-only, spaceship-plus-method, and neither, recommending the method for audience fit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Python-style key functions as a candidate and folded them in: key-based sorting composes with a compare method and belongs in the sorting API design regardless of this ballot.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping the method now while reserving `<=>` for later and rejected the reservation: unratified futures are not law, and the spelling stays free either way.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with Ruby and PHP migration comfort and C with zero surface growth. B still buys brevity only inside rare comparator bodies; C still leaves tie-breaking to hand-rolled Bool logic.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A by asking whether deriving six operators from one method is magic beginners cannot trace. The derivation is the same one every peer language ships and diagnostics can name the source method, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Default Int overflow model: arbitrary precision
decisions.gist: What happens when the default Int gets too big.
decisions.lesson: Jet's default Int is fixed-width today and the program stops with a panic when a result overflows (D-NUMOPS1). Overflow is not a beginner mistake; it is a machine limit leaking through. Python removed the limit entirely: its int grows as needed, so factorials, big powers, and money math in small units just work. The cost is a check on arithmetic and a slower path for huge values. This decision sets the default; fixed-width expert types exist regardless.
decisions.story: Nadia, a biology student, computes 25 factorial for a probability. It is a 26-digit number. In Python she has the answer before her coffee cools. In Jet today her program panics mid-run with an overflow message she has no tools to understand.

options.name: Int grows without limit; fixed widths are the expert opt-in
options.detail: The default Int is arbitrary precision with a fast path for machine-sized values, exactly Python's model. Overflow stops existing for beginners. Experts who need exact machine behavior reach for fixed-width types, where overflow traps by default and wrapping or saturating is an explicit named choice. Gain: a whole class of runtime crashes disappears and exact math just works. Loss: arithmetic carries a small-versus-big check, and foreign-function boundaries must range-check.
options.technical: Small-int fast path in machine words, spilling to heap digits past roughly 63 bits, per I9 identical across AOT, JIT, interpreter, and web. Fixed-width `I8..I128`, `U8..U128` keep trap-on-overflow plus explicit `wrapping_*` and `saturating_*` methods. Amends D-NUMOPS1 for default Int only. Crossing to fixed-width or FFI range-checks with a real diagnostic.
options.code:
print(factorial(25))     // 15511210043330985984000000
print(2 ^ 200)           // exact, 61 digits
sensor: U8 = 300         // error: 300 does not fit in U8

options.name: Keep fixed-width Int with panic on overflow
options.detail: Status quo. Gain: predictable machine-speed arithmetic everywhere and no representation split. Loss: correct-looking math crashes at runtime on big inputs, the message teaches machine trivia beginners should never need, and Python migrants lose exactness they took for granted.
options.technical: No change. D-NUMOPS1 stands as ratified.
options.code:
print(factorial(25))
// panic: attempt to multiply with overflow

options.name: Fixed-width Int that wraps silently
options.detail: The C model: overflow wraps around modulo the width. Gain: fastest possible arithmetic, no checks at all. Loss: factorial(25) returns a confidently wrong number with no error, the worst possible outcome for scientific work and a direct violation of safe-by-default.
options.technical: Wrapping two's-complement arithmetic on the default Int.
options.code: print(factorial(25))   // 7034535277573963776, silently wrong

options.name: Fixed-width Int that saturates
options.detail: Overflow pins the result at the maximum value. Gain: no crash and the error stays visible as an extreme value. Loss: silently wrong results that additionally look plausible in aggregates, and no mainstream language uses this default, so it surprises everyone equally.
options.technical: Saturating arithmetic on the default Int.
options.code: print(factorial(25))   // 9223372036854775807, silently wrong

comparisons.note: Default integers grow without limit; the scripting standard.
Fixed-width, panics in debug, wraps in release; experts choose explicitly.
Doubles by default, lossy past 2^53; BigInt bolted on later.

recommendation.why: The mission is magic for beginners with expert control behind opt-in. An Int that simply holds the answer is that magic, proven by the exact languages Jet aims to beat, while fixed-width types keep every expert capability explicit.

whyNot.reason: A panic explains a machine limit to a person doing math homework; the crash is safe but the experience fails the mission.
Silently wrong answers are disqualifying for a language whose pitch is trustworthy computation.
Saturation is silent wrongness with a plausible face, and no precedent recommends it as a default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Default-Int arithmetic pays a small-versus-big check and FFI boundaries need range checks. That is acceptable because hot numeric code moves to fixed-width or Float types anyway, which is where experts already live.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared unlimited growth, panic, wrap, and saturate, recommending unlimited growth as the mission answer.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added checked-Result arithmetic and compile-time range types as candidates. Both push expert ceremony into everyday sums, so they were folded into the fixed-width expert surface where they belong.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested panic-by-default with an opt-in BigInt type and rejected it: the beginner still crashes first, and two integer defaults split the ecosystem, the JavaScript BigInt lesson.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with its predictable performance and Rust precedent, the strongest honest rival. It still trades a beginner-facing crash for a cost experts can already escape.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on hot-loop performance, memory layout of spilled ints, and I9 parity cost across four tiers. The small-int fast path bounds the common case, Python and Erlang prove the model at scale, and parity work is implementation effort, which never ranks a ballot, so A survives.

decisions.title: Plain short names for the named Core containers
decisions.gist: What each named container type is called.
decisions.lesson: Core ships eight named containers beside the bracket forms for list and map. Several names are computer-science jargon. Deque, Bag, BitSet, and ByteBuffer do not tell a new reader what the type does. This choice picks the one canonical name for each container. The names appear in code, docs, errors, and search results every day.
decisions.story: Mia is new to programming. She needs a line of jobs where the first job in is the first job out. She scrolls the container list and stops at Deque. The name tells her nothing. She leaves the editor to search the web instead of writing the next line.
decisions.inWild:
// A build farm, written with the current names.
pending :: Deque.from(jobs)          // what is a Deque?
urgent  := PriorityQueue.from(jobs)
retries := Bag.from(failed_ids)      // a bag of what, kept how?
flags   := BitSet.from(ports)
wire    := ByteBuffer.from(packet)

options.name: Owner slate: Set, Rank, Queue, PriorityQueue, Tally, Cache, Bits, Bytes
options.detail: Rename the jargon rows to one short word each. Deque becomes Queue. SortedSet becomes Rank. Bag becomes Tally. BitSet becomes Bits. ByteBuffer becomes Bytes. Set, Cache, and PriorityQueue keep their names. Every name is one common word except PriorityQueue. Queue names the both-ends structure, so it also covers last-on-first-off use without a separate Stack type.
options.technical: Amends the D-COLLBREADTH1 and D-ITERTOOLS1 rosters. Type names only; no keyword or sigil change, so Syntax.rs is untouched. HashMap and BTreeMap stay reserved. One rename sweep across Prelude, sema, docs, examples, and snapshots.
options.code:
pending :: Queue.from(jobs)          // take front, add back
urgent  := PriorityQueue.from(jobs)  // most important first
scores  := Rank.from(results)        // unique, always in order
retries := Tally.from(failed_ids)    // counts repeats
flags   := Bits.from(ports)
wire    := Bytes.from(packet)

options.name: Keep the current names
options.detail: No change. Set, SortedSet, Deque, PriorityQueue, Bag, Cache, BitSet, ByteBuffer stay. Readers who know other languages find familiar words. Beginners keep hitting Deque, Bag, and ByteBuffer, which do not describe behavior in plain English.
options.code:
pending :: Deque.from(jobs)
urgent  := PriorityQueue.from(jobs)
scores  := SortedSet.from(results)
retries := Bag.from(failed_ids)
flags   := BitSet.from(ports)
wire    := ByteBuffer.from(packet)

options.name: Descriptive slate: Roster, Rail, Priority, plus Queue and Stack aliases
options.detail: SortedSet becomes Roster. Deque becomes Rail, with Queue and Stack as thin aliases that signal which ends you use. PriorityQueue becomes Priority. Tally, Bits, and Bytes as in option A. Beginners searching for a queue or a stack find those exact words. The cost is three names for one structure and one invented word, Rail.
options.technical: Queue and Stack are transparent aliases of Rail with the same methods. Alias rows join the D-COLLBREADTH1 roster.
options.code:
pending :: Queue.from(jobs)     // alias of Rail
undo    := Stack.from(edits)    // alias of Rail
urgent  := Priority.from(jobs)
scores  := Roster.from(results)

options.name: Industry slate: match Rust and Java spellings
options.detail: Rename toward the names experienced developers already know. HashSet, BTreeSet, VecDeque, BinaryHeap, Multiset, Cache, BitSet, ByteBuffer. Zero learning cost for people arriving from Rust or Java. Maximum jargon for beginners, and several names describe the implementation rather than the behavior.
options.code:
pending :: VecDeque.from(jobs)
urgent  := BinaryHeap.from(jobs)
scores  := BTreeSet.from(results)
retries := Multiset.from(failed_ids)

comparisons.note: Ships jargon and plain names side by side: deque and heapq are jargon, while Counter is exactly option A's Tally.
comparisons.code:
from collections import deque, Counter
retries = Counter(failed_ids)

comparisons.note: Names containers after their implementation: VecDeque, BinaryHeap, BTreeSet. Precise for experts, opaque for beginners.
Keeps the surface tiny: Array, Set, Dictionary in the standard library; Deque and Heap live in a separate package.

recommendation.why: Every renamed row becomes a word a beginner already knows: Queue, Rank, Tally, Bits, Bytes. Names that were already plain stay put, so the change is small and complete.

whyNot.reason: Keeps Deque, Bag, and ByteBuffer, the exact names that send new readers to a search engine instead of the next line of code.
Buys Stack discoverability at the price of three names for one structure and the invented word Rail, which explains nothing by itself.
Optimizes for people who already know another language and abandons the beginner facet that Jet leads with.

recommendation.tradeoff: Queue names a both-ends structure, so it also supports last-on-first-off use that a strict queue would not. PriorityQueue stays the one long compound name. Both accepted by the owner in chat on 2026-08-05.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the owner slate, the current names, and a descriptive slate, and recommended the owner slate for plain-word coverage.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested acronym names such as FIFO and FILO and an industry slate matching Rust and Java. FIFO cannot name the priority structure, so only the industry slate joined the menu as option D.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested Rail with Queue and Stack aliases on top of the owner slate. The owner rejected the extra aliases, so the hybrid stays recorded as option C rather than the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option: B gained its familiarity argument, C its search-discoverability argument, D its zero-relearning argument for experienced arrivals.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked Heap as a shorter PriorityQueue name, but its plain meaning is a disordered pile and it collides with memory vocabulary. The remaining Queue wrinkle is recorded in the tradeoff and survives.

decisions.title: How a file declares an app program
decisions.gist: How a source file tells the toolchain it is an app to serve, not a script to run once.
decisions.lesson: Today a web app is a function named `app` that returns `WebApp`. The toolchain sniffs for that name and splices in a hidden `run() { app().serve() }` entry. So the entry that actually runs is one you never wrote. Files can also hold `run`, `dev`, and `app` together, which forces a precedence table nobody should have to learn. This choice picks one visible rule for what an entry is.
decisions.story: Mia builds her first site and `jet run site.jet` serves it, which feels great. Later she adds a plain `fn run()` to print a debug line. Her server silently stops serving, because the hidden rule says her new function now outranks `app`. Nothing in her file explains what happened.

options.name: Named builder function (today)
options.detail: Keep `fn app() => WebApp` as a magic name. The toolchain detects it and synthesizes a hidden serving entry. You can also write `run` and `dev`, and a fixed precedence table decides which one wins. Gain: shipping code keeps working unchanged. Loss: three competing entry names, an invisible synthesized entry, and the silent-outranking trap in the story.
options.technical: Detection is name plus return type. A file with `app` and no `run` gets `fn run() { app().serve() }` appended before load. `run` beats `app`, and `dev` beats both under `jet dev`.

options.name: The entry returns the program
options.detail: One entry, `run`. Its return type says what the program is. No return means a script that executes and exits. Returning `App` means the value describes an application, and the runtime serves it. `jet dev` serves the same value with watch, reload, and hot swap added. An expert can still write `fn dev()` to replace the dev default entirely. Gain: one visible rule, no hidden entry, no precedence table. Loss: existing `fn app()` files migrate.
options.technical: The runtime interprets the entry's returned value. Tooling such as `jet explain --web-graph` statically evaluates the returned builder chain, and reports a diagnostic when the chain is not statically known. `fn <command>()` remains the ratified override hook for a command's default metaprogram, today only `dev`.

options.name: Marker on the entry
options.detail: Keep one entry name but mark it: `#App fn run()`. The marker, not the type, declares the program kind. Gain: the declaration is loud and searchable. Loss: the marker duplicates what the return type already proves, so the two can disagree, and every new program kind needs a new marker ratified.
options.technical: Sema must reconcile marker and return type and diagnose mismatch. The marker namespace grows one entry per program kind.

options.name: No magic: call serve yourself
options.detail: No detection at all. A server is a script that happens to call `.serve()` at the end. Gain: nothing is hidden, and the beginner rule is just "programs run top to bottom". Loss: the app description never escapes the entry, so `jet dev` cannot re-serve the same value in watch mode, and `jet explain` cannot read the graph without guessing where the chain is. Every command that wants the graph re-sniffs the body.
options.technical: Static graph extraction must pattern-match a call chain inside an executed body, which breaks as soon as the chain is built through a variable or helper.

comparisons.note: The entry is a value of type Program. The runtime interprets it, and the same value drives dev tooling like the time-traveling debugger.
comparisons.code:
main : Program () Model Msg
main = Browser.sandbox { init = init, update = update, view = view }

comparisons.note: An app is a value conforming to App. The framework runs it, and previews reinterpret the same value without a second entry point.
Routes and pages are exported descriptions. `next dev` and `next build` reinterpret the same exports rather than asking for a second program.

recommendation.why: The signature the user writes is the whole rule. The return type separates a script from an app, and the same value feeds run, dev, build, and explain. New program kinds arrive as new types, which the language already knows how to extend.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a hidden synthesized entry, a name sniff, and a precedence table, and the story's silent-outranking trap stays in the product.
The marker restates what the return type already proves, which creates a disagreement case to diagnose and a marker to ratify per program kind.
Serving inside the body hides the app from every tool. Dev mode, graph explain, and deploy all need the description without executing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The returned builder chain must be statically known for tooling to read the graph. A chain built through arbitrary runtime control flow gets a diagnostic asking for a static description.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared today's named builder with a value-returning entry and recommended the value form, because one visible signature replaces a hidden entry and a precedence table.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the marker form and the fully explicit serve-yourself form. A manifest-declared entry kind was folded into the marker option, since both restate what the type proves.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested marker plus value together and rejected it as two spellings of one fact. It kept one hybrid piece: the expert `fn dev()` override survives inside the recommended option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the explicit form with a documented chain-extraction convention and strengthened today's form by documenting its precedence. Both still hide the program from at least one tool.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked static extraction with chains built via helpers and conditionals. The repair is a named diagnostic that asks for a statically known chain, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One App type or one type per target
decisions.gist: Whether Jet has one App type for every target, or a separate type per platform.
decisions.lesson: The app builder currently returns `WebApp`, a type whose name bakes in where the program runs. Native UI, and any future platform, would each need a sibling type. Where a program runs is already stated elsewhere, by the `#Target` marker or the package manifest's `target:` field. This choice decides whether the platform lives in the type name or stays where it is.
decisions.story: Ravi ships a web dashboard as a `WebApp`. His team then wants the same product as a native desktop app. The program is the same routes, views, and actions, but the type name says web, so the retarget starts with a rename and a fork.

options.name: One type per target (today's path)
options.detail: Keep `WebApp` and add siblings like `NativeApp` as platforms arrive. Gain: each type lists only what its platform supports, so misuse fails at the name. Loss: one product forks per venue, shared code needs a common wrapper, and every new platform mints a new type with its own builder surface.
options.technical: Each target type carries its own builder methods and its own runtime interpretation. Cross-target code must be generic over an app trait or duplicated.

options.name: One App, target set by marker or manifest
options.detail: One `App` type describes any application. The platform comes from the existing `#Target` marker or the manifest's `target:` field, never from the type. Using a capability the chosen target cannot honor is a compile-time diagnostic that names the target. Gain: one program retargets by changing one setting, and beginners learn one type. Loss: some misuse surfaces at target check rather than at the type name.
options.technical: Sema checks the app value's capabilities against the resolved target and reports a registered diagnostic on mismatch, for example `.csr()` under a native target. `WebApp` is deleted, and in-repo examples migrate in the same change.

options.name: Target as a type parameter
options.detail: One generic type, `App(Web)` or `App(Native)`, so the platform is visible in the signature but the type is shared. Gain: misuse still fails at the type, and shared code can be generic. Loss: the platform now threads through every signature that touches an app, and the same fact is stated twice once a `#Target` marker or manifest is present.
options.technical: Capability methods constrain the parameter, so `.csr()` exists only on `App(Web)`. Sema must still reconcile the parameter with `#Target` and the manifest, and diagnose disagreement.

comparisons.note: One app type runs on mobile, web, and desktop. The target is a build setting, not a type, and unsupported plugins fail per target at build time.
comparisons.code:
void main() => runApp(const MyApp());
// flutter build web | apk | macos — same MyApp

comparisons.note: One Application class, targets picked in the project file. Platform-only APIs are guarded per target rather than by separate app types.

recommendation.why: The platform is deployment information, and Jet already has a ratified home for it in `#Target` and the manifest. One App keeps one program retargetable by one setting, which is the one-mechanism rule applied to applications.

whyNot.reason: It forks the product per venue and mints a new type and builder surface for every future platform.
It states the target twice once a marker or manifest exists, and threads deployment info through every signature that touches an app.

recommendation.tradeoff: A target-only capability is caught by the target check instead of by the type name. The diagnostic must therefore name the capability, the target, and the fix plainly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared per-target types with one marker-driven App and recommended one App, because the platform already lives in `#Target` and the manifest.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the generic `App(Target)` form and considered a structural capability-set type. The structural form was folded into the generic option, since both move deployment into signatures.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested one App with an optional visible parameter for experts. It was rejected as two spellings of one fact, which invites disagreement between parameter, marker, and manifest.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened per-target types with a shared app trait, and the generic form with parameter inference. Both still fork or thread the platform through code that never cares about it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked one App with capability misuse caught late and with mixed-target workspaces. Registered per-target diagnostics and the manifest's per-member target answer both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One word for named auxiliary entries
decisions.gist: Pick one word for named auxiliary entry functions across the marker and the CLI.
decisions.lesson: A named auxiliary entry is a function you can invoke by name, like a database migration. Today the marker says `#Job fn`, but the CLI says `jet run --task` and `jet tasks`. Two words for one thing means every user learns the pair and every doc explains it. This choice picks the single word.
decisions.story: Priya writes `#Job fn migrate()` and then types `jet run --job migrate`, which fails. The flag is `--task`, and nothing connects the two words. She files it as a bug, but it is a naming split we shipped.

options.name: Unify on job
options.detail: The marker stays `#Job fn`, and the CLI becomes `jet run --job <name>` and `jet jobs`. Gain: the word you write is the word you type, and it does not collide with anything else in the language. Loss: the two CLI spellings change, and shipped docs and muscle memory migrate once.
options.technical: Rename `--task`/`--task=` to `--job`/`--job=` and `jet tasks` to `jet jobs`. Migrate help text, examples, snapshots, and docs in one change, with no alias left behind.

options.name: Unify on task
options.detail: The CLI stays, and the marker becomes `#Task fn`. Gain: the smaller diff, since only the marker changes. Loss: `Task` is already Jet's concurrency type, so `#Task fn` reads as an async declaration and the collision follows the word into docs, search, and teaching forever.
options.technical: Rename the `#Job` marker to `#Task` and migrate examples and snapshots. The concurrency `Task` type keeps the same spelling in the same files.

options.name: A fresh third word
options.detail: Retire both words for something unclaimed, for example `#Op fn` with `jet run --op` and `jet ops`. Gain: no collision with anything, ever. Loss: both surfaces migrate, and the new word teaches nothing that `job` does not already teach.
options.technical: Rename marker and CLI together and migrate all consumers. The word must be registered in Syntax.rs with this decision id.

comparisons.note: A Job is a run-to-completion unit of work, distinct from long-running services. The word carries exactly this meaning to a large audience already.
Cargo shipped `cargo check` and kept every verb aligned with its docs. Verb-flag drift is treated as a bug, not a style choice.

recommendation.why: Job matches the marker already in the language, reads as a schedulable unit of work, and collides with nothing. The word you write becomes the word you type everywhere.

whyNot.reason: Task is the concurrency type, so the same word would name two unrelated mechanisms in the same file.
A fresh word migrates both surfaces and buys nothing that job does not already deliver.

recommendation.tradeoff: The CLI flag and the list command change spelling once, and anything that memorized `--task` or `jet tasks` must relearn one word.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared unifying on job against unifying on task and recommended job, because task collides with the concurrency type.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the fresh-word option and considered keeping both words with aliases. Aliases were dropped as a standing greenfield violation rather than an option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested job in the CLI with task kept as a doc synonym. It was rejected, since a sanctioned synonym recreates the split this ballot exists to close.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened task with its smaller diff and prior CLI familiarity, and the fresh word with a collision-free future. Both still lose on the type collision or on teaching cost.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked job with the scheduling connotation of cron jobs. That connotation matches these entries, which can be scheduled or invoked by name, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Jobs as program subcommands, with a typed scope
decisions.gist: Whether jobs become subcommands of the program itself, and which audience a bare `#Job` gets by default.
decisions.lesson: A job is a named auxiliary entry, like a database migration. Under this design the job dispatcher is program semantics, not a build artifact. The same argv contract holds on every tier, so `jet run app.jet -- migrate` on plain source and `./myapp migrate` on the built binary hit identical routing. That retires the separate `--job` flag. The marker's argument is a real enum, `.Ship`, `.Dev`, or `.Internal`, so the audience is typed and extendable. The open choice is the default for a bare `#Job`.
decisions.story: Sam deploys a compiled app, and release night needs the migration job. Meanwhile a teammate left `#Job fn wipe_test_data()` in the same package. Whether that second job silently ships as `./myapp wipe_test_data` is exactly the default this ballot picks.

options.name: Bare word table, everything ships
options.detail: Every `#Job` becomes a subcommand on every tier, and hiding one uses an untyped marker word like `#Job(hidden)`. Gain: maximum magic, what works in dev works in production with zero extra marks. Loss: the word table is a closed compiler list rather than a type, and the teammate's wipe job ships unless someone remembers a word for it.
options.technical: Marker arguments are bare identifiers validated against a compiler table. New audiences mean compiler changes, and tooling cannot complete or type-check them.

options.name: Typed scope enum, ship by default
options.detail: The audience is the enum, and a bare `#Job` means `.Ship`. Gain: the beginner's first job survives deploy with no extra marks, and the enum gives experts typed control. Loss: the default answers the story badly, since the wipe job ships unless its author remembered `.Dev`.
options.technical: The scope is a Prelude-owned enum. Dispatch and `--help` derive from it identically on every tier under the parity rule.
options.code:
#Job fn migrate() { ... }             // = #Job(.Ship), ships
#Job(.Dev) fn wipe_test_data() { ... } // author must remember this
#Job(.Internal) fn tick() { ... }      // never a subcommand

options.name: Typed scope enum, dev by default
options.detail: A bare `#Job` means `.Dev`, a subcommand everywhere the toolchain runs the program, but stripped from release builds. Shipping is the explicit act, `#Job(.Ship)`. The release build prints what it stripped and names the fix. Gain: full magic while developing, and a production binary whose surface is deliberate. Loss: the release-night migration needs `.Ship` on it, one mark, taught by the build output.
options.technical: Dev tiers, `jet run`, `jet dev`, and debug builds, dispatch every job. Release builds dispatch `.Ship` jobs only and list stripped jobs in the build summary. `.Internal` jobs are callable from code and the scheduler, never from argv. The enum is Prelude-owned, so all tiers share one meaning.

options.name: Typed enum, no default
options.detail: A bare `#Job` is a diagnostic, and every job states its scope. Gain: no default to argue about, and every audience is visible at the declaration. Loss: the very first job a beginner writes fails to compile until they learn an enum, which is ceremony the magic facet exists to avoid.
options.technical: Sema rejects a scope-less `#Job` with a fix-it listing the three variants.
options.code:
#Job fn migrate() { ... }
// error: `#Job` needs a scope — .Ship, .Dev, or .Internal

comparisons.note: Management commands ship with the deployed app and run in production, which teams rely on for migrations. Nothing separates dev-only commands, so they ship too.
comparisons.code:
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py wipe_test_data   # also there, forever

comparisons.note: Scripts run from source with no build, and the runner strips nothing, so dev scripts ride into every environment that has the manifest.
comparisons.code:
npm run migrate
npm run seed:demo

comparisons.note: Feature flags gate code out of release binaries explicitly, and cargo reports what a build included. Deliberate release surface is the norm.

recommendation.why: While you develop, every job just works from plain source with no build and no flags. What ships is exactly what was marked to ship, the build says what it stripped, and the enum keeps the whole surface typed and extendable.

whyNot.reason: An untyped word table is a closed compiler list, and its ship-everything default sends the wipe job to production.
The typed enum is right, but ship-by-default still answers the story with an exposed wipe job.
Requiring a scope on the first job a beginner ever writes is ceremony before the first success.

recommendation.tradeoff: A production-needed job carries one explicit `.Ship` mark. The release build's stripped-jobs summary teaches that mark at exactly the moment it matters.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft exposed every job with an untyped hide word. Owner review reshaped it, a typed scope enum, tier-uniform argv dispatch, and a safe release default became the frame.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass compared ship-by-default, dev-by-default, and no-default over the enum, and kept the word-table form as the baseline. A per-package manifest allowlist was folded into dev-by-default, since the `.Ship` mark is that allowlist at the declaration.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined the enum with tier-uniform dispatch and the stripped-jobs build summary, which became the recommended option. It also merged the old dev-time flag path into program argv, retiring the second invocation spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened ship-by-default with the zero-marks deploy story and no-default with total explicitness. One still ships the wipe job, and the other taxes the first job ever written.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked dev-by-default with the forgotten `.Ship` on release night and with job names colliding with run flags. The build summary names the stripped job and its fix, and the dispatcher reserves job names before flag parsing, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.comment: Enum must cover all cases

decisions.title: How CLI arguments reach an app entry
decisions.gist: How command-line arguments flow into the parameters of an entry that returns an App.
decisions.lesson: Script entries already turn their parameters into typed command-line flags, so `fn run(count: Int)` accepts `--count=3` with type checking. An app entry returns a program value instead of running to completion, which raises the question of whether the same parameter magic applies. This choice decides how a served app receives arguments, and what happens when an argument does not fit.
decisions.story: Leah serves her app locally and wants it on another port. She expects `jet run site.jet -- --port=9000` to just work, the way flags already work on her scripts. If apps need a different ceremony for the same idea, that is the day the language stops feeling coherent to her.

options.name: Parameters are flags, one rule for every entry
options.detail: The script rule applies unchanged: app entry parameters become typed flags, values flow in before the value is built, and defaults keep the zero-argument path working. An incompatible argument is a launch-time diagnostic naming the flag, the expected type, and the fix. Experts customize names, validation, and help text with the ratified CLI field markers. Gain: one rule, no new ceremony. Loss: the signature becomes the binary's public flag surface.
options.technical: Argument mapping runs before the entry is called, identically for Unit and App entries. The extraction of the static app graph is unaffected, since parameters only feed builder arguments. Field markers from the ratified CLI field-marker decision provide renames, validation, and docs.

options.name: The builder reads arguments explicitly
options.detail: App entries take no parameters, and the value asks for arguments itself, for example `.port(args.get("port"))`. Gain: the app value owns its whole configuration in one visible chain. Loss: apps and scripts follow different rules for the same idea, argument reads scatter through the chain untyped until checked by hand, and the beginner's expectation from the story breaks.
options.technical: An `args` accessor is exposed to the builder chain. Type checking happens per read site, and there is no derived `--help` surface unless each read also declares metadata.

options.name: Apps take no CLI arguments
options.detail: Served programs configure through the manifest and environment variables only, never argv. Gain: deployment config lives in declarative files, which some platforms prefer. Loss: the quick local override in the story requires editing a file or exporting a variable, and scripts and apps split into two rules.
options.technical: App entries must have an empty parameter list, enforced by a diagnostic. Config values arrive through the manifest's settings or the environment API.

comparisons.note: The dev server accepts direct flags for the quick path and a config file for the durable one. Users reach for the flag first.
Server config arrives as typed CLI flags on the runner, and the app object stays free of argv handling.

recommendation.why: It is the rule users already learned on scripts, applied without exception. Compatible arguments flow in with types checked, incompatible ones fail with a named fix, and the expert path is the already-ratified field markers rather than new machinery.

whyNot.reason: It splits apps from scripts, moves type checking to each read site, and loses the derived help surface.
It removes the quick local override entirely and forces file edits or environment exports for a one-off port change.

recommendation.tradeoff: The entry signature is the binary's public flag surface, so renaming a parameter renames a flag. The field markers give experts stable names when the signature needs to move.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared extending the script flag rule against builder-owned reads and recommended the shared rule, because one mechanism should serve both entry kinds.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the no-argv option and considered a dedicated config-struct parameter. The struct form was folded into option A, since a struct parameter already works under the field markers.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested auto-mapped parameters plus a builder-side args accessor together. It was rejected, because two ways to read the same flag invite drift between them.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened builder reads with a typed accessor sketch and the no-argv form with twelve-factor deployment practice. Both still break the expectation the script rule already set.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked flag-surface stability across refactors and collisions with job subcommand names. Field-marker renames and reserved-word checks in the dispatcher repair both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Which commands an entry function can override
decisions.gist: Whether test and bench, like dev, can be customized by writing a function named after the command.
decisions.lesson: Each toolchain command runs a default metaprogram over your code. For `jet dev` that default is watch and hot swap, and a user-written `fn dev()` already replaces it. Test and bench have no such hook, so custom setup like starting a database before a suite means wrapper scripts outside the language. This choice decides how far the override rule extends, and what an override receives.
decisions.story: Noor's integration tests need a database container running first. Today she wraps `jet test` in a shell script that every teammate and CI job must find and remember. The setup she wants is ten lines of Jet, with nowhere to put them.

options.name: Dev only (today)
options.detail: Keep the override hook for dev and nothing else. Gain: test and bench runs are always the stock harness, so a green run means the same thing everywhere. Loss: real setup and teardown needs live outside the language in wrapper scripts, and dev stays an unexplained special case.
options.technical: No new detection. The dev override remains the single command hook.
options.code:
fn dev() { devserver.start(port: 4000) }   // works today
fn test(suite: TestSuite) { ... }          // never called, silently dead

options.name: Every command overridable, bare replacement
options.detail: Writing `fn test()` or `fn bench()` replaces that command's default entirely, the way `fn dev()` does. Gain: one uniform rule with full control. Loss: the override starts from nothing, so reaching the actual discovered tests means reimplementing discovery, and most overrides would rebuild the harness badly.
options.technical: Detection matches the dev rule, name only. The override body receives nothing and must locate and execute blocks through library calls if it wants them.

options.name: Every command overridable, suite handed in
options.detail: Same uniform rule, but the override may declare a parameter and receive the command's discovered work as a value, a `TestSuite` or `BenchSuite`. Discovery, filtering, and reporting stay the compiler's job, and the override orchestrates around them. A no-parameter override still fully replaces the default. Gain: setup, teardown, custom order, and custom reporting become ordinary Jet code. Loss: a bad override can skip work and print green.
options.technical: The suite value carries the discovered blocks after `--filter` is applied, with `run()`, iteration, and result access. `jet test --default` and `jet bench --default` ignore overrides, and verification contexts use that flag so an override can never mint CI green. Suite types are Prelude-owned under the I9 parity rule.

options.name: Hooks instead of overrides
options.detail: Keep the stock harness in charge and expose fixed extension points, like `#TestSetup fn` and `#TestTeardown fn`. Gain: the harness can never be skipped, so green stays trustworthy without a flag. Loss: every new customization needs a new ratified hook, and reordering or custom reporting never fits a fixed hook list.
options.technical: Each hook is a new marker with its own detection and ordering rules. The hook set grows per use case and per command.

comparisons.note: A crate can replace the default test harness per target, and most never do. The escape hatch existing does not corrupt ordinary runs.
conftest.py customizes collection, fixtures, and reporting in the language itself, which is a large reason teams standardize on it.
TestMain receives the run as a value and wraps it with setup and teardown. Discovery stays the toolchain's job.

recommendation.why: It makes the override rule one sentence covering every command, and hands the override the discovered suite so orchestration is ordinary code. Discovery stays the compiler's job, and the default flag keeps verification honest.

whyNot.reason: It leaves real setup needs in wrapper scripts and keeps dev as an unexplained exception to its own rule.
A bare override cannot reach the discovered blocks, so any useful customization starts by reimplementing discovery.
Fixed hooks grow a marker per use case and still cannot express reordering or custom reporting.

recommendation.tradeoff: An override can skip the suite and print green. The `--default` flag exists for verification contexts, and a run under an override says so in its output.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared dev-only against a uniform override rule and recommended uniformity with a suite parameter, because setup needs are real and discovery should not be reimplemented.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added bare replacement and fixed hooks. A manifest-declared harness path was folded into bare replacement, since both swap the whole runner without reaching the discovered blocks.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced the recommended option itself, combining uniform overrides with the suite value from the Go TestMain shape. Bare and hooked forms stayed as separate options.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened hooks with a minimal two-hook set and dev-only with its trustworthy-green property. Both still fail custom ordering and reporting, which the story generation needs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked false green from overrides that skip the suite. The `--default` flag, an override notice in output, and verification contexts pinning `--default` repair it, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Bench runner parity with the test runner
decisions.gist: Whether `jet bench` gains the same targets and selection that `jet test` already has.
decisions.lesson: `jet test` accepts a file, a directory, or a project, walks directories recursively, and selects by name with `--filter`. `jet bench` accepts exactly one file, cannot walk a module, and cannot run a single region. The two markers were ratified as siblings, but their runners drifted apart. This choice decides whether and how the runner surfaces stay parallel.
decisions.story: Owen keeps a bench block beside each hot function across a dozen files. Before merging an optimization he wants one number per region, but `jet bench` takes one file at a time. He writes a shell loop, loses the summary, and stops running benches at all.

options.name: Status quo, one file at a time
options.detail: Keep bench as a single-file command. Gain: nothing moves. Loss: module-wide numbers need shell loops, one region cannot be run alone, and the sibling markers keep strangers for runners, which is drift and not a decision anyone made.
options.technical: No change. The asymmetry stays undocumented behavior.
options.code: for f in src/*.jet; do jet bench "$f"; done   # Owen's shell loop

options.name: Parity where meaning carries over
options.detail: Bench accepts the same targets as test, a file, a directory walked recursively, or a project, and gains `--filter` for region names. Assertion-specific flags stay test-only, since coverage and snapshots have no bench meaning, and benches always run one at a time for timing integrity. A standing rule keeps future runner surface changes applied to both commands or explicitly carved out. Gain: the sibling promise becomes real and stays real. Loss: none beyond the migration itself.
options.technical: Bench reuses the test runner's target resolution and recursive walk. `--filter` matches region names after discovery. `--shuffle`, `--coverage`, and `--update-snapshots` remain test-only. Multi-file output is one line per region plus a per-file heading, and `--json` emits one record per region.
options.code:
jet bench src/                       // every region under src/, serial
jet bench src/ --filter="fib"        // just the fib regions
jet bench .                          // whole project, one summary

options.name: One command for both
options.detail: Fold bench into test, for example `jet test --bench`, so one runner owns both modes. Gain: a single surface can never drift. Loss: the command stops matching the marker you wrote, and timing runs inherit test defaults like parallelism that corrupt measurements. It also reverses the direction to keep the two parallel.
options.technical: One discovery pass tags blocks by kind, and a mode flag selects which kind executes. Timing integrity needs mode-conditional defaults inside one runner.
options.code:
jet test src/ --bench --filter="fib"   // benches via the test command
jet test src/                           // tests only — flag decides meaning

comparisons.note: `cargo test` and `cargo bench` share the same target and filter grammar, so knowledge transfers between them with one word changed.
comparisons.code:
cargo test parser::
cargo bench parser::

comparisons.note: One command runs both, with `-bench` selecting regions by regex. It works, but timing runs inherit test flags and the pairing confuses newcomers.

recommendation.why: The markers were ratified as siblings, so the runners should keep the same promise. Parity restores directory and project targets plus name selection, keeps timing-hostile test flags out, and pins the pair against future drift.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a shell loop where a command should be, and leaves the sibling promise broken by accident.
It reverses the direction to keep the two parallel, and timing runs inherit test defaults that corrupt measurements.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two commands must now evolve together, so every future runner change pays a small check against the parity rule or names an explicit carve-out.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the status quo with target-and-filter parity and recommended parity, because the single-file limit is drift rather than a ratified design.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added folding bench into test and considered a shared lower-level runner command. The shared runner was folded into the merge option, since both trade the marker-matching command away.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested parity plus a merged discovery pass internally. It kept shared target resolution as an implementation note and rejected surfacing one command, which is the merge option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the status quo with scripting composability and the merge with a never-drifts guarantee. Neither survives the story or keeps timing defaults clean.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked parity with long project-wide bench runs and filter-name collisions across files. Serial execution with per-file headings and path-qualified names in output repair both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Arrow loop bodies in statement position
decisions.gist: Whether a loop can take a `->` body as a statement, the way if arms already do.
decisions.lesson: The arrow already gives lightweight bodies in two places. An if arm runs `-> expression` with or without braces, and a finite loop yields values with `loop x, xs -> expression`. But the loop form is legal only where the values are collected. A loop that just does something still requires braces, even for one call. This choice decides whether the arrow body also works as a plain statement, and on which loop headers.
decisions.story: Dana writes `if hit -> score += 1` all day, so she types `loop pair, joined -> print(pair)` and gets an error. The braces she must add hold one statement. The language taught her a rule and then applied it to only half the constructs.

options.name: Status quo, braces for statement bodies
options.detail: Arrow loops stay expression-only. Gain: the arrow on a loop always means values are being collected, one signal with one meaning. Loss: the one-statement loop keeps ceremony the if arm does not, and the story's inconsistency stays in the product.
options.technical: No change. Statement-position arrow loops keep their current diagnostic.
options.code:
loop pair, joined { print(pair) }        // required
loop pair, joined -> print(pair)         // error, today and after

options.name: Statement arrows on finite-source loops only
options.detail: The arrow body becomes legal as a statement, but only on the loop headers that can already yield, finite sources. Gain: the statement form and the value form stay one grammar rule. Loss: condition-only and infinite loops still demand braces, so Dana's rule breaks again one construct later, on `loop running -> tick()`.
options.technical: Statement position discards the body value. A non-unit body in statement position gets a lint naming the `::` collection form. Condition-only and bare infinite headers keep their brace requirement.
options.code:
loop pair, joined -> print(pair)     // ok
loop n < 10 -> n += 1                // still an error
loop running -> tick()               // still an error

options.name: Statement arrows on every loop header
options.detail: In statement position, every loop header takes an arrow body, finite, condition-only, or bare infinite. Value position stays exactly as ratified, finite sources with non-unit yields. Gain: one sentence covers the arrow everywhere, a lightweight body for any control-flow construct. Loss: the same spelling collects in value position and discards as a statement, which one docs paragraph must teach.
options.technical:
The grammar allows `-> statement` after any loop header in statement position, with the body value discarded. A non-unit body in statement position gets a lint naming the `::` collection form and the `&` write form. The write form binds each element through the memory model's write handle, `loop v, &values`, so in-place change is a visible header fact. The infinite-yield bar stays for value position, since an infinite collection cannot terminate.

The body rule is line-based per D-BODY-ARROW1. A loop whose whole form fits one line uses `->`. A longer body uses a brace block opening on the next line, one statement per line. The formatter picks by width and round-trips both forms, with a stability test.

options.name: A second separator for statement bodies
options.detail: Keep the arrow for yields and add a different spelling for one-statement bodies, for example `loop pair, joined: print(pair)`. Gain: collecting and discarding never share a spelling. Loss: a new sigil to ratify and teach, two lightweight-body forms in one language, and the if arm already discards with the arrow, so the separation is not even consistent.
options.technical: A new separator token enters the grammar, Syntax.rs, the formatter, and the teaching surface, duplicating the arrow's role.
options.code:
loop pair, joined: print(pair)       // new spelling
doubled :: loop v, values -> v * 2   // arrow kept for yields
if hit -> score += 1                 // but if still discards with ->

comparisons.note: Match arms take one expression or a block after the arrow, in statement or value position alike, and the value is simply discarded when unused.
The one-line body after a colon works on every compound statement, if, for, and while, so the rule transfers between constructs.
comparisons.code:
for pair in joined: print(pair)
while running: tick()

recommendation.why: It finishes the rule the if arm already teaches, a `->` body is the lightweight form of any control-flow body. Statement position discards, value position collects, and the ratified value-form restrictions stay untouched.

whyNot.reason: It keeps brace ceremony on one-statement loops and leaves the arrow rule applying to only half the constructs.
It moves the inconsistency one construct over, since condition-only and infinite loops still refuse the body form the user just learned.
A second separator duplicates the arrow's job and still disagrees with the if arm, which discards with the arrow today.

recommendation.tradeoff: One spelling collects in value position and discards in statement position. The discard lint on non-unit statement bodies keeps the accidental case loud, and one docs paragraph teaches the split.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the status quo with statement arrows on all headers and recommended all headers, because the if arm already set the discard rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the finite-only middle ground and a second-separator spelling. An expression-statement rule making bare arrow loops expressions everywhere was folded into option C, since discard-in-statement-position is that rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested finite-only statement arrows plus a separator for the infinite headers. It was rejected as two body spellings split by header kind, which is harder to teach than either pure option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the status quo as a one-signal reading of the arrow and the separator option with never-ambiguous collection. Both still contradict the if arm the user learned first.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the collect-versus-discard split and nested arrow chains like a loop feeding an if. The non-unit discard lint answers the split, nesting already parses in value position today, and the formatter stability test guards round-trips, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.comment: Same rule as the more general arrow syntax for non pattern matching/if statements. For inline/fitting/single item statements/expressions, use arrow. For multiline, auto convert to {…} block

decisions.title: One line-based body rule for every head
decisions.gist: Whether every body is `-> body` when it fits one line and a brace block past that, with `=` retired from bodies.
decisions.lesson: A body follows a head, a function signature, an if condition, a loop header, or a dispatch arm. Today three spellings split that job. Functions use `= expression`, effect guards use a bare statement with no arrow, and arms use `->`. This choice tests one line-based rule instead. A body that fits on one line is `-> body`. A longer body is a brace block that opens on the next line. The formatter picks by width, so the writer never chooses. Values route to any consumer and drop otherwise, on every form alike.
decisions.story: Ana writes `if err -> return err` on day one and loves it. Then she writes a one-line function and must switch to `=`, and a one-line guard where the arrow is suddenly illegal. Three spellings, one idea. She asks which one the language actually believes in.

options.name: Keep the three spellings (today)
options.detail: Functions keep `=`, effect guards stay arrowless, arms keep `->`. Gain: each spelling carries a nuance, the equation reading on functions and the bare guard's brevity. Loss: the beginner learns three body forms for one idea, and the formatter cannot collapse or widen a body without changing which spelling it uses.
options.technical: No change to D-ARROW-CONTROL1, D-IFGUARD1, or the function grammar.

options.name: One line-based rule, arrow or block
options.detail: Every head takes `-> body` when the whole form fits one line, and a brace block otherwise, with the body starting on the next line. Functions join the rule, effect guards gain the arrow, and `=` retires from bodies to mean values only. The writer never chooses, since the formatter widens or collapses by line width. Gain: one sentence teaches every body in the language. Loss: the equation reading of `= expression` disappears.
options.technical:
Amends D-ARROW-CONTROL1, D-IFGUARD1, and the D-IF3 effect form. Inside arm tables `->` stays before a block, since it also separates head from body. Self-delimiting heads take the bare block. Marker-scoped regions such as `#Unsafe("reason") { … }`, `#Test("name") { … }`, and `#Bench("name") { … }` always keep braces, even for one statement. Their braces state the extent of a fact, the audited region, the registered test, the timed region, and are not bodies, so the arrow never applies to them.

Blocks hold one statement per line under S6, and a block's final expression is its value. A dropped non-unit arrow value in statement position gets a lint naming `::` collection and the `&` write form. The formatter emits the arrow form for one-line bodies, widens past width to a block, and round-trips both, with a stability test.

options.name: Blocks only for functions, arrows only for control flow
options.detail: Functions always take a brace block, and the arrow stays a control-flow mark. Gain: the arrow keeps one narrow meaning, and function bodies have exactly one shape. Loss: the most common function, one expression, pays braces and an extra line, and the guard split with `if` remains untouched.
options.technical: The `=` form is deleted and one-line function bodies are written as blocks. Control flow keeps today's arrow rules unchanged.

comparisons.note: Arrow functions use one rule, an expression body or a brace body, and it transfers to every arrow a user ever writes.
comparisons.code:
const area = (w, h) => w * h
const log = (m) => { console.log(m) }

comparisons.note: The equation form is today's Jet function spelling. Kotlin accepts carrying it as a permanent second body form beside braces.
comparisons.code: fun area(w: Int, h: Int): Int = w * h

comparisons.note: Match arms keep the fat arrow before both expressions and blocks, which is the same head separator rule this ballot keeps inside arm tables.

recommendation.why: One structural sentence covers every body, the arrow for one line, braces past it, chosen by the formatter and never by the writer. Each symbol keeps one role, `=>` for callables, `->` for bodies, `=` for values.

whyNot.reason: Three spellings for one idea tax the beginner and block the formatter from resizing a body without respelling it.
It taxes the most common function shape with braces and an extra line, and leaves the guard split in place.

recommendation.tradeoff: The equation reading of `= expression` is given up, and `=> Int -> body` places two arrows adjacent. Each arrow keeps one fixed role, which is what keeps the adjacency readable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft extended the arrow to function bodies for uniformity and recommended it over the equation form and braces-only functions.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested unifying on `=` instead, which dies on `if c = a` colliding with assignment, and a marker-based body form, which restates what the grammar already shows. Both folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried value-marking arrows and owner review killed them for forcing a value-versus-action choice on every body. The line-based rule replaced them, with the arrow kept inside arm tables as the head separator.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the equation form with its math reading and Kotlin precedent, and braces-only with its narrow-arrow economy. One keeps three spellings for one idea, the other taxes every one-liner.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the arrow adjacency in `=> Int -> body`, S6 legality of collapsed blocks, silent value drops, and one-line `#Unsafe` regions losing their audit weight. Fixed symbol roles, the width-based formatter, the discard lint, and the marker-region carve-out that keeps scope braces mandatory repair all four, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Markers must live in the registry — no drift, no exceptions
decisions.outcome: D-MARK-REG1 — mandatory registration: a marker exists if and only if it is a registry row. No marker may be parsed, checked, formatted, highlighted, or reflected outside Policy::APPLIED_RULES; every active row must be fully implemented end to end or retired. Drift in either direction is a defect enforced by CI guards (name-literal scan, per-row end-to-end coverage, generated editor grammars). Owner words (2026-08-05): 'We must make all markers REQUIRED to be registered in the registry, no exceptions for drift, no tolerance. Not acceptable to have marker drift from registry.'
decisions.comment: D-MARK-REG1 — mandatory registration: a marker exists if and only if it is a registry row. No marker may be parsed, checked, formatted, highlighted, or reflected outside Policy::APPLIED_RULES; every active row must be fully implemented end to end or retired. Drift in either direction is a defect enforced by CI guards (name-literal scan, per-row end-to-end coverage, generated editor grammars). Owner words (2026-08-05): 'We must make all markers REQUIRED to be registered in the registry, no exceptions for drift, no tolerance. Not acceptable to have marker drift from registry.'

decisions.title: Impure joins the reason law
decisions.gist: Whether an Impure block must say why.
decisions.lesson: Three block markers unlock checked power: Unsafe, Nondeterministic, and Impure. The first two demand a written reason. Impure's reason is optional today, which contradicts the block-plane ruling that names it beside the other two. This ballot settles Impure's obligation.
decisions.story: An auditor sweeps a service for authority blocks before a release. Every Unsafe block explains itself in one line. A bare Impure block says nothing, so the auditor must reconstruct intent from diff history.

options.name: Reason required
options.detail: Every Impure block carries a written reason, exactly like Unsafe and Nondeterministic. A bare block becomes an error whose fix asks for the reason. All three authority gates then read identically.
options.technical: The registry signature becomes reason: String with no default. Existing bare blocks migrate with a one-line reason added.

options.name: Reason stays optional
options.detail: The signature keeps its optional reason. The spec records Impure as a lighter gate than the other two, and audit sweeps accept bare blocks.

options.name: No reason parameter at all
options.detail: Impure becomes a plain switch with no reason slot. Writers who want to explain themselves use an ordinary comment; the gate stops pretending to collect audit text.

comparisons.note: The undocumented_unsafe_blocks lint makes every unsafe block carry a SAFETY comment. Teams enable it because bare unsafe rots.
comparisons.code:
// SAFETY: the pointer is live for this call
unsafe { ptr.read() }

recommendation.why: One law for all three authority gates is easier to teach and to audit, and it matches the block-plane ruling already on the books.

whyNot.reason: A lighter gate splits the authority story into two rules and leaves audit sweeps blind on one of three gates.
Removing the slot forbids even willing writers from explaining themselves where the gate is, and comments are invisible to tooling.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing bare Impure blocks need a one-line reason added during migration.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared requiring the reason with keeping it optional and recommended requiring it, for one authority law.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested reason-required-under-policy-only and a lint-level nudge. Both re-create the split rule this ballot exists to close, so option C was added instead as the honest opposite.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried optional-with-audit-flag, where bare blocks pass but audits list them. That is B with extra machinery, so it was folded into B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: comments are cheaper and the block already draws the eye. It still loses tooling visibility.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with reason fatigue producing copy-paste reasons. The same risk already exists for Unsafe and has not materialized in the examples, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.comment: Let’s make them optional BUT ones that are not provided should be easily auditable with tool chain and can be considered warnings or errors with build settings or ci/cd pipelines

decisions.title: How a SQL block names its row type
decisions.gist: The lawful spelling for the row type on an inline SQL block.
decisions.lesson: An inline SQL block can name the row type it produces. Today that is written with angle brackets, the only marker in the language that takes them. The registry row declares no parameters, so the spelling is typeable but never ratified. This ballot picks the lawful spelling.
decisions.story: Ana writes a dashboard query and wants each row typed. She copies the angle-bracket spelling from the one existing example, and nothing in the spec says whether that spelling is law.

options.name: Ordinary call argument
options.detail: The row type rides the one marker call grammar: SQL takes the type name as its argument. The angle spelling retires with a teaching fix. No new grammar anywhere.
options.technical: Registry signature: SQL(row: Type = none). Type-valued marker arguments follow the ratified argument-type ruling; the compiler checks the query's columns against the named type.

options.name: Ratify angle brackets
options.detail: Markers gain a type-parameter feature and the angle spelling becomes law. SQL reads like a generic call from host languages, and the signature schema grows to carry it.

options.name: No argument; the binding's declared type decides
options.detail: The block takes no type at all. The row type flows from the declared binding type. An unannotated binding in expression position is an error that asks for one.

comparisons.note: The row type is a generic argument on the query call.
comparisons.code: let rows = sqlx::query_as::<_, Row>("SELECT id, name FROM users");

comparisons.note: The row type is the ordinary generic argument of Query.
comparisons.code: var rows = conn.Query<Row>("SELECT id, name FROM users");

recommendation.why: The one call grammar already carries every other marker argument, and a type name is an ordinary argument under the ratified argument-type ruling. It works in every position with no new grammar.

whyNot.reason: A type-parameter feature for exactly one marker is a second grammar bought for one registry row.
Context typing fails in positions without a declared type, so a beginner hits an error the explicit argument never causes.

recommendation.tradeoff: SQL blocks read slightly less like generic calls from host languages that use angle brackets.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the call-argument spelling with ratifying angle brackets and recommended the call argument for grammar economy.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a named argument, a scope member inside the block, and full inference. The first two are spellings of A and were folded in; inference became option C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried the call argument with inference as a fallback when the argument is omitted. Two ways to say one thing violates the one-mechanism rule, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its host-language familiarity and C with its zero-ceremony reading on annotated bindings.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with type-versus-value ambiguity in the argument slot. The argument-type ruling already gives type names a lawful value form there, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One placement law for markers; the five forms retire
decisions.gist: One rule for where a marker sits.
decisions.lesson: The compiler's marker table gives every marker one of five written forms: Bare, Call, BareOrCall, Block, and Prefix. The audit found the five forms describe one shape. A marker sits right before the code it rules. This ballot decides whether the spec keeps five categories or one law. No current spelling changes under any option.
decisions.story: Sam adds a new marker row to the compiler. Under five forms, Sam must first pick a category, and that pick quietly invents grammar. Under one law, Sam declares a name, a signature, and legal targets. The written shape then follows on its own.

options.name: One placement law
options.detail: A marker, or one bracket group, sits right before its target. Parentheses appear exactly when arguments are written. Empty parentheses are an error the formatter fixes. The form column leaves the registry. Every current spelling stays legal.
options.technical: The registry row schema becomes: name, signature, legal targets, repeatable, status, inheritance. Formatter layout rule: own line above types, functions, and methods; inline before fields, parameters, bindings, statements, and blocks. S82 is rewritten to the one law.

options.name: Keep the five forms
options.detail: The spec keeps Bare, Call, BareOrCall, Block, and Prefix as documented law. Every new marker picks one category. Nothing changes today, and the category stays a coarse reading aid in the registry.

options.name: Two grammars: attached and scoped
options.detail: Attached markers get the one placement law. Scoped block markers keep a separate grammar section because a brace body follows them. Two rules replace five.

comparisons.note: One attribute grammar covers every attribute. Placement legality is per-attribute data, never a grammar class.
Attributes declare their legal targets in data (AttributeUsage), not through written-form categories.

recommendation.why: One sentence teaches the whole plane, and every future marker is a data row instead of a grammar decision. The audit showed the categories already collapsed: Known is filed Prefix while Track is filed Bare for the same written shape.

whyNot.reason: Five categories describe one shape, so each category names a difference that does not exist, and the table already holds contradictory filings.
A scoped rule differs only in what its target is, not in where the marker sits. A second grammar section rebuilds the split this rebuild removes.

recommendation.tradeoff: The registry loses a coarse hint about how each marker is usually written. The signature and legal-target columns carry that information with more precision.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one placement law against the current five forms and recommended the law because every form reduces to marker-before-target.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested postfix pragmas, always-bracketed lists, and keyword-per-marker designs, all rejected as respellings that break ratified stacking or casing law. Option C was added as the strongest genuine split.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried the one law plus a dedicated scoped-block appendix. That is option A with clearer spec prose, so it was folded into A's technical detail.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: the form column does feed tooling menus today. A keeps that value because completion menus read the legal-target column instead.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with empty-parentheses ambiguity and same-line declaration markers. Both resolved as formatter rules, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Repeating one marker on one target
decisions.gist: What happens when the same marker is written twice on one target.
decisions.lesson: Today the same marker can be attached twice to one declaration, and the compiler accepts it silently. Some markers repeat with real meaning: a function can state several Pre contracts. This ballot decides the default rule and how meaningful repeats are declared.
decisions.story: Riley merges two branches. Both branches added Inline to the same function, so the merged file carries it twice. Nothing warns, and the duplicate ships as noise the next reader must puzzle over.
decisions.inWild:
#[Inline, Inline]              // merge artifact — accepted silently today
fn price(cents: Int) => Int = cents * 3

#[Pre(n > 0, "n must be positive"), Pre(n < 100, "n must stay small")]
fn take(n: Int) => Int = n     // two contracts — repetition with meaning

options.name: Error by default; the registry marks repeatable rows
options.detail: Writing one marker twice on one target is an error with a remove-the-repeat fix. Rows where repetition carries meaning are marked repeatable in the registry: Pre, Post, and allow.
options.technical: The check joins the E0999 family and runs in the shared validation pipeline, so it covers every site. The repeatable column is ordinary registry data under D-MARK-REG1.
options.code:
#[Pre(n > 0, "n must be positive"), Pre(n < 100, "n must stay small")]
fn take(n: Int) => Int = n      // legal: Pre is repeatable

#[Inline, Inline]
