fn price(cents: Int) => Int = cents * 3
// error: `#Inline` is already applied to this function — remove the repeat

options.name: Keep silent acceptance
options.detail: The duplicate stays legal and the last copy wins. No new error, no new registry column. A lint could flag it later without a ballot.
options.code:
#[Inline, Inline]     // compiles clean; the second copy wins
fn price(cents: Int) => Int = cents * 3

options.name: Error for every marker; no repeatable rows
options.detail: All repeats are errors with no exception column. Several contracts combine into one condition with and, carrying one combined message.
options.code:
#Pre(n > 0 and n < 100, "n must be between 1 and 99")
fn take(n: Int) => Int = n   // one contract, one blunt message

comparisons.note: Repeating is an explicit opt-in on the annotation declaration; unmarked annotations cannot repeat.
AllowMultiple is false by default on every attribute; repeats are opt-in per attribute.

recommendation.why: A silent duplicate is nearly always a typo or a merge artifact, and the registry already owns per-row facts. Meaningful repetition stays first-class for contracts.

whyNot.reason: Silence hides mistakes today and lets two copies quietly disagree later when one of them gains arguments.
Merging contracts into one condition produces one blunt failure message where separate contracts each explain their own violation.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more registry column, and every future row must state whether it repeats.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared erroring with today's silent acceptance and recommended the error because duplicates are almost always accidents.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a warning-only rule and a formatter-dedupe rule, folding both into B since neither stops the copies from diverging. Option C was added as the strict alternative.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried error-by-default with a formatter auto-remove fix. That is option A's fix-it text, so it was folded into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a future lint and strengthened C with its one-law simplicity and zero new columns.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with repeated Doc lines and several allow lints on one declaration. Marking allow repeatable resolves it, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Two mechanisms share the name HTML
decisions.gist: Separate names for the page-pairing marker and the inline HTML block.
decisions.lesson: A file-level marker pairs a Jet web file with its host page. A block marker embeds inline HTML. Both are spelled HTML today, and the block form has no registry row. One name for two mechanisms breaks the one-name-one-meaning rule the marker renames established.
decisions.story: Kim reads a teammate's web module. The top of the file says HTML with a path, and the middle of a function says HTML with a brace body. Kim assumes they are one feature and hunts for a connection that does not exist.

options.name: Block keeps HTML; the pairing marker gets its own name
options.detail: Inline HTML keeps the name that says what the block contains. The file-pairing marker takes a name that says what it does. Candidate names, owner picks one at ratification: Page, Hosts, Mount, Serves.
options.technical: Both mechanisms get registered rows with full signatures. The old file-level HTML spelling retires with a teaching fix to the chosen name.

options.name: Register both under one name
options.detail: Two rows share the name HTML with site-dependent signatures. On a file it means pairing; on a block it means inline HTML. Nothing renames, and readers carry the double meaning.

options.name: Retire the pairing marker
options.detail: Page pairing moves to the package manifest. Source files stop naming their host page, and HTML means only the inline block.

comparisons.note: The file format owns the pairing, and the embedded template block has its own name. Two jobs, two names.

recommendation.why: Each name then says exactly one true thing: the block contains HTML, and the file marker names the page it serves. The rename is one teaching fix.

whyNot.reason: One name meaning two things at two sites is exactly the confusion the marker hygiene ruling paid to remove.
The manifest is far from the code it describes, and a reader at the top of the file loses the pairing information they want most.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rename with a teaching fix for existing files.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared renaming the pairing marker with registering the shared name twice and recommended the rename for one-name-one-meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested renaming the block instead and folding pairing into Target, rejecting both because the block's name is its content and Target rules build partitions. Option C was added from this pass.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried the rename plus manifest pairing as an override for generated sites. That is a future manifest feature independent of this naming choice, so it was set aside.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B, since site-dependent signatures become expressible after the registry rebuild, and strengthened C's single-source-of-truth story.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A over churn in existing web examples and candidate-name collisions. The sweep found few files, and none of the candidate names collide with registry rows or traits, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Integer power when the exponent sign is unknown
decisions.gist: What an integer power returns when nobody knows the exponent sign until the program runs.
decisions.lesson: You already chose that `2 ^ -1` is 0.5 and returns a Float. That rule reads the minus sign in the source text. Jet checks types before the program runs. When the exponent is a variable, no one knows its sign yet. The compiler must still pick one result type. This choice decides that type, and what happens when the exponent turns out to be negative.
decisions.story: Sam writes a loop that doubles a counter: `total = 2 ^ step`. The variable `step` comes from a file. Sam expects exact whole numbers. One day the file holds -3. Jet must either hand Sam a fraction, stop the program, or refuse to compile the line.

options.name: Stay exact, stop on a negative exponent
options.detail: An integer raised to an integer stays an exact integer. If the exponent turns out negative while the program runs, the program stops with a clear message. A written minus sign still gives a Float, so `2 ^ -1` is still 0.5. Gain: counting and sizing code keeps exact whole numbers, which is what almost every loop wants. Loss: a negative exponent from data stops the program instead of returning a fraction.
options.technical: `Int ^ Int -> Int`. The result type never depends on a runtime value. A written negative literal exponent keeps the ratified `Int ^ Int(<0) -> Float` rule, decided in sema from the source text. A runtime-negative exponent traps, using the same trap family as divide by zero and overflow. The trap message and its diagnostic code come from one Prelude symbol shared by every tier.

options.name: Always return a Float when the sign is unknown
options.detail: If the compiler cannot see that the exponent is zero or more, the answer is a Float. Nothing stops the program. Gain: a negative exponent from data returns a fraction, exactly like the written case, so one rule covers both. Loss: ordinary counting code quietly loses exact whole numbers. `2 ^ step` in a loop returns 1024.0 instead of 1024, and large values lose digits.
options.technical: `Int ^ Int -> Float` unless sema proves the exponent is a non-negative constant. Proof comes from literals and from constant folding only. A variable of type Int always widens. Float results follow the platform double rules, so exactness is lost above 2^53.
options.code:
let step = config.read_int("scale_step")
print(2 ^ step)   // 1024.0, a Float, even when step is 10

let n = 10
print(2 ^ n)      // 1024, exact: n folds to a constant
print(2 ^ 62)     // exact
print(2 ^ step)   // loses digits past 2^53

options.name: Make the author state the intent
options.detail: Jet refuses to compile `2 ^ step` when nothing proves the sign of `step`. The message offers two fixes: check the sign first, or make the base a Float. Gain: no surprise fraction and no surprise stop, because every power says what it means. Loss: real ceremony on ordinary code. Every power over a variable needs an extra line, even where a negative value is impossible in practice.
options.technical: `Int ^ Int` is an error when sema cannot prove the exponent is non-negative. Proof comes from a literal, a constant, a checked branch, or a non-negative integer type. The error carries a registered code with a fix that offers a guard or a Float base.

options.name: Split the spellings
options.detail: `^` means exact integer power and only accepts an exponent that cannot be negative. A separate `math.pow` covers fractions and negative exponents, and always returns a Float. Gain: each spelling has one meaning and one result type, with nothing to learn about proofs. Loss: `2 ^ -1` stops meaning 0.5, which reverses a rule you already chose, and textbook formulas need rewriting.
options.technical: `^` takes a non-negative integer exponent type. A negative literal is a compile error. `math.pow(base, exponent) -> Float` covers every other case. This retires the ratified `Int ^ Int(<0) -> Float` rule and needs that decision amended.
options.code:
print(2 ^ 10)         // 1024, exact Int
print(2 ^ -1)         // compile error, use math.pow
print(math.pow(2, -1))// 0.5, a Float

let step = config.read_int("scale_step")
print(math.pow(2, step))  // always a Float

comparisons.note: Types are checked while the program runs, so the sign is always known. Jet cannot copy this directly.
The exponent type cannot hold a negative number, so the question never arises. Overflow stops the program in debug builds.
There is no power operator. The library function takes and returns floating point numbers only.
There is no power operator. The library covers floating point, and exact integer power needs a written loop.
The power function is floating point only. Exact integer power is not in the standard library.

recommendation.why: Almost every power over a variable is counting, sizing, or scaling, and those need exact whole numbers. Option A keeps them exact. A negative exponent from data is a bad input, and Jet already stops on divide by zero and overflow, so the behaviour is familiar. The written rule you ratified stays untouched.

whyNot.reason: It quietly turns exact counting into floating point. `2 ^ step` returning 1024.0 breaks index and size code, and silently loses digits past 2^53.
It puts a guard or a conversion on every power over a variable. That is ceremony on ordinary code, and the beginner surface pays for a rare input.
It reverses your ratified rule that `2 ^ -1` is 0.5, and it splits one idea across two spellings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bad configuration value stops the program instead of returning a fraction. That is accepted because a negative exponent in integer code is a data fault, and a clear stop beats a silent change of number type.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the gap left by the ratified rule: the written case is decided, the computed case is not. It compared staying exact against widening to Float, and recommended staying exact.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the author-states-intent option and the split-spelling option. It also tested returning an optional or a checked result, and dropped that because it adds a new mechanism for one operator.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested proving the sign from checked branches and adding that proof to the exact option. The proof rule was folded into option C, because bolting it onto A would make the same line compile or fail depending on distant code.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option: constant folding for B, a two-way fix hint for C, and a clean library boundary for D. Each option now reads as the strongest honest version of itself.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the recommendation with the config-file case, where a bad value stops a running program. The stop survived, because every alternative changes the result type of ordinary counting code.

decisions.title: Which number types Core ships beyond whole and decimal
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a complex number type and an exact fraction type.
decisions.lesson: Jet ships four number types today: Int for whole numbers, Float for measured numbers, BigInt for whole numbers of any size, and Decimal for exact base-ten money. The Core surface ledger compares Jet against eleven languages. Four operations it scores as missing are not missing functions at all. They are accessors on types Jet does not have: the real and imaginary parts of a complex number, and the top and bottom of an exact fraction. This choice decides whether those types exist.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a signal filter. Every step multiplies complex numbers, and the textbook writes them as one value. In Jet he carries two Float variables through every function and writes the multiply rule out by hand each time. One sign error in the middle of it costs him an afternoon.

options.name: Ship both, as ordinary Core types
options.detail: `Complex` and `Fraction` join Int, Float, BigInt and Decimal. Complex carries two Floats and answers the arithmetic operators. Fraction carries two whole numbers, stays exact, and reduces itself. Gain: signal, control and geometry code reads like its textbook, and exact ratios stop drifting the way Floats do. Loss: two more types every beginner sees in the Core listing, and two more sets of operator rules to learn.
options.technical: `Complex` is a struct of two Float fields, `real` and `imaginary`, with `+ - * /`, `abs`, `conjugate` and `polar`. `Fraction` is a struct of two Int fields, `numerator` and `denominator`, kept reduced with a positive denominator, with `+ - * /` and exact comparison. Division by a zero denominator is refused where every other zero divisor is. Neither is a default; both are opt-in by naming them.
options.code:
use core.math as math

filter :: Complex.{ real: 0.5, imaginary: -0.5 }
print(filter * filter)          // Complex(0.0, -0.5)
print(filter.abs())             // 0.7071067811865476

third :: Fraction.{ numerator: 1, denominator: 3 }
print(third + third + third)    // 1/1, exactly
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)         // false, the Float answer

options.name: Ship Complex only
options.detail: `Complex` joins Core. Exact fractions stay out, because `Decimal` already answers the money case that most people reach for. Gain: the numeric work that most obviously needs a type gets one, and the Core listing grows by a single name. Loss: exact ratios still drift. A program that adds a third three times still does not get one, and the workaround is to carry two whole numbers by hand.
options.technical: `Complex` as in option A. `numerator` and `denominator` are recorded as declined against this decision id, so the ledger stops scoring them.

options.name: Ship Fraction only
options.detail: `Fraction` joins Core. Complex numbers stay out, on the grounds that they belong with the compute and signal libraries rather than in the Core every program loads. Gain: exact ratios for schedules, gearing, sampling rates and probabilities, which are common in ordinary programs. Loss: complex arithmetic stays hand-written, and the textbook formula and the Jet code stop looking alike.
options.technical: `Fraction` as in option A. `real` and `imaginary` are recorded as declined against this decision id, and complex support is left to a later compute library.

options.name: Ship neither, and record the decline
options.detail: Core keeps four number types. Both are recorded as deliberate declines with this decision id, so they stop being scored as gaps and stop resurfacing. Gain: the beginner surface stays as small as it is now, and neither type has to answer the hard questions about operators, ordering and printing. Loss: Jet stays behind eleven compared languages on both, and anyone doing signal or exact-ratio work writes the type themselves.
options.technical: No new Core types. `real`, `imaginary`, `numerator` and `denominator` are marked declined against this decision id in the Core surface ledger. A user-written struct is the answer, and nothing in Core blocks that.

comparisons.note: Complex is built into the language with its own literal. Exact fractions are a standard-library module.
comparisons.code:
z = 1 + 2j
from fractions import Fraction
Fraction(1, 3) * 3   # Fraction(1, 1)

comparisons.note: Both are built in, and both take part in the ordinary numeric tower.
Neither is in the standard library. Both live in widely used external packages.
Complex is built into the language with two widths. Exact fractions are in the big-number package.
Neither is in the standard library. Complex is in the official numerics package.

recommendation.why: Both types answer a question a program cannot answer well by hand. Complex arithmetic written out at every call site is where sign errors hide, and Float ratios drift in exactly the places people assume they will not. Neither type costs the beginner anything until it is named, and both are ordinary structs with ordinary operators.

whyNot.reason: It leaves exact ratios drifting. Sampling rates, gearing and probabilities are ordinary programs, not specialist ones.
It leaves the textbook formula and the Jet code looking different, which is where sign errors in signal code come from.
It keeps Jet behind eleven compared languages on both, and hands every user the same hand-written multiply rule to get wrong.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two more names in the Core listing, and two more sets of operator rules to document. That is accepted because neither appears until a program names it, and the alternative is hand-written arithmetic in the places most likely to be wrong.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the choice as four ledger rows that are accessors on absent types rather than missing functions. It compared shipping both, either one alone, and neither.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a single numeric-tower type covering both, and shipping them outside Core in a compute package. The tower was dropped because it hides two different sets of operator rules behind one name, and the package split was folded into option D, whose answer is already a user-written type.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping Complex in Core and Fraction in a compute package. It was rejected because exact ratios turn up in ordinary scheduling and sampling code, not in specialist numeric work.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option, giving D a full worked user-written type and giving B and C an explicit decline id so a declined row stops being scored.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the recommendation on beginner surface. Both types survive because neither appears until a program names one, and both behave as ordinary structs with the operators already ratified.

decisions.title: How fine a Duration measures
decisions.gist: The smallest slice of time a Duration can hold.
decisions.lesson: A Duration in Jet counts whole milliseconds. That is the smallest slice it can hold, so a Duration cannot say 250 microseconds, and `core.time` has no way to build one. Eleven compared languages all measure finer. This choice decides how fine Jet measures, and it cannot be changed later without changing every stored Duration.
decisions.story: Mira times a database call to tune an index. The call takes 400 microseconds. Jet reports it as 0 milliseconds, so every run looks the same and she has nothing to tune against. She drops to raw integers and carries her own unit by hand.

options.name: Nanoseconds, in a 64-bit count
options.detail: A Duration counts whole nanoseconds. It reaches about 292 years, which covers timeouts, benchmarks and retry schedules, and it matches what an operating system clock actually reports. Gain: every measurement a program can take is representable, and no unit is lost on the way in. Loss: a Duration can no longer hold a span longer than 292 years, so calendar-scale arithmetic must use dates rather than durations.
options.technical: `Duration` becomes an i64 nanosecond count. `DurationUnit` gains `Nanoseconds` and `Microseconds`. `core.time` gains `nanoseconds` and `microseconds` constructors beside the existing four. `in(unit)` keeps returning a whole number and keeps refusing a span that leaves the range. Existing millisecond values scale by 1_000_000 at construction; no stored format changes, because Duration is not serialized as a raw count.
options.code:
gap :: time.microseconds(400)
print(gap.in(Unit.Nanoseconds) ?? 0)   // 400000
print(gap.in(Unit.Milliseconds) ?? 0)  // 0, still whole

budget :: time.hours(2)
print(budget.in(Unit.Seconds) ?? 0)     // 7200

options.name: Microseconds, in a 64-bit count
options.detail: A Duration counts whole microseconds. It reaches about 292 thousand years, so calendar-scale spans stay representable. Gain: fine enough for almost every measurement a program takes, with a range nobody will hit. Loss: nanosecond timing is still lost, which is the resolution a profiler and a hardware clock report, so benchmark work still rounds.
options.technical: `Duration` becomes an i64 microsecond count. `DurationUnit` gains `Microseconds`. `core.time` gains a `microseconds` constructor. A nanosecond reading from the clock is rounded to the nearest microsecond on the way in, which is a lossy conversion the caller cannot see.
options.code:
gap :: time.microseconds(400)
print(gap.in(Unit.Microseconds) ?? 0)   // 400

// A nanosecond reading rounds on the way in.
print(time.start().elapsed().in(Unit.Microseconds) ?? 0)

options.name: Two numbers: whole seconds and a nanosecond part
options.detail: A Duration carries a whole-second count and a nanosecond remainder, the way an operating system reports time. Gain: full nanosecond resolution with no range limit worth worrying about, so both a benchmark and a century are exact. Loss: a Duration stops being one number, so comparing and adding cost more, and the type is harder to explain than a count.
options.technical: `Duration` becomes a struct of an i64 second count and a u32 nanosecond remainder, matching the shape of a POSIX timespec. Arithmetic normalizes the remainder. `in(unit)` keeps its contract.
options.code:
gap :: time.nanoseconds(400)
print(gap.in(Unit.Nanoseconds) ?? 0)    // 400

long :: time.hours(1_000_000)
print(long.in(Unit.Hours) ?? 0)          // 1000000, still exact

options.name: Keep milliseconds, and record the decline
options.detail: Duration stays a whole-millisecond count. Sub-millisecond timing is recorded as a deliberate decline with this decision id, so it stops being scored as a gap. Gain: nothing changes, and the type stays the simplest thing it could be. Loss: Jet cannot express a measurement that eleven compared languages can, and anyone timing a fast operation leaves the type behind and carries raw integers.
options.technical: No change. `microseconds` and `nanoseconds` are marked declined against this decision id in the Core surface ledger.
options.code:
// Timing a fast call stays outside the type.
started :: time.start()
lookup(index, key)
print(started.elapsed().in(Unit.Milliseconds) ?? 0)   // 0

comparisons.note: A duration is a 64-bit nanosecond count, reaching about 292 years.
A duration is whole seconds plus a nanosecond remainder, with no practical range limit.
A timedelta stores days, seconds and microseconds, so microsecond is the finest slice.
A duration carries seconds and attoseconds, finer than a nanosecond.
A TimeSpan counts 100-nanosecond ticks.

recommendation.why: A nanosecond count is what the operating system clock reports, so nothing is lost between the clock and the type. It stays one number, which keeps comparison and arithmetic cheap and the type easy to explain. The 292-year reach covers every span a Duration is for; a longer span is a calendar question, and dates answer that.

whyNot.reason: It rounds the clock reading on the way in, and the caller cannot see it happen. Benchmark work is exactly where that matters.
It gives up one number for a range nobody reaches. Two fields cost more on every compare and add, and are harder to explain.
It leaves Jet unable to express a measurement all eleven compared languages can, and pushes timing work out of the type entirely.

recommendation.tradeoff: A Duration can no longer hold more than about 292 years. That is accepted because a span that long is a calendar question, and `Date` answers it exactly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared nanosecond, microsecond and two-field representations against keeping milliseconds, and recommended nanoseconds for matching what the clock reports.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a floating-point second count and a unit carried alongside the number. The float was dropped because it loses exactness at large spans, and the carried unit because it makes two durations of the same length compare unequal.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a nanosecond count that widens to two fields past its range. It was rejected because a type that changes shape at a threshold is harder to reason about than either shape alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option, giving D an explicit decline id and giving C the timespec shape that makes it genuinely exact at both ends.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the 292-year reach with scheduling and archival cases. Those are calendar spans measured between dates, not durations, so the limit survives.

decisions.title: Collection helpers: run at once, or only when read
decisions.gist: Decide when list helpers like map and filter do their work.
decisions.lesson: Today list.map(f) returns a lazy view. The work happens only when something reads the view, and reading it twice does the work twice. The eager choice runs the work at the call and returns a plain list. The lazy spelling stays available behind one visible word. This amends the ratified lazy default from D-ITERTOOLS1.
decisions.story: Marcus filters a list of orders, then counts the result twice while debugging. Under the lazy default his filter runs twice, and a print inside it fires twice. He spends an hour filing a bug against his own code. Under the eager default the second count is free and the print fires once.
decisions.inWild:
open_orders :: orders.filter((o) => o.open)
print(open_orders.count())
print(open_orders.count())   // lazy: filter runs AGAIN here

loop o; open_orders { ship(o) }   // lazy: and a third time here

options.name: Eager on containers, .lazy opt-in
options.detail: Helpers on a real list, map, or set run at once and return a plain collection. Writing .lazy first gives the same vocabulary as a deferred view for large or infinite work. Streams and file lines stay naturally lazy because they arrive over time. Gain: no invisible re-running, results are inspectable in a debugger. Loss: long chains build intermediate lists unless the optimizer fuses them.
options.technical: Amends D-ITERTOOLS1. [T].map returns [T]; [T].lazy.map returns Iter<T>; Iter adapters unchanged. Sources that are already streams (files.lines, Stream, channels) keep returning Iter. The optimizer may fuse adjacent eager adapters when the intermediate is unobservable.
options.code:
names :: users.filter((u) => u.active).map((u) => u.name)
print(names.len())   // free: names is a plain list

big.lazy.map(parse).filter(ok).first(10)   // deferred, visibly

options.name: Keep the lazy view default
options.detail: Status quo. Helpers return a lazy Iter view, and collect, to_list, or a reducer materializes it. Gain: chains never build intermediate collections, matching Rust's zero-cost model. Loss: reading a view twice silently repeats the work and its effects. This is the documented multiple-enumeration trap that bites C# LINQ users at every level.
options.technical: D-ITERTOOLS1 as ratified. Adapter methods return Iter<T>; to_list()/collect()/reducers materialize.
options.code:
names :: users.filter(active).map(name)   // no work yet
print(names.count())   // work happens
print(names.count())   // work happens again, silently

comparisons.note: Collections are eager; asSequence() opts into lazy with the same method names. Widely praised as the beginner-safe split.
Enum is eager, Stream is lazy, same shape. Laziness is a module choice you can see.
LINQ is lazily deferred by default. Silent multiple enumeration is one of its most documented bug classes.
comparisons.code:
var q = xs.Where(p);
q.Count(); q.Count(); // enumerates twice

recommendation.why: Eager defaults make results real things a beginner can print, count, and debug. The deferred trap disappears, and experts keep the identical lazy vocabulary behind one word.

whyNot.reason: The lazy default trades an invisible correctness hazard for a performance property most code never needs. When the work is big, .lazy is one visible word away.

recommendation.tradeoff: Chained eager helpers can allocate intermediate lists. Accepted: fusion can remove most of it, and the hot-path escape is explicit and cheap.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared eager-with-opt-in against the ratified lazy default and recommended eager on the multiple-enumeration evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered a caching lazy view that memoizes on first read, and per-call-site inference from the expected type. Both were rejected as hidden machinery and folded into the two honest models.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed A is already the hybrid: eager containers plus naturally lazy streams plus an explicit lazy view. No stronger combination emerged.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: Rust proves lazy defaults work when the type system makes views unmistakable, and fusion is guaranteed rather than best-effort. Jet's beginner tier cannot lean on that type literacy.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with the 10-million-row case and effectful map closures. The .lazy escape handles scale, eager order actually tames effect surprises, and A survived with the fusion note made honest: best-effort, not guaranteed.

decisions.title: Adopt the extended Core API design rules
decisions.gist: Adopt the new Core API design rules.
decisions.lesson: Jet already has eight ratified API laws. The research behind docs/proposals/corelib-overhaul.md found proven moves those laws miss: call-site reading tests, enum options over booleans, typed domain values, defaults over overload families, and visible laziness. This ballot decides whether the extended rule set becomes review law for every Core API.
decisions.story: Priya teaches a first-year class with Jet. Her students copy a call like round(3.7, mode: .Down) from the docs and understand it without help. Sam, an expert on her team, audits the same function's defaults from one table in its docs and overrides two of them. The rules exist so both experiences hold across every Core module, not just the well-tended ones.

options.name: Adopt every rule
options.detail: All Part A rules become law. Every new or changed Core API must pass them in review, the same way L1 to L8 work today. Call sites are judged by reading them aloud. Options are enums. Every magic default is listed in one docs table with its override. Gain: one consistent library and a mechanical review test. Loss: longer reviews, and some existing APIs get drift cards.
options.technical: Extends the ratified rubric in docs/spec/stdlib-api-laws.md per the mapping table in the proposal. C1-C3 call site, D1-D4 defaults and options, F1-F3 failure, T1-T3 types, N1-N2 naming, L-A to L-D layering, E1-E2 evolution. Existing drift is carded, not grandfathered.
options.code:
// Passes review under the full rule set:
parse(text, on_error: .Lenient)
list.sorted()      // no side effect: past participle
list.sort()        // mutates: imperative verb

// Fails review:
parse(text, true)              // D4: boolean option
find_or_minus_one(items, x)    // F2: sentinel

options.name: Adopt call-site and option rules only
options.detail: C1-C3, D1-D4, F1-F3, and N1-N2 become law. The layering, type, and evolution rules stay as written guidance. Gain: the most visible wins land with less review weight. Loss: guidance without law is how libraries drift. A module could still ship only a streaming API, or keep a superseded spelling alongside its replacement.

options.name: Keep L1 to L8 unchanged
options.detail: No new rules. The current rubric already covers naming, fallibility, ownership, effects, allocation, diagnostics, examples, and one-way. Gain: nothing changes. Loss: the measured failures the research catalogs stay legal: boolean options, sentinel returns, stringly paths, silent laziness, overload families.

comparisons.note: Its API Design Guidelines are enforced doctrine, and the reason its call sites read as sentences.
The counterexample: accretion with no naming authority. Its own repair RFCs concluded the damage is permanent.

recommendation.why: Every rule is backed by a measured success and a measured failure in the research. Enforcing all of them is what keeps the library consistent when many agents write it.

whyNot.reason: Unenforced guidance drifts. The layering and evolution rules prevent the two most expensive failures on record: hostile stdlib tiers and permanent duplicate idioms.
The current rubric permits boolean options, sentinels, and silent laziness. Each is a documented, measured source of bugs and friction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core reviews check more rules, and existing APIs that break them get drift cards. That work is accepted: effort never outweighs the beginner experience.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full adoption, partial adoption, and the status quo, recommending full adoption on the strength of the cited evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered adopting rules per-domain and a lint-only variant with no review law. Both were folded in: per-domain adoption is B's shape, and lints can implement several rules mechanically under A.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested law-for-new-APIs with guidance-for-existing. That is already A's shape, since existing drift becomes cards rather than instant violations, so no separate option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: the current rubric plus taste has produced good recent APIs like core.crypto. It still leaves the banned patterns legal for the next author.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's review cost and the risk of rule-lawyering over judgment. The rules are phrased as call-site tests, the cost argument is void under the effort doctrine, and A survives.

decisions.title: File paths: plain text or a real type
decisions.gist: Decide whether a file path is a plain String or a Path type.
decisions.lesson: Today every Core path is a plain String, and core.path holds free helper functions like join and parent. A Path type knows it is a path: it joins with methods and chains calls, and cannot be confused with ordinary text. Beginners keep typing quoted strings either way, because path functions would accept both. This amends the ratified plain-String rule from D-FILES-WRITE1.
decisions.story: Ana builds a report tool on Linux and a teammate runs it on Windows. Her dir + "/" + name concatenation produces a broken path in the bug report. With a typed Path, dir / name joins correctly on every system, and the broken spelling cannot be written at all.
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as fs
use core.path as path

// today: strings and free functions, nesting inside out
full :: path.join(path.join(base, "logs"), day)
fs.write(full + ".txt", text)?   // works until it does not

options.name: Path type, strings accepted everywhere
options.detail: Path becomes a real type with join and other methods. Every Core function that takes a path accepts a plain String or a Path, so beginners never construct anything. core.path free functions are deleted because the methods replace them. Gain: correct joining on every system, chainable calls, and a reviewer can see what is a path. Loss: one more type in the mental model.
options.technical: Path in the prelude (see D-CORE-PRELUDE1). Core signatures use String | Path via ratified union types. Join with Path methods such as .join and .parent; no path-join operator is part of this ballot. core.path free functions are deleted per evolution rule E1. Expert Path-only APIs may take Path alone; default Core doors keep String | Path.
options.code:
log :: Path.home().join("logs").join("{day}.txt")
fs.write(log, text)?
fs.read("notes.txt")?          // plain string still fine
print(log.parent().exists())

options.name: Keep plain String paths
options.detail: Status quo. Paths stay Strings, helpers stay free functions in core.path. Gain: no new type, nothing migrates. Loss: separator bugs stay writable, path code nests inside out, and nothing distinguishes a path from any other text in review or in types.
options.code:
full :: path.join(base, name)
fs.write(full, text)?
fs.write(base + "/" + name, text)?   // the bug stays writable

options.name: Path type, Path required
options.detail: Path exists and every Core signature demands it. Strings convert explicitly. Gain: maximum type rigor, no union in signatures. Loss: every quick script pays a conversion call for zero safety gain, since a literal string is already unambiguous. This is the ceremony Rust pays with PathBuf, a known beginner tax.
options.code:
fs.read(Path.from("notes.txt"))?   // ceremony on line one
log :: Path.home().join("logs")
fs.write(log.join("today.txt"), text)?

comparisons.note: pathlib replaced stringly os.path and is the most praised stdlib upgrade on record. But both survive forever, which is its own cautionary tale.
Path/PathBuf are required types with explicit conversions. Correct, and routinely cited as early-lesson friction.
Plain strings plus filepath.Join free functions. Works, but nothing stops broken concatenation.

recommendation.why: The typed path removes a whole bug class and reads better, while the union keeps the beginner surface at zero ceremony. Deleting core.path in the same change avoids the permanent double idiom Python is stuck with.

whyNot.reason: Strings keep the separator bug writable and path code nested inside out. The research rates this the clearest before-and-after lesson in any stdlib.
Requiring Path taxes every quick script with conversions that add no safety, since literal strings are already unambiguous at these call sites.

recommendation.tradeoff: Signatures carry String | Path unions, and one more type exists. Accepted: the union is invisible at call sites, which is where the rules say clarity is judged.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared typed-with-union, status quo, and typed-required, recommending the union form on the pathlib evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered a distinct-type alias over String and compile-time path literal checking. The alias gives no joining algebra, and literal checking works under A too, so both folded in.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced A itself: C's type with B's call-site freedom. It was already the base recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: plain strings match how shells and configs pass paths in, and D-FILES-WRITE1 chose them deliberately. Boundary input stays text under every option, so the argument covers the edge, not the algebra.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested Path-only Core doors and rejected them as beginner tax. Owner feedback also removed pathlib-style slash join from examples; methods stay the join surface for this ballot.

decisions.title: Prelude policy and the safe additions
decisions.gist: Adopt written rules for what needs no import, plus five safe additions.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no written rule for what lives in the prelude, the set of names that work with zero imports. The research derives seven membership criteria and two safety mechanics from what nine languages praise and regret. The proposed additions are eprint, input, assert and assert_eq, the time entry points, and the Path name. Contested candidates go to a separate ballot.
decisions.story: A student's first lesson is print("hi"), then name :: input("who? "). No imports, no ceremony, and the first test is assert_eq(add(2, 2), 4) with a rich diff when it fails. Years later at a company, the same person gets a compiler warning when a teammate shadows input with a local variable, and the code still means what it says.
decisions.inWild:
// a complete first script, zero imports
name :: input("your name? ")
print("hello {name}, today is {Date.today()}")
assert_eq(name.trim().len() > 0, true)

options.name: Adopt the policy and the additions
options.detail: The seven criteria become law: measured frequency, total and safe, names never semantics, no better home, first-hour coverage, one fixed set, collision-conscious names. Shadowing lets the user win with a compiler warning. New names land only at epoch boundaries with a migration lint. The five safe additions ship. Gain: first-hour zero ceremony with enterprise-safe mechanics. Loss: five more ambient names.
options.technical: Adds to the existing ambient set (print, panic, built-in types, Val/None/Ok/Err, ?, ??, ?.): eprint(value), input(prompt: String = "") -> String ? IOError, assert(cond), assert_eq(a, b) with structural diff, type names Clock, Instant, Date, Duration, Path, plus Clock.now() and Date.today() as the blessed doors. Every entry is total or returns a Result. No implicit conversions ever enter the prelude.
options.code:
eprint("warn: {msg}")
line :: input()?
assert_eq(parse(line), Ok(42))
print(Clock.now() - start)

options.name: Policy only, no new names
options.detail: The criteria and mechanics become law, but the ambient set stays as it is today. Each addition returns later as its own epoch-gated proposal. Gain: maximum caution about ambient growth. Loss: the first hour keeps its measured friction now, and five separate future ballots re-litigate what the criteria already answer.
options.code:
use core.io as io
name :: io.input("your name? ")   // the import a first lesson must explain

options.name: No written policy
options.detail: Keep deciding prelude membership case by case. Gain: nothing binds future choices. Loss: every language that grew its ambient surface without criteria regrets specific entries, and the regrets proved permanent. Haskell never removed head; Python polices builtin shadowing with third-party linters.
options.code: // no code changes; the risk is in future additions

comparisons.note: 71 builtins cover the whole first year, the most praised beginner surface anywhere. Silent shadowing is its enterprise cost.
RFC 3114 is the only written membership rubric on record, and additions ride editions with a migration lint. The criteria here adapt it.
comparisons.code: // 2021 edition added only TryFrom, TryInto, FromIterator

comparisons.note: JEP 512 is a thirty-year correction: hello-world ceremony was pedagogically harmful by Oracle's own account.

recommendation.why: The criteria turn every future prelude fight into a checklist, and the five additions all pass it cleanly: high frequency, total or Result-returning, no resolution magic, and no better home.

whyNot.reason: It re-litigates five names the criteria already decide, and keeps measured first-lesson friction for no safety gain.
Case-by-case is how every studied regret happened. Unsafe or ill-chosen ambient names proved effectively permanent everywhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: Five more ambient names can collide with user variables. Accepted: the user wins with a warning, so a collision costs one message, never a bug.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft wrote the seven criteria, the two mechanics, and the additions table, recommending adoption as one slate.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a Java-25-style mode-gated beginner prelude and a user-extensible prelude. Mode gating splits what a name means by file kind, and extensibility breaks the uniform-vocabulary criterion, so both were rejected as options and recorded as comparisons.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass moved the contested entries out to D-CORE-PRELUDE2 so this slate contains only entries every criterion passes. That split is the hybrid.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: caution about ambient growth is exactly what the epoch gate exists for. But the gate governs future additions either way, so caution now buys nothing the mechanics do not already provide.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked assert in production, input on headless systems, and Clock as a variable name. Assertions compile per profile, input returns a Result like any I/O, and shadowing warns and works, so the slate survived.

decisions.title: Contested prelude entries: files and random
decisions.gist: Decide whether file reading and random numbers need zero imports.
decisions.lesson: Both candidates pass the frequency test in every measured segment, and both are effectful with a clean one-line import home, so the membership criteria pull in opposite directions. Python puts open in its builtins and owns the best first-script story. Rust left random out of its standard library entirely, and a third-party crate became near-universal.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a ten-line script that reads a word list and picks a random line for a game with his kids. With both additions the script has zero imports. Without them it starts with two use lines and works exactly the same. The question is what the first real script should look like.
decisions.inWild:
words :: read_file("words.txt")?.lines().to_list()
print(random.choice(words))

// versus with imports:
use core.[files as fs, math.random]
words :: fs.read("words.txt")?.lines().to_list()
print(random.choice(words))

options.name: Files and random both ambient
options.detail: read_file, write_file, file_exists, and a random family (random, choice, shuffle) all join the prelude. Gain: the frequency champion set is fully covered, and most first scripts need zero imports. Loss: ambient random invites seeding and reproducibility questions the prelude cannot answer, and the effectful ambient surface doubles.
options.code:
text :: read_file("data.txt")?
n :: random(1..10)
write_file("out.txt", "{n}: {text.len()}")?

options.name: File trio only
options.detail: read_file, write_file, and file_exists join the prelude. Random stays in core.math.random. Gain: the single highest-friction first-script need is covered, and the effect marker keeps the file access visible in signatures. Loss: game-flavored beginner scripts still need one import.
options.technical: read_file(path: String | Path) -> String ? IOError with =[FS]=>; write_file and file_exists likewise. They are the same functions as fs.read/fs.write/fs.exists, re-exported, not a second mechanism.
options.code:
text :: read_file("data.txt")?
write_file("out.txt", text.to_upper())?

use core.math.random as random   // one line when needed
print(random.choice(text.lines().to_list()))

options.name: Random family only
options.detail: random, choice, and shuffle join the prelude. Files stay behind use core.fs. Gain: playful beginner scripts run import-free. Loss: this inverts the measured frequency order, since file work outranks random in every segment past the first week.
options.code:
n :: random(1..6)
use core.fs as fs
text :: fs.read("data.txt")?

options.name: Neither
options.detail: Both stay behind their one-line imports. Gain: the ambient surface stays free of effectful I/O beyond printing and input. Loss: the first real script keeps two lines of ceremony, and the top measured friction question in programming history, checking whether a file exists, stays behind an import.
options.code:
use core.fs as fs
use core.math.random as random

comparisons.note: open and input are builtins; random imports. Its first-script dominance in education is the measured result.
Excluded random from std; the rand crate became one of the most downloaded artifacts in the ecosystem. Absence distorted nothing safely.
Random is in the default-imported kotlin package; file I/O needs java.io or kotlin.io paths.

recommendation.why: File reading is in the agreement set for every segment. It is also the top import-tax win. Random stays under math.random with a short alias or list entry.

whyNot.reason: Ambient random raises seeding and reproducibility policy the prelude cannot carry. Its home is one obvious line away and scopes that policy cleanly.
It covers the smaller need and skips the larger one. Frequency evidence orders files first in every segment past week one.
It preserves measured friction for the most common first script to protect a purity line that print and input already crossed.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two effectful names join the ambient set. Accepted: both carry the FS effect marker and return Results, so nothing fails invisibly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft laid out the four combinations and recommended the file trio on frequency order and friction evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered ambient JSON and an ambient http_get as further frequency champions. Both fail the no-better-home criterion harder than random does, and neither is week-one material, so the candidate set stayed at two.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested read_file ambient with write_file behind the import. Splitting a natural pair fails the naming-grammar rule and saves one name, so the trio stayed whole.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened D: an ambient surface without filesystem access is a real security-review simplification. But effect markers give reviewers the same visibility per function, which is the stronger form of the same guarantee.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked B with sandboxed and web targets where read_file cannot succeed. The function exists on every tier and returns its error like any FS call, so parity holds and B survived.

decisions.title: Adopt the Core namespace tree
decisions.gist: Pick the final map of Core modules, with consistent nesting and no short-door one-offs.
decisions.lesson: Core grew a large flat list and a few grab-bags. Nesting is fine because callers can alias, and a grouped module use can bind several modules in one line. Inventing parallel short roots like core.json beside encoding.json is worse than teaching one path.
decisions.story: Deepa builds a small tool. She imports files, http, and JSON in one list, aliases files as fs, and keeps guessing module homes because each parent answers one question.

options.name: Consistent nested tree
options.detail: Keep core.files. Nest random under math, fmt under text, and net or crypto leaves under their parents. Merge env and os into sys. Delete core.io by splitting it. Do not add core.json. Gain: one home per question and no duplicate short doors. Loss: people learn nested paths once, then alias.
options.technical: Tree in docs/proposals/corelib-overhaul.md Part B. http.get and http.post stay on the parent. Grouped module use is D-CORE-USELIST1. Deletions include core.io and core.path. Renames include science.measurement to units.
options.code:
use core.[files as fs, http, encoding.json, math.random]
print(http.get(url)?.text()?)
print(random.int(1..6))

options.name: Adopt minus named rows
options.detail: Take the tree except rows the owner lists to keep flat. Gain: smaller change. Loss: the root list stays uneven in exactly the places nesting was meant to clean up.
options.code: use core.random as random   // still a root sibling of math

options.name: Short-door exceptions
options.detail: Keep nesting for most modules, but add parallel short roots such as core.json or rename files to fs. Gain: slightly shorter use paths for a few hot modules. Loss: two spellings for the same module, which breaks the one-way rule.
options.code:
use core.json as json
use core.encoding.json as json   // both exist

options.name: Grow core.io
options.detail: Fold args and log into core.io. Gain: fewer imports for some CLIs. Loss: a larger grab-bag and denser io. prefixes on mixed jobs.
options.code:
use core.io as io
io.spec(...)
io.info("hi")

comparisons.note: Nests true siblings such as math/rand and keeps short import aliases at the call site.
Kept os.path beside pathlib. Duplicate homes are the failure this tree avoids.
Item selective import already groups with as. Module lists should follow that rename story.

recommendation.why: Consistent nesting plus aliasing and grouped use gives one home per question without parallel short doors. Grab-bag merges stay rejected.

whyNot.reason: Leaving hot leaves flat keeps the uneven root list the nesting pass exists to fix.
Short-door exceptions recreate two spellings for one module, the documented os.path failure.
Folding args and log into io rebuilds the grab-bag this overhaul removes.

recommendation.tradeoff: People learn nested paths such as encoding.json and math.random. Accepted: alias and grouped use make the call site short after that one lesson.

reviewPasses.base: Rewrote the tree ballot around consistency, keeping core.files, and dropping core.json.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Retested short-door exceptions and io merges as their own options so the owner can pick them explicitly.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested nesting everything except random. That is still a one-off, so it stayed inside B rather than a fifth choice.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened short doors with alias examples. They still create two module paths for JSON, so A wins.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked ceremony on nested hot paths. Grouped use with last-segment defaults and http parent re-exports repair the common scripts.

decisions.title: Grouped use list spelling
decisions.gist: How one use line imports several names from a module path, and how you rename them.
decisions.lesson: People often need several Core modules in one file. Stacked use lines add clutter. Jet already groups item names in braces. This choice picks one list shape for groups and keeps the as rename rule next to each name.
decisions.story: Ravi wants files, http, and JSON in one line. He wants short local names and the same as keyword he already uses on a single import.

options.name: One list with brackets
options.detail: Use square brackets for every grouped use. Write as next to a name when you want a shorter local name. If you skip as, the local name is the last part after the final dot. Also move today’s item groups from braces to the same list. Gain: one list shape and one rename rule. Loss: existing brace item imports must migrate.
options.technical: Amends S16 and D-SELIMPORT1. use path.[a as x, b] binds modules or items from path. Default local name is the last path segment. use math.[sin, cos as c] replaces use math.{sin, cos as c}. No wildcards. Greenfield: delete the brace group form in the same change.
options.code:
use core.[files as fs, http, encoding.json, math.random]
use math.[sin, cos as c]
fs.read("in.txt")?
http.get(url)?
json.parse(text)?
random.int(1..6)

options.name: Brackets for modules only
options.detail: Add module lists in brackets, but keep item groups in braces. Gain: no item-import migration. Loss: two group shapes for the same kind of job.
options.code:
use core.[files as fs, http]
use math.{sin, cos as c}

options.name: Trailing alias list
options.detail: Write the paths in one list and the local names in a second list after as. Gain: as stays after the whole group, like a single import. Loss: the two lists must match by position, and a rename sits far from its path.
options.code: use core.[files, http, encoding.json] as [fs, http, json]

options.name: Colon pairs
options.detail: Write path: name pairs inside the list. Gain: each rename sits beside its path. Loss: it looks like a record, and it drops the as keyword.
options.code: use core.[files: fs, http: http, encoding.json: json]

options.name: No grouped use sugar
options.detail: Keep one use line per module or item path. Gain: no new syntax. Loss: common scripts keep stacking use lines.
options.code:
use core.files as fs
use core.http as http
use core.encoding.json as json

comparisons.note: A single import already uses as. Item groups use braces today. Option A moves groups to the same list shape Jet uses for lists.
comparisons.code:
use core.files as fs
use math.{sin, cos as c}

comparisons.note: Rename sits next to the imported name, not in a second list.
comparisons.code: from math import sin, cos as c

comparisons.note: Grouped use also puts as beside each path.

recommendation.why: One list shape matches Jet list grammar. as stays beside the name it changes. The last-dot rule gives short names for nested paths such as encoding.json without a second spelling.

whyNot.reason: Two group shapes for the same job force people to remember braces versus brackets.
A second alias list breaks when lengths drift and moves the rename away from its path.
Colon pairs drop as and read like building a record.
It leaves the stacked use lines nested Core trees make more common.

recommendation.tradeoff: Brace item groups must migrate to brackets in one change. Accepted: greenfield rules prefer one form, and the rename rule does not change.

reviewPasses.base: Rewrote the ballot so brackets are the only group list, and explained last-dot naming in plain words.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Kept trailing alias lists and colon pairs as clear losing options. Added modules-only brackets so the owner can keep brace item groups if wanted.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested brackets for modules while also allowing braces. That is option B, not a separate hybrid.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened option B as a smaller migration. It still leaves two list shapes, so A remains the clean rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked last-dot clashes when two paths share an ending. Duplicate local names are errors that need as, which repairs that case.

decisions.title: Post-switch health proof for jet deploy
decisions.gist: What must pass after a host switch before jet deploy treats that host as healthy.
decisions.lesson: A bad switch can lock you out of a remote machine. D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1 already requires health checks and rollback on fail. This choice defines the default health bar after switch, including whether Jet must prove it can still reach the host.
decisions.story: Olive deploys a change that breaks SSH. Without a strong default check, the host stays on the bad generation and she cannot fix it from her laptop.

options.name: Control reach plus declared health
options.detail: After switch, Jet must reconnect from the controller and run the host health checks you declared. Both must pass. Experts can turn off reconnect for planned SSH or network changes on the same rollout object. Gain: lockouts roll back by default. Loss: network changes need an explicit opt-out.
options.technical: Amends D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1 health meaning. Default health gate is controller reconnect confirm within timeout AND declared host health probes. Expert field e.g. rollout.controlPlaneConfirm: false or per-host override. Failed reconnect triggers the same rollback-and-stop path. Intentional SSH/IP/port changes require the opt-out in source and appear in proof.

options.name: Declared host health only
options.detail: After switch, only the host health checks you declared must pass. Jet does not require a fresh controller reconnect. Gain: SSH and IP changes are easier. Loss: a host can pass local checks while you can no longer reach it.
options.technical: Health gate is declared probes only (services, files, scripts). No mandatory post-switch controller reconnect. Rollback still runs when declared health fails.

options.name: Reconnect only
options.detail: After switch, Jet only proves it can reconnect. Declared service health is optional. Gain: strong lockout defense with a tiny default. Loss: a reachable host can still run a broken app until you add checks.
options.technical: Default gate is controller reconnect confirm only. Declared health probes remain available but are not required for success.

options.name: Opt-in reconnect confirm
options.detail: Default is declared host health only. Reconnect confirm is an expert flag you turn on. Gain: beginners face less friction on network edits. Loss: the safe lockout defense is off until someone remembers the flag.
options.technical: Default matches option B. Experts set rollout.controlPlaneConfirm: true (or magicRollback: true) to require reconnect.

comparisons.note: Magic rollback confirms the machine is still reachable after activation. You must disable it to change SSH, IP, or port on purpose.
comparisons.code:
# deploy-rs README
# magicRollback confirms post-activation connectivity
# disable for intentional SSH/IP/port changes

comparisons.note: Generated fleet scripts treat a remote health file as enough. That is weaker than reconnect proof and is not product closeout.

recommendation.why: Lockout is the costly failure for remote deploy. Reconnect plus declared health matches the safe default people expect from deploy-rs, and keeps expert opt-out on the same rollout object.

whyNot.reason: Local health can pass while the controller cannot reach the host, so Olive stays locked out.
A reachable host can still run a broken service if app health is optional by default.
The safe lockout defense stays off until someone turns a flag on, which fails the beginner magic bar.

recommendation.tradeoff: Planned SSH or network changes need an explicit opt-out in source. Accepted: that friction is cheaper than a silent lockout, and proof shows the opt-out.

reviewPasses.base: Compared reconnect-plus-health, health-only, reconnect-only, and opt-in reconnect. Recommended reconnect plus declared health with expert opt-out.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Also tested no post-switch gate and external watchdog only. Folded those into B and D because they drop first-party lockout defense.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Kept reconnect and declared health together as option A instead of a third hybrid row. Opt-out stays on the same rollout object.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B for network edits and D for explicit control. Both still leave lockout protection off by default.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked false reconnect success on a stale bastion path. Proof must bind controller identity and target host so a wrong hop cannot clear the gate.

decisions.title: Connect identity versus activation privilege
decisions.gist: How jet deploy separates the login used to reach a host from the privilege used to activate a generation.
decisions.lesson: D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 already requires typed target and authority fields. Remote tools often log in as a normal admin user and activate as root. This choice sets the default split beginners get, and what must show in proof.
decisions.story: Kai deploys from CI to three servers. He wants SSH keys on a wheel user, not root login, and he still needs root to activate the system generation.

options.name: Split connect and activate by default
options.detail: Each target has a connect user and an activate user. The beginner default connects as a normal wheel user and activates as root. Root for both stays allowed when written. Gain: safer SSH defaults with clear proof. Loss: first setup must grant keys and passwordless privilege before the first deploy.
options.technical: Amends D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 authority fields. Typed connectUser and activateUser (names may match existing surface). Default when omitted: connectUser=wheel-class deploy user policy, activateUser=root for system profiles. User-env profiles may activate as the owning user. Proof records both identities. Preflight fails closed if keys or privilege path are missing.

options.name: One user for both roles
options.detail: One user field covers SSH and activation. Beginners use root for both. Gain: fewer fields. Loss: root SSH becomes the easy path and weaker hosts are common.
options.technical: Single user field on deploy.target. Activation uses the same account as SSH. No first-class connect/activate split in the default surface.

options.name: Forbid root SSH
options.detail: Connect user must be non-root. Activation is always root for system profiles. Gain: strong SSH policy. Loss: labs and recovery hosts that need root SSH become second-class or blocked.
options.technical: Sema rejects connectUser == root. System activation always escalate to root through a declared privilege path.

options.name: SSH config owns identity
options.detail: Jet stores only the host label. OpenSSH config picks the user. Activation privilege stays implicit. Gain: familiar for operators. Loss: Jet cannot type-check or prove the full authority graph from source.
options.technical: Conflicts with D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 proof-visible authority. Would reintroduce inventory outside Jet source.
options.code:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host web1
  User deploy

# Jet source has no connect/activate users
fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }

comparisons.note: Profiles set user for activation and sshUser for the SSH login. Docs recommend a wheel user for SSH and root for activation.
D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 already requires typed target and privilege facts in source and proof. This ballot picks the beginner default shape.
comparisons.code:
# from D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1=A
# host target/authority fields are proof-visible

recommendation.why: Split identities match real remote deploy practice and keep root SSH optional. Beginners get a safer default while experts can still write root for both.

whyNot.reason: One user field pushes beginners toward root SSH and hides the privilege boundary.
A hard ban on root SSH blocks valid lab and recovery setups that Jet should still allow explicitly.
Authority outside Jet source breaks typed proof and conflicts with D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1.

recommendation.tradeoff: First deploy needs keys and a privilege path on the host. Accepted: that setup cost is the price of a safe default, and preflight names the missing piece.

reviewPasses.base: Compared split users, one user, forbid-root SSH, and SSH-config identity. Recommended split connect and activate with wheel-plus-root defaults.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Also tested sudo-only without typed activate user and agent-forwarding only. Folded those into A and D as incomplete authority graphs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Kept optional root-for-both inside A instead of a separate hybrid row, so one mechanism covers beginner and expert.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B for tiny fleets and C for hard policy shops. B still weakens SSH defaults; C over-blocks recovery hosts.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked missing NOPASSWD or key setup as silent hangs. Preflight must fail closed with a clear diagnostic before switch.

decisions.title: JetOS install trust without App Store gatekeeping
decisions.gist: How jetos stops malware while still letting people install and run software they choose or build.
decisions.lesson: Apple treats central review and signing locks as security. Those locks also block owner-built apps, peer share, plugins, and fast local tools. jetos already has generations, Flatpak policy, hangar hashes, and Studio risk gates. This choice sets the default trust law for installs. It must protect beginners and keep owner freedom. The same law covers any future jetos device class unless a later ballot changes it.
decisions.story: Maya builds a small drawing app on her jetos laptop and wants her friend to try it tonight. She also wants her parents' laptop to resist random malware from a download. She needs one system that allows her share and still protects the family machine.
decisions.inWild:
# Maya shares a local package with a friend (must work without Jet review):
$ jet pack ./doodle
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
# friend sees capability prompt, not a rejection

# Studio Apps install from catalog:
# Install "Music Player" -> sandboxed; Photos access needs an explicit grant

# After a bad install:
$ jet os generations rollback
# previous generation returns; provenance still names the package

options.name: Capability-first freedom
options.detail: Anyone may install software they choose or build. Third-party and foreign apps start with almost no power. The user grants files, network, devices, or agents later. Hangar hashes and optional publisher signatures feed trust UI. They never block an owner-built local install. Generations and rollback repair bad installs. There is no central review and no category ban.
options.technical: Default runtime policy for user apps and Flatpak refs is deny-by-default capabilities with explicit grants in Studio or Jet config. System hangar closures keep supply-chain integrity (hash, sign/verify, locks). Owner-local packages and jet run paths skip notarization. Catalog ranking may prefer signed publishers; ranking is not a hard gate. Family or enterprise lock modules may tighten policy as expert opt-in.
options.code:
# config.jet — beginner default stays free to install, tight to run
apps.flatpak.permissions.default: .Deny

# friend installs Maya's package
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
grant needed: Documents (read)
# after grant, app runs; no Jet notary step

options.name: Notarization gate
options.detail: Only packages signed by Jet-approved keys or a central notary may run. Unsigned code is blocked unless a hard developer mode is on. That blocks many casual malware installs. Owner-built and peer-shared software become second-class. This repeats the App Store shape jetos is trying not to copy.
options.technical: Hard gate at activation: signature required against a Jet trust root. Local unsigned installs fail closed outside developer mode. Catalog and peer share both hit the same gate.
options.code:
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
error: package is not notarized by Jet
hint: enable developer mode, or submit for review

options.name: Warn-only open install
options.detail: People may install and run anything with full host power. Unknown publishers only show warnings. Maximum freedom and simple plumbing. One hostile package can own the machine. Beginners get alerts instead of real limits.
options.technical: No default capability jail for GUI apps. Trust UI is advisory. Generations still roll back if the user notices damage in time.
options.code:
$ jet install ./free-game.jetpkg
warning: unknown publisher
# proceeds with full user powers

options.name: Curated beginners, free experts
options.detail: The default profile installs only from a curated catalog under sandbox rules. An expert profile unlocks free install. Safer default story. It teaches that real power lives in another mode. Beginners may never learn grants. The catalog risks becoming a soft App Store.
options.technical: Two named profiles in config. Beginner profile rejects non-catalog refs. Expert profile matches option A or C. Mode switch is explicit.
options.code:
profile: .Beginner
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
error: beginner profile allows catalog apps only
hint: switch profile to .Expert

options.name: Disposable VM per app
options.detail: Every GUI app runs in a disposable microVM with gated portals. Strong isolation for hostile binaries. High cost in battery, memory, and desktop fit. Terminal tools and light apps pay a heavy tax. Portal grants are still required, so this does not replace a capability model.
options.technical: App launch always goes through a microVM or equivalent strong boundary. Portals mediate files and devices. Native hangar system services stay outside this path.
options.code:
$ jet install music-player
# launches inside app-vm; Documents access via portal prompt

comparisons.note: Central review and signing locks block whole categories. Security and rent seeking stay hard to separate.
comparisons.code: # no peer install path without Apple approval

comparisons.note: Apps can ship widely. Permissions start tight. Users grant more later. Closest open model to option A.
Hardened Android with stronger sandbox defaults and user control. Still a phone OS with store pressure around it.
comparisons.code: # install unknown apps allowed; sandbox remains

comparisons.note: Bad system changes roll back. Provenance and immutability help recovery. They do not replace app capability grants.

recommendation.why: Capability-first freedom matches jetos goals. Beginners get real limits by default. Owners can build and share without Jet review. Hangar identity, Studio risk gates, and generations already cover supply chain and recovery. The store stays a discovery surface, not a notary.

whyNot.reason: A notarization gate recreates App Store lock-in and blocks the kid-builds-and-shares story.
Warnings without capability limits leave beginners open to full-host malware.
A beginner-only catalog becomes a soft store and hides grants behind an expert mode.
Always-on microVMs add heavy cost and still need the same grant model for portals.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users can approve too many grants. Studio risk classes and clear prompts must keep that rare. Expert family locks can tighten later without changing the default.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared capability defaults, notarization, warn-only installs, split beginner profiles, and per-app VMs. It recommended capability-first freedom.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested mandatory antivirus scanning and web-of-trust-only installs. Those folded into identity signals and expert policy under option A, not separate defaults.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and added catalog ranking by signatures, generation rollback, and optional family locks. Those stay helpers, not hard gates.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened notarization with fast local developer mode and strengthened curated beginners with one-click expert escape. Each still blocks or hides owner freedom.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested peer-share malware, users who grant everything, and signed-but-hostile publishers. Sandbox defaults, rollback, provenance, and honest trust UI repair those cases, so option A remains.

decisions.title: Primary dirty units for Jet incremental builds
decisions.gist: Which units Jet marks dirty so an edit does not force a full rebuild.
decisions.lesson: Swift and Xcode often rebuild far more than the edit needs. Progressive caches fail, so teams treat clean builds as ritual. Jet already plans query caches, module checks, and sealed package objects. This choice locks how those layers share dirty work. It must match C++-style small units without a second build system.
decisions.story: Priya changes one helper inside module util.math. She wants Jet to recheck that module and its dependents only. She does not want the whole app or every package to rebuild. She also wants a warm second build to restore sealed package objects when nothing in them changed.
decisions.inWild:
# edit only util.math
$ jet build --timings
# expect: util.math dirty; dependents rechecked; unrelated packages restored from cache

$ jet build --timings   # no edits
# expect: no world recheck; sealed objects hit cache

options.name: Three-layer dirty model
options.detail: Editor and warm check reuse item and file queries. Batch builds dirty a Jet module when its interface fingerprint changes, and recheck dependents only. Link and distribute sealed package objects under the ratified library reuse law. Small edits stay small. Package cache stays honest.
options.technical: Layer 1: jet-queries + IncrementalSemaCache item reuse (D-LSP1 path, promoted to batch by #1026). Layer 2: module interface fingerprint invalidates importers only. Layer 3: D-LIB-REUSE1=B sealed package artifacts for compile/link restore. No path skips sema or diagnostics on a cache hit that still needs checking.
options.code:
# util.math changes a private fn body → item/module local recheck
# util.math changes a pub signature → dependents recheck
# unrelated pkg.ui → sealed object cache hit

options.name: Package-only dirty units
options.detail: Any file change dirties the whole package artifact. Simple mental model. Small modules inside a large package still pay a full package tax. Fine editor reuse may still exist, but batch builds stay coarse.
options.technical: Invalidation key is package source digest only. Module fingerprints are not used for batch dirty sets.
options.code: # one-line edit in util.math rebuilds all of package util

options.name: File-only dirty units
options.detail: Dirtiness is per source file with no module interface layer. Easy to implement. Cross-file modules and generic APIs still force broad conservative rechecks. It underuses Jet modules as units.
options.technical: Query keys stay file-scoped. No module interface fingerprint. Package sealed objects may still cache link outputs.
options.code: # changing math.jet always rechecks every file that imported any symbol from it

options.name: Whole-program always
options.detail: Every build rechecks the full program. Maximum simplicity and no cache bugs. Large projects become Swift-like multi-minute no-change builds. Rejects the video lesson.
options.technical: No batch incremental sema. Caches may still store final binaries only.
options.code: $ jet build   # always full check, even with zero edits

comparisons.note: Translation units and interfaces limit rebuild fan-out when headers stay stable.
comparisons.code: # change .cpp → rebuild one object; stable .h → dependents stay

comparisons.note: Crate-level artifacts with fingerprint invalidation; fine queries inside rustc.
Module planning and weak incrementality often rebuild too much; clean becomes ritual.

recommendation.why: Three layers match Jet's existing law: queries for warm work, modules for batch dirty sets, sealed packages for link restore. Priya's one-module edit stays bounded. It is the C++-style split without a second build tool.

whyNot.reason: Package-only dirty sets punish large packages for a one-module edit.
File-only dirty sets ignore Jet modules as the natural interface boundary.
Whole-program always recreates the Xcode no-change multi-minute failure mode.

recommendation.tradeoff: Module interface fingerprints must be exact. A wrong fingerprint either trusts stale code or over-invalidates. Hostile tests on #1023 own that risk.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared three-layer dirty sets, package-only, file-only, and whole-program builds. It recommended three layers.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested function-only dirty sets as a fifth default. That stays an internal query optimization under layer 1, not a separate owner default.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept three layers and required sealed package hits to still honor sema when interfaces change. No merge created a fourth product mode.
