reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened package-only with internal file tips and file-only with import graphs. Each still misses module-scale batch dirty sets.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested wrong interface fingerprints and cache hits that skip diagnostics. Hostile corpus rules on #1023 repair those, so three layers remain.

decisions.title: How Jet fails when type checking gets too hard
decisions.gist: What Jet does when a type check would take too long or get too complex.
decisions.lesson: Swift sometimes says it cannot type check an expression in reasonable time. The span is often too wide. People then reshape working code to please the compiler. Jet diagnostics are a product. The checker must stay honest and local. This choice sets the bound and the failure shape.
decisions.story: Omar writes a nested UI builder that type-checks on a small sample and hangs on a real screen. He needs a clear error at the real problem site. He must not be told to rewrite style because the compiler gave up.
decisions.inWild:
# pathological nested builder
ui.column:
  ui.row: ... # deep inference

# required outcome under the winner:
error[E????]: type check hit its bound near this call
  --> app.jet:84:12
   |
84 |   ui.row: ...
   |            ^
 Why: this expression exceeded the type-check bound
 Fix: split the expression or add a type annotation here

options.name: Bound plus pinpoint diagnostic
options.detail: Type checking has an explicit bound. When the bound hits, Jet emits a normal diagnostic at the best local span. The message never says the compiler merely gave up on the whole program. Users annotate or split at that site. Refactoring only to soothe the checker is treated as a Jet defect to fix.
options.technical: Sema carries a type-check bound (steps or recursion depth) separate from comptime interpreter fuel. Diagnostics use a registered code with What/Why/Fix and a UI snapshot (I4). No approximate types. I3 stays: codegen never invents unchecked meaning.
options.code:
error[E????]: type check hit its bound near this call
 Fix: add a type annotation or split this expression

options.name: Unbounded complete checking
options.detail: The checker always runs to a full answer or an ordinary type error. No complexity bound. Some programs may hang the compiler. Matches classic batch compilers. Fails Omar's hang case.
options.technical: No type-check fuel. Process-level timeouts stay outside sema.
options.code: $ jet check app.jet   # may not return

options.name: Timeout with guessed types
options.detail: On timeout, Jet invents approximate types and continues. Builds feel fast. Wrong programs may pass. Breaks sema-as-gatekeeper.
options.technical: Would violate I3. Listed to reject clearly.
options.code:
# warning: approximated types after timeout
$ jet build   # may ship wrong code

options.name: Ban deep type-level builders
options.detail: Jet forbids language features that create SwiftUI-like checker explosions. Strong prevention. Also blocks useful nested DSLs that stay within a bound. A bound with pinpoint errors already covers the failure mode.
options.technical: Syntax or sema rejects nested builder depth above a fixed limit even when checking is cheap.
options.code: error: nested builder depth 8 is not allowed

comparisons.note: Unable to type check this expression in reasonable time often points at a wide span.
comparisons.code: error: unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time

comparisons.note: Mostly completes or gives a normal error; pathological cases still exist but culture rejects compiler-soothing refactors as the product.
comparisons.code: error[E0277]: the trait bound is not satisfied

comparisons.note: Instantiation depth and complexity limits emit local diagnostics.
comparisons.code: error TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep

recommendation.why: A bound with a pinpoint diagnostic keeps sema honest and local. Omar sees where to annotate. Jet never ships guessed types. Useful nested DSLs still work when they stay within the bound.

whyNot.reason: Unbounded checking allows compiler hangs on real UI code.
Guessed types after timeout break sema as the only gatekeeper.
A hard ban on deep builders blocks healthy DSLs that a bound already keeps safe.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bounds need tuning on a corpus. Too tight annoys experts. Too loose still feels like a hang. #1023 owns measurement after ratification.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared bound-plus-pinpoint, unbounded checking, guessed types, and a hard builder ban. It recommended bound-plus-pinpoint.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested process kill-only timeouts and always-require-annotations modes. Those folded into ops policy and local annotation fixes under option A.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and allowed shallow DSL nesting inside the bound. No guessed types were added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened unbounded checking with external watchdog scripts and strengthened the builder ban with allow-lists. Each still hangs or over-blocks.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested wide spans and silent approximates. Option A requires a registered local diagnostic and forbids approximates, so it remains.

decisions.title: Adopt the carrier plus knowledge foundation
decisions.gist: Whether the type checker gets one shared foundation for every compile-time fact.
decisions.lesson: Jet proves facts about values in about ten separate ways: ranges, units, lengths, shapes, lanes, states, tags, effects, exactness, and function obligations. Each way has its own code, its own errors, and its own gaps. The proposal makes them one mechanism. A type becomes a runtime carrier plus registered knowledge, and the checker folds knowledge through the program with one engine. This choice sets the foundation for the rest of the slate.
decisions.story: Rowan spends a week in the checker fixing a units bug. The unit's dimension is stored as text inside a hidden type name, so the fix is string surgery. The same week Rowan finds that two function types each equal a third type but not each other. Every fix lands in a different private mechanism, and no fix helps the next one.
decisions.inWild:
#UnitFamily(Time) { ms, s }
a :: 500ms                  // distinct Float, minted by the unit plane
task.timeout(500ms)         // same spelling, hidden nanosecond table

Severity :: distinct Int(0..10)                        // range machinery one
#Invariant("value >= 0 && value < 4")
Index4 :: distinct Int                                 // range machinery two

buf: [U8#4]                 // compile-time number, third private encoding
m: Matrix<3, 4>             // compile-time number, fourth private encoding

options.name: One foundation: carrier plus knowledge
options.detail: Every compile-time fact joins one substrate with one registry. Ranges, units, lengths, states, and obligations share registration, checking, and reflection. Type equality becomes transitive again. Shipped programs keep their exact behavior; this changes how the compiler holds what it already knows.
options.technical: Type carries a knowledge vector. Identity is carrier plus identity-bearing facts, declared per plane. Obligations compare by subsumption, which restores transitive equality. All knowledge erases before the typed IR, so codegen and every execution tier are untouched.
options.code:
info :: Severity.reflect()
print(info.facts)          // range 0..10

speed :: Meter.reflect()
print(speed.dimensions)    // Length^1  (a real value, not a hidden string)

options.name: Targeted defect fixes, no shared foundation
options.detail: Fix the known defects one by one: make function-type equality transitive, store dimensions as structured data, and merge the two range spellings. The ten mechanisms stay separate. Each future feature, such as matrix shapes or uncertainty, adds its own new machinery.
options.technical: Hand-edit the equality rules in the type comparison, replace the dimension string with a struct field, and keep every per-feature check where it lives today.
options.code:
// same programs, same fixes, ten private mechanisms remain
m: Matrix<3, 4>            // matrix work still invents encoding number five

options.name: Fix equality now, decide the foundation later
options.detail: Repair the one live soundness defect, the non-transitive function-type equality, and defer the foundation question until after the current epoch. The number-slate work that is already ratified gets built on today's machinery in the meantime.
options.technical: One patch to the type comparison. Everything else waits.
options.code:
// bigint Int, Complex, and Ordering land on the old machinery,
// then move again if a foundation is adopted later

comparisons.note: Units of measure are a special compiler feature. They never generalized to other fact kinds, so ranges and states needed unrelated tools.
Const generics, typestate patterns, and newtype units grew separately. Each is its own feature with its own limits, which is the fragmentation this ballot removes.
comparisons.code:
struct Meters(f64);
fn get<const N: usize>(a: [u8; N]) {}

recommendation.why: One substrate turns ten mechanisms into one, so every plane gains the same checking, naming, and reflection. The eleven ratified but unbuilt number decisions then land once, on the final foundation.

whyNot.reason: The fixes repair symptoms and keep the fragmentation, so shapes and uncertainty would become mechanisms eleven and twelve.
The number slate is unbuilt right now, so deferring means building it twice: once on old machinery and once after the foundation arrives.

recommendation.tradeoff: The checker's core becomes one larger shared piece instead of ten small private ones. A defect in the shared engine reaches every plane, so the engine needs the strongest test coverage in sema.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one shared foundation against per-feature fixes and recommended the foundation, because ten private mechanisms keep producing the same class of defect.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested two more shapes: adopting the foundation for new planes only, and moving facts into a separate tool outside the checker. Both split the model in two, so they were folded into option B.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether option C's quick equality fix belongs inside option A. It does: adopting A starts with that exact repair, so no separate hybrid option is needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose targeted fixes are smaller reviews that touch nothing working, and C, whose one soundness patch is the minimal honest move. Both stand as real choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's blast radius, since one shared engine can break every plane at once. The phased shape repairs this because phase one changes no surface and must keep every test green.

decisions.title: The number tower: one grid, and BigInt folds into Int
decisions.gist: How Jet's number types relate to each other, and whether BigInt survives as a separate name.
decisions.lesson: Jet ships Int, Float, F32, the sized widths, BigInt, Decimal, and Fraction, with Complex ratified and coming. Each pair has hand-written conversion rules. A ratified decision already makes the default Int arbitrary precision, which is exactly what BigInt was for. The proposal arranges every number type on one grid with two axes: which mathematical world the value lives in, and how well the bits know the value. Conversion rules then follow from the grid instead of a table.
decisions.story: Priya teaches a first programming class with Jet. A student asks why 300 does not fit in a U8 but fits in an Int, and why BigInt exists at all when Int never overflows. Priya wants one answer that covers all three questions, not three separate rules to memorize.
decisions.inWild:
n :: factorial(25)        // 15511210043330985984000000, exact
sensor: U8 = 300          // error: 300 is outside 0..255
big :: BigInt(2) ^ 200    // why does this type still exist?
half :: 7 / 2             // 3.5, a Float
third :: Fraction(1, 3)   // exactly one third

options.name: Adopt the grid; retire BigInt into Int
options.detail: Every number type becomes one cell of the grid. A sized width like U8 becomes Int plus a proven range and a one-byte layout; its spelling and behavior do not change. BigInt retires, because the arbitrary-precision Int already holds every value it held. The four errors that police mixing Int with BigInt retire with it.
options.technical: Axis one is the value world: whole, ratio, real, complex. Axis two is the knowledge grade: exact unbounded, exact bounded, approximate, measured. The ratified widening law, value-set containment, becomes the theorem that a subset needs no conversion. One interval prover replaces the width table, the range-type checks, and the fixed-list index proof.
options.code:
n :: 2 ^ 200              // exact Int, no BigInt call
sensor: U8 = reading      // checked exactly like distinct Int(0..255)
price :: Decimal("19.99") // stays: base-10 exactness is real knowledge

options.name: Adopt the grid; keep BigInt as an opt-in name
options.detail: The grid is adopted, sized widths become range facts, but BigInt stays as an explicit type for people who want heap-backed numbers spelled out. Int and BigInt hold the same values and still refuse to mix without conversion.
options.technical: Same grid, plus one duplicate cell: two exact unbounded whole-number types with a conversion pair between them.
options.code:
a :: 2 ^ 200              // Int, exact
b :: BigInt(2) ^ 200      // same value, different type
c :: a + b                // still an error without a conversion

options.name: Keep the flat menu
options.detail: No grid. The arbitrary-precision Int is built as its own feature, BigInt stays, and every conversion pair keeps its hand-written rule. Each future numeric type extends the table by hand.
options.technical: The widening function and range table stay as written today, and Complex joins them with new hand-written arms.
options.code: // behavior today, plus bigint Int bolted on beside BigInt

comparisons.note: One int with arbitrary precision and no separate big-integer type. Beginners never meet overflow, which is the model the ratified Int decision already chose.
The numeric tower tracks exactness through arithmetic. Exact stays exact until an inexact value enters, which is the second axis of the grid.

recommendation.why: The grid gives one answer to every conversion question, and it explains the whole ratified operator slate as consequences of one model. Retiring BigInt removes a duplicate mechanism the bigint Int decision already made redundant.

whyNot.reason: Two names for the same values split every library signature in two and keep four dead mixing errors alive.
The hand-written table grows with every new type, and the same subset rule keeps being rediscovered one arm at a time.

recommendation.tradeoff: Any code that names BigInt migrates to Int in one repository-wide sweep. Greenfield law allows it, and the sweep deletes code rather than adding it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the grid against the flat menu and recommended the grid, because the ratified widening law is already subset reasoning in disguise.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a single unified Number type covering every world. The number-type ballot already rejected that shape for hiding two operator rule sets behind one name, so it was not added.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option B, the grid with BigInt kept. It is a real coherent design, so it stays on the menu rather than folding away.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with the audit-trail argument that an explicit BigInt marks where heap numbers may appear, and strengthened C because hand-written arms are locally readable. Both remain honest choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether U8 as a range fact keeps byte layout in lists and at FFI boundaries. It does, because layout is a separate fact from range, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One spelling for value-range rules
decisions.gist: How a checked value range is written on a distinct type.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two spellings for the same rule. A range in parentheses, distinct Int(0..10), and a rule inside a text string, #Invariant with a quoted comparison. The checker's prover only understands straight-line whole-number bounds, and every such bound is an interval. So the string form adds a hand-rolled string parser but no checking power. One shipped example uses both forms in sixteen lines.
decisions.story: Sam writes a board game and wants a die type that only holds 1 through 6. The docs show two ways to say it, one in parentheses and one in a quoted string. Sam cannot tell which one the compiler really checks, so Sam writes both on the same type to be safe.
decisions.inWild:
Die :: distinct Int(1..6)

#Invariant("value >= 1 && value <= 6")
Die2 :: distinct Int

// both mint a checked whole-number type; only the spelling differs

options.name: Range form only
options.detail: distinct Int(1..6) becomes the one spelling. The #Invariant marker retires, and the index prover reads range facts directly. The same range facts describe the sized widths, so U8 and Die fail with the same error shape.
options.technical: The range becomes an interval fact on the plane registry. The prover for fixed-list indexing consumes interval facts instead of parsed strings. The marker row retires under law zero with a replacement note.
options.code:
Die :: distinct Int(1..6)
roll: Die = 7        // error: 7 is outside 1..6
faces: [String#6]
name :: faces[roll.raw() - 1]   // proven in bounds, no runtime check

options.name: Keep both spellings
options.detail: The range form and the string form both stay. Programs keep compiling unchanged, and the two mechanisms keep their separate parsers and error paths.
options.technical: No change. The string parser and the range checker remain side by side.
options.code:
Die :: distinct Int(1..6)
#Invariant("value >= 1 && value <= 6")
Die2 :: distinct Int    // still legal, still a second mechanism

options.name: Predicate form becomes the one spelling
options.detail: A real expression replaces both forms: distinct Int(value >= 1 && value <= 6). It reads like code instead of a string, and the range form becomes shorthand for it. The danger is a promise the checker cannot keep, because today it proves intervals only.
options.technical: The parser accepts a boolean expression over value. The checker accepts only expressions it can reduce to an interval and rejects the rest, so the surface allows more than the prover delivers.
options.code:
Die :: distinct Int(value >= 1 && value <= 6)
Even :: distinct Int(value % 2 == 0)   // error today: not an interval

comparisons.note: Range types are first-class and forty years old. The range is part of the type, not an annotation beside it.

recommendation.why: The range form says exactly what the checker proves, no more and no less. Retiring the string form deletes a parser, a second error path, and a duplicate mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Two spellings of one rule is the exact defect the one-mechanism invariant exists to prevent.
A predicate spelling promises checking the prover cannot deliver, so most predicates would be errors and the form would teach distrust.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rules beyond a single interval, such as evenness, get no spelling for now. When a stronger prover exists, a fresh ballot can widen the surface honestly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the three spellings and recommended the range form, because the prover is interval-only and the string form adds only a parser.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review looked for rules the string form can express and the range form cannot. Within what the prover accepts there are none, so no new option was added.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested range-now, predicate-later as one option. That is option A plus a future ballot rather than a third design, so it folded into A's tradeoff line.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C, since a predicate surface is the honest long-term shape if the prover grows, and B, which needs zero migration. Both remain real choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the multi-clause invariants from the shipped example. Every one reduces to a single interval, so nothing expressible is lost and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Time joins the unit plane
decisions.gist: Whether durations and instants become ordinary unit-plane quantities with one literal system.
decisions.lesson: The spelling 500ms means three different things today. In user code it mints a distinct Float through a unit family. Inside a timeout call it is a nanosecond count from a hidden table. Inside a schedule marker it is a nanosecond count from a second hidden table. The real Duration type is a fourth thing, reachable only through core.time calls. A ratified decision already moves Duration to a nanosecond count, the same resolution the hidden tables use.
decisions.story: Noor sets a timeout with 500ms and it works. On the next line she writes the same 500ms into a binding, gets a different type, and the sleep function refuses it. The same spelling changed meaning between two adjacent lines, and nothing in the code explains why.
decisions.inWild:
task.timeout(500ms)          // hidden nanosecond table, works
wait :: 500ms                // distinct Float, if a Time family is in scope
sleep(wait)                  // error: sleep wants a Duration
d :: time.milliseconds(500)  // the only path to a real Duration

options.name: Duration and Instant become Time quantities
options.detail: Duration becomes the delta quantity of a canonical Time unit family, stored as a 64-bit nanosecond count per the ratified resolution decision. Instant becomes the matching point quantity. Every 500ms resolves through the one unit plane, in user code, timeouts, and schedules alike. Both hidden suffix tables are deleted.
options.technical: The Time family is the one unit family with a fixed integer carrier, per the ratified nanosecond decision. Point and delta reuse the affine machinery temperatures already use. Timeout and schedule sites accept the Time delta type instead of reading raw suffix tables.
options.code:
wait :: 500ms               // a Time delta, everywhere
task.timeout(wait)          // same value, same type
sleep(500ms)                // works: one meaning
later :: now() + 5min       // point plus delta gives a point
speed :: 12meter / 2s       // time finally joins unit algebra

options.name: Keep Duration separate; route the literals to it
options.detail: Duration stays its own core type outside the unit plane. Unit literals like 500ms build a Duration when a Duration is expected, so the two hidden tables die and the adjacent-lines trap closes. Time still cannot participate in unit algebra, so meters divided by seconds stays impossible.
options.technical: The literal path gains a Duration destination rule. The unit plane and the Time family remain unrelated to Duration.
options.code:
wait :: 500ms               // Duration when one is expected
speed :: 12meter / 2s       // still an error: Duration has no dimension

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Keep all three systems and the constructor-only Duration. The nanosecond resolution decision is implemented inside the existing type, and the spelling keeps meaning different things by position.
options.technical: No change beyond the ratified resolution work.
options.code:
task.timeout(500ms)   // table one
#Every(5min)          // table two
wait :: 500ms         // unit family, incompatible with both

comparisons.note: Time units participate in ordinary unit algebra, so speed is meters over seconds with no special time type.

recommendation.why: One meaning for one spelling, everywhere, and time joins the algebra that already handles every other physical dimension. Three parallel systems become zero special cases, which a prior audit already flagged as owed.

whyNot.reason: It closes the literal trap but leaves time outside unit algebra, so speed, frequency, and rates stay hand-rolled.
Three systems for one concept, and the same spelling keeps changing meaning between adjacent lines.

recommendation.tradeoff: The Time family becomes the one unit family with a fixed integer carrier, a privilege other families do not get. That asymmetry is real and must be documented plainly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full unification against the literal-only repair and recommended full unification, because the resolution decision already moved Duration onto the tables' own unit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested retiring Duration entirely in favor of a plain nanosecond Int. That loses the point and delta distinction instants need, so it was folded into option A's design notes.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option B, unifying literals while keeping the type separate. It is a coherent stopping point, so it stays on the menu.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: the hidden tables are small, frozen, and fast to read. It strengthened B as the smallest change that closes the user-facing trap.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's fixed carrier, because unit conversions on an integer carrier must stay exact. Nanosecond scales for every shipped time unit are exact integers, so the law holds and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One home for compile-time numbers in types
decisions.gist: Whether list lengths, matrix shapes, vector lanes, and dimension exponents share one substrate.
decisions.lesson: A compile-time number inside a type is written four ways in the compiler today. Fixed-list lengths are a numeric field with a placeholder zero for symbols. Vector and matrix sizes are numbers hidden inside a generated type name. Lane counts are a match on the type's name string. Dimension exponents are a separate map. None of these can see the others, and the coming matrix surface would add a fifth. The proposal gives them one substrate called a measure, with each use declaring how its numbers combine.
decisions.story: Kai picks up the matrix design card. Multiplying a 3 by 4 matrix with a 4 by 2 matrix must answer a 3 by 2 at compile time, and a mismatch must be a clear error. The compiler already tracks list lengths and vector sizes, but each lives in a private encoding Kai cannot reuse, so the card starts by inventing encoding number five.
decisions.inWild:
a: [Float#3]              // length, private encoding one
m: Matrix<3, 4>           // shape, private encoding two
v: F32x4                  // lanes, private encoding three
speed :: 12meter / 2s     // exponents Length^1 Time^-1, encoding four

options.name: One measure substrate
options.detail: Lengths, shapes, lanes, and exponents become measures: compile-time numbers attached to types through the plane registry. Each use declares its combination rules. Joining two lists adds lengths. Matrix multiply matches inner sides and composes outer sides. Multiplying quantities adds exponents. Surfaces do not change; the encodings underneath become one.
options.technical: Measures are declared literals or module value parameters, never computed by user code, so the ratified wall that compile-time evaluation cannot create types stands. Symbolic lengths from generic modules resolve at specialization exactly as today, without the placeholder-zero sentinel. This amends the stored encoding that D-COMPUTE-TYPE1 chose for vector and matrix sizes while preserving its semantics unchanged.
options.code:
fn join<T>(a: [T#N], b: [T#M]) => [T#(N + M)]   // declared rule: add
c :: Matrix<3, 4> * Matrix<4, 2>                // shape 3 by 2, checked
bad :: Matrix<3, 4> * Matrix<5, 2>              // error: inner sides 4 and 5 differ

options.name: Unify lengths and shapes only
options.detail: Fixed-list lengths and matrix shapes merge, which unblocks the matrix card. Lane counts stay a name match and dimension exponents stay a separate map, so reflection over those stays partial and the two old encodings remain.
options.technical: One shared length-and-shape representation. Lanes and exponents untouched.
options.code:
c :: Matrix<3, 4> * Matrix<4, 2>   // checked
v: F32x4                           // still a string match inside sema

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Keep all four encodings and let the matrix card add its own fifth. Every future shaped type repeats the choice.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: // four private encodings today, five after the matrix card

comparisons.note: Const generics give one substrate for numbers in types. Arrays, SIMD lanes, and matrix crates all use it rather than private encodings.
comparisons.code: fn join<const N: usize, const M: usize>(...) -> [T; N + M]

recommendation.why: One substrate deletes four encodings, hands the matrix card its foundation, and makes every measure reflectable through the same registry as every other fact.

whyNot.reason: It leaves lanes and exponents as string encodings, so reflection stays partial and the cleanup returns as a future card.
The fifth encoding is already scheduled: the matrix card cannot proceed without shape checking somewhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: Measure rules like adding lengths live in the compiler's plane declarations, not in user code. Users who want richer compile-time arithmetic over measures do not get it, and that wall is deliberate.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one substrate against the status quo and recommended the substrate, because the matrix card makes a fifth private encoding otherwise inevitable.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested full user-facing compile-time arithmetic over measures, the const-generics shape. It reopens a wall ratified as rejected for v1, so it was recorded as out of scope rather than added.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option B, the minimal merge that unblocks matrices. It is a genuine stopping point, so it stays on the menu.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B and C: each encoding today is small, local, and fast to read on its own. The cost is only visible across features, which is where the audit found it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the symbolic-length case, where a module parameter length must not regress equality checking. The substrate keeps symbol identity until specialization, matching today's behavior without the sentinel, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The conservation law for precision
decisions.gist: Whether one written law governs every step that loses precision, and how such steps are spelled.
decisions.lesson: Jet already refuses silent precision loss in two places with two vocabularies. Crossing a number to a smaller floating type requires the word approx. Converting a unit inexactly requires a rounded conversion method with an explicit mode. The rule behind both is the same and nowhere written down: knowledge about a value never disappears silently. Ratifying the law makes every future surface follow it by obligation instead of by accident.
decisions.story: Elena tunes a sensor pipeline. She converts a reading to a 32-bit float with approx, then converts kelvin to celsius with a rounded conversion naming its rounding mode. Both lines drop digits. She asks why the language has two unrelated words for the same event, and whether the next feature will add a third.
decisions.inWild:
r: F32 = approx(reading)   // spelled precision loss, numbers
c :: Celsius.from_kelvin_rounded(k, .NearestEven, digits: 1)   // spelled loss, units
total :: price * 3         // Decimal: exact, no spelling needed

options.name: Ratify the law; keep both spellings
options.detail: The law enters the spec: knowledge grows silently, is lost only at a spelled step, and erases at runtime. The two existing spellings stay, because each names its own operation well. Approx marks accepting a representation's precision; rounded conversions name a mode because rounding direction matters there.
options.technical: The law binds every future surface: any operation that discards range, exactness, unit, state, or classification must require a spelled step, checked in sema. Existing spellings are grandfathered as the law's two instances.

options.name: Ratify the law; merge to one vocabulary
options.detail: The law enters the spec and the two spellings become one destination-owned family. Approx retires, and precision-losing widenings use rounded conversion methods with a default mode. Every lossy step then reads the same way at every call site.
options.technical: The float crossing becomes a destination-owned rounded conversion with a nearest-even default. The approx marker and its rewrite retire.
options.code:
r :: F32.from_float_rounded(reading, .NearestEven)
c :: Celsius.from_kelvin_rounded(k, .NearestEven, digits: 1)

options.name: No law; keep case-by-case rules
options.detail: Each surface keeps deciding its own precision story. The two existing rules stay as local decisions, and future surfaces choose freely, including choosing silence.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: // today's behavior; the next surface may round silently

recommendation.why: The law is the valuable part: it turns two good local decisions into a promise every future surface must keep. The two spellings each carry real information, so merging them buys uniformity and costs clarity.

whyNot.reason: The merged form makes the common float crossing wordier and pushes a rounding mode where intent, not direction, is the point.
Without the law, the third vocabulary arrives with the next lossy surface, and silence stays a legal choice.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two words remain for one class of event. The spec must teach that the law, not the word, carries the rule.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared law-plus-both-spellings against a full merge and recommended keeping both, because each spelling names a genuinely different operation.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested extending the law to a compiler flag that forbids all lossy steps per package. That is a policy key, not a law question, so it was recorded for the policy plane instead of added here.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested one word with an optional mode argument. It collapses into option B with a default, so it folded there.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, where one vocabulary is one lesson with audit value, and C, where local rules let each surface fit its domain exactly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's grandfathering, since two spellings could drift into three by precedent. The law's wording closes this by requiring new surfaces to reuse an existing spelled form or ballot a new one.

decisions.title: Uncertainty as a knowledge grade
decisions.gist: Whether measured values carry their uncertainty through arithmetic automatically.
decisions.lesson: Jet already stores uncertainty in two disconnected places. Unit scales can be declared as measured constants with a stated uncertainty and source. The science library pairs a value with an uncertainty as a plain type. Neither propagates: multiplying two measured values today forgets the error bars unless the programmer combines them by hand. An earlier ballot on tracked uncertainty was deferred. The carrier-plus-knowledge foundation makes it a natural grade of numeric knowledge instead of a whole feature.
decisions.story: Dr. Okafor models a rocket burn. Every constant carries error bars from the standards body, and the report needs a confidence interval on the burn time. Today she propagates sigma by hand on paper beside the code. One missed square root and the published interval is wrong.
decisions.inWild:
g :: measurement(9.80665, uncertainty: 0.00001)
m :: measurement(12.0, uncertainty: 0.1)
f :: m * g        // the error bars must combine; today you do it by hand

options.name: Opt-in measured grade with propagation
options.detail: Measurement becomes the measured grade of numeric knowledge. Arithmetic and the math functions propagate uncertainty by the standard first-order rules. Exact values are zero-uncertainty, so mixing works without ceremony. Nothing changes for any program until a measurement enters it, and printing shows the value with its uncertainty.
options.technical: Propagation uses first-order linear approximation with uncorrelated inputs, stated plainly in the docs. Correlated errors are out of scope and documented as such. Measured unit scales produce measured conversion results, connecting the two existing homes of uncertainty. A companion literal spelling, value ± uncertainty, is proposed in the surface section of the proposal; the plain measurement call is the canonical form either way.
options.code:
g :: 9.80665 ± 0.00001            // proposed literal; plain form below
m :: measurement(12.0, uncertainty: 0.1)
f :: m * g
print(f)          // 117.68 ± 0.98

options.name: Library-only, no propagation
options.detail: Keep the current shape: the measurement type stores a value and an uncertainty, and combining them stays a manual call. The hand-propagation risk the story shows remains the user's job.
options.technical: No change to arithmetic. The library may add helper combinators.
options.code: f :: propagate_mul(m, g)   // correct only if the right helper is chosen

options.name: Tracked uncertainty on every numeric type
options.detail: The original deferred idea: every number in the language carries an uncertainty slot, and all arithmetic propagates it. Beginners meet error bars whether or not they want them, and every numeric carrier grows a second field.
options.technical: Every numeric value pairs with an uncertainty at runtime, doubling numeric storage and touching every tier.
options.code: x :: 3.0          // secretly 3.0 ± 0.0 everywhere

comparisons.note: Uncertainty propagation lives in add-on packages that wrap numbers. Adoption is high in science because hand propagation is the leading error source.
comparisons.code:
from uncertainties import ufloat
f = ufloat(12.0, 0.1) * ufloat(9.80665, 0.00001)

recommendation.why: Propagation is the error-prone step a machine should own, and the opt-in shape keeps every beginner program untouched. It also connects the measured unit scales the language already ratified to the arithmetic they belong in.

whyNot.reason: Storage without propagation keeps the dangerous half manual, which is the exact failure in the story.
It taxes every number in every program for a concept most programs never meet, against the beginner-first ranking.

recommendation.tradeoff: First-order uncorrelated propagation is an approximation. The docs must state its limits plainly so results are not over-trusted.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared opt-in propagation against the library status quo and recommended propagation, because hand-combined sigma is the leading real-world error source.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added option C, the always-on tracked grade from the deferred ballot, so the owner sees the full spectrum from manual to universal.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested propagation as a compiler policy toggle per package. That is option A's opt-in expressed worse, so it folded into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose library combinators are honest and never wrong about correlation, and C, whose universal tracking can never be forgotten at a call site.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on correlated inputs, where first-order rules understate error. The repair is documented scope plus a correlation-aware library escape for experts, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The plane law: registered, nameable, reflectable, readable
decisions.gist: Whether every fact plane obeys the registration and reflection law markers already obey.
decisions.lesson: Marker law zero fixed marker drift: a marker exists exactly when it is a registry row. Tags, states, and effects were unified behind one internal registry earlier. But dimensions never joined, reflection reports no dimensions at all, and markers on fields, methods, and variants reflect as bare name strings instead of typed records. The proposal extends the marker law to every plane: registered, nameable, reflectable, and shipped as readable prelude source.
decisions.story: Ibrahim writes a derive that reads a type's reflection data. Struct-level markers arrive as typed records, field markers arrive as bare names, and the meters unit on a field is invisible entirely. He ships string matching and hopes the names never change.

options.name: Plane law for every plane, reflection completed
options.detail: Every fact plane lives in one registry. A plane exists exactly when registered, its facts are nameable, reflection reports them as typed values, and the compiler's planes ship as readable prelude source. Reflection gains dimensions, and marker arguments become typed records on fields, methods, and variants, matching the type level.
options.technical: Extends the marker registration law to dimensions, measures, exactness, and classifications. Reflection's remaining string fallbacks are removed. Drift guards walk every registered plane end to end, the same pattern the marker rebuild uses.

options.name: Complete reflection only
options.detail: Reflection gains dimensions and typed marker records everywhere, which fixes today's lying surface. No registration law extends to the other planes, so a future plane can ship half-registered and drift returns the way markers drifted before their law.
options.technical: Reflection work only. No new registry obligations.
options.code:
print(info.fields[0].dimensions)   // works
// but the next plane may ship without reflection at all

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Reflection stays partial and each plane keeps its own registration habits. Derive authors keep string matching.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: m :: info.fields[0].markers[0]   // still a bare string

recommendation.why: The marker rebuild proved the pattern: a registration law plus drift guards ends an entire defect class. Extending it to every plane finishes the job once instead of re-fighting drift plane by plane.

whyNot.reason: It fixes today's surface but not the cause, so the next plane can drift exactly as markers did before their law.
Reflection keeps lying to derive authors, and string matching keeps shipping in user code.

recommendation.tradeoff: Registration becomes a hard gate for anyone adding a plane to the compiler. That friction is the mechanism working as designed.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full law against reflection-only completion and recommended the law, because the marker history shows completion without a law decays.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested exposing the registry itself as a queryable value at compile time. That reopens the wall against computed types, so it was recorded as out of scope.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested law-for-new-planes with old planes grandfathered. Grandfathering is how drift survives, so it folded into option B's weakness rather than standing alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, which delivers every user-visible gain of A with less compiler ceremony, and C, which avoids churn while the marker rebuild is mid-flight.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's timing against the live marker migration cards. The repair is sequencing, because the law lands as those cards close and reuses their drift guards rather than racing them.

decisions.title: Inline refinements in type position
decisions.gist: Whether a value range can be written directly in a type position, without minting a named type first.
decisions.lesson: Today a checked range requires a named distinct type, even when the range matters at exactly one parameter. The carrier-plus-knowledge model says a range is knowledge on a type, so the type position should be able to carry it directly. This also makes the sized widths teachable: U8 is exactly Int with the range 0..255 and a one-byte layout, and the inline form lets the docs say so in code.
decisions.story: Tomas writes a brightness function that accepts 0 through 100. The honest options today are a bare Int with a runtime check he must remember, or declaring a named distinct type for one parameter of one function. He ships the bare Int, and the bad value arrives a month later.

options.name: Inline ranges anywhere a type is written
options.detail: Int(0..100) is legal in any type position: parameters, returns, fields, bindings. Literals check at compile time; unproven values convert fallibly, exactly as U8 works today. Naming stays available through distinct when identity matters. Two inline types with the same base and range are the same type.
options.technical: The inline form is structural: identity is carrier plus interval fact. distinct stays the nominal wrapper. The same checking already ratified for range types applies unchanged, including the literal-only bounds rule from D-RANGE-VALUE1; only the requirement to pre-declare a name is removed.
options.code:
fn set_brightness(level: Int(0..100)) { ... }
set_brightness(150)                       // compile error: 150 is outside 0..100
level :: Int(0..100).from_int(raw) ?? return   // unproven: fallible, like U8
volume: Int(0..11) = 11                   // fields and bindings too

options.name: Named types only
options.detail: The ratified status quo: every checked range is a named distinct type. One-off constraints keep paying the naming ceremony, and casual code keeps shipping bare Int with hope.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
Brightness :: distinct Int(0..100)
fn set_brightness(level: Brightness) { ... }

options.name: Inline on parameters only
options.detail: The inline form is allowed on function parameters, where the one-off need is most common, but not on fields, returns, or bindings. The surface gains a where-can-I-write-this rule that must be learned and diagnosed.
options.technical: Parser accepts the form in parameter position only; other positions get a targeted error naming distinct.
options.code:
fn set_brightness(level: Int(0..100)) { ... }   // ok
volume: Int(0..11) = 11                          // error here: name it instead

comparisons.note: Anonymous subtype constraints can appear directly at the use site, and named subtypes exist for reuse. Forty years of practice says both are wanted.
comparisons.code:
subtype Die is Integer range 1 .. 6;
procedure Roll (D : Integer range 1 .. 6);

recommendation.why: The fact travels with the position that needs it, so the cheapest path becomes the checked path. It also turns the sized-width story into one teachable line: U8 is Int(0..255) with a one-byte layout.

whyNot.reason: Naming ceremony at every one-off constraint keeps bare Int the path of least resistance, which is how unchecked values ship.
A position-dependent grammar rule is a new thing to learn and diagnose, and it saves nothing once the general form exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: Structural inline types mean two spellings can name the same type, one anonymous and one distinct. The docs must teach when identity matters, which is the existing distinct lesson.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared inline-anywhere against named-only and recommended inline, because the one-off case is the common case and it currently ships unchecked.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested inline forms for other knowledge kinds, like units in type position. Ranges are the only case with ratified checking behind them today, so the ballot stays scoped to ranges.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option C, parameters-only, as the minimal surface. It stands as a real choice rather than folding, since parameters are where the need concentrates.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: every checked range having a name keeps signatures self-documenting and greppable. That is a genuine style position, not a strawman.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's structural identity with the two-spellings confusion and with diagnostic length for inline types. Identity follows the interval fact and diagnostics print the inline form verbatim, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Imaginary literals ride the unit-literal path
decisions.gist: How an imaginary number is written: a 4i literal, or constructor calls only.
decisions.lesson: Complex numbers are ratified and coming. The remaining question is spelling. The lexer already reads a number glued to a suffix as one unit literal, which is how 500ms and 12.50usd work. The imaginary unit fits that exact machinery: 4i is a number on the imaginary axis, and mathematics has written it that way for two centuries. The alternative is constructor calls only, which reads like plumbing in any formula longer than a line.
decisions.story: Lena ports a signal-processing filter from a textbook. The book writes coefficients like 0.5 + 0.8i. With constructors only, every coefficient becomes a call, the formula stops looking like the book, and she transcribes one real part into an imaginary slot without noticing.

options.name: The 4i literal
options.detail: A numeric literal with the suffix i is an imaginary number. Real plus imaginary reads exactly like the textbook: 0.5 + 0.8i. The lexer path is the shipped unit-literal path, so no new grammar exists, and the identifier i alone remains an ordinary variable name.
options.technical: The suffix resolves through the same table-free literal machinery as unit suffixes, minting the imaginary component of the ratified Complex type. Only the suffix form is special: bare i is untouched, and shadowing risks are the same as any unit suffix in scope.
options.code:
z :: 3 + 4i
print(z * z)              // -7 + 24i
print(abs(3 + 4i))        // 5.0
h :: 0.5 + 0.8i           // reads like the book

options.name: Constructor only
options.detail: Complex values are built with the ordinary constructor and named parts. No literal exists. Formulas become call chains, and positional real-versus-imaginary mistakes are on the reader.
options.technical: No lexer change; the ratified struct constructor is the only spelling.
options.code:
z :: Complex.{real: 3.0, imaginary: 4.0}
h :: Complex.{real: 0.5, imaginary: 0.8}

options.name: The im suffix
options.detail: Same literal idea with a two-letter suffix, avoiding any collision with a loop variable named i. The cost is reading distance from written mathematics, which uses i.
options.technical: Identical machinery to option A with a different suffix string.

comparisons.note: Imaginary literals use the j suffix from electrical engineering. Loved by users, mocked for the letter.
Uses the im suffix to keep i free for loops. Users report it reads slightly off the page but never collides.

recommendation.why: It reads exactly like mathematics, and it costs zero new machinery because the unit-literal path already exists. The deeper point stands on its own: an imaginary number really is a number with a unit.

whyNot.reason: Formulas stop looking like formulas, and positional constructor slots invite the exact transcription error the story shows.
The collision it avoids does not exist, because only the suffix position is special and bare i stays an ordinary name.

recommendation.tradeoff: A numeral immediately followed by i can no longer mean multiplication-by-juxtaposition in some future surface. Jet has no such surface, so the cost is theoretical.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the i literal against constructor-only and recommended the literal, because it reuses shipped machinery and matches written mathematics.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Julia's im suffix and checked Python's j; j was folded into C's analysis as the same collision-avoidance idea with a worse letter.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping both i and im. Two spellings of one literal violates the one-mechanism invariant, so it was rejected rather than folded.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, which needs no lexer consideration at all, and C, which is the shipped Julia compromise with real-world mileage.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the loop-variable collision and with unit-family shadowing. Bare i is untouched because only the suffix position is special, and shadowing follows the shipped unit-literal resolution rules, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Precise by default: the exact numeric world
decisions.gist: Whether ordinary numbers are exact by default, with approximation as an expert opt-in.
decisions.lesson: The whole-number default is already exact: the ratified bigint Int removed overflow for beginners. Fractions did not get the same move. A decimal literal today is a binary float, so a tenth plus two tenths does not equal three tenths. This ballot decides whether the rest of the default world becomes exact too. It is an explicit amendment to the ratified division rule: division still leaves the whole numbers, but its landing world becomes exact. Float, F32, and U8 remain the expert path.
decisions.story: Amara writes her first budgeting script. She adds three items priced 19.99 and gets 59.96999999999999. Nothing in her code mentions floating point; she typed ordinary prices and ordinary math. She concludes the language is broken, because for her purpose it is.
decisions.inWild:
price :: 19.99
total :: price * 3
print(total)              // today: 59.96999999999999
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  // today: false
share :: 7 / 2            // today: Float 3.5 (exact by luck)
third :: 1 / 3            // today: 0.3333333333333333, error forever after

options.name: Exact default world
options.detail: Decimal literals are exact Decimal values. Division of exact values lands in exact rational territory: a result with a finite decimal prints as a decimal, otherwise it prints as a fraction and stays exact. Functions that truly leave the rationals, like square root and sine, answer approximate and say so. Experts opt into Float or F32 at the declaration, and hot code gets today's machine arithmetic unchanged.
options.technical: Amends three ratified rules by name. D-INTDIV1: division still maps whole to rational, but the landing default is exact instead of Float. D-EXPSEM1 and D-EXPNEG1: a written negative exponent gets the same exact landing. D-NUMTYPE1: its Fraction-is-opt-in-by-name clause relaxes, because plain division can now answer an exact ratio. Exact values use machine-word fast paths with spill, the bigint Int playbook. Sized widths and Float keep every ratified behavior once named, mixing with an approximate operand answers approximate under the one widening law, and narrowing still requires approx.
options.code:
price :: 19.99
print(price * 3)          // 59.97, exactly
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  // true
third :: 1 / 3
print(third)              // 1/3
print(third * 3 == 1)    // true
r :: sqrt(2.0)            // approximate: sqrt leaves the rationals
fast: Float = 19.99       // expert opt-in: machine float, today's speed

options.name: Exact wholes, approximate fractions
options.detail: The ratified status quo. Whole numbers are exact and never overflow; anything fractional is a binary float unless the programmer names Decimal or Fraction. The budgeting story stays broken by default, and the fix is knowing which type to ask for.
options.technical: No change: D-INTDIV1 stands as ratified, decimal literals stay Float.
options.code:
price :: 19.99            // Float
print(price * 3)          // 59.96999999999999
exact :: Decimal("19.99") // correct, if you know to ask

options.name: Exact by policy, float by default
options.detail: Defaults stay as ratified, and a package policy flips a project into the exact world. Teams that care opt in once per package. Two worlds then exist, and any code snippet means different things depending on an invisible setting.
options.technical: A policy key switches literal typing and the division landing type per package scope.
options.code:
policy: .{ exact_math: true }
// same source now means different values in different packages

comparisons.note: Decimal literals are exact rationals by default, so a tenth plus two tenths equals three tenths. Floats exist and are opt-in. This is the closest shipped precedent.
Exact int by default, binary float for fractions, with Decimal and Fraction as opt-in library types. This is option B, and its float surprises fill beginner forums.

recommendation.why: It finishes the move the bigint Int decision started: the default world is simply correct, and every restriction is chosen on purpose. Beginners get right answers; experts lose nothing and gain a visible audit of where approximation enters.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the single most famous beginner footgun as the default experience, in a language whose constitution ranks the beginner experience above performance.
One spelling with two meanings across packages breaks reading, teaching, and copy-paste, which is worse than either consistent world.

recommendation.tradeoff: Exact rational arithmetic costs more than machine floats, and long chains can grow big denominators. The small-value fast path and the one-word Float escape bound the cost, and the constitution spends performance rank to buy beginner rank.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the exact default against the ratified status quo and recommended exact, because the bigint Int precedent shows the default-correctness move works.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the per-package policy shape and considered decimal-only exactness without fractions; the latter folded into A's printing rule since both keep exact values underneath.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested exact decimals with approximate division. Splitting literals from division reintroduces the surprise at the first divide, so it folded into B rather than standing alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose model is Python's and battle-tested, and C, which gives teams an explicit contract. Both remain honest choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with denominator blowup in long simulations and with FFI boundaries expecting floats. Fast paths plus the one-word Float escape answer the first, and crossings already range-check under ratified law, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One authority model for effects, caps, policy, budgets, and trust
decisions.gist: Whether Jet builds all authority checks on one shared model.
decisions.lesson: Nine parts of Jet decide who may do what. Effect rows, #Caps and #Grant, the #Policy ladder, package budgets, build effects, comptime purity, the REPL gate, plugin sandboxes, and the trust store each carry their own vocabulary and rules. They already obey the same law: a scope may only shrink what its parent allows, and every exception is written down. This choice decides whether that law gets one implementation or stays spread across nine.
decisions.story: Maya runs a small billing service with two dependencies and a deploy agent. Her auditor asks one question: what can this system touch? Today the compiler, the package manifest, the build runner, and the trust store answer in four vocabularies. She wants one answer she can hand to the auditor.

options.name: One substrate
options.detail: All nine mechanisms become readers of one rights tree, one holds-set relation, one tighten rule, and one gate record. Nothing users type changes. The compiler, the budget, the sandbox, the REPL, and the trust store give the same answer with the same names. Ratified-but-unbuilt work (the agent executor, jetos install trust, the sandbox proof) lands on this substrate instead of adding more copies.
options.technical: One foundation module owns the root table, the subsumption lattice (effect_covers), the scope ladder (D-MARK-SCOPE1), and the gate ledger. Effects.rs, Policy.rs, EffectBudget.rs, BuildEffects.rs, both purity checkers, and the REPL authorizer become consumers. Semantics live in the substrate per I3/I9; generated Rust stays byte-identical.

options.name: Law on paper only
options.detail: The spec states the attenuation law and each mechanism must cite it, but every engine keeps its own code. Cheapest to adopt. Drift between the copies remains possible, and the ratified agent and jetos work still each build their own engine.
options.technical: A spec section names the law and lists the nine mechanisms as instances. No shared code. New authority features must reference the section in their ballots.

options.name: One vocabulary, nine engines
options.detail: Merge the six closed name tables into one rights tree so every surface uses the same names, but keep each mechanism’s own checking engine. Users see consistent words. The same tighten law still runs in nine places with nine error surfaces, and boundary features still need bespoke types.
options.technical: EFFECT_ROOTS, BuildEffect, PolicyKey, trust authority kinds, and plugin capabilities merge into one table in jet-foundation. Resolution code stays where it is.

options.name: Keep nine models
options.detail: Decline. Each boundary keeps its own model and vocabulary. No re-founding work. The word capability keeps six meanings, the spec and code keep drifting, and every future boundary (agents, jetos, remote builders) adds another copy.

comparisons.note: One runtime policy oracle over ambient authority. Retired: hand-written policy for real dependency trees collapsed to grant-everything, and every sensitive call site had to opt in forever.
comparisons.code: grant { permission java.security.AllPermission; }; // what real policy files said

comparisons.note: The compiler checks the trust chain across the whole import graph. The strongest prior art for making authority a static, transitive fact rather than a runtime hope.
comparisons.code: {-# LANGUAGE Safe #-} -- a Safe module cannot import untrusted code

comparisons.note: Default-deny with explicit allow flags works, but the grant unit is the whole process, so one needy dependency widens everyone.
comparisons.code: deno run --allow-net app.ts  // every module now has the network

recommendation.why: One substrate makes every authority answer agree, heals the drift at its root, and lets the ratified agent, jetos, and sandbox work land as instances instead of copies ten, eleven, and twelve. It also makes the safety story teachable in one sentence.

whyNot.reason: Paper cannot stop drift. The spec already said ten roots while the compiler shipped twenty-eight, with the stale count baked into user-facing explain text.
Shared names with nine engines still checks one law nine ways, keeps nine error surfaces, and leaves boundary features building bespoke authority types.
The fragmentation is already user-visible, and two more authority consumers are ratified and about to be built on nothing.

recommendation.tradeoff: A single substrate concentrates risk: a bug in the shared lattice touches every check at once. That is acceptable because one heavily tested lattice is safer than nine partly tested ones, and the golden suite pins generated output byte-for-byte.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one substrate, a documented law, a shared vocabulary without shared engines, and the status quo. It recommended the substrate because agreement between checkpoints is the point.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested a dynamic runtime authority object and split language-side and toolchain-side substrates. The runtime shape repeats the SecurityManager failure and was rejected, and the split shape was folded into option C as its strongest form.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried document-now-unify-later and vocabulary-now-substrate-later stagings. Both let the agent executor build on the old engines meanwhile, creating the tenth copy this ballot exists to prevent, so no hybrid survived.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a conformance test suite that checks each engine against the documented law, and strengthened C by including the manifest schemas in the merged vocabulary. Both improvements are kept in those options as written.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with substrate bugs propagating everywhere and the refactor disturbing erasure. The golden suite pins byte-identical output and phase A changes no surface, so A remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: Heal the effect root table: FFI languages become leaves
decisions.gist: What the closed list of effect roots actually is.
decisions.lesson: D-EFF4 ratified ten closed effect roots. Since then, sixteen language-binding ballots each added a root (Go, Java, Lua, and so on), plus Browser and Secret, without amending D-EFF4. The code now has twenty-eight roots, the spec and the E1221 explain text still say ten, and D-FFI-PY1 promised a Py root that was never added. This choice picks the true closed list and where foreign-language calls live in it.
decisions.story: Tom reads the Jet book, learns the ten effect roots, and audits a teammate’s service. He finds =[Java]=> in a signature. No documentation he owns mentions a Java effect, and jet explain tells him the vocabulary has ten roots. He no longer trusts the list he learned.

options.name: One FFI root, languages as leaves
options.detail: The closed table becomes thirteen roots: the ratified ten plus FFI, Browser, and Secret. The sixteen language roots become leaves: FFI.Go, FFI.Java, FFI.Lua, and the promised FFI.Py and FFI.Octave arrive as leaves too. A bound like =[!FFI]=> forbids all foreign calls at once. Existing rows migrate in one pass and the old flat spellings are deleted.
options.technical: Amends D-EFF4/D-EFF5 (root list) and the effect clause of each D-FFI-*1 ruling. Honors D-FFI-PY1 and D-FFI-OCTAVE1 by delivering their effects as leaves. Ancestor subsumption (D-EFFTREE1) already gives FFI covering FFI.Go. E1221 text and the stale Effects.rs comments are corrected in the same change.

options.name: Bless the flat thirty
options.detail: Keep every language as its own root and add the missing Py and Octave. Amend D-EFF4/5 and the explain text to list thirty roots. No migration. The teaching story grows from ten words to thirty, and forbidding all foreign calls takes sixteen prohibitions.
options.technical: Facts.rs becomes the ratified list verbatim. D-EFF4/5 amended to thirty. No row changes anywhere.

options.name: Ten teaching roots, system roots documented apart
options.detail: Keep the ratified ten as the beginner vocabulary. Everything else (language roots, Browser, Secret) becomes a documented system register that ordinary teaching never mentions. Code keeps compiling as today. Two registers of the same kind of name is a second vocabulary wearing a disguise.
options.technical: No code change. Spec gains a system-roots appendix. E1221 text says ten user roots plus system roots.

comparisons.note: Preview 1 shipped a flat rights bitmask per handle. The grain was wrong and unwinding it took a full redesign. Grant shape calcifies early.
comparisons.code: // preview1: fd_rights: u64 bitmask -> preview2: typed interfaces

comparisons.note: STORAGE bundled all files under one grant. Narrowing it later (Scoped Storage) took years of migrations.

recommendation.why: One FFI root restores a small closed list that teaches in a breath, makes forbid-all-foreign-calls one word, and honors the two rulings whose promised roots never shipped. The tree already supports it: leaves and subsumption are ratified and built.

whyNot.reason: Thirty flat roots make the closed set a memorization exercise and a sixteen-term prohibition row the price of purity from foreign code.
Two registers of one vocabulary is drift by design. The audit that found this problem started from exactly such a split.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing =[Go]=> style rows migrate to =[FFI.Go]=> in one repository-wide pass. That is churn without behavior change, accepted because the flat spellings were never ratified as a set.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the leaf collapse against blessing the flat table and recommended the collapse for teachability and single-word prohibition.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the two-register option and tested folding all foreign-language effects into Exec. The Exec fold was rejected because a JVM call and spawning a process are different risks an auditor must tell apart.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried A with Browser and Secret also demoted to leaves under IO or a new Data root. Neither has a natural parent among the ten, so the hybrid was rejected and both stay roots.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its real virtue: a flat table has no hierarchy rules and never surprises anyone with subsumption. C gained its clearest framing as a documentation-only fix.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether FFI subsumption hides which language a dependency uses, and it does not: exact leaves stay in rows, budgets, and the ledger. The migration was checked against the examples and formatter round-trip traps, so A holds.

decisions.title: Memory floors ride the rights tree
decisions.gist: Whether memory floors and effect rules share one ladder.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two tighten-only ladders. The effect system checks rows and #Caps regions on one lattice. The #Policy ladder checks memory floors (no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded, gc) and the unsafe mode on a second lattice with its own error code. Both enforce the same rule: inner scopes may only tighten. This choice decides whether the memory floors become denials on the rights tree (new Mem leaves) or keep their separate engine.
decisions.story: Ana writes firmware for a flight-data recorder. Certification asks: prove this package never allocates after boot and never touches the network. Today those are two proofs from two systems with two vocabularies. She wants one proof from one system.

options.name: One ladder, spellings kept
options.detail: Mem.Alloc, Mem.Rc, and Mem.Gc become rights on the tree. #Policy(no_alloc) keeps its exact spelling and meaning but now records a Mem.Alloc denial on the same ladder #Caps uses. Nothing users type changes, diagnostics keep their codes, and a certification audit reads one ledger.
options.technical: Amends D-MEM-FACTS1=B in substrate only: same facts, same transitivity, expressed as tree denials. PolicyKey memory variants retire; the unsafe mode stays a policy value (it is a gate mode, not a right). arena_bounded(N) carries its limit as gate data. E0355 remains the diagnostic for policy-shape errors.

options.name: Full respell as effect denials
options.detail: Retire the memory keys from #Policy and write floors as prohibitions: =[!Mem.Alloc]=> on functions, deny: [Mem.Alloc] in manifests. One mechanism and one spelling, but the friendly floor words (no_alloc) disappear and arena limits need a new home.
options.technical: Amends D-MEM-FACTS1 and D-POLICY-WORD1. #Policy keeps only non-memory arguments. arena_bounded needs a parameterized-denial form the row grammar does not have today.

options.name: Two ladders stay
options.detail: Decline. Memory floors keep their own lattice and error family. The certification story stays split and the substrate keeps two implementations of the tighten rule.

comparisons.note: Fused all of aliasing and authority into one six-mode lattice that every beginner faces. Lesson taken: fold the substrate, not the beginner surface — the floor words stay.
comparisons.code: iso | val | ref | box | trn | tag  // mandatory vocabulary, day one

comparisons.note: no_std and #![forbid(unsafe_code)] are separate systems from the borrow checker. Certification audits there also stitch multiple proofs.

recommendation.why: One ladder gives embedded and certification work a single proof and deletes a duplicate lattice. The floor words stay because they read better than row noise, and the unsafe mode stays a gate setting, which keeps the model honest.

whyNot.reason: It trades the ratified, readable floor words for row noise and has no good answer for parameterized floors like arena_bounded.
It keeps two implementations of one rule and a permanently split audit story for exactly the users who audit hardest.

recommendation.tradeoff: Mem joins the root table, so the closed list grows by one root. That is acceptable because the alternative is a whole parallel lattice for three names.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared substrate fold, full respell, and status quo, recommending the fold because it unifies proof without touching ratified spellings.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested an Unsafe root and per-type floors such as no_alloc on a struct. Unsafe stays a gate with modes rather than a held right, and per-type floors are not this decision, so both were folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried A plus optional row spellings (=[!Mem.Alloc]=> as sugar for the same denial). That reintroduces two spellings of one mechanism, against I8, and was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a concrete manifest form for limits and strengthened C by naming its real virtue: zero migration risk to certified code. Both are reflected in the option details.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A on arena_bounded, since a limit is not a set-membership fact; the denial carries its limit as gate data, as grants entries already carry per-dependency data. Tighten-only (D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1) survives unchanged as the ladder law, so A holds.

decisions.title: Name the authority value that crosses boundaries
decisions.gist: What the carried rights-set value is called, and whether it is one type.
decisions.lesson: When rights cross a boundary the compiler cannot see past — into a spawned process, a plugin, or a session — they must travel as a value. Jet has four designs for that value today: the unnameable #Grant handle, the ratified-but-unbuilt ProcessAuthority, the plugin capability list, and the REPL grant copy. The type name Capability is currently accepted anywhere a type is legal but can never be constructed. This choice picks one type and its name.
decisions.story: Priya builds a CI agent in Jet. She spawns a build in a workspace, hands a plugin its rights, and opens a debug session. Three handoffs, and today each would use a different type with a different shape. She wants to write one thing three times.

options.name: Authority — one Prelude type
options.detail: One type named Authority carries a rights set across every boundary. The #Grant handle has this type, process.workspace() returns it, plugins receive it, sessions hold it. It can only be narrowed, never widened, and it never participates in dispatch. The dead-end phantom is fixed by making the real type exist.
options.technical: Amends D-AGENT-EXEC2 naming: ProcessAuthority becomes Authority (ProcessPlan and ProcessReceipt stay). Reopens the type-unification audit’s post-v1 note on typed handles, value form only. Facts stay facts (D-FACTMODEL1): Authority is ordinary data, no type selection, no dispatch. Narrowing is the only operation family (with/without). Construction keeps the ratified PascalCase convention from D-AGENT-EXEC2: Authority.workspace(...), not a lowercase namespace call.
options.code:
a :: Authority.workspace()         // proposed
a2 :: a.with(FS.Write, "out/")      // extend only within holds; else E0712
process.run("jet build", a2)
plugin.load("lint", a2.without(FS.Write))

options.name: Caps — match the marker
options.detail: Same one-type design, named Caps to rhyme with #Caps(...). Shortest name, already half-taught by the marker. The rhyme cuts both ways: #Caps narrows a static scope while the value crosses runtime boundaries, and one word for both may blur that line.
options.technical: Identical semantics to option A. Amends D-AGENT-EXEC2 naming the same way.
options.code:
c :: Caps.workspace()
process.run("jet build", c.with(FS.Write, "out/"))

options.name: Clearance — plain-word metaphor
options.detail: Same one-type design, named Clearance: what you have been cleared to do. Reads naturally in security prose and to newcomers. It is a fresh word with no anchor in existing Jet surface, so it adds a vocabulary item instead of reusing one.
options.technical: Identical semantics to option A.
options.code:
c :: Clearance.workspace()
process.run("jet build", c.with(FS.Write, "out/"))

options.name: Bespoke types per boundary
options.detail: Honor D-AGENT-EXEC2 exactly as ratified: ProcessAuthority for processes, plugin capabilities for plugins, session grants for the REPL, and the #Grant handle stays unnameable. Each boundary gets a type shaped for its job. Three shapes to learn, and narrowing rules are re-stated per type.
options.technical: No amendment. The phantom-type regression is fixed separately by scoping marker-argument names to marker positions (card #1501).

comparisons.note: One handle type with a rights mask; duplication may only reduce rights. One narrowing rule serves the whole OS.
Linear capability values threaded from main, no ambient authority anywhere. Proof the value form works in a language, unproven at ecosystem scale.
Everything the guest may touch is a handle it was explicitly given at instantiation.
comparisons.code: // no ambient open("/etc/passwd") inside the sandbox

recommendation.why: One type with one narrowing rule serves processes, plugins, and sessions alike, lands the ratified agent design as an instance, and turns the Capability dead end into a real, teachable thing. Authority is the plainest word for exactly what the value is.

whyNot.reason: Caps names the static marker; reusing it for the runtime value blurs the static/boundary line the model works hard to keep sharp.
Clearance is a good word with no anchor: it adds vocabulary where Authority reuses the concept the whole model is named for.
Three bespoke shapes re-state the same narrowing law three times and leave the phantom type a permanent trap to re-fix.

recommendation.tradeoff: Renaming ProcessAuthority amends a ratified naming ruling before any code exists. That is the cheapest possible moment to amend it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft posed one-type-versus-bespoke and a name menu, recommending one type named Authority.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass weighed Warrant, Permit, and Leash, folding them into C as the best fresh-word representative. A generic parameterized form like Authority[FS.Read] re-enters the withdrawn typed-handle design and touches the facts-never-dispatch wall, so it stays out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried one type with per-boundary aliases (ProcessAuthority = Authority). Aliases are exactly the parallel-spelling drift greenfield law forbids, so the hybrid was dropped.
