No silent override anywhere — not even a profile over a declared default. Every override becomes an explicit conflict to resolve by editing a file. This is today's ratified law for Config facts, applied to the whole plane.

comparisons.note: mkDefault (1000) and mkForce (50) are the priority spelling A keeps for system/fleet. NixOS's regret is not priorities — it is five parallel composition mechanisms beside them.
Order-independent unification kills the last-file-wins bug class, but plain defaults-then-override needs special defaults machinery even there.
Profile precedence is fixed and undocumented in places; there is no explain command, so effective values are folklore.

recommendation.why: A states as one law what Jet ratified in three pieces: D-MARK-SCOPE1's nearness in source, the composition conflict rule per layer, and D-JOS's audited pin. The beginner story stays one sentence: the value written closest to the act wins, and jet explain shows the chain.

whyNot.reason: Numbers in everyday code tax every user for a problem only fleets have. NixOS shows the table becomes folklore.
Extending pure conflict everywhere refuses the commonest act in configuration — a profile overriding a declared default on purpose — and turns it into an error to hand-resolve.

recommendation.tradeoff: The law has two directions (innermost wins in source, outermost-explicit wins across layers) plus one pin. That is three things to teach, softened because each was already ratified separately and one explain chain shows them all.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared nearest-wins, priorities-everywhere, and conflict-everywhere, and recommended nearest-wins as the generalization of ratified precedent.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested last-write-wins (rejected: ambient order, banned by D-BUILDPROFILE1) and per-fact custom merge functions (rejected: Gradle-shaped unbounded logic). Owner feedback then added the missing source rungs — item and file — completing the ladder.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced A's current form: nearness kept for source scopes, C's per-layer conflict rule kept within each layer, and B's priorities kept as the system/fleet pin only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass rewrote C honestly as the ratified composition law extended unchanged, not an exotic import — its no-silent-override guarantee is real. It strengthened B by noting one mechanism is easier to specify than two.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's original framing twice: it called the CLI the nearest scope (backwards under D-MARK-SCOPE1) and pinned the amendment on the noun ballot D-ECO-SLICENAME1 instead of the composition law. Both are restated — two directions plus a pin, amendment on the composition rule — and A survives.

decisions.title: Settings and module value parameters: one substrate
decisions.gist: Whether settings and generic-module value parameters become one mechanism.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two features that accept the same five value types (Bool, Int, Char, String, fieldless enum), evaluate them with the same purity rules, and reject the same expressions. One is generic-module value parameters (D-GENMOD-VALUE1). The other is settings (D-CONF-KEY1). Today they are checked by two code paths and cannot mix: no fact is a legal value argument. This ballot decides one substrate or two, and names the two D-GENMOD-VALUE1 clauses that one substrate amends.
decisions.story: Elin tunes a cache per deployment. Her module takes a slot count: module cache<slots: Int>. Her package declares a setting cache_slots. She writes module tuned = cache<$build.settings.cache_slots> and wants it to just work — a fact is a value, and the parameter wants a value.

options.name: One substrate
options.detail: One value substrate: settings and module value parameters share one evaluator, one fuel budget, one diagnostic family. Nothing on the module page changes — cache<slots: Int> is spelled exactly as ratified. The one visible gain: a fact becomes a legal value argument, so module tuned = cache<$build.settings.cache_slots> works. Each profile produces its own cached specialization, and jet explain traces the value into the instantiation.
options.technical:
Amendment one: D-GENMOD-VALUE1's closed-expression rule extends to admit facts as value arguments. Today it rejects any non-literal reference.

Amendment two: the ratified [T#capacity] layout carve-out (S26/S76/D-FIXARR1) extends to fact-fed Int parameters. A build fact may size a fixed array, exactly as a different literal instantiation does today. A profile change produces a different cached specialization; the existing E0859 fingerprint path keys on argument values.

Unchanged: the parameter-list grammar keeps no defaults and no named arguments; defaults and names live at the settings declaration only. S26 otherwise stands: values specialize bodies and the one ratified layout slot, never type identity or dispatch.

Spelling note: the examples use the ratified D-GENMOD2 punctuation. D-CONF-GENSPELL1 decides the final spelling (<types>(values) and :: binding); this ballot is independent of that choice.

options.name: Two mechanisms, a documented wall
options.detail: Keep them separate on purpose: module parameters are code, settings are data, and never the twain. Facts stay illegal as value arguments, and module instantiation stays hermetic — a module's meaning never depends on who built it. The wall is written into the spec so the sameness of the rules is declared a boundary, not a seam.

options.name: Full syntactic unification
options.detail: Go further: the package itself is spelled as a generic module with value parameters, and settings are its parameter list. One concept on the page, but the whole ratified manifest surface (identity:, the D-ECO nouns) is respelled for no new power.

comparisons.note: Functors are the ancestor of D-GENMOD; nobody feeds build config into them because the build system is a separate world. Jet can close that gap.
comparisons.code: module Tuned = Cache(struct let slots = 64 end)

comparisons.note: comptime values flow freely from build options into generic code — the composition A wants — because there is one value world.

recommendation.why: The rule sets are already identical; A makes the identity real and buys composition — facts flow into modules, and explain chains reach instantiations. One diagnostic family teaches both features, and both amendments are small and named.

whyNot.reason: The wall preserves two copies of one rule set and forbids the composition users will ask for first. A coincidence this exact is a seam.
It respells the ratified D-ECO manifest surface for zero new capability. The unification A buys is semantic, not orthographic.

recommendation.tradeoff: Instantiation errors can now involve facts, so diagnostics must name the contributing home in the message, and a fact-sized [T#capacity] layout can change between profiles. Both costs are visible in jet explain, but they are real.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared unification with a documented wall and recommended unification because the two rule sets are already identical.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added option C, the full syntactic merge, found while testing how far the identity extends. It also tested facts-in-type-position and rejected it against S26 without balloting.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A-plus-C for new packages only. Two manifest spellings for one ecosystem violates one-mechanism (I8), so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: hermetic instantiation is a real guarantee — a module's meaning never depends on the build that ran it. Owner feedback drove a clarity rewrite: the lesson now states the unification in plain terms and the example uses the $ fact-read spelling.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass surfaced two silent amendments the first draft skipped: the closed-expression rule and the [T#capacity] layout carve-out reaching facts. Both are now named in A's technical text with the fingerprint answer, and A survives with the amendments owned.

decisions.title: Provenance facts: a binary names its own build
decisions.gist: Whether a binary can name the exact source and toolchain that built it.
decisions.lesson: No comptime path exists for build provenance. A program cannot learn the git commit or toolchain that built it, so crash reports carry only a hand-maintained version string. Comptime inputs are closed today to embed_file/embed_bytes (D-CTIO1) and find (D-CTFIND1/2, Tier 1 under D-CTEFFECT1). This ballot proposes, as a named amendment to that closed input list, one more Tier-1 locked input: the repository state. It also decides what stays out for reproducibility.
decisions.story: Fatima runs three replicas of a service. A crash report says version 3.0.0. Two commits shipped under 3.0.0 last week because a hotfix did not bump the version. She bisects blind between them at 2am.

options.name: Source and toolchain stamps, no timestamp
options.detail: Two facts join the plane: build.stamp.git (the commit hash, -dirty suffixed for an unclean tree, absent outside a repository) and build.stamp.toolchain (the jet version). Each read is recorded in .jet/lock, so a --locked rebuild reprints the same stamp. A build timestamp is deliberately absent: wall-clock time is not a fact about the source, and the lock cannot pin it.
options.technical: Amends the closed comptime-input list (D-CTIO1/D-CTFIND1/2 family): the repository state becomes a Tier-1 locked input under D-CTEFFECT1 — hashed, recorded in .jet/lock, reproducible from the lock; never Tier 2, never #Impure. build.stamp.git is a String? fact; optional facts are readable on the plane but are not legal module value arguments, so D-GENMOD-VALUE1's Tier-0 set is unchanged. build.stamp.toolchain is a String fact.

options.name: Stamps plus a lock-pinned timestamp
options.detail: Everything in A, plus build.stamp.at: a timestamp captured once when the lock is written and replayed from the lock afterward. Rebuilds stay reproducible because the value comes from the lock, not the clock — but the fact describes the lock file's history, not the source.
options.code:
print("built {build.stamp.at}")   // when the lock was cut,
// not when this binary was built — a fact that lies politely

options.name: No stamp facts
options.detail: Provenance stays a tooling concern: jet inspect names the commit and toolchain from the lock and receipts, but no program can read them. Crash banners keep hand-maintained strings, and the 2am bisection stays blind. The comptime input list stays exactly as ratified.

comparisons.note: Stamps vcs.revision into every binary by default; the ecosystem treats it as table stakes for operations.
No first-party answer; the vergen build script fills the gap with env-var stringly plumbing.
SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH exists because timestamps are the classic reproducibility leak — the reason A excludes them.

recommendation.why: A gives crash reports and support tooling the one fact they need — which source built this binary — while keeping the same-input-same-binary law intact. The dirty suffix keeps the stamp honest during development.

whyNot.reason: A pinned timestamp is a fact about the lock file, not the source. It answers no question bisection asks and invites time-based logic that reproducibility forbids.
Provenance only an operator can query never reaches the crash report, which is where Fatima meets it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The ratified comptime input list grows by one entry, and builds outside a repository read an absent value, so banner code handles the missing case once with ??.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared stamps-without-timestamp, stamps-with-timestamp, and tooling-only provenance, and recommended the first for reproducibility.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested richer stamps (branch name, remote URL, builder identity) and folded them out: branch and remote are mutable labels, and builder identity is a receipt concern (D-ECO-RECEIPTSTORE1).
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A plus an opt-in timestamp behind a flag. A flag that breaks reproducibility when set is a trap with a switch, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: receipts (ratified, unbuilt) will carry full provenance for operators regardless, and C alone leaves the ratified comptime input list untouched.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass caught the first draft calling stamps Tier-0 while D-CTEFFECT1 makes ambient reads tiered; A now names the amendment and places stamps at Tier 1, locked like find. It also caught String? against the Tier-0 value set, answered by barring optional facts from module arguments, and A survives as restated.

decisions.title: One meaning for the word profile
decisions.gist: End the name clash: profile names four ratified things today.
decisions.lesson: Four ratified features share one word, across five surfaces. Build profiles are optimize bundles (release, debug, ci) behind --profile and its sugar --release (D-BUILDPROFILE1). TargetProfile (crates/jet-foundation/src/TargetProfile.rs:12) is a board/triple machine identity for firmware builds — internal, its user surface deliberately unbuilt. Environment profiles own the profiles: field (D-ENV-PROFILE1) plus --env-profile and an env-namespace --profile flag (D-ENV-FACET1). Package and user profiles share a generation engine (D-JPK-PROFILE1). This ballot decides which meaning keeps the word, and what the others are called.
decisions.story: Gus builds firmware for a sensor board. He reads about build profiles in the CLI help and meets target profile in the freestanding docs (D-WD11). He guesses jet build --profile=board.sensor_v1, gets E1219 unknown profile, and files a docs bug that is really a naming bug — the word taught him the wrong flag.

options.name: Profile means the optimize bundle; the rest are renamed
options.detail: release, debug, and ci keep the word, matching --profile and its ratified sugar --release. The board identity is a machine description; before its unbuilt surface ships, it is renamed into the machine vocabulary and selected beside triples with --target. Environment profiles become presets (amends D-ENV-PROFILE1's field and flag spelling). Package/user profiles are already generation snapshots and take the generation word (amends D-JPK-PROFILE1's wording only). Each rename is an amendment named here; none changes behavior.
options.technical: TargetProfile renames into the machine axis (--target=<triple|board>), not the targets: manifest field (artifact kinds, D-TGT1-4) and not build-graph targets (D-BUILDTARGET1) — those two keep their own words, and E1216 stays as-is. The board surface is unbuilt (TargetProfile.rs:3-4 defers user diagnostics to a follow-up surface ballot), so this rename lands before any user meets the old name. D-ENV-PROFILE1: profiles: becomes presets:. D-ENV-FACET1: --env-profile and the env-namespace --profile flag become --preset. D-JPK-PROFILE1: prose adopts generation.

options.name: Machines keep profile; bundles become modes
options.detail: The firmware side takes the word when its surface ships; release and debug become modes with a --mode flag. The unbuilt concept gets the word, and the common ratified surface is respelled — including the --release sugar for --profile=release.

options.name: Keep all four meanings
options.detail: Do nothing. Docs disambiguate with build profile, target profile, environment profile, and package profile on every mention, and E1219 keeps catching the crossover guess at run time instead of the vocabulary preventing it.

comparisons.note: Profiles are exclusively optimize bundles; targets are exclusively machines. The clean split is why nobody confuses them.

recommendation.why: A gives each question one word: profile answers how hard to optimize, target answers what machine, preset answers which environment. It keeps the ratified --profile/--release surface unchanged and renames the three others while two of them have no shipped user surface to break.

whyNot.reason: It respells the common ratified surface (--profile=release, --release) to hand the word to a surface that has not shipped.
The clash keeps generating the exact error Gus hit, and every doc pays a four-way disambiguation tax forever.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four amendments land at once (TargetProfile, D-ENV-PROFILE1, D-ENV-FACET1, D-JPK-PROFILE1 wording), and board names join triples under one --target flag, so that flag accepts two name shapes for one question.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft treated this as a two-meaning clash (bundles vs boards) and recommended renaming the board side to target.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass found the clash is four-way across five surfaces, not two-way: environment profiles hold profiles: (D-ENV-PROFILE1) plus two selection flags (D-ENV-FACET1), and package/user profiles (D-JPK-PROFILE1) also hold the word. A was widened to rename all of them, each as a named amendment.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested renaming only the board side and leaving environment profiles alone. That leaves profiles: in env modules one field away from build profiles, so the four-way fix was kept.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: E1219 does catch the crossover today with a real diagnostic, and the board surface being unbuilt means the collision is mostly latent. It strengthened B by noting mode is Xcode's word for the same bundle.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's flag sharing: --target must tell a board name from a triple, and no manifest declares boards today. Sequencing answers it — the board surface is unbuilt, so its follow-up ballot defines the declared home and name shapes, and the rename lands before anything breaks.

decisions.title: Adopt the failure law: one report, three routes
decisions.gist: One law for every failure: one report, delivered once, on the route its attribution picks.
decisions.lesson: Jet has many failure mechanisms: error values, contracts, traps, panics, exit codes, and compile diagnostics. They grew separately. Seventeen mechanisms now deliver failures, with four runtime renderers and different wording per tier. This ballot decides whether Jet adopts one law that says what a failure is and which route it takes. The law would guide every later failure decision.
decisions.story: Maya is in her first week with Jet. Her program reads past the end of a list. The message looks nothing like the friendly compile errors she has seen. She asks `jet explain` about it, but runtime stops have no code to explain.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build app.jet && ./build/app
panic: the list has 3 items, so position 10 doesn't exist
  --> app.jet:12

$ jet run app.jet
panic: index out of bounds: the index is outside the list

# Same program, same bug, two different stories — and no code to look up.

options.name: Adopt the full law
options.detail: Every failure is one product: a report with a code, a message, a why, a fix, and a source location. Attribution picks the route. A promise the world broke returns as a value in the signature. A promise code broke stops the program with attribution. A substrate failure stops and is contained at the nearest boundary. Routes change only at spelled boundaries, such as a task join or the process edge. No failure is lost or reworded on the way.
options.technical: Ratified law becomes theorems: E0401/E0402 must-use and `.drop("reason")` are delivery-exactly-once on the value route. I2/exit 101 is substrate attribution. The S36 exit table is the process-edge boundary conversion. D-VALIDATE1's three layers are the attribution split. D-INTBIG1 deletes a failure case; D-NUMOPS1 traps are code promises; `U8.from_int(n)?` is world data. D-CANCELMODEL1=C's unwind engine is the containment machinery.

options.name: Name the taxonomy only
options.detail: The spec names the three kinds of failure — error, breach, fault — as guidance. No mechanism changes and no unification is owed. Future decisions may cite the names. The seventeen delivery mechanisms, four renderers, and tier drift stay as they are until each is fixed on its own.

options.name: No law — decide case by case
options.detail: Keep deciding each failure question as it comes up. Each new surface picks its own delivery, wording, and exit behavior. This is the current state.

comparisons.note: The closest prior art. Recoverable errors live in signatures; bugs abandon the isolation unit and are not catchable; contracts are checked or proven. Its report: most error-handling code disappeared.

Result and panic split the first two kinds well, but whether a panic unwinds is a build flag, so libraries cannot reason about it. The std Error type shipped hollow and the ecosystem routed around it.
comparisons.code:
fn read() -> Result<String, io::Error>  // value route
panic!("broken invariant")               // breach — but abort or unwind?

comparisons.note: The fault route done properly: a crash is contained by the process boundary and a supervisor restarts from known-good state. Containment is what makes fail-fast affordable.
comparisons.code:
% a crashed worker never corrupts a peer;
% the supervisor's restart rule is data

recommendation.why: The law explains every ratified failure rule Jet already has, so it is not a new direction — it is the name of the existing one. With the name in law, the seventeen shadow mechanisms become one product with three doors, and every future surface knows its route before it ships.

whyNot.reason: Names without obligations leave the four renderers, the tier drift, and the exit-code collisions in place. The next feature drifts again, and the names become documentation of a wish.
Case-by-case is how seventeen mechanisms happened. It produced the 101 collision, the silent contract skip, and an entry rule that refuses every typed error family.

recommendation.tradeoff: The law is binding. A future feature must deliver its failures on one of the three routes, and a genuinely new route needs an owner amendment. That constraint is the point, and it is the accepted cost.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full law, taxonomy-only naming, and case-by-case. It recommended the full law because every ratified rule already fits it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested failure as a knowledge plane and as a signature effect. Both folded into the value route because they restate attribution with more ceremony.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested taxonomy-now with obligations-later, and it collapsed into option B. Deferred obligations are dropped obligations, so no new option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B as better spec prose and C as maximal future freedom. Both still leave the seventeen-mechanism drift in place.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the law with cancellation and with web-tier stops. Cancellation is a boundary event and the web keeps the report text, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: The default error is a real value — its name and constructor
decisions.gist: What the default error value is called and how a program builds one.
decisions.lesson: Today the default error type is a plain string inside the compiler. S80 ratified a structured form — message, optional code, optional source — but it was never built. No program can construct one, read its fields, or walk a cause. Separately, two names circle one idea: `Err(...)` is what people write, `Error` is what signatures say. This ballot picks the shape and the name.
decisions.story: Priya ships a command-line tool. A config load fails three calls deep. Her user sees `parse failed` with no file and no cause. Priya already writes `Err("parse failed")`; she wants that exact line to produce a real value with a chain, not a bare string.

options.name: One word: Err is the constructor and the type
options.detail: `Err("msg")` builds the default error — the line beginners already write becomes the constructor, with nothing new to learn. Labels add the rest: `Err("msg", code: "CFG404")` and `Err("msg", cause: e)`. The `code` label is a short string, so registered codes and app codes ride one field. Programs read `.message`, `.code`, and `.cause`. In signatures the type is spelled `Err` (`Config ? Err`), and mostly it is not written at all: bare `T ?` already implies it.
options.technical: Amends S80's builder spelling and renames the default error type `Error` to `Err`. In an Err-arm position `Err(e)` wraps a typed error value as today; with a string message and labels it constructs the default error. The value route carries message, code, and cause; why, fix, and location dress the report when a boundary renders it. `Error` as a type name is deleted, not aliased. `Type::Named("Error") => String` in `Codegen/Context.rs:1325` dies.

options.name: Err constructs, Error stays the type name
options.detail: Same structured value and labels, but signatures keep the ratified type name: `Config ? Error`. Two related names remain: one for building, one for naming. The pairing matches today's spelling exactly, at the cost of a beginner question — why does `Err(...)` make an `Error`.
options.code:
return Err("parse failed", cause: e)
fn load() => Config ? Error { ... }

options.name: The ratified builder chain
options.detail: Build S80 exactly as written: `Error.message("…")` starts, `.code(n)` and `.with_source(e)` chain on. Three calls spell what one constructor says, and the spelling differs from how every other core value is built.

comparisons.note: std shipped Error without context, chaining, or a constructor story; the ecosystem built it twice outside std. The lesson: ship the authoring and reporting ergonomics in core, first.
One shape everyone builds inline: {:error, reason}. The reason travels as a value and the whole ecosystem agrees on the spelling. That agreement is what a single short name buys.

recommendation.why: The line beginners already write becomes the whole feature: `Err("msg")` is the constructor, and the type name in signatures is the same word. One name, no builder chain, no explaining why `Err` makes an `Error`. The cause chain and labels give experts the structure peers had to import.

whyNot.reason: Keeps two names for one idea and the beginner question that comes with them. The type name is almost never written, so keeping `Error` preserves ceremony nobody sees value from.
Three chained calls to state one value, and a spelling no other core type uses. The corelib doctrine's own rule (D4) says options are labels.

recommendation.tradeoff: One word does two jobs: `Err` wraps a typed error in an arm position and constructs the default error from a message. Context separates them cleanly, but the overload is real and documented.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one-name Err, split Err/Error names, and the ratified builder chain. One name won because the beginner's existing line becomes the constructor.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested shipping no default error and a trait-only interface. Both folded out because the default type keeps the bare fallible spelling one word, and trait-only repeats Rust's hollow std.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass asked whether the builder chain could stay as sugar over the constructor. Two public spellings for one construction lost, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass credited B with zero renames of ratified text and C as verbatim delivery of S80. Neither removes the two-name question beginners actually ask.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the Err overload with `Err(e)` where e is itself a default error. That case is wrap-through and behaves identically either way, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Delete the Fallible trait: error conversion has one rail
decisions.gist: Whether the dead Fallible trait dies, and how the one conversion rail is spelled.
decisions.lesson: Two mechanisms exist for turning one error type into another. The declared conversion `impl Source => Target { … }` is ratified, shipped law (D-ERR-CONV). Its shape is deliberate: a conversion is a function from source to target, so `self` is the source and the body returns the target. The second mechanism, the `Fallible` trait, does not work: it is registered nowhere and no program can implement it. Its diagnostic (E2402) teaches a fix that is itself a hard error. This ballot decides whether the trait dies and how the rail is spelled.
decisions.story: Sam returns a custom enum from a helper inside a fallible function. E2402 tells him to implement `impl StoreErr: Fallible`. The parser rejects that spelling. He searches the whole repository for one working `Fallible` implementation and finds zero.

options.name: Delete the trait; keep the ratified arrow spelling
options.detail: The `Fallible` trait, `to_error`, and the compiler's `TryConvert::Fallible` arm are removed. Error conversion has exactly one mechanism: the declared conversion `impl Source => Target`, now usable with the default error as the target. One rule bends: a conversion into the default error may name a foreign source type, the case E2406's fix text used to send to the dead trait. E2402 and E2406 are rewritten to teach the one rail.
options.technical: Amends D-ERR2's Fallible clause and D-LIB3's `?`-conversion registration. The orphan rule (E2406) keeps its meaning for typed targets; the default-error-target carve-out replaces the trait as the foreign-type escape. Removes `TRAIT_FALLIBLE`/`FN_TO_ERROR` constants, the sema arm at `CheckerInfer/fallible.rs`, and the `Fallible` block in `docs/reference/syntax-surface.jet`. E2402's and E2406's what/why/fix and their UI snapshots are re-registered (I4). Default-error name per D-FAIL-ERROR1.

options.name: Delete the trait; respell the rail as `as`
options.detail: Same deletion, same single rail, different spelling: `impl Source as Target { … }` reads "treat a StoreErr as an Err". For readers who find the arrow lambda-like, this trades the function shape for a relational one. Amends D-ERR-CONV's ratified spelling and migrates the shipped `=>` conversions in the same change (greenfield: the old form is deleted).

options.name: Build Fallible for real
options.detail: Register `Fallible` as a real trait, make the default error constructible, and keep both rails: the trait for conversions into the default error, declared conversions for typed targets. Two mechanisms stay, split by target type.
options.technical: Requires trait registration plus the same constructor work. The `?` lowering keeps both arms. I8 pressure: two rails for one job, split by an invisible rule (target is the default error vs anything else).

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: The trait stays unregistered, E2402 keeps its impossible fix, and conversion into the default error stays unreachable for user types. Nothing is deleted and nothing starts working.
options.code: // E2402 keeps teaching a spelling the parser rejects.

comparisons.note: One rail: `?` applies `From::from`, and the impl is function-shaped for the same reason — a conversion is a function. It is the most copied piece of modern error design.
comparisons.code: impl From<StoreErr> for AppErr { fn from(e: StoreErr) -> Self { … } }

comparisons.note: Typed and untyped throws form one lattice with `any Error` as an endpoint, not a second mechanism. Conversion to the general form is the same rule everywhere.
comparisons.code: func get() throws { try readStore() }   // one rule, any error

recommendation.why: Every `Fallible` implementation anyone could write is one declared conversion with the default error as the target, so deleting the trait removes a mechanism and loses nothing. The arrow spelling stays because it is ratified, shipped, and honest: a conversion is a function from source to target, and the form says so.

whyNot.reason: `as` reads like a cast that reinterprets a value, which this is not — the body builds a new value. The arrow's function shape is the accurate one once it is explained, and it is already shipped law.
Two rails for one job, split by whether the target happens to be the default error. That is the I8 violation this slate exists to remove, built on purpose.
Ships a registered diagnostic whose fix cannot compile. That is a product defect under I4, not a neutral default.

recommendation.tradeoff: No trait means no generic bound spelled "any error convertible to the default". Nothing loses this today — the trait never worked, so no such generic code exists.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared deletion with the ratified spelling, building the trait for real, and the status quo. Deletion won because declared conversion already covers every case.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the `as` respelling as a genuine option after the owner flagged the arrow as unfamiliar. It also rejected auto-derived silent conversions, which D-ERR2's ratified text forbids.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass asked whether the trait could survive as internal machinery. The conversion table already is that machinery, so the trait would be a name with no body.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its best reading — relational, cast-free prose — and credited C with giving the concept a documentable name. Both still lose to one honest rail.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the orphan rule, whose fix text sends owners of neither type to the dead trait. Repaired: a conversion into the default error may name a foreign source and E2406 is retexted, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Every runtime stop is a registered report on every tier
decisions.gist: Whether traps, contracts, require, panic, and #Todo become one registered report family with one renderer.
decisions.lesson: Compile failures are products: 1064 registered codes with what, why, and fix text. Runtime stops have four codes, four renderers, and wording that differs by tier. The JIT drops the source arrow. `?? panic("msg")` prints `panic: panic` under `jet run`. `#Todo` and several raw Prelude panics exit with 101, the code reserved for compiler bugs. This ballot decides whether every stop becomes one registered report, identical on AOT, JIT, the interpreter, and the web tier.
decisions.story: Diego's program stops in CI, which runs the AOT build. He reruns locally with `jet run` and gets different words for the same bug, with no file and line. He greps the codebase for the CI wording and finds nothing he can act on.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build app.jet && ./build/app
panic: the list has 3 items, so position 10 doesn't exist
  --> app.jet:12

$ jet run app.jet
panic: index out of bounds: the index is outside the list

$ jet run port.jet    # n :: load() ?? panic("could not load the port")
panic: panic

options.name: One report family, one renderer
options.detail: Every stop — arithmetic trap, bounds trap, contract failure, `require`, `panic`, `#Todo` — carries a registered code in the E30xx runtime family. One renderer lives in the Prelude, so every tier prints the same words, the same what/why/fix, and the same source arrow. `jet explain` answers runtime codes. Tests can assert a specific stop with `.expect_fail(E3010)`. Web-tier throws carry the same report text. `#Todo` moves from exit 101 to a real stop at exit 70.
options.technical:
Implements I4 at run time and I9 for failure: engines marshal, the Prelude owns the report. The ratified trap message strings from the math slate (for example "divided by zero", D-FLOORDIV1; D-MODSEM1) are kept word for word as the message line. E3001/E3005 keep their codes.

E3001's registered rich frame — the source-line box and the debug-build safe locals (D-OBS1/D-OBS2) — is kept; samples here are abbreviated. The `CmdProve` diagnostic reconstructor, the JIT's own wording in `jet-jit/src/Collections.rs`, and the raw `panic!` sites in the Prelude are deleted or rerouted. Runtime `.err.out` examples join the tier-parity ledger. The `panic:` prefix in spec renderer text becomes the `Stop` frame; no ratified decision pins that prefix.
options.code:
$ jet run app.jet     # identical under jet build, dev, interpreter
Stop [E3010]: the list has 3 items, so position 10 doesn't exist
  --> app.jet:12 in run
 Why: reading past the end of a list has no answer to give.
 Fix: check the position first, or use `list.get(i)` for a maybe-value.

$ jet explain E3010   # works like any compile code

options.name: Unify wording and spans only
options.detail: One renderer and identical wording with the source arrow on every tier, but no registered codes for traps. The `panic:` voice stays. `jet explain` stays compile-only, and tests cannot name which stop they expect.
options.code:
$ jet run app.jet
panic: the list has 3 items, so position 10 doesn't exist
  --> app.jet:12 in run
// same words everywhere, but nothing to explain or assert on

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Four renderers, five runtime codes, tier-different wording, lost arrows, and the 101 collisions stay. Each defect is fixed piecemeal if a card happens to cover it.
options.code:
panic: panic          # jet run, message lost
// #Todo → exit 101, same code as a compiler bug

comparisons.note: Panic messages are free text with no registry. Users search the web for wording, and tools cannot classify stops. Jet's compile side already solved this with registered codes; the runtime side never got the same treatment.
comparisons.code: thread 'main' panicked at 'index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 10'

comparisons.note: A failed runtime check names its check kind (range, overflow, assertion). Naming the kind is what lets proof tools and tests target it.
comparisons.code: raised CONSTRAINT_ERROR : app.adb:12 range check failed

recommendation.why: Registered codes make runtime failure a product with the same guarantees as compile diagnostics: stable wording, an explain entry, a snapshot, and a name tests can assert. One renderer in the Prelude is what I9 already demands — engines marshal, meaning lives once.

whyNot.reason: Fixes the drift but keeps stops anonymous. Tests still assert "something stopped", docs still cannot link a stop, and `jet explain` stays half-blind.
Keeps `panic: panic`, the lost arrows, and #Todo exiting on the compiler-bug code. Every one of those is a live defect with a repro.

recommendation.tradeoff: Registered codes freeze runtime messages as snapshot-tested product copy. Changing a message becomes a deliberate bless, exactly as it is for compile diagnostics. That weight is the point.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full registration, wording-only unification, and the status quo. Registration won because anonymous stops cannot be explained, asserted, or tracked.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested machine-readable stop events and per-tier renderers with shared strings. The first is an output mode inside option A, and the second restates the defect.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested codes for new stops only. Two generations of stops would coexist forever, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass credited B with the cheapest parity fix and C with its live repair cards. Neither gives stops a name.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the web claim, where no process or exit code exists. The guarantee scopes to the report text a thrown error carries, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Contracts run on every tier, erase under proof, and blame the right site
decisions.gist: How #Pre/#Post checks are delivered: which tiers run them, when proof removes them, and where blame points.
decisions.lesson: D-PREPOST1 says contracts are checked in every build. Today only AOT builds check them. `jet run` skips them silently and prints the wrong answer with exit 0. The failure arrow points at the marker line, not the failing call. This ballot decides the delivery: every tier checks, the type system's proofs erase checks it can discharge, and the report blames the party that broke the promise.
decisions.story: Ana adds `#Pre(cents > 0, "cents must be positive")` to a billing function. Her test through `jet run` passes with -100 and ships. The production AOT build stops on the same input. Now she trusts neither the test run nor the contract.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet run fee.jet          #  #Pre(cents > 0, …) on add_fee
total: -95                 # exit 0 — the contract never ran

$ jet build fee.jet && ./build/fee
#Pre contract failed: cents must be positive
  --> fee.jet:1            # the marker line, not the call that broke it

options.name: Every tier checks; proof erases; blame lands right
options.detail: Contracts get a real place in the compiler's middle layer, and the check itself lives in the Prelude, so AOT, JIT, and the interpreter all run the same one. A `#Pre` breach points at the call site, because the caller broke the promise. A `#Post` or `require` breach points at the body, because the callee broke its own. When a range fact already proves the condition — for example the argument is `Int(1..)` — the runtime check is not emitted at all.
options.technical: Delivers "checked in every build" on every tier, and names one amendment to D-PREPOST1: erasure-under-proof joins the ratified explicit per-module strip as a second, proof-keyed disposition. The strip opt-out stays as ratified. Erasure rides the type-system v2 interval plane (D-TYPE2-* are ratified) and mirrors D-TYPE2-REFINE1's move: proof first, check as fallback. The report is D-FAIL-BREACH1's E3005 either way. Requires a TIR contract node; today none exists, which is why two tiers skip contracts.

options.name: Every tier checks; no erasure
options.detail: All tiers run every contract, always. Blame still lands at the right site. No check is removed by proof, so a contract's cost is paid even where the types already guarantee it.

options.name: Make AOT-only the law
options.detail: Amend D-PREPOST1's text down to reality: contracts are an AOT feature, and `jet run` documents that it skips them. Development runs and shipped binaries behave differently by design.
options.code:
$ jet run fee.jet
total: -95            # documented: contracts are off here

comparisons.note: The same Pre/Post annotation is a proof obligation and a runtime check. Proven means erased; unproven means checked. This is the only industrial system where one annotation serves both, and it is the direction option A opens.
comparisons.code:
procedure Debit (Amount : Positive)
  with Pre => Amount > 0;   -- proven: no check emitted

comparisons.note: Contract checking is a build switch, so shipped programs behave differently from tested ones. That is the trap option C would make law.
comparisons.code: -- assertions disabled in release: require clauses vanish

recommendation.why: It delivers what the ratified text already promises, on every tier, and points blame where attribution says it belongs. Erasure makes contracts free exactly where the type system is strong, which rewards writing better types instead of punishing them.

whyNot.reason: Pays at run time for facts the checker already proved, and contradicts the erasure rule knowledge already follows under the ratified type-system slate.
Makes the development-run lie the default. D-PREPOST1's ratified strip is an explicit per-module opt-out; C turns silent skipping into the norm for every `jet run`, the split I9 exists to forbid.

recommendation.tradeoff: With erasure, a contract's runtime cost depends on what the checker proves, so identical-looking calls can differ in cost. The observable behavior never differs: the same breach yields the same report.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared delivery with erasure, delivery without erasure, and codified AOT-only. Erasure won because it matches the ratified knowledge rules.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested folding contracts into validate blocks or refinement types. The ratified D-VALIDATE1 layering forbids the first, and the second reopens more than this slate needs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested erasure-as-lint, keeping every check and warning when provable. It nags exactly the best-typed code, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass credited B with uniform cost and C with truthful documentation. Both still ship a worse promise than the ratified one.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked blame through generated call frames and attacked erasure soundness. Blame uses the nearest user-written frame and erasure keys only on ratified range facts, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Entry fallible by default; errors report and exit 1; 101 is the compiler's
decisions.gist: Whether run() is fallible by nature, and what each exit code means.
decisions.lesson: Programs fail by nature, yet a beginner's first `?` today forces the signature `fn run() => () ?` — ceremony before the first file read. The exits are undesigned too. An untyped entry error prints a bare string and exits 1 with no frame. `CryptoError` gets a full frame and exit 70, or 101 for its Internal case. Every other typed family is refused (E0122). `#Todo` and raw Prelude panics exit 101, the code reserved for compiler bugs. This ballot fixes the entry and the law.
decisions.story: Maya's first program reads a file. The compiler makes her write `=> () ?` before `?` works, and she asks what `()` means on day one. Marco, in CI, has the opposite problem: exit 1 sometimes means a compile error and sometimes a reported failure, and 101 sometimes means a Jet bug and sometimes his own `#Todo`.

options.name: Fallible-by-nature entry; report and exit 1; 101 compiler-only
options.detail:
`fn run()` is fallible by default: `?` works inside with no annotation, ever, for the default case. An unhandled error at the process edge is a value delivered to the operating system. The full report prints with its journey, and the process exits 1: the work failed, the program did not break.

An expert pins the family like any other narrowing: `fn run() ? StoreErr`. A breach or program-side fault exits 70. Exit 101 belongs to Jet's own defects alone: `#Todo` becomes a real stop at 70, raw Prelude panics become reports, and the `CryptoError` special case is deleted.
options.technical:
Named amendments: S80's entry clause (implicit fallible `run`; E0122 and its allow-list die), the architecture exit table's producer column, S36's producer note, and E3001's registered entry text. Exit 70 widens from panic/require to every stop, and exit 1 gains the runtime-reported error. The pinned form rides D-FAIL-UNIT1's spelling.

Deletes the `CryptoError` arm in `Codegen/Items.rs`. Direct `process::exit(70)` sites in the scheduler, streams, and FFI route through the one boundary so cleanup runs. The five code numbers stay; 1 keeps covering "a reported problem" from either compile time or run time.

options.name: Fallible entry, but unhandled errors exit 70
options.detail: Same implicit entry and cleanup, but an error leaving `run` counts as a stop: full report, exit 70. Scripts see one code for "this program did not finish", whether it reported or broke.

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Beginners keep typing `=> () ?` at the entry, the three entry behaviors stay, and the 101 collisions stay as shipped.
options.code:
fn run() => () ? { ... }    // ceremony on day one
// #Todo still exits on the compiler-bug code

comparisons.note: main returning Err prints the error and exits 1; a panic exits 101. The reported-versus-broke split at the process edge is the same one option A draws — but Rust still makes main declare its Result type.
comparisons.code: fn main() -> Result<(), io::Error> { … }   // Err → print + exit 1

comparisons.note: Code 70 is EX_SOFTWARE, "internal software error". A program that cleanly reports a failed job is not an internal error; 1 is the general failure code. Option A matches the convention Jet's table already borrowed 70 from.

A script needs zero ceremony to fail: an uncaught exception prints a traceback and exits 1. The beginner never declares that their program can fail — it simply can. Option A gives that default with a designed report instead of a traceback.

recommendation.why: Programs are fallible by nature, so the default entry says nothing and everything works — the beginner's first `?` costs zero ceremony. At the edge, a reported error and a broken program are different facts with different codes, and 101 finally means one thing: file a Jet bug.

whyNot.reason: Folds "the work failed" into "the program broke", so operators lose the one distinction the failure model exists to draw. It also breaks the sysexits meaning Jet's own table cites for 70.
Keeps day-one ceremony the owner has rejected, user code exiting on the compiler-bug code, and an entry rule that refuses every typed error family.

recommendation.tradeoff: Exit 1 covers both a compile diagnostic and a runtime reported error. Scripts that need the difference read the stderr frame, not the code. Accepted because the five ratified codes stay stable and 1 already means "a reported problem".

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared implicit-entry with exit 1, implicit-entry with exit 70, and the status quo. Exit 1 won because a reported error is not a broken program.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested user-chosen codes and a new dedicated code for runtime errors. The first already exists as core.process.exit, and the second breaks the never-repurpose rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested exit 1 by default with a build-policy switch to 70. A deployment knob on failure meaning is the Rust panic-strategy scar, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass credited B with simpler coarse alerting and C with violating no ratified text. The day-one ceremony and 101 collisions still condemn C.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the implicit entry for hiding fallibility from readers. The entry is one known function whose nature every program shares, and experts pin the family when the fact matters, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: How a fallback sees the error: ambient err, no lambda
decisions.gist: How the fallback after a failed call can read the error it replaces.
decisions.lesson: The fallback operator gives a default, but the error vanishes. The arm table can bind it, but that is many lines for one log call, so people swallow. A lambda binder was drafted and rejected as ceremony. This ballot picks the lightest spelling that lets a fallback see the failure.
decisions.story: Lena reads a port from config with a fallback of 8080. It works. Operations asks her to log why the default was used. Her one-line read must not become an eight-line arm table or a lambda — or she will go back to swallowing on the next file.

options.name: Ambient err inside the fallback
options.detail: Inside a fallback expression, `err` simply names the failure. No lambda, no binder, no parentheses — the upgrade from swallowing to handling costs one word. The name is in scope only inside the fallback, the way `result` is in scope only inside `#Post`. On an optional's fallback there is no failure to name, so writing `err` there is a compile error.
options.technical: `err` is a contextual name bound within the fallback expression of the operator on a fallible value; it is the report (D-FAIL-ERROR1 shape). Shadowing a user binding named `err` raises a lint. Fallible-only; optionals reject it. The ratified `?? (next)` value form (D-ORRETURN-CANON1) is untouched — no binder grammar exists to collide with it. A `return` inside a fallback block returns the fallback value.

options.name: Arm-style binder: ?? e -> expr
options.detail: The fallback may open with a binder and arrow, matching the arm-table shape people already know: `?? e -> expr`. Explicit binding, light ceremony, one new form on the operator's right side.
options.code: port :: read_port() ?? e -> { log.warn("using default port: {e}") ; return 8080 }

options.name: A method: .or_else
options.detail: The operator stays exactly as it is. A method on fallible values takes a function from the error to the fallback. The everyday fallback and the logging fallback use different spellings.
options.code: port :: read_port().or_else((e) => { log.warn("default: {e}") ; return 8080 })

comparisons.note: catch blocks bind `error` implicitly, with no binder written. The closest shipped precedent for an ambient name, and it reads fine in practice — nobody asks where `error` came from.
catch binds the error inline with |err|. Explicit, but the binder ceremony is exactly what makes quick fallbacks skip it.
unwrap_or_else takes a closure over the error — the method-plus-lambda shape option C mirrors, and the reason quick Rust code reaches for unwrap_or instead and drops the error.

recommendation.why: The upgrade from swallowing to handling should cost one word, not a rewrite. An ambient `err` is the magic-with-control pattern Jet already uses for `result` in `#Post`: invisible until needed, fully defined when read, and the lint keeps shadowing honest.

whyNot.reason: The binder and arrow are small but real ceremony on every use, and they buy nothing over the ambient name — the bound value is always the same one failure.
Splits the fallback across two spellings and adds a lambda, so the everyday form and the responsible form look unrelated. That gap is exactly why people keep swallowing.

recommendation.tradeoff: `err` is a name the fallback scope provides rather than one the code binds. The precedent (`result` in `#Post`, Swift's `error`) shows it reads well, but it is one more contextual name to know.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the ambient name, an arm-style binder, and a method. The ambient name won because the upgrade from swallowing must cost one word.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a lambda binder and a guard-style statement. The lambda was rejected by the owner as ceremony, and the guard form restates the arm table.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass asked whether the ambient name and the arm binder should both ship. Two spellings for one job on day one lost.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B as the explicit-binding purist's choice and C as the chain-composition choice. Neither makes the first log line a one-word change.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked shadowing, nesting, and the optional plane. The lint covers shadowing, the innermost fallback owns `err` when fallbacks nest, and optionals reject the name, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Compile time is one Jet program
decisions.gist: Whether the compiler's own rules are written in Jet or stay written in Rust.
decisions.lesson: Jet runs code before your program runs. You write some of it: #Known bindings, derive bodies, and fn build. The compiler writes the rest in Rust: the marker table, the effect roots, the dimension table, and the DSL block list. Both halves do the same job. Only your half can be read, extended, or reflected. This choice decides whether the two halves become one.
decisions.story: Priya writes a payments library. She wants a #Audited marker so every call logs its owner. Today she cannot. The marker table is a Rust array inside the compiler. Her only paths are a build entry that runs at the root, or a fork of Jet. She ships a code-review checklist instead.

options.name: One program: rules are Jet declarations
options.detail: Every rule the compiler applies becomes a declaration in Prelude Jet source. The 99 marker rows, the effect roots, and the dimension table move out of Rust. Users can write their own. Nothing a beginner types changes. Experts gain a surface that is readable, reflectable, and extensible.
options.technical: Policy::APPLIED_RULES retires. Marker names resolve through ordinary name resolution, so there is exactly one parse path. The four checks of D-MARK-FORM1 (vocabulary, site, signature, duplicates) read a declaration instead of a Rust row. This makes D-VERDICT-1455-1 structurally true rather than enforced by CI scan. D-RULEARG-TYPES1=A generates fourteen marker-argument enums from this table; it reads declarations instead, with no change to what it generates.

options.name: State the laws, keep the Rust tables
options.detail: Write the two laws into the spec so future work has one rule to check against. Leave every table in Rust. This costs almost nothing and settles the argument about what belongs at compile time. It gives users no new power and leaves the four registries separate.
options.technical: Law 1 (compile-time code only adds) and Law 2 (proved knowledge erases) enter docs/spec/philosophy.md. D-METAMUTATE1 gets restated as an instance of Law 1. No code moves.

options.name: Fix each defect on its own
options.detail: Treat the findings as a list of bugs. Repair the 30 markers that bypass the registry, merge the two derive engines, and unify the two splice paths. Each fix is small and safe. The closed tables stay closed, and the next feature adds a fifth registry.
options.technical: This is the path already in flight: cards #1456 through #1461. It closes the drift but keeps registration in Rust, so the door D-CTMARKER1 reserves stays shut.

options.name: Markers only
options.detail: Move the marker table to declarations and stop there. Type planes, the rights tree, and build facts keep their own tables. This is the smallest change that opens user markers. It leaves four registries as three, and the same question returns with the next proposal.
options.technical: Fulfills D-VERDICT-1455-1 alone. D-TYPE2-PLANE1, the authority rights tree, and D-CONF-PLANE1 each keep a separate table with the same law.

comparisons.note: The compiler's own reader and expander are Racket programs. This is why a Racket user can extend the language without touching the implementation.
The derive table is closed, so every extension needs a separate proc-macro crate with its own build and its own dependency tree.
comparisons.code: // serde-derive: a whole second crate to add one row

comparisons.note: There is no attribute plane at all. Rules spend keywords instead, which keeps the compiler closed and the keyword set growing.

recommendation.why: You ratified this law twice already. Marker law zero and the plane law both say a rule must be registered, nameable, and reflectable. Option A is the only one that makes both true, because a declaration in Jet is readable by definition. It also deletes six Rust tables instead of adding a seventh.

whyNot.reason: A law with no mechanism is what happened in July. D-MARKSIG1 ruled one registry and the compiler drifted anyway, because nothing failed when it did.
It repairs the drift and keeps the cause. Registration stays in Rust, so the next feature mints a fifth table and the same audit runs again.
It solves the marker plane and leaves three registries stating one law in three places. The cohesion problem is the finding, not a side effect.

recommendation.tradeoff: The Prelude grows and the compiler shrinks. Some rules that are a Rust one-liner today become a declaration plus a body. That is the right trade, because a rule the user cannot read is a rule the user cannot trust.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared moving the tables to Jet against leaving them in Rust. It recommended moving them because two ratified laws already demand readable registration.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the markers-only option and the fix-the-bugs option. It also tested and dropped a generated-declarations path, because a generated file is not writable by users.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested option D as a first phase of option A. That is now the implementation shape, not a separate choice, so the options stayed as written.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting that cards #1456 to #1461 already fund most of the repair. It also strengthened option B.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked compile speed and beginner error quality. Declarations cache like any Prelude item and the four checks are unchanged, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: How generated code is written
decisions.gist: Whether code that Jet generates is written as a string or as real code.
decisions.lesson: Three parts of Jet generate Jet source: user derives, the build entry, and generic modules. Generic modules write real code with parameters. The other two build a string and hand it to the parser. A string is not checked until someone uses it, every brace must be doubled, and the editor cannot help. This choice decides whether all three use one form. What a body holds is decided separately by D-META-BODY1.
decisions.story: Sam writes a derive that adds a summary method to any struct. He spends an hour on a build error that points inside his generated text. The cause is a single brace he forgot to double. The compiler could not tell him sooner, because until expansion his code is just a string.

options.name: Real code with holes
options.detail: A derive body contains Jet members, not a string. The header already names the trait and the type, so no inner impl is written. The parser checks the body when you write it. Braces are braces. The formatter and the editor work inside it.
options.technical: The body parses at definition time into an item template. Splices are typed holes filled at expansion. E2710 disappears as a user-facing class, because generated text can no longer fail to parse. D-CTCODEGEN1 still holds: the filled template enters sema like hand-written source. The derive T.Trait spelling is unchanged, as D-METADERIVE1 requires. b.generate takes the same block of items, so the build entry needs no separate form.

options.name: A code block you can nest
options.detail: Generated code sits inside a marked block that can appear anywhere a value can, including inside the build entry. This is the same idea as option A, but the block is a value you can pass and combine. It is more flexible and adds one concept.
options.technical: A code { … } block is a first-class comptime value of a code type. It composes, so a helper function can return one. This is the quotation form used by Scala 3 and Template Haskell. It sits close to a stage type, which S26 does not currently name.

options.name: Keep strings
options.detail: Leave emit() as it is. Nothing breaks, and the mechanism is already shipped and understood. Every derive author keeps doubling braces, keeps writing quotes inside quotes, and keeps finding mistakes only when someone uses the derive.
options.technical: The re-lex and re-parse path at Bundle.rs:1654-1697 stays, with E2710 as the failure mode. The second splice implementation in apply_dollar_splices stays beside Expr::ComptimeSplice.

options.name: Generic modules do the job
options.detail: Delete derives and express the same work as generic modules, which already take parameters and already hold real code. This removes a mechanism instead of improving one. It cannot read a type's shape, so it cannot replace #Codable.
options.technical: A generic module is parameterised by types and values, never by a type's field list. Making it read TypeInfo would turn it into a derive under another name.

comparisons.note: String mixins let you build source by joining text. Errors point into the joined result, and tools cannot see inside until it is already text.
Scala 2 macros were untyped and unsound. Scala 3 replaced them with typed quotation, which is option B's shape.
A macro returns a syntax tree, not text, so Xcode shows the expansion inline.

recommendation.why: Option A gives every benefit the string form lacks and adds no new concept. The body is code, so the parser, formatter, and editor already know what to do. It also deletes the second splice implementation and the E2710 error class.

whyNot.reason: It adds a code value and moves close to a stage type. A block of items covers both derives and b.generate, so nothing needs a first-class value yet.
Doubling every brace is a tax on every derive author, and the mistake is found by the user of the derive, not its writer.
A generic module cannot read a type's field list, so it cannot express #Codable. Deleting derives would remove capability.

recommendation.tradeoff: A derive body can no longer generate arbitrary text, so a generator that assembles code from a data file must produce items rather than characters. That is the intended limit, and it is what makes the body checkable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared real code against strings and recommended real code, because a string is only checked when someone uses it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the nestable code block and the delete-derives option. It also tested a text form with checked interpolation, which was folded into option C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether option B could ship later on top of option A. It can, because a code value is an extension of an item template, not a different design.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting that emit is shipped, understood, and covered on every execution tier today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested code that must be built from a schema file at build time. Option A handles it by generating items in a loop, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.comment: Both option A and b. A is the simple case, b is the expert case

decisions.title: What a user-written rule may do
decisions.gist: How much power a rule written by a user gets, compared with a rule written by the compiler.
decisions.lesson: A marker applies one named rule to the next thing you write. Today the compiler owns 99 of them and a user owns none, except through a derive, which only works on types and only adds methods. This choice decides what a user-written rule may do: record a fact, add code, or both, and at which sites.
decisions.story: Ravi runs a platform team. Every service function that touches the network must carry a timeout. He can check this in the build entry, but only at the root, and the error points at a function far from the rule. He wants the rule to sit on the function it governs.

options.name: Rules may record facts and add code
options.detail: A user declares a rule with a signature and legal sites, exactly like a compiler rule. A rule with no body records a fact. A rule with a body adds code. This is the same power the compiler has, so #Codable and #Inline stop being special.
options.technical: The four checks of D-MARK-FORM1 run unchanged against the declaration. Law 1 still holds: a rule adds items and facts, and can never change or shadow what the user wrote. Additive-only is checked, not trusted, as D-BUILDGEN1 already requires.

options.name: Rules may record facts and reject code
options.detail: A user rule can record a fact and raise a diagnostic, but never add code. This gives Ravi his timeout rule at the right site with a good error. Nobody can generate code, so #Codable stays a compiler feature and boilerplate stays hand-written.
options.technical: This is D-METADEPTH2's read-only enforcement moved from the build entry down to the attachment site. The diagnostic API keeps the code, what, why, and fix shape that I4 requires.

options.name: Types only, as today
options.detail: Keep the current rule. A user rule is a derive: it attaches to a type and adds methods. Functions, fields, blocks, and files stay closed. This is the smallest change and keeps every current guarantee. Ravi's rule stays in the build entry.
options.technical: known_derive_names stays the only dynamic half of the marker vocabulary, as it is today at Bundle.rs:1234-1239.

options.name: Nothing: the compiler owns every rule
options.detail: Close the door fully and delete user derives too. The vocabulary becomes one closed table with no exceptions, which is the simplest thing to audit. Every library that needs a rule must ship a build entry or a patch, and #Codable-style boilerplate stays a compiler privilege.
options.technical: This retires D-METADERIVE1 and the reserved D-CTMARKER1 door. The registry becomes fully static, so the CI drift guards in D-VERDICT-1455-1 get simpler.

comparisons.note: A derive macro is the successful case because its scope is closed: input is a type, output is an impl. An attribute macro can rewrite the function it sits on, and reading the code no longer tells you what runs.
An annotation processor may add new files and may never change the annotated class. That rule is why reading a Java class is still reliable.
A source generator adds a partial class. The author must open the seam with the partial keyword, so the extension is never a surprise.

recommendation.why: Option A is the only one where a user rule and a compiler rule are the same kind of thing. That is what makes the vocabulary one table instead of two. Law 1 keeps it safe: a rule adds, and can never change what you wrote.

whyNot.reason: It fixes Ravi's case and leaves boilerplate as a compiler privilege. A library author still cannot ship the derive their users need.
It keeps the rule that a derive works on types only, which is why org rules live in the build entry, far from the code they govern.
It removes a shipped capability and makes every library that needs a rule fork the compiler or ship a build entry.

recommendation.tradeoff: A user rule that adds a method can collide with a hand-written one. The collision must be an error naming both sites, which costs a diagnostic and a check. That is the price of not letting generation shadow anything.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full user rules against types-only derives. It recommended full rules, because the closed table is the cause of the drift and the missing surfaces.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the reject-only option and the close-the-door option. It also tested rules limited to new sites, which was folded into option A as a site list.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping option B first and option A later. That is the implementation order, not a separate choice, so the options stayed as written.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D by noting a fully static table makes the drift guards simpler and the audit surface smaller.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether an adding rule becomes an attribute macro. It cannot, because Law 1 forbids changing or shadowing user code, and additive-only is checked.

decisions.title: Who may declare a text block language
decisions.gist: Whether a library may add a checked text block such as GraphQL, the way the standard library adds SQL.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two text blocks: #SQL and #HTML. Inside them you write another language, and Jet checks it. The list is closed to two entries, fixed in the compiler. D-DSLBLOCK1=A ratified that closure to stop libraries from changing Jet's grammar. This ballot asks whether the closure can be narrowed to what it was protecting, without opening the grammar.
decisions.story: Mei ships a GraphQL client. Her users write query strings that fail at run time on a typo. She wants a #GraphQL block that checks the query against the schema at compile time, exactly as #SQL checks a query against a table. She cannot, so her users keep shipping typos.

options.name: Open the text region, keep the grammar closed
options.detail: A library may declare a block rule. Jet reads the block boundary with its own grammar and hands the inside to the library as text. The library checks it and adds code. Jet's grammar never moves, because the braces are always Jet's braces.
options.technical: Amends D-DSLBLOCK1=A. The closure narrows from the marker name to the grammar. STDLIB_DSL_BLOCK_MARKERS retires. The block body is one lexical region delimited by the marker grammar, so no library can change how Jet parses anything outside it.

options.name: Open it, but only under a grant
options.detail: Same power as option A, but a project must permit each block language in its manifest before the block parses. This makes the surface visible in one file per project. It adds a step for every user of every library that ships a block.
options.technical: Amends D-DSLBLOCK1=A and adds a manifest key. The grant rides the existing chain from D-BUILDSCOPE1: flag, then package, then workspace.

options.name: Keep it closed, add rows by ballot
options.detail: The list stays in the compiler. When a block language earns its place, it is added by a decision, as SQL and HTML were. This keeps the audit surface at two entries and keeps every block checked by the compiler team. Mei waits for a ballot.
options.technical: D-DSLBLOCK1=A stands unchanged. Each new row is a syntax decision under I7 and a compiler patch.
options.code:
// Only SQL and HTML exist.
#SQL<Row> { select id from users }

options.name: Retire text blocks
options.detail: Delete #SQL and #HTML and let every embedded language be an ordinary checked function call on a string. This removes a mechanism and one closed table. It also loses compile-time checking of the query, which is the reason the blocks exist.
options.technical: Retires D-DSLBLOCK1 and D-SQL-ARG1. Checking moves to a comptime function over a string literal, which cannot report a span inside the string as precisely.
options.code:
// proposed under D
rows :: sql.query<Row>("select id, name from users")?

comparisons.note: #lang lets a file choose its whole reader. It is the most powerful version of this and the reason Racket tooling must be built per language.
A function-like proc macro takes a token stream, so sqlx can check a query at compile time. The cost is a separate crate and expansion the reader cannot see.
String mixins let any library assemble source text. This is the version Jet refuses, because the grammar and the tooling lose their footing.

recommendation.why: D-DSLBLOCK1 was written to stop third-party grammar mutation, and option A keeps that stop exactly. Jet still parses the block boundary, so no library can change how any other file reads. What opens is the inside of one clearly marked region, which is text either way.

whyNot.reason: The grant protects against grammar mutation, which option A already prevents structurally. It taxes every user for a risk that is no longer present.
It makes every embedded language wait on the compiler team, and the surface frequency audit shows embedded query languages are common work.
It removes compile-time checking of the query, which is the only reason these blocks exist rather than plain strings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bad block library can give bad errors inside its own region. Jet cannot check another language for the author. The block still reports a span, so the error lands in the right place even when its text is poor.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared opening block rules against keeping the closed list. It recommended opening, because the ratified closure protects the grammar and the grammar does not move.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the grant option and the retire option. It also tested a curated registry of blessed block libraries, which was folded into option C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested option A with an opt-out for projects that want no block languages. That belongs in lint policy, not in this decision.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting two entries are trivially auditable, and every shipped block is checked by the compiler team.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether a block rule can become a reader macro. It cannot, because Jet owns the delimiters and the region never extends past them.

decisions.title: One effect model, or two
decisions.gist: Whether compile-time code declares what it touches the same way run-time code does.
decisions.lesson: Run-time code says what it touches with an effect set, written =[FS]=>. Compile-time code says the same thing a different way: a fixed list of allowed calls, three tier names, and its own diagnostics. Two vocabularies describe one idea. There are also two checkers, which report the same mistake as E0951 or as E3401. This choice decides whether they merge.
decisions.story: Lena writes a build step that reads a schema file. She already knows how to declare a file effect, because she does it in every service she ships. At compile time none of that applies. She learns a second vocabulary to say the same sentence.

options.name: One model at both stages
options.detail: Compile-time code declares effects with the same syntax as run-time code. The three tiers stay exactly as ratified, but they stop being a separate vocabulary and become what the effect set already says. One checker, one diagnostic family, one thing to learn.
options.technical: Amends D-CTCORE1: the allow-list of pure Core calls retires, because the effect set already carries the fact. D-CTEFFECT1's tiers are unchanged in meaning. Tier 0 is an empty effect set. Tier 1 is a recorded effect. Tier 2 needs #Impure plus permission. The two checkers at Sema/Purity.rs and Comptime merge, retiring one diagnostic family.

options.name: Merge the checkers, keep both vocabularies
options.detail: Fix the duplication that hurts most: two checkers proving the same property with two diagnostic families. Users still learn tier names at compile time and effect sets at run time, but a mistake now reports once, with one message.
options.technical: Effects.rs's fixpoint absorbs Purity.rs's recursive walk. E3401 and E0951 collapse to one family. D-CTCORE1 and D-CTEFFECT1 stay as written.
options.code:
// Surface unchanged; one error instead of two spellings of it.
#Known cfg :: embed_file("app.toml")

options.name: Keep both
options.detail: Leave the two models alone. Compile-time and run-time really do differ: one runs on the build machine, one on the user's machine. Separate names make that difference obvious. The cost is two checkers, two diagnostic families, and a second vocabulary to learn.
options.technical: D-CTCORE1 and D-CTEFFECT1 stand unchanged. The Purity and Effects duplication stays, as flagged in authority-one-model.md:118.

comparisons.note: build.rs has no effect declaration at all. Any build script may read anything, which is the documented supply-chain hole.
comptime code is restricted by what the evaluator supports, not by a declared effect. The rule is real but unwritten.
comparisons.code: comptime { const x = readFile(); }  // rejected, no declaration involved

comparisons.note: Builds are pure by default and impure inputs must be pinned by hash. This is the same tier idea Jet ratified, expressed once rather than twice.

recommendation.why: The stage a function runs at does not change what it touches. An effect set already says the thing the tier names say, so one vocabulary covers both. This also deletes the allow-list, which is the last place where being allowed at compile time is a hard-coded list rather than a declared fact.

whyNot.reason: It repairs the duplicated checker and leaves the duplicated vocabulary, so a user still learns two ways to say the same sentence.
