recommendation.why: A deletes two spelling islands with one rule the user already knows from functions: <> types, () typed values, :: bound once. The instantiation is literally the D-GENERIC-CALL1 call shape, and fact arguments (D-CONF-MODULE1) land in a value position that looks like one.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the small island and keeps the big one: a mixed angle list that functions forbid, one keystroke away from the function form that works.
Two documented islands, forever, in the feature the settings unification is about to make more common.
Hiding the module keyword saves six characters and costs the reader the item kind. A namespace deserves to announce itself.

recommendation.tradeoff: One mechanical migration touches every generic module in the tree (spec, examples, fixtures), and empty-parens conventions must be documented once. The value-parameter semantics move nowhere; only punctuation does.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full function mirror, the binding-only fix, and the status quo, and recommended the mirror for the one-rule reading.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a #-pin spelling for value params (the number-pin sigil reading) and keyword-free instantiation. The pin spelling died as a third island; keyword-free became option D.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A's declaration with C's = binding. It fixes the list and keeps the binding island, so it lost to full A; B remains for the reverse preference.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C (const-generics familiarity for Rust arrivals; zero migration) and D (S2 uniformity taken to its logical end).
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's call-shape reading: does cache<Int>(64) look like a runtime call at module scope? No — module declarations are item position, where no call is legal, and the module keyword disambiguates, so A survives.

decisions.title: Map type spacing: [K:V] or [K: V]
decisions.gist: Whether the map type is written [K:V] with no space or stays [K: V].
decisions.lesson: The map type is spelled with brackets and a colon. A map from names to ages is [String: Int] today, with a space after the colon, and the formatter enforces that space. This ballot decides whether the type form tightens to [String:Int]. Map literal entries like ["ana": 31] and field declarations like age: Int are separate forms. They keep their spacing unless an option says otherwise.
decisions.story: Sam scans a signature: fn tally(votes: [String: Int]) => [String: Int]. The space inside each bracket pair makes every map read as two pieces, and the whole signature as four. Sam wants each type to read as one compact shape.

options.name: [K:V] in type position
options.detail: Type spellings tighten: [String:Int], including empty-literal heads like [String:Int].{}. A type now reads as one compact unit. Literal entries and field declarations keep their space, so value-position colons stay consistent with fields. The loss: the type no longer mirrors the literal's spacing exactly.
options.technical: Amends the written form of the S64 / D-LISTMAP-CANON1 canonical map type. The formatter emits no space around the colon in type position only. Nested forms follow the same rule: [[U8]:String].
options.code:
votes: [String:Int]
ages :: [String:Int].{}
ages["ana"] = 31
print(["ana": 31])   // literal entries keep the space

options.name: Tight everywhere
options.detail: Types and map literal entries both drop the space: [String:Int] and ["ana":31]. One spacing rule for every map colon. The loss: literal entries stop matching record fields like .{x: 1} and field declarations like age: Int, which keep their space. The inconsistency moves into value code everyone writes daily rather than going away.
options.code:
votes: [String:Int]
print(["ana":31])
point :: Point.{x: 1, y: 2}   // fields still spaced

options.name: Keep [K: V]
options.detail: The status quo. One universal rule with no exceptions: a colon is always followed by a space, in types, literals, and fields alike. The loss: type signatures stay visually wide, and a map type keeps reading as two pieces.
options.code: fn tally(votes: [String: Int]) => [String: Int] { ... }

comparisons.note: Dictionary types are written tight.
comparisons.code: var votes: [String: Int]   // Swift's own formatter keeps the space

comparisons.note: Type hints keep a space after the colon only in annotations, not in dict display.

recommendation.why: A map type reads as one compact shape, the way Sam scans it, while every value-position colon keeps the one-space rule it shares with fields.

whyNot.reason: Tightening literals breaks their rhyme with record fields and field declarations, so the spacing inconsistency moves into everyday value code.
The type form stays wide, and a signature with two maps keeps reading as four fragments.

recommendation.tradeoff: The type no longer mirrors the literal exactly: [String:Int] against ["ana": 31]. That gap is accepted because type position and value position already read differently.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared tightening the type form against the status quo and recommended the tight form because a type should scan as one unit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added tight-everywhere as option B. Spacing both sides of the colon ([K : V]) was also tried and cut as a wider spelling nobody asked for.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A width-dependent hybrid - tight when short, spaced when long - was rejected. Spacing that depends on content makes two spellings of one type.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The status quo gained its strongest case: one universal colon rule with zero exceptions is the easiest rule to teach and to format.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack used nested and generic forms such as [String:Lru<K, V>], where inner commas still carry spaces. The tight bracket pair still delimits the map cleanly, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Alias declarations: bind with :: or keep =
decisions.gist: Which mark a type alias uses: the binding mark :: or the current =.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two marks for giving something a value. name :: value binds a new name. name = value changes something that already exists. A type alias introduces a new name for a type. Today the alias line spells it with the update mark: alias Parsed<T> = T ? AppError. This ballot decides whether alias keeps = or moves to the binding mark ::.
decisions.story: Mia is three days into Jet. She learned that total :: 0 binds a new name and total = total + 1 updates it. Then she reads alias Parsed<T> = T ? AppError in a teammate's file and pauses. Nothing is being updated here, so why the update mark?

options.name: Keep alias X = Y
options.detail: The alias line keeps =. It reads like the alias forms in Rust, TypeScript, and Go, so imported habits work unchanged. It also matches the function expression body fn f() => T = expr, where = likewise means 'is defined as'. The loss: = does two jobs. In statements it updates an existing thing, but on an alias line it introduces a name.
options.code:
alias Parsed<T> = T ? AppError
alias Rows = [[String]]

retries :: 3          // a new name binds with ::
retries = retries - 1 // = updates it

options.name: Bind with alias X :: Y
options.detail: One rule: every new name arrives through ::. The alias line reads exactly like a value binding, so what Mia learned on day one carries over. = keeps its single job of updating what already exists. The loss: people arriving from Rust or TypeScript will type = out of habit, and the alias line no longer matches the function body =.
options.technical: Amends D-TYPEALIAS1 spelling only. Scope is unchanged: transparent aliases for shortening generic spellings, not newtypes. A diagnostic on alias X = Y offers the :: fix.
options.code:
alias Parsed<T> :: T ? AppError
alias Rows :: [[String]]

retries :: 3   // same mark, same meaning: a new name

options.name: Drop the keyword: Parsed<T> :: T ? AppError
options.detail: A type alias becomes a plain binding whose right side is a type. It is the shortest spelling. The loss: nothing marks the line as an alias, so a reader cannot tell a type alias from a value binding until they resolve the right side. The keyword also fences aliases to their ratified narrow scope, and losing it opens a side door toward general type programming.

comparisons.note: Type aliases use =.
Every compile-time definition - constants, types, procedures - binds with ::.
Type aliases use =.

recommendation.why: Every new name in Jet arrives through one mark. A beginner who knows retries :: 3 reads the alias line correctly on first sight, and = keeps its single job of updating what already exists.

whyNot.reason: It keeps = doing two jobs. The alias line looks like an update but updates nothing.
Without the keyword a type alias is indistinguishable from a value binding at a glance, and the fence that keeps aliases in their narrow ratified scope loses its anchor.

recommendation.tradeoff: The alias line now differs from Rust and TypeScript muscle memory, and from the function body form fn f() => T = expr, which keeps its ratified = spelling.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping = against binding with :: and recommended :: because an alias line introduces a name rather than updating one.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added dropping the keyword entirely as option C. A colon-free alias X Y form was also tried and cut as unreadable rather than genuinely distinct.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid accepting both marks on alias lines was rejected. One construct with two spellings breaks the one-spelling rule (S14).
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option A gained its strongest case: = matches the ratified function expression body and every mainstream alias syntax, so imported intuition works unchanged.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack pressed the function body = as a counterexample to 'definitions bind with ::'. The claim was narrowed to name introduction - the body = defines a body, not a name - and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Expression fences: expand integer-literal ranges
decisions.gist: Whether $[0..3]$ in an expression fence expands to one entry per number.
decisions.lesson: A fence repeats a statement once per entry: print(pick_str($[0, 1, 2, 3]$)) runs four prints. Binding fences already accept a name range: $[ t1..t8 ]$ makes eight names. But in an expression fence, 0..3 is a single Range value, so $[0..3]$ makes one statement copy that receives a Range. This ballot decides whether integer-literal ranges expand into entries, and how a real Range still passes through a fence.
decisions.story: Priya tests a function against inputs 0 through 9. She writes print(pick_str($[0..9]$)) expecting ten runs, because $[ t1..t8 ]$ taught her that fences understand ranges. She gets one run, with a Range as the argument.

options.name: Integer-literal ranges expand; parentheses keep a Range
options.detail: A bare ascending integer-literal range entry expands to one entry per number: $[0..3]$ means $[0, 1, 2, 3]$, matching the binding-fence rule. To pass a real Range through a fence, parenthesize the entry: $[ (0..3) ]$ stays a single Range value.
options.technical: Expansion applies only when both endpoints are integer literals and the range ascends: lo..hi with lo <= hi, or lo..<hi with lo < hi. Any other range entry is a normal expression entry. The formatter keeps entry-level parentheses around a range entry - they carry meaning there. Amends D-VERDICT-1320-1; binding-fence rules and E0369 are unchanged.
options.code:
print(pick_str($[0..3]$))    // pick_str(0), pick_str(1), pick_str(2), pick_str(3)
run($[ (0..3) ]$)             // one copy: run(0..3) with a Range value

options.name: Status quo: a range entry is a Range value
options.detail: No change. Every expression entry substitutes token for token, so 0..3 stays one Range argument and repeated inputs are written out. The gain: zero special cases in the fence rule. The loss: the binding fence and the expression fence read the same but treat a range differently, which is the trap Priya hit.
options.code:
print(pick_str($[0, 1, 2, 3]$))   // spell out every input
run($[ 0..3 ]$)                    // one copy: run(0..3)

options.name: Explicit expansion mark
options.detail: Bare ranges stay Range values. A marked entry expands - for example $[ each 0..3 ]$ becomes four entries. The gain: no bare spelling silently changes meaning, and expansion is visible at the entry. The loss: a second mark for a meaning the binding fence already carries bare, so the common case pays ceremony.
options.code:
print(pick_str($[ each 0..3 ]$))   // four copies, marked
run($[ 0..3 ]$)                     // one copy: a Range value

comparisons.note: The ratified precedent: a range in a binding fence already means one name per step.
Hardware languages expand a literal range into repeated statements at compile time.
comparisons.code: for (i = 0; i < 4; i = i + 1) begin : gen ... end

recommendation.why: Both fence positions keep one story - a range in a fence means one entry per step - and the parenthesized escape keeps every Range expressible.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the trap Priya hit: the same spelling means expansion in one fence position and a single value in the other.
It adds a second mark for a meaning the binding fence already carries bare, so the common case pays ceremony to avoid an ambiguity parentheses already resolve.

recommendation.tradeoff: Parentheses become meaningful inside a fence entry: $[0..3]$ and $[ (0..3) ]$ differ. That is accepted because passing a literal Range through a fence is rare, and the parenthesized spelling states it plainly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared bare expansion against the status quo and recommended expansion so both fence positions treat a range the same way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added an explicit expansion mark as option C. Comptime expansion of any known iterable was considered, folded into C as its natural extension, and set aside as scope creep.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid expanding literal ranges bare while requiring a mark for computed ranges collapsed into option A, which restricts expansion to integer literals outright.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The status quo gained its strongest case: token-for-token substitution with zero special cases is the simplest possible law and stays literally true.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack pressed the parenthesized escape: a formatter that strips parentheses would silently change meaning. Option A now names the formatter obligation to keep entry-level parentheses, and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Two markers spell #Policy: pick the one owner of the name
decisions.gist: Which mechanism keeps the name #Policy: call wrappers, or compiler rules.
decisions.lesson: D-CALLPOLICY1 ratified #Policy(retry(3), trace("users.load")) as the marker for callable wrapper chains. A shipped marker already spells #Policy(no_alloc): a scoped compiler rule, legal at the same grammar position. Same name, two meanings. The ratified ballot never checked against the shipped marker. Separately, D-AUTHORITY-MEM1 already retires four of the old marker's six keys, so the old #Policy is shrinking either way.
decisions.story: Ana reads a codebase and sees #Policy(no_alloc) on one function and #Policy(retry(3)) on the next. One forbids the function something at compile time; the other wraps its calls at run time. Nothing on the page says these are different machines.

options.name: One grammar, told apart by argument shape
options.detail: Both meanings keep the name. A bare name like no_alloc means a compiler rule; a call like retry(3) means a wrapper chain. No rename, no migration. The cost is a silent rule: adding parentheses to an argument flips which machine reads it, and no error says so.
options.code:
#Policy(no_alloc)          // compiler rule
#Policy(retry(3))          // wrapper chain
#Policy(no_alloc, retry(3)) // both machines, one list

options.name: Rename the wrapper marker
options.detail: The shipped compiler-rule marker keeps #Policy. The new wrapper marker takes a fresh name: #Wrap, #Around, #Apply, #Relay, or #Escort. This reopens D-CALLPOLICY1's spelling, ratified two days ago, and the wrapper cards re-land on the new name.

options.name: Retire the old marker; #Policy means wrappers only
options.detail: MEM1 already moves the four memory keys onto the rights tree as denials. The two survivors follow their own laws home: the unsafe permission becomes an authority manifest entry, and explicit_units becomes a typed setting on the fact plane. The PolicyKey table deletes, and #Policy has exactly one meaning: the ratified wrapper chain.
options.technical: no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded, gc: rights-tree denial rows per D-AUTHORITY-MEM1 and D-AUTHORITY-MEM2. unsafe: an allow/deny entry in the authority manifest per D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1. explicit_units: a typed setting per D-CONF-KEY1. Scope inheritance (organization to block) rides the manifest and scope law that already governs those planes. The denial row rides the signature effect arrow, in the return position. It never stands above a function; only markers stand there.

options.name: Merge: compiler rules join the wrapper chain grammar
options.detail: One registry row, one list: #Policy(no_alloc, retry(3)). Compiler rules and runtime wrappers become entries of one chain. The reader still cannot tell which entry does what, and the two behaviors share nothing but a comma.
options.code:
#Policy(no_alloc, retry(3), trace("users.load"))
+fn load_user(id: UserId) => User ? DbErr { ... }

comparisons.note: Decorators wrap calls, and linter pragmas constrain code, and they never share a name. The split option C creates is the split Python already has.
Attributes share one syntax for both kinds, like option A, and readers must know each attribute to know its machine.

recommendation.why: Every old key already has a better home under this week's ratified law, so the collision resolves by finishing that migration. The name then has one meaning, the newest ratified spelling stands unchanged, and no shape rule or rename is needed.

whyNot.reason: A silent shape rule flips meaning when parentheses appear, with no error. Two machines behind one name is the confusion, not a fix for it.
It reopens a spelling the owner ratified two days ago, and the newest ruling owns the name.
Compile-time constraints and runtime wrappers share nothing but a comma. One list with two behaviors hides which entry does what.

recommendation.tradeoff: The old marker cannot delete until the unsafe and explicit_units keys land in their new homes, so #1396 gains two small dependencies on the authority and settings cards.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared shape disambiguation, renaming the new marker, retiring the old marker, and merging, and recommended retiring the old marker because its keys already have ratified homes.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review hunted more options: banning #Policy at Function scope for rules, and a mandatory prefix like #Policy(rule: no_alloc). Both were folded into A as tactics, since each still leaves two machines behind one name.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested C plus a temporary shape rule during migration. Rejected: greenfield law forbids a transition grammar, and the migration is one coherent change.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with a rich name menu (#Wrap, #Around, #Apply, #Relay, #Escort) and confirmed any of them reads well at the call site. B still reopens a two-day-old ratification.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked C's claim that every key has a home: unsafe and explicit_units were unhoused. The ballot was repaired to name their exact destinations, the manifest and the settings plane, and the recommendation survives with those two dependencies made explicit.

decisions.title: The spawn surface: four spellings, or the ratified taskgroup block
decisions.gist: How Jet code starts tasks and fans work out.
decisions.lesson: Two ratified decisions, D-CONC-JOIN1 and D-CONC-SCHED1, already cite a spawn surface named D-CONC-SPAWN1. That ballot was never raised. The ratified D-CONC-GROUP1 blessed the older taskgroup block instead. The board now holds two spawn surfaces, and each one deletes the other's work. This ballot settles which one is law, so the concurrency implementation cards can start.
decisions.story: Rio writes a crawler. They want many fetches in flight with a cap of four workers. Today they import core.tasks, open a taskgroup block, and wrap every call in a lambda. They ask why starting work needs this much ceremony when calling a function needs none.
decisions.inWild:
use core.tasks as tasks
taskgroup g {
    a :: g.task => sum_range(1, 25)
    b :: g.task => sum_range(26, 50)
    results :: g.all([a, b])
    print(results[0] + results[1])
}
h :: tasks.spawn(() => work())
h.join()

options.name: Four spellings: task, all, race, any, group
options.detail: Starting work looks like calling a function. No import, no lambda wrapper. task f() starts one child. all, race, and any fan out and need no handles. group g(limit: n) covers dynamic counts with a worker cap. The taskgroup block, g.task, g.all, and tasks.spawn are deleted. D-CONC-GROUP1's law survives: a group may still be named in any borrow position, now as the Group value.
options.technical: task expr spawns a child of the current scope; an unbound handle is joined at scope end per D-CONC-JOIN1. all/race/any keep their ratified fail-fast, cancel-losers, first-Ok meanings. group g(limit: N) { } joins every child at the closing brace. Group can never be stored. Amends the spelling of D-TASKSCOPE1, D-NURSERY1, D-CONCCOMB1, and D-TASKGROUP-PARAM1; their laws carry over.

options.name: Keep the ratified taskgroup block
options.detail: D-CONC-GROUP1 stays as ratified and the proposal's spawn section is struck. Spawning keeps the core.tasks import, the taskgroup block, and the lambda wrapper. D-CONC-JOIN1 and D-CONC-SCHED1 must then be corrected, because their ratified text and code samples show the four spellings.
options.code:
use core.tasks as tasks
taskgroup g {
    a :: g.task => sum_range(1, 25)
    b :: g.task => sum_range(26, 50)
    results :: g.all([a, b])
}
h :: tasks.spawn(() => work())
h.join()

options.name: Handles only: task everywhere, combinators as calls
options.detail: One spawn form: task f() returns a handle. all, race, and any become ordinary functions over handles, not blocks. The grammar gains one form instead of four. The cost: race and any must not start work early, so their arguments go back inside lambdas, and every fan-out is handle bookkeeping.
options.code:
a :: task sum_range(1, 25)
b :: task sum_range(26, 50)
(x, y) :: all(a, b)

winner :: race(() => slow(), () => fast())

options.name: One keyword, nested: task, task.all, task.race, task.any, task.group
options.detail: Option A surface, spelled under one keyword. task f() starts one child. task.all, task.race, and task.any fan out with no handles. task.group g(limit: n) covers dynamic counts. Only task becomes a reserved word; all, race, any, and group stay free for user names. This spelling came from owner feedback on this ballot.
options.technical: Same laws as option A: scope-end joins per D-CONC-JOIN1, the ratified fail-fast, cancel-losers, and first-Ok meanings, and group joins at the closing brace. The parser reads task and an optional selector, so the grammar gains one head form, not four. Autocomplete after task. lists the whole concurrency surface.

comparisons.note: launch and async inside a coroutineScope block; children are joined at scope end, like option A's group.
async let spawns a child with no lambda; TaskGroup covers dynamic counts. Swift ships both, close to option A.
comparisons.code:
async let a = sumRange(1, 25)
print(await a)

recommendation.why: It keeps everything option A wins: spawning reads like calling a function, and the two newest ratified decisions keep their surface. It reserves one word instead of four, so all, race, any, and group stay available as user names.

whyNot.reason: It reserves all, race, any, and group as block keywords. Those are common user identifiers; any and all are everyday function names.
It keeps the import and lambda ceremony, and it forces corrections to two newer ratified decisions that already show the bare spellings.
Fan-out becomes handle bookkeeping, and race and any need lambdas again so they do not start work early. The ceremony returns through the back door.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every fan-out site pays a short task. prefix, and D-CONC-JOIN1 and D-CONC-SCHED1 need their code samples respelled to the nested forms.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the proposal's four spellings with the ratified taskgroup block and recommended the four spellings, because two newer ratified decisions already cite them.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a handles-only surface, which became option C, and a keep-both surface. Keep-both was folded out because two spawn forms for one job break the one-mechanism rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested four spellings plus a kept tasks.spawn expert call. It lost: task f() already is the low-level form, so the extra call would duplicate it exactly.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose block is explicit about scope and keeps ratified text, and C, which is the smallest grammar. Each still pays lambda ceremony at every spawn.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the four new grammar forms of A as scope creep against formatter round-trip and tier parity. All four lower to the same scheduler calls that exist today, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Where a bounded arena limit lives after memory keys leave #Policy
decisions.gist: How code declares: this function may allocate at most N bytes.
decisions.lesson: D-AUTHORITY-MEM1 chose option B: memory floors become effect denials, written =[!Mem.Alloc]=> on functions and deny: [Mem.Alloc] in manifests, and the memory keys leave #Policy. The ratified option text left one hole it named itself: arena_bounded(65536) carries a number, and denial rows carry none. Until the number has a home, the memory-floor implementation card cannot start.
decisions.story: Sam ships a firmware package for a device with 64 KB of spare RAM. The embedder asks for a written promise: this package never allocates past that line. Sam had #Policy(arena_bounded(65536)); after MEM1 that spelling is retired and nothing yet replaces it.

options.name: Parameterized denial row
options.detail: The denial row grammar gains arguments. A plain denial stays =[!Mem.Alloc]=>; a bounded one is =[!Mem.Alloc(above: 65536)]=>, and manifests write deny: [Mem.Alloc(above: 65536)]. One mechanism carries both the floor and the number, in the one place a reader already checks.
options.technical: The rights tree row for Mem.Alloc accepts an optional above: Bytes argument. The authority gate records the number in the audit ledger with the denial. Sema enforces the unbounded form statically where it can and the bounded form at the allocator, on every tier. The row rides the signature effect arrow, in the return position, never a line above the function.

options.name: A typed setting on the fact plane
options.detail: The bound becomes a typed build fact, arena_ceiling :: Bytes, on the settings plane the build/config law just created. The denial row stays parameterless. The reader must now check two places to learn one memory law: the row for the floor, the setting for the number.

options.name: One surviving #Policy spelling for bounds
options.detail: #Policy(arena(65536)) stays only for the bounded case. This reopens what MEM1 retired two days ago: the memory keys were removed from #Policy so that memory law has one mechanism. The friendly spelling returns, and so does the second mechanism.
options.code:
#Policy(arena(65536))
fn decode_frame(input: Bytes) => Frame { ... }

options.name: No declarative bound: an arena API in code
options.detail: The bound is not a declaration. Code opens a bounded arena and runs inside it: arena(65536).run { }. Simple and explicit, but a manifest can no longer promise a cap to an embedder, which is the case MEM1 exists for.

comparisons.note: Allocation bounds are values in code: a FixedBufferAllocator over a fixed buffer, like option D. Zig has no declarative package-level cap.
comparisons.code:
var buf: [65536]u8 = undefined;
var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buf);

comparisons.note: The cap is an external runtime flag (-Xmx), not a fact the code carries. Nothing in the package declares it.

recommendation.why: MEM1 chose one mechanism for memory law: the rights tree. Giving the denial row an argument keeps the number inside that one mechanism, visible at the same line a reader already checks, and the audit ledger records it with the denial.

whyNot.reason: It splits one memory law across two planes, so the floor and its number live in different places and can drift apart.
It reopens the retirement MEM1 made two days ago and restores the second mechanism that vote removed.
It loses the declarative promise. A package could no longer state its cap to an embedder, which is the very case this law serves.

recommendation.tradeoff: The row grammar gains arguments, and every consumer of rights rows — sema, the gate, the audit ledger, reflection — must carry the number through.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a parameterized row, a settings-plane fact, a surviving #Policy key, and a code-only arena API, and recommended the parameterized row for staying inside MEM1's one mechanism.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a refinement-type spelling on the function's return type and a comptime assertion. Both were folded out: they state the bound where no embedder or manifest can read it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested row-plus-API: the declarative row for promises and the arena API as its runtime enforcement. That is not a separate option; option A already implies an enforcing allocator, so the pairing was noted inside A's technical text.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: typed settings are real law now and give the bound a typed home with provenance. It still leaves the floor and the number in two places.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether above: opens the row grammar to arbitrary predicates. The repair is a closed argument list registered per right, and with that fence the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Task failure: the one ? rail, or a separate outcome type
decisions.gist: What a program reads when a task it waits on has failed.
decisions.lesson: Today a task failure hides in strings: exception() returns text like "cancelled", and a child panic can kill the process. The ratified D-CONC-OUTCOME1 answered this with a separate TaskOutcome type read through outcome(). The final proposal replaced that with a simpler law: join() is fallible like any other call, on the same ? rail every other error uses. The two answers delete each other's work, so one must win before the outcome card can be built.
decisions.story: Priya fans out three scrapes and one times out. She wants the other two results and a fallback for the third. Today she compares exception() against the string "cancelled" and hopes the spelling never changes.

options.name: join() is fallible: T ? TaskFailure
options.detail: One rail for every error in the language. join() returns T ? TaskFailure, so ?? gives a fallback and the arm table tells failures apart. TaskFailure is a normal enum: .Cancelled, .DeadlineBlown, .Panicked(reason). It converts up to app error families like every other error. trace(), exception(), and the separate TaskOutcome and TaskStatus types are deleted.
options.technical: all { } returns its tuple on the same rail. A joined child's panic becomes .Panicked(reason) instead of killing the process. Conversion rides the one rail of D-FAIL-CONV1. Amends D-COROUTINE1's handle surface and retires D-CONC-OUTCOME1's TaskOutcome/TaskStatus surface.

options.name: Keep the ratified TaskOutcome type
options.detail: D-CONC-OUTCOME1 stays as ratified: outcome() consumes the handle and returns a typed TaskOutcome, with TaskStatus for the running states. Failure reading is a second door beside the ? rail: results travel one way, task failures another. The trace() and exception() strings still retire.

options.name: Failure on the rail, plus a status() probe
options.detail: join() returns T ? TaskFailure as in option A. A non-consuming status() probe is added for liveness: running, paused, finished. Failure travels the one rail; watching a live task is a separate read. The probe is a second window onto the task, and supervisors are its only known reader today.

comparisons.note: JoinHandle.await returns Result<T, JoinError>; JoinError tells cancellation from panic. The same one-rail shape as option A.
try await task.value throws like any call; CancellationError rides the normal error path.

recommendation.why: A task failure is an error, and Jet's failure law says every error is one report on one rail. With option A the fallback, the arm table, and the conversion rules a person already knows all work on tasks unchanged.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a parallel concept beside results: a second consuming read with its own type, which ?? and error conversion cannot touch.
The probe adds a second window whose one known reader is a supervisor, and the service-plane cards own supervision. The core task type should not carry it.

recommendation.tradeoff: D-CONC-OUTCOME1, ratified days ago, is retired, and the outcome-card work already sliced against it must be re-sliced onto TaskFailure.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the ratified TaskOutcome type with fallible join() and recommended the rail, because it reuses the failure law instead of adding a parallel concept.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested exceptions, a status-code integer, and callback-style completion handlers. All were dropped: each is a second failure vocabulary that the ratified failure law forbids.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option C: rail plus a liveness probe. It stays on the menu because liveness is a real need, but supervision cards already own it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose consuming outcome() is race-free and whose enum is honest. It still leaves the fallback operator and error conversion useless on tasks.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a joined child that panics, which must become .Panicked(reason) on every tier instead of killing the process. That work equals what OUTCOME1 needed, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: String's remaining 34 ledger gaps: decline, ship, or ship the high-frequency few
decisions.gist: Which of String's 34 remaining ledger names ship directly on String, and which route to an existing mechanism.
decisions.lesson: Card #1476 gave String 30 methods. The surface ledger still lists 34 more names other languages ship on their string type. Each name already has a Jet route somewhere else. The usage-frequency report (docs/research/corelib-api-usage-frequency-2026-08-06.md) ranks how often real code performs each operation. Jet's philosophy sets friction in proportion to that frequency: the most common work must be the shortest call.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a log cleaner in Jet. She trims a line, then wants the number inside it. She types line.trim().to_int(), the way Ruby's to_i chains, and wonders whether Jet forgot number parsing on text or expects a detour through another type.

options.name: Decline all 34, route each to what Jet already ships
options.detail: None of the 34 names add a workflow Jet is missing. Mutation verbs like clear and push do not fit an immutable String. Sequence names like map, fold, and first already exist on List and Iter once text becomes a list of characters or bytes. parse, tofloat, match, and matches already live on Int, Float, and core.regex. concat duplicates the plus operator and interpolation. The rest are niche buffer operations two languages ship, covered today by slice, replace, and the shipped surface.
options.technical:
Immutable-string declines: clear, push, pop, remove, and write. String is an immutable value. Rebuild text with plus, replace, or slice instead of mutating it in place.

Iter and List declines: all, map, fold, skip, chunk, droplast, indexed, flatmap, each, max, min, scan, first, last, get, and codepointat. These are sequence operations, not text operations. Call chars or bytes first, then use the existing List or Iter method.

Number-parsing declines: parse and tofloat. Int.parse and Float.parse already convert text to a number with one error type.

Pattern-matching declines: match and matches. core.regex already owns pattern matching under D-REGEXENGINE1.

Concatenation decline: concat. The plus operator and string interpolation already join text.

Validity decline: isvalid. A live String is always valid UTF-8 by construction. String.from_bytes already reports invalid bytes as an error when text is built from a byte buffer.

Niche buffer declines: replacerange, isprint, intern, indexofany, lastindexofany, chop, and rpartition. Each is a low-traffic operation only two of eleven compared languages ship.

options.name: Ship all 34 as new String methods
options.detail: String grows a second copy of the Iter vocabulary, a second parse path, and a second match method, all living beside the mechanisms Jet already ships elsewhere. Every text tutorial now has to say which of two spellings to use for map, parse, or match, and the answer changes by container.
options.technical: Each of the 34 names ships as a string_method_return case in Collections.rs plus a matching jet_str_* Prelude function in UnicodeString.rs. Sequence names like map, fold, and first duplicate the List/Iter case arms already registered for those same names. parse and tofloat duplicate Int.parse and Float.parse. match and matches duplicate core.regex.is_match and core.regex.matches. concat duplicates the existing plus operator lowering for String plus Add.

options.name: Ship the high-frequency names as direct spellings; route the rest
options.detail:
The frequency report marks parse-to-number as a dominant string operation and regex tests as heavy, recurring work. Those names ship directly on String: to_int and to_float (the ledger's parse and tofloat, spelled to match to_string) plus match and matches. Each one is a spelling of a mechanism Jet already ships — Int.parse, Float.parse, and the one core.regex engine — so no second mechanism appears.

Every other name stays routed. Mutation verbs clash with immutable String. Char-level sequence work sits below the frequency line, where one chars() call is proportional friction. concat stays declined because plus and interpolation are already the shortest spelling.
options.technical:
to_int() and to_float() call the same Prelude parse functions Int.parse and Float.parse use today. They return the same result with the same error meaning. matches(pattern) answers a yes-or-no test by routing to core.regex.is_match. match(pattern) returns the first match through the same engine. Both carry the engine's existing bad-pattern error shape.

Declines unchanged from option A: mutation verbs (clear, push, pop, remove, write); the sequence family, still one chars() or bytes() call away; concat; isvalid; and the niche buffer names.

comparisons.note: Ruby puts number parsing and regex tests straight on String, the shape option C adopts. Jet keeps the parse error where Ruby's to_i silently returns 0 on junk.
Kotlin's CharSequence mirrors most of Iterable, so all, map, and first exist twice: once as a sequence operation and once as a string operation.
Rust keeps text parsing on the destination type through FromStr, the route option A keeps and option C shortens with a direct String spelling.

recommendation.why: The frequency report shows parse-to-number is everyday string work and regex tests recur constantly. Option C makes those the shortest possible calls, which is what friction-proportional-to-frequency demands. Underneath, each new name is a spelling of one existing mechanism, so the expert model stays single-engine.

whyNot.reason: It weighs all 34 names the same and leaves dominant operations behind a detour, taxing the most common text work to keep a rule tidy.
It ships a second copy of the sequence vocabulary and synonyms that save no keystrokes, growing what a beginner must learn without cutting friction anywhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: Docs must say plainly that to_int, to_float, match, and matches are the one parse mechanism and the one regex engine. Char-level sequence work still detours through chars().

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped the 34 names into six families, each already answered by an existing Jet mechanism, and recommended declining all of them.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked isprint and indexofany for a real gap instead of a duplicate. Both still routed to an existing mechanism or a two-witness niche buffer method.
reviewPasses.hybrid: After the owner's philosophy question, this pass was rerun with the usage-frequency report as the scale. Parse-to-number and regex tests crossed the dominance line, and that split became option C, now the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: shipping the full 34 would let a newcomer type any name they already know without a detour. Option C keeps that welcome exactly where the traffic justifies it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked option C as reopening dual mechanisms. It survives: the four new names call the one parse mechanism and the one regex engine, and every still-declined name keeps a one-call route.

decisions.title: Set's last 4 order-dependent methods: decline, ship all, or ship the order-producing pair
decisions.gist: Whether Set answers shuffle, sort, indexof, and indexed directly, when a Set keeps no positions.
decisions.lesson: Card #1478 shipped 11 more Set methods and closed most of the surface ledger. Four names remain: shuffle, sort, indexof, and indexed. A hash-backed Set keeps no positions, so today all four route through to_list. The usage-frequency report ranks sorting among the most common operations in all real code, and dedupe-then-sort is an everyday idiom. A fifth name, flatten, stays declined either way: Set elements must be Hash and Eq, so a Set can never hold nested containers.
decisions.story: Sam is building a card-shuffling game in Jet. The deck lives in a Set so duplicate cards are impossible. Sam types deck.shuffle() expecting a shuffled hand back, the way deck.to_list().shuffle() already works, and wonders why Set itself has no shuffle.

options.name: Decline all 4, route through to_list
options.detail: None of the 4 names add a workflow Jet is missing. shuffle and sort already exist on List. Calling to_list first, then shuffle or sort, reaches the exact result Set.shuffle or Set.sort would compute. indexof and indexed ask for a position, and a hash Set keeps no position for any element. A direct answer would only expose an implementation detail, not a meaning a caller can rely on.
options.technical:
shuffle, sort: both already exist on List, and Set already converts to a list. A Set-native shuffle or sort would be a second spelling of the same List call, reached one method earlier.

indexof, indexed: Rust's HashSet keeps no stable enumeration order across inserts and removals. A Set-native indexof or indexed would return a real Int, but that Int would carry no meaning beyond this one call. A List's index or enumerate answers over a sequence with a real position instead.

flatten: declined regardless of outcome. Diagnostic E0506 requires Set elements to implement Hash and Eq, so a Set element can never be a list or another set. flatten needs a Set of nested containers to unpack, and Jet's type checker never allows that Set to exist.

options.name: Ship all 4 on Set with a documented arbitrary order
options.detail: Set gains shuffle, sort, indexof, and indexed directly. Each one runs by first walking the Set in whatever order Rust's HashSet currently keeps, then applying the same List logic. The docs would say the starting order before shuffle or sort is arbitrary, and that indexof or indexed answers that same arbitrary order.
options.technical: Each of the 4 names ships as a new sema case, routed through the same to-list-then-List machinery already built for filter, map, fold, each, all, min, and max. indexof and indexed need one more caveat in the docs: the position they return stays valid only until the next add or remove on that Set.

options.name: Ship sort and shuffle, each returning a List; decline indexof and indexed
options.detail:
sort and shuffle both turn an unordered Set into an ordered List, and that is a real, common step: dedupe with a Set, then sort the result. Both ship directly on Set and return a new List, running the same List logic to_list plus sort runs today.

indexof and indexed stay declined for meaning, not tidiness. A hash Set has no positions, so the number they return changes after any add or remove. Code that needs positions converts to a List, where the position is real.
options.technical:
Set.sort() and Set.shuffle() route through the same to-list-then-List machinery already built for filter, map, fold, each, all, min, and max. Each returns a fresh List and never mutates the Set. sort's output is deterministic no matter what internal order the Set walks. shuffle's output is uniform for the same reason.

indexof and indexed stay declined: Rust's HashSet keeps no stable enumeration order, so any Set-native position is an implementation leak dressed as an answer.

comparisons.note: Kotlin's Set inherits Iterable, so sorted and withIndex exist on Set too, always over an unspecified encounter order.
Swift's Set exposes sorted and enumerated the same way, both documented as running over the Set's undefined order.

recommendation.why: Sorting is a top-tier operation in the usage-frequency report, and a Set exists to dedupe, so Set-to-sorted-List is among the most common things a Set does. Option C makes that one call while running the same List mechanism underneath. It still refuses to hand back a position that means nothing.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a top-tier operation behind a to_list detour on every dedupe-then-sort, taxing the most common Set workflow to avoid a second spelling of one mechanism.
indexof and indexed would return positions that silently change after any mutation. That reads like a real index, and a beginner has no way to know it is not.

recommendation.tradeoff: Set gains two names whose results are Lists, not Sets. Docs must say the input order never matters: sort is deterministic and shuffle is uniform.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped shuffle/sort with indexof/indexed as one order-dependent family and recommended declining all four through to_list.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked whether sort deserves its own bucket, since a sorted result is deterministic regardless of a Set's internal order. That split later became the seam option C ships along.
reviewPasses.hybrid: After the owner's philosophy question, this pass was rerun with frequency as the scale: sort and shuffle ship directly, while indexof and indexed stay out. The earlier sort-only hybrid grew to include shuffle because both produce an order rather than pretending to read one.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: shipping all four lets a newcomer from Kotlin or Swift type the name they already know without a to_list detour, and matches those two languages exactly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether Set.sort hides the arbitrary internal order from learners; the output is fully determined by the elements, so it does not. It re-confirmed declining indexof and indexed, since to_list keeps the arbitrary order visible instead of minting an index that quietly changes.

decisions.title: Iter's last six ledger gaps: decline or ship
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adds six more Iter methods that rename features it already has, or add a second consumption model.
decisions.lesson: Card #1479 gave Iter thirteen new methods. The surface ledger still lists six more names other languages ship on their iterator type. Five of the six are synonyms: fill, cycle_n, and duplicate are repeat; tostring is join; clip and iterator are to_list and collect; compact is filter. The sixth, next, asks for a hand-held cursor Jet's Iter model does not have. Jet's philosophy sets friction in proportion to frequency, and a synonym cuts no friction: the canonical call is already the same length.
decisions.story: Sam is porting a Python generator pipeline to Jet. Python's iterator protocol calls next(it) by hand to pull one item at a time and keep the cursor between calls. Sam reaches for it.next() on a Jet Iter and finds nothing, then wonders whether Jet's iterators are missing basic stepping.

options.name: Decline all six, route each to what Jet already ships
options.detail: None of the six cuts any friction. The five synonyms rename calls that are already one short method under the canonical name, so shipping them saves zero keystrokes and doubles what a reader must learn for each capability. next would add a second, stateful way to consume a sequence beside the for-loop and the lazy adapters. Every workflow next serves already has a one-call route: chunk for pairwise reads, take and skip for bounded steps, a loop for walking.
options.technical:
Synonym declines: fill/cycle_n/duplicate -> Iter.repeat(n). tostring -> Iter.join(sep). clip/iterator -> Iter.to_list()/collect(). compact -> Iter.filter(f).

Consumption-model decline: next. Jet's for-loop and iterator adapters consume a full Iter value each time; there is no live cursor object a caller holds and advances by hand. Adding next(self) would need a second, stateful iterator protocol running beside the existing one — a second mechanism for the same job, unlike the one-mechanism spellings above.

options.name: Ship all six as new Iter methods
options.detail: Iter grows five methods that duplicate repeat, join, to_list, and filter under new names. It also grows a sixth, next, that adds a stateful cursor object living beside the existing for-loop and lazy-adapter model. Every sequence workflow now has two ways to repeat, render, materialize, and filter. It also gains a new way to walk a sequence that behaves differently from every other Iter consumer.
options.technical:
fill, cycle_n, and duplicate each ship as one more case in Iter's method table. Every one calls the same repeat logic repeat already uses.

tostring ships as a second text-rendering method beside join. clip and iterator ship as two more spellings of to_list and collect. compact ships as filter with a fixed predicate.

next ships as a new stateful method with a held cursor value and a new Prelude function. It also needs matching AOT, JIT, and interpreter lowering that mutates and returns that cursor across calls. No other Iter method has this shape.
options.code:
nums :: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

five_pairs := nums.fill(2)
line := nums.tostring()
materialized := nums.clip()
nonzero := nums.compact()

it := nums
first := it.next()
second := it.next()

comparisons.note: Python's next(it) advances a live generator/iterator object and raises StopIteration at the end; Jet's for-loop and lazy adapters already own that walk without exposing a mutable cursor.
comparisons.code:
it = iter([1, 2, 3])
first = next(it)
second = next(it)

comparisons.note: Ruby's Array#cycle(3) repeats the whole array three times, the same job Jet's repeat(n) already does under a different name.

recommendation.why: Friction in Jet shrinks in proportion to frequency, and every operation these six names cover is already one short call under its canonical name. A synonym cuts nothing and grows the beginner surface. next would buy a second consumption model whose workflows already have one-call routes.

whyNot.reason: Shipping the six saves no keystrokes anywhere, since repeat, join, to_list, and filter are already the same length. It adds five duplicate names to learn plus a stateful cursor unlike every other Iter consumer.

recommendation.tradeoff: A programmer arriving with fill, compact, tostring, clip, or next as muscle memory looks up the canonical name once. If a stepping workflow ever appears with no one-call route, the answer is a new adapter, not a cursor.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped the six names into a synonym set (four names already answered by repeat, join, to_list, or filter) and a model-mismatch case (next), recommending decline for both groups.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked whether next could ship as a read-only peek instead of a full stateful cursor. A peek still needs somewhere to remember the last position between calls, which is the same held-cursor problem, so the finding stood.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid shipping the synonym names as thin aliases was tested and dropped. An alias saves no keystrokes, since the canonical call is the same length, so it fails the friction-per-frequency test while doubling the names a beginner must learn.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: a newcomer typing fill, compact, tostring, clip, or next by muscle memory from another language would find it immediately instead of detouring to repeat, filter, join, or a for-loop.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether declining next leaves a real workflow stranded. Every pattern the six names cover already has one working route — pairwise stepping is one chunk call — so no workflow is stranded.

decisions.title: The small-cluster ledger's 75 remaining names: decline or ship anyway
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adds 75 competitor names across 15 small modules that a check already found a working route for.
decisions.lesson: Card #1481 checked 81 rows the surface ledger flagged as missing across 17 small modules. Four were real gaps and now ship. The other 75 already have a working Jet route. Two lenses grade every row. First, frequency: does declining tax a path real code takes often? Second, name quality: is Jet's existing spelling actually the better API? Where a competitor's spelling is better, Jet replaces its own name outright — it never keeps two.
decisions.story: Priya ports a Go service to Jet. She reaches for sync.Lock, testing.Run, and reflect.Set out of habit, and cannot find any of them under core.sync, core.testing, or core.reflect. Each time the missing name turns out to already have a working Jet answer, once she knows where to look.

options.name: Decline all 75; keep whichever spelling is the better API
options.detail:
Every one of the 75 names already reaches its result in equal or fewer keystrokes under Jet's canonical name, so declining taxes no frequent path. The only cost is one docs lookup, and the core-library reference names the existing route beside each declined name.

Each pair was also judged on merit: had a competitor spelling been the better API, Jet's would be replaced outright, never aliased. In this sweep the current names win or tie every head-to-head: v4 over uuid4, query_one over first, next over read, float_range over uniform.
options.technical:
core.sync (12 names: broadcast, clear, lock, put, rlock, signal, trylock, unlock, wait, thread, timer, locked). Jet's core.sync is CRDT data sync — SyncText, SyncCounter, SyncMap, SyncList. The competitor evidence is Go, Python, and Ruby's sync or threading package: Mutex, RWMutex, Cond, Event. That is a different domain; it only shares the word "sync". Jet's safety design omits raw shared-memory locks. core.tasks owns concurrency instead. put duplicates the already-shipped map_set.

core.encoding.xml (9 names: close, copy, end, flush, indent, name, nodetype, write, clear). close, flush, and write already ship as XMLWriter.finish, flush, and write. end, indent, name, and nodetype ask for incremental SAX-style tag control. Jet parses every format into one shared DataTree value instead, by design (D-SERDE13=B). copy and clear each have one witness language and no consistent competitor meaning.

core.process (8 of 9 names: id, kill, wait, spawn, output, success, exitcode, start). id, kill, wait, spawn, output, and success already ship on ProcessChild, ProcessResult, and ProcessSpec. exitcode already ships as ProcessResult.code. start already ships as ProcessSpec.spawn(). Only exited, a non-blocking poll, was a real gap. It ships with this card.

core.db (8 names: close, commit, name, first, raw, rollback, copy, count). close, commit, and rollback already ship on DBConnection and DBScope. first already ships as query_one(). count duplicates query(...).len(). raw would open an unaudited escape from the portable DB-plugin-wire protocol every backend goes through. name and copy have no consistent competitor meaning.

core.testing (7 names: benchmark, fail, main, run, runtests, skip, stop). Jet already defines and runs tests through #Test and #Bench marker blocks, plus the jet test and jet bench commands. Every one of these 7 names asks for that same capability, spelled as a function call instead of a marker.

core.reflect (8 names: clear, copy, equal, get, set, getfile, getmodule, loadfile). reflect.of(x) is deliberately a read-only structural snapshot. It keeps no runtime type registry and allows no field write by string name (I1). get, set, clear, copy, and equal would all need that registry. getfile, getmodule, and loadfile ask for dynamic runtime code loading, which a compiled, ahead-of-time language does not do.

core.http (4 names: cancelrequest, copy, first, postform). first already ships as HTTPHeaders.first. postform already ships as the request builder's .form(...) call. cancelrequest duplicates the deadline every request already takes. copy has one witness language.

core.tls (4 of 6 names: start, handshake, verifyhostname, copy). start already ships as tls.client(). handshake happens inside client() automatically, by design; there is no separate step. verifyhostname is mandatory already, visible as TLSPeerIdentity.verified_server_name; Jet gives no way to turn it off. copy has one witness language. The other 2, ciphersuites and tlsversion, are real gaps needing a native TLS-bridge change; they move to a follow-up card, not this ballot.

core.uuid (3 of 5 names: join, uuid1, uuid4). uuid4 already ships as v4. uuid1 is MAC-address-based, an older and weaker format; Jet declines it in favor of the already-shipped, safer v7. join matches no real UUID operation in any compared language. parse and v5 were real gaps. They ship with this card.

core.binary (2 names: pipe, readchar). JetReader is a fixed in-memory byte-buffer parser (D-SHIFT1), not a stream. pipe asks for a stream-to-stream copy, a different mechanism. readchar asks for character decoding, which belongs to core.text's Cursor, not a byte reader.

core.encoding.csv (3 names: flush, read, fieldsizelimit). flush already ships as CSVWriter.flush. read already ships as CSVReader.next, matching every other stream reader's name. fieldsizelimit already ships as the shared EncodingLimits.max_item_bytes, one cross-format limit instead of a CSV-only one.

core.random (2 names: random, uniform). Both already ship, as float() and float_range(a, b).

core.args (2 names: parse, parseargs). Both already ship as ArgsSpec.parse(argv), Jet's one declarative CLI-parsing route.

core.encoding.json (1 name: dump). Already reachable as to_string() plus a file write, or the streaming JSONWriter.

core.mem (2 names: replace, copy). replace duplicates the take operator (^) plus assignment, which already swaps a value out. copy has one witness language and duplicates plain assignment for Copy values.

options.name: Ship all 75 as new, second spellings
options.detail: Every declined name ships anyway, even where Jet already reaches the same result another way. A newcomer from Go, Python, or Ruby can type the exact name they already know, in every one of the 15 modules, without learning Jet's existing spelling first.
options.technical: Each name ships as its own new function or method. Where a Jet spelling already exists, the new name routes to the same result. v4 stays, and uuid4 becomes a second name for it; query_one stays, and first becomes a second name for it. Where none exists yet, real new surface ships instead: raw shared-memory locks for core.sync, dynamic module loading for core.reflect, a second XML DOM alongside DataTree for core.encoding.xml.
options.code:
// Every module keeps its existing name AND gains the competitor's name.
uuid.v4()
uuid.uuid4()              // new: identical result, second spelling

reader.next()
reader.read()              // new: identical result, second spelling

// Modules with no existing answer gain a new mechanism outright.
lk := sync.Lock.new()
lk.lock()                  // new: a raw mutex, alongside CRDT SyncMap

v := reflect.of(config)
v.set("port", 9090)        // new: field write by string name, breaks I1

comparisons.note: Go's sync package is OS-level locking; its separate CRDT-style types live in third-party packages. Jet keeps the CRDT half under core.sync and the safety half under core.tasks, never both under one name.
unittest defines a test as a class with methods Python's own runner discovers and runs. Jet's #Test marker plus jet test plays the same role without a base class to inherit.

recommendation.why: Declining costs no friction anywhere: every one of the 75 results is already equal or fewer keystrokes under Jet's canonical name. The sweep's four real gaps ship with the card, and the two real TLS gaps moved to a follow-up card, so real friction still gets fixed. Safety declines (raw locks, reflect writes) keep the beginner default safe: concurrency routes through core.tasks, and reflection stays read-only by design.

whyNot.reason: It gives every reader two names for one result while cutting no friction, since the existing call is already as short. For core.sync and core.reflect it also reopens raw locks and string-keyed field writes that Jet's safety design deliberately left out.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reader who reaches for a familiar name from Go, Python, or Ruby and does not find it must learn Jet's existing spelling once. docs/reference/core-library.md names the existing route right next to every declined name.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped the 75 names by module and matched each to its existing Jet route, recommending a decline with the route named for every one.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked whether any module deserved a partial ship — for example shipping core.sync's raw lock as an expert escape hatch. Declined: Jet's whole concurrency story routes through core.tasks, and a second raw-lock mechanism would fork that story for one competitor package.
reviewPasses.hybrid: After the owner's philosophy question, every pair was regraded by frequency and by name quality, and no declined name beats its Jet route on either scale. The regrade also fixed the standing rule: when a competitor's spelling is the better API, Jet renames its own, never aliases.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: a beginner arriving from Go or Python reaches for the name their prior language taught them, and if that name does not exist, they have to search. That friction is real for exactly one lookup per name, once.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Shipping reflect.set or a raw core.sync lock as an audited #Unsafe escape hatch was tested and dropped. No request for either has ever reached the backlog, so it would be speculative scope, not a real gap.

decisions.title: What a Library output hands to another language
decisions.gist: Whether Jet can be compiled into a library that C, Python, or Swift calls directly.
decisions.lesson: D-LIB-REUSE1=B already settled how Jet reuses Jet. Sealed package objects restore from cache, and no binary layout is promised. It said nothing about the other direction. Today nothing lets a C or Python program call into compiled Jet code. Jet's foreign-function work all runs inbound: Jet calls C, Python, Dart, and Rust through generated bridges. This choice decides whether the arrow ever points outward, and through which door.
decisions.story: Marcus maintains a log parser for a data team. He rewrote it in Jet and it is four times faster. The team's pipeline is Python and will stay Python for years. He wants to ship the parser as something their Python code imports, without rewriting the pipeline or standing up a server.
decisions.inWild:
# what Marcus wants to hand his team
import flightlog

records = flightlog.parse(open("gate.log", "rb").read())
print(len(records), "records")

# what he can do today: nothing.
# Jet reads C, Python, Dart and Rust.
# Nothing reads Jet.

options.name: WebAssembly is the only door out
options.detail: Library stays a Jet-to-Jet output. Any other language reaches Jet through the sandboxed WebAssembly component Jet already builds. One export path, one safety story, no new memory contract. Marcus ships a component, and his team loads it with a Python WebAssembly runtime.
options.technical: Reuses target: plugin (D-PLUGIN1=B, D-DEP-WASM1=A) and its ApiFreeze-frozen pub surface (D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1=A). No native artifact, no header, no calling convention of Jet's own. Host capabilities stay at zero, so the guest cannot open files or sockets.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
name: "flightlog"
target: plugin

pub fn parse(bytes: [Byte]) -> [Record] { … }

$ jet build
  built target/flightlog.wasm (component)

# Python side needs a wasm runtime and a byte copy per call
import wasmtime

options.name: Native library plus a C header
options.detail: Library can also produce a static and a shared native library, with a generated C header beside it. The exported surface is the entry module's pub items. Any language with a foreign-function interface can call it. Marcus gets a .so and a .h, and writes the Python wrapper himself.
options.technical: The boundary uses the C calling convention, not a Jet ABI. Jet promises nothing about its own layout, so the no-stable-ABI stance under D-LIB-REUSE1=B is unaffected. The exported surface freezes through Sema::ApiFreeze, so a breaking change is a diagnostic. Ownership of returned buffers is stated in the header and enforced in sema.

options.name: Native library plus generated bindings per language
options.detail: Everything in the header option, plus Jet generates the caller-side binding file for each language you name. Marcus writes no wrapper. He names python in the output, and jet build produces the module his team imports. The same generator that reads foreign libraries today runs in reverse.
options.technical: Mirrors the ratified inbound binder direction (D-FFI-UNIFY1=A, D-FFI-PY1=A) with one shared surface description. The native artifact and the C header are still produced, so a language with no generator is never blocked. Binding files are build outputs, never checked-in source. The frozen pub surface is the single source for header, bindings, and version check.

options.name: Cross a process boundary, never a memory boundary
options.detail: Jet never links into a foreign process. Other languages reach Jet by running it as a service and calling it. Jet generates the client for the caller's language. No memory contract ever crosses a language line, so no foreign bug can corrupt Jet's heap. Marcus ships a small service and a Python client.
options.technical: Reuses the ratified Service output and service topology (D-SERVICE1=D, D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A). Transport is local by default. No header, no calling convention, no shared allocator. Every call pays serialisation and a context switch.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
outputs: .{ api: .Service.{ entry: serve, clients: [python] } }

$ jet build
  built target/flightlog-service
  built target/clients/flightlog.py

# Python side
import flightlog
records = flightlog.connect().parse(data)   # over a local socket

comparisons.note: Emits staticlib and cdylib with a C boundary. Callers get a header, and each ecosystem builds its own wrapper generator on top, such as PyO3 or cbindgen.
c-archive and c-shared build modes generate the header for you, but the runtime must start before the first call.
Exports to C only through explicit annotations, and its own stable interface stays Swift-to-Swift.
comparisons.code: @_cdecl("parse") public func parse(_ p: UnsafePointer<UInt8>) -> Int32

comparisons.note: export fn produces a C symbol, and the generated header is a first-class build output rather than a side tool.
comparisons.code: export fn parse(ptr: [*]const u8, len: usize) callconv(.C) i32 { … }

recommendation.why: Generated bindings are the only option where the caller writes no glue. It also finishes an arrow Jet already draws in the other direction, using the same frozen public surface for the header, the bindings, and the version check.

whyNot.reason: A WebAssembly component forces the caller to adopt a runtime and copy bytes across the guest boundary. Marcus cannot hand his team something they simply import.
A raw header stops one step short of usable. Every ecosystem then writes its own wrapper generator, which is the same work done many times outside Jet.
A process boundary adds a socket, a lifecycle, and serialisation cost to a call that was a function. It also cannot serve a caller who must run in one process, such as a game host.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet takes on the ownership rules at the boundary: who frees a returned buffer, and what a foreign caller may hold across calls. That contract is stated in the exported surface and checked in sema, so it is a design cost, not a safety hole.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared no native export, a C header, generated bindings, and a service boundary. It recommended generated bindings because the caller writes no glue and the inbound binder machinery already exists.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a Jet-specific foreign protocol, a C++ class surface, and a Python-only special case. All three folded into the bindings option as generator targets rather than separate owner choices.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed the bindings option already contains the header option, so both artifacts ship together and a language with no generator is never blocked. It also kept the WebAssembly path alive for untrusted callers, since that path is already ratified law.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option: WebAssembly gives one safety story, a header is the widest common denominator, and a service isolates faults completely. Each remains the strongest choice for its own audience.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked layout leakage and buffer ownership. The boundary uses C's frozen convention rather than Jet's, and the exported surface must state ownership so sema can check it.

decisions.title: What a loaded Jet library is allowed to do
decisions.gist: The powers a Jet library gets when a running Jet program loads it.
decisions.lesson: D-LIB-REUSE1=B ratified that a Jet program can load a Jet library while it runs. Both sides must come from the same compiler version, and a mismatch is a checked error. It did not say what the loaded code may then do. Jet already has a second way to load code: a sandboxed WebAssembly plugin with zero host powers, and no gate to widen that. Two ways to load code need one clear boundary between them.
decisions.story: Rosa ships a flight-sim game in Jet. She wants community aircraft mods that run at full speed inside her render loop. A mod needs to read its own model and texture files. It must never read her players' save files or open a network socket she did not expect.

options.name: Declared effects, granted at load
options.detail: A loadable library declares what it does, in the same way any Jet package does. The host states what it grants when it loads one. A library asking for more than the host grants is refused before it runs, with a clear error. Rosa grants read access to the mods folder, and nothing else.
options.technical: Reuses the existing package effect declaration and effect checking (the machinery behind E1258). The compiler already proves a package cannot use an effect it did not declare, so the declaration in the artifact is enforceable, not advisory. Load compares the artifact's declared effect set against the host's grant, then refuses or proceeds. Artifact provenance and signature verification come from D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1=D.

options.name: Loading native code is an audited trust decision
options.detail: Loading a Jet library is a trust act the host author signs, in an audited region with a written reason. The loaded code then runs with the host's full powers. Untrusted third-party code must use the sandboxed WebAssembly plugin instead. Rosa writes one audited line, and accepts every mod she ships.
options.technical: Spelled like the existing audited region: an explicit block with a required reason string, which appears in audit output. No effect comparison happens at load. The sandboxed plugin path stays the only route for code the host author has not vetted.

options.name: Same powers as linking
options.detail: A loaded library behaves exactly like a library linked at build time. Same process, same powers, no gate and no ceremony. Whoever loads it takes responsibility. Rosa writes one line and every mod can do whatever her game can do.

options.name: Same contract as the sandboxed plugin
options.detail: A loaded Jet library gets exactly what a WebAssembly plugin gets: no host powers at all. The host passes in every value the library needs, and takes back every result. The two loading paths then differ only in speed and portability, never in what code may do. Rosa hands each mod its textures and gets back draw commands.
options.technical: One capability law across both substrates, matching the ratified zero-capability plugin contract and its E1258 refusal to widen. All input and output crosses the boundary as values. No ambient file, network, process, or clock access exists inside a loaded library.

comparisons.note: dlopen gives the loaded object every power the process holds. Nothing is declared and nothing is checked.
A guest gets only the imports the host passes in. This is the model Jet's ratified plugin target already follows.
comparisons.code: // host chooses which imports exist; the guest cannot reach anything else

comparisons.note: The security manager tried to police loaded code at run time with a policy file. It was deprecated for removal because run-time policy proved unenforceable in practice.
Mod hosts hand the guest a restricted environment table. Enforcement is a convention of the host, not the language.

recommendation.why: Jet's compiler already proves a package cannot use an effect it did not declare. That turns the declaration inside an artifact into an enforceable fact, so the host can grant a precise set instead of choosing between all powers and none.

whyNot.reason: An audited trust act is all-or-nothing at the load site. It teaches hosts to sign one blanket reason rather than say what a mod may do.
A mod can then read save files and open sockets the host never intended, and nothing in the artifact or the audit output says so.
Zero powers blocks the ordinary case of a mod reading its own assets, and it copies the WebAssembly contract without adding anything the WebAssembly path lacks.

recommendation.tradeoff: The grant is only as good as the artifact's provenance, because a file that was not built by this compiler could claim anything. That is acceptable because the load already verifies compiler identity, digest, and signature before mapping anything.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared granted effects, an audited trust act, unrestricted loading, and full sandbox parity. It recommended granted effects because Jet's effect checking makes a declared set enforceable rather than advisory.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a signed publisher allowlist, a per-call permission prompt, and a separate process per mod. The first folded into provenance checks, and the other two were dropped as run-time policy Java already proved unworkable.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested granted effects combined with an audited region for hosts that want no gate. The audited form collapses into a grant of everything, so it needs no separate spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option on its own terms. Unrestricted loading is simplest, sandbox parity gives one law for both substrates, and an audited act names a human behind every load.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked forged effect declarations and stale grants. Compiler identity, digest, and signature verification happen before mapping, so a forged artifact fails the pin rather than the grant.

decisions.title: How a package asks for a loadable library, and what it is called
decisions.gist: The word for a loadable Jet library artifact, and where a person asks for one.
decisions.lesson: D-LIB-REUSE1=B ratified that Jet can build a library another Jet program loads while it runs. Nothing yet says how a person asks for one, or what the file is called. Jet already has nine closed output kinds, and Library is one of them. The manifest vocabulary is also settled: a package states its facts in text, and commands act on them. This choice fits the new artifact into that vocabulary before any parser work starts.
decisions.story: Rosa is setting up her flight-sim game for community mods. She opens a mod package's manifest to say what it should build. She wants one obvious line, and she wants a reader of that manifest to know at a glance that this package ships something loadable.
decisions.inWild:
# a community mod package, today
name: "skyhawk"
version: "0.3.1"
deps: .{ simkit: "^4" }
outputs: .{ ??? }        # nothing here means "a thing Rosa's game loads"

# and on the command line
$ jet build
  built target/skyhawk          # an executable. not what Rosa needs.

options.name: A field on the Library output
options.detail: Library already exists as an output kind. A field on it says this library is also loadable at run time. No new word enters the language, and a reader sees the fact in the manifest. The file is called skyhawk.jetlib.
options.technical: Adds one manifest field to the ratified Library output payload under D-ECO-OUTPUT-PAYLOAD1=A. The closed nine-kind set from D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A stays closed. No token, keyword, or sigil enters Syntax.rs, so I7 needs only this decision identifier. Suffix candidates for the owner: .jetlib, .jlib, .jetso, .pylon.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Library.{ entry: Skyhawk, loadable: true } }

$ jet build
  built target/skyhawk.jetlib (Jet 1.4.2)

# the host
mod := Mod.load("./mods/skyhawk.jetlib")?

options.name: Its own output kind, named for the mount
options.detail: A loadable library is a different thing from a library you link, so it gets its own name in the closed set.
