An aircraft carries an external store on a pylon, and a pylon is cleared for one airframe. That matches a file cleared for one compiler version. The file is called skyhawk.pylon.
options.technical: Adds a tenth kind to the closed Output set, which D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A explicitly allows by ratified addition. Kind-name candidates for the owner: Pylon, Hardpoint, Jetway, Pod, Attach. Matching suffix follows the chosen noun.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Pylon.{ entry: Skyhawk } }

$ jet build
  built target/skyhawk.pylon (Jet 1.4.2)

# the host
mod := Mod.load("./mods/skyhawk.pylon")?

# a stale file
error[E1xxx]: skyhawk.pylon was built by Jet 1.4.1; this program uses Jet 1.4.2
  fix: rebuild the mod with the same Jet version

options.name: A build flag, nothing in the manifest
options.detail: The package says nothing. Whoever builds it asks for the loadable form on the command line. This keeps the manifest vocabulary untouched, and lets one package be built either way. The file is called skyhawk.jetso.
options.technical: One new value on an existing build flag, with no manifest field and no new output kind. The fact lives only in a build invocation, so a reader of the package cannot see it. Suffix candidates for the owner: .jetso, .jso, .jetlib.
options.code:
# pkg.jet — unchanged
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Library.{ entry: Skyhawk } }

$ jet build --emit shared
  built target/skyhawk.jetso (Jet 1.4.2)

# and Rosa's build script must remember the flag, forever
$ jet build          # silently builds the linkable form instead

options.name: Any library is loadable, with no declaration
options.detail: Nothing is declared and no flag is passed. Any Library output can be loaded, and the compiler produces the loadable form when a host asks for it. The least ceremony possible. A package cannot state that it is not meant to be loaded.
options.technical: The loadable artifact becomes a derived output of every Library, produced on demand and cached under the same artifact identity. No manifest field, no flag, no new kind. Package authors lose the ability to refuse run-time loading.
options.code:
# pkg.jet — unchanged, nothing added ever
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Library.{ entry: Skyhawk } }

# the host names a package, not a file
mod := Mod.load("skyhawk")?
  # builds or restores the loadable form on first use

comparisons.note: The manifest declares the artifact shapes, and the file suffix follows the platform.
A build mode flag decides, and nothing in the module file records the choice.
The package manifest names the product and its kind explicitly.
Loadable code is the normal unit and needs no separate declaration, which is the closest match to the no-declaration option.

recommendation.why: A field on Library keeps one word for one concept and keeps the ratified nine-kind set closed. The fact stays in the manifest where a reader finds it, which is the settled rule that facts live in text.

whyNot.reason: A tenth kind splits one concept into two words. Every reader must then learn when a library stops being a Library.
The manifest no longer says what the package ships. The fact survives only in build scripts, which is exactly where facts get lost.
Every library silently becomes a loading target, and an author has no way to refuse. Run-time loading is a real surface and should be stated.

recommendation.tradeoff: The word Library then covers both a package you link and a file you load. That is acceptable because both are the same code, and the field says which artifacts the build produces.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a field on Library, a new output kind, a build flag, and no declaration at all. It recommended the field because it adds no new word and keeps the fact in the manifest.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a marker on the entry module, a separate loadable manifest file, and a naming convention by folder. All three moved the fact away from the output list without making it clearer.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a field plus an override flag for one-off builds. The flag adds a second source for one fact, so the field alone stands.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option. A dedicated noun reads well aloud, a flag keeps one package flexible, and no declaration is the shortest path for a mod author.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the field for overloading one word across two artifact shapes. Both shapes come from the same code and the same frozen surface, so one word stays honest.

decisions.title: The select wait in valid Jet syntax
decisions.gist: How Jet spells waiting on several channels at once.
decisions.lesson: D-CONC-CHAN1 was ratified with a note from you. The direction stands: channels are builtin values, a loop drains a receiver, and waiting on several sources becomes an arm table. But the worked spelling in that ballot is not valid Jet. S68 law says if is the only branching keyword. S68 arm heads are values, patterns, or Bool expressions, never a binding paired with a source. This ballot picks the spelling that makes the ratified wait table real inside that law.
decisions.story: Kofi writes a worker. It drains a job queue, listens for a control message, and retries after 100ms of silence. He wants wait code he can read once and trust, in the same shape the rest of his Jet code uses.

options.name: select is the readiness table
options.detail: A new select table stands beside if. The if table branches on values. The select table branches on which source is ready. Each arm head is a binding and a source, in the exact shape the drain loop already uses. An after arm takes a normal time value. An optional else arm makes the wait non-blocking. The chain, the dead read arm, and the group requirement are deleted.
options.technical: Amends one S68 sentence: if remains the only value-branching keyword, and select is the one readiness table. Arm heads are binding, source pairs mirroring loop binding, source. after takes any Time delta expression (D-TYPE2-TIME1=A). else fires when no source is ready at entry. Expression position follows the if value-table law: arm results unify, or the table yields unit. select is reserved only at statement or expression head. Member and field names such as query.select() stay legal. A closed source stops matching. Cancellation at the wait follows D-CANCELMODEL1=C.

options.name: A Core function and the if table
options.detail: No new keyword. A builtin function waits on the sources and returns one event value. The existing if table then tells the arms apart. The event type names its arms by position, because a type cannot borrow the names of your local bindings. Every wait costs one extra line, and the arms read First and Second instead of jobs and control.
options.technical: tasks.select2, tasks.select3, and so on, one per arity, each returning a generated enum with positional variants plus TimedOut. after is a named argument taking a Time delta. The if dispatch over the result is ordinary S68. No parser or grammar change.

options.name: The readiness table rides subjectless if
options.detail: No new keyword. A subjectless if table whose arm heads are a binding and a source is the wait. A comma head can never be a Bool expression, so the parser knows this table waits. The table shape, the after arm, and the else arm are exactly option A's. The cost: an if statement can now block, and the reader learns that from the arm shape, not the keyword.
options.technical: Amends the subjectless table law (D-IFGUARD1): a table whose every head is binding, source is one atomic readiness wait. Mixing readiness heads and Bool heads in one table is a registered diagnostic. after takes a Time delta expression (D-TYPE2-TIME1=A). else fires when no source is ready at entry. Expression position follows the if value-table law. The whole table compiles to one wait, so there is no test-then-read race. select stays a free identifier everywhere. Cancellation at the wait follows D-CANCELMODEL1=C. A closed source stops matching.

options.name: Merge the sources, loop the result
options.detail: Waiting on several sources becomes stream composition. A merge builtin joins the sources into one stream, a tick source supplies the timeout, and the drain loop is the wait. Repeating waits read well. A single one-shot wait still needs the merge, a next call, and the same positional variant names as option B.
options.technical: merge(a, b, ...) yields a stream of a generated positional enum. every(duration) is a tick source on the Time rail. One-shot wait is merged.next() with a fallback. No parser change. The stream machinery follows the ratified stream lifecycle law (D-CONC-STREAM1).

comparisons.note: Go spells both common shapes as control flow. Ranging drains a channel, and select with case arms waits on several. Neither is a method chain.
Rust has no select in the language, so a macro fakes the table shape. The macro body has its own grammar that rustfmt and rust-analyzer handle poorly.

recommendation.why: One branching keyword stays the whole law. The wait keeps option A's table shape, named sources and all, without reserving a word or amending the S68 keyword sentence. The comma head marks the wait, and the arm head is the drain loop head, so learning one form teaches the other.

whyNot.reason: It reads the same as D but reserves select and adds a second branching keyword, which costs an S68 amendment for no extra clarity.
The arms lose the source names, an arity family of functions grows without bound, and every wait costs an extra binding line.
It answers a control-flow question with stream plumbing. A single wait needs a merge call, a next call, and nameless positional variants.

recommendation.tradeoff: An if can now block. The arm shape announces it, but readers must learn that one table form waits. Accepted: the shape is loud, the after and else arms flag it further, and the keyword count stays at one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a select keyword table, an arity function family dispatched by if, and merged streams. It recommended the keyword table because the wait stays control flow with named sources.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested Bool readiness heads inside a plain if table and an alternation form in the loop head. Bool heads lie about atomicity and the loop alternation cannot format, so both were folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Option D came from your direction on this ballot: it merges the if keyword with option A arm shape. The comma head keeps the whole table one atomic wait, so the earlier atomicity objection does not apply.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B gained a named TimedOut variant and keyword arguments, and option C gained every(duration) ticks that make timeouts ordinary sources. Positional variant names remain the floor for both.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack on D asked whether a reader can mistake a waiting if for a testing if. The comma heads, the after arm, and the mixed-table diagnostic mark the wait, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: fmt simplify: catalog, surface, and default
decisions.gist: Whether jet fmt may rewrite code to its simplest ratified spelling, and how you turn that on.
decisions.lesson: jet fmt fixes spacing and layout but never changes the shape of your code. A simplify mode would re-emit the most concise ratified spelling with the same meaning. The starter catalog has four rewrites. Braced single-return bodies become = expr one-liners (card #1512). Else-if chains become one arm table. A struct literal drops a type name the context already knows. A listed run of integers in a fence becomes a range. Each rewrite cites its ratified law and proves the same program. The ballot picks the catalog, surface, and default.
decisions.story: Priya inherits a Jet service written by three people in three styles. She wants one command that makes the whole repo read like current canonical Jet, without changing what it does.

options.name: Opt-in flag: jet fmt --simplify
options.detail: Plain jet fmt stays exactly as it is. The rewriter runs only when you ask for it with one flag. Teams canonicalize a repo in one deliberate run, and nobody's code changes shape mid-edit. The in-repo corpus migrates once with the flag as part of this work.
options.technical: The flag shares the fmt engine and AST. Each catalog rewrite carries its decision ID and an AST-equality check: emit, re-parse, compare. The ratified branch-shape law (D-BRANCH-FMT1=C, fmt does not change branch shape) stays intact for default runs. The catalog grows only by ratified law, never by heuristic.

options.name: Simplify is the default fmt
options.detail: Every jet fmt run emits the simplest spelling. One canonical form everywhere, enforced by the tool everyone already runs. This amends the fresh branch-shape ruling, and code changes shape under your cursor on every save.
options.technical: Explicitly amends D-BRANCH-FMT1=C (ratified 2026-07-28): fmt would now change branch shape. Same catalog, same AST-equality proof. An escape flag to skip simplify would be needed for teaching material that shows the verbose forms.
options.code:
$ jet fmt src/        # every run rewrites shape

fn mirror(p: Point) => Point = .{x: -p.x, y: p.y}

options.name: A separate command: jet simplify
options.detail: The rewriter gets its own verb next to fmt. The split makes the intent loud, but there are now two commands that both reformat code, and every guide must explain when to run which.
options.technical: Same engine and catalog under a second CLI entry. fmt law untouched. Editors would need a second format-on-demand action.
options.code:
$ jet simplify src/
$ jet fmt src/        # still needed for layout

options.name: Lint hints only, no batch rewriter
options.detail: No rewriter. Lints point at the simpler spelling and editors offer a quick fix, one site at a time. Nothing ever rewrites your file wholesale, but a repo can never be canonicalized in one run.
options.technical: One L-code per catalog entry, each citing its decision ID. Quick-fix payloads reuse the same AST emitters, so a later batch mode could still be built on top.
options.code: src/geo.jet:4: L0510 this body can be `= expr` (jet fmt cannot fix this automatically)

comparisons.note: gofmt fixes layout only. The shape rewriters live in a separate opt-in tool, gofmt -r and gopls modernizers, and Go has kept that split for a decade.
rustfmt never changes shape. cargo clippy --fix applies shape rewrites as an explicit second step.

recommendation.why: One flag gives whole-repo canonicalization on demand while plain fmt stays predictable. It honors the fresh branch-shape ruling instead of amending it, and it still lets this repo migrate to one canonical form in a single run.

whyNot.reason: It amends a branch-shape ruling you ratified nine days ago, and code changing shape on every save punishes people mid-edit.
A second command that also reformats is two tools for one job, and every guide must teach the split.
Site-at-a-time hints can never canonicalize a repo, so the one-canonical-form goal stays out of reach.

recommendation.tradeoff: fmt gains a mode, so its docs and tests cover two behaviors. Accepted: the default stays frozen and the mode is one flag with one catalog.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an opt-in flag, a default rewrite, a separate command, and lint hints. It recommended the flag because repos canonicalize on demand while the default stays predictable.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-rewrite flags, a config-file toggle, and an editor-only action. All collapsed into the four menu options because they only move where the same switch lives.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of the flag plus D's lint hints was tested: the lint names the simpler spelling and the flag applies it. It was folded into option A's technical path since the lint codes can land later without a new ballot.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened with an escape flag for teaching code, and option D with quick-fix payloads that reuse the batch emitters. Both remain honest versions of themselves.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack tried a rewrite that changes comment placement or drops a needed paren, breaking the same-program promise. The AST-equality check after every rewrite catches both, so the flag survives with the catalog gated on ratified law.

decisions.title: Where shared Prelude semantics live in the source tree
decisions.gist: Which folder holds the one shared implementation every execution tier calls.
decisions.lesson: Invariant I9 demands one implementation of every language behavior, and it names the folder: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude. The compile-time interpreter lives in a crate that is not allowed to depend on the codegen crate. So a behavior that the compile-time interpreter must also run cannot live in the named folder. The outcome carrier hit this wall. The code now lives in the foundation crate, which every engine can reach. The invariant's purpose is intact; only its named path is wrong.
decisions.story: An agent finishes the outcome carrier and must make the compile-time interpreter call the same jet_partial function the compiled program calls. The named Prelude folder is unreachable from that interpreter's crate. The agent either duplicates the function, breaks the crate seam, or moves the file. Duplication is the exact drift I9 exists to prevent, so the agent moved the file and flagged the invariant text.

options.name: Amend I9: shared semantics live in the Prelude parts
options.detail: The invariant stops naming one folder. It instead says: semantics live only in the embedded Prelude parts, and today those parts live in jet-foundation and crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude. Every engine must call those functions. Nothing moves. The carrier stays where every tier can already reach it.
options.technical: I9 text change only. The prelude assembly order in Codegen/mod.rs and Codegen/Web.rs remains the single source of truth for what is a Prelude part. A new part is legal in either crate; the comptime-reachable parts must sit in jet-foundation.

options.name: Move every Prelude part into jet-foundation
options.detail: One folder again, but a reachable one: all Prelude semantics migrate from the codegen crate into jet-foundation. The invariant keeps naming exactly one home. Larger one-time move; the codegen crate keeps only emit and marshalling.
options.technical: Relocate crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/** into jet-foundation prelude modules; codegen includes them verbatim as it already does for Outcome.rs. No behavior change; include order preserved; golden output byte-identical.
options.code:
// I9 (amended): Semantics live only in crates/jet-foundation/src/prelude/**.
// jet-codegen embeds those files verbatim; no semantic code remains in codegen.

options.name: Keep I9's folder; carve out the carrier by name
options.detail: The invariant text stays. A ratified carve-out names Outcome.rs as the one permitted exception, with its reason. Every future comptime-reachable behavior needs its own carve-out, so this choice recurs.
options.technical: No code change. The carve-out record must name the file, the I6 seam reason, and its removal condition (a future dependency restructure that makes the named folder reachable).

comparisons.note: Rust's core library sits below every backend for the same reason: the lowest crate everyone may depend on holds the shared meaning.
comparisons.code: // libcore is reachable from every consumer; codegen backends never define language semantics.

recommendation.why: Option A states the real rule the code already follows: one embedded Prelude, every engine marshals onto it. It fixes the text without moving working code or inviting repeat exceptions.

whyNot.reason: A large file move with zero behavior change; the single-folder purity it buys is cosmetic, and the move risks churn in every open branch.
A named exception recurs every time the compile-time tier needs a new behavior, and a growing exception list is weaker law than an accurate rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two legal homes instead of one folder. That is acceptable because the prelude assembly list, not the folder path, is what engines actually share.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared amending the text, moving all parts to the foundation crate, and a named carve-out, and recommended the amendment because it matches the shipped, working shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested two more shapes: letting comptime depend on codegen, and duplicating the carrier per crate. Both die on ratified law — the I6 seam and I9's anti-drift purpose — so neither joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tried A now with B as a scheduled migration. That adds a standing obligation with no behavior gain, so the passes stayed separate options.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by noting verbatim embedding makes the move mechanical, and C by giving the carve-out a concrete removal condition. Both stand as their best selves.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A: two homes could invite semantic code sprawl into any foundation file. The repair names the prelude assembly list as the authority — a file is a Prelude part only when embedded — so A survives.

decisions.title: What the environment-module selector flag is called
decisions.gist: The command-line flag that picks one environment module needs a name that no longer says profile.
decisions.lesson: The ratified one-word ruling keeps the word profile for exactly one meaning and renames the rest. The rename card found a flag the ruling's fold list mislabeled: --env-profile does not select a preset composition, it selects one env.<name> module from the manifest. Folding it into --preset would make one flag mean two different things. The flag kept its old spelling, so a user still types the retired word today.
decisions.story: Rowan keeps two environment modules in one package: env.dev with a local database and env.ci with a hermetic one. To enter the second, Rowan types jet enter --env-profile ci. Every other surface stopped saying profile; this flag still does, and Rowan wonders whether it is the old system or the new one.

options.name: --env <name>
options.detail: The flag names the axis it selects: an environment module. Short, matches the env.<name> spelling in the manifest, and cannot be confused with --preset. The loss: --env reads slightly generic next to commands that already live inside an environment.
options.technical: Rename EnvProfileFlag and its parse row to Env; retired --env-profile teaches the replacement with a registered diagnostic, same pattern as the E1300 row --profile already has.
options.code:
$ jet enter --env ci
entered env.ci (hermetic database)

$ jet enter --env-profile ci
error[E1301]: `--env-profile` is retired
  fix: type `--env ci` — the flag now names the environment module directly

options.name: --enter <name> positional on enter
options.detail: jet enter ci: the subcommand already means entering an environment, so the module name rides as its positional argument and no flag exists at all. Smallest surface. The loss: other commands that accepted --env-profile (run, test) still need a spelled flag, so this option only removes the flag in one place.
options.technical: enter takes an optional positional env module; other commands keep a flag (whatever this ballot picks for them) — so option B must pair with A or C for the general case.
options.code:
$ jet enter ci
entered env.ci (hermetic database)

$ jet test --env ci   # non-enter commands still need the flag

options.name: --environment <name>
options.detail: The full word, no abbreviation. Unambiguous and self-teaching, at the cost of eleven characters where every sibling flag is short. Tab completion softens the cost.
options.technical: Same mechanical rename as option A with the long spelling; --env could be accepted as its documented short form only if the owner wants both, which reintroduces two spellings for one thing.
options.code:
$ jet enter --environment ci
entered env.ci (hermetic database)

comparisons.note: nix develop .#ci selects a named devShell with a positional attribute — the enter command and the selector are one gesture, like option B.
--profile selects optional service groups; the overload of the word profile across tools is exactly why Jet retired it.

recommendation.why: The flag's whole job is picking an env.<name> module, and --env says exactly that in the manifest's own spelling. It works uniformly on every command, not just enter.

whyNot.reason: It only removes the flag on enter; every other command still needs a spelled flag, so the ballot's question returns immediately.
The long word buys no clarity over --env, because the manifest itself spells the axis env.

recommendation.tradeoff: --env is one more short global flag to learn. That is acceptable because it replaces a retired spelling users must unlearn anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared --env, an enter positional, and --environment, and recommended --env for matching the manifest spelling on every command.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a namespaced preset value and keeping the old flag; neither joined the menu because one re-merges the two axes and the other keeps a retired word.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review paired option B's positional on enter with option A's flag elsewhere. That is two spellings for one selection, so the combination was rejected and the options stayed separate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by noting enter is by far the most-typed site, and C by noting completion erases its length cost. Both stand as real choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked --env as colliding with the env.jet file and manifest env blocks. That is agreement — flag, file, and block name one axis — so A survives.

decisions.title: One law for every compiler-held fact
decisions.gist: Whether one written law governs every fact the compiler holds.
decisions.lesson: The compiler proves facts about the program: a value's range, a scope's rights, a task's duty, a place's write window, a build setting. Four ratified rethinks each gave their facts a rule, and all four rules say the same thing in different words. A fact may move toward safety silently. Every move away from safety needs one written word at the site. This ballot decides whether that sentence becomes one recorded law, or stays as four separate rules.
decisions.story: Ana learns Jet from the book. The numbers chapter says knowledge is conserved. The security chapter says rights only shrink. The packages chapter says policy only tightens. The concurrency chapter says a task must be joined. Four chapters, four rules to memorize. Her teammate asks what the safety model is, and she cannot answer in one sentence.

options.name: One written law in the spec
options.detail: The spec states the law once: a fact moves toward safety silently, and every move away is one written word, recorded for audit. The four ratified per-plane rules become named instances of it. Teaching, docs, and diagnostics can point at one sentence. Gain: one safety story. Loss: the law is prose only, so a future plane could forget to follow it.
options.technical: The law enters docs/spec/philosophy.md and syntax-decisions.md as a recorded decision. D-TYPE2-EXACT1, D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1, D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1, D-CONF-MERGE1, D-FLOWTYPE1, and D-CONC-JOIN1 are listed as instances. No ruling changes.

options.name: Law plus a guarded registry
options.detail: Everything in option A, and the plane registry enforces it. Every registered fact plane must name its safe direction and its gate words in its registry row. A plane without them fails the same guard that already protects marker law zero. Gain: no future plane can drift from the law. Loss: registry rows carry two more required columns.
options.technical: The D-META-REG1 table gains two columns per plane: safe_direction and gates[]. A CI guard mirrors the marker drift-guard: a plane row missing either column fails the build. Existing planes are backfilled in the same change.

options.name: Keep four separate rules
options.detail: No umbrella law. Each rethink keeps its own rule, vocabulary, and chapter. Gain: nothing moves, and no wording debate happens now. Loss: the same law stays written four times, new planes copy whichever wording their author read last, and the one-sentence safety story never exists.

comparisons.note: Pony unified its concurrency and memory safety into one deny-capability table. One rule made the system teachable where prior actor languages had scattered rules.
comparisons.code:
// Pony reference capabilities: one matrix of what is denied.
// iso, trn, ref, val, box, tag - every alias rule reads off one table.

comparisons.note: Rust never stated one law across borrow checking, Send/Sync, const rules, and unsafe. Each is taught separately, and learners report the total model as the hard part.

recommendation.why: The registry guard is what made marker law zero real, and the same guard makes this law real. Implementation cards #1517-#1579 are about to add planes, so the check must exist before they land.

whyNot.reason: A prose-only law repeats the pre-law-zero marker story, where five ad-hoc forms grew because nothing checked new arrivals.
Keeping four wordings leaves the fifth rethink free to mint a fifth, and the one-sentence safety story never exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every plane author must declare a safe direction and gate list, even for a plane with no gates. That is two lines per plane, and it is the audit trail working.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a spec-prose law with keeping four separate rules and recommended the written law for the one-sentence safety story.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the guarded-registry option and considered a diagnostics-only variant. The diagnostics-only variant was folded into the vocabulary ballot D-FACT-WORD1, where it belongs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested prose law now with a guard later. It collapsed into option B, because the guard is two registry columns and delaying it invites drift during the #1517-#1579 builds.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C: it costs nothing today and avoids a wording debate. It still leaves the law unwritten while sixty implementation cards build fact planes.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked B with planes that have no meaningful safe direction, such as pure bookkeeping rows. The registry accepts a declared none value for such planes, so the guard survives and B stands.

decisions.title: One word for the one-way rule
decisions.gist: Which word names the safe move and the escape in errors and docs.
decisions.lesson: Five words currently name the same one-way rule. Policy and config say tighten. Rights say attenuate. Flow types say narrow. Number knowledge says conserve. Facts erase. A user who meets all five reasonably believes Jet has five different rules. This ballot picks one word pair for the law in diagnostics and docs. Exact operation names stay: flow narrowing keeps its technical name, and no user-typed spelling changes.
decisions.story: Sam hits three errors in one afternoon. One says a package may only tighten policy. One says rights may only attenuate. One says a conversion would lose knowledge. He searches the docs for three different rules and files a confused issue asking how they relate. They are the same rule.

options.name: Tighten and loosen
options.detail: Facts tighten silently. A gate loosens, and loosening is always spelled. Two ratified rules already say tighten, so this option renames the least. Plain everyday words. Gain: smallest migration, reads naturally at every plane. Loss: tighten reads oddly for duty, where the safe move is finishing a job rather than shrinking something.
options.technical: Diagnostic copy and docs adopt tighten and loosen as the law words. attenuate, conserve, and law-level narrow retire from prose. Operation names stay: flow narrowing, widening conversions, and every user-typed spelling are untouched.

options.name: The ratchet and the release
options.detail: Facts ratchet toward safety. Every escape word is a release, and a release is always written. One vivid picture that works for all four planes, including duty. Gain: memorable, teaches itself, names the gate family too. Loss: ratchet is a workshop metaphor, not a plain word, and it translates poorly.
options.technical: Docs name the law the ratchet. Diagnostic copy says moves toward safety and names the release word. The gate ledger and the release family share the release name.

options.name: Toward safety and away
options.detail: No metaphor at all. Diagnostics say a fact only moves toward safety here, and name the written word that allows the move away. Gain: nothing to learn, no metaphor to translate, works for every plane including duty. Loss: longer phrases in error text, and no single noun for the law when docs need to cite it.
options.technical: Diagnostic copy adopts the toward-safety phrase. Docs cite the law as the one-way law. attenuate, conserve, and tighten retire from law-level prose but stay legal in local descriptions.

options.name: Keep the five words
options.detail: Each plane keeps its own vocabulary and only the docs note the family resemblance. Gain: zero migration, each word stays locally precise. Loss: the confusion in the story stays real, error copy never converges, and every future plane picks a sixth word.

recommendation.why: Tighten is already ratified language in two places, it is a plain everyday word, and one word pair makes every error teach the same law. The duty plane reads acceptably as tightening what the value may still do.

whyNot.reason: Ratchet is a metaphor the simple-prose rule would flag, and it adds a word to learn where a plain one exists.
The toward-safety phrase is honest but wordy, and the law still needs a noun the docs can cite.
Keeping five words preserves the exact confusion this ballot exists to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: Duty errors fit the tighten frame least naturally, so their copy leans on the owes phrasing rather than the law word. That is one plane with softer wording, against four that align exactly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared tighten, ratchet, and keeping five words, and recommended tighten for continuity with ratified text.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the no-metaphor toward-safety option and tested narrow and widen as the pair. Narrow lost because flow narrowing already owns that word as an operation name.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested tighten in errors with ratchet as the doc nickname. Two names for one law recreates the original problem, so the hybrid was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened D: local words are locally precise, and attenuate is standard security vocabulary. It still leaves users finding five rules where there is one.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked tighten with the duty plane, where nothing shrinks. The owes phrasing repairs duty copy without breaking the law word, so A survives with that carve-out recorded.

decisions.title: One ledger for every gate
decisions.gist: Which escape words land in the one audit list.
decisions.lesson: A gate is one written word that moves a fact away from safety: #Unsafe, #Scrub, approx, .Force, grants, detach. The ratified authority ledger (D-AUTHORITY-GATE1) already collects the rights gates behind jet inspect authority. The other gate families, such as taint scrubs and precision drops, live only in source text. This ballot decides how far the one ledger reaches. It generalizes D-AUTHORITY-GATE1 and changes no gate spelling.
decisions.story: Priya reviews a payment service before a compliance audit. She needs every place the code stepped off the safe path: unsafe regions, dependency grants, scrubbed customer data, forced build settings, and precision drops in the interest math. Today that is one CLI command, a lockfile diff, a trust file, and a repo-wide grep, assembled by hand into a spreadsheet.
decisions.inWild:
# today - the exceptions live in four places
jet unsafe
git diff jet.lock
cat ~/.jet/trust
rg "#Scrub|approx\(|wrapping\(" src/

# the authority ledger (ratified) covers only the rights rows:
jet inspect authority

options.name: Full ledger, grouped by kind
options.detail: Every gate lands in one ledger: unsafe regions, impure marks, grants, trust and .Force, taint scrubs, duty drops, and precision demotions. jet inspect gates prints counts per kind with security kinds expanded first, and filters select one kind. Gain: one list is the whole audit, and CI can refuse new gates without sign-off. Loss: numeric code can log thousands of demotion rows, so the tool must summarize well.
options.technical: The gate record generalizes D-AUTHORITY-GATE1. Each entry: site, gate word, kind, reason where ratified law requires one. Compile-time only; no runtime cost. jet inspect authority remains as the rights-kind filter of the same ledger.
options.code:
$ jet inspect gates
rights   2   src/dma.jet:41 #Unsafe "MMIO: manual 4.2"
              pkg.jet grants image-codec: FS.Read
taint    1   src/etl.jet:88 call of #Scrub(Pii) fn hash_email
build    1   pkg.jet stamp.at forced via .Force
exact   214  (summarized; jet inspect gates --kind exact)
duty     1   src/jobs.jet:12 detach

options.name: Security gates only
options.detail: The ledger holds the gates a security reviewer needs: unsafe, impure, grants, trust, .Force, and taint scrubs. Precision demotions and duty drops stay in code only, found by grep. Gain: a short, high-signal list with no numeric noise. Loss: simulation and money code lose the precision audit, and the law's on-the-record clause holds for only half the gate family.
options.technical: Same record shape as A, restricted to the rights and taint kinds plus .Force. approx, wrapping, and detach never enter the ledger.
options.code:
$ jet inspect gates
src/dma.jet:41  #Unsafe "MMIO: manual 4.2"
src/etl.jet:88  call of #Scrub(Pii) fn hash_email
pkg.jet         grants image-codec: FS.Read
pkg.jet         stamp.at forced via .Force
# precision drops: rg "approx\(" src/   (outside the ledger)

options.name: Keep the authority ledger as ratified
options.detail: No generalization. jet inspect authority ships as D-AUTHORITY-GATE1 wrote it, and other gates stay source-only. Gain: nothing new to build or decide. Loss: the audit crawl in the story stays real for every non-rights gate, and each future plane will propose its own inspector.
options.code:
$ jet inspect authority
gates:
  src/dma.jet:41  #Unsafe "MMIO: manual 4.2"
  pkg.jet         grants image-codec: FS.Read
# scrubs, demotions, forced settings: grep by hand

comparisons.note: cargo-geiger counts unsafe but nothing collects allows, feature forcing, and lossy casts in one place. Auditors assemble the picture from separate tools.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo geiger        # unsafe only
$ rg "as f32" src/    # lossy casts by grep

recommendation.why: The law says every gate is on the record, and one grouped ledger is that clause made real. Certification work reads one list, and the kind grouping keeps numeric rows from burying security rows.

whyNot.reason: Half a ledger reopens the audit crawl for exactness and duty, exactly where money and simulation code need the record.
Stopping at the ratified rights ledger invites one bespoke inspector per future plane, which is the fragmentation this slate exists to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: Heavy numeric code produces large exact-kind sections, so the default view must summarize them to counts. That is a presentation cost, accepted to keep the record complete.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a full ledger with the ratified rights-only ledger and recommended the full ledger for the one-list audit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the security-only middle option and considered a per-plane inspector family. The inspector family was rejected as the fragmentation pattern itself.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the kind grouping and summarized counts from a separate presentation idea into option A, so the full ledger ships with noise control built in.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: a short list auditors actually read beats a complete list they skim. The counts-first default in A answers the same concern.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with ledger bloat from hot numeric loops and with reason-ceremony creep. Summarized counts answer bloat, no gate gains a new required reason, and A survives.

decisions.title: One way to read what the compiler knows
decisions.gist: How code reads a compiler-held fact: the $ sigil, reflection methods, or tools only.
decisions.lesson: The compiler knows a value's range, a function's effects, a type's states and units. Reading that knowledge is currently uneven. Build facts read as $build.profile (D-CONF-READ1). The metaprogramming rethink made $ the one mark for a compile-time name (D-META-STAGE1). Type reflection is partly typed and partly strings, and state names cannot be written at all. This ballot picks the one reading surface. It extends D-CONF-READ1 and D-META-STAGE1 and completes D-TYPE2-PLANE1's typed reflection.
decisions.story: Marco writes a derive that generates an audit table for every type in his payments package. He needs each field's range, unit, and tags. Today the ranges are readable, the units arrive through a different call, and the state names come back as mangled strings he must parse.

options.name: The $ mark reads every plane
options.detail: Reading a fact is one act, one mark: T.$range, f.$effects, Order.$states, $build.profile. Every registered plane answers as typed values, in comptime code and derive bodies. The string fallback dies. Gain: one lesson covers every fact read, and the build-fact spelling generalizes instead of staying special. Loss: the $ position grammar grows from build facts and splices to member position on types and functions.
options.technical: Extends D-META-STAGE1: $ marks a compile-time name, so a fact read is $ in member position. Facts return typed values from the D-META-REG1 registry. Comptime only; S26 holds, facts are values and never mint types. TypeInfo remains the aggregate view and loses its string fallback.
options.code:
// one act, every plane (proposed):
Severity.$range          // 0..10
send_report.$effects     // [Net, DB.Read]
Order.$states            // [.Draft, .Confirmed, .Shipped]
Meters.$dimension        // Length
$build.profile           // ratified today - same act, build subject

options.name: Typed reflection methods only
options.detail: Complete D-TYPE2-PLANE1 as written: T.reflect() returns fully typed data for every plane, and the string fallback dies. The $ mark stays where it is ratified, on build facts and splices. Gain: no grammar change, one aggregate object per type. Loss: two reading stories remain, because build facts read with $ and type facts read with a method.
options.technical: TypeInfo gains typed fields per registered plane: ranges, dimensions, states, effects, marker args. No new $ positions. Reflect.rs string paths are deleted.
options.code:
// reflection completes, $ stays build-only:
info :: Order.reflect()
info.states              // [.Draft, .Confirmed, .Shipped] - typed
info.fields[0].range     // 0..10
$build.profile           // still the separate build spelling

options.name: Tools read facts, code does not
options.detail: jet explain and the language server answer what is known here, but programs cannot read facts beyond today's ratified surfaces. Gain: zero language change, and no risk of programs depending on checker internals. Loss: derives and comptime code keep parsing strings or go without, and the phantom reflection gap stays.
options.code:
$ jet explain value order
order: Order   state: Confirmed (set at line 12)
               tags: Pii (from field email)
// in code: only today's partial reflect() remains

recommendation.why: The metaprogramming rethink already ratified $ as the one mark for a compile-time name, and a fact is a compile-time name. One act for one idea is the whole point of the capstone.

whyNot.reason: It keeps two reading stories, so the build plane stays a special case forever and the one-lesson claim fails.
It leaves derive authors parsing strings, which is the exact defect the evidence table documents.

recommendation.tradeoff: The $ member-position grammar must be specified carefully so it cannot be mistaken for runtime field access. Accepted: the mark is already defined as compile-time-only, and the checker rejects runtime positions.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared $ reads with completing typed reflection and recommended $ reads for the one-act story.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the tools-only option and tested a facts() standard-library call. The library call was folded into option B as the same design behind a longer name.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed A already contains B: the aggregate reflect() view remains as the bulk read, and $ is the per-fact read. No separate hybrid option was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: tools cover the human questions and freeze no surface. It still leaves generated code without typed fact access, which derives need today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A for grammar creep and for programs branching on checker internals. The mark stays comptime-only under S26 and facts never dispatch under D-FACTMODEL1, so the walls hold and A survives.

decisions.title: Home the orphan facts, retire the phantom types
decisions.gist: Which stray compiler facts join the registry, and phantom fact names stop compiling in signatures.
decisions.lesson: Some compiler-held facts live outside every registry: send-safety is a stray flag, #Track provenance and view provenance are unreadable, maturity and failure attribution are unregistered. Separately, about eighteen fact-menu names such as Capability and State are accepted in function signatures today, then every call fails, and no value can ever exist. This ballot decides which orphans become registry rows and confirms that phantom names are refused at the signature with a fix-it.
decisions.story: Lena writes fn audit(c: Capability) after reading an error message that mentioned Capability. It compiles. Every call site then fails with a type error, and there is no way to make the value. She loses an hour before learning the name was never a type.

options.name: Home the user-facing orphans
options.detail: Facts with user-visible meaning join the registry as typed, readable rows: send-safety, failure attribution, #Track and view and unit-scale provenance, and maturity. Prover internals such as uninit tracking and exhaustiveness stay engine-side, matching the prover wall in D-FACT-OWN1. Phantom fact-menu names are refused at the signature with a fix-it naming the real path. Gain: every fact a user can meet is nameable and readable. Loss: prover internals stay unreflectable.
options.technical: Each homed fact becomes a D-META-REG1 registry row with typed members. Marker-argument menus stop resolving as general types in core_type_known; the diagnostic names the real value type where one exists, such as the authority value.

options.name: Home everything
options.detail: Every fact the compiler holds joins the registry, including uninit tracking and exhaustiveness. Phantom rejection lands the same way. Gain: complete uniformity, and tools can show even prover internals. Loss: registry rows for facts no user can act on, and the prover wall blurs, because engine-internal state becomes a public surface the checker must keep stable.
options.technical: As A, plus registry rows for definite-assignment and exhaustiveness facts. Those rows expose intermediate prover state, which then falls under reflection stability rules.

options.name: Phantom fix only
options.detail: Refuse phantom names in signatures with fix-its, and home nothing. Gain: the user trap closes with the smallest change. Loss: send-safety stays a stray flag while the concurrency cards build on it, and provenance, attribution, and maturity stay unreadable.

recommendation.why: Homing the user-facing orphans finishes what the four rethinks started, and the prover wall keeps engine internals free to change. The phantom fix closes a real beginner trap the audit documented.

whyNot.reason: Publishing prover internals freezes checker implementation details as API, trading engine freedom for reflection nobody asked for.
It leaves send-safety as a stray flag exactly while cards #1557-#1565 build the crossing checker on top of it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The line between user-facing fact and prover internal is a judgment call recorded per fact. Accepted: the ballot lists the assignment explicitly, so the line is written down, not folklore.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft homed every orphan and refused phantoms. The recommendation later narrowed after the prover wall took shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review split homing into user-facing and everything variants and added the phantom-only floor. It also checked for further orphans and confirmed maturity and unit-scale provenance belong on the list.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested phantom fix now with homing later. That is option C wearing a schedule, and it leaves the concurrency cards building on the stray flag, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: complete uniformity is the simplest rule and tools benefit. The stability cost to the checker stands, because published shapes cannot change freely.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's fix-it quality: a refusal without a real alternative just moves the dead end. Each refused name must name its living counterpart, the menu without one says so plainly, and A survives with that requirement recorded.

decisions.title: The ownership wall: prover, not plane
decisions.gist: Whether the borrow checker stays its own engine or becomes a registered fact plane.
decisions.lesson: Fact planes fold facts through code with small per-operation rules: ranges add, units multiply, rights meet as sets. The borrow checker is different. It tracks places, aliases, and time: which windows overlap, which owner moved, which view outlives what. That is flow analysis, not algebra. This ballot decides whether that difference becomes a recorded wall, so no future card tries to rebuild ownership as a plane, while the facts ownership proves still register like all others.
decisions.story: Next spring an agent picks up a card that says unify the fact planes. Without a recorded wall it spends a week flattening the borrow checker into plane rules, breaks view invalidation, and the review has no ratified sentence to point at when rejecting the patch.

options.name: Ratify the wall
options.detail: The borrow checker is a prover, never a plane. The sigil surface stays closed as ratified. The facts the prover publishes, such as sendability, view provenance, and moved-ness, register as read-only rows so tools and other planes can consume them. Gain: the engine stays free to be a real program analysis, and its outputs still join the one model. Loss: one mechanism is formally outside the plane registry.
options.technical: Records: ownership checking follows D-MEM1, D-SHAPE-PLACE1, and D-MEM-VIEWRET1 as its own analysis. Published facts enter the D-META-REG1 table as prover-supplied rows. No plane algebra is defined for windows.

options.name: Ownership becomes a plane
options.detail: Windows and moves register as a plane with combination rules, and the checker becomes that plane's algebra engine. Gain: complete uniformity, one registry with no exceptions, window facts reflect like all others, and one guard checks every plane including this one. Loss: alias analysis does not decompose into per-operation rules, so the registered algebra must delegate to the engine, and forcing the frame invites a rebuild that loses precision.

options.name: Leave it undecided
options.detail: No ruling either way. Gain: no decision to maintain. Loss: the question returns on every unification card, and the next agent has no ratified sentence to cite, which is how the week in the story gets spent.
options.code: // status quo: the boundary lives in reviewers' heads

comparisons.note: Rust's borrow checker is its own engine, and Send/Sync are auto-derived facts published from it. The split works and nobody proposes merging the two frames.
comparisons.code:
// borrowck: flow analysis over MIR
// Send/Sync: structural facts other systems consume

recommendation.why: The evidence shows ownership already obeys the one-way law at its surface while its engine is genuinely different inside. Naming that split keeps both truths and stops future rebuild attempts.

whyNot.reason: It gains a registry entry and risks a precision-losing rebuild, because alias analysis has no per-operation rule table to register.
It spends future reviewer time relitigating a boundary this audit has already proved twice.

recommendation.tradeoff: The registry carries prover-supplied rows that no plane algebra backs, a small irregularity accepted to keep the engine honest.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft stated the wall and recommended it, with full absorption as the alternative.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the leave-undecided option and checked whether duty should sit behind the same wall. Duty stays a plane, because discharge rules are per-operation and D-CONC-UNIT1 already ratified that.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the published-facts-register clause from a separate idea into option A, so the wall and the registry stop being rivals.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with the uniformity argument and the reflection gain. Both survive in A through the published rows, without forcing the engine into the plane frame.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A as an excuse wall that future proposals could hide behind. The wall is scoped to the alias engine only, and its published facts must register, so nothing else can shelter under it and A survives.

decisions.title: One flow-fact store with one join rule
decisions.gist: How the checker stores per-binding facts that change along control flow.
decisions.lesson: Six separate stores track facts that change as code flows: moved bindings, uninit fields, typestate, optional narrowing, taint, and view windows. Each store hand-writes its own branch-merge logic, and two of the merges are dead code, so typestate and partial-init simply keep whatever the last-walked branch left. This is machinery, but it decides whether the concurrency and type-v2 cards build one engine or six more copies.
decisions.story: A user writes an if/else where one branch confirms an order and the other cancels it. After the join the compiler believes whichever branch it happened to walk last. The bug report lands next winter, and the fix gets written twice, once per store, because there is no shared join.

options.name: One store, planes supply joins
options.detail: One flow-fact store on the checker holds every per-binding fact. Each plane supplies only its join rule for branch merges, and the walker applies joins uniformly at every if, loop, and arm table. The six stores and the twelve one-off checker columns migrate in. Gain: joins can no longer be forgotten, and new planes get flow tracking for free. Loss: one large internal migration through the checker.
options.technical: Store keyed by binding and plane. Join called at every control-flow merge point by the shared walker. Sema-only; no TIR or codegen change; generated Rust stays byte-identical. Lands as phase A of the implementation shape, before cards #1517-#1579 build on it.

options.name: Shared join contract, separate stores
options.detail: The stores stay where they are, but each must implement one join interface, and a guard test lists every store and asserts its join is live. Gain: the dead-join class of bug dies with a much smaller change. Loss: six data shapes remain, new planes still hand-roll storage, and the walker still calls six merge paths.
options.technical: A JoinFacts trait over the existing stores plus a registry-driven test that fails when a store lacks a live join. No storage migration.
options.code:
// each store implements join(); a guard test enumerates them
// State.rs join_after: now called, or the build fails

options.name: Fix the two dead joins as bugs
options.detail: Wire up the typestate and uninit merges, change nothing structural. Gain: the known soundness holes close this week. Loss: the seventh store gets hand-written by the next card, and the next forgotten join waits there.

recommendation.why: The concurrency and type-v2 cards are about to add more flow-tracked planes. One store built first means those cards add join rules, not storage engines, and the forgotten-join bug class ends.

whyNot.reason: It keeps six shapes and six merge paths, so every new plane still pays the storage tax the capstone exists to delete.
It patches two symptoms of a structure that has already produced dead code twice, and leaves the structure.

recommendation.tradeoff: One wide internal migration through the checker before feature cards land. Accepted: effort is expendable, and the migration is phase A with every test staying green.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the unified store with fixing the dead joins and recommended the store for the by-construction guarantee.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the shared-contract middle option and checked whether view facts belong in the store. They do as storage, while their invalidation logic stays with the ownership prover per D-FACT-OWN1.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested contract-now, store-later. Sequencing both costs more than building the store once before the feature cards, so the hybrid was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: it is the honest minimal soundness fix and ships immediately. It still leaves the next plane hand-rolling store number seven.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A over loop fixpoints and merge-order subtleties that six bespoke stores currently dodge. The shared walker must document its fixpoint rule once, which is strictly fewer places to get it wrong than six, so A survives.

decisions.title: Adopt the one-tree name model
decisions.gist: Is a name one thing: a member at one point in one tree?
decisions.lesson: Today a name can reach you through five doors: two import forms, a file-reference declaration, automatic discovery, and the prelude. The shadowing rule has one law and four exceptions. Inside the compiler, six separate stores resolve names, and two of them disagree about package visibility. This ballot decides the founding model. The other eight D-NAME ballots each stand alone, but they all read cleaner on top of this one.
decisions.story: Maya teaches Jet to a high-school class. A student asks: where does the name print come from, and why does use sometimes take quotes? Maya has no one-sentence answer today. Under the model, she says: every name lives in one tree; you declared it, your project has it, or the prelude aliases it.

options.name: Adopt: one tree, one law, one ledger
options.detail: A name is a member at one point in one tree. A declaration attaches it. An alias (use, prelude) only points at it. Declarations never collide; a declaration replaces an alias, never another declaration. The four shadowing exceptions become one rule. Inside the compiler, sema writes one name ledger and every engine and tool reads it. The six follow-up ballots then shape the surface.
options.technical: Law: attach/alias. E0118 and E0105 become the collide clause. D-PRELUDE-LAW1 user-wins, the Reader/Cursor guard, and FFI in-situ shadowing become the replace clause. D-GENMOD-IDENTITY1 (aliases never mint identity) becomes a theorem. Backend: generalize reference_anchors and import_targets into one sema-owned table; codegen, JIT, interpreter, LSP, REPL, and devserver consume it. One mangle function. Fixes the pub(package) divergence: codegen filters today read bare is_pub only (Codegen/Imports.rs:83).

options.name: Law and ledger only, surface unchanged
options.detail: Adopt the attach/alias law and the one compiler ledger, but keep today's import and visibility spellings exactly as they are. The compiler gets simpler and the exceptions get one explanation. The page a user reads does not improve.
options.technical: Same internal consolidation as A. S16, D-VISDEFAULT2, and the prelude table stay untouched. The six follow-up ballots would be moot.

options.name: Reject: keep five doors
options.detail: Keep today's model. Each door and each exception stays its own rule. No compiler consolidation is scheduled. The duplicated resolvers keep drifting; the pub(package) divergence stays open until fixed piecemeal.
options.technical: No change. The B1-B9 duplicate list from the audit remains the maintenance surface.

comparisons.note: Zig removed usingnamespace because hidden name origins forced the compiler to discover namespace contents. One visible tree avoids that whole class.
comparisons.code:
// Zig: @import returns a value; a file is a struct
const scoring = @import("scoring.zig");

comparisons.note: Go's one loved property: every non-universe name is greppable to its source. The tree keeps that property with jet project parts.

recommendation.why: One sentence answers every beginner question about names, and one ledger ends the compiler's six-store drift. Every ratified naming rule already fits the law, so nothing fights it.

whyNot.reason: An internals-only rethink leaves the five doors on the page. The owner has rejected exactly that shape of outcome before.
The five doors and four exceptions stay unexplained, and the sema/codegen visibility divergence stays live.

recommendation.tradeoff: The follow-up migrations touch many examples and snapshots at once. That is accepted: each follow-up ballot is one coherent greenfield change that deletes the replaced form.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared adopt, internals-only, and reject, and recommended adopt because the law already covers every ratified rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a two-tree design (project tree plus separate core universe) and a Zig-style files-are-values design. Both folded into A: roots are just top members of one tree, and module-as-value is already ratified for generic modules.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether B plus one surface fix beats A. It does not: the surface wins come from the follow-up ballots, which need the model named and ratified first.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: today's doors each have a ratified rationale and shipped tests. It still leaves four shadowing exceptions and two disagreeing visibility checkers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the ledger as a new mechanism, but it generalizes the existing reference_anchors and import_targets tables and deletes six ad-hoc stores. Mechanisms fall from six to one, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Project files visible without imports
decisions.gist: Do your own project files need an import line?
decisions.lesson: Today a second file in your project needs a use line with quotes, or a module declaration that only imports. U3 already rules that discovered modules merge into one whole and never import each other. This ballot decides whether that rule reaches every file, and fixes the explicit spellings an expert keeps. It amends S16 (D-S16-USE, D-MOD1/2, D-MOD-DIR) and U3/D-SHAPE-MODULEINTERNAL1's outermost-construct and discovery-naming clauses, and touches D-CALLDUAL1's scope wording. The project-wide refusal switch is its own ballot, D-NAME-AUDIT1.
decisions.story: Sam is thirteen and writes a game. The main file grows, so Sam cuts the enemy code into enemies.jet. Today the game breaks until Sam learns two import spellings and picks the right one. Under option A the game keeps running, because enemies was already part of the tree.

options.name: Whole project tree, with a full ledger
options.detail:
Every project file is a module named by its filename; a directory is a namespace. Siblings and subdirectories are visible everywhere in the project with no use line. The file-reference module declaration is deleted.

Three exits ship with the magic. jet imports FILE prints every name a file resolved, the member path, the source file, and the door it came through. use project.path is the explicit spelling for any member, including _name internals. use "…/file.jet" as name imports any file by relative path; only out-of-tree files need it, and the ledger flags them.
options.technical: Deletes the file-reference module declaration and in-tree quoted imports (S16, D-MOD1, D-MOD-DIR). The quoted form survives with one job: importing a file outside the project tree, with as required. module name { } inline grouping stays, but nests under its file's namespace — this amends U3's single-outermost-construct and declared-name-discovery clauses. The common case, one declaration matching the filename, keeps its path unchanged. Project roots enter file scope as implicit aliases, so D-CALLDUAL1's no-global-search wording gets one edited sentence. Collisions stay E0105/E0118.

options.name: Same directory only
options.detail: Files in the same directory see each other with no import line. Anything in another directory still needs a use line with a tree path. Smaller magic radius; deep projects keep import ceremony. The jet imports ledger and the explicit spellings apply the same way.
options.technical: Same deletions and exits as A. Cross-directory reach requires use grades.curve or use project.grades.curve.

options.name: Keep explicit imports
options.detail: Every cross-file name keeps an import line, as today. The two spellings could still be merged editorially, but a beginner's second file still fails until an import is learned.
options.technical: No change to S16. The tree model still holds; the project root is simply not ambient. jet imports still has value as a resolution viewer.

comparisons.note: Python requires imports even for sibling files, and sys.path rules are a famous teaching wall. The loved part is only that a file is a module.
Rust requires mod declarations to mount files, and mod.rs versus file naming confused a generation. Jet's U3 discovery already removed the mount step for declared modules.
Java's compact source files auto-see their package neighbors; the same code stays valid in a full project. Growth without rewrites is the goal here too.
comparisons.code: // same file compiles in both modes

recommendation.why: Splitting a file is the third most frequent operation in real code, and option A makes it free. Provenance survives and improves: jet imports lists every resolved name with its source, and the explicit spellings cover every case, including files outside the tree.

whyNot.reason: A directory boundary is an arbitrary magic radius. The first subdirectory brings the ceremony back, at the exact moment a project starts to grow.
It keeps ceremony on the most common growth step and keeps two import spellings alive for the same job.

recommendation.tradeoff: A large project sees more ambient roots, so a new file can collide with an existing module name. That is accepted: the collision is a clear E0105 at compile time, and the D-NAME-AUDIT1 switch restores strictness without changing meaning.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared whole-tree, same-directory, and explicit imports, and recommended whole-tree because it deletes two spellings and frees the most common refactor.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an opt-in marker per file and an editor-inserts-imports answer like goimports. Both folded into A's exits: the switch is the opt, and tooling needs no inserted lines when the tree is ambient.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review first proposed a package.jet compile switch for explicit imports, then demoted it to a lint and split it into D-NAME-AUDIT1. A compile mode would make one source mean different things per package.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with Go's provenance argument: an import line per file is greppable. A keeps the property through jet imports, which lists the exact resolution per file with its source.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked name collisions, accidental coupling, and untracked out-of-tree reach. Compile-time E0105, the _name exit, pub fences, and the ledger's out-of-tree flag contain all three, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Where the prelude lives
decisions.gist: Is the prelude a readable Core module or a compiler table?
decisions.lesson: The prelude is the set of names every file sees with no use line. Today it lives as a closed list inside the compiler's Rust source, and each call site matches those names by string. The ratified list, its membership criteria, and its epoch-gated growth (D-PRELUDE-LAW1, D-CORE-PRELUDE1/2) are not in question here. This ballot only picks the home: where the list is written and how the compiler applies it. It amends the D-PRELUDE-LAW1 mechanism and D-PRELUDEX1 wording, not their rulings.
decisions.story: Ana reviews a security-sensitive service. She asks: exactly which names can appear in this code without an import, and what do they resolve to? Today the answer lives in compiler source she has to trust. Under option A she opens one short Core file and reads the whole list.

options.name: A readable Core prelude module
options.detail: Core ships one short prelude module: the ambient basics are declared there, and the rest are pub use aliases into the ratified Core tree. The compiler opens it for every file. The full ratified list moves — including the four comptime-gated names, whose gate lives on the declarations and is untouched by aliasing. Growth stays ballot-gated as decided. Your declaration still replaces a prelude alias, with the ratified warning. #NoPrelude still opts a file out, and anyone can read what is ambient.
options.technical: core/prelude.jet carries the whole D-PRELUDE-LAW1 registry (always-ambient and comptime-gated names) plus the ratified D-CORE-PRELUDE1/2 additions. Names with no module home (print, panic, require) are declared in the prelude module itself; their meaning stays in Prelude/CoreLib per I9. Member spellings follow the ratified D-CORE-TREE1 tree and are settled by card #1576. Sema injects the aliases once at file scope instead of per-call-site string matching (core_surface.rs:183 and the scattered shadow guards retire). Libraries still cannot inject: only Core owns the file, enforced as today.

options.name: Keep the compiler table
options.detail: The list stays in compiler source, matched per call site. Behavior is identical for users who never ask where names come from. Reading the ambient surface keeps requiring compiler-source trust, and the per-builtin shadow guards stay scattered.
options.technical: No change. PRELUDE_ALWAYS_IDENTS and PRELUDE_COMPTIME_IDENTS remain the registry; ratified additions extend the Rust arrays.
options.code:
// user code identical; the list lives in
// crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs

options.name: Mode-gated prelude
options.detail: Two ambient sets: a bigger list for single-file programs, the small ratified list inside packages. Scripts get more magic; the same code can stop compiling when it moves into a package, which breaks grow-without-rewrite.
options.technical: Java JEP 512 shape. Requires defining the mode boundary and a migration lint for names that fall out of scope on package promotion.

comparisons.note: Rust's prelude is an ordinary module of re-exports, grown per edition with a migration lint. That is the proven growth path Jet's epoch gating already mirrors.
comparisons.code: // std::prelude::rust_2021 is just pub use lines

comparisons.note: Elixir's Kernel is readable source with per-name opt-out. Jet's #NoPrelude plus shadowing gives the same exits.

recommendation.why: The ambient surface becomes something a person can read, hover, and audit, while the list, its criteria, and its growth gate stay exactly as ratified. The compiler deletes scattered per-builtin guards.

whyNot.reason: A closed compiler table is the one shape every audit flags: names users see but cannot read the source of.
Code that compiles alone must keep compiling inside a package. Two ambient sets break that promise at the worst moment.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler must bootstrap the prelude module before user files, adding one ordering rule to module loading. That is accepted; Units.jet injection already proves the pattern.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a Core module, the current table, and a mode-gated set, and recommended the module because it makes the ambient surface readable without changing the list.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-project prelude extension and a no-prelude-ever design. Both were rejected as ratified-law violations: D-PRELUDEX1 forbids injection, and the ambient floor is already decided.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review took C's growth idea and folded it into A: any future bigger-script set would be another readable Core module behind its own ballot, not a compiler mode.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: a table is trivially fast and cannot be shadowed by a broken Core checkout. A keeps both properties because Core ships with the compiler.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked bootstrap ordering, user edits to a vendored file, and the comptime-gated four. Core is compiler-shipped and read-only, and the gate rides the declarations, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The visibility set
decisions.gist: How many ways can Jet spell who sees a name?
decisions.lesson: Today visibility has six spellings: pub, priv, #PubFile, pub(package), soft-public pub _name, and the module-level _name discovery skip. Two of them give the underscore different meanings. Private-by-default (S18) is not in question. This ballot picks the set of marks. It amends D-VISDEFAULT2 and D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1, and option A redefines the current pub module spelling, which today makes the module visible while members still need pub. Option C would also amend D-PUBPKG1.
decisions.story: Ben publishes his first Jet library. He wants: a public API, one internal helper he may delete, and one function only his workspace uses. Today that tour needs four spellings and a file marker. Under option A it is pub, _name, and pub(package) — each with one meaning.
decisions.inWild:
// today, one library file
#PubFile
fn api() { }                 // public because of the marker
priv fn secret() { }         // opt-out keyword
pub(package) fn shared() { } // wait - was pub redundant here? (E0414)
pub fn _legacy() { }         // soft-public, warns outside
// elsewhere: module _draft skips discovery - same _, different meaning

options.name: Four marks, one meaning each
options.detail: pub opens an edge; pub(package) fences at the package; _name means internal everywhere - skipped from discovery, callable, warns outside, never a promise. pub module makes a public-by-default subtree at the attach point, replacing the #PubFile file marker. priv keeps its one existing job - opt a member back to private inside such a subtree. On a file that is its own module, a leading pub module line does what #PubFile did. Fewer spellings, and the underscore stops meaning two things.
options.technical: Deletes #PubFile and the separate L0601 soft-public rule; the E0412-E0418 family retargets from the marker to pub module. priv stays legal only inside a public-by-default subtree, exactly today's E0413 shape. _name unifies D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1 and U3's discovery skip into one story. This redefines today's pub module (module visible, members still private) into public-by-default; the old meaning falls out of pub on the declaration plus per-member defaults.

options.name: Keep today's six spellings
options.detail: No change. Each spelling has a ratified rationale and shipped tests. The underscore keeps two meanings, and library files keep the marker-plus-keyword pattern.
options.technical: S18, D-VISDEFAULT2, D-PUBPKG1, D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1, and U3 stay as written.

options.name: Minimal: pub and underscore only
options.detail: Two marks: pub opens, _name is internal. pub(package), #PubFile, and priv are deleted. The workspace fence disappears, so package-only APIs become soft convention instead of a checked rule.
options.technical: Amends D-PUBPKG1 in addition to D-VISDEFAULT2 and D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1. E0605 package enforcement retires.

comparisons.note: Go has one visibility idea (capitalized exports) and it is loved for zero ceremony. But its missing package fence bred internal/ directory conventions.
comparisons.code: func Letter(n int) string  // public by case

comparisons.note: Rust's pub(crate), pub(super), pub(in path) zoo is the cautionary tale. Jet already rejected everything but pub(package) (E0411).

recommendation.why: Every mark keeps exactly one meaning, the file marker stops fighting the module tree, and the checked package fence survives. Ben's tour is pub, pub(package), and _name.

whyNot.reason: Six spellings for three ideas, and the underscore means two different things depending on where it appears.
Deleting the package fence trades a checked boundary for a naming convention, which the enterprise pass cannot accept.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing #PubFile and priv code migrates to pub module in one greenfield change. That is accepted; the migration is mechanical and examples are few.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the unified mark set, the status quo, and a Go-style minimal set, recommending the unified set for one-meaning-per-mark.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested visibility-by-casing and per-item export lists in a module head. Casing collides with the ratified casing law; export lists duplicate pub use doors, so both folded away.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option A's pub module: it keeps #PubFile's real value (public-by-default regions) but moves the flip to the attach point the tree already has.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: every spelling is shipped, tested, and ratified, so keeping them costs no migration. It still leaves two meanings of underscore.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked pub module: _name alone is callable, not private, so the first draft lost true privacy inside public subtrees. Keeping priv inside the flip repairs it, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: use inside module bodies, and one meaning for .[ ]
decisions.gist: May a module body hold use lines, and what does .[ ] always mean?
