Gain: the chain becomes readable today and enforceable per project. Loss: an unattested dependency still resolves by default.
options.technical: Implements D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1=D (attaches the deferred live verifiers) on the authority-block rail (#1570). The ratified D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1 trust vocabulary is { default, ci, services } with allow/prompt/deny; the require: row (values none | logged | attested) is a named amendment adding new vocabulary to that block. Exact spelling is the owner's. E1204 hash enforcement unchanged.

options.name: Require attestation by default
options.detail: Unattested dependencies fail resolve unless the manifest lowers the bar. Gain: the strongest default. Loss: most of today's ecosystem is unattested, so nearly every project's first resolve fails on day one. The practical lesson from npm and Go is that adoption grows from visible-by-default, not mandatory-at-birth.

options.name: Tooling only: show, never enforce
options.detail: The inspect surface ships; no manifest row exists. Gain: zero resolve behavior at stake. Loss: the project that needs enforcement — the one Mia works at — has a report and no lever, and the deferred verifiers stay deferred with nothing pulling them live.
options.code:
$ jet inspect provenance textkit   // readable
// and no way to make any of it required

comparisons.note: Provenance shipped as a visible badge first; registries and orgs then ratcheted requirements. Visibility created the demand that made enforcement adoptable.

The checksum database is enforced silently for everyone — the layer analogous to Jet's E1204 — while identity and build proof stayed out-of-band. Jet already matches the enforced layer; this ballot adds the readable ones.

recommendation.why: It turns typed-but-dead trust machinery into a chain anyone can read today and any project can require tomorrow, on the authority rail the owner already ratified for exactly this kind of choice.

whyNot.reason: It breaks nearly every resolve in an ecosystem that is not attested yet, and the precedent shows visibility-first is what makes requirement adoptable later.
A report without a lever leaves the highest-stakes projects exactly where the story starts: able to describe the gap, unable to close it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The default accepts unattested dependencies, so a project must opt into the stronger posture. That is accepted: the posture is one manifest row, and the inspect output names every dependency that would fail it before the switch is flipped.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared verify-and-show, require-by-default, and tooling-only, and recommended verify-and-show with a manifest requirement lever.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested review attestations (the cargo-vet axis) as a fourth layer. It folded out as future work — a different proof with its own ecosystem, and the chain surface can add its line later without a new decision.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested B-for-new-projects, A-for-existing. That is A plus a template default, recorded in A's notes for the jet new scaffold rather than balloted separately.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: shipping read-only first is a smaller change and still answers Mia's CTO. It answers the question and still cannot act on the answer.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's require row with a broken registry log — attested deps failing resolve during a log outage. The posture check reads locally cached attestations pinned in the lock, so an outage degrades to the cached proof; the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Single-line function bodies: = or ::
decisions.gist: Which symbol attaches a one-line body to a function.
decisions.lesson: A concise function is `fn area(r: Float) => Float = 3.14 * r * r` (D-ARROW-CONTROL1). Definitions elsewhere are moving to `::`: aliases (D-ALIAS-OP1) and module instantiation (D-CONF-GENSPELL1) both made the switch. The owner asked whether the function body should move too, since the line binds a name to its logic. The split under test: `::` defines a thing; `=` fills a slot inside a thing being defined — defaults, discriminants, reassignment.
decisions.story: Nate reads three one-line definitions in a row: an alias with `::`, a module with `::`, a function with `=`. The function is the odd one out, and he has to remember why.
decisions.inWild:
alias Parsed<T> :: T ? AppError            // ratified, D-ALIAS-OP1
module int_cache :: cache<Int>(64)         // ratified, D-CONF-GENSPELL1
fn area(r: Float) => Float = 3.14 * r * r  // today, D-ARROW-CONTROL1

options.name: :: defines, = fills
options.detail: The one-line body binds with `::`, matching every other one-line definition. The rule becomes teachable in one sentence: defining a named thing uses `::`, filling a slot inside a definition uses `=`. Reassignment, parameter defaults, field defaults, and enum discriminants are slot-fills and keep `=`. Every existing single-line function migrates by formatter.
options.technical: Amends D-ARROW-CONTROL1=A. S83 multi-heads move with it (`fn area(Circle(r: Float)) => Float :: 3.14 * r * r`). Unchanged `=` sites: reassignment (S2), parameter defaults (S61/D-NARG1), field defaults (D-FIELDDEF1=C), enum discriminants (D-META-CONST1=A), index write (S39/D-API-STORE1). The parser is unambiguous: after a return type, `::` can only open a body. Named honestly: D-ALIAS-OP1's rejected option kept the fn `=` on purpose, and ratifying this overrides that recorded reasoning.

options.name: Keep =
options.detail: No change. The body keeps `=`, the spelling D-ALIAS-OP1's own reasoning chose to preserve when aliases moved. The cost is the story above: three one-line definitions, two symbols, and a rule that only history explains.
options.technical: No change. D-ALIAS-OP1's rejected-option text stands as the recorded rationale: the alias move was argued precisely so the fn body `=` could stay.
options.code: fn area(r: Float) => Float = 3.14 * r * r

options.name: Retire the single-line form
options.detail: Braces only: every function body is a block. The symbol question disappears, and every concise helper pays two braces and a line for it. The measured corpus is full of one-line helpers, so this taxes the common case to dodge a one-token choice.
options.technical: D-ARROW-CONTROL1's `= expression` production is removed; formatter rewrites to braces.

comparisons.note: Every definition uses `=`, uniformly — the opposite consistency. The lesson is that one symbol for definition reads well; which symbol matters less than using it everywhere.
Expression bodies use `=` while properties use `=` too, but locals use different keywords — a mixed record that never settled a define-versus-fill split.
comparisons.code: fun area(r: Double): Double = 3.14 * r * r

recommendation.why: One reading for every one-line definition: name, shape, `::`, meaning. The fill-sites keep `=`, so the split is one teachable sentence instead of a history lesson.

whyNot.reason: It preserves the last definition still spelled `=`, and the reason it survived was an argument about aliases, not about functions.
It deletes a loved concise form and taxes every small helper to avoid answering a one-token question.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every existing single-line function migrates, and D-ALIAS-OP1's recorded rationale is overridden by name. Accepted: the formatter does the whole migration, and the overridden reasoning is quoted here rather than silently dropped.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the `::` body, keeping `=`, and braces-only, and recommended `::` for the define-versus-fill split the ratified alias and module moves already started.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested dropping the operator entirely and reusing the arm arrow for bodies. Both collide with existing grammar or overload an arm token, so both folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid — `::` for functions, `=` elsewhere — is option A itself, since defaults and discriminants are slot-fills by the stated law. No separate entry needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned with D-ALIAS-OP1's own recorded reasoning, quoted rather than paraphrased. Option C gained the honest note that it ends the symbol debate permanently.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack: migration churn across every example and golden, plus overriding a recorded rationale. Both costs are named in the tradeoff, the formatter owns the churn, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The statement test-bind: subject == pattern ?? route
decisions.gist: How one line tests a shape, binds its names, and exits on the miss.
decisions.lesson: S31 already lets `==` test a pattern and bind names inside an `if` head. In statement position that power is missing, so breaking down a result costs an arm table even when the miss should simply leave. This ballot makes the statement form law: subject first, the test spelled `==`, the miss answered by a written `??` route that must leave. It replaces S74's pattern-left refutable bind, which is ratified but has zero code.
decisions.story: Kofi validates a request: parse the id, load the record, serve it. Each step is one test and one exit. Today each test is an arm table, and the happy path drifts one indent to the right per check.

options.name: Test, then a route that must leave
options.detail: The statement reads left to right: the subject, the shape it should have, and the written answer for the miss. The route must leave the surrounding flow, which is exactly why the bound names are safe afterward. Inside a loop, `?? next` is the skip, written out loud. A test with no route binds nothing.
options.technical:
The grammar already parses this shape: `==` builds a pattern test at any expression site, and the fallback operator wraps it at the loosest rung. New written law: the route must diverge (`return`, `break`, `next`, `panic`). A value route is illegal because the bound names would be unproven. Names survive the statement only when the route is present. E0405 gains one named exception: a pattern-test left side with a diverging route. A plain value test (`x == 5` with a route) is legal and binds nothing.

Amends S31 (binding scope extends past the statement when the route diverges), S74 (the unbuilt pattern-left form is retired; card #1652 re-points here), and D-FAIL-BIND1. Ambient `err` reaches these routes only when the missed subject carried a failure value, as in an `.Ok` test over a fallible type. A pure shape miss has no `err`, and using it is a compile error that says why. Byte patterns ride the same engine.
options.code:
parse_id(raw) == .Ok(id) ?? return reject(err.message)
load(id) == .Ok(rec) ?? return reject(err.message)
serve(rec)

version == "v{major:Int}.{minor:Int}" ?? return usage()
use(major, minor)

loop r, readings {
    r == .Ok(reading) ?? next
    record(reading)
}

options.name: Keep S74's pattern-left bind
options.detail: Build the ratified spelling as written: the pattern sits left of `::` and the route follows. The adversarial audit found three problems. The shape before the subject reads backwards, the failure is invisible until the route, and the leading dot, quote, and bracket forms collide with shipped statement grammar.
options.technical: Requires new statement-start dispatcher arms ordered before the scope-member statement (D-DOTSCOPE1) and string-literal statements. This is the S74 text made real, unchanged.
options.code:
Val(n) :: maybe_port() ?? return
.Ok(rec) :: load(id) ?? return reject(err.message)

options.name: Arm tables only
options.detail: No statement form. Every shape test stays a table, which is always explicit and always exhaustive-checked. The cost is the rightward drift in the story above, multiplied by every check in every validation path.
options.technical: No change. Card #1652 closes as will-not-build with an S74 amendment retiring the promised form.

comparisons.note: guard-let is the closest precedent for option A: the test is announced, the else block must leave, and the bound name survives because it did.
comparisons.code:
guard let id = parseId(raw) else { return reject() }
serve(load(id))

comparisons.note: let-else gives the same guarantee with the pattern on the left — the order option B uses and the audit rejected for Jet.

recommendation.why: It is the S31 test everyone already reads, allowed to stand alone, with the miss written on the line. Subject first, spoken left to right, and the grammar parses it today.

whyNot.reason: The shape arrives before the subject, the failure is invisible, and the leading-token forms collide with shipped statement grammar.
It keeps the rightward drift that makes validation code hard to read, which is the whole cost this ballot exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: `==` now sometimes binds in statement position, and `??` accepts one non-fallible left side. Accepted: both powers are announced by visible tokens on the same line, and the diverging-route law keeps every surviving binding proven.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the statement test-bind, the S74 pattern-left form, and tables-only, recommending the test-bind for its reading order and zero new parse rules.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a dedicated try-bind sigil and a keyword form. The sigil fixed nothing about ordering and added a fourth bind operator, so both folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping S74's spelling for enum shapes only would run two orders for one construct. It was dropped as the exact disease this slate treats.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned as the ratified text made real, with its parser costs written down. Option C gained the honest note that tables stay canonical for two-sided handling.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The audit attacked `Bool` left sides, the plain value test, and binding scope. The repairs are written law: diverging routes only, no route means no binding, and the E0405 exception is named.

decisions.title: Tier parity: resolve I9 against the interpreter carve-out
decisions.gist: Decide once whether the interpreter tier must match AOT exactly, because two ratified texts currently disagree.
decisions.lesson: Invariant I9 says every tier preserves one meaning for every feature. A later ratified verdict, D-VERDICT-1254-1, says in full: "Full JIT/AOT parity required, but the user-visible law is byte-identical default-run behavior. Interpreter-tier parity is a lower concern; implementation may close gaps or route around the interpreter." Both are law today, and the open question is only the interpreter tier. The gap is not abstract: the interpreter silently skips view-range bounds checks (card #1616). One text must win.
decisions.story: A teacher demos Jet with jet run. A student indexes past a view's end. On the teacher's laptop, nothing happens; the interpreter skips the check. Compiled for homework submission, the same program stops with a bounds error. The student's first lesson about Jet is that it disagrees with itself.

options.name: Full parity, no carve-out
options.detail: The interpreter is a first-class tier. Every safety check and every semantic holds there. D-VERDICT-1254-1 is superseded and says so with a link. The jit_gaps ledger and card #1616 become blocking work.
options.technical: Supersedes D-VERDICT-1254-1. I9 text unchanged. Every Prelude semantic reachable from deopt calls the same Prelude symbol; the one-home guards from D-ONCE-LAW1 enforce it.

options.name: A named carve-out (amends I9)
options.detail: This option amends I9 to permit one guarded exception registry. The interpreter may lag, but only on surfaces named in that list, and never on safety checks. I9's text names the list's home. Anything not listed must match, and silent new gaps still fail.
options.technical: I9 text amended to cite an interpreter-exceptions registry. Safety checks (bounds, overflow, unsafe gates) are never listable. The list ratchets: entries carry a removal condition.

options.name: Demote the interpreter to a dev shim
options.detail: Accept the verdict's direction fully: the interpreter is a development convenience, not a semantic tier. jet run warns when deopt runs code whose meaning is unproven there. I9 text shrinks to AOT, JIT, and web.

recommendation.why: Safety is rank one and the interpreter is the tier beginners touch first through deopt. A skipped bounds check there is a memory-safety story, not a performance story. One meaning everywhere is also the cheapest rule to guard.

whyNot.reason: A listed carve-out is a standing ledger of differences, and this audit shows ledgers of allowed drift grow until someone closes them as done with 48 entries still inside.
A permanent warning teaches every beginner that jet run is not really Jet. That trades the first-hour experience away to save engine work, which the constitution forbids weighing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Full parity makes some future features land slower, because the interpreter path must ship in the same change. That is the do-it-right rule already written in the philosophy.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the contradiction, offered full parity, a named carve-out, and demotion, and recommended full parity on the safety rank.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered deleting the interpreter tier entirely and JIT-only dev. Both collapse into option C's honesty question and were folded there.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested full parity for safety checks plus a listed lag for everything else. That is exactly option B, so no new option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the never-listable safety rule and a removal condition per entry, and strengthened C with an explicit user-visible note instead of silence.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with the cost of blocking features on interpreter work and with deopt surfaces that genuinely cannot apply. The existing owner-ratified carve-out mechanism in I9 already handles true cannot-apply cases, so A survives without a standing lag list.

decisions.title: Retired spellings: the enforcement mechanism
decisions.gist: Pick what happens when code uses a retired spelling, so renames stop living forever.
decisions.lesson: Greenfield law says a replaced form is deleted in the same change. Nothing enforces it. The ratified entry file run.jet has zero adopters; the retired main.jet has 94. The ratified manifest name has 7 files; the retired one has 45. A retirement today ships as a memo. This ballot makes it ship as code: an error, a rewrite, and a ratchet test.
decisions.story: The owner ratifies run.jet as the entry file. Three weeks later a new contributor copies an example, names the file main.jet, and everything works silently. The ratified decision exists only in the ledger. Nobody is wrong, and the migration never happens.
decisions.inWild:
$ ls my-app/
main.jet   pkg.jet        # both retired names, both accepted in silence today
$ jet run my-app/main.jet
Hello!                    # no notice, no nudge, forever

options.name: Hard error with a fix line
options.detail: A retired spelling is a compile error with what, why, and fix, and jet fix performs the rename on demand. Old trees stop building until touched once. The strictest reading of greenfield law.
options.code:
$ jet run my-app/main.jet
Error [E13xx]: `main.jet` was retired; the entry file is `run.jet`
 Why: one canonical entry name (D-VERDICT-678-1)
 Fix: run `jet fix --rename-entry` to rename it
// E13xx is provisional; the real code is assigned at registration
$ jet fix --rename-entry
renamed: main.jet -> run.jet

options.name: Auto-rewrite with a notice
options.detail: jet fmt and jet fix rewrite retired spellings mechanically and print what they did. The compiler accepts the old form for one release window and says so each time. That window is a compatibility exception, so greenfield law requires this option to carry an owner-ratified carve-out naming its exact scope and removal condition. Errors appear only where a rewrite cannot be mechanical.
options.code:
$ jet fmt
rewrote: pkg.jet -> package.jet   (retired name, D-ECO-FILEROOT1)
$ jet run my-app/main.jet
note: `main.jet` is retired; this build accepted it and renamed guidance applies

options.name: Both, split by category
options.detail: Pure renames auto-rewrite with a notice. Retirements that change meaning or structure hard-error with a fix line. Every retirement declares its category when it lands, and both roads end at the same ratchet: a test asserting the retired form's in-repo count is zero.
options.technical: A retirement row: {old, new, category: rename|semantic, error code, rewrite rule?, ratchet test}. The row is the one home; loader silence is no longer a possible outcome.
options.code:
// retirement row (proposed):
retire main.jet -> run.jet        category: rename    rewrite: yes   ratchet: 0 files
retire payload:{} -> name:/version:  category: semantic  error: E1206   ratchet: 0 files
$ jet fmt        # renames just happen
$ jet build      # semantic retirements stop the build with the fix

comparisons.note: Editions pair a hard boundary with cargo fix, which rewrites mechanically; retired forms do not linger silently inside one edition.

recommendation.why: Renames and meaning changes deserve different force. A rename that a tool can perform should never cost a human a build break, and a meaning change should never be rewritten silently. One row shape carries both and ends at zero either way.

whyNot.reason: Hard-erroring a pure rename makes the tool ask a human to do what the tool can do itself.
A notice on a semantic change lets a program's meaning shift under a formatter run, which is exactly the silent move the fact law forbids.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every retirement must now declare its category and ship its row. That is one line of ceremony per retirement, paid by the person retiring, not by users.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered hard error, auto-rewrite, and the category split, recommending the split because renames and meaning changes deserve different force.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested grandfathering old trees permanently and a telemetry-driven deprecation clock. Permanent grandfathering is the current silent failure with paperwork; clocks without enforcement decay, so neither joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed C is itself the hybrid of A and B and checked it stays coherent: one row shape, two forces, one ratchet.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with jet fix on demand and B with a one-release acceptance window, making both their strongest honest selves before judging.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked C's category field: who decides rename versus semantic? Repair: the retirement row is part of the retiring change and reviewed with it, and a wrong category is a normal review finding, not a new mechanism.

decisions.title: The corpus law: say it once, with a guard
decisions.gist: Adopt one law for the whole corpus: every truth has one home, every other appearance is rendered from it, and each law ships with a guard.
decisions.lesson: The audit found 18 cases where one job is implemented by several hand-kept copies: two schedulers, three effect-root lists, four copies of one error message, two decision ledgers. Each copy is kept in sync by comments or habit. The fact law you ratified already forbids this for program facts. This ballot extends the same rule to the compiler, its tables, its messages, and its records.
decisions.story: An agent fixes the deadline error text in the scheduler. Three other copies keep the old wording. The test suite stays green, because every test only checks that the text exists somewhere. A month later, two tiers print different errors for the same failure, and nobody knows which one is law.

options.name: The law plus mandatory guards
options.detail: Every unified truth registers its home, the surfaces rendered from it, and a guard test. A registered truth without a guard fails lint. New second copies fail the build. This is the fact-law row shape, applied to the corpus itself.
options.technical: A truth row: {name, home, renderers[], guard}. Guards are cheap uniqueness tests: assert one definition site, or diff derived output against the home. tower lint gains a corpus-law pass that fails a row with no guard.

options.name: The law as doctrine, guards optional
options.detail: Adopt the one-home rule as written policy. Guards are recommended, not required. Reviewers enforce the rule by reading. No registry, no lint pass. Lighter to run, but the audit shows review alone did not stop the existing hundred copies.

options.name: Per-slate policing only
options.detail: No corpus-wide law. Each ratified slate keeps policing its own area, as the report slate and fact slate do today. Cross-domain forks, like one error text living in four crates, stay nobody's job.

comparisons.note: rustc generates its diagnostics index and its option tables from single declarative homes; a second copy cannot drift because it does not exist.
comparisons.code: // rustc: declare_lint! / diagnostic structs -> rendered docs, JSON, and checks from one source

recommendation.why: The audit is the proof: doctrine without guards produced about one hundred copies, four live forks, and a green test suite through all of it. A guard turns the next fork into a red build the same day.

whyNot.reason: Doctrine alone already failed. AGENTS.md forbids parking work in jit_gaps.txt, and the file holds 48 entries.
The worst forks cross slate lines. Four copies of one error text span three domains, so per-slate policing never sees the whole animal.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every future unification must also write its guard row. That is one small test per truth, and it is the only thing that has ever kept two copies equal.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared mandatory guards, optional guards, and per-slate policing, and recommended mandatory guards because the evidence shows reviews alone missed a hundred copies.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested two more shapes: a one-time cleanup sweep with no standing law, and generating all code from one schema. The sweep decays like jit_gaps did, and full generation is a build-system rewrite folded into option A's guard idea.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried doctrine now, guards later. It collapsed into option B, because a guard promised later is a promise, and the audit is a museum of expired promises.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a quarterly audit cadence and C with a named cross-slate owner. Neither repair catches a fork the day it lands, which is the job.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with guard rot: a weak guard passes while meaning drifts. Repair: a guard must diff behavior or count definition sites, never just check existence, and A survives with that rule in the row shape.

decisions.title: One word, one mechanism: stream and yield
decisions.gist: Give the words stream and yield exactly one meaning each in Jet's spec and docs.
decisions.lesson: The word stream names six unrelated things today: the generator type Stream<T>, a codec reader mode, file-line iteration, the Event type's description, a future analytics type, and scheduler internals. The word yield is a suspension keyword, yet the spec also calls eager list-building loops yielding loops. No user spelling is wrong; the vocabulary is. A newcomer cannot ask what Jet means by streaming and get one answer.
decisions.story: A newcomer reads that encoding supports streaming, finds Stream<T> in the reference, and writes a codec loop expecting yield to work inside it. It does not; codec readers are a different machine with the same name. Their mental model breaks on a word, not on a rule.
decisions.inWild:
fn count() => Stream<Int> { yield 1 }        // a real Stream: suspends
reader :: json.reader(file)                   // the spec calls this streaming too
loop line, handle.lines() { }                 // and this
ev :: event.new<Int>()                        // "a typed occurrence stream" — also this

options.name: Stream<T> owns the word
options.detail: Only the generator type is called a stream. Codec modes are readers and writers, which their API already says. Events are events. Eager loops become collecting loops. One spec page defines the vocabulary and every other page links it. Zero user spellings change.

options.name: Rename the type, free the word
options.detail: The generator type becomes Seq<T> or Flow<T>, and stream becomes the umbrella word for all values-over-time surfaces, with one page mapping the family. A real user spelling changes, and every existing example migrates under the retirement mechanism.
options.code:
fn count() => Seq<Int> { yield 1 }   // renamed type
// "streaming" now legally describes readers, events, and Seq alike

options.name: Glossary only
options.detail: Keep all current wording and add a glossary page that disambiguates the six uses. Lowest churn of the three: no prose sweep, no doc lint, and readers of older material meet no renamed terms. The six meanings stay live, with the page as the map.
options.code:
// docs/spec gains one page: the six senses of "stream", each linked to its mechanism
// existing prose untouched; new prose free to use any sense

recommendation.why: The generator type is the only surface where the word does work: it names a language mechanism with suspension law behind it. Everything else already has a better word in its own API, so prose just starts using those words.

whyNot.reason: It spends a real breaking rename to buy an umbrella word, and umbrella words are how six meanings happened.
A glossary documents the collision without ending it, and the next spec page re-collides.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some prose becomes slightly longer, saying reader or collecting loop where stream used to blur. That is the cost of one meaning per word.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared narrowing the word, renaming the type, and a glossary, recommending narrowing because every other surface already owns a better word.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested banning the word entirely and renaming Event to Topic. Banning punishes the one legitimate owner, and the Event rename is out of scope here, so neither joined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested narrowing plus a glossary page, and folded it in: option A already includes the one vocabulary page, so no separate option exists.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with real candidate names and C with a linked glossary that costs nothing and breaks nothing. C is the right pick for an owner who values zero churn over one-word-one-meaning.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with enforcement: prose rules rot. Repair: the vocabulary page is a truth row under D-ONCE-LAW1, and a doc lint flags the retired senses, so A survives with teeth.

decisions.title: One spelling to request a derived capability
decisions.gist: Pick the single way a type asks for a built-in capability like Comparable, and end the second spelling.
decisions.lesson: Today a struct can request Comparable two ways: a marker before the type (#Comparable) or a body line (derive Comparable, D-USERDERIVE1). Both fill the same field; the parser proves they converge. The same keyword also means something else entirely: derive T.Trait { } defines a provider (D-METADERIVE1). One job with two spellings, and one keyword with two jobs.
decisions.story: A reviewer reads two structs in one file. One says #Comparable above its name; the other says derive Comparable inside its body. They check the compiler to learn whether these differ. They do not — and the keyword they just studied means definition, not request, three files later.
decisions.inWild:
#[Printable, !Debug]
struct Visible { value: Int }        // marker spelling

struct Score {
    points: Int
    derive Comparable                 // body-line spelling, same effect
}

derive Money.Wire { ... }             // same keyword, different job: defines a provider

options.name: Marker requests, keyword defines
options.detail: #Comparable and friends are the one request spelling. The body line derive Comparable retires through the retirement mechanism, with fmt rewriting it to the marker. The derive keyword keeps only its provider-definition meaning from D-METADERIVE1. Amends D-USERDERIVE1; keeps D-METADERIVE1.
options.code:
#Comparable
struct Score { points: Int }          // the one way to ask (bare form; #[A, B] only for two or more, D-MARK-STACK1)

derive Money.Wire { ... }             // the one thing `derive` means
// jet fmt rewrites:  derive Comparable  ->  #Comparable

options.name: Body line requests, marker narrows
options.detail: derive Comparable inside the body is the one request spelling, keeping requests next to fields. Markers keep every non-derive rule (#Layout, #State) but stop carrying derive names. The keyword then means request in a body and define at top level, split by position. Amends the marker table's derive rows.

options.name: Keep both, document equivalence
options.detail: Both spellings stay and the spec states they are one feature with two entry points, like inline versus external methods. Zero migration for the shipped corpus, and authors keep the adjacency choice per type. The reviewer's question from the story stays a live question.
options.code:
// status quo, plus one spec sentence:
// "#Comparable and `derive Comparable` are the same request."

comparisons.note: One spelling: the attribute. No body-line alternative exists, so the question never arises.

recommendation.why: Markers already carry every other declaration-site rule, so requests join the family the reader already knows. The keyword then has one meaning, and fmt can migrate the corpus mechanically.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the keyword meaning two things by position, which is the exact one-word-two-mechanisms defect this slate exists to end.
The structural-flexibility rule covers where code lives, not two spellings of one request; I8 calls that a second mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: Types with many derives stack markers above the name rather than lines in the body. The bracket list form keeps that compact.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared marker-only, body-line-only, and keep-both, recommending marker-only because markers already own declaration-site rules.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a third spelling, deriving inside an impl block, and folding requests into trait syntax. Both add mechanisms rather than delete one, so neither joined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested marker-only requests while keeping the body line as fmt-rewritten sugar. That is option A with the retirement mechanism doing exactly that, so it folded in.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the adjacency argument for long files, and C with the structural-flexibility precedent for one feature with two entry points. Each now states its best honest case.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with the distinct-type wrinkle, where capability markers set booleans instead of derives. Repair: that unification is the type slate's row and A only fixes the spelling, so A survives scoped.

decisions.title: The plugin package kind gets its own word
decisions.gist: Stop using the word wasm for two unrelated mechanisms: the browser compute bucket and the sandboxed plugin kind.
decisions.lesson: Two mechanisms share one word. #Target(Wasm) marks a function for the browser's compute bucket inside a web package. target: plugin compiles a whole package into an isolated Component Model guest — its point is isolation, not the instruction set. A user searching the spec for wasm gets two disjoint stories with disjoint diagnostics.
decisions.story: A developer builds a browser app with #Target(Wasm) functions. Later they want a safe third-party extension point and find target: plugin described as wasm too. They assume the two compose, spend an afternoon, and learn the only shared thing is the compiler's internal ISA choice.
decisions.inWild:
#Target(Wasm) fn crunch(rows: List<Row>) => Stats { ... }   // browser compute bucket

// package.jet of an extension:
name: "mathkit"
target: plugin        // sandboxed guest, loaded by core.plugin — also called wasm in docs

options.name: Rename the kind to sandbox
options.detail: target: sandbox says what the mechanism is for: an isolated, capability-free guest. The wasm word stays only where the browser bucket genuinely means the browser ISA. The old kind name retires through the retirement mechanism. Amends D-PLUGIN1 naming.

options.name: Rename the browser marker instead
options.detail: #Target(Wasm) becomes #Target(Compute), pairing naturally with #Target(JS) as the view bucket. The plugin kind keeps its name and the word wasm leaves the marker surface. Amends the web partition marker vocabulary.
options.code:
#Target(Compute) fn crunch(rows: List<Row>) => Stats { ... }
#Target(JS)      fn render(s: Stats) => Html { ... }

options.name: Keep both, add a disambiguation page
options.detail: Both names stay and the spec adds one page separating the stories. No manifest migrates and no term anyone has learned changes. The word keeps two meanings, with the page as the boundary marker.
options.code:
// docs: one page, two sections — the browser bucket and the sandbox kind,
// each naming the other as "not this"

recommendation.why: The plugin kind's user-facing promise is isolation, so its name should say sandbox; nobody chooses it for the instruction set. The browser bucket genuinely is the wasm target, so its name stays truthful.

whyNot.reason: It renames the surface that was telling the truth and keeps the name that was not.
A page that explains a collision preserves it, and search still returns two stories for one word.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing plugin manifests migrate one field value under the retirement mechanism's rename category.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared renaming the kind, renaming the marker, and documenting both, recommending the kind rename because isolation is that mechanism's actual promise.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested renaming both surfaces and folding plugins under the web partition. Renaming both fixes a collision that one rename already ends, and the fold is false: the mechanisms share nothing but an ISA.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested sandbox as the kind plus Compute as the marker. It adds a second rename without removing a second collision, so it folded back to A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the Compute/JS symmetry argument and C with its zero-migration guarantee. C is the right pick for an owner who wants no manifest churn this epoch.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with ecosystem expectations: developers search for wasm plugins. Repair: docs keep the word as an implementation note on the sandbox page, so discovery survives while the surface name tells the truth.

decisions.title: One policy ladder for every audited escape
decisions.gist: Give the three audited escape markers one org-policy ladder, and retire the one-off --allow-impure flag.
decisions.lesson: Three markers share one shape: write a reason, step off the safe path. Behind them sit three unrelated depths. #Unsafe has a five-scope, six-mode policy ladder with an org file. #Impure has a single CLI boolean. #Nondeterministic has nothing. The shared audit ledger is already ratified (D-FACT-GATE1, card #1571); this ballot decides only the policy half.
decisions.story: A team lead forbids unsafe code org-wide with the policy file and believes the org is locked down. A contractor's build script passes --allow-impure, and comptime code reads the network during builds. The lead never sees it, because the org file governs one marker of three.
decisions.inWild:
#Unsafe("pointer stays local") { ... }        // governed by org policy file
#Impure("reads a feature flag") { ... }        // governed by a CLI bool, invisible to policy
#Nondeterministic("samples entropy") { ... }   // governed by nothing

options.name: One ladder for the family
options.detail: The unsafe policy ladder generalizes: one policy surface names all audited escapes, with the same five scopes and modes. The one-off --allow-impure spelling retires, replaced by one family flag the org file can refuse — solo scripts need no policy file. A beginner still writes one marker and one sentence.
options.technical: PolicyKey::Unsafe generalizes to per-gate keys sharing one PolicyValue shape and one resolution order (Organization, Package, Module, Function, Block). The env-var org hook covers the family. All three land in the ratified gates ledger.
options.code:
// org policy file, after:
#Policy(unsafe: .Forbid, impure: .GateOnly, nondeterministic: .Default)

$ jet build --gate impure=allow      // the per-invocation escape, one spelling for the family
$ jet build --allow-impure
Error [E21xx]: `--allow-impure` was retired; use `--gate impure=allow` (org policy may refuse it)

options.name: Ladders per marker, shape shared
options.detail: Each marker gets its own policy key and file section, all using the same six-mode shape, but set independently with no shared default. More knobs, same coverage, and a lead must remember to set all three.
options.code:
#Policy(unsafe: .Forbid)
#Policy(impure: .Forbid)          // forgotten? impure stays open
#Policy(nondeterministic: .Forbid)

options.name: Ledger only, ladders stay uneven
options.detail: Ship the ratified gates ledger and stop there. Visibility becomes uniform; control stays three different shapes. The contractor story remains possible, now with better logs.

recommendation.why: The family shares one meaning, so it should share one control surface. One ladder makes the org file the whole answer to who may step off the safe path, which is what a lead actually asks.

whyNot.reason: Independent knobs with no shared default recreate today's hole: the marker you forgot is the one the contractor uses.
Seeing an escape is not governing it; the audit's missing-exit standard requires the refusal switch, not only the ledger.

recommendation.tradeoff: The org policy file gains two fields, and the old flag spelling retires with a teaching error pointing at the family flag.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one ladder, per-marker ladders, and ledger-only, recommending one ladder because the family shares one meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested folding taint scrubs and #Transact undo declarations into the same ladder. Both are different shapes, propagating facts rather than scoped escapes, so the family stayed three.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested one ladder with per-marker overrides. That is what option A already is: one default surface whose fields may differ per gate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C by pairing the ledger with a CI query teams could alert on. It remains observation without refusal, but it is C's strongest honest form.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with policy-file blast radius: one bad org file could block builds org-wide. Repair: the existing six-mode vocabulary already includes permissive modes, and scope resolution keeps local overrides where policy allows, so A survives.

decisions.title: One decision ledger
decisions.gist: Pick the one home for ratified decisions, because the spec and Tower currently disagree about what the law even is.
decisions.lesson: The spec cites about 927 decision IDs as law. Tower holds 505 records. 675 cited IDs have no Tower record, and 253 Tower IDs appear nowhere in the spec. The drift linter scans a directory that now holds a README. Verdicts can silently contradict each other with no supersession link; the comptime keyword was ratified immutable one day and retired the next, both records still standing. Nobody can query whether an ID is current law.
decisions.story: An agent drafts a proposal and cites a ratified decision it found in the spec. The dedupe reviewer cannot verify it: the ID has no Tower record, no status, no date. Hours go to archaeology that a one-line query should answer — this audit paid that cost repeatedly, today.
decisions.inWild:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs decision show D-MEM1
not found                       # yet the spec cites D-MEM1 as ratified law in 30 places

options.name: Tower is the home; the spec renders
options.detail: Every spec-cited ID gets a Tower record in a one-time import, with status and source span. The spec keeps its prose, but a decision block's canonical fields come from the store. The lint walks docs/spec and fails on any ID with no record. Supersession links become mandatory on verdicts.
options.technical: Import builds records from spec citations with status ratified-by-spec until reviewed. tower lint --docs gains a spec-walking pass. decision add gains a required supersedes field when the same surface is re-decided.
options.code:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs decision show D-MEM1
D-MEM1  ratified  source: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2210  supersedes: —
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs lint --docs
E_DRIFT: docs/spec/spec.md:1180 cites D-XYZ9 — no record

options.name: The spec is the home; Tower links
options.detail: The spec's declaration of itself as canonical stands. Tower records become pointers into spec spans, and the lint verifies every Tower ID resolves to a live spec citation and the reverse. Queries answer from the index the lint builds.
options.code:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs decision show D-MEM1
D-MEM1 -> docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2210 (indexed; spec text is the record)

options.name: Two ledgers with a sync guard
options.detail: Both stay authoritative for their halves, and a guard fails when an ID exists in one and not the other. The 675-and-253 gap becomes a burn-down list. Ends silent drift without moving either home, and keeps two write paths forever.
options.code:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs lint --docs
E_SYNC: 675 spec-only ids, 253 tower-only ids — sync required before merge

recommendation.why: Law you cannot query is folklore. Tower already has status, dates, options, and ratification mechanics; the spec has prose. Give the structured half the record and the prose half the rendering, and the one query works.

whyNot.reason: A 5,900-line prose file as the record means status and supersession stay regex archaeology forever.
Two write paths is the disease this whole slate treats; a guard makes the symptom loud without curing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time import of several hundred spec-cited IDs, each landing with a source span and a provisional status until touched.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared Tower-as-home, spec-as-home, and guarded dual ledgers, recommending Tower because the record needs queryable status and supersession.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a third store, one file per decision in git, and generating the spec from Tower entirely. The per-file store is Tower with worse tooling, and full generation is a later step A does not preclude.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced A's final shape: Tower holds the record while the spec keeps the prose and renders canonical fields, which is the workable middle of A and B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a built index making spec spans queryable, and it stands for an owner who wants prose primacy preserved exactly as declared today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's import quality: 675 records minted from citations could be noise. Repair: imported records carry a provisional status and their source span, so review happens lazily and nothing is invented.

decisions.title: One verb per job in Core collections
decisions.gist: Make one verb mean one job across List, Map, and Set, and bless the constructor spelling the corpus actually uses.
decisions.lesson: Today replace means three jobs: swap-by-value on List, upsert on Map, canonical-swap on Set. Remove-and-return is pop on Map but take on Set. The API law documents Type.from_x() conversions, yet bare .from() is the most common real form, with 32 call sites and no rule blessing it. Each inconsistency is small; together they mean nobody can guess a collection API without reading it.
decisions.story: Someone who just used map.pop(key) writes set.pop(value). It does not exist; Set spells the same job take. Their fix is a search through two API pages for a distinction that carries no meaning.
decisions.inWild:
displaced :: prices.replace("eggs", 3.99)   // Map: upsert, returns displaced
swapped  :: names.replace("Bob", "Rob")     // List: swap first equal value
back     :: seen.take(id)                    // Set: remove-and-return
gone     :: prices.pop("eggs")              // Map: remove-and-return — same job, other verb

options.name: Adopt the verb table
options.detail: One table fixes the family. The verb pop means remove-and-return on every collection, matching the verb beginners arrive knowing. The verb replace keeps only the List swap meaning, and Map upsert stays add per the ratified storage law. Bare .from() is written into the naming law as the conversion constructor. The from_x() shape stays reserved for source-qualified variants. Retired verbs go through the retirement mechanism.
options.technical: Amends the storage-verb table around D-API-STORE1 and the D-STDRUBRIC1 constructor idiom list. Both IDs are spec-only today with no Tower record; B9's amendment lands wherever B8 homes the decision record. The verb table is a truth row: stdlib docs, CLI verb choices, and future API review render from it.
options.code:
gone :: prices.pop("eggs")      // one verb, every collection
back :: seen.pop(id)
names.replace("Bob", "Rob")     // replace = swap, List only
Set.from([1, 2, 3])              // bare .from blessed in the law it already dominates

options.name: Match the substrate
options.detail: Align verbs with Rust's std where they differ, so people arriving from the backend's own ecosystem guess right: pop, insert, and HashSet's take and replace keep Rust's meanings. Consistency comes from the neighbor language rather than from an internal table.
options.code:
prices.pop("eggs")               // Rust's verb, kept
seen.take(id)                    // Rust's verb, kept
seen.replace(v)                  // Rust's canonical-swap, kept — three meanings stay

options.name: Document the map, change nothing
options.detail: Keep every verb and add a cross-collection table to the docs. Nothing ships, nothing renames, and no golden output changes. The guessing failure stays, with a shorter search.
options.code: // docs table: "remove-and-return: Map.pop / Set.take" — a legend for the maze

comparisons.note: pop means remove-and-return on dict, list, and set alike; one verb, one job, and beginners guess right.

recommendation.why: Guessability is the beginner surface: one verb per job means the second collection you learn is free. The table picks pop because the ballot's own evidence shows it is the verb people arrive knowing. The table also becomes the review rubric, so the next API cannot reintroduce a synonym.

whyNot.reason: It imports Rust's own inconsistencies, and Jet's users are not required to know the backend exists.
A legend for the maze leaves the maze; the audit's standard is deleting the second spelling, not mapping it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing code using the retired verbs migrates through the retirement mechanism's rename category, mechanically.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an internal verb table, Rust alignment, and documentation-only, recommending the table because guessability is the beginner surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass swept the wider verb space, including has, add, and open across modules. This ballot stays scoped to collections where the collisions are proven, and the table's later rows carry the full-surface sweep.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested the table with Rust's verbs as tie-breakers when jobs match. That rule folded into A: where meanings already agree, nothing changes anyway.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B for FFI-heavy users who context-switch into Rust daily, and C for owners who want zero golden churn. The adversarial pass then forced A to justify its verb pick against the Python comparison, which flipped the choice to pop.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's original take pick with the ballot's own Python row and story, and A now picks pop. It also attacked churn: the retirement mechanism's rename category makes each migration one fmt run.

decisions.title: The at-sign: build it, reassign it, or state the reservation
decisions.gist: Decide the at-sign's future: fulfill its reservation, narrow it, publish it, or make @ the one word for both at-a-place and at-compile-time.
decisions.lesson: The at-sign has one ratified, working meaning: the package-reference source separator, as in textkit#1.2.0@vendor (D-JPK-REF1). It also carries a documented reservation for locations and sources, with no feature behind it. Meanwhile the dollar sign is ratified as the compile-time mark and the fact-read spelling (D-FACT-READ1: T.$range, $build.profile). That dollar surface is law without code today. A respelling now is cheap; the same change later is a corpus-wide break. Option D amends the dollar law; the others leave it alone.
decisions.story: A language-curious expert hits the reserved-sigil error, goes looking for the location feature it advertises, and finds nothing: no type, no roadmap card, no design note. The reservation is a promise only the error message remembers.

options.name: Design the promised feature
options.detail: Mint a design card for locations and sources as a real typed surface, with @ as its sigil, homed to the epoch that owns distributed and packaging work. The reservation gains a due date and a designed shape. No syntax ships until that design ratifies.

options.name: Narrow the reservation to the packaging meaning
options.detail: The packaging separator becomes the sigil's whole official meaning. The location promise is withdrawn from the teaching error and the reserved-space docs. This amends the reservation text only, never D-JPK-REF1 itself. A future location feature would need to claim new space on its own merits.

options.name: Keep the reservation, publish it
options.detail: The reservation stays, and it becomes a visible row: jet inspect reserved lists it with its written condition for minting, and the teaching error links there. The promise becomes auditable and falsifiable instead of living only inside an error string.
options.code:
$ jet inspect reserved
@   live: package-reference source separator (D-JPK-REF1)
    reserved: locations, addresses   condition: distributed-execution design epoch

options.name: @ is the word at: place and compile time
options.detail: Prefix @ becomes the compile-time mark and the fact-read spelling, replacing $ everywhere: @config, T.@range, @build.profile. Infix @ keeps its ratified at-a-source meaning unchanged. The location reservation folds into the same word: a future at-a-machine feature rides @, so where and when share one story. This amends D-FACT-READ1's spelling half and the ratified comptime-mention mark — the read semantics stay, the glyph changes. The dollar sign is freed; its next job is D-ONCE-DOLLAR1's question.
options.technical: Amends: D-FACT-READ1 (spelling only; the one-mark-per-registered-plane law stands) and the $ comptime-mention rule. Untouched: D-JPK-REF1 semantics. Migration: mechanical respell of the shipped $ surface (comptime splices, the layout selector) via the retirement mechanism; the fact-read organs are unbuilt, so most of the change is spec text.

recommendation.why: One word carrying one meaning — at — across place and time is the strongest use of the glyph, and the packaging surface already teaches it. The swap is near-free today because the dollar read surface is law without code; that window closes as the fact organs land.

whyNot.reason: It spends design effort on the location half alone, before its epoch, and leaves the when-versus-where split standing.
It quietly forecloses the distributed future to save one ledger row, and the at-compile-time reading dies with it.
Publishing the reservation is honest but spends nothing and unifies nothing; it is the right floor, not the best ceiling.

recommendation.tradeoff: The comptime mark attaches to every mention of a comptime name, so a heavier glyph raises visual density in comptime-heavy files — and two fresh ratifications get their spelling amended.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft mis-read the sigil as unused; review rebuilt it around D-JPK-REF1 and scoped the question to the reservation's unfulfilled half, recommending publication.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the owner-raised swap: prefix @ as the compile-time mark, unifying at-a-place with at-compile-time. It also re-tested freeing @ as an identifier character and decorator use; both still lose.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed D is itself the unifying hybrid. It keeps B honesty about the live packaging meaning, keeps A path to the location future, and adds the when reading under one word.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C as the epoch-rule floor that spends nothing, and A as the only option that delivers the location promise on its own. Both stand for owners weighing those highest.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked D with glyph density on every comptime mention and with amending two fresh ratifications. The density cost is real and accepted in the tradeoff; the amendment is named, and the unbuilt read surface makes the migration window genuinely cheap now.

decisions.comment: This also must replace the macro expansion $[…]$ which would become @[…]@

decisions.title: The ratified UI-tree spelling was never built: ship it, amend it, or decide with the architecture
decisions.gist: Decide what happens to the ratified dot-construction UI spelling that no shipped code uses.
decisions.lesson: The spec ratifies typed dot-construction for UI trees, spelled .Button.{ label: "OK" } (recorded as D-UITREE1, which itself has no Tower record). Nothing was ever built: no Button type exists, and every shipped example and test uses the function-call surface, ui.box and ui.button. A reader trusting the ratified text writes code that does not compile. Separately, card #1588 is an open evaluation of one canonical UI architecture. This ballot decides the spelling's fate.
decisions.story: A developer reads the ratified decision text, writes .Button.{ label: "OK" }, and gets a parse error. They check the examples, find ui.button("OK"), and now hold two official answers: the ratified one that fails and the shipped one the spec does not teach.

options.name: Build the ratified spelling
options.detail: The dot-construction tree ships in the UI epoch: nameable widget types, .Button.{ } construction, and migration of the function-call examples. The ratified text becomes true. Until it ships, the spec marks the spelling unbuilt.

options.name: Amend the text to the shipped surface
options.detail: This ballot amends the ratified decision: the function-call constructors become the recorded UI surface, and dot-construction for UI trees is withdrawn. The spec tells the truth today, and a future architecture may still propose a new surface through its own ballot.
options.code: tree :: ui.box([ui.button("OK", on_click: done)])   // now also the ratified story

options.name: Mark unbuilt now, decide with the architecture
options.detail: The minimal gate ships immediately: the spec marks the spelling ratified-but-unbuilt so no reader is misled. The spelling decision itself waits for card #1588's architecture evaluation, because the tree syntax should serve whichever architecture wins. This ballot then reopens with that evidence.
options.code:
// spec, today: ".Button.{ } is ratified and unbuilt; the shipped surface is ui.*"
// spelling decided together with the #1588 architecture result

recommendation.why: The tree spelling and the UI architecture are one design surface, and the architecture evaluation is already open. Deciding the spelling first risks deciding it twice; the honest gate costs one spec sentence now.

whyNot.reason: It spends a future epoch's design budget now, before the architecture it must serve is chosen.
It ratifies the stopgap surface as final while the evaluation that could justify something better is still open.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spec carries an admitted unbuilt marker for a while, which is the truthful state anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared building now, amending to the shipped surface, and deferring with a gate, recommending the gated deferral tied to the open architecture card.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested deleting the UI-tree promise entirely and building a third spelling. Deletion is option B with less honesty, and a third spelling multiplies the defect, so neither joined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed C already combines A and B: it ships B's honesty sentence now and preserves A's build path for the epoch.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with the do-it-right principle and B with the spec-tells-the-truth-today principle. Both stand as real picks for owners who weigh those highest.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked C as a decision that just re-queues itself. Repair: C names its reopening condition, the #1588 evaluation result, so it cannot drift as an unowned deferral.

decisions.title: One naming lexicon for every surface, or one per tool
decisions.gist: Decide whether the ratified naming and abbreviation law also governs CLI verbs, flags, manifest keys, and file names.
decisions.lesson: Inside .jet source, naming is law: plain English words, a closed abbreviation list, fixed acronym casing. Outside it, nobody governs. jetpack says uninstall where the stdlib says remove. Some CLI verbs are kebab-case and some are smashed together. dry-run is a flag on one command and a subcommand word on its sibling. The abbreviation list allows len and fmt but the CLI ships deps, pkg, a11y, semindex, and sbom unexamined. The audit found the same concept named differently on two surfaces repeatedly.
decisions.story: A user who learned remove from the collections API types jetpack remove and is told the verb is uninstall. The language taught them a word; the tool speaks a different one.
decisions.inWild:
names.remove("Bob")        // the stdlib verb
$ jetpack uninstall http    # the tool verb for the same job
$ jet fix --dry-run         # preview as a flag
$ jet codemod dry-run plan  # preview as a word

options.name: One lexicon, every surface
options.detail: The ratified source-naming law extends to CLI verbs, flags, manifest keys, and tool file names. One blessed-abbreviation list and one acronym table govern all of them, rendered from one home per the corpus law. Violations retire through the retirement mechanism, mechanically where possible.
options.code:
$ jetpack remove http       # the stdlib verb, everywhere
$ jet fix --dry-run
$ jet codemod --dry-run plan   # preview is a flag, one spelling
// deps:, a11y, sbom: each either joins the blessed list by ballot or renames

options.name: Two lexicons, both written
options.detail: Source keeps its law; the CLI and manifests get their own written convention honoring command-line tradition, including its short verbs and abbreviations. Each lexicon has one home and a guard, but they are allowed to differ, and the remove versus uninstall split becomes official.

options.name: Per-tool freedom
options.detail: No new law. Each tool keeps naming as it likes, and review taste is the only guard. Zero migration and zero new rules, at the cost of the story's collision staying permanent and ungoverned.
options.code: // status quo: the next tool picks its own verbs

comparisons.note: One naming voice across the language, standard library, and go tool subcommands; gofmt-era users never meet a second lexicon.
comparisons.code: $ go mod tidy   // plain words, one casing, tool and library agree

recommendation.why: The beginner meets Jet as one product, and every second lexicon is a second thing to learn. The source law already works; extending its reach deletes a whole class of collisions the audit proved are live.

whyNot.reason: It writes the collision into law: the same job keeps two official names, and every future surface must pick a side.
Ungoverned naming is how uninstall, a11y, and dry-run-the-word happened; keeping it guarantees more.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some familiar command-line spellings rename or must earn a place on the blessed list by ballot.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one lexicon, two written lexicons, and per-tool freedom, recommending one lexicon because the beginner meets Jet as one product.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested aliasing both verbs everywhere and a lexicon for verbs but not flags. Universal aliases are two spellings with extra steps, and a half-scope lexicon leaves the flag collisions standing.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested one lexicon with a short blessed-exception list for entrenched command-line terms. That is option A as written, since the blessed list already exists for exactly this.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the unix-tradition argument, and it stands for an owner who wants the CLI to feel native to shell users first. C gains zero-churn honesty.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with ecosystem familiarity: users expect sbom and a11y in security and web tooling. Repair: the blessed list takes new rows by ballot, so familiar terms can earn their place explicitly instead of by drift.

decisions.title: The hash glyph's four jobs: keep them positional, or rename the colliding one
decisions.gist: Decide whether # keeps four position-split jobs, or the interpolation selector stops borrowing marker names.
decisions.lesson: One glyph does four jobs, split by position: applied-rule markers (#Debug before a type), fixed-size lists ([T#4]), package version pins (textkit#1.2.0), and interpolation format selectors ("{x#Fixed(2)}"). Three never collide in a reader's mind. The fourth does: {u#Debug} borrows the literal marker name Debug, but is not a marker, is never checked against the marker table, and carries its own error codes. Same glyph, same word, two judgment systems.
decisions.story: A learner who just wrote #Debug above a struct writes "{user#Debug}" in a string and reasonably believes it is the same feature. When their custom marker works in one position and not the other, the error text has no shared vocabulary to explain why.
decisions.inWild:
#Debug
struct User { name: String }      // a marker: judged by the rule table

print("{user#Debug}")             // a format selector: same word, different machine
prices :: [Float#4]                // a size: third job
deps: { textkit: "lib#1.2.0" }    // a pin: fourth job

options.name: Keep four jobs, write the one law
options.detail: All four spellings stay. The positional split becomes written law in the canonical syntax file and the reserved-space listing, and the selector's docs stop calling its arguments markers. The dot glyph already carries nine positional jobs under ratified law, so the precedent is established.
options.code:
// unchanged surface; Syntax.rs and jet inspect reserved record all four jobs
print("{user#Debug}")   // documented: a format selector, not the #Debug marker

options.name: The selector stops borrowing #
options.detail: Interpolation selectors move to a spelling that cannot be mistaken for a marker, such as a colon: {x:Fixed(2)}, {user:Debug}. Markers, sizes, and pins keep #. The one genuine mind-collision is deleted, and the format language gains room to grow without shadowing marker names. Migrated mechanically per the retirement mechanism.
options.code:
print("{user:Debug}")
print("{distance:Unit(km)}")
print("{x:Fixed(2)}")   // format language, visibly not the marker plane

options.name: The size separator moves instead
options.detail: Fixed-size lists respell ([T * 4] or similar) and # keeps rules, pins, and selectors. This trades the low-confusion job away while keeping the high-confusion pair, so it only wins if the size spelling has independent problems.
options.code:
prices :: [Float * 4]
print("{user#Debug}")   // the marker-name collision remains

comparisons.note: Format specs live after a colon inside braces, a lane that never collides with decorators or attributes.

recommendation.why: Three of the four jobs never share a reader's headspace; the selector does, because it borrows the marker plane's own names. Moving it to a colon deletes the one real confusion and matches the format-spec lane every mainstream language already teaches.

whyNot.reason: The dot precedent covers positions that never swap names; {u#Debug} versus #Debug shares the word itself, which documentation cannot un-collide.
It spends a migration on the job nobody confuses and keeps the one people do.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every interpolation selector in the corpus migrates once, mechanically, under the retirement mechanism.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared documenting the four jobs, moving the selector, and moving the size separator, recommending the selector move because it deletes the only name-level collision.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested retiring selectors entirely in favor of method calls inside interpolation. That trades a format language for expression noise in every string, so it did not join the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested keeping # while banning marker-name reuse in selectors. A name-ban inside one spelling is a lexicon patch on a structural collision, so it folded into A's honest form.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with the dot-glyph precedent and ratified positional law, and C with a genuine check of the size spelling. A stands as the zero-churn pick.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked B with churn and with colon overload risk in future format specs. The migration is mechanical under the retirement mechanism, and the colon lane is reserved to selectors alone, so B survives.

decisions.title: The dollar sign's next job, if the at-sign takes compile time
decisions.gist: Decide what the freed dollar sign does next; this only takes effect if D-ONCE-AT1 picks the swap.
decisions.lesson: If D-ONCE-AT1 chooses option D, the at-sign becomes the compile-time mark and the dollar sign is freed. Prime one-character syntax space is scarce: today only a handful of glyphs remain unclaimed. This ballot decides whether the dollar sign is reassigned at once or held with a published reservation. If D-ONCE-AT1 picks any other option, this ballot closes as moot and the dollar sign keeps its ratified compile-time job.
decisions.story: A maintainer sees the swap land and asks what the dollar sign now means. The honest answers are nothing yet, or a new job chosen deliberately — not a leftover glyph that three parser paths still half-recognize from its old life.
decisions.inWild:
// after the swap, these are the candidate futures for $:
home :: env.$HOME              // config surfaces read the environment
names.map(f => f.upper())       // today
names.map($.upper())            // or: a shorthand parameter
emit { fn get_$name() = $body } // or: $ stays only inside emit templates

options.name: Publish the reservation, assign later
options.detail: The dollar sign goes into jet inspect reserved with the candidate jobs named and a minting condition: each candidate arrives by its own ballot when its feature area reaches design. Nothing is spent on speculation, and no parser path keeps a half-meaning.
options.code:
$ jet inspect reserved
$   reserved: unassigned (freed by D-ONCE-AT1=D)
    candidates: environment access, shorthand parameter, template splice
    condition: the owning feature area reaches its design epoch

options.name: Environment and config access
options.detail: The dollar sign reads the environment in config surfaces: $HOME in env.jet and deploy files, matching decades of shell folklore exactly where config authors expect it. Ordinary program code does not use it, keeping the glyph rare by design.

options.name: Shorthand closure parameter
options.detail: The dollar sign becomes the implicit parameter in short closures: names.map($.upper()), pairs with $1 and $2 for arity two. A large everyday ergonomic surface — deliberately the opposite of a rare job, for an owner who wants the glyph earning daily rent.
options.code:
names.map($.upper())
scores.filter($ > 90)
pairs.sort_by($1.age <=> $2.age)

options.name: Template splice only
options.detail: The dollar sign returns to its original job and nothing else: splices inside comptime emit templates, where shell and template folklore already point. Outside emit blocks it becomes free space again, reserved and published as in option A.
options.code:
emit { fn get_$name() => $ty = self.$field }
// outside emit: $ is reserved, listed, unassigned

recommendation.why: The epoch rule: freed space is spent when a feature area earns it, not the day it opens. A published reservation keeps every candidate alive, and each future assignment arrives with its own design evidence.

whyNot.reason: Environment access is real but belongs to the config domain's own design pass, where its typing and audit story live.
A daily-ergonomics surface deserves its own worked design against Jet's existing closures, not a rider on a glyph swap.
Keeping a half-job alive re-creates the situation this slate exists to end: one glyph, one leftover meaning, three parser paths.

recommendation.tradeoff: The glyph sits idle for a while, visibly, in the reserved listing.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reserving, environment access, shorthand parameters, and splice-only, recommending the published reservation under the epoch rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested currency and unit literals and a pipeline hole marker. Units already ride #UnitFamily and the pipeline design is unstarted, so both fold into the reservation's candidate list.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested splice-only plus a published reservation for the rest, which is exactly option D as written, so no new option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the config-folklore fit and C with the daily-rent argument. Each stands as a real pick for an owner who wants the space earning now.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A as deferral dressed as discipline. Repair: the reservation row names its candidates and its minting condition, so every deferral is falsifiable and owned.

decisions.title: How block-construct markers are stored after parsing
decisions.gist: Whether a parsed block construct also keeps a separate marker record.
decisions.lesson: Card #1456 unified marker reading. One shared reader reads every hash-name marker, and bindings keep a plain list of marker records. Block constructs like #Unsafe and #Context still have their own dedicated tree nodes. Those nodes store the marker's arguments as typed fields. Storing a second marker record beside those fields would say the same fact twice. This choice decides the one storage shape for block constructs, plus #Todo, #Tainted, and the tag-prefix operator in expression position.
decisions.story: Priya writes a formatter pass that must find every marker in a file. Bindings hand her one marker list. Block constructs hand her twelve different node shapes. She asks which shape is the one truth, and today the answer differs by position.

options.name: The construct node is the record
options.detail: Dedicated nodes keep their typed fields, and no separate marker record is added. The registry still owns every name. Tools get one uniform accessor that yields any construct's marker row and arguments, derived from the fields. Gain: no fact is stored twice, and the checker keeps precise typed fields. Loss: the uniform view is an accessor, not a stored field.
options.technical: Stmt variants keep their shapes. A registry-derived accessor (marker_row()) maps each block-construct node to its Policy::APPLIED_RULES row plus argument values. The retained markers: Vec<Marker> list stays binding-only. The shared parse-path reader from #1456 is unchanged.

options.name: Retain a marker record on every construct
options.detail: Each block node carries the parsed marker record beside its typed fields. Gain: every marker in a file is findable the same way, as a stored value. Loss: the same fact lives in two places. An edit that changes one copy and not the other ships silent drift, and every consumer must know which copy is authoritative.
options.technical: Add marker: Marker to the twelve block-construct Stmt variants plus the #Todo, #Tainted, and tag-prefix expression nodes. A single-writer rule makes the record authoritative; fields become derived views. Formatter and reflection read the record; sema reads the fields.

options.name: One generic marker-block node
options.detail: Dissolve the dedicated variants into one node: a marker record plus a body, the same shape bindings use. Gain: one storage mechanism for every marker position. Loss: construct-specific typed fields leave the tree. Every checker and codegen consumer reads arguments through accessors, and the one-time refactor crosses parser, sema, TIR, and formatter.
options.technical: Stmt::Marked { marker: Marker, body: Block } replaces the twelve variants. Typed argument accessors are generated from the registry row schema, so malformed arguments are still rejected at parse time. Sema match arms key on marker.name instead of variant.

comparisons.note: Attributes stay uniform token records on every node, read on demand through typed parsers — the shape option C proposes.
comparisons.code: #[cfg(unix)] fn f() {}  // syn: Attribute { path: cfg, tokens: (unix) }

comparisons.note: Each statement kind is its own typed AST node with dedicated fields — the shape option A keeps.
comparisons.code: // SwiftSyntax: GuardStmtSyntax { conditions, body } — no generic wrapper

recommendation.why: The node already records every fact the marker states, in typed fields the checker verifies. The registry supplies the name. Nothing is stored twice, and the uniform tooling view is one derived accessor.

whyNot.reason: It stores the same fact in two places, and the two copies can drift apart silently.
It trades precise typed fields for accessor indirection across the whole checker, with no user-visible gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Tools that want one flat marker list call a shared accessor instead of reading one stored field. That accessor is written once and derived from the registry, so it cannot drift.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared typed fields, a duplicate record, and one generic node. It recommended typed fields because no fact is stored twice.
