reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested erasing markers after checking and a side table of records. The first lost the source shape the formatter needs; the second folded into option B as the same duplication.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass added a registry-derived accessor to option A, yielding any construct's marker row in one call. This closes option B's uniformity gain without duplicate storage.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option B a single-writer rule with fields as derived views. Option C gained typed accessors generated from the registry row schema.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked option A with the formatter walk and a future reflection walk; the shared accessor answers both. Drift between fields and registry names is already caught by the D-MARK-REG1 scans, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: select() element types: one generic door or an Int-only law
decisions.gist: Pick whether select can receive from a channel of any type, or is Int-only and says so.
decisions.lesson: Sema accepts `.recv(rx)` on any `Receiver<T>` and only asks that the arms agree on T. Both runtime doors take i64: `jet_scheduler_select_int_channels` and its timed twin. The Cranelift bridge calls the same door. So a `Receiver<Str>` select is a promise the runtime cannot keep. The gap is undocumented today. This ballot picks which side becomes the truth.
decisions.story: A user builds a task group with a `Str` channel for log lines. The checker accepts the select and says nothing. The value then has no door to come through at run time.
decisions.detail: Sema: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerTaskGroup.rs, `infer_taskgroup_select` at line 698 and `infer_select_recv` at line 769. Runtime: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs:2422 and crates/jet-codegen/src/SchedulerHost.rs:139. Cranelift: crates/jet-jit/src/Concurrency.rs:807 calls the timed Int door. Whatever wins must hold on AOT, `jet run`, and the interpreter per I9, with the meaning in the Prelude.

options.name: Generic select on any T
options.detail: Widen the scheduler door to a type-erased channel handle, so select carries any element type. Sema keeps its current promise, and the doc comment becomes true without any new restriction.
options.technical: One Prelude function takes erased handles and returns the winning arm plus its payload slot. Emit, Cranelift, and interpreter marshal only.
options.code:
(tx, rx) :: tasks.channel<Str>()
tx.send("log line")
line :: g.select().recv(rx).wait()   // Str, Float, or a struct: all work
print(line)

options.name: Int-only, rejected in sema with a diagnostic
options.detail: Sema errors on a non-Int element type with what, why, and fix. The doc comment states the restriction. Users tag work with an Int and read the payload after the select.

options.name: Scalars now, aggregates rejected
options.detail: The door carries a tagged 64-bit value, so Int, Float, and Bool all work. Aggregates such as `Str` and structs are rejected in sema with the same diagnostic shape as option B.
options.code:
(tx, rx) :: tasks.channel<Float>()
temp :: g.select().recv(rx).wait()    // ok: Int, Float, Bool

(tx2, rx2) :: tasks.channel<Str>()
g.select().recv(rx2).wait()
// Error [E13xx]: `select` carries scalars only; `Str` is not one

recommendation.why: The bug is a silent promise, not a missing feature. The smallest complete fix makes the checker say what the runtime already does. It costs one diagnostic and one doc line, and it holds on every tier at once.
recommendation.tradeoff: Users who want a typed select must send an Int signal and read the payload after. That is one extra line, and it is visible instead of silent.

whyNot.reason: A type-erased scheduler handle is new runtime machinery on three tiers to serve a case nobody has hit yet.
A scalar tier is a third rule to teach, and it still rejects the `Str` case the report actually names.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered a generic door and a sema rejection, and recommended the rejection because it closes the silent promise now.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested auto-boxing every payload and a compiler-inserted Int tag channel. Both hide a type change from the user, so neither joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced option C, which serves scalars through a tagged word and rejects the rest.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option A a single Prelude entry so the tiers stay marshalling only, and gave option B a fix line that names the workaround.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether option B blocks a real program. Any payload still arrives through `rx.receive()` after the select, so the pattern stays available.

decisions.title: Lower-level Core doors: fold into one ladder or ratify the split
decisions.gist: Pick how a lower-level Core API relates to its friendly sibling, so `expert` stops being an unexplained second door.
decisions.lesson: `core.crypto.expert.hkdf_sha256` takes raw bytes. Its `core.crypto` sibling takes typed keys. Neither door mentions the other, and no decision governs the split. One split already has a rule: `core.random` against `core.crypto.random`, ratified as D-RANDSPLIT1 and taught by an example. Card #1579 makes layering law and grandfathers nothing, so the two shapes cannot both stand.
decisions.story: A user reaches for HKDF, finds two functions with one name, and picks the one whose arguments compile. Nothing tells them one door is the lower rung. They ship the raw-bytes call by accident.
decisions.inWild:
use core.crypto as crypto
use core.crypto.expert as expert

key :: crypto.hkdf_sha256(...)     // typed keys
raw :: expert.hkdf_sha256(...)     // raw bytes, no cross-reference, no rule
decisions.detail: Sema routes all three module names together: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_call.rs lines 179 and 366. `core.http.client` is a ratified builder (D-HTTPLIB2=B, D-HTTPLIB4=B, D-HTTP-CLIENT2=A) but still states no rung boundary against `core.http.get`. Evidence: card #1725 and the xcut-ladder tables in docs/proposals/corpus-say-it-once.md.

options.name: One module, two rungs
options.detail: Fold the lower-level function back into its base module under a name that says what it gives up. The `expert` module goes away, so there is one import and one page per subject.
options.code:
use core.crypto as crypto

key :: crypto.hkdf_sha256(key: k, salt: s, info: i)      // default rung
raw :: crypto.hkdf_sha256_bytes(key: kb, salt: sb, info: ib)  // lower rung
// core.crypto.expert is retired; imports move in one change

options.name: Keep the split, ratify and teach it
options.detail: Two modules stay. Every split carries a decision id, a cross-reference line in both doors, and one golden example showing the same result through each. This copies the rule D-RANDSPLIT1 already sets for random.
options.technical: The layering law gains one row shape: base module, lower module, decision id, example path. A split without a row fails the layering check.

options.name: No rule; each module states its own shape
options.detail: Nothing changes in the code. Layering stays a per-module habit, and the four drifts on card #1725 close as documentation only.
options.code:
use core.crypto.expert as expert
raw :: expert.hkdf_sha256(...)   // unchanged: no cross-reference, no example, no rule

recommendation.why: The precedent already exists and works. D-RANDSPLIT1 keeps two doors and makes the boundary teachable, and the same row closes every other split at once. No API is deleted and no caller moves.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each split costs a decision id, two doc lines, and one example. That is paid by the person who adds the split, not by users.

whyNot.reason: Folding raw-bytes calls into the friendly module puts the sharp tool in the beginner's first import.
That is today's silence with paperwork, and card #1579 rules out grandfathering.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered folding into one ladder against ratifying the split, and leaned on the random precedent.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a compiler-enforced rung attribute on every Core item. That is a new mechanism for a four-case problem, so it stayed out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass checked whether some subjects fold and others split. Mixing both leaves users guessing which shape a subject uses, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option A a name suffix that states the cost, and gave option B a row shape the layering check can read.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked who decides that a split is worth keeping. The answer is the ballot for that split, reviewed with the change that adds it.

decisions.title: policy.auto_derive: a deny entry or its own boolean
decisions.gist: Pick whether refusing auto-derive is spelled on the generic deny list or stays a private boolean key.
decisions.lesson: Five project-wide refusal switches exist in five shapes. `policy.lints.deny` is the one generic list, ratified as D-LINTPOLICY1=A, and it takes lint codes. `policy.auto_derive` is an `Option<bool>` with its own parser, its own malformed-value diagnostic, and its own codegen check. Card #1570 collapses the authority keys but has not landed. The question is which surface auto-derive uses.
decisions.story: A team wants to refuse auto-derive across the project. They already deny lints by code in one list. They then learn that this one refusal lives somewhere else, in a different shape.
decisions.detail: policy.auto_derive is a bespoke boolean beside the general lint policy. Owner law (2026-08-07): config surfaces take names, never codes — see card #1748. Any migration lands on the NAMED deny list (deny: [auto_derive]), not a code.

options.name: Migrate to the named lint deny list now
options.detail: auto_derive registers as a named lint; policy.lints.deny: [auto_derive] replaces the boolean via the #1718 retirement rename. Depends on #1748 (named lint selection in config). Example: policy { lints { deny: [auto_derive] } }.
options.code: deny: [auto_derive]

options.name: Wait for the #1570 authority block
options.detail: Keep the boolean until the one authority block in the package manifest ships, then fold the knob into it. One migration for users instead of two.
options.code: policy { auto_derive: false }

options.name: Keep the boolean as a stated exception
options.detail: Ratify the boolean as the one blessed policy toggle and record why it stands outside the lint plane. No migration ships.
options.code: policy { auto_derive: false }

recommendation.why: One policy plane with named entries reads clearly and deletes a bespoke boolean. The named deny list is the general mechanism the say-it-once law points at.
recommendation.tradeoff: Option A waits on card #1748 landing named lint selection; the boolean survives until then.

whyNot.reason: The authority block has no landed design date, so the coat survives indefinitely.
Blessing a bespoke boolean beside a general mechanism contradicts I8 and the say-it-once law.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered migrating now, waiting for the authority block, or keeping a documented exception, and recommended migrating now.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a general manifest key-to-lint mapping table. That is a mechanism for one key, so it stayed out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass checked accepting both spellings for a window. Two live spellings for one refusal is the exact drift this card closes.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option B a single combined migration note, and gave option C a stated reason on the spec page.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether a lint code fits a build behaviour. Lint codes already name behaviours the build refuses, so the shape holds.

decisions.title: The print family: which spellings survive
decisions.gist: Five print spellings greet a beginner today. Choose the surviving set.
decisions.lesson: The first hour of Jet shows ambient print, io.print, io.println, io.sprint and io.repr with no stated difference. I8 wants one mechanism with a small beginner surface. No ratified decision picks the survivors; D-ONCE-VERB1 rules collection verbs only.
decisions.story: The corpus audit found the five spellings introduced together in examples/features/io/io_surface.jet:5-7 as a sweep. A beginner cannot tell which one to reach for. The say-it-once law asks for one home per job.
decisions.inWild: Python ships one print with an end parameter. Rust splits print and println. Swift ships one print that ends the line. Each language that kept many spellings teaches them forever.
decisions.detail: Sources: examples/features/io/io_surface.jet:5-7; BUILTIN_PRINT at crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs:173; jet_std_io_sprint at crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/IoLineStream.rs. D-PRELUDEX1 ratified the qualified io.* spelling under #NoPrelude, so the ambient survivor keeps a qualified twin. Interpolation "{x}" already builds strings, and "{x=}" already labels values, which covers sprint and much of repr.

options.name: One print, line-ending, with its qualified twin
options.detail: Ambient print(x) prints x and ends the line. io.print is its #NoPrelude twin per D-PRELUDEX1. io.println and io.sprint retire by fmt/fix rename; sprint callers become "{...}" interpolation. io.repr retires; repr output comes from the "{x=}" selector or a repr format selector. Example: print("hi") replaces io.println("hi"); s := "{user}" replaces io.sprint(user).
options.code: print("done: {n}")

options.name: The print/println pair
options.detail: print(x) writes without a newline; println(x) ends the line, matching Rust and C. io.sprint and io.repr retire the same way as option A. Beginners learn two verbs on day one. Example: print("loading"); println(" done").
options.code: println("done: {n}")

options.name: Keep all five and teach them
options.detail: The five spellings stay. The io_surface example and the docs gain one table naming each job. No retirement ships. The beginner surface stays five wide.
options.code: io.sprint("{n}")

recommendation.why: One verb with the newline included is the beginner default every survey of first programs supports. Interpolation already covers string building and labeled debug output, so the other spellings are second homes.
recommendation.tradeoff: Printing without a newline needs an explicit io call or a later ballot. Rust habits expect println, and option A retires that muscle memory.

whyNot.reason: Two verbs double the day-one surface to serve the rarer no-newline case, which the qualified io form can carry instead.
Five taught spellings for one job is the exact coat the say-it-once law deletes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft carried the one-verb option and the Rust-style pair, and recommended one verb because the newline default serves the first program.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tried an end parameter on print, Python style. It adds a named argument to the day-one verb, so it stays out of the menu and waits for a real need.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced option C, keep and teach, as the no-retirement floor.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option A its migration route: fmt/fix renames through the #1718 retirement table, and interpolation absorbs sprint and repr callers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked what breaks without a no-newline print. Progress meters do; the qualified io form or a later ballot carries them, and the ratchet counts the survivors.

decisions.title: How a plane, a right and a build fact are written in Prelude source
decisions.gist: Which written form carries a non-code registry row and its law columns.
decisions.lesson: Marker rows now live in Prelude Jet source. The same registration table also holds knowledge planes, scope rights and build facts. Those ten rows still sit in a Rust array. Each carries the two law columns the ratified fact law asks for. One says which way its facts move for free. The other names the written words that move them the other way. This ballot decides the written form those rows take, so the law reads in source.
decisions.story: Sam wants to know why a range narrows for free but never widens. Today the answer is a Rust file Sam cannot open. Sam wants to read one line that says the direction and the escape words, next to the marker rows that already read that way.

options.name: One new word: fact
options.detail: A non-code row is written `fact Name(...)`, with the same dollar-marked facts a marker declaration uses. What it attaches to is one more fact. Gain: the word matches what the row is, and one word covers all three kinds. Loss: one new keyword.
options.technical: Add KW_FACT and a fact_decl parser reusing marker_decl_param_list. Registry.rs reads Prelude/Facts.jet the way Policy reads Prelude/Markers.jet. NON_CODE_ROWS and PRELUDE_GATES are deleted.
options.code:
fact Exactness($holds: .Value, $safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, raw, wrapping])
fact Rights($holds: .Scope, $safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Unsafe, Impure, Grant])
fact Sendability($holds: .Value, $safe: .None, $proved_by: ownership)

options.name: Three new words: plane, right, fact
options.detail: Each kind gets its own word, so the declaration names the kind without a fact. Gain: the reader sees the kind at the left margin. Loss: three keywords for one table, and a fourth kind later needs a fourth word.
options.technical: Add KW_PLANE, KW_RIGHT and KW_FACT, all parsed by one shared routine. The keyword sets RowTarget.
options.code:
plane Exactness($safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, raw, wrapping])
right Rights($safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Unsafe, Impure, Grant])
fact BuildSettings($safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Force])

options.name: Reuse the marker word
options.detail: A non-code row is a marker declaration with no site and a fact naming what it holds. Gain: no new keyword, one form for the one table. Loss: the word marker stops meaning a thing a writer types before a target, which is what it means everywhere else.
options.technical: No parser change at all. Registry.rs reads the same Prelude/Markers.jet and splits the rows on the $holds fact.
options.code: marker Exactness($sites: [], $holds: .Value, $safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, raw, wrapping])

options.name: Leave them in Rust
options.detail: The ten non-code rows stay a Rust array. Gain: no new syntax and no work. Loss: half the one table reads in source and half does not, and the fact law stays unreadable to the people it governs.
options.code: // crates/jet-foundation/src/Registry.rs keeps NON_CODE_ROWS.

recommendation.why: One word for one table matches the ratified ruling that the four kinds differ only in what they attach to, and it keeps a fourth kind from needing a fourth keyword.

whyNot.reason: Three words for one table teach a split the table does not have.
Calling a knowledge plane a marker breaks the one word a beginner already learned.
Half the table readable in source is the drift the registration card set out to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new keyword, and the word fact is already used in prose for what these rows hold.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one new declaration word with leaving the ten non-code rows in Rust, and recommended the new word so the whole table reads in source.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review asked whether the row could be a type declaration or a package setting. Both were dropped: a row is compiler vocabulary, not a user type, and a package file cannot carry compiler law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested writing the planes now and the rights later. It collapsed, because the two law columns are the same columns for all three kinds and a split leaves a second Rust table alive.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D: no syntax, no work, and the guard in Registry.rs already checks the law columns. It still leaves half the one table unreadable to the people the law governs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked option A with the prover rows, which carry no direction and no gate. They already state a none direction and name a prover, so the shared form holds and A stands.

decisions.title: Where a contributor's secret values may live
decisions.gist: Which storage places the Jet vault supports for secret values.
decisions.lesson: Jet projects declare named secrets, and the vault stores the values in one encrypted file inside the repository. Some people and companies do not allow secret values in git at all, even encrypted. Other tools let each contributor keep values in a store they already use, while the project only declares names. This choice decides which storage places Jet supports.
decisions.story: Riley joins a Jet project at a company that forbids committing secret material to git, even encrypted. The project declares three API keys. Riley already keeps every credential in the company password manager. Today the vault offers only the in-repo encrypted file, so Riley cannot use it at all.

options.name: Repo vault only (today's law)
options.detail: The one place a value can live is the encrypted file in the repository, shared through git and unlocked per recipient. Zero setup for new contributors, and it works offline. People who must not put secret material in git cannot use the vault at all.
options.technical: Status quo D-JPK-SECRET1=A: .jet/secrets.age, age-style recipients file, memory-only decrypt at activation, every read carries the Secret effect.
options.code:
$ jetpack secrets set stripe-dev sk_live_x
ok: stored in .jet/secrets.age
$ git add .jet/secrets.age   # encrypted, committed, shared
# policy shops: no path forward

options.name: Blessed provider fleet
options.detail: Jet ships native backends for common stores: the repo file, the system keyring, and major password managers. Each contributor picks one, and the project only declares names. Every backend is code Jet must build, test, and keep working on three platforms forever.
options.technical: Per-backend native integrations (keyring APIs, manager CLIs or APIs), a provider registry, and per-platform CI coverage for each backend.
options.code:
$ jetpack secrets provider use bitwarden
$ jetpack secrets get stripe-dev
ok: fetched from Bitwarden
# Jet now owns Bitwarden, 1Password, Vault, keyring... code

options.name: Repo vault plus system keyring
options.detail: Two built-in places: the shared repo file, or the contributor's own system keyring. This covers the no-secrets-in-git rule with no third-party code. People who live in external password managers must copy values into one of the two by hand.
options.technical: One extra native backend: Secret Service on Linux, Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows. No external-manager integrations.
options.code:
$ jetpack secrets provider use keyring
$ jetpack secrets set stripe-dev sk_live_x
ok: stored in the system keyring (repo untouched)
# password-manager users: copy values in by hand

options.name: Repo vault default plus one command bridge
options.detail: The repo file stays the beginner default with nothing to configure. An expert may declare one provider command, per project or per user; Jet runs it to fetch a named value into memory. Any store works through this one mechanism, including keyrings and password managers. The command runs only after the existing trust prompt.
options.technical: One provider contract: the command receives the secret name, prints the value on stdout, and a non-zero exit fails activation with a registered diagnostic. Keyring and manager recipes ship as documented presets, not code paths. Values never touch argv, logs, or the hangar.
options.code:
# default: unchanged
$ jetpack secrets set stripe-dev sk_live_x   # → .jet/secrets.age

# expert, per user: any store through one contract
$ jetpack config set secrets.provider "bw get password jet/{name}"
$ jet run
trust: this project fetches secrets with `bw ...` — allow? [y/N] y
ok: stripe-dev fetched (memory only)

comparisons.note: One declared contract, 27 provider backends; each contributor picks their own store. The contract idea is the lesson; maintaining the fleet is the cost.
Encrypted values live in git and contributors hold keys. Same shape as Jet's vault today, and the same objection from no-secrets-in-git shops.
Plaintext files outside git: easy, leaky, and unshareable. The thing both Jet's vault and SecretSpec exist to replace.
comparisons.code: STRIPE_KEY=sk_live_x   # sits in plaintext on every machine

recommendation.why: One extra mechanism serves every external store, so the vault keeps its zero-setup default while the no-secrets-in-git rule stops excluding whole companies.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the vault unusable for anyone whose policy forbids secret material in git.
A backend fleet is permanent upkeep across three platforms, and every backend invites behavior drift.
It serves keyring users but still shuts out password-manager and central-vault users.

recommendation.tradeoff: A provider command is arbitrary code that can read secrets. That is accepted because it runs only after the existing first-entry trust prompt, and the beginner default never runs one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the status-quo repo file with a native provider fleet and recommended one generic command bridge over per-vendor backends.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested SOPS-file import, per-secret provider pins, and a hosted Jet secrets service. They folded into the fleet and bridge options because the storage place is the only real axis.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the keyring from a native backend into a documented bridge preset, so option D covers option C's use case without a second code path.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option A with its offline and zero-drift virtues and credited option B with first-run polish that a raw command cannot match.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the bridge as a secret-stealing vector and a beginner trap. The trust prompt, the untouched repo-file default, and a registered failure diagnostic repair both, so D stands.

decisions.title: What a keyless --no-sign publish does to registry metadata
decisions.gist: When an unsigned publish may skip the registry metadata refresh.
decisions.lesson: A publish writes two trust records. The package author's signature is optional with --no-sign; D-PKGSIGN1 ratified that choice. The registry metadata chain uses the registry root key and protects every consumer. A publisher without a key or pin cannot refresh it. Today, keyless --no-sign fails with E2607 even when a new registry has no chain. A publisher-side skip would break resolution for pinned consumers on an established registry.
decisions.story: Sam starts a private registry for a game-jam team. He publishes the first package with --no-sign; no root key exists, and no consumer has a pin. The command fails with E2607 even though the registry has no chain. Ada runs the same command without a key on her company's signed registry. A silent metadata skip there would break her teammates' resolution of older signed versions.
decisions.inWild:
Sam's release script runs this command:

$ jet publish game-core --no-sign

The new registry has no checkpoint or sparse metadata, so the command succeeds. Against the company's established signed registry, the same command fails with E2607.

options.name: Registry-side gate
options.detail: Skip the metadata refresh only when the registry repository has no checkpoint and no sparse metadata. This identifies a never-signed registry. Established chains always refresh. Ada fails closed with E2607, while Sam's first publish works.
options.code:
$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry jam
published game-core 0.1.0

$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry company
error[E2607]: registry metadata chain cannot be refreshed

options.name: Always require a chain
options.detail: Every publish requires a signable root key. --no-sign still creates or uses a local registry key for the metadata layer, but it leaves the author signature empty. Sam must run keygen once.
options.code:
$ jet keygen --registry jam
created registry root key
$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry jam
published game-core 0.1.0

options.name: Retire keyless registries
options.detail: Unsigned registries are unsupported. --no-sign leaves only the author signature empty on an otherwise signed chain. The keyless test path is deleted.
options.code:
$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry jam
error: unsigned registries are unsupported

recommendation.why: A lets Sam publish the first package to a registry with no chain. It still protects established registries because the repository must lack both a checkpoint and sparse metadata before refresh is skipped.

whyNot.reason: B makes Sam create a root key before the first publish. It rejects the new keyless registry even though no metadata chain exists to refresh.
C removes keyless registries and deletes their test path. It avoids the edge case by banning the use case instead of checking registry state.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds a registry-repository check before refresh can be skipped. The check must treat either existing artifact as an established chain.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compares a registry-side gate, a required chain, and retired keyless registries. It recommends A because it permits a new empty registry without weakening an established chain.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a publisher-side skip, a local pin check, and a manual override. Those tactics do not distinguish a new registry from an established one, so they stay inside the three main options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested option A with option B's local key creation. That still requires Sam to create a key, so it adds no value to the recommended gate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option on its own terms. A protects old signed versions, B gives every registry a signed chain, and C removes an unsafe deployment class.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested missing checkpoints, stale sparse metadata, and a keyless publisher on an established registry. A fails closed in the established case and skips only an absent chain, so it remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: How grad is spelled and which inputs it differentiates
decisions.gist: Pick the gradient call shape and the way experts select target inputs.
decisions.lesson: Autodiff APIs settled into three shapes. Julia's Zygote uses one direct call, gradient(f, x, y), one gradient per input, widely praised as the cleanest read. JAX uses a transform, grad(f), which composes but yields the double call grad(f)(x, y) that reads like multiplication with a tuple. Swift spells named arguments, gradient(at: x, of: f). PyTorch hides a tape behind loss.backward(): beginner magic, expert-criticized hidden state. Jet wants one readable call for beginners and explicit targets for experts, with the double-parenthesis shape banned.
decisions.story: Priya trains a support-ticket ranker. Her loss takes weights, a batch, and labels. She wants gradients for weights only, and her teammate Sam just wants a one-line gradient of a toy function without learning any transform vocabulary.
decisions.detail: All options ban the inline double call grad(f)(x, y): a derivative function, where one exists, must be bound to a name before it is called. One mechanism underneath (I8): every spelling lowers to the same jvp/vjp core. Option E exists because the owner asked whether A and B combine; they do, on arity.

options.name: Direct call, Julia shape
options.detail: Beginners write one call that looks like every other Jet call and get every gradient back. Experts add wrt: with parameter names to select targets, and value_and_gradient to keep the loss value. No transform object exists on the surface, so the multiplication-lookalike shape cannot appear.
options.technical: compute.gradient(f, args..., wrt: [names]) evaluates f at args and returns a named tuple of gradients for the selected differentiable Tensor parameters, all of them when wrt is absent. compute.value_and_gradient returns (value, gradients). wrt names are compile-time checked against f's signature; a wrong name is a diagnostic naming the real parameters.

options.name: Bound transform, JAX shape
options.detail: grad(f, wrt: ...) returns a derivative function that must be bound to a name first; calling it inline is a style diagnostic. Composes naturally for higher-order derivatives, but beginners must learn that grad returns a function, and the binding step is ceremony for one-shot use.
options.technical: compute.grad(f, wrt: [names]) => fn with f's input contract returning the selected gradients. The formatter and L-lint flag an immediate call on the result, so grad(f)(x, y) never appears in idiomatic code. Higher-order: gg :: compute.grad(compute.grad(f)).
options.code:
d_loss :: compute.grad(loss, wrt: [w])
weight_grad :: d_loss(w, b, l)
options.tradeoff: Best composition story; worst beginner story.

options.name: Named arguments, Swift shape
options.detail: gradient(of: f, at: x, y) reads like a sentence and can never be mistaken for multiplication. Verbose for the common case, and Jet call sites do not otherwise lead with prepositional labels, so it imports a foreign idiom.
options.technical: compute.gradient(of: f, at: args..., wrt: [names]) with the same semantics as option A. Purely a spelling variant; the labels of/at are fixed words in the signature.
options.code: g :: compute.gradient(of: loss, at: w, b, l, wrt: [w])

options.name: Method on the function value
options.detail: Every differentiable function value carries .gradient and .value_and_gradient methods, so autodiff reads like any other Jet method chain. Most native to Jet's uniform method surface; risks surprising members appearing on every fn value, and needs a rule for which fns are differentiable.
options.technical: loss.gradient(w, b, l, wrt: [w]) with option A semantics. The member exists only on fns whose signature is differentiable (all-Tensor path); elsewhere the member is absent and gets the standard no-such-method teaching diagnostic.
options.code: grads :: loss.gradient(w, b, l, wrt: [w])

options.name: One name, two arities: direct call plus bound transform (recommended)
options.detail: One spelling, compute.gradient, does both jobs. Given the function and its inputs it evaluates immediately, exactly like option A: pure beginner magic. Given only the function (and optional wrt:) it returns the derivative function for binding, exactly like option B: full transform power for composition and reuse. No double-parenthesis shape can appear because the transform result must be bound before call, and the direct form never returns a function. This beats Julia, which lacks the first-class transform, and JAX, which lacks the direct call.
options.technical: compute.gradient(f, args..., wrt: [names]) evaluates and returns the named gradient tuple. compute.gradient(f, wrt: [names]) with zero value arguments returns a derivative fn with f's input contract; the formatter and lint reject calling that result inline. value_and_gradient carries the same dual arity. Both forms lower to the one vjp core (I8). Higher-order derivatives compose through the transform arity: g2 :: compute.gradient(compute.gradient(f)).

comparisons.note: JAX selects function arguments by index and can request one or several gradients.
comparisons.code:
jax.grad(f, argnums=0)(x, y)
jax.grad(f, argnums=(0, 1))(x, y)

comparisons.note: Swift makes the differentiated arguments visible at the call site.
comparisons.code: valueWithPullback(at: x, y) { x, y in f(x, y) }

comparisons.note: PyTorch asks for the input tensors whose gradients the caller needs.

recommendation.why: One name serves the whole ladder: beginners get a direct call that reads like any Jet call, experts get a first-class derivative function for reuse and higher-order composition. Both arities lower to the one vjp core, so no second mechanism exists. The banned inline double call keeps every call site unambiguous.

whyNot.reason: Pure direct call has no reusable derivative function, so training loops re-derive per step and higher-order composition needs new vocabulary later.
Transform-only forces every beginner through bind-then-call ceremony for one-shot gradients.
Prepositional labels import a foreign idiom Jet uses nowhere else, and still lack the transform form.
Members appearing on function values by differentiability is surprising, and the rule for which fns qualify leaks type-system detail into completion.
Accepting E means accepting arity overloading on one core name; if that ever reads as too clever, option A remains the safe subset.

recommendation.tradeoff: One name returning two kinds by arity is a real cost: a reader must see the argument list to know whether a value or a function came back. The bind-before-call rule and the zero-value-argument rule keep the two shapes visually distinct at every site.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compares all-input, named, indexed, and closure-selected targets. Each option uses the same two-argument function and shows the returned gradient shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested target values, closure wrappers, all inputs, named inputs, and indexes. Target values folded into closure selection because a value cannot name a stable function parameter.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested all-input mode with named narrowing. It kept named selection as one contract and treated closure wrapping as an existing composition pattern.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened every option. All-input mode favors short model code, named mode favors intent, index mode favors generated code, and closure mode favors existing language rules.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested parameter renames, reordered parameters, unused inputs, and captured data. It made selector failures compile-time errors and kept named selection as the recommendation.

decisions.title: The vjp carrier: how value and pullback travel together
decisions.gist: Pick what compute.vjp returns and how the pullback is applied.
decisions.lesson: Julia's pullback returns a pair, value and a pullback function, bound to two names and applied later: praised because both halves are named and no call ever touches another call's parenthesis. JAX's vjp returns the same pair; users who inline it get vjp(f, x)[1](seed), a shape nobody defends. Enzyme and Futhark treat vjp as an explicit seeded primitive for experts only. Jet wants named, discoverable halves for beginners and explicit seeds for experts, never an adjacent-parenthesis chain.
decisions.story: Sam has a loss value and wants the gradient too, cheaply. Dana writes a custom training loop and needs to push three different seed vectors through one recorded pass without recomputing the forward run.
decisions.inWild:
// one forward pass, three seeds, no recompute
rec :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l)
print(rec.value)
g1 :: rec.pull(seed_a)
g2 :: rec.pull(seed_b)
g3 :: rec.pull(seed_c)
decisions.detail: All options ban inline double calls; a pullback is always a named thing before it runs. One mechanism underneath (I8): grad in D-COMPUTE-GRAD1 is defined as vjp with a scalar unit seed, whichever spelling wins.

options.name: Typed record with pull method (recommended)
options.detail: vjp returns one typed value with named members: .value for the forward result, .pull(seed) to run the recorded pass, and .grads as the beginner shortcut for the unit seed. Discoverable through completion, impossible to mis-order, and the record type gives experts a place for future cost and memory controls. Combines with a two-name destructure: (val, pull) :: compute.vjp(f, x, y) works because the record destructures positionally, so option B is a free subset, mirroring the unified shape recommended in D-COMPUTE-GRAD1 option E.
options.technical: compute.vjp(f, args...) => VjpRun. Members: value: Tensor; pull(seed: Tensor) => named gradient tuple; grads => pull(unit seed) for scalar outputs, diagnostic otherwise. VjpRun holds the tape; dropping it frees the recording under normal ownership rules. VjpRun destructures as (value, pull) for Zygote-style call sites.
options.code:
rec :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l)
step :: compute.sgd_step(w, rec.grads.w, 0.01)

// expert seeds
jtj_row :: rec.pull(basis_row)

options.name: Two-name destructure, Julia shape
options.detail: One call returns (value, pull) and the destructure names both halves at the call site. Familiar to every Zygote user and needs no new type; the pullback is a plain function value, so future expert controls have no natural home.
options.technical: compute.vjp(f, args...) => (Tensor, fn(Tensor) => gradient tuple). The formatter flags any expression that calls the second tuple slot without binding it first.
options.code:
(val, pull) :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l)
grads :: pull(seed)

options.name: Expert-only seeded primitive, Enzyme shape
options.detail: vjp takes the seed up front and returns gradients directly; no pullback value exists. Simplest surface and one call per seed, but every extra seed pays a full forward pass again, which is exactly the cost the recorded pullback exists to avoid.
options.technical: compute.vjp(f, args..., seed: Tensor) => named gradient tuple. Multiple seeds mean multiple forward passes; a note in docs points batch-seed users at grad or a future batched API.
options.code: grads :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l, seed: s)

comparisons.note: JAX returns the primal value and a pullback function as a pair.
comparisons.code:
value, pullback = jax.vjp(f, x, y)
grads = pullback(cotangent)

comparisons.note: Swift exposes a value and a pullback from one differentiation call.
Zygote returns the primal result and a function that applies the reverse step.
comparisons.code:
value, back = Zygote.pullback(f, x)
grads = back(cotangent)

recommendation.why: The typed record is discoverable, safe for beginners through .grads, explicit for experts through .pull(seed), and subsumes the Julia destructure as sugar. It gives future cost and memory controls a typed home.
recommendation.tradeoff: A new public type enters the compute surface; its member set becomes API the freeze must track.

whyNot.reason: Accepting A accepts one more named type in core.compute; if the surface must stay type-minimal, B is the closest subset.
A bare tuple gives the pullback no home for future controls and no discoverable members.
Seed-up-front repays a full forward pass per seed, the exact cost a recorded pullback exists to avoid.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compares a named tuple, a dedicated handle, and a callable closure. Each option shows one score evaluation followed by a value read and a pullback call.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested an unnamed tuple, a named record, a handle, and two closures. The unnamed tuple folded into the named tuple because field names help readers without adding a mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested a tuple whose pullback also had handle methods. It created two access paths for one value, so the draft kept the tuple and ordinary closure separate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option. The tuple favors composition, the handle favors lifecycle control, and the closure favors one compact call surface.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested repeated pullback use, saved results, and missing value access. The tuple keeps both outputs explicit without inventing callable-object behavior.

decisions.title: How a host grants and calls a loaded library
decisions.gist: How a host grants paths and calls a function from a loaded mod.
decisions.lesson: A loadable library is compiled Jet code that a running host uses. An exported function is an entry point, such as on_tick(dt). An effect is a power such as file read or network access. D-LIB-DYNTRUST1 says the library declares effects and the host grants an equal or narrower set before mapping. It does not ratify the grant spelling. bd19-rev flagged the path gap. Read access to ./mods must not become read access to every file. This ballot chooses the call and grant shapes while keeping Mod.load(path)?.
decisions.story: Rosa maintains a flight-sim game with community mods. Each frame, the host loads f16.jetlib, grants read access to ./mods, and calls on_tick(dt). She wants a beginner path that reads like a normal method call and an expert path that can bind or select exports without hiding authority.

options.name: Typed member call with a load grant
options.detail: Jet checks the exported surface and exposes each public function as a typed member. The load line shows the file and its grant in one place. Beginners write mod.on_tick(dt); experts can bind mod.on_tick before a call. The cost is one grant record at every load site.
options.technical: grant: is a load-only named argument. Its value maps effect names to normalized path sets. The loader checks declared effects against the grant before mapping. mod.on_tick resolves only an exported function with a checked signature. A path grant covers descendants of ./mods, not sibling paths.

options.name: Lexical grant block with typed members
options.detail: The host opens one trusted region around the load and its calls. Authority ends at the closing brace, which makes review scope clear and can cover several mods. The loaded value still has typed members. The cost is a block for a single load.
options.technical: #Grant(caps: .{ read: ["./mods"] }) reuses the existing scoped-grant marker and adds path entries. The marker supplies the library's load-time authority; it does not change the library declaration. The loader checks each load inside the block before mapping. The handle and loaded values cannot escape the block.

options.name: Explicit export handle with a load grant
options.detail: After loading, the host asks for one exported function and binds it to a name. This fits dispatch tables and repeated calls because the function handle is explicit. It adds a line and moves a fixed export name from compile time to load time.
options.technical: mod.export("on_tick")? returns a typed function handle after the loader checks the frozen export table. The handle carries the export signature and the library lifetime. A missing name or wrong signature is a checked error. The grant remains path-scoped at the load call.
options.code:
mod := Mod.load("./mods/f16.jetlib", grant: .{ read: ["./mods"] })?
tick := mod.export("on_tick")?
tick(dt)

options.name: Dynamic named call with a grant record
options.detail: The host passes an export name and arguments to one dynamic call. This fits mod registries that discover names at run time. A typo becomes a checked run-time error, and the fixed on_tick case reads less like an ordinary call.
options.technical: mod.call("on_tick", dt)? resolves the name against the frozen export table and checks the argument shape before entering the library. The call returns the exported result or a checked call error. The grant record still maps read to normalized paths. The host cannot use this call to bypass the declared-effect check.
options.code:
mod := Mod.load("./mods/f16.jetlib", grant: .{ read: ["./mods"] })?
mod.call("on_tick", dt)?

// typo: checked error before entry
mod.call("on_tik", dt)?
error: export on_tik was not found

comparisons.note: Rust hosts open a library, get a named symbol, and call the typed handle. The unsafe boundary and ABI rules remain visible.
Lua exposes module functions as table fields, so mod.on_tick(dt) is the easy call shape. Hosts often pass a restricted environment separately.
A component host gets an export from an instance and passes imports at instantiation. It favors explicit handles over ambient grants.
comparisons.code:
instance := linker.instantiate(module, imports)?
tick := instance.export("on_tick")?
tick(dt)

recommendation.why: Option A keeps the common mod call as a normal typed member call. Its load line shows the exact path grant, so authority and code use stay together. Binding the member gives experts a named function without adding a second call mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Choosing A accepts one visible grant argument at each load. That repetition is useful because authority stays beside the load.
B hides the grant in a surrounding block. It can cover several loads, but a distant block can make one mod's authority harder to audit.
C adds an export lookup and shifts fixed-name errors to load time. It helps registries but adds ceremony to the common fixed export.
D supports name-driven registries, but it gives up compile-time export-name checks. A typo and argument mismatch surface later than typed member access.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option A adds a named argument and path normalization to every dynamic load. It accepts that repetition to keep authority local, preserve typed calls, and let experts bind a checked export.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared typed member access, a lexical grant, an export handle, and a dynamic call. It recommended the typed member form because it serves the fixed mod path and still lets experts bind the function.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The broad pass tested interface binding, a capability object, and a first-call prompt. Binding folded into typed members, the object duplicated the grant record, and the prompt delayed authority until after load.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested a typed member call inside a lexical grant block. It kept the block as a separate option because its wider scope changes audit behavior, not just spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened every option for its target user. A serves fixed mods, B serves grouped loads, C serves expert dispatch tables, and D serves name-driven registries.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested forged effect claims, sibling paths, missing exports, and wrong arguments. The recommendation keeps identity and effect checks before mapping, and keeps every call typed or checked before entry.

decisions.title: The default error on the exported web wire
decisions.gist: How an exported `Err` becomes a value that JavaScript and a Wasm host can use.
decisions.lesson: `JetErr` is Jet's default error value: a message, optional code, and optional recursive cause. The internal shape is settled. No ratified law covers how a compound default error crosses an exported web boundary. JavaScript and Wasm need one stable wire value that preserves these facts. The boundary therefore needs one versioned encoding, while adapters may present native errors or data.
decisions.story: Rui ships one profile loader as a browser app and a Wasm library. A missing profile is normal input failure, not a code stop. Rui needs JavaScript callers to use normal `try` and `catch`. A Wasm host needs stable fields for logs and retry rules. One wire must keep both code and cause chain.

options.name: Native `JetError` chain
options.detail: JavaScript gets a normal rejected Promise with a typed `JetError`. Beginners use `try` and `catch`. Experts read `message`, `code`, and recursive `cause`. Wasm hosts get the same fields as a plain record. The shape has no version tag, so future wire changes can break machine clients silently.
options.technical: Map `Err` to a `JetError` that extends JavaScript `Error`. Set `name`, `message`, and `code`, with absent code as `null`. Map one Jet cause to `Error.cause`. A raw Wasm host sees `{message, code, cause}`. The JS bridge throws once for the web edge. No full `jet.report/v1` object crosses.

options.name: `jet.report/v1` envelope
options.detail: JavaScript still gets a typed `JetError`, but its `report` field uses the existing machine-report schema. Tools can share one decoder with compiler and test reports. The schema gives every failure a full report frame. `JetErr` lacks why, fix, and source, so the boundary must add generic values or the schema must change.
options.technical: Encode the outer error as `jet.report/v1`. Set `moment` to `run`, `severity` to `error`, and `what` from `message`. Set `why` and `fix` to boundary text. Flatten the recursive Jet cause into the schema's `cause` array. A missing Jet code needs `null` support or a reserved placeholder. The JS bridge throws `JetError` with this report. A Wasm host receives the report object.

options.name: Tagged outcome at the raw edge
options.detail: The Wasm host gets an explicit success or failure record. Experts can branch without exceptions. The JavaScript adapter still throws a typed `JetError`, so browser code keeps target-native rejection. The outer tag makes every fallible export uniform, but it wraps successful values too.
options.technical: Use `JetOutcomeWire<T> = {tag: "Ok", value: T} | {tag: "Err", error: JetErrWire}`. `JetErrWire` has `message`, `code`, and recursive `cause`. The raw Wasm adapter returns the tagged record. The JS bridge unwraps `Ok` and converts `Err` to `JetError`. This option has no schema tag for `JetErrWire` itself.

options.name: Versioned `jet.err/v1` plus native adapters
options.detail: The wire mirrors `JetErr` and adds one stable schema tag. JavaScript gets a native `JetError` with `message`, `code`, and recursive `cause`. Experts can inspect those fields or call `toJSON()`. A Wasm host gets the same record as data. `jet.report/v1` remains a renderer shape, so no why, fix, or source data is invented.
options.technical: Define `JetErrWire = {schema: "jet.err/v1", message: String, code: String|null, cause: JetErrWire|null}`. Define a fallible edge as `{tag: "Ok", value: T} | {tag: "Err", error: JetErrWire}`. The JS bridge maps `Err` to `JetError` and maps cause nodes to `Error.cause`. The Wasm host decodes the tagged value. A report renderer may adapt the value to `jet.report/v1` when full What, Why, Fix, or source data exists.

comparisons.note: `Result<T, E>` is a strong Wasm precedent. `Ok` becomes a JavaScript value. `Err` becomes a JavaScript exception carrying the converted error. The boundary favors native JavaScript control flow, but the error shape depends on `Into<JsValue>`. Source: https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/result.html

`google.rpc.Status` is a durable cross-language shape. It has an integer code, a message, and repeated typed details. It separates stable classification from extensible detail. It does not model one linked cause directly. Source: https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/rpc/status.proto

JavaScript `Error` supports a recursive `cause` value. The platform keeps the outer message useful for people and the cause useful for machines. It is strong for native JS ergonomics, but it is not a versioned wire schema. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error/cause

Problem Details is the established HTTP JSON shape. It uses `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and `instance`, with extension members. It is strong for HTTP responses, but `JetErr` does not carry all of those facts. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html

recommendation.why: D keeps D-FAIL-MODEL1's value facts and D-FAIL-EDGE1's target-native delivery. One small recursive record maps exactly to `JetErr`. The schema tag prevents silent drift. JavaScript beginners use normal `try` and `catch`. Experts read stable fields or call `toJSON()`. Raw Wasm hosts branch on the explicit outer tag. `jet.report/v1` remains a renderer schema, so it does not force invented why, fix, or source fields.

whyNot.reason: A native error chain feels right, but it has no version tag or raw decoding contract. A host must guess field meaning, and a future field change can break it silently.
B gives tools one decoder, but `JetErr` does not contain why, fix, or source. Generic values would misstate the report. It also turns one recursive cause into many diagnostic objects.

C gives Wasm hosts control, but it adds a wrapper to every success and still leaves the error record unversioned. JavaScript callers gain a second public branch model when native rejection already fits the target.

recommendation.tradeoff: The wire adds one small schema tag and a boundary adapter. JavaScript receives a rejection instead of a fulfilled result for `Err`, and Wasm hosts decode one outer tag. This cost buys stable machine data without changing Jet's internal carrier or success ABI.

reviewPasses.base: The first pass compared four boundary contracts. Only D covers the JS and raw Wasm hosts without changing the internal value or bending the report schema.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The wide pass tried JS-only exceptions, binary status codes, RFC 9457, and a bare record. Each misses a host, adds a second schema, invents facts, or drifts unversioned.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Combining A native errors, C tagged edge, and a versioned record reproduces D exactly. The B envelope on top only reintroduces invented diagnostic fields.
reviewPasses.cooperative: C strengthened with the versioned record and a throwing JS adapter becomes a usable contract. It is then the D design plus a success wrapper with worse beginner ergonomics.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack targeted versioning overhead, adapter drift, and recursive decoding bugs. D survives: one fixed tag field, a wire record that mirrors the settled JetErr, and one shared encoding both adapters consume.

decisions.title: Program allocator: how a program swaps or wraps its memory allocator
decisions.gist: How a Jet program names the allocator that serves every allocation in it.
decisions.lesson: Every program needs memory while it runs. An allocator is the part that hands out that memory. Most programs never think about it and use a hidden default. Sometimes you want to swap it or wrap it: count every byte, cap total use, trace leaks, or use a faster allocator for a game. Rust calls this the global allocator. Jet has scoped allocators (arenas, fixed buffers) but no way to change the allocator for a whole program.
decisions.story: Last night a test program looped and quietly ate 34 gigabytes. The machine ran out of memory and the kernel killed every agent session on it. Overnight work was lost. A capped wrapping allocator would have stopped that program in seconds with a clear error. Nate wants every Jet program to be able to name such an allocator — the same power Rust's global allocator gives, in one clean Jet spelling.

options.name: Profile fact in package.jet
options.detail: The package file names the program allocator, the same way freestanding targets already name theirs. Code does not change. Beginners never see it. The build dossier shows it, so audits see exactly which allocator shipped.
options.technical: Extends the ratified D-TARGET-ALLOC1 typed profile fact from freestanding profiles to hosted programs. The fact names any value whose type implements the core allocator trait. Sema validates it; codegen routes the program heap through it on every tier (I9). Absent fact = hidden default, unchanged.

options.name: Marker on one binding in the entry file
options.detail: A marker names one binding as the program allocator, like Rust. The choice lives in code, so it travels with the source and needs no package file. Sema rejects two markers or a marker outside the entry file.
options.technical: New ratified marker (I7) valid on one top-level binding in the entry module. Duplicate marker and wrong-placement diagnostics required. Same allocator trait and tier-parity rules as option A.

options.name: Scoped allocator block
options.detail: A block makes everything inside it allocate through a named allocator, like Jai and Odin contexts. Wrapping run() covers the whole program. Fine control, but the ambient rule must answer hard questions: what happens across task boundaries, stored values, and returns.
options.technical: Ambient allocator as dynamic scope. Needs defined behavior for values that outlive the block, task spawn inheritance, and interaction with arenas and #Region. Highest semantic surface of the four.

options.name: No program allocator — scoped only
options.detail: Keep today's surface: hidden default plus explicit arenas and fixed buffers where you choose them, like Zig's explicit style. Honest and simple, but there is no way to wrap every allocation, so caps, counting, and leak tracing stay impossible program-wide.
options.technical: Status quo. D-REGION1 arenas and D-FIXED-BACKING1 fixed buffers remain the only user-facing allocators.

comparisons.note: One attribute on one static swaps the program allocator.
No global. Every function takes an allocator argument; maximum honesty, maximum ceremony.
An implicit context carries the allocator; blocks override it in scope.
Replace global operator new and delete anywhere in the program; powerful and famously easy to get wrong.
comparisons.code: void* operator new(std::size_t n) { return my_alloc(n); }

recommendation.why: Freestanding Jet already names its allocator as a typed profile fact (D-TARGET-ALLOC1, ratified). Extending that one fact to hosted programs keeps one mechanism for every target (I8). The allocator is a whole-program shipping fact, so it belongs beside the program's other shipping facts, visible in the audit dossier. Beginners never touch it; experts get swap, wrap, cap, and trace with one line.

whyNot.reason: It hides a whole-program fact inside one source file and adds a new marker plus placement diagnostics. Once freestanding uses profile facts, a marker is a second mechanism for the same fact.
An ambient scoped allocator must answer escape, storage, and task-boundary questions that arenas and #Region already answer. It duplicates Jet's existing scoped tier at high semantic cost.
It leaves counting, capping, and tracing impossible program-wide. Last night's crash is the direct cost of that gap.

recommendation.tradeoff: Swapping allocators means editing package.jet, not just code. A quick experiment touches configuration. That is one clear named line, and the choice stays where audits can see it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a package profile fact, a Rust-style entry marker, a scoped ambient block, and the status quo. It recommended the profile fact because freestanding targets already ratified exactly that shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also weighed a build flag, linker-level interposition, and per-package allocators. The first two folded into option A as spellings of the same fact; per-package allocators were dropped for creating two heaps in one program.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested profile fact plus scoped block together, but arenas and #Region already are Jet's scoped tier, so it collapsed back to option A. Wrapper composition (mem.Counting.over) was kept so one fact also covers wrapping.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option: the marker is greppable and mirrors Rust habits, the block matches Odin and Jai practice, and the status quo is Zig's honest explicitness. Each option now shows its best real form.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked option A on custom allocators, test harnesses, and config friction. The fact accepts any user allocator value, tests set it in their env profile, and the recommendation survived unchanged.

decisions.title: The CLI system: the program struct, shared flags, and the standard pack
decisions.gist: How a program declares its commands and shared flags, and how much the common case gets for free.
decisions.lesson: A program with subcommands wants three things: add a command with almost no ceremony, declare a shared flag once, and get standard behavior such as --verbose and --version for free. Today each subcommand needs its own struct, an enum variant, and a dispatch arm; nothing is shared and nothing is free. This choice picks the whole shape, so the most common cases carry the least friction.
decisions.story: Priya builds a deploy tool: plan, apply, rollback. Today that is three structs, one enum, and a three-arm dispatch before any logic. She wants --verbose everywhere, so she types it three times and rollback drifts. A teammate runs `deploy --verbose apply` and gets an unknown-subcommand error. Adding a fourth command means touching four places.

options.name: Each command declares its own
options.detail: Keep today's law. Every subcommand struct lists every flag it accepts, including repeated ones. Nothing is shared, nothing is free, and nothing is hidden. The cost is the ceremony the story shows: struct plus variant plus dispatch arm per command, duplication of shared flags, and silent drift.
options.technical: No change. D-CLIFLAG1 stands: no root flag namespace; argv before the subcommand token must be the subcommand name.

options.name: App struct with a command enum field
options.detail: The entry takes one #CLI struct. Its scalar fields are the shared flags; one enum-typed field is the subcommand. Shared flags parse before or after the subcommand word. Per-command ceremony stays: each new command is still a struct, a variant, and a dispatch arm.
options.technical: E1308 extends: the entry parameter may be a #CLI struct containing exactly one enum-of-#CLI field. Shared scalars parse anywhere in argv; variant fields parse after the token. A shared-versus-variant name collision is a compile-time error.

options.name: The bare map registry
options.detail: The program is a map from command names to functions; each function's parameter list is its flags. Adding a command is one function and one line. But shared flags need a separate mechanism, inline member docs move to parameters, and the map is a second program shape next to the struct everyone already knows.
options.technical: #CLI on a registry binding of function values declares the entry. The literal is read at compile time; each callable must have CLI-mappable parameters. Shared flags arrive through a hoisted #CLI struct parameter.

options.name: Marker registration on each function
options.detail: Each command function carries its own marker, Cobra-style. No registry at all — the marker is the registration. The cost is a scattered surface: no single place lists the program's commands, ordering is unclear, and discovering the full shell surface means reading every file.
options.technical: #Command(name?) on a top-level function registers it as a subcommand. Command list order follows declaration order across files, which imports can reshuffle.

options.name: The program struct: fields are flags, callable members are commands
options.detail: One #CLI struct is the whole program. Scalar fields are shared flags with the same #Doc and = defaults as today. A callable member is a command: bind an existing function with =, or define a method whose self reads the shared flags. The member name is the command word; member #Doc is its help summary. #CLI(Standard) grants working --verbose, --quiet, --color, and --version with automatic wiring. One-command tools skip the struct entirely: parameters on fn run are the flags. Growth never rewrites: signature, then struct, then members.
options.technical:
Member kinds split at compile time: scalar fields become root flags parsed anywhere in argv; callable members become subcommands named by their lowercased member name. A method's self is the parsed shared-flag struct, read-only. A bound function may declare one parameter of the struct's type to receive shared flags; its remaining scalar parameters, S61 `= expr` defaults, and parameter #Doc define that command's flags.

#CLI(Standard): --verbose/-v and --quiet/-q drive core.log level, --color=auto|always|never honors NO_COLOR, --version prints the package version. Bare #CLI keeps only auto --help. jet inspect expand shows every inferred piece.

Flag-versus-command name collisions and callable members inside #Codable structs are compile-time errors. Callable members are not data: never constructed, serialized, or positional. Zero arguments or root --help prints the command list with member #Doc summaries and exits 0 (existing orientation law).

E1308 extends to param-direct entry: fn run(path: Path, threshold: Int = 100) maps parameters as flags. Amends D-CLIFLAG1: the enum subcommand form is deleted (greenfield). The dossier, embedded schema, and completions carry command names and summaries; signature changes surface in the existing breaking-shape report.

comparisons.note: A struct declares configuration and lists subcommand types in one place — the closest prior art for option E's program struct.
Function signatures become CLI flags with defaults and help from annotations — the parameter mapping options C and E share.
A plain dict of callables becomes the whole CLI — option C's map, but untyped and runtime-reflected.
Imperative AddCommand registration plus PersistentFlags — option D's scatter with extra ceremony; the video mine that raised this ballot.

recommendation.why: The program struct keeps the struct surface Jet already ratified and absorbs the registry into it. Fields are flags, callable members are commands, and one #Doc and one = expr rule serve every member kind. The most common actions become the cheapest: one signature for a one-command tool, one member per new command, one marker argument for the standard pack. Shared flags reach commands through self with no injection mechanism to learn, and the whole shell surface is one readable struct.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the ceremony and the silent drift the story shows, and root-position flags stay errors.
It fixes shared flags but keeps struct-plus-variant-plus-dispatch ceremony for every command, so the most common action stays the most expensive.
The map is a second program shape whose shared flags and member docs need separate mechanisms the struct already owns.
Scattered markers leave no single place that lists the program, so the shell surface becomes implicit and hard to audit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Struct members now come in two kinds, data and callable, and the derive must keep them apart from construction, serialization, and positional filling. That is accepted: the kinds are visually distinct in source, every misuse is a compile-time error, and the payoff is one struct that is the whole program.

reviewPasses.base: The draft was rebuilt twice: first around a bare map registry, then, on owner direction, around the program struct. The final menu ranks five shapes by friction on the most common actions.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested auto-discovery of public functions, an imperative add() builder, and manifest files, and kept marker-per-function as option D. The rest folded away: implicit surface, runtime ceremony, or truth split across files.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced the recommendation itself: option B's struct and option C's registry fuse into E, where callable members are the registry entries. Owner review resolved the member-kind question to both bound and method forms and deleted the standalone map.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with compile-time map checking and B with the Standard pack, which composes with any winner. C still splits shared flags from commands; B still pays per-command ceremony.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked E: flag-versus-command name collisions, callable members leaking into #Codable serialization, self mutation expectations, bound-function signature drift, and positional ambiguity. Compile-time collision and serialization errors, read-only self, the existing breaking-shape report, and named-value-wins repair those, so E survives.

decisions.title: Command files: which mark makes one
decisions.gist: Which mark, if any, sets a command file apart from every ordinary Jet file.
decisions.lesson: Four commands can be replaced by a function of the same name: run, build, dev, and test. That function may live in any file. A command file is the optional home for one of them, and it sorts where its name puts it. This choice picks the mark that name carries. D-ONCE-AT1 already reserved `@` for locations, addresses, and sources, and left the location half to a later ballot. The underscore ladder gives none, one, and two their own meanings: ordinary, disabled, machine space.
decisions.story: Ravi joins a team and opens a package with thirty files at the root. He wants the entry point and the build override. He scrolls the listing, misses run.jet between record.jet and streams.jet, and greps for `fn run` instead. In Python he would have seen __init__.py at the top without looking.
decisions.inWild:
// today — the two files a reader wants are scattered
README.md
api.jet
billing.jet
package.jet
queue.jet
run.jet
streams.jet

// option A — `@` is 0x40, above every letter
@build.jet
@run.jet
README.md
api.jet
billing.jet
package.jet

// option B — `_` is 0x5F, below every capital
README.md
__build.jet
__run.jet
api.jet
billing.jet
package.jet

options.name: `@` marks a command file
options.detail: The four optional homes are `@run.jet`, `@build.jet`, `@dev.jet`, and `@test.jet`. `@` sorts above every letter, so the set opens each listing. Every tool still sees them: `ls`, `rg`, `fd`, and a `*.jet` glob all match. Jet already reads `@` as at a location, and a filename is a location. Gain: one mark, already taught, visible everywhere. Loss: `@run` renders as a mention in Markdown and chat, so prose needs backticks.
options.technical: Mints the location half of D-ONCE-AT1, which that decision left to a later ballot. Prefix `@` on a filename names a command location. Infix `@` stays the package-source separator under D-JPK-REF1, and prefix and infix never meet. At package root, `@` is legal only in front of a command name; `@notes.jet` raises an error. The underscore ladder keeps its identifier-only meaning, so `__` never becomes user-typeable on files. Amends D-VERDICT-678-1: `run.jet` loses reserved status.

options.name: `__` marks a command file
options.detail: The four homes are `__run.jet`, `__build.jet`, `__dev.jet`, and `__test.jet`. The underscore ladder extends to filenames: none is ordinary, one is disabled, two is machine space. Gain: the ladder already exists, and readers coming from Python know the shape on sight. Loss: `_run.jet` and `__run.jet` differ by one character and mean opposite things, and `__` gains a second user-typeable meaning.
options.technical: Amends D-NAME-SIGIL1 so machine space covers compiler-recognized files as well as generated symbols. Identifiers stay forbidden. At package root, `__` is legal only in front of a command name. The disable rule keeps matching exactly one leading underscore, so `___run.jet` disables a command file. Sorts below capitals, so `README.md` still opens the listing. Amends D-VERDICT-678-1: `run.jet` loses reserved status.

options.name: No mark; plain names and a homing lint
options.detail: The names stay ordinary words: `run.jet`, `build.jet`, `dev.jet`, `test.jet`. A lint asks a package with several files to home each override in the matching name. Gain: nothing renames, and a beginner's first file stays a plain word. Loss: the files sort into the middle of the listing, so the surfacing that started this choice never arrives.
options.technical: No ladder or sigil amendment, and no change to any ratified spelling. Adds the homing lint plus four conventional filenames as documentation-level convention. `run.jet` keeps the status D-VERDICT-678-1 gave it. Command functions stay discoverable wherever they are declared.

comparisons.note: `@` names a repository address: `@rules_go//go`. The mark reads as at this source, which is the same word Jet gives it.
`__init__.py` and `__main__.py` sit in the interpreter's dunder namespace. They sort near the top, and the spelling still feeds a tutorial industry.
`build.zig` is a plain-name command file at the root. Every Zig reader knows it, and it still sorts under b like any other file.

recommendation.why: `@` sorts above every letter and stays visible to `ls`, ripgrep, fd, and shell globs. It carries a meaning Jet already teaches, so the rule costs one character and no new concept. It also leaves the underscore ladder untouched.

whyNot.reason: The mark works, but `_run.jet` and `__run.jet` differ by one character and mean opposite things. It also gives `__` a second user-typeable meaning that the ladder did not have.
Plain names home the code without surfacing it. `run.jet` still hides between `record.jet` and `streams.jet`, which is the itch that opened this decision.

recommendation.tradeoff: `@run` reads as a mention in Markdown, chat, and issue trackers, so every mention in prose needs backticks. A URL escapes it to `%40`, which shows up in registry and raw links. Scaffolds and the missing-command diagnostic must carry the one-sentence rule so the mark never needs a tutorial.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a marked command file against plain names and against tooling alone, and found that only a mark puts the four files at the top of every listing.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a leading dot, bang, tilde, capitals, and a command directory. A dot hides the file from `ls`, ripgrep, fd, and `*.jet` globs, bang and tilde fight shells, capitals sort unreliably, and a directory buries the entry.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a command directory holding many named entries. It was dropped because `#Job fn` under D-JPK-TASKRUN1 already names extra entry points, so a third naming mechanism would break I8.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with scaffold comments and a `jet map` listing, and strengthened B with a diagnostic that names the disabled twin. Both improve, and neither gains sort-to-top surfacing.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on mention rendering in Markdown and chat, on URL escaping to `%40`, and on the visual echo of infix `package@source`. Backticks cover prose, command files are never fetched by name, and prefix never meets infix in the grammar.

decisions.title: FFI namespaces use the one import form
decisions.outcome: No separate import grammar for FFI. Single import stays c.lib; multiple libraries use c.[lib1, lib2], the same .[ ] form every other namespace uses.
decisions.comment: No separate import grammar for FFI. Single import stays c.lib; multiple libraries use c.[lib1, lib2], the same .[ ] form every other namespace uses.

decisions.title: Command functions: override or requirement
decisions.gist: What run, build, dev, and test do when the matching function is absent.
decisions.lesson: Each of the four commands can be replaced by a function of the same name. D-BUILDENTRY1 already rules that `jet build` runs `fn build` when it is defined, and the batteries pipeline when it is not. This choice decides whether the other three follow that same law, and what a file argument on the command line selects. It also decides what happens when two files define the same command.
decisions.story: Mara writes one file and types `jet test`. Nothing overrides anything, so she expects the stock harness to find her checks and run them. A month later her team adds `fn test` to start a database first. Same command, same file, one extra step and no new rule to learn.
decisions.inWild:
// no command function anywhere — every command still works
jet run    → runs the file
jet build  → standard compilation
