jet dev    → watch, then re-run run
jet test   → stock harness over every #Test

// a file argument names the target, not the lookup
jet build main.jet   → the package override, scoped to main.jet
jet test parser.jet  → the stock harness, scoped to parser.jet

options.name: One law: every command function is an optional override
options.detail: An absent function means stock behavior. Run executes the file, build compiles it, dev watches and re-runs run, and test runs the stock harness. A file argument sets scope, not lookup, so a package override still applies when you name a file. Two definitions of one command raise an error. Gain: one sentence covers four commands. Loss: `run.jet` gives up its reserved status.
options.technical: Generalizes D-BUILDENTRY1 to run, dev, and test. A command function is discovered by declaration across the package, which matches D-JPK-FILENAME2 and the shape of E1239. A duplicate raises a new error listing every file that declares it, and lint policy can soften it to a warning. Amends D-VERDICT-678-1 so `run.jet` is an ordinary filename. Only a `fn build` inside the named file outranks the package override.

options.name: The entry is required; the other three are optional
options.detail: A package must declare `fn run` or be a single script file. Build, dev, and test keep their stock behavior when nothing overrides them. Gain: `jet run` never has to guess what a package meant. Loss: two rules where one would do, and a library package must declare an entry it will never run.
options.technical: Keeps the reserved-entry half of D-VERDICT-678-1 and generalizes D-BUILDENTRY1 to dev and test only. A package with no `fn run` and no script body raises a missing-entry error even when it ships no executable. Duplicate handling matches option A.

options.name: No search; an override counts only in a declared home
options.detail: A command function counts only inside its own command file or `package.jet`. A `fn build` written in `util.jet` is ordinary code and nothing calls it. Gain: resolution is one file lookup, and no scan can surprise a reader. Loss: the command file stops being optional, so a one-file script can never override its own command.
options.technical: Replaces package-wide discovery with a fixed lookup table of command files plus `package.jet`. Duplicates become impossible by construction, so the duplicate error is not needed. The command-file mark stops being optional for any project that overrides anything.
options.code:
// util.jet
fn build(b: BuildContext) { … }   // ordinary function, never called by `jet build`

comparisons.note: `build.zig` is the only home for the build graph, and a project without one cannot be built by the build command at all.
Every command works with no user code, and `build.rs` is a pure addition. Nothing is required before it is wanted.
comparisons.code: cargo test   // works with zero configuration

comparisons.note: A missing script is an error, so each command a project wants must be written out before it will run once.
comparisons.code: npm run dev   // fails without a dev script

recommendation.why: One sentence covers four commands, and it is the sentence D-BUILDENTRY1 already ratified for build. Nothing is required before it is wanted, so a single file and a large package obey the same rule. A file argument never silently drops the project's own override.

whyNot.reason: A library package gains a required entry it never runs, and a reader learns two rules instead of one. The guess it prevents does not happen, because a missing entry already has a stock answer.
A single-file script could not override its own build or test, which is the case the optional design exists to protect. It also makes the command-file mark mandatory.

recommendation.tradeoff: Without a command file the compiler scans the package to find each override, where a command file is a direct hit. `run.jet` loses reserved status, so D-VERDICT-678-1 needs that amendment recorded. Scaffolds ship a commented example override rather than a copy of the real default, so a generated project never freezes today's build logic.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one uniform override law against a required entry and against explicit homes only, and found the uniform law already half-ratified in D-BUILDENTRY1.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a manifest script table, a registration call inside `package.jet`, and per-command rules kept as they are. Each adds a second place to look for the same answer, and none removes a rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a required entry with optional everything else, which is option B. It was kept as an option rather than folded, because the entry question is genuinely separable from the other three.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review added the scoping rule that keeps a package override alive when a file argument is present, and the duplicate error modelled on E1239. Both fixes belong to every option.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on scan cost and on the silent-override risk when a stray `fn dev` sits in an unrelated file. The duplicate error removes the stray case, and a command file removes the scan.

decisions.title: The four frozen epoch-3 cards: which ones stay
decisions.gist: Decide which of the four frozen epoch-3 cards belong in epoch 3.
decisions.lesson: Four epoch-3 cards are frozen. A frozen card is owner-only. No agent may plan it, home it, or close it. Two of them were frozen by an old instruction that a later ratified decision has since answered. One was deferred by an owner verdict. One is held back on purpose as the last card of the epoch. Epoch 3 cannot finish while any of them sit in the owner lane.
decisions.story: Nate asks for epoch 3 to run start to finish with no further owner input. An agent sweeps the board and reaches the four frozen cards. It cannot touch them, so it stops and asks. That single stop is the thing this ballot removes.
decisions.inWild:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs card update '#1462' --milestone e3-bucket-1 --by architect
tower: card #1462 is frozen — owner-only until the owner moves it out

$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs card list --epoch e3 --phase frozen
#480   E3-UL9: mobile native UI (iOS/Android) + app-store pipeline
#677   Typed project compile-latency budgets
#775   Proposal: checked transaction regions (rollback on failure)
#1462  Full suite red: seven truthfulness checks fail on master

options.name: All four run in epoch 3
options.detail: Unfreeze every card and build all four inside epoch 3. Epoch 3 then also carries phone and tablet apps, store signing, and a parked language proposal. That is a large addition to an epoch already holding more than two hundred open cards.
options.code:
# Owner runs four unfreeze commands, then agents work them like any other card.
tower card update '#480'  --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#677'  --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#775'  --phase planning --by owner
tower card update '#1462' --phase ready --by owner

options.name: Split by whether the design is settled
options.detail: Build the two cards whose design is settled. Move the two that are not out of epoch 3. Compile budgets and the red test suite stay. Phone and tablet apps and the rollback proposal leave.
options.code:
# Settled, so they stay:
tower card update '#677'  --phase ready --by owner   # D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1 = C
tower card update '#1462' --phase ready --by owner   # plan and criteria already written

# Not settled, so they leave:
tower card update '#480' --epoch e11 --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#775' --epoch e11 --phase planning --by owner

options.name: All four leave epoch 3
options.detail: Move every frozen card to a later epoch. Epoch 3 closes on the cards that are already moving. Nothing is lost, but the red test suite then stays red inside epoch 3, and no card holds the fix.
options.code:
tower card update '#480'  --epoch e11 --by owner
tower card update '#677'  --epoch e11 --by owner
tower card update '#775'  --epoch e11 --by owner
tower card update '#1462' --epoch e11 --by owner

options.name: Split, and run the test-suite card last
options.detail: Same split as option B, with one added rule. The red-test card runs as the final card of epoch 3, after every other card lands. Its own log already asks for this. That keeps agents from fixing the same test twice.
options.technical: #1462 moves to bucket 4 with the highest workOrder in the epoch. Its exit criterion stays: `cargo test --test truthfulness` passes with no weakened check and no grown allowlist. #677 moves to bucket 2 and implements D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1 outcome C.
options.code:
# Settled work joins the buckets:
tower card update '#677'  --phase ready --milestone e3-bucket-2 --by owner
tower card update '#1462' --phase ready --milestone e3-bucket-4 --workOrder 9999 --by owner

# Unsettled work leaves:
tower card update '#480' --epoch e11 --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#775' --epoch e11 --phase planning --by owner

$ tower card list --epoch e3 --phase frozen
(no cards)

comparisons.note: Rust moves an unfinished feature to the next train rather than holding the release. The train ships on its date.
comparisons.code:
feature not ready -> next milestone
release date -> fixed

comparisons.note: Work that misses the merge window waits for the next cycle. Nothing sits half-in.
comparisons.code: merge window closes -> queue for next cycle

recommendation.why: It clears the owner lane completely, keeps the work whose design is already ratified, and records the order the red-test card needs. Epoch 3 then has no card an agent cannot touch.

whyNot.reason: It adds phone and tablet apps and store signing to epoch 3, which an owner verdict already deferred on 2026-07-13.
It makes the right split but leaves the red-test card unordered, so a worker may run it early and repeat the same fix later.
It leaves the failing test suite inside epoch 3 with no card that owns the fix, so the epoch would close on red.

recommendation.tradeoff: Compile-latency budgets stay in epoch 3 and add real work. That is accepted because the owner already ratified their design as outcome C.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping all four, splitting them, and moving all four out. It recommended the split, because two cards have ratified designs and two do not.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested deleting the two parked cards and merging them into later epoch umbrellas. Both were dropped because they lose the mined design work with no gain.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review added the run-last rule for the red-test card, taken from that card's own log. It became option D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the all-in option by noting that mobile work has three ratified design decisions and a written seven-slice plan. The 2026-07-13 deferral verdict still outranks that readiness.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what happens if the truthfulness suite fails for a cause outside epoch 3. The card's criteria already allow splitting such a cause into its own card, so option D survives.

decisions.title: Public-key encryption in Core: keep one mechanism, or add the RSA shape
decisions.gist: Decide whether Core gains an RSA-style public-key encrypt and decrypt surface.
decisions.lesson: Core already encrypts to a recipient's public key. The mechanism is a sealed box built on X25519. Eleven other languages expose a second shape as well: make a key pair, encrypt with the public half, decrypt with the private half. That shape is RSA. Adding it needs either a large-number library Core does not have, or a second way to do work the sealed box already does. Card #1473 blocks on this and records six ledger rows as unimplemented.
decisions.story: Ravi moves a payment service to Jet. The bank he talks to hands out an RSA public key and will not change. Ravi searches Core for a way to encrypt with it, finds only the sealed box, and cannot tell whether Jet declined RSA on purpose or forgot it.
decisions.inWild:
// What Core has today: encrypt to a recipient, decrypt with the matching secret.
use jet.crypto.[seal, open, keypair]

keys :: keypair()
box  :: seal(keys.public, "card token")
plain :: open(keys.secret, box)?

// What Ravi needs, and cannot write today:
bank_key :: rsa_public_from_pem(read("bank.pem")?)?
blob     :: bank_key.encrypt(payload)?   // no such call exists

options.name: Decline RSA, and say so
options.detail: Core keeps the sealed box as its only public-key encryption. The six ledger rows close as a stated refusal with a reason and a pointer to the sealed box. Ravi still cannot talk to the bank from Core.

options.name: Add RSA on a new library
options.detail: Core gains generate_key, public_encrypt, private_decrypt, and their partners, built on a vetted outside large-number library. Ravi's code works. Core takes its first outside cryptography dependency, and two mechanisms now do one job.
options.technical: This adds an external crate to the Core build. Invariant I6 keeps compiler seam crates on path dependencies only, so this needs a named carve-out. Invariant I8 keeps one mechanism per job, so the sealed box and RSA both need a stated role.
options.code:
use jet.crypto.[rsa_generate_key, rsa_public_encrypt, rsa_private_decrypt]

keys :: rsa_generate_key(2048)?
blob :: rsa_public_encrypt(keys.public, payload)?
back :: rsa_private_decrypt(keys.secret, blob)?

options.name: Add RSA, written inside Core
options.detail: Same surface as option B, with the large-number arithmetic written by hand inside Core. No outside library joins the build. Hand-written large-number arithmetic is where timing leaks live, so this trades a dependency for a safety risk.

options.name: Decline in Core, ship an interop package
options.detail: Core keeps one mechanism, as in option A. RSA lives in an ordinary Jet package outside Core, built on the existing bridge that already carries outside libraries. Ravi adds one dependency and his code works. Core stays small and beginners never meet RSA.
options.technical: The package uses the standard bridge template that other outside libraries already use, so no new dependency enters any crate under `crates/`. The refusal note in core.crypto names the package, so the ledger rows close as routed rather than missing.

comparisons.note: Go ships RSA in its standard library and also ships a modern sealed-box style package. Both live side by side, and its own docs steer new code away from RSA.
libsodium refuses RSA on purpose. It offers one sealed-box shape and tells callers to use a separate library when a peer demands RSA.
comparisons.code:
crypto_box_seal / crypto_box_seal_open
// no RSA at all

comparisons.note: Rust's standard library ships no cryptography. RSA arrives as a separate crate that projects add when a peer needs it.

recommendation.why: Ravi can talk to the bank, Core keeps one public-key mechanism, and no outside cryptography library enters the compiler build. The refusal becomes a route instead of a dead end.

whyNot.reason: It leaves a real interop need with no answer, so anyone who must meet an RSA peer leaves Jet for that work.
It puts an outside cryptography library in the compiler build and gives one job two mechanisms in the same namespace.
Hand-written large-number arithmetic in Core carries timing-leak risk that no test in this repo would catch.

recommendation.tradeoff: RSA users add one dependency instead of finding the call in Core. That is accepted because RSA is interop with older peers, not the shape Jet teaches.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared declining RSA against adding it on an outside library, and recommended declining, because the sealed box already performs the same job.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added a hand-written option and a package option. It also tested hiding RSA behind an expert door in Core, which was dropped because it still puts the library in the build.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review joined the refusal with a route, so Core stays one mechanism while the interop need still gets an answer. That became option D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the outside-library option by pairing it with a named expert module and a steer in the docs. It still adds a second mechanism to the same namespace.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what happens when no package exists yet. The answer is that card #1473 must name the package and its first release, so option D now carries that requirement.

decisions.title: What `*` means between two matrices
decisions.gist: Which multiplication the `*` key writes when two matrices sit beside it.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no matrix arithmetic today. Matrix work goes through functions such as `compute.matmul(a, b)`. Two multiplications exist in this field. One composes two matrices as transformations. The other multiplies matching cells. Every language must decide which one the `*` key writes, and how the other one is written. Two square matrices accept both meanings without complaint, so a wrong choice returns a wrong number instead of an error.
decisions.story: Priya ports a physics notebook from MATLAB. She writes `a * b` for two three-by-three rotations. The line is well shaped under either reading, so nothing warns her. Her simulation drifts for a week before she finds the cause.

options.name: `*` composes; a leading dot multiplies cells
options.detail: The spelling MATLAB and Julia use, and the one a textbook writes. `*` between two matrices is composition. A leading dot asks for cell-by-cell work: `.*`, `./`, `.^`. Ported formulas read the same in Jet as on the page. The cost is that `*` reads two ways, and two square matrices accept both.
options.technical: New infix tokens `.*`, `./`, `.^` with compound forms. `*` between `Matrix<M, K>` and `Matrix<K, N>` gives `Matrix<M, N>` on the D-TYPE2-MEASURE1 substrate; a mismatch names both inner sides. `^` on a square matrix is repeated composition. Amends D-LINALG1, which today defines `*` as element-wise plus matrix-times-vector and puts matrix-times-matrix on `.matmul()`.
options.code:
oriented :: pose * spin          // Matrix<3, 3>, composed
lit      :: gain .* spin         // Matrix<3, 3>, cell by cell
scaled   :: gain ./ spin
raised   :: gain .^ 2
squared  :: pose ^ 2             // pose * pose

wide :: Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
bad  :: pose * wide
// Error: inner sides 3 and 4 do not match.

options.name: `*` always multiplies cells; composing is `.matmul`
options.detail: Every arithmetic operator means cell by cell on every math value, everywhere. Composition is the named method `.matmul(b)`. No symbol changes meaning and no new symbol is added. The cost is that the textbook formula becomes a chain of method calls.
options.technical: `*`, `/`, `^`, `/%` and `%` are cell-by-cell on equal shapes. `.matmul(b)` matches inner sides and composes outer sides. Matrix power is `.power(n)`. Amends D-LINALG1 by removing its matrix-times-vector reading of `*`, so the symbol never changes meaning by operand type.
options.code:
oriented :: pose.matmul(spin)    // Matrix<3, 3>
lit      :: gain * spin          // Matrix<3, 3>, cell by cell
scaled   :: gain / spin
raised   :: gain ^ 2             // every cell squared
squared  :: pose.power(2)

bad :: gain * Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
// Error: cell-by-cell work needs equal shapes; 3 by 3 and 4 by 2 differ.

options.name: `*` multiplies cells; a new `@` composes
options.detail: Python added exactly this in 2014, after twenty years of one library shipping both readings of `*`. The two multiplications are visibly different in the source and neither changes meaning by operand type. The cost is one more symbol, and `@` is not a symbol mathematics uses.
options.technical: New infix token `@` at the same precedence as `*`, left grouping, with compound `@=`. `Matrix<M, K> @ Matrix<K, N>` gives `Matrix<M, N>`; `Matrix<M, N> @ Vec<N>` gives `Vec<M>`. All other operators stay cell-by-cell. Amends D-LINALG1's matrix-times-vector reading of `*`.
options.code:
oriented :: pose @ spin          // Matrix<3, 3>
lit      :: gain * spin          // Matrix<3, 3>, cell by cell
chained  :: pose @ spin * gain   // groups left to right: (pose @ spin) * gain
raised   :: gain ^ 2             // every cell squared

bad :: pose @ Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
// Error: inner sides 3 and 4 do not match.

options.name: The type says which multiplication it is
options.detail: Two shape-typed values share one storage. `Matrix<M, N>` is a transformation and multiplies by composition. `Grid<M, N>` is a table of numbers and multiplies cell by cell. No symbol is overloaded and none is added: `*` asks the type, which is the rule the rest of the language already follows. Crossing between the two is one written word and copies nothing.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>` and `Grid<M, N>` are two readings of one `Tensor<T>` buffer (D-COMPUTE-TYPE1). `m.cells()` gives a `Grid` view, `g.as_map()` gives a `Matrix` view; both are views under D-SHAPE-PLACE1, not copies. `*` dispatches through the ordinary operator hook (D-OPDEF1) rather than a closed compiler table. `^` composes on `Matrix` and raises each cell on `Grid`. `/` between two `Matrix` values is refused, naming `.solve` and `.cells()`. Amends D-LINALG1's closed-family operator table.
options.code:
oriented :: pose * spin                       // Matrix values compose
lit      :: gain.cells() * spin.cells()       // Grid values multiply cells
back     :: lit.as_map()                      // read the result as a map again
raised   :: gain.cells() ^ 2                  // every cell squared
squared  :: pose ^ 2                          // pose * pose

bad :: pose / spin
// Error: two transformations do not divide.
// Use `.solve(...)` for a system, or `.cells()` to divide cell by cell.

options.name: A leading dot means element by element, for operators and for calls
options.detail: Julia's full rule. `*` composes, and a leading dot on any operator or any function call means it applies to every element. One idea covers `a .* b`, `a .+ 1`, and `sqrt.(a)`, so no function needs an element-by-element twin. The cost is that `*` still reads two ways for two square matrices.
options.technical: Extends option A: the dot prefix generalizes to call position, so `f.(x)` applies `f` to every element of `x` and composes with the existing operator dots. `*` behaves exactly as in option A.
options.code:
oriented :: pose * spin          // composed
lit      :: gain .* spin         // cell by cell
shifted  :: gain .+ 1.0          // add to every cell
roots    :: math.sqrt.(gain)     // one rule, applied to a call

bad :: gain .* Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
// Error: element-by-element work needs equal shapes.

options.name: The type says which; the dot asks for cells where the plain operator would compose
options.detail:
Option D decides the meaning, and the leading dot from option A returns as the one way to override it. `Matrix` composes under `*`. `Grid` and lane vectors multiply cells under `*`, which is already law (D-VECARITH1). A leading dot is legal only on a `Matrix`, where it means cells: `pose .* spin`. Where `*` is already cell by cell the dot is refused, so no meaning has two spellings.

The textbook line types as written. A ported MATLAB line types as written. Two square matrices never accept both readings.
options.technical: Extends option D. New infix tokens `.*`, `./`, `.^`, `.+`, `.-` with compound forms, accepted ONLY where the left operand composes under the plain operator (today: `Matrix<M, N>`). On `Grid`, lane vectors, and scalars the dot form is a sema error naming the plain operator. Call-position dot (`f.(x)` from option E) is NOT adopted: call fan-out was retired by ratified D-VERDICT-1324-1, and `.[` already carries member spread under D-SPREAD1=A. `^` stays take in prefix position (D-MEM1=A) and power in infix position; `.^` must be lexed against that.

comparisons.note: `*` composes and a leading dot means cell by cell. The oldest form, and the one textbooks match.
comparisons.code:
C = A * B;
D = A .* B;

comparisons.note: Same as MATLAB, plus the general rule that a dot on any call applies it to every element.
comparisons.code:
C = A * B
D = A .* B
E = sqrt.(A)

comparisons.note: `*` is cell by cell and `@` composes. The `@` symbol was added to Python because an earlier matrix type gave `*` the other meaning, and both readings shipped side by side.
comparisons.code:
C = A @ B
D = A * B

comparisons.note: `*` is cell by cell and composition gets its own spelled symbol.
comparisons.code:
C <- A %*% B
D <- A * B

comparisons.note: The type carries the reading. A matrix composes; asking for its array view multiplies cell by cell, over the same storage.
comparisons.code:
C = A * B;
D = A.array() * B.array();

recommendation.why:
It keeps every gain of the current recommendation and pays back its one cost. The type still settles what `*` means, so the two-square-matrix trap cannot happen and no symbol reads two ways. The dot returns as a real override, so a person porting a formula writes the line they know on the value they hold, with no conversion step.

The dot is not a new idea here. `.[` already spreads a member across a list, and `.Variant` already reaches into a type. Distributing an operator across cells is the same idea, one level down.

whyNot.reason: Two square matrices accept both readings, so a person who meant cells gets a composed answer and no error.
The textbook formula becomes a method chain for the scientific audience the ratified `^` spelling was chosen to serve.
It adds a symbol mathematics does not use, and a reader arriving from MATLAB still types `*` and quietly gets cells.
Correct, but a porter must write `.cells()` at the crossing point, so a formula that reads the same in every other language does not read the same here.
Its call half reintroduces call fan-out, which ratified D-VERDICT-1324-1 removed, and `*` still reads two ways for two square matrices.

recommendation.tradeoff: Five new infix tokens, and a MATLAB porter who writes `.*` on a Grid gets an error instead of a result. That error is the teaching moment and needs registered what/why/fix text under I4. `.cells()` stays for a chain that is cellwise throughout; the dot is for one expression.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the textbook `*` against a cell-by-cell `*` with a named `matmul`, and recommended the textbook reading because the ratified `^` spelling already chose the mathematics-tool audience.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Julia's general dot rule as option E and the type-carried reading as option D. It folded away a Unicode multiplication sign and a no-operators-at-all surface, since neither changed who decides the meaning of a line.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review found that option D already is the combination: it keeps the textbook line of option A and the one-meaning-per-symbol promise of option B. The recommendation moved from A to D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with the point that a named multiply never guesses, and C with Python's history, where `@` was added because one library shipped both readings of `*` at once.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked D for making data work wordy at every crossing. Reductions and cell helpers now sit on both types, so a crossing appears only where two values combine cell by cell, and the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How a matrix is written down
decisions.gist: What separates one row of a matrix from the next in source code.
decisions.lesson: A matrix is a grid, and source code is lines of text. Jet builds every other typed value with `Type.{ ... }`, and rows must be told apart inside those braces. The spelling decides whether a small matrix reads like the grid it is. It also decides whether a matrix can sit on one line as a function argument. A vector is a plain comma list under every option.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a two-by-two rotation directly inside a call and wants it on one line. He also keeps an eight-by-two design matrix at the top of the same file. That one should look like the table the numbers came from.

options.name: A line break ends a row
options.detail: Rows sit under each other, so the source shows the grid. Nothing is counted by eye and no separator is learned. The cost is that a matrix cannot be written on one line, so a small rotation inside a call spans four lines.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` a newline ends a row and commas separate cells within a row. The declared shape checks the row count and each row width. `Vec<N>.{ ... }` stays a comma list.

options.name: A semicolon ends a row
options.detail: The MATLAB and Julia spelling. A matrix fits on one line anywhere an expression fits, and ported code carries over unchanged. The cost is a tall literal: it becomes one long line, or the reader counts semicolons to find the rows.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` a `;` ends a row. Jet already uses `;` as a within-header separator in a loop head, so the character is not new. A newline is ordinary whitespace here.

options.name: Each row is an ordinary list
options.detail: Nothing new is learned: a matrix is built from list values, the way NumPy builds one. The cost is two extra brackets on every row, and the value reads as a list of lists rather than as a grid.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` each element is a `[Float#N]` row and the element count is `M`. Both counts come from the declared shape.

options.name: No literal at all; build with named functions
options.detail: Matrices come from `Matrix.rows(...)`, `Matrix.columns(...)`, or a flat list plus a row count. No grammar is added and the building step names itself. The cost is that the most common small matrix stays a function call, so the grid never appears in the source.
options.technical: `Matrix.rows(a, b, c)` and `Matrix.columns(a, b)` take fixed lists and infer the shape from their measures. `Matrix.of(flat, rows: n)` checks that the length divides evenly.
options.code:
design :: Matrix.rows([1, 4], [1, 7], [1, 8])       // Matrix<3, 2>
flat   :: Matrix.of([1, 4, 1, 7, 1, 8], rows: 3)    // Matrix<3, 2>
apply(turn: Matrix.rows([0, -1], [1, 0]))

options.name: A row ends at the line end, or where a semicolon says so
options.detail: One idea with two ways to say it: a row ends where the line ends, or where a `;` ends it. A tall matrix is written as the grid, and a small one fits on one line inside a call. Nothing is counted by eye in either shape.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` both a newline and a `;` end a row, and a `;` at a line end is redundant rather than wrong. Commas separate cells within a row. The declared shape checks the row count and each row width, so a short row names the row index and both counts. `Vec<N>.{ ... }` stays a comma list.

comparisons.note: Semicolons end rows and spaces separate cells. The space rule is a known trap, because a leading minus reads as either a separator or a sign.
Semicolons end rows on one line, and a line break ends a row in the multi-line form. Both spellings are ordinary.
Rows are lists inside a list. No grammar is involved, and the brackets are the price.
A flat vector plus a row count, filled down the columns by default. The fill order surprises people.

recommendation.why: It writes both shapes people actually need. A design matrix read from a table looks like that table, and a two-by-two rotation fits inside the call that uses it. Neither form asks the reader to count separators, because the declared shape checks every row and reports the row that is short.

whyNot.reason: A two-by-two inside a call has to break over four lines, which pushes small matrices out of expressions.
A tall literal becomes one long line, or the reader counts semicolons to find where the rows are.
Every row carries two extra brackets, and the value reads as a list of lists instead of a grid.
The most common small matrix stays a function call, so the grid never appears in the source at all.

recommendation.tradeoff: A row ends in two ways, which is one more thing to read. It stays one rule stated twice: a row ends where the line ends, or where a semicolon says it ends.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the line-break grid against the MATLAB semicolon and the list-of-lists spelling, and recommended the line break because a design matrix should look like its source table.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added constructor-only building as option D and tested MATLAB's space-separated cells. Spaces were dropped, because a leading minus then reads as either a separator or a sign.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the line break with the semicolon into option E, which writes the tall grid and the one-line matrix with one rule. The recommendation moved to E.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: list rows add no grammar at all, and a ragged row is caught by the declared shape under every option, not only under C.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what a short row reports. Option E now states that the error names the row index and both counts, which is what makes the missing separator readable, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: When two different shapes may combine
decisions.gist: Whether a short side repeats itself to meet a bigger one, and when.
decisions.lesson: Subtracting a column mean from every row of a table is everyday work. The mean has one row; the table has eight. Letting the short side repeat is called broadcasting, and it saves a written loop. It is also the best known source of quiet wrong answers in array code, because a repeat that was never intended still produces a well-formed result. Jet knows every shape at compile time, so this choice decides how much of that convenience is worth keeping.
decisions.story: Sara centres eight brake readings by their column means. In an earlier Python project she wrote the mean the wrong way round, got an eight-by-eight answer instead of eight-by-two, and lost an afternoon to a chart that looked plausible.

options.name: A short side repeats itself, on the shapes as written
options.detail: The NumPy and Julia rule. Any axis of extent one repeats to meet the other side, and a plain vector takes whichever axis fits. Nothing is written and everything lines up. The cost is that a vector with no stated direction guesses, and a guess that goes the wrong way still produces a well-formed answer.
options.technical: Axes align from the last one. An axis of extent one repeats. A `Vec<N>` is treated as a row when the column count is `N`, and as a column when the row count is `N`. All of it resolves at compile time on the D-TYPE2-MEASURE1 substrate.
options.code:
mean :: x.mean(along: .Rows)     // Matrix<1, 2>
centred :: x - mean              // Matrix<8, 2>

gain :: Vec<8>.{ 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 }
y :: Matrix<8, 1>.zeros()
odd :: y - gain                  // Matrix<8, 8> — accepted, and rarely meant

options.name: Only a single number spreads; every other repeat is written
options.detail: A number combines with any shape. Anything else must have equal shapes, and a repeat is spelled out. Nothing ever expands behind your back. The cost lands on the most common line in this area: centring a table by its column means has to say the repeat out loud.
options.technical: Scalar with matrix is allowed. Two matrices must have equal shapes. `m.repeat_rows<N>()` and `m.repeat_columns<N>()` produce the expanded value, checked against the declared measures.
options.code:
mean :: x.mean(along: .Rows)                 // Matrix<1, 2>
centred :: x - mean.repeat_rows<8>()         // Matrix<8, 2>
halved  :: x / 2.0                           // a number still spreads

slip :: x - mean
// Error: 8 by 2 and 1 by 2 differ. Write `.repeat_rows<8>()` to repeat the row.

options.name: A vector repeats along the one axis it matches
options.detail: A number spreads everywhere. A vector whose length matches exactly one axis repeats along that axis. A vector whose length matches both axes is refused, and the message names the two ways to say which was meant. The cost is that two one-wide axes can still expand each other into a bigger result.
options.technical: `Vec<N>` with `Matrix<M, N>` repeats down the rows; `Vec<M>` with `Matrix<M, N>` repeats across the columns. When `M == N` the combination is refused and names `.as_row()` and `.as_column()`. Matrix-with-matrix follows the extent-one rule.

options.name: Nothing repeats; the operation names the axis
options.detail: Shapes must match exactly for every operator. When a shorter value is meant to apply along an axis, the operation says which axis by name. Every repeat is visible at the place it happens. The cost is that ordinary arithmetic turns into method calls, and the axis is already visible in the shapes.
options.technical: Operators require equal shapes, except with a single number. `x.minus(v, along: .Rows)` and `x.times_cells(v, along: .Columns)` carry the axis as a named argument and check the length against that axis.
options.code:
centred :: x.minus(mean, along: .Rows)
scaled  :: x.times_cells(gain, along: .Columns)
halved  :: x / 2.0

slip :: x - mean
// Error: 8 by 2 and 1 by 2 differ. Use `x.minus(mean, along: .Rows)`.

options.name: A one-wide axis repeats, and direction is always part of the type
options.detail: An axis of extent one repeats silently, so centring a table stays one clean line. Nothing is ever guessed, because every value states its direction in its own type: a bare vector says `.as_row()` or `.as_column()` before it meets a matrix. A combination that would repeat both sides into a bigger result is refused and names the spelling that means it.
options.technical: Matrix with matrix follows the extent-one rule on the D-TYPE2-MEASURE1 substrate. `Vec<N>` has no direction, so it never combines with a matrix directly; `.as_row()` gives `Matrix<1, N>` and `.as_column()` gives `Matrix<N, 1>`, both views. When both sides carry an extent-one axis on different sides, the combination is refused and names `.outer(...)`. Reductions such as `.mean(along: .Rows)` already return a directed result, so the common path needs no extra word.

comparisons.note: Axes align from the last one and a one-wide axis repeats. A vector has no direction, which is why the one-column and one-dimension mix-up is the most reported array bug.
comparisons.code:
x - x.mean(axis=0)          # fine
y - g                       # y is (8,1), g is (8,) -> (8,8), rarely meant

comparisons.note: Since R2016b the same repeat happens automatically, but every value is already a matrix with a direction, so the direction is never guessed.
A short vector is recycled down the columns whether or not the length divides evenly, with a warning at most. A long-standing complaint.
comparisons.code:
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3)
m - c(1, 2)     # recycles down the columns, warns

comparisons.note: Repeating happens only where a dot asks for it, so the expansion is visible in the source.

recommendation.why: It keeps the line people write every day, subtracting the column means from a table, and removes the step where a direction is guessed. Direction lives in the type, so a reader can see from the shapes which side repeated. The one silent expansion that grows both sides is refused and names the spelling that means it.

whyNot.reason: A vector with no stated direction guesses an axis, which is the step that turns an eight-by-two answer into an eight-by-eight one.
Centring a table by its column means, the most common line in this area, has to spell out the repeat every time.
It refuses only the case where one length matches both axes, and still lets two one-wide axes expand each other into a bigger result.
Naming the axis on every operation turns ordinary arithmetic into method calls, and the axis is already readable in the shapes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A hand-built `Vec<N>` must say `.as_row()` or `.as_column()` before it meets a matrix. Reductions already return a directed result, so that word appears only where a bare vector enters an expression.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the NumPy repeat rule against a numbers-only rule, and recommended the numbers-only rule because a wrong repeat still produces a well-formed answer.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the axis-as-argument option and the direction-in-the-type option. It tested a marked region where repeating is switched on, and folded it away because a marker moves the question rather than answering it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined free repeating with typed direction into option E, which keeps the clean centring line and deletes the guessing step. The recommendation moved from B to E.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, since a written repeat is always readable, and strengthened C, since compile-time shapes already catch most mismatches without any rule at all.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review found that option E still let two one-wide axes expand each other into a bigger result. Option E now refuses that case and names the outer-product spelling, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How a user caches a pure function's results
decisions.gist: How a Jet user reuses a slow function's past answers.
decisions.lesson: A slow function called twice with the same input does the same work twice. Keeping past answers removes the second run. Jet has the bounded Cache collection, so a user can build that store by hand today. The hand-built version puts a lookup and a save inside every function that wants it. This choice decides who owns the store and how a user asks for one.
decisions.story: Priya builds a shipping quote page. Every quote calls a rate lookup that walks a large table. The same few zones repeat all day, so the same slow lookup runs again and again. She wants the repeat lookup to be free without a store, a check and a save inside her rate function.

options.name: A marker on the function
options.detail: You write one marker above a pure function. Jet keeps one store for that function and answers repeat calls from it. The body stays about its own job. The name does not change, so existing callers and recursive calls are served too. A size argument sets the limit.
options.technical: `#Memo` prefixes a `fn` whose effect row is empty. Sema rejects any other function with a registered code. The key is the argument tuple and reuses the existing hashable check. The store is one `Cache<K, V>` per function, bound 128, least-recently-used eviction; `#Memo(bound: none)` removes the limit. `name.cache()` reports hits, misses, size and bound. A return type of `Iter<T>` is rejected, because a stored iterator is spent after one read. Semantics live in one Prelude part that AOT, the JIT and the interpreter call.

options.name: The caller keeps the store
options.detail: No new syntax. Core gains one helper on Cache that looks up a key and computes the value when it is missing. The user makes the store, names it and decides its size. The store is plain code the user can read, share between functions and clear.
options.technical: Add `Cache.get_or_add(key, compute)`. It returns the stored value, or calls `compute(key)`, stores the result and returns it. Nothing checks purity, because the store is ordinary data. Nothing checks the key beyond the existing `Cache<K, V>` hashable bound. A recursive function must call itself through the store by hand.

options.name: Jet decides on its own
options.detail: No user surface at all. Jet stores results for pure calls it judges slow and repeated. Nobody writes a store, a marker or a size. The cost is that memory use and speed change without anything in the source saying so, and the user cannot turn it off for one function.
options.technical: The compiler picks memoized call sites from a cost model over pure calls. Storage size, eviction and lifetime are compiler policy. Reproducible builds need that policy pinned, or two builds of one source differ in memory use. There is no per-function opt-out and no report.

options.name: A memo value in Core
options.detail: No new syntax. Core gains one function that takes a pure function and returns a caching version of it. The user binds that version to a new name and calls it. The store rides along with the new name and can be reported on or cleared.
options.technical: `core.memo(f, bound: n)` accepts an `fn(K) =[]=> V` and returns `fn(K) =[]=> V` with an attached `Cache<K, V>`. Purity is a type bound, so an impure argument fails at the call. The original name keeps its old behaviour, so recursive calls inside `f` are never served from the store.

comparisons.note: A decorator on the function, keeping the name. The store is bounded at 128 by default and reports hits, misses and size. A second unbounded decorator was added later for one job, which is the wart to avoid.
A library function wraps a function and returns a caching one under a new name. This is option D. Recursive calls inside the original still miss the store.
comparisons.code:
(def fast (memoize zone-rate))
(fast 3)  ; walks the table
(fast 3)  ; answered from the store

comparisons.note: Nothing in the standard library. Users reach for an outside crate that adds an attribute above the function, which is the shape of option A.

recommendation.why: The marker keeps the function's name, so every existing caller and every recursive call is answered from the store with no other edit. Jet already proves a function is pure with the empty effect row, so the one rule that makes stored answers safe is checked by the compiler instead of written in a comment.

whyNot.reason: The store, its size and its lifetime go back into the user's code for every function that wants caching, and a recursive call inside the function still runs the slow path.
A store nobody asked for spends memory nobody can see, and no reader of the source can tell whether a call was answered from it.
The stored answers live under a new name, so recursive calls and every existing caller keep running the slow path until each one is edited.

recommendation.tradeoff: A marker is new user-typed syntax, so it needs a registered spelling, a formatter rule and its own diagnostics. Jet accepts that cost because the marker family already exists, and every other option puts the bookkeeping back into function bodies.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a marker, a caller-held store and an automatic compiler store. It recommended the marker because the function keeps its name, so recursion and existing callers are covered.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the Core memo value that Clojure uses. It folded per-argument keys, time-based expiry and a shared store between functions into the marker's arguments rather than padding the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a marker that also hands back its store. The marker now reports hits, misses, size and bound, so the expert path needs no second mechanism beside it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the caller-held store with a get_or_add helper and gave the automatic option a size limit. Both still hide the store or repeat it in every function.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the marker with recursion, unhashable arguments, lazy returns and unbounded growth. The empty effect row, the existing hashable check, a stated refusal for Iter returns and a bounded default answer each attack, so the marker stands.

decisions.title: How you read one cell, one column, and one window
decisions.gist: The spelling that picks part of a matrix out of the whole.
decisions.lesson: Reading part of a matrix is constant work: one cell, a whole column, a block of rows. Jet already settled what a partial read gives you. A bare projection is a read window, `&` makes it writable, and `~` copies it. Today a matrix cell is read with a function call, and only the first axis can be windowed. This choice is the spelling inside the brackets, and whether a single index drops that axis while a range keeps it.
decisions.story: Tom pulls the second column out of a design matrix to plot it, then doubles that column in place to change its units. Today he writes `compute.get(t, [0, 1])` for one cell, and the language can only window the first axis for him.

options.name: One bracket, one slot per axis
options.detail: Rows and columns get a slot each inside a single bracket. A range in a slot picks a band, and `..` means the whole axis. A single index drops its axis, so one cell is a number. The cost is that the two most common reads, a whole row and a whole column, are written as punctuation.
options.technical: `m[i, j]` gives the cell type. `m[range, j]` and `m[i, range]` give `Vec<N>`; `m[range, range]` gives `Matrix<M, N>`. `..` in a slot means that whole axis. Every result is a place under D-SHAPE-PLACE1, so `&m[.., 1]` is the write window and `~m[.., 1]` copies. Ranges are ordinary values (D-RANGE-VALUE1).
options.code:
cell   :: m[0, 1]              // Float
column :: m[.., 1]             // Vec<8>
block  :: m[0..<4, 0..<2]      // Matrix<4, 2>
&m[.., 1] *= 2.0               // write window over that column

options.name: Chained brackets, a row at a time
options.detail: A matrix reads like a list of rows, so `m[0]` is a row and `m[0][1]` is a cell. Nothing new is learned beyond list indexing. The cost is that the two axes stop looking alike: a row is punctuation and a column needs a method.
options.technical: `m[i]` gives `Vec<N>` and `m[i][j]` gives the cell type. `m[range]` windows the first axis, matching today's `Tensor` behaviour. Columns are only reachable through `.col(j)`.
options.code:
cell   :: m[0][1]              // Float
row    :: m[0]                 // Vec<2>
column :: m.col(1)             // rows come first, so a column needs a method
block  :: m[0..<4]             // Matrix<4, 2>

options.name: Named methods only
options.detail: Every read says what it is in words: `m.at(i, j)`, `m.row(i)`, `m.col(j)`, `m.window(...)`. Nothing has to be decoded and the argument order is labeled. The cost is that a method call is not a place, so editing a column in place needs a second surface that the bracket form does not need.
options.technical: Reads are methods returning views. A method call is not part of a place under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. So `&m.col(1)` is not a write window. In-place edits use named mutating methods such as `m.scale_column(j, by: v)`.
options.code:
cell   :: m.at(0, 1)
column :: m.col(1)
block  :: m.window(rows: 0..<4, cols: 0..<2)
m.scale_column(1, by: 2.0)     // the in-place edit needs its own method

options.name: Labeled slots
options.detail: Each slot carries the axis it means: `m[row: 0, col: 1]`. The order can never be swapped by mistake, and a single-axis read needs no filler. Jet already writes labeled arguments this way. The cost is two labels on every read, and the labels stop helping past two axes, where they turn into invented names.
options.technical: `m[row: i, col: j]` and `m[col: j]` are index expressions with labeled slots, following the existing labeled-argument surface. Omitting a label means that whole axis. Results are places, so `&m[col: 1]` is a write window.
options.code:
cell   :: m[row: 0, col: 1]
column :: m[col: 1]
block  :: m[row: 0..<4, col: 0..<2]
&m[col: 1] *= 2.0

options.name: One bracket per axis, with named readers for the whole-axis case
options.detail: Brackets carry cells, bands and windows, and `.row(i)` and `.col(j)` are the readable names for a whole axis. A single index drops that axis and a range keeps it, so a one-row matrix and a plain row are both writable with no extra flag. Everyday reads are words and precise reads are brackets.
options.technical: `m[i, j]` gives the cell type; `m[i, ..]` and `m[.., j]` give `Vec<N>`; `m[0..<1, ..]` gives `Matrix<1, N>`. `..` means the whole axis. `.row(i)` is `m[i, ..]` and `.col(j)` is `m[.., j]`. All bracket results are places under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. So `&m[.., 1]` is the write window and `~m[.., 1]` copies. A method call is not a place, so an in-place edit is written on brackets. Ranges are ordinary values (D-RANGE-VALUE1).
options.code:
cell   :: m[0, 1]              // Float — a single index drops that axis
column :: m[.., 1]             // Vec<8>
kept   :: m[0..<1, ..]         // Matrix<1, 2> — a range keeps the axis
block  :: m[0..<4, 0..<2]      // Matrix<4, 2>
first  :: m.row(0)             // the readable name for m[0, ..]

&m[.., 1] *= 2.0               // write window: doubles the column in place
keepsafe :: ~m[0..<4, ..]      // an owned copy that outlives `m`

comparisons.note: One bracket with a slot per axis. A single index drops that axis and a slice keeps it, which is the rule most array users already carry.
comparisons.code:
cell = m[0, 1]
col  = m[:, 1]
kept = m[0:1, :]

comparisons.note: Parentheses with a slot per axis, and a colon for the whole axis. Indexes start at one.
One bracket per axis, but a single-column read silently becomes a plain vector unless a flag says otherwise. That flag is a long-standing complaint.
comparisons.code:
col  <- m[, 2]
kept <- m[, 2, drop = FALSE]

comparisons.note: One bracket per axis with a colon for the whole axis, and a view is asked for by name when no copy is wanted.

recommendation.why: The two reads people write most, a row and a column, become words instead of punctuation, and everything else stays one bracket with one slot per axis. Because a range keeps its axis, a one-row matrix and a plain row are both writable without the extra flag other languages carry. Bracket reads stay places, so the same line that reads a column can edit it.

whyNot.reason: Without the named readers, the two most common reads are written as punctuation and `m[.., 1]` has to be decoded.
A row is punctuation while a column is a method, so the two axes stop looking alike in the source.
A method call is not a place, so editing a column in place needs a second surface that brackets do not need.
Every read grows two labels, and the labels turn into invented names as soon as a value has more than two axes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A single index drops its axis, so `m[0, 1]` is a number while `m[0..<1, 0..<1]` is a one-by-one matrix. That difference is learned once, and it removes the flag other languages need for the same job.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one bracket with a slot per axis against chained brackets and named methods, and recommended the slot form because both axes then read alike.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added labeled slots, which Jet can already write, and checked whether an index needs a new value type. Ranges are already values under D-RANGE-VALUE1, so nothing new was needed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the bracket form with named row and column readers, and folded in the rule that a range keeps its axis while a single index drops it. The recommendation moved to that combination.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened D, since labeled slots read well for two axes and refuse a swapped argument order outright, and strengthened C for the same clarity in words.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the drop rule with the single-row case that other languages need a flag for. A one-wide range keeps the axis, so no flag is needed and the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How you solve a system and fit a line
decisions.gist: The spelling that answers a system of equations and fits a line to measurements.
decisions.lesson: Fitting a line to measurements is the most common reason anyone reaches for a matrix. The algebra is one step: solve a system of equations. A square system has one exact answer. A tall system, which is what measured data gives, has no exact answer and takes the closest one instead. Those are two different questions with two different ways to fail, and this spelling decides whether a reader can tell which one ran.
decisions.story: Ana fits a line to eight brake tests. Her system is tall, so no exact answer exists and she wants the closest one. In R she writes `lm(dist ~ speed)` and is finished. In Jet today she writes a chain of fallible function calls.

options.name: A backslash solves
options.detail: The MATLAB and Julia spelling. `x \ y` answers exactly when the system is square and takes the closest answer when it is tall. Ported code carries over and the fit is one short line. The cost is a symbol nobody can guess, which also hides which of the two questions was answered.
options.technical: New infix `\` at division precedence. `Matrix<N, N> \ Matrix<N, K>` is the exact solve; `Matrix<M, N> \ Matrix<M, K>` with `M > N` is the closest answer. Both are fallible: a square system that cannot be solved and a tall system with dependent columns both report failure. A wide system is refused.
options.code:
exact :: a \ b ?? panic("singular")     // a is Matrix<2, 2>
fit   :: x \ y ?? panic("no fit")       // x is Matrix<8, 2>: the closest answer
print("intercept {fit[0, 0]}  slope {fit[1, 0]}")

options.name: Two named methods, one per question
options.detail: `x.solve(y)` answers a square system exactly. `x.least_squares(y)` takes the closest answer for a tall one. The call says which question was asked, so a reader never has to check a shape to know what came back. The cost is that people arriving from MATLAB will look for a backslash first.
options.technical: `.solve(y)` accepts `Matrix<N, N>` only; on a tall matrix it is a compile error naming `.least_squares`. `.least_squares(y)` accepts `Matrix<M, N>` with `M >= N`. Both are fallible and report a dependent-column failure rather than a quiet answer. `\` is registered as an unknown operator whose message names both methods. Expert routes reuse the same names on a stored factorization: `x.qr().least_squares(y)`.

options.name: One named method that reads the shape
options.detail: `x.solve(y)` answers exactly when the matrix is square and takes the closest answer when it is tall. One name to learn, and the shape picks the behaviour at compile time. The cost is that a reader of the call cannot tell which of the two questions was answered without going to find the shape.
options.technical: `.solve(y)` accepts `Matrix<M, N>` with `M >= N` and chooses the exact or closest route from the measures. Fallible in both routes. The compiler can report the chosen route on request, but the call site does not carry it.
options.code:
exact :: a.solve(b) ?? panic("singular")     // a is Matrix<2, 2>: exact
fit   :: x.solve(y) ?? panic("no fit")       // x is Matrix<8, 2>: closest
print("intercept {fit[0, 0]}  slope {fit[1, 0]}")

options.name: Free functions in the module
options.detail: `la.solve(x, y)` and `la.least_squares(x, y)` sit beside the other library entries, and the module name says where the work happens. The cost is that the surface stops reading like the rest of the matrix API, which is method-shaped, and a call breaks a chain in the middle of an expression.
options.technical: Module-level functions with the same shape rules and the same fallible results as option B.
options.code:
exact :: la.solve(a, b) ?? panic("singular")
fit   :: la.least_squares(x, y) ?? panic("no fit")
print("intercept {fit[0, 0]}  slope {fit[1, 0]}")

options.name: A fitting surface above the algebra
options.detail: `la.fit(speed, stop)` answers the question people actually have and hands back a value with a named intercept, slope and prediction. This is the level R users work at, and it is one line. The cost is that it answers only the straight-line case, and it puts model fitting inside the algebra surface.
options.technical: `la.fit(xs, ys)` returns a `Fit` value carrying `.intercept`, `.slope`, `.predict(x)` and `.residuals()`. The algebra stays available underneath through the option B method pair, which the fit calls.
options.code:
line :: la.fit(speed, stop) ?? panic("no fit")
print("intercept {line.intercept}  slope {line.slope}")
print("12 mph stops in {line.predict(12)} feet")

// The algebra is still reachable:
beta :: x.least_squares(y) ?? panic("no fit")

comparisons.note: One backslash covers both questions and picks by shape.
The same backslash, with a factorization available by name when the same system is solved many times.
comparisons.code:
beta = X \ dist
F = qr(X); beta = F \ dist

comparisons.note: Two separate named functions, one per question, in the linear algebra module.
`solve` does the algebra, but the everyday answer to this exact task is a model-fitting function, not matrix algebra at all.
comparisons.code:
beta <- solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% dist)
fit  <- lm(dist ~ speed)

recommendation.why: The two questions fail in different ways, so the call should say which one was asked. A reader of `x.least_squares(y)` knows a closest answer came back without going to look at a shape. A square system that cannot be solved reports failure instead of quietly returning an approximation, which is the mistake this area is known for.

whyNot.reason: A backslash is a symbol no new reader can guess, and it hides which of the two questions the shape decided to answer.
One name covers two questions, so the call site no longer says whether an exact answer or a closest one came back.
Free functions read against the rest of the matrix surface, which is method-shaped, and they break a chain mid-expression.
It answers only the straight-line case and moves model fitting into the algebra surface, while still hiding which algebra ran.

recommendation.tradeoff: People arriving from MATLAB and Julia will type a backslash and not find it. That character reports a message naming both methods, so the search ends on the first attempt.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the backslash against a pair of named methods, and recommended the pair because the two questions fail in different ways.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added free functions, a single shape-reading name, and a fitting surface above the algebra. It also tested a factorization-first surface and folded it into option B as the expert route for repeated solves.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested pairing the named methods with the fitting value. The fitting value stays its own option, because it answers only the straight-line case and would move model fitting into the algebra surface.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened A, because one symbol covers both questions the way two whole fields already write them. It strengthened E with Rs evidence that most people want the fit, not the algebra.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what a MATLAB reader does when the backslash is missing. That character now reports a message naming both methods, and `.solve` on a tall matrix names `.least_squares`, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Whether matrix types are always there or asked for
decisions.gist: Whether a program can write a matrix without importing anything first.
decisions.lesson: Every Jet program starts with the names the language always provides: numbers, text, lists, `print`. Everything else is asked for with `use`. Matrix work spans a wide range. A two-by-two rotation inside a game loop is arithmetic. A determinant, a decomposition and a fast Fourier transform are a library. This choice decides which of those a program gets without asking, and therefore how much every beginner sees in front of them forever.
decisions.story: Ben writes a twenty-line script to fit a line through eight readings. The first thing he has to work out is whether a matrix is already there, or which module holds it. Every extra step at that point is a step where he goes back to Python.

options.name: Everything is always there
options.detail: Types, literals, arithmetic, and the whole algebra library need no import. Nothing stands between a person and a matrix. The cost is that determinants, decompositions and transforms sit in front of every beginner, and most programs never touch one.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>`, `Vec<N>`, and the full `core.linalg` surface enter the always-available name set. Every name appears in completion and in the beginner listing.

options.name: Everything is asked for
options.detail: One import brings the whole surface, exactly like every other core module. The file states what it depends on, which a reader auditing a program can see at a glance. The cost lands on the smallest use: a matrix literal does not type-check until the import is written.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>` and `Vec<N>` resolve only through `use core.linalg`. An unimported use reports the ordinary unknown-type message naming the module.

options.name: The small fixed sizes stay; the general shapes are asked for
options.detail: Today's fixed graphics types stay always available, and the shape-typed general forms need the import. Game and graphics code changes nothing. The cost is two families of matrix type living side by side, when the small ones are already names for the general ones.
options.technical: `Vec2/3/4` and `Mat3/Mat4` stay in the always-available set as D-LINALG1 has them. `Matrix<M, N>` and `Vec<N>` resolve through `use core.linalg`.

options.name: Arithmetic is always there; the algebra is asked for
options.detail: Types, literals, indexing, transpose, `+ - *` and reductions need no import, the way `+` on numbers needs none. Solving, determinants, decompositions and transforms come with `use core.linalg`, the way `sqrt` comes with `core.math`. A rotation or a small sum never meets an import, and the always-available set grows by two names rather than by a library.
options.technical: Always available: `Matrix<M, N>`, `Vec<N>`, their literals, indexing and windows, transpose, `+`, `-`, `*`, `.mean()`, `.sum()`. Asked for with `use core.linalg`: solving, least squares, determinant, inverse, decompositions, eigenvalues, transforms. Shape-typed matrices are fixed size, so they sit in the heap-free `core` runtime layer (D-RINGLAYER1); the dynamic `Tensor` stays in the allocating layer.

options.name: `core.compute` owns them
options.detail: One import covers every array shape, from a two-by-two rotation to a device tensor, and `core.linalg` stops being a separate name. The cost is that a rotation then arrives with the device, placement and transfer surface attached, which a rotation has no reason to see.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>` and `Vec<N>` resolve through `use core.compute`, which already owns `Tensor<T>` under D-COMPUTE-TYPE1. `core.linalg` retires and its fixed types move across.

comparisons.note: Matrices are the base type of the language. Nothing is imported, ever, and that is the whole pitch.
Arrays and their arithmetic are always there; decompositions and solvers need one standard-library import.
Everything is asked for, including the array type itself. This is the single most repeated line in scientific Python.
comparisons.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])

comparisons.note: Matrices, arithmetic, determinants and solving are all in the base language with no import.

recommendation.why: It follows the split Jet already uses for numbers: arithmetic is always there, and `core.math` is asked for when `sqrt` is needed. A person writing a rotation or a small sum never meets an import, which is where scripting users are lost. The names in front of every beginner grow by two types instead of by a whole library.

whyNot.reason: Determinants, decompositions and transforms sit in front of every beginner, and most programs never use one.
A matrix literal does not type-check until an import is written, which is ceremony on the smallest possible use.
It keeps two families of matrix type, and the small fixed ones are already names for the general shape-typed ones.
It ties a two-by-two rotation to the device, placement and transfer surface, which a rotation has no reason to see.

recommendation.tradeoff: A line has to be drawn between arithmetic and algebra, and it has to hold as the library grows. The line is written out: types, literals, indexing, transpose, `+ - *` and reductions are always there, and everything else is asked for.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared putting the whole surface always in reach against putting all of it behind an import, and recommended the import to keep the beginner listing small.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the split home, the two-family option matching today's fixed graphics types, and folding the whole surface into `core.compute`.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the two, giving arithmetic to the always-available set and algebra to the import, which is how numbers and `core.math` already divide. The recommendation moved to that split.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: one import is one line, and it makes the dependency visible to a reader auditing what a program touches.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the split as a line that will drift as the library grows. Option D now writes the line out as a list, and the fixed-size types also fit the heap-free runtime layer, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: A computed field that is slow: how a user asks for the answer to be kept
decisions.gist: How a user asks Jet to keep the answer of a slow computed field instead of working it out on every read.
decisions.lesson: A computed field is a formula over its sibling fields. D-FIELDPOL1 makes it run again on every read, which is always correct and never stale. When the formula is slow, every read pays. The only fix today is to add a second plain field and fill it by hand, which is the bookkeeping computed fields removed. D-MEMO1 already answers this for functions with a `#Memo` marker. This choice picks the field spelling, and must agree with that one.
decisions.story: Mara models a supply route. Her `Leg` struct has a computed `distance` that walks a road graph. A report reads `distance` inside a sort, so the same walk runs thousands of times and the report takes a minute.

options.name: Keep it, and clear it when a source changes
options.detail: You mark the field. Jet keeps the answer after the first read. When any sibling the formula reads is written, the kept answer is dropped and the next read works it out again. Nothing can go stale. Mara marks one field and her report is fast.
options.technical: `#Memo` prefixes the field. The compiler already knows which siblings a computed field reads, because D-FIELDPOL1 orders them and rejects cycles. The same set drives the clear. A write to any of them clears the kept answer. `.{ }` copies and patches start empty. The formula must be pure, the same rule `#Memo` sets for a function.

options.name: Keep it, and never clear it
options.detail: The same marker keeps the answer, but nothing ever drops it. It is simple and fast. A patch that changes a source leaves the old answer in place, so a field can report a number that no longer matches its own formula.

options.name: A second arrow says it is kept
options.detail: No marker. A different arrow spells the kept form: `=>` works it out each read, `==>` keeps it. The struct reads as one table with no prefix. It costs a new arrow that a reader must learn, and it does not match the function spelling.

options.name: Nothing new; write it down by hand
options.detail: Jet adds no surface. A user who needs the answer kept adds a plain field and fills it in the constructor. It is honest about the cost and adds nothing to learn. It also returns the bookkeeping that computed fields removed, and the hand-filled field can go stale with no warning.

options.name: Keep it, and let the user say when to clear it
options.detail: The marker keeps the answer, and the user names the siblings that should clear it. It gives exact control for a formula that reads something the compiler cannot see. It also lets a user name the wrong set and ship a stale field.
options.technical: `#Memo(on: [from, to])` names the clearing set. With no argument, the set is every sibling the formula reads, which is option A's rule.

comparisons.note: Python keeps the answer forever and clears nothing. Its own documentation warns that the object must not change.
Swift has a lazy stored property that runs once. It never clears, and it cannot appear on a value type that gets copied and patched.
comparisons.code: lazy var distance: Double = shortest(from, to)

comparisons.note: Vue keeps a computed value and drops it when a source it read changes. That clear-on-source-change rule is the same one option A uses.

recommendation.why: Mara marks one field and gets the speed, and no reading can ever disagree with the formula. The compiler already tracks the sibling set, so the rule needs nothing new to be exact.

whyNot.reason: It lets a field report a number its own formula no longer produces, which is the silent wrong answer Jet refuses by default.
It adds a second arrow for a job a marker already spells on functions, so one idea would have two shapes.
It returns the hand bookkeeping that computed fields removed, and the hand-filled value can go stale with no warning.
It puts the clearing set in the user's hands, so a wrong list ships a stale field that reads as deliberate.

recommendation.tradeoff: A write to any source clears the answer even when the formula would return the same number. That is accepted because a correct field beats a slightly faster one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping the answer with clearing it against keeping it forever, and recommended clearing, because a computed field must never disagree with its own formula.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the second-arrow spelling, the do-nothing option, and a user-named clearing set. It dropped a time-limit option, because a clock cannot tell whether a source changed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested folding the user-named set into the recommendation as an expert door. It stayed a separate option, since the automatic set is already exact and a second spelling would weaken it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the do-nothing option by noting that a hand-filled field is visible and costs nothing to learn. It still returns the bookkeeping computed fields were built to remove.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked about a formula that reads something outside the struct, which the compiler cannot track. Option A already requires a pure formula, so that case is refused rather than silently kept.

decisions.title: What an automatic fix promises before a tool applies it
decisions.gist: How much Jet promises about an automatic fix.
decisions.lesson: Jet reports can carry a machine-applicable edit. Editors and `jet fix` apply those edits, and coding agents apply them in a loop without a person reading each one. Today the report says nothing about how much to trust an edit. A rename and a guess look identical. This choice decides what Jet promises when it offers a fix, and what a tool may safely do with that promise.
decisions.story: Priya is porting a 40-file service to Jet. She starts an agent, closes her laptop, and lets it run overnight. The agent applies every fix Jet offers, rechecks, and repeats. In the morning she needs two things: the errors are gone, and nothing was silently changed into something she did not mean. She never reads the individual edits.
decisions.inWild:
# The agent's overnight loop. It never reads the fix sentence.
while jet check src/ --json > reports.jsonl; do
  jq -c 'select(.fix_edits | length > 0)' reports.jsonl | apply-edits
  [ $? -eq 0 ] || break
done

# Two reports from one run. Which of these is safe to apply unread?
{"code":"E0102","what":"nothing named `pirnt` exists here",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"print"}]}

{"code":"E0311","what":"this value is used after it moved",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"value.copy()"}]}

options.name: Four grades, the vocabulary Rust already uses
options.detail: Every edit carries one of four words: safe, may-be-wrong, has-placeholders, or unknown. Tools choose which grades they apply. Gain: a reader who knows Rust knows this at once, and tools written for that model port over. Loss: three of the four words mean some version of 'do not trust this', so the tool author still has to pick a policy Jet never states.
options.technical: Adds `applicability` to `jet.report/v1` with the closed enum `safe`, `maybe_incorrect`, `has_placeholders`, `unspecified`. Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1. `jet fix` applies `safe` only. Every grade needs a registry entry and a golden.

options.name: One class: an edit exists only when it is always right
options.detail: Jet offers an edit only when applying it is correct every time. A repair that depends on what the author meant carries no edit at all. The fix sentence still teaches the person what to do. Gain: no grades to learn, and no tool ever has to choose a policy. Loss: helpful-but-uncertain suggestions become prose only, so an agent cannot act on them mechanically.
options.technical: No new field. The rule moves to the raise site: a checker attaches an edit only when the repair is determined by the program, not by intent. `fix_edits` stays as specified. A guard test fails any diagnostic that attaches an edit for an ambiguous repair.
options.code:
{"code":"E0102",
 "fix":"did you mean `print`?",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"print"}]}

{"code":"E0311",
 "fix":"copy the value, or move the later use above this line",
 "fix_edits":[]}

$ jet fix src/
src/a.jet: applied 1 fix

options.name: Two words: safe and suggested
options.detail: An edit is either safe to apply unread or a suggestion a person should look at. Tools apply safe edits and show suggestions. Gain: one bit, easy to explain, and it keeps uncertain suggestions usable by an editor. Loss: 'suggested' hides real differences — a placeholder to fill in and a plausible guess get the same word.
options.technical: Adds `applicability` to `jet.report/v1` with the closed enum `safe`, `suggested`. Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1. `jet fix` applies `safe`; `jet fix --suggested` prompts. Editors show suggestions as code actions.

options.name: Safe means proved: applying every safe edit always makes progress
options.detail: Same two words as C, but 'safe' becomes a promise Jet keeps and tests. Applying every safe edit and rechecking must reduce the report count and must never add a new problem. A loop that runs to zero is guaranteed to end. Gain: an unattended agent can trust the loop, not just the edit. Loss: a repair that cannot be proved to make progress ships as a suggestion until someone proves it.
options.technical: Adds `applicability` with the closed enum `safe`, `suggested`. Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1. Adds a conformance property: for any source, applying all `safe` edits and rechecking yields strictly fewer reports and introduces no report absent from the previous round. Fixture-proved per release; a violation is a release blocker.
options.code:
{"code":"E0102","applicability":"safe",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"print"}]}

$ jet fix src/ --loop
round 1: applied 12 fixes, 31 reports remain
round 2: applied 9 fixes,  4 reports remain
round 3: applied 0 fixes,  4 reports remain
stopped: 4 reports need a person (suggested, not safe)
