comparisons.note: Four grades. They are advisory: nothing promises the repair loop ends, and `cargo fix` can apply an edit that leaves new errors behind.
`gofmt -r` and `go fix` apply only rewrites that are correct by construction. There is no grade because nothing uncertain is ever offered.
comparisons.code: $ go fix ./...   # rewrites only what it can do exactly

comparisons.note: One bit: a rule is fixable or it is not. Fixes are applied in rounds until nothing changes, with a round cap when a pair of rules disagree.
comparisons.code: $ eslint --fix src/   # loops internally, caps at 10 passes

recommendation.why: It is the only option that promises something about the loop rather than about one edit. An agent working unattended needs to know the run ends and never goes backwards. That promise is testable, so Jet can hold itself to it every release.

whyNot.reason: Four words describe Jet's confidence but promise nothing about what happens after an edit is applied. Three of them mean 'do not trust this', so each tool still invents its own policy.
One class is honest and needs no vocabulary, but it throws away every uncertain repair. An editor can show a suggestion safely, and this option gives it nothing to show.
Two words are the right shape, but 'safe' stays an opinion. Without a proved progress rule, a safe edit can still add a new problem and a loop can run forever.

recommendation.tradeoff: A repair nobody has proved to make progress ships as a suggestion, so `jet fix` starts narrower than it could. That is the right way round: the promise is only worth having if it always holds.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared Rust's four grades against a single always-right class. It recommended the four grades because they are familiar and let editors show uncertain repairs.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the two-word option and the proved-progress option, then checked Go, which offers nothing uncertain, and ESLint, which loops in capped rounds. That surfaced the real question: the loop, not the label.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the two-word vocabulary with the always-right discipline and added the progress property. The result became option D, and the recommendation moved there because a promise about the loop beats a label on an edit.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each loser: Rust tooling ports to option A unchanged, option B needs no tool policy at all, and option C gives editors a real suggestion path. All three remain honest choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the progress property with edits that conflict inside one round and spans that shift after an earlier edit. Stating the property over a whole round, with spans reapplied against the round's starting text, repairs both attacks.

decisions.title: One-line function bodies: two ratified rulings disagree
decisions.gist: Which mark attaches a one-line function body: the arrow or the double colon.
decisions.lesson: Two ratified decisions give the same surface two different answers. D-BODY-ARROW1=B says every head takes `-> body` on one line, and functions join that rule. D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A says a one-line function body binds with `::`. Neither is built yet, and neither appears in the syntax record. Two cards wait to build opposite spellings. A third card teaches the formatter to emit `= expr`, which both rulings retire. One ruling must win before any of them starts.
decisions.story: Mia writes her second Jet file. She types a one-line function and the formatter rewrites it. Later she reads a one-line `if` and sees a different mark for what looks like the same act. She asks which mark means body. Today Jet has two ratified answers for her, so nobody can teach her one.

options.name: The arrow takes every body
options.detail: One sentence teaches every body in the language. A head takes `-> body` when the whole form fits one line, and a brace block otherwise. Functions, guards, loops and arms all read the same. The cost is two arrows in one function line: `=> Float` names the result and `->` opens the body. The reader must hold two arrow meanings on the same line.
options.technical: Honors D-BODY-ARROW1=B as ratified and drops D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A. `=` retires from bodies and keeps its slot-fill jobs: reassignment, parameter defaults, field defaults, enum discriminants, index write. Card #1454 builds it. Cards #1812 and #1512 retarget.

options.name: The double colon defines, the arrow maps
options.detail: Two words with two jobs, and each says what it does. `::` gives a name a meaning, so a function body binds like every other definition. `->` sends a head to a body, so guards, loops and arms keep the arrow. A function line then carries one arrow, not two. The cost is that the body rule needs two sentences instead of one.
options.technical: Honors D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A for function bodies and keeps D-BODY-ARROW1=B for control heads, with a named scope boundary between them. Both ratified texts survive under that boundary. `=` still retires from bodies. Matches D-ALIAS-OP1=B, which already binds an alias with `::`. Card #1812 builds the function half; card #1454 builds the head half.

options.name: The double colon takes every body
options.detail: Every one-line body binds with `::`, heads included. One mark, one sentence, and it is the mark a beginner already met on day one. The cost is heavy. A guard reads `if ready :: run()`, which says a name is being defined when none is. Arm tables lose the arrow that separates head from body.
options.technical: Overturns D-BODY-ARROW1=B in full and extends D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A past its stated scope. It also reopens D-ARROW-CONTROL1=A, which gave `->` the selected-value and yielded-value job. Arm tables would need a separate rule, because `->` there separates head from body inside a block.

options.name: The equals sign keeps function bodies
options.detail: Nothing changes. A one-line function body stays `= expr`, which is what ships today and what most languages with this form use. The formatter work on card #1512 lands as written. The cost is that `=` then means both define and fill, and Jet already chose `::` for every other definition, including aliases.
options.technical: Overturns both D-BODY-ARROW1=B and D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A. It also breaks the rule D-ALIAS-OP1=B set on 2026-08-06, where a new name arrives through `::` and `=` only updates what exists. Card #1454 and card #1812 both close as rejected.

comparisons.note: Expression-bodied members use an arrow. The result type sits before it, so one line carries one arrow.
comparisons.code: public double Area(double r) => 3.14 * r * r;

comparisons.note: Same arrow form. The return type is a bare word, not an arrow, so the two never collide.
Uses the equals sign for a one-line body, and keeps braces for longer ones.
comparisons.code: fun area(r: Double): Double = 3.14 * r * r

comparisons.note: Added an endless method in 3.0 with the equals sign, after twenty-five years of braces only.
A one-line body is a keyword, not a sign. It reads as prose and never collides with a type arrow.

recommendation.why: Each mark says one thing. `::` gives a name a meaning, in a binding, an alias, and now a function body. `->` sends a head to a body, in a guard, a loop, and an arm. A function line keeps one arrow, so `=> Float` still reads as the result and nothing competes with it. This is also the newer ruling, and it is the one that examined function bodies directly.

whyNot.reason: It puts two arrows on one function line. `fn area(r: Float) => Float -> 3.14 * r * r` asks the reader to hold two arrow meanings three words apart.
It reads `if ready :: run()` as a definition when nothing is being defined, and it takes the arrow out of arm tables, where the arrow separates head from body.
It keeps `=` meaning both define and fill. Jet already ruled the other way for aliases on 2026-08-06, so this answer splits one rule across two surfaces.

recommendation.tradeoff: The body rule takes two sentences, not one. That is acceptable because the two sentences name two different acts, and each mark then means exactly one thing everywhere it appears.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft set the two ratified rulings side by side and recommended the double colon for function bodies, because it matches the alias rule ratified one day earlier.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the current equals form and a colon-everywhere form, so the menu covers all four end states a card on the board could build. It also gathered five peer languages; none uses a double colon, and the arrow languages all keep a bare return type, which Jet does not.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review found that the two rulings need not fight, because a named scope boundary keeps both ratified texts alive. That boundary became the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave the arrow its real prize, one sentence for every body, and gave the equals sign its peer evidence from Kotlin and Ruby. Neither answer survived the two-arrow line or the alias rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the boundary as arbitrary, and it held, because the split is by act and not by construct. It also tested the return type against the body mark and found no parse ambiguity.

decisions.title: One text for the jetos boot default: the record and the code disagree
decisions.gist: Which bootloader and kernel a fresh jetos machine starts with.
decisions.lesson: One ratified decision now has two texts. The board record for D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1=A reads systemd-boot with a Linux long-term kernel. The syntax record, the jetos plan, and the shipped code all read Limine with the CachyOS kernel. A second ratified decision from the same day, D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, carries a first-party CachyOS kernel package, which the long-term kernel text does not allow. Three boot cards are queued against the Limine text. One owner line ends the split.
decisions.story: Sam installs jetos on a spare laptop. The machine must boot, roll back to the last generation, and show a menu that names each one. Sam does not choose a bootloader. Jet does, once, and every later card builds on that answer.

options.name: systemd-boot with the long-term kernel
options.detail: The default boot path is systemd-boot and the kernel is the Linux long-term release. This is what the ratified board record says today. It is the quiet, conservative answer, and it matches what most declarative Linux systems ship. The cost is that three queued cards, the syntax record, the jetos plan and the shipped code all say something else, so all of them change.
options.technical: Keeps the D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1=A record as stored. Requires amending docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4501, docs/plans/epoch-7/native-jetos.md, and the shipped jetos boot code, and reworking cards #909, #409 and #910. D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A must also be reopened, because it ratifies a first-party CachyOS kernel package.

options.name: Limine with the CachyOS kernel
options.detail: The default boot path is Limine and the kernel is the CachyOS package. This is what the syntax record, the plan and the code already say, and it is what the sibling kernel decision from the same day ratifies. It also gives jetos a faster desktop kernel by default. The cost is that the stored decision text is wrong today and must be corrected so one text exists.
options.technical: Amends the D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1 record to match its own rendered form at docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4501. Agrees with D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, the first-party CachyOS kernel package with exact source, config, patches and hashes. Cards #909, #409 and #910 proceed as written. Expert override of the kernel package and boot entry fields is unchanged either way.

comparisons.note: Ships systemd-boot as the modern default and a long-term kernel, with GRUB still available.
Ships Limine as an option beside its own tuned kernel, which is the pairing option B names.
Uses GRUB2 with boot loader specification entries, so menu entries are files rather than a generated script.

recommendation.why: It is the answer already written into the syntax record, the plan and the shipped code, and the only one that agrees with D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A from the same day. Choosing it corrects one stored sentence. Choosing the other rewrites four places and reopens a second ratified decision.

whyNot.reason: It contradicts D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, which ratifies a first-party CachyOS kernel package on the same day and the same card. It also forces a rewrite of the spec, the plan, the code and three queued cards.

recommendation.tradeoff: A tuned desktop kernel carries more patches than a long-term release, so jetos owns more upstream tracking. That is accepted because the kernel package is first-party and already ratified with exact source and hashes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft set the stored decision text against the rendered spec text and recommended the rendered form, because the code and the sibling kernel decision both agree with it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a third answer, GRUB, and a fourth, no default with an install-time prompt. Both were dropped: no card, plan or line of code asks for either, and a prompt moves a settled choice onto the beginner.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether the loader and the kernel can be decided apart. They can, but nothing on the board wants that split, so the menu stays two coherent pairings.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review made the conservative answer as strong as it can be. A long-term kernel with systemd-boot is the least surprising pairing for a declarative system, and NixOS ships it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether the stored record is right and the spec is the error. It could be, which is exactly why this needs an owner line rather than an agent judgement, and the ballot names both texts.

decisions.title: Where should an interpreter view-bounds failure be tested?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet proves an interpreter view-bounds failure.
decisions.lesson: The interpreter already performs the shared bounds check. D-INTERP-DIAG1, ratified on card #1483, maps this runtime failure to a panic with exit 70. Card #1616 still requires a compile diagnostic snapshot. Both requirements cannot be true at once.
decisions.story: Mara runs a program that creates a view outside a list. Jet must stop before any invalid access. She also needs a test that fails if one execution tier ever accepts the view.
decisions.inWild:
values := [1]
outside :: &values[2..2]

$ jet run --interpret main.jet
Error [E0953]: can't view 1 items from 2 to 2 (inclusive)
# exit 70

options.name: Test the runtime trap in the runtime suite
options.detail: Keep the ratified exit-70 runtime trap. Delete the stale compile-diagnostic fixture and prove the same message and failure across AOT, default run, and forced interpreter. This keeps each test suite about one product surface.
options.technical: Retarget #1616 to the tier-parity runtime test. Amend #1601 criterion 3 to remove tests/ui/view_mut_bounds_interpreter.stderr. Preserve D-INTERP-DIAG1 and the shared E0953 bounds predicate.
options.code:
assert_tiers_fail(
  source: "outside :: &values[2..2]",
  code: "E0953",
  exit: 70,
)

options.name: Teach the diagnostic suite to capture runtime traps
options.detail: Keep the ratified exit-70 runtime trap and keep the UI fixture. Change the snapshot harness so a nonzero interpreter run records panic output instead of reporting no errors. One suite then covers compile reports and runtime traps.
options.technical: Preserve D-INTERP-DIAG1. Extend diagnostic_snapshots only for RunOutcome::Ran with a nonzero exit. The golden stores stderr and exit status, not a Problems value.

options.name: Turn the failure back into a compile diagnostic
options.detail: Restore the old Problems/E0953 snapshot. The interpreter rejects the view before execution, so the diagnostic suite remains unchanged. This reopens the ratified rule that runtime interpreter failures use panic output and exit 70.
options.technical: Amend D-INTERP-DIAG1 for view bounds. Source/Interpreter.rs must return RunOutcome::Problems for this case instead of RunOutcome::Ran.
options.code:
$ jet check main.jet
error[E0953]: can't view 1 items from 2 to 2 (inclusive)

comparisons.note: Rust tests compile diagnostics and runtime panics in separate suites. An out-of-bounds dynamic index is a runtime panic.
comparisons.code:
let xs = vec![1];
println!("{}", xs[i]); // panics when i is outside the vector

comparisons.note: A dynamic bounds failure is tested by running code and checking IndexError, not by a parser snapshot.

recommendation.why: The bounds check already works. A runtime parity test proves the safety contract at the surface where it occurs and keeps the ratified exit-70 rule intact.

whyNot.reason: It makes one snapshot harness interpret two different products. Future readers cannot tell whether a fixture tests a compiler report or a runtime failure.
It reopens a ratified interpreter rule even though the current runtime behavior is safe and consistent.

recommendation.tradeoff: The stale UI fixture is deleted. The same case remains protected by a stronger three-tier runtime test.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a runtime parity test with a mixed snapshot harness and a compiler diagnostic. It recommended the runtime test because the failure occurs during execution.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested keeping both suites and removing the case. Keeping both duplicates proof, while removing it loses tier safety coverage.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the useful part of the stale fixture with the runtime test: keep the exact E0953 message, but assert it in the three-tier runtime matrix.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the mixed harness option by limiting it to nonzero interpreter outcomes. It still gives one suite two meanings.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether deleting a golden weakens diagnostics. It does not, because no compile diagnostic exists under ratified law and the runtime test checks code, message, exit, and tier parity.

decisions.title: Close cards before milestone review
decisions.outcome: A card closes when its nonempty observable exit criteria are all met with concrete evidence, its patch is integrated into the milestone stream, and no known blocker contradicts the evidence. Do not require a per-card reviewer or duplicate proof. At the milestone boundary, run one composed targeted test sweep and one fresh-context review of the integrated milestone diff; reopen owning cards and criteria for findings, fix and review the correction delta, verify criteria, then explicitly verify the milestone.
decisions.comment: A card closes when its nonempty observable exit criteria are all met with concrete evidence, its patch is integrated into the milestone stream, and no known blocker contradicts the evidence. Do not require a per-card reviewer or duplicate proof. At the milestone boundary, run one composed targeted test sweep and one fresh-context review of the integrated milestone diff; reopen owning cards and criteria for findings, fix and review the correction delta, verify criteria, then explicitly verify the milestone.

decisions.title: Storing a read-only view: semantic copy with a visibility ladder
decisions.gist: What happens when a program stores a zero-copy view in a list, struct, or cache.
decisions.lesson: A view is a zero-copy look into a string or list. Today a program cannot store one anywhere: the compiler rejects the store with E2307 and its fix text says to write `~` and copy. So the most common memory error demands a fix the compiler could apply itself. This choice decides who applies that fix: the language, a source rewriter, or the user. Write-through views (ViewMut) keep the error under every option, because a copy there would break write-back.
decisions.story: Ana writes her first parser. She splits each line with `.before(":")` and pushes the pieces into a list. The compiler stops her, tells her to sprinkle `~` on every push, and she does it without understanding why. Her file now has eleven sigils that all mean 'the compiler made me'.

options.name: Language semantic plus visibility ladder
options.detail: Storing a read-only view stores a copy. That is what the construct means, on every tier, with nothing injected into the file. Experts climb rungs. `jet audit copies` lists each copy with its size. The editor can show ghost `~` hints. `jet fmt --explicit-copies` writes real sigils on request. `policy: .{ copies: .Explicit }` in package.jet restores the error project-wide. Gain: the most common memory error stops existing and behavior stays fully predictable. Loss: a reader of plain source does not see the copy until they ask a tool.
options.technical: Amends D-MEM-VIEWRET1 boundary behavior: a read-view store lowers to the same code as an explicit `~` store. E2307 retires for read views and stays for ViewMut. D-SHAPE-COPY1 is untouched: `~x` remains the only copy spelling; the semantic inserts no second spelling. The package policy key rides D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1 and only tightens. The compiler never edits user source; `jet fmt --explicit-copies` is the invited, deterministic materializer.
options.code:
cache :: [ha, hb]          // works: a store IS a copy

$ jet audit copies
cache.jet:6  `ha` stored into `cache` as a copy (5 bytes)

$ jet fmt --explicit-copies   // you invite the ink
cache.jet: 2 copies written as `~`

# package.jet — perf-strict projects refuse the magic
policy: .{ copies: .Explicit }

options.name: Compiler writes the sigil into your file
options.detail: On compile or format, the toolchain inserts a real `~` at every view store, so the file always shows every copy. Gain: plain source is always explicit. Loss: your diff grows characters you did not type, agents get edited out from under themselves, and `~` stops meaning 'the author chose this'. It also breaks the toolchain norm that no command modifies user source uninvited.
options.technical: Would need a mandatory format-on-build step and a rule for code the formatter cannot reach (generated sources, patches in review).

options.name: Keep the error
options.detail: E2307 stays as shipped. The user types `~` at every store. Gain: every copy is author-written and visible in plain source forever. Loss: the beginner's first parser still fails on the language's most common memory error, and the fix remains mechanical typing the compiler already knows.
options.technical: No change. Probe P04j documents today's behavior on both tiers.

comparisons.note: Stored borrows force lifetime parameters onto every enclosing type; most users call `.to_owned()` by hand — option C's world with more ceremony.
comparisons.code: struct Tok<'a> { s: &'a str }   // the annotation tax Jet avoids

comparisons.note: Substrings share the backing array silently: convenient like option A, but with no receipt, no refusal switch, and surprise retention of large buffers.
comparisons.code: tok := line[0:3]   // keeps all of `line` alive, invisibly

recommendation.why: The store keeps one meaning everywhere: it behaves exactly as if the user wrote `~`, because that is the defined semantic. Beginners never meet the error. Experts get a receipt, a manual spelling, and a project-wide refusal.

whyNot.reason: A build that rewrites source churns diffs and review, and a machine-inserted `~` no longer tells a reader the author chose that copy.
It keeps the most common memory error alive to demand typing the compiler already prints in its own fix text.

recommendation.tradeoff: Plain source hides small copies until a tool is asked. We accept this because the copies are cost-only facts with a ledger, and `policy: .{ copies: .Explicit }` restores full visibility where cost is the product.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the language semantic, source injection, and today's error, and recommended the semantic because it removes the error without changing any meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested copy-on-write strings, implicit gc promotion, and editor-only ghosts as full options. All three were folded away: copy-on-write hides cost worse than a ledger, the owner rejected silent gc at checkpoint, and ghosts alone need an IDE.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass moved the best part of option B into option A: `jet fmt --explicit-copies` gives B's always-explicit file to anyone who wants it, on request instead of by force.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened option C: its error text now names the store, the owner, and the exact fix, which is the strongest honest version of keeping the wall. It still fails the beginner on their first parser.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked hidden cost on hot paths and ViewMut ambiguity. The policy key restores the error for perf-strict projects and write-through views never copy silently, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Capability sigils across the FFI boundary
decisions.gist: Whether an expert can lend or give memory to foreign code without copying it.
decisions.lesson: Today every FFI crossing copies: E0702 bans `&` and `^` in extern signatures, and each side frees its own copy. That rule is a perfect beginner floor and kills cross-boundary double-frees by construction. But it is also the only tier: no lending, no ownership handoff, no way to hold a handle that C allocated. This choice decides what the expert tier looks like above that floor.
decisions.story: Mo embeds Jet in an audio engine. Every 100 MB sample buffer he passes to a C DSP routine is duplicated first, once per call, on the real-time thread. He reads the E0702 fix text, drops the sigil, and ships the copies because there is nothing else to type.

options.name: The same three sigils, checked across the border
options.detail: `&` lends for exactly one call: the foreign side may read, must not keep, and no copy happens. `^` gives ownership away: the foreign side owns and frees it, and the Jet name dies. `#Close(fn)` puts a returned foreign handle on Jet's `close(^)` protocol, so the foreign free runs exactly once or the program does not compile. Gain: zero new vocabulary and zero-copy crossings, with who-frees-what written in the signature. Loss: a foreign library can break a `&` promise it made; the blast radius is the declared extern block.
options.technical: Amends the D-FFI-UNIFY1 frame's by-value-only law. E0702 narrows from a ban to a gate: sigils are legal in extern signatures as an opt-in tier; the by-value floor stays the default and the beginner card is unchanged. `#Close` reuses the existing consuming-cleanup machinery (S63 opaque handle precedent from D-FFI-CPP1).

options.name: Keep by-value only; zero-copy lives behind #Unsafe
options.detail: One rule, no new surface: everything copies, and an expert who needs zero-copy builds raw-pointer plumbing inside an `#Unsafe` gate. Gain: the two-sentence FFI card stays the whole story. Loss: the hottest crossings in kernel, audio, and embedding either pay copies forever or hand-roll unchecked pointer protocols the compiler cannot audit as signatures.
options.technical: No change to E0702. Zero-copy paths use `*T` under D-CAP9 inside `#Unsafe` gates.

options.name: New transfer keywords instead of sigils
options.detail: Spell the tier with words: `loan`, `gift`, and `bind` as parameter markers in extern signatures only. Gain: the border reads like a contract document, and foreign-only words cannot be confused with local sigils. Loss: three new keywords that mean exactly what `&`, `^`, and `#Close` already mean, which breaks one-mechanism discipline and doubles what a reader must learn.
options.technical: New extern-only parameter grammar; sigils stay banned. Same checking machinery as option A under different spelling.

comparisons.note: Zero-copy FFI is spelled with raw pointers plus `unsafe` and a comment; ownership transfer is `Box::into_raw` discipline by convention.
`withUnsafeBufferPointer` scopes a loan to a closure — the loan idea, but as a library shape rather than a signature fact.

recommendation.why: The sigils already carry these exact meanings everywhere in Jet. The expert tier costs zero new vocabulary, and the contract lives in the signature where the checker and the reader both see it.

whyNot.reason: It sends every serious embedder into `#Unsafe` to hand-roll the same protocol without checking, which is more danger for less clarity.
Three new keywords restate what the sigils already say; two spellings for one meaning breaks the one-mechanism rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: A foreign library can violate a lend it accepted. We accept this because the violation is contained to the declared extern block, which is already the audited trust surface, and Decision G's fence can contain the library wholesale.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared sigils-across, by-value-only, and keyword verbs, and recommended sigils because the meanings already exist and the signature becomes the contract.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested callback support, a marshalling-annotation DSL, and per-library trust levels as options. Callbacks were scoped out as a follow-up decision; the DSL and trust levels folded into Decision G's fence rather than this spelling choice.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass merged option C's `bind` idea into option A as `#Close(fn)`, keeping the attribute shape Jet already uses instead of a new keyword.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened option B: with Decision F's sentries, hand-rolled unsafe crossings are at least watched in dev. It still leaves the contract in comments.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked lying foreign code and re-entrancy during a lend. Violations stay contained to the declared extern block, and D-MEM-GUARANTEE1's fence can seal a distrusted library, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: freeze and ^-captures for tasks
decisions.gist: How tasks receive data that is read-only, or handed over, instead of locked.
decisions.lesson: Shared<T> is today's only door to other tasks: a lock-guarded handle whose every read and write runs inside a closure. That is right for state that genuinely mutates concurrently. But read-only data pays a lock per read, and handing a batch to one worker has no spelling at all — a plain capture of a mutable local is rejected with E1101. This choice decides whether the two missing verbs exist.
decisions.story: Rae ships a renderer. Eight tasks read one asset table that never changes after load, and every name lookup acquires a lock. Her profiler shows contention on data that has no writer. She asks what the lock is protecting and the honest answer is: the absence of a word for 'this is immutable now'.

options.name: freeze for sharing, ^ for handoff, Shared for shared-mutable
options.detail: `freeze(x)` returns a deeply immutable value; bare captures of frozen values are legal because no race can exist, and writing to one is a compile error. `^x` in a capture gives the value to the task — the same meaning `^` has at every callsite — and the old name dies with the existing use-after-move error. Gain: the price of sharing is visible in the source, and locks remain only where mutation is real. Loss: two new facts to teach beside Shared.
options.technical: Extends D-TASKBORROW1: group children may capture frozen values bare and may consume owned values with `^`. E1101's fix menu gains both exits. `freeze` is a prefix verb like `close`; deep immutability is a type-level fact the prover already models for `::` bindings, extended to a runtime-constructed value. Shared and Cell are untouched.

options.name: Keep Shared and Cell as the only door
options.detail: No new verbs. All cross-task data crosses through lock-guarded closures. Gain: one tool to teach, no migration. Loss: read-only data pays a lock per read forever, and a handoff keeps meaning wrap-or-copy; the E1101 rejection stays correct but exitless.
options.technical: No change. Probes P09, P09c document today's behavior.
options.code:
counter :: Shared.new(Counter.{ hits: 0 })
counter.read(v => v.hits)   // even a read takes the lock

options.name: Compiler elides read locks instead of new verbs
options.detail: Keep the Shared surface and let the compiler skip the lock when it proves no writer exists after a point. Gain: existing code speeds up with no new words. Loss: performance now depends on an invisible proof. The same line gains or loses a lock when a distant write appears, which breaks the owner's predictability rule. The handoff case is not addressed at all.
options.technical: Whole-program freeze inference over Shared<T> values; no surface change; E1101 unchanged.
options.code:
assets :: Shared.new(load_assets())
a.read(v => v.names[id])   // maybe a lock, maybe not — depends on analysis elsewhere

comparisons.note: Arc<T> shares immutably without a lock, and moving into a thread is a closure capture — both verbs exist; Jet's version spells them with one function and its existing sigil.
Reference capabilities (`val`, `iso`) prove the same two facts in the type system, at the cost of a six-capability lattice Jet folds into two verbs.
comparisons.code: let a: Assets val = recover val load() end

recommendation.why: The rule becomes one teachable sentence — give it, freeze it, or lock it — the price of sharing is visible in the source, and data-race freedom stays a compile-time fact in all three.

whyNot.reason: It keeps charging a lock for data with no writer and leaves the handoff intent with no spelling.
It makes performance depend on an invisible whole-program proof, so the same line gets slower when distant code changes — unpredictable by construction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two new facts to teach beside Shared. We accept this because each is one sentence, and the compiler's capture error names which of the three the program needs.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the two new verbs, the status quo, and lock elision, and recommended the verbs because they make the sharing price visible and complete the capture story.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested channels-only messaging, region transfer from the blind design, and per-field freezing. Channels exist already and answer a different shape; region transfer folded into `^`-captures; per-field freezing was dropped as a second mechanism for one fact.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass checked whether elision (option C) could ride under option A as an optimizer detail. It can later, safely, because freeze makes the fact explicit first; the ballot keeps them separate so semantics never depend on analysis.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened option B with a documented pattern page for wrap-and-read. It remains a lock on read-only data.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked freeze-then-mutate, double-freeze, and `^`-capture teachability. Writing to frozen is a compile error naming the freeze site, and misuse after `^` hits the existing E0121, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Dev-tier sentries for #Unsafe gates
decisions.gist: Whether anything watches unsafe code at runtime while you develop.
decisions.lesson: An #Unsafe gate is audited at compile time: its reason is mandatory (E3112) and its raw operations carry named obligations that `jet inspect unsafe` reports. At runtime, nothing watches it — a bad index inside a gate is silent corruption, exactly as in C. Jet is uniquely placed to fix this because the default `jet run` already executes on the dev tier, where a watcher can live without touching release performance. This choice decides whether that watcher exists and when it is on.
decisions.story: Teo pastes a ring-buffer #Unsafe block from a forum into his first audio program. His index math is off by one. The program plays fine on his machine for a week, then corrupts a sample buffer on stage. The audit surface had approved the gate; nothing had ever watched a single run.

options.name: Sentries on by default in dev; release silent; hardened profile opts in
options.detail: Every default `jet run` guards raw operations inside #Unsafe gates: freed memory is quarantined and poisoned, and writes are bounds-checked against the gate's declared storage. A violation is a located runtime fault naming the gate, the obligation, and the fix. Each fault feeds the `jet audit memory` ledger, so `jet fix memory` can repair it statically. Release builds carry zero sentries; the hardened profile ships with them. Gain: beginners get a watched runtime for free and experts ship silence. Loss: dev-tier unsafe code runs slower, which can mask timing bugs.
options.technical: Extends D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1: obligations gain runtime discharge evidence on the dev tier. New R08xx runtime-fault report family, registered and snapshot-tested like every diagnostic (I4). I9 is preserved by construction: sentries observe, they never change meaning; all tiers run identical semantics. The hardened shipping profile is card #1888.
options.code:
$ jet run audio.jet
Runtime fault [R0801]: raw write outside `ring`'s storage
  --> audio.jet:4, in #Unsafe gate audio.jet:3
 Why: `p` points 8 bytes past the buffer the gate's reason names
 Fix: clamp `head` before the write — obligation `valid_ptr` was not met on this run

$ jet run --release audio.jet    # zero sentries, zero cost
$ jet build --profile=hardened   # ship WITH sentries (#1888)

options.name: Sentries exist but are opt-in even in dev
options.detail: The same machinery behind a flag: `jet run --guard`. Gain: dev runs behave identically to release by default, so timing differences never surprise an expert. Loss: the people the watcher protects most — beginners pasting unsafe code — never turn it on, because they do not know it exists.
options.technical: Same R08xx family and ledger integration; default off.
options.code:
$ jet run audio.jet            # naked, as today
$ jet run --guard audio.jet    # watched, on request

options.name: Compile-time audit only
options.detail: Today's behavior: reasons, obligations, and `jet inspect unsafe` stand alone. Gain: no runtime machinery anywhere, one fewer subsystem. Loss: between the audit and production, nothing observes a single run; the gap where unsafe bugs actually live stays dark.
options.technical: No change. Probes P07b and P07d document the shipped audit surface.
options.code:
$ jet inspect unsafe audio.jet
gate audio.jet:3  reason: "ring buffer owns its slots…"
  raw_write  required=[valid_ptr, aligned]  discharged=static
$ jet run audio.jet
(silent corruption — nothing watches the run)

comparisons.note: Debug builds carry safety checks that release drops — the same dev-watched shape, but for the whole language rather than scoped to declared unsafe gates.
comparisons.code: zig build -Doptimize=Debug   // checked; ReleaseFast strips it

comparisons.note: AddressSanitizer is the industry's bolt-on version: opt-in, whole-program, 2x cost, and reports raw addresses instead of gates and obligations.

recommendation.why: The dev tier already runs every default `jet run`, so the watcher costs release nothing and covers exactly the population that cannot debug corruption: beginners inside #Unsafe gates. Faults name the gate, the obligation, and the fix.

whyNot.reason: Default-off protects the experts who need it least and abandons the beginners it was built for.
It leaves the entire runtime lifetime of unsafe code unobserved — the exact gap where these bugs live.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dev runs of unsafe code are slower than release runs, which can hide timing-sensitive bugs until a release build. We accept this because `--release` is one flag away and the sentries never change what any tier computes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared default-on dev sentries, opt-in sentries, and audit-only, and recommended default-on because it watches the population that cannot self-protect at zero release cost.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested making raw pointers tracked fat pointers everywhere (the Fil-C shape). It was rejected as a default for cost and for changing what #Unsafe means per flag, and routed to D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 as the per-dependency fence.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass connected sentries to the scaffolding loop: faults write the same ledger `jet fix memory` drains, so a watched failure becomes a static repair instead of a report.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened option B with a first-run hint suggesting --guard when a file contains #Unsafe. It still relies on the user opting into their own protection.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked false faults on exotic pointer arithmetic and the dev/release timing gap. Sentries scope to the gate's declared storage and the timing gap is stated in the tradeoff, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: The memory-safety guarantee dial: contain and harden
decisions.gist: How a project turns 'this binary cannot corrupt memory' into a checkable fact.
decisions.lesson: Safe Jet is proven memory-safe by the compiler, with or without gc. The prover cannot vouch for exactly two things: your #Unsafe gates and foreign code. Today no switch states or checks a whole-binary safety claim that covers them. This choice decides where that claim lives. The owner ruled at checkpoint that it must not couple to gc. Coupling would make one library run fenced or naked depending on its caller's scope.
decisions.story: Priya ships a payments service that links a vendored XML parser from 2011. Security asks her one question: can anything in this binary corrupt memory? Today her honest answer is a shrug toward the vendor. She wants a switch that makes the answer yes, and a command that proves it.

options.name: Own dial: contain per dependency, harden per binary, inspect prints the truth
options.detail: Two policy keys in package.jet. `contain:` lists dependencies whose pointers become tracked handles inside a fence. A wild write there faults with a report instead of corrupting your heap, and only that dependency pays the 2-4x cost. `harden: true` keeps the dev sentries in release and contains every foreign dependency. `jet inspect guarantees` prints the per-component truth: proven, watched, fenced, or TRUSTED. Gain: one switch produces an honest, checkable whole-binary claim. Loss: two new policy keys to learn, and fenced dependencies pay real overhead.
options.technical: Extends D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1 with `contain` and `harden` keys; both only tighten, preserving the policy law. Fencing compiles the named dependency with tracked-handle pointers (the Fil-C shape) at its extern boundary — the same audited surface E0702 governs. R9 preserved: single files need no manifest; their guarantee line reads 'your code: proven; externs: trusted'. Freestanding targets report 'no runtime layer — prover plus audit only' instead of pretending.
options.code:
# package.jet                    (proposed keys, ratified policy shape)
policy: .{
    contain: ["libxml"],
    harden:  true,
}

$ jet inspect guarantees
your code            proven      compile time
#Unsafe gates (2)    watched     sentries (dev always; release via harden)
libxml (contained)   fenced      cannot corrupt your heap; 2-4x inside fence
libz                 TRUSTED     outside the guarantee — named, not hidden
verdict: contain libz to make this binary's no-corruption claim total

options.name: Couple containment to gc
options.detail: Foreign calls made from #Policy(gc) scopes run contained; gc off means no fence. Gain: one switch fewer, and 'gc on' reads as 'fully safe'. Loss: the same library runs fenced or naked depending on which scope calls it — one library, two meanings. Enabling gc for a cache silently makes FFI on that path 2–4x. And it implies non-gc Jet is unsafe, which is false: the prover guarantees safe Jet with gc off.
options.technical: Fence activation becomes a property of the calling scope's policy rather than the dependency; call-graph-dependent codegen for extern shims.
options.code:
#Policy(gc)
fn handle(req: Request) { xml.parse(req.body) }   // fenced here…
fn batch(path: String)  { xml.parse(read(path)) } // …naked here. Same library.

options.name: No containment; sentries and audits are the whole story
options.detail: Drop the fence. Dev sentries watch your #Unsafe gates, the extern boundary stays audited, and untrusted C stays untrusted. Gain: no new keys, no fence machinery. Loss: the vendored-C question keeps its shrug — there is no switch that makes the whole-binary claim true, and no command that states which components are outside it.
options.technical: No change beyond D-MEM-SENTRY1.
options.code:
# security asks: can this binary corrupt memory?
# answer: 'probably not?' — no switch, no report

comparisons.note: Proves the fence is real: memory-safe C via tracked capability pointers at 1.5–4x — the exact mechanism option A scopes to the dependencies you distrust instead of the whole program.
comparisons.code: fil-c compiles unmodified C, every pointer checked

comparisons.note: cargo-geiger counts unsafe in dependencies but nothing fences them; the guarantee stays social.
comparisons.code: cargo geiger   // a report, not a boundary

recommendation.why: It gives the owner's question one honest switch. With harden on and every dependency contained or proven, the binary cannot corrupt memory, and `jet inspect guarantees` names the components that claim rests on.

whyNot.reason: One library would run fenced or naked depending on its caller's scope — dual meaning — and an unrelated lifetime convenience would silently tax FFI.
It leaves the vendored-code question unanswerable: no switch produces the claim and no report names what is trusted.

recommendation.tradeoff: Contained dependencies pay 2–4x inside the fence. We accept this because the price is opt-in, per dependency, printed in the report, and paid only for code you chose not to trust.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the standalone dial, gc-coupling, and no containment, and recommended the dial because it decouples trust from lifetime management and makes the claim checkable.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested process isolation (sidecar workers), wasm-sandboxing dependencies, and CHERI-only hardening. Sidecars exist for the polyglot FFI tiers already; wasm sandboxing folded into the fence as a possible backend; CHERI is deploy-time hardening orthogonal to the policy surface.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass merged the inspect report into the dial as its mandatory receipt: a guarantee switch without a per-component truth table is a vibe, not a fact.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened option B with scope-lifted fencing (fence the library if ANY scope is gc) to remove dual meaning. That repairs consistency but still couples cost to an unrelated choice, and the owner's checkpoint ruling rejected the coupling.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked fence-boundary laundering and report staleness. Pointers crossing out of a fence are a checked error at the extern boundary and the report is computed per build, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Trust model for the community package channel
decisions.gist: How much checking a package must pass before the community channel serves it.
decisions.lesson: Jet's registry will accept packages from outside authors. Arch's user repository shipped malware twice: a hijacked download in 2018, and a remote-access trojan in July 2025 under a lookalike name. Telling users to read the install script stopped neither one. Jet's signing types exist, but live signature checks are not built yet (JP6B). This ballot picks the trust model before the channel opens; cards #1912 (names) and #1913 (liveness) supply two of the gates.
decisions.story: In July 2025, an Arch user installed `librewolf-fixed-bin` from the community repository. The name read like a repaired build of his browser. It was a remote-access trojan, and it ran for two days before removal. Jet's community channel will meet the same attacker on day one, so the owner picks the trust model now.
decisions.inWild:
# A new Jet user needs a QR library for an invoice app.
$ jet add qrcode
# The index offers three candidates:
#   qrcode        1.4.2   signed - 40k installs
#   qrcode-fast   0.9.1   signed - 210 installs
#   qr-code       1.4.3   unsigned - published yesterday
# Which of these may exist at all, and what each one had to
# pass before appearing here, is what this ballot decides.

options.name: Reviewed-only channel
options.detail: A human reviews every publish before anyone can install it. Users get the strongest trust story, and the loudest video comments asked for exactly this. The cost is a queue: every release waits for a reviewer, and a small reviewer pool becomes the growth limit. Review quality also decays; Arch's history shows curation staff rot into orphans and rubber stamps.
options.technical: Machine gates still run first: live signatures (E1246/E1247), fail-closed audit (#431), and the name policy (#1912). A publish then enters a pending state; approval is a signed entry in the transparency log (D-JPK-REGISTRY1=D). E2610 is a placeholder code; the final number lands with implementation.
options.code:
$ jet registry publish
  packed qrcode 1.4.2 (sha256 9f2c...) - signed (key jrk1q...)
  gates: signature ok - audit ok - name ok
  submitted for review: queue position 14, median wait 6 days
  track: jet registry status qrcode@1.4.2

# a consumer, before approval:
$ jet add qrcode@1.4.2
Error [E2610]: `qrcode 1.4.2` is awaiting review and cannot be installed
 Why: this channel serves human-reviewed releases only
 Fix: install the last reviewed release: jet add qrcode@1.4.1

options.name: Open channel behind mandatory machine gates
options.detail: Anyone publishes, and the registry blocks a release unless it passes every machine gate: live author signature, fail-closed advisory audit, name policy, and maintainer-liveness rules. A clean publish is live in minutes, so the ecosystem grows at full speed. The loss is what the gates cannot see: a brand-new trojan, self-signed under a plausible name, passes every one. No human ever looks, and users who asked for curation do not get it.
options.technical: Gates: JP6B signature verification live (E1246/E1247), a server-side `jet inspect audit` that fails closed with no advisory database (#431), edit-distance and reserved-suffix name checks (#1912), and liveness rules (#1913). Transport and log stay per D-JPK-REGISTRY1=D. E2608 is a placeholder code; the final number lands with #1912.
options.code:
$ jet registry publish
  packed qrcode-fixed-bin 1.0.0 (sha256 44aa...) - signed (key jrk1x...)
Error [E2608]: name `qrcode-fixed-bin` is rejected by the registry name policy
 Why: the suffix `-fixed-bin` is reserved; the name imitates a repaired
      build of the existing package `qrcode`
 Fix: publish under a distinct name, or send the `qrcode` maintainer a patch

# a clean publish, minutes later:
$ jet registry publish
  packed qrsuite 1.0.0 (sha256 71bd...) - signed (key jrk1x...)
  gates: signature ok - audit ok - name ok - maintainer ok
  published qrsuite 1.0.0 - live (transparency log #88231)

options.name: Two labeled tiers: curated core, gated community
options.detail: One registry, two labeled tiers. The core tier is a small set with human review on top of every machine gate. The community tier is open to anyone behind the same machine gates, and its label says so at install time. Beginners get a safe default, and the ecosystem still grows. The loss: users must learn two trust levels, and core needs a standing reviewer group that the liveness rules must keep alive.
options.technical: One publish path; the tier is a registry property. Core promotion is a signed review entry in the transparency log (D-JPK-REGISTRY1=D). A workspace can pin `tier: core` in the `policy:` namespace (D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1=D). E2609 is a placeholder code. No tier opens before the machine gates are live.
options.code:
$ jet add qrcode
  added qrcode 1.4.2  [core - reviewed - signed]

$ jet add leftpadx
  added leftpadx 0.3.0  [community - machine-gated - signed]
  note: community tier has no human review; see jet inspect info leftpadx

# a workspace whose policy: block forbids the community tier:
$ jet fetch
Error [E2609]: `leftpadx 0.3.0` is community-tier, but policy requires `tier: core`
 Fix: remove the dependency, or add a scoped exception in policy:
      (id, exact package edge, reason, expiry)

options.name: No community channel in v1
options.detail: The registry serves first-party packages only, and the owner revisits the choice after the gates ship. Third-party code arrives through direct source roots pinned by hash, which the lockfile already guards. The gain is zero new attack surface while signatures are unbuilt. The loss is real: no shared names, no discovery, no advisories, no yank. Users trade the registry for raw repository links, which is the same attacker with less metadata.
options.technical: Direct roots and locks already ship (D-JPK-PROVIDERS2=D; E1204 hash checks, E2604 integrity). The git spelling shown is illustrative; the exact root form follows D-JPK-PROVIDERS2. E2611 is a placeholder code.
options.code:
$ jet registry publish
Error [E2611]: this registry does not accept third-party packages yet
 Why: the community channel is deferred until signature verification is live
 Fix: share the repository link; consumers pin it by revision:
   deps: { qrcode: "github.com/mara/qrcode#rev=9f2c1a7" }

# the consumer side still verifies hashes on every fetch:
$ jet fetch
  fetched qrcode (rev 9f2c1a7) - hash ok - locked in .jet/lock

comparisons.note: Fully open and unreviewed: no signatures, no name policy. It shipped a hijacked package in 2018 and a remote-access trojan in July 2025. The advice to read the build script failed in practice; the trojan was caught after install.
comparisons.code:
$ yay -S librewolf-fixed-bin   # lookalike name, unreviewed
# installs a remote-access trojan; detected post-install via /tmp payload

comparisons.note: Open publish with first-come names and no human review. Signing and audit are optional extras, not publish gates, so known-bad releases still land.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo publish   # live in seconds; no review, no signature gate
$ cargo audit     # optional extra tool; many projects never run it

comparisons.note: Reviewed-only: every new package waits in the NEW queue for a human. Trust is high and incidents are rare, but intake is slow and reviewer capacity is the hard limit.
comparisons.code:
# a new package waits days to months in the NEW queue
# https://ftp-master.debian.org/new.html

comparisons.note: A labeled two-tier design. Official repositories are reviewed; COPR is a clearly separate user tier that a user must enable by hand, with a warning that names the risk.
comparisons.code:
$ dnf copr enable alice/qrtools
# warning: COPR is not reviewed by Fedora; use packages at your own risk

recommendation.why: The tier model gives beginners one safe default and keeps the channel open. Every install line names the exact trust level, so the registry never claims more checking than it did. That inverts the failure behind the Arch incidents. The machine gates stay mandatory in both tiers, and no tier opens before they are live.

whyNot.reason: A human queue on every publish makes the reviewer pool the growth limit of a young ecosystem, and Arch's orphan history shows curation staff decay into rubber stamps.
The loudest comment strata said they would not use an uncurated repository. A fresh, self-signed trojan under a clean name passes every machine gate, and nothing tells the user that no human looked.
Closing the channel pushes third-party code to raw repository links: the same attacker with less metadata, no advisories, no yank, and no name policy at all.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two labeled trust levels are more to learn than one, and the core tier needs a standing reviewer group kept honest by the liveness rules (#1913). That is accepted because the label is truthful and the beginner default is safe.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reviewed-only, open-with-gates, and a labeled two-tier registry, and recommended the tier model because it keeps a safe default without closing the channel.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added a real fourth option: no community channel in v1, with third-party code through hash-pinned source roots. Publish deposits and web-of-trust vouching were folded into the gate option as tactics, not separate designs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved one rule into every open option: no channel accepts a publish until live signatures, fail-closed audit, and the name policy exist. It also put the tier label into the install output itself, not only on package pages.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave reviewed-only a queue target and signed review receipts, and gave open-with-gates an explicit machine-gated label so it never implies human review. It credited the v1-closed option with the hash-locked source roots that already ship.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the tier model with reviewer rot, label blindness, and a poisoned core package. Liveness rules (#1913), the tier line in every `jet add` output, and signed review receipts in the transparency log repair all three, so the tier model stands.

decisions.title: Jet as an embeddable engine for foreign hosts
decisions.gist: How a C, Python, or Rust program embeds and calls Jet code.
decisions.lesson: Lua's whole niche is embedding. A host program creates a fresh Lua state that can do nothing, then registers a few narrow, validated functions. Jet ships only the reverse direction: a Jet host loads sandboxed WebAssembly (WASM) plugins with zero capabilities (E1258). No spec text says how a foreign host embeds Jet. This choice picks Jet's embedding story, or records that it has none.
decisions.story: Mara runs a Python risk system at a brokerage. Operators need a small command language that can halt a bad order but can never touch the network or disk. Lua is the default answer for this job: a Lua state starts empty, and the host adds three checked functions. Mara would rather write the rules in Jet, with real types and tests. Today no document tells her how a Python process can call Jet at all.
decisions.inWild:
# risk_host.py — what Mara wants to write
engine = jet.load("guards.wasm")            # sandboxed: no file, net, or clock
verdict = engine.call("max_order", qty, price)
if verdict == 0:
    reject(order)

# what she writes today instead (Lua, sandbox by convention)
lua = LuaRuntime(register_eval=False)        # hope this closed every door
lua.globals().halt = halt_checked            # one leaked global undoes it

options.name: libjet: a C-ABI engine library
options.detail: Ship a linkable library that any C, Python, or Rust host calls. The host creates a state, registers narrow functions, and loads Jet source at run time. This is Lua's exact model: rules reload without a rebuild, and every language with C bindings can use it. The loss is safety by convention: every registered pointer and every crossing value is checked only by host discipline. That is the exact weakness Jet's plugin sandbox exists to remove. It also puts a second embedding mechanism beside the component substrate.
options.technical: libjet packages the interpreter tier; I9 keeps its meaning identical to AOT. New C surface: jet_new/jet_register/jet_call_float, state lifetime, error strings, and memory ownership at the edge. D-LIB-REUSE1=B refuses a stable Jet ABI; the C convention at the edge is allowed, but the engine API itself becomes a frozen public contract.

options.name: WASM component: one artifact, both directions
options.detail: Commit that the plugin artifact is also the embedding artifact. `jet build --target=plugin` already makes a standard WASM Component; this option documents and tests that a C or Python host loads that same file with an off-the-shelf runtime. The sandbox holds by construction: the component imports nothing (E1258), so the host gets Lua's empty state as compile-time law, not discipline. The loss: exports stay Int/Float until #1906 widens them, calls pay WASM overhead, and the host must ship a component runtime.
options.technical: Artifact: D-PLUGIN1=B component, WIT world `jetplugin`, built through `rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` plus `wasm-tools` (D-DEP-WASM1=A). Interface frozen by `Sema::ApiFreeze` (E1257 on breaking change). Deliverable: host-side golden tests (C via the wasmtime C API, Python via wasmtime-py) and one spec section. Host-provided imports (Lua-style host capabilities) need a fresh decision; E1258/I1 make zero imports the law today.
options.code:
$ jet build guards/ --target=plugin
  built target/guards.wasm              # a standard WASM Component

# risk_host.py — any language with a Component Model runtime
from wasmtime.component import Component, Linker, Store
store = Store()
guards = Component.from_file(store.engine, "target/guards.wasm")
inst = Linker(store.engine).instantiate(store, guards)  # zero imports: empty state
print(inst.call(store, "max-order", 500, 101.25))       # 0 -> reject the order

# the sandbox is compile-time law, not host discipline:
$ jet build guards/ --target=plugin     # if guards.jet tried to read a file
error[E1258]: a plugin can't use any effect

options.name: Native library export only (already ratified, unbuilt)
options.detail: Declare the ratified native export (D-LIB-EXPORT1=C) Jet's whole embedding answer. `jet build` emits a static and shared library, a C header, and named language bindings; the host calls Jet at native speed with no extra runtime. The gain is speed and one artifact per platform. The loss is the niche itself: there is no sandbox, so the host must trust the Jet code like its own. Logic is fixed at build time; operators cannot load new rules while the system runs.
options.technical: Exported surface: the entry module's `pub` items, frozen by `Sema::ApiFreeze`; the C calling convention at the edge, no stable Jet ABI (D-LIB-REUSE1=B). The loadable `.jetlib` path (D-LIB-DYNTRUST1=A) is Jet-host-only and compiler-identity pinned, so it cannot serve a foreign host.

options.name: Explicit v1 non-goal
options.detail: Write one spec paragraph: embedding Jet in a foreign host is out of scope for v1, revisit when a named user asks. The gain is zero new promises while the plugin substrate and #1906 settle. The loss is the evidence itself: embedding is Lua's whole adoption niche, and hosts that need it will pick Lua now and not return. The stopgap for trusted code is the ratified native export once it is built.
options.technical: Spec text lands next to the plugin section (docs/spec/spec.md) and names the two ratified neighbours: D-PLUGIN1=B for Jet-as-host and D-LIB-EXPORT1=C for trusted native export. A later request reopens this as a fresh decision; nothing here forecloses option A or B.
options.code:
docs/spec/spec.md — recorded text:

  Embedding Jet in a foreign host program is a non-goal for v1.
  Jet-as-host loads sandboxed plugins (D-PLUGIN1=B, E1258).
  A host that trusts its Jet code can wait for the ratified
  native export (D-LIB-EXPORT1=C, unbuilt). A request from a
  named user reopens this decision.

options.name: Both targets of one export surface
options.detail: Jet keeps one typed export surface and lowers it to two artifacts. A native C-ABI library serves embedded, kernel, and performance-critical C and C++ hosts that cannot carry a separate runtime. A WASM component serves hosts that want the sandbox. The developer picks a build target, not a different language surface. The loss is two artifact pipelines to keep at parity.
options.technical: One #Export surface (D-LIB-EXPORT1=C) with two lowerings: `jet build --lib` emits a .so/.a plus a generated C header; `jet build --target=component` emits a wasm component. Same export list, same type-lowering table, one Prelude implementation per I9. Sandbox guarantees exist only on the component artifact and the docs say so plainly.

comparisons.note: The canonical embedded engine. A fresh state exposes nothing; the host registers validated C functions. Production uses include a sandboxed command line inside a financial system and a hardware fan-speed gate. Its safety is host discipline: one forgotten global reopens the door.
The bar for option A: one C-ABI artifact that every language binds, with a decades-stable API. Anything called libjet gets measured against this standard of edge discipline.
comparisons.code:
sqlite3 *db;
sqlite3_open(":memory:", &db);   /* one library, every host language */

comparisons.note: The component route in the wild: compile logic to one .wasm file, then load it from Python, Go, C, or the browser with a stock runtime. Sandbox by construction, capabilities only where the host grants them.

recommendation.why: One export surface reaching both worlds serves the whole mission. Jet replaces low-level languages only if a C or C++ system can link it with no extra runtime. Sandbox-first hosts still get the component artifact, and the developer learns one surface and picks a target.

whyNot.reason: A C-ABI engine alone abandons hosts that want sandboxed, hot-reloadable guest code.
A component alone locks out kernels, embedded targets, and performance-critical C and C++ systems that cannot ship a wasm runtime.
The ratified native export gives no embedding story for sandboxed hosts and leaves the component ABI single-purpose.
A non-goal cedes the embedding niche entirely while the mission targets exactly those systems.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two artifact pipelines must stay at parity from one export surface. That is accepted: the owner rules that playing well with performance-critical C and C++ systems is not optional.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a C-ABI engine, component embedding, native export, and a recorded non-goal. It recommended component embedding because there the sandbox is law, not host discipline.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a source-interpreting engine crate, `.jetlib` loading for foreign hosts, and a subprocess pipe protocol. All three folded in: option A owns source loading, D-LIB-DYNTRUST1=A makes `.jetlib` Jet-host-only, and the pipe stopgap joined the non-goal option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed option B is two-sided: the same artifact, WIT world, and interface freeze serve Jet-as-host (`core.plugin`) and Jet-as-guest, and #1906 widening pays both directions at once. The option text now states this.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review held option A to SQLite's single-artifact standard and gave option C its honest strength: trusted code at native speed under ratified law. Option D gained a stopgap pointer to the native export.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked host runtime weight, Int/Float-only exports, and the missing host-capability story. The tradeoff now names the first two, and host-provided imports are marked as a fresh future decision, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: wasm32-wasi as a user-facing server target
decisions.gist: Whether `jet build` gains a server-side WebAssembly target.
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly (wasm) is a portable binary format. WASI is the system interface that lets a wasm program run outside a browser. Some hosting platforms run only wasm, because it starts fast and the host can sandbox it. Today `jet build --target=wasm32-wasip1` fails with E3302, because Jet ships no standard library for that target. Jet's browser target (`--target=web`) is separate and stays. This choice decides whether Jet promises a server wasm target, records a no, or routes wasm work through plugins.
decisions.story: Priya runs a platform team. Her company hosts tenant code on a wasmtime fleet, where every handler is one wasm module. She likes Jet and wants tenants to write handlers in it. She copies the build command from her platform docs and gets E3302. She must now tell her tenants whether Jet will ever build for this platform.
decisions.inWild:
# Priya follows her platform's docs:
$ jet build handler.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Why: rustc doesn't have the standard library for this target compiled in, or the target triple is not recognised.
 Fix: Run `jet self doctor --target=wasm32-wasip1` to see what's missing, or `rustup target add wasm32-wasip1` to install it.

# She retries with a space instead of `=` (open defect, card #1899):
$ jet build handler.jet --target wasm32-wasip1
built: build/handler        # native binary — the flag was silently ignored

# Her wasm host then rejects build/handler: not a wasm module.

options.name: Full supported server target (wasm32-wasip2)
options.detail: Jet ships wasm32-wasip2 as a real server target: stdlib port, CI lane, and full tier parity (I9). Preview 2 carries wasi-sockets, so a Jet server can actually listen and serve, which preview 1 could not. The gain is every platform that deploys wasm server-side becomes a Jet platform. The cost is a stdlib port and a permanent CI lane, paid up front.
options.technical: Target triple wasm32-wasip2; sockets via wasi-sockets, filesystem via wasi-filesystem, entropy rides the existing CryptoEntropy wasi shims. E3302 retires for this triple. The example matrix and golden corpus gain a wasip2 column per I5/I9; no carve-out.
options.code:
$ jet build server.jet --target=wasm32-wasip2
built: build/server.wasm
$ wasmtime serve build/server.wasm
listening on 0.0.0.0:8080

options.name: Recorded non-goal for v1.x
options.detail: Jet says no, in writing. Native binaries are Jet's server story; a container wraps them when a platform needs isolation. The build error for wasi triples then names this decision, so nobody waits for a port that will not come. Gain: one server path, the whole standard library everywhere Jet claims to run, and no I9 carve-out. Loss: teams on wasm-only platforms cannot deploy Jet there in v1.x. The record names a revisit trigger: WASI preview 2 sockets settle and real user demand appears.
options.technical: No new target. The decision record lists the revisit trigger. E3302 gains a triple-specific message for `wasm32-wasi*` that cites D-WASISRV1 instead of suggesting `rustup target add`, which would mislead here. Card #1899 (space-form `--target` silently ignored) is fixed separately; a recorded no makes the correct rejection reachable by both spellings.
options.code:
# Today the error suggests installing a target Jet cannot use:
$ jet build server.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Fix: Run `jet self doctor --target=wasm32-wasip1` to see what's missing, or `rustup target add wasm32-wasip1` to install it.

# After this option ships, the same command names the decision:
$ jet build server.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Why: server-side WebAssembly is a recorded non-goal for v1.x (D-WASISRV1). Jet servers ship as native binaries.
 Fix: build a native binary with `jet build server.jet`, or package it in a container for your platform.

options.name: WASI only through the plugin surface
options.detail: Jet keeps sandboxed wasm where it already exists: `target: plugin` packages, which build as WASM Components and run fully sandboxed. A native Jet server loads tenant plugins and calls them. Gain: the sandbox case is served today, with a hard capability boundary — plugins are deny-by-default with zero host capabilities (E1258). Loss: a plugin cannot open a socket or read a file, so it can never be a server by itself. Platforms that want one wasm module per service still get nothing.
options.technical: No new target. Plugins compile via `rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` plus `wasm-tools component` (E1259) and export all-`Int` or all-`Float` functions in v1 (E1260). E1258 and I1 forbid widening plugin capabilities, so this option cannot grow into a server story later without a new decision.
options.code:
# jetpack.toml of the sandboxed part:
[package]
name = "scorer"
target = "plugin"

$ jet build
built: build/scorer.wasm      # WASM Component, zero host capabilities

# A native Jet server embeds it:
plugin := Plugin.load("build/scorer.wasm")
result := plugin.call("score", [42])

# A plugin that touches the OS does not build:
Error E1258: A plugin can't use any effect.

options.name: Preview target under an I9 carve-out
options.detail: Jet ships the target now, marked preview, with an owner-ratified I9 carve-out that lists what is missing. A program that avoids the missing parts builds and runs today. Gain: early adopters and wasm platforms get a real artifact now, and the port grows in public. Loss: a beginner's program passes the toolchain, then stops at the first `core.net` call. Carve-out lists also grow stale, and recent tier drift (the `#Todo` AOT defect) shows how such gaps leak raw internals to users.
options.technical: The carve-out names the excluded modules (`core.net`, `core.exec`, threads) and the diagnostic that rejects them at compile time, in the E3301 style. CI runs the supported subset under wasmtime. The carve-out expires when WASI preview 2 sockets land or the owner renews it.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
warning: wasm32-wasip1 is a preview target (D-WASISRV1 carve-out): core.net, core.exec, and threads are unavailable
built: build/tool.wasm
$ wasmtime run --dir=. build/tool.wasm
processed 3 files

# The first socket call is a compile-time stop:
$ jet build httpd.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error: `net.listen` is not available in a wasm32-wasip1 build (preview carve-out D-WASISRV1).
 Fix: build a native binary with `jet build httpd.jet`, or keep this program off `core.net`.

comparisons.note: Go 1.21 shipped `GOOS=wasip1` as a port, not a first-class target. `net.Listen` fails at run time because WASI preview 1 has no sockets. Server use never arrived; the port serves plugins and scripts.
comparisons.code:
$ GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o main.wasm .
$ wasmtime run main.wasm
panic: listen tcp :8080: operation not permitted

comparisons.note: Rust keeps `wasm32-wasip1` at tier 2. The standard library compiles, but sockets and threads return errors at run time. Real servers on wasm use host worlds such as `wasi:http` instead of the target's own stdlib.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build --target wasm32-wasip1   # builds
// std::net::TcpListener::bind(...) -> Err(Unsupported) at run time

comparisons.note: Wasm platforms answer the socket gap by owning the socket in the host: `wasmtime serve` speaks the `wasi:http` proxy world and hands the program one request at a time. Any future Jet server target would take this shape, not a ported `core.net`.
comparisons.code:
$ wasmtime serve app.wasm
Serving HTTP on http://0.0.0.0:8080/

recommendation.why: A full wasip2 target serves users where they already deploy instead of telling them Jet does not go there. The sockets objection dissolves at preview 2, and the owner accepts the up-front stdlib and CI cost for user benefit.

whyNot.reason: A recorded non-goal cuts out every team whose platform is wasm-first, for no user-facing gain.
Plugin-only WASI serves embedding, not deployment; a server team cannot ship its whole program as someone else's plugin.
A preview target under an I9 carve-out ships two meanings of the same program, which is the drift I9 exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: A permanent stdlib port and CI lane for one more target. Accepted by owner direction: more work up front for the benefit of users.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a full standard-library port, a recorded non-goal, and a plugins-only route. It recommended the non-goal because WASI preview 1 cannot carry Jet's server standard library.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the preview target under an I9 carve-out as a fourth option. A separate 'export a component from any package' variant folded into the plugin option, because both are host-embedded wasm.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the improved E3302 message into the non-goal option, so a no still teaches. The error now names the decision, the native path, and stops suggesting `rustup target add`.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the full target with the `wasi:http` host-world shape and the existing `CryptoEntropy` shim. It gave the preview option an explicit carve-out list with an expiry rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the non-goal with the serverless cold-start case and the polyglot-host case. The plugin surface, the container path, and the recorded revisit trigger absorb both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How Jet enforces the panic law in libraries
decisions.gist: How the compiler makes libraries follow the panic law.
decisions.lesson: Stdlib law L2 says a function returns `T ? E` for expected failure and panics only for programmer error. Today nothing checks this. A library can stop the whole program on bad input, and no surface reports it. Jet's own examples corpus holds 842 `panic(` calls, and flagship serde examples model `?? panic("bad json")`. Rust tried opt-in lint walls, and unwraps still spread through README examples. This ballot picks the one route that enforces the law.
decisions.story: Priya maintains confkit, a small config library that other teams embed. Her parse_port stops the process on a bad value. An on-call engineer's service dies at 3am because one environment variable held "abc". Priya wants the compiler to tell her, before release, which of her functions can stop someone else's program.

options.name: Function-level #NoPanic proof marker
options.detail: You mark a function #NoPanic. The compiler then proves that the body and every reachable callee cannot stop. A panic call, an unproven trap, or an unmarked callee is a compile error. The gain is a caller-visible guarantee on exactly the functions that promise it. The loss is a second wall mechanism: Jet already has the =[!E]=> prohibition arrow for "this call graph never does X", so a new marker adds a parallel spelling.
options.technical: A new attribute plane beside #Pre and #Post. Obligations: no reachable panic, #Todo, require, or unproven E30xx trap site. Refinement facts (#1549) and #Pre facts discharge obligations under D-FAIL-TIER1 proof-keyed erasure. A callee needs the marker, or the checker reproves its whole body. The proposed diagnostic code E0755 is new.

options.name: Refinements only, no new wall
options.detail: No new surface. Refinement types such as Int(0..100) (#1549, ready) prove panic sites away where authors adopt them. Bounds and range facts move into signatures, trap checks erase, and runtime values convert fallibly. The gain is safer signatures with no annotation ceremony, and faster code where proofs land. The loss is that nothing obliges a library to adopt them. A panic on expected failure still compiles silently, so law L2 stays an honor system.
options.technical: Rides #1549 (D-TYPE2-SPELL1) and D-FAIL-TIER1 unchanged: a range proof removes a check, the unproven case keeps it.
