Enforcement pressure comes only from the L2 review rubric in docs/spec/stdlib-api-laws.md, which reviews stdlib additions but never third-party or example code. jet prove --lens refinements already grades the evidence.

options.name: jet check policy wall with a panic budget
options.detail: A package sets a panic budget in package.jet, and jet check fails the build when the count of panic sites grows. This generalizes the shrink-only continuous-integration gate proposed for the examples corpus (#1903) to any package. The gain is a wall that covers a whole corpus at once and is easy to read. The loss is that a count cannot tell a legal programmer-error panic from an illegal expected-failure panic. The wall also lives beside the compiler, the exact place where Rust's clippy walls decayed.
options.technical: Extends the D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1 policy: namespace, next to lints: { deny: [...] } and effect budgets. Host and org policy narrows, never widens. The count is syntactic: explicit panic( sites per package, budget shrink-only in continuous integration. Trap sites, #Todo, and require are not counted, so the wall misses implicit stops entirely.

options.name: Panic joins the effect tree as a deniable row
options.detail: Panic becomes a row that the shipped prohibition arrow and the manifest deny list already know how to enforce. A signature writes =[!Panic]=>. A package writes effects: { deny: [Panic] } in package.jet, and E1220 already names a panicking dependency. The compiler proves that denied scopes cannot stop: expected failure must become T ? E, and programmer-error stops must move behind #Pre or refinement facts that callers prove. One mechanism covers one function, a whole package, and its dependency graph.
options.technical: Reuses D-PROP1/D-PROP2 (=[!E]=>, E0749) and the D-AUTHORITY-MEM1=B denial precedent (deny: [Mem.Alloc]). Adds one denial-only row and amends the D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 closed table by this ballot. Discharge: refinement proofs (#1549) and #Pre facts under D-FAIL-TIER1 proof-keyed erasure; jet prove --lens refinements shows the evidence. A #Pre on a denied function transfers the stop obligation to callers: a denied caller must prove it, an undenied caller keeps the runtime check at the call site (D-FAIL-TIER1 blame rule).

comparisons.note: The no_panic crate enforces panic freedom with a linker trick, outside the type system. Clippy's unwrap_used wall is off by default, and the Don't Panic video shows unwraps spreading through README examples anyway.
comparisons.code:
# clippy.toml walls are off by default; the video's own errata corrected this
# [lints.clippy]
# unwrap_used = "deny"        # opt-in, per crate, decays

#[no_panic]                    // third-party crate; enforced by a linker trick
fn parse_port(raw: &str) -> u16 { raw.parse().unwrap() }

comparisons.note: SPARK mode proves absence of runtime errors for marked units. Obligations come from contracts, and the prover erases checks. This is the discharge model option D borrows.
Error unions !T force callers to handle expected failure, which matches T ? E. But @panic and unreachable compile anywhere, and nothing proves a call graph panic-free.

recommendation.why: Denial rides surfaces Jet already ratified: the =[!E]=> prohibition arrow, the manifest deny list, and proof-keyed erasure. One spelling scales from one function to a package to its dependency graph. Enforcement is at compile time, so denied code pays nothing at runtime and often runs faster, because proved checks erase. And it enforces exactly law L2: expected failure is forced into T ? E, while programmer-error stops stay legal behind contracts that callers prove.

whyNot.reason: It gives the same guarantee as option D but mints a second wall mechanism beside the shipped =[!E]=> arrow. Two spellings for "this call graph never does X" breaks I8.
Proofs without an obligation enforce nothing. A library that panics on bad input still compiles silently, so law L2 stays an honor system. That is the failure Rust already demonstrated.
A count cannot tell a legal programmer-error panic from an illegal expected-failure panic, so it blocks the wrong sites and excuses implicit traps. Walls outside the compiler decay, as clippy's did.

recommendation.tradeoff: Denial is only as strong as the prover. Some code that never stops in practice cannot be admitted yet, and it must return T ? E, add facts, or stay undenied. We accept this because that escape shape is the shape law L2 prefers anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a #NoPanic marker, a refinements-only route, and a jet check budget wall. It recommended the marker for its caller-visible, per-function guarantee.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review searched the ratified record and found the shipped prohibition arrow =[!Net]=> (D-PROP1) and the manifest denial precedent deny: [Mem.Alloc] (D-AUTHORITY-MEM1=B). It added option D, which spells the same guarantee in those existing surfaces.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review folded the marker's function guarantee, the budget wall's package scope, and the refinement proofs into option D: one denial row, discharged by proofs. The recommendation moved from A to D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each loser on its own terms. Option B gained the L2 review rubric as an adoption path, option C gained the shrink-only budget #1903 needs anyway, and option A gained whole-call-graph checking with #Pre discharge.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked D where the prover is too weak: denied code that never stops in practice may not compile. The repair names three exits (return a fallible result, add facts, stay undenied) and records the D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 amendment by name, so D survives.

decisions.title: In-toolchain exercise runner (`jet learn`)
decisions.gist: Whether the Jet toolchain ships a built-in exercise runner for new users.
decisions.lesson: New users learn a language by writing small programs and reading the errors. Rust learners needed three outside resources plus a mentor to pass the first wall. The tool they loved, rustlings, runs failing exercises in a watch loop with a hint command. It lives outside the toolchain, so its hints drift from the installed compiler. Jet already ships teaching diagnostics (I4), `jet explain`, and a `jet dev` watch loop that reruns in 42 milliseconds. This ballot decides where a person's first hours with Jet live.
decisions.story: Priya is a Python developer who installs Jet on a train with no network. `jet new` gives her a project and one next-step line. Ten minutes later she hits her first ownership error. She wants a guided next exercise, not a search engine. What Jet answers here shapes her whole first day.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet new pricing-tool
Created pricing-tool. Next: cd pricing-tool && jet run src/main.jet

$ jet run src/main.jet
Hello from Jet!

## Ten minutes later, her first real edit hits the wall:
error[E0120]: `name` was not moved here, so it cannot be returned as-is
  fix: return a copy: `return ~name;` — or take ownership with `name: ^String`

$ jet explain E0120     ## explains this one error, well
## ...but nothing suggests what to learn or try next.
## She opens a browser tab to search. The train has no network.

options.name: `jet learn` — exercise runner in the toolchain
options.detail: The toolchain ships a short exercise track. `jet learn` opens the next failing exercise inside the `jet dev` watch loop. The user edits, saves, and sees the real compiler error in about 42 milliseconds. `jet learn hint` gives exercise context and points at `jet explain` for the live diagnostic. Exercises install with the compiler, so hints never drift from the errors. Gain: one offline path from install to competence. Loss: the toolchain carries a curriculum, and every language change must keep it current.
options.technical: One new CLI verb plus an exercise set versioned with the toolchain. The runner reuses the `jet dev` watcher and rerun engine; no second watch mechanism (I8). Hints hold exercise context only; error explanations stay in the I4 registry behind `jet explain`. Exercises run on the default tier and under `--release`, so the track respects I9 tier parity. Each exercise names its matching docs chapter, so prose depth stays on the site while the loop stays local. In CI the exercise suite doubles as end-to-end coverage of the teaching diagnostics.
options.code:
$ jet learn
Jet track: 24 exercises. Opening 01_values/give_back.jet.
watching give_back.jet — edit and save; results show here.

error[E0120]: `name` was not moved here, so it cannot be returned as-is
  fix: return a copy: `return ~name;` — or take ownership
       with `name: ^String`

$ jet learn hint
This exercise is about ownership markers.
`~` returns a copy. `^` takes the value itself.
Full explanation: jet explain E0120

## She writes `return ~name;` and saves — rerun in 42ms:
give_back.jet passed — 1 of 24. Next: 01_values/numbers.jet

options.name: Interactive track on the docs site
options.detail: The curriculum lives on the documentation site as editable examples that run in the browser. There is no new CLI verb. Writers update lessons without a toolchain release, and a person can start before installing anything. Loss: the loop breaks. The browser compiler can lag or lead the installed one, the hints are not the live diagnostics, and the track disappears offline.
options.technical: Needs a web build of the compiler, or a server sandbox, kept in step with every release. Page diagnostics render in the browser and never connect to `jet explain` on the user's machine.
options.code:
## Browser: jet-lang.org/learn, lesson 1 — editable pane (site runs Jet 1.2)
fn shout(name: String) -> String {
    return name
}
[ Run ]
error[E0120]: `name` was not moved here, so it cannot be returned as-is

## She installs Jet to keep going. The train loses signal.
$ jet --version
Jet 1.0.0                   ## older than the site build
## Lesson 7 uses syntax her compiler rejects. The site is unreachable.

options.name: Explicit non-goal: the compiler is the curriculum
options.detail: Jet declares that the compiler teaches, and ships no curriculum. `jet new` prints one next-step line, `jet dev` reruns on save, teaching diagnostics explain each error, and the examples corpus shows working programs. Gain: no curriculum to maintain, and full pressure stays on making every diagnostic teach. Loss: nothing orders the first hours. The Rust evidence shows this exact gap: strong compiler errors still left learners needing three outside resources and a mentor.
options.technical: No new surface. The bet is that I4 what/why/fix diagnostics plus the examples corpus replace an ordered track. The Rust study is the counterexample on record.
options.code:
$ jet new hello
Created hello. Next: cd hello && jet dev src/main.jet

$ cd hello && jet dev src/main.jet
Hello from Jet!

## She experiments, hits E0120, and reads a good explanation:
$ jet explain E0120

## Then: silence. No next exercise, no ordered path.
## She asks a search engine what to try next. No network on the train.

options.name: Exercise pack as a registry package
options.detail: The curriculum ships as a normal package on the Jet registry. `jet add jet-katas` fetches it, and the exercises run with `jet dev` like any project. Writers release lessons on their own schedule, and the toolchain stays lean. Loss: this recreates the rustlings failure. The pack version and the compiler version drift apart, the first fetch needs a network, and hints can quote errors the installed compiler no longer prints.
options.technical: No new CLI verb. The pack is exercises plus a `#Test`-style checker that marks an exercise done. Version pinning narrows drift but cannot remove it: a pack tested on one compiler meets users on another.
options.code:
$ jet add jet-katas
error: network unreachable          ## first day, on the train

## Later, with network:
$ jet add jet-katas
$ jet dev katas/01_values/give_back.jet
warning: jet-katas 1.4 targets Jet 1.2; you run Jet 1.0
## The hint file quotes an error message Jet 1.0 does not print.

comparisons.note: rustlings is a separate install and repository. Its watch loop with `hint` is the mechanic learners love, but it versions apart from rustc, so exercises and hints break on toolchain changes.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo install rustlings
$ rustlings watch
$ rustlings hint intro1

comparisons.note: The official tour runs in the browser against a remote sandbox. It gives a good first hour, but it is not the local toolchain, and no bridge leads from a local compiler error back into the tour.
comparisons.code: ## tour.golang.org — browser only; the `go` CLI has no learn verb

comparisons.note: Elm bet everything on teaching compiler errors plus a written guide, with no exercise runner. The errors are loved, but learners still assemble their own practice path.
comparisons.code: ## elm-lang.org/docs — guide and famous errors; no `elm learn`

recommendation.why: Jet already owns the two pieces learners love: teaching diagnostics and a 42-millisecond watch loop. `jet learn` joins them into one offline path that is always the same version as the compiler. The Rust evidence is direct: the loved mechanic is the hint inside the watch loop, and the failure is that it lives outside the toolchain.

whyNot.reason: A browser track breaks the loop this decision exists to protect: it can drift from the installed compiler, its hints are not the live diagnostics, and it vanishes offline.
Rust ran this experiment. Strong compiler errors without an ordered practice path still cost learners three outside resources and a mentor.
A registry pack recreates the rustlings failure: the pack and the compiler version apart, hints quote errors the installed compiler does not print, and the first fetch needs a network.

recommendation.tradeoff: The toolchain now carries a curriculum, and every language change must update its exercises. That cost buys a live gain: the exercise suite runs in CI as end-to-end proof that the teaching diagnostics still teach.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an in-toolchain runner, a docs-site track, and an explicit non-goal. It recommended the runner because it joins the shipped watch loop and teaching diagnostics into one offline path.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the registry exercise pack as a fourth genuine option. It folded editor-plugin and video-course ideas into the docs-site option, because both leave the toolchain unchanged.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved one docs idea into the runner: each exercise names its matching docs chapter for prose depth, while the loop stays local. No separate hybrid option was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the non-goal with the `jet new` next-step line and strengthened the pack with version pinning. Pinning narrows drift but cannot remove it, and the non-goal still leaves no ordered path.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked curriculum staleness: exercises inside the toolchain could rot like docs. The repair is structural — the exercise suite runs in CI so a breaking language change fails the build, and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Observing allocation failure on freestanding and embedded targets
decisions.gist: How a freestanding or embedded Jet program sees and handles a failed memory allocation.
decisions.lesson: When a program asks for memory and none is left, something must happen. Today Jet aborts on every tier: Prelude Mem.rs line 64 routes the failure straight to an abort. On a server that default is fine. On a microcontroller there is no operating system to catch the fall, memory is tiny, and running out is normal. E3303 already tells embedded users to configure their own allocator. This ballot decides how such a program observes the failure instead of dying.
decisions.story: Maya ships firmware for a battery soil sensor with 32 kilobytes of memory. A storm produces a burst of oversized radio packets. Parsing one asks for more memory than the device has. Today the firmware aborts, the watchdog reboots it, the burst repeats, and the node reboot-loops all night. A day of field data is lost. Maya wants the parse to fail as a value so the firmware can drop that packet and keep sampling.

options.name: Fallible allocation family: try_ calls return T ? AllocError
options.detail: Collections and constructors gain try_ forms that return the value or an AllocError. Code that expects exhaustion calls the try_ form and branches on the result. Plain calls keep today's abort, so hosted beginners see no change. Gain: the failing call site itself can recover, which is what a device needs. Loss: the standard library carries a second, fallible spelling of each allocating operation.
options.technical: New Core enum AllocError carries the requested bytes and the allocator name. Family: List.try_new, List.try_with_capacity, try_push, try_reserve, Map.try_insert, String.try_push, mem.Arena.try_alloc. The allocator's raw entry point returns failure as a value; plain APIs convert it to today's abort, try_ APIs return it. One Prelude entry point serves every tier (I9) and the D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 fact. E0402 still rejects an ignored fallible result.

options.name: Allocation as a substitutable seam only
options.detail: The allocator becomes a swap point like Jet's effect roots: tests and embedded profiles substitute their own implementation. A fail-nth implementation gives SQLite-style fault loops for card #1916 with no new API on collections. Gain: one seam powers testing and embedded policy together. Loss: without a fallible return type, the failing call site still cannot branch. The substituted allocator can only record the failure, abort, or reset.
options.technical: Rides the ratified D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 profile fact: the named allocator value is the seam, and a test env profile names mem.FailNth. No new effect root is needed because the fact already selects the implementation per profile. Observation stays program-level (the implementation's failure action), never value-level.

options.name: Failure policy fact plus one program out-of-memory handler
options.detail: The allocator fact grows an on_fail policy: abort, or call one named handler. The handler gets the failed request, can log to the UART, free caches, and reset the device cleanly. This matches common firmware practice: one central out-of-memory response. Gain: no new API on collections, and one place to audit. Loss: the failing call site never sees the failure, so local recovery like dropping one packet is impossible.
options.technical: Extends the D-TARGET-ALLOC1 / D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 facts with on_fail: .Abort | .Handler(fn(mem.AllocRequest)). The handler runs on the failing thread. If it returns, the allocation retries once, then aborts. This mirrors the shape of Rust's set_alloc_error_hook.

options.name: Keep abort everywhere; retract the embedded claim
options.detail: No new surface. Allocation failure aborts on every tier, and the docs stop promising that freestanding programs can handle exhaustion. The E3303 fix text changes to say the allocator must be sized so it never fails. Gain: nothing to design, and one behavior everywhere. Loss: Jet gives up the embedded reliability story. Card #1916's out-of-memory loops can never prove a graceful path, because no graceful path can exist.
options.technical: Status quo in Prelude Mem.rs:64. Requires edits to the E3303 fix text and to docs/reference/embedded.md so the claims match the behavior.

comparisons.note: Every allocating call returns error.OutOfMemory and callers write try. Maximum honesty, constant ceremony — even on servers where exhaustion is not worth handling.
Aborts by default through handle_alloc_error, with stable opt-in try_reserve on collections. The abort default plus a try_ opt-in shipped and held up in production.
malloc returns NULL. SQLite proves every out-of-memory path by failing the nth allocation in a loop until a clean pass — possible only because failure is a value.
comparisons.code:
p = sqlite3_malloc(n);
if( p==0 ) return SQLITE_NOMEM;

comparisons.note: Two mechanisms at once: a thrown bad_alloc and new(nothrow) returning null. A cautionary tale of a split surface that every codebase must police by convention.
comparisons.code:
int* p = new (std::nothrow) int[n];
if (!p) { /* handle */ }

recommendation.why: Only a failure value at the call site lets firmware drop one packet and continue, which is the whole point of observing exhaustion. The try_ family delivers that through the ratified T ? E mechanism and the L2 fallibility law, with no new error machinery. Hosted beginners keep today's abort default untouched. It also completes card #1916: a fail-nth allocator plus try_ calls reproduces SQLite's proof loop as an ordinary Jet test.

whyNot.reason: A seam alone selects who fails, not how code recovers. Without a fallible return the failing call still cannot branch, so the graceful path a fault loop wants to prove never exists.
One central handler cannot make a local decision. Dropping one oversized packet while keeping the rest needs the failure at the call site, and a retry-then-abort handler never provides that.
It retracts the promise E3303 already makes and blocks card #1916's acceptance criterion. The board raised this card because that embedded story is worth keeping.

recommendation.tradeoff: The standard library gains a second, fallible spelling for each allocating operation, and both spellings must stay in step forever. Rust accepted the same cost for try_reserve, and L2 already defines which spelling a caller must use.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared try_ calls, a substitutable allocator seam, one central handler, and honest retraction. It recommended try_ calls because only a value at the call site permits local recovery.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Zig-style all-fallible allocation, C++-style unwinding, and a reserve-then-infallible model. Unwinding contradicts freestanding panic=abort, all-fallible breaks the hosted default, and reservation folded into option A as try_reserve.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined A and C: try_ calls for deliberate recovery, with the machine's existing panic policy fact covering plain calls. That pairing became a technical note under A instead of a fifth option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each loser: the seam already owns its swap point through D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1's fact, the handler matches real firmware reset practice, and retraction received the exact doc edits it needs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A as a second spelling (I8) and on tier parity. L2 assigns the two spellings distinct meanings, and the try_ family lowers through one Prelude entry point on every tier (I9), so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Test declarations and fault injection: one signature, one loop
decisions.gist: How a test tells the harness which effects to make fail.
decisions.lesson: A test is a function with a name and a claim, spelled #Test fn. Fault injection is the missing half: SQLite fails allocation or I/O call N in a loop, checks recovery, and repeats until no new site appears. Two drafts died on review. A nested .faults member hid the contract in the body. A row suffix put failure marks where rows never carry them. Deny is not reusable either: it proves the effect never happens, while injection fails a happening effect.
decisions.story: Priya ports a config store to Jet. Her write path looks correct, but a full disk at the wrong moment once corrupted the store in production. She wants the harness to fail every Fs.Write her test reaches, one call at a time, and prove the store recovers after each one. She opens the testing chapter and wants to read the whole contract in the signature line.

options.name: faults argument on the #Test marker
options.detail: The marker the harness already owns gains one argument: #Test(faults: [Fs.Write]) names the effects the harness must fail. The loop is the harness's: fail each reachable call site once, re-run, stop when no new site appears. The body sees each injected failure as the ordinary error value and handles it like real code. Plain asserts after the fallible section are the recovery check. The common test stays exactly #Test fn with nothing added. Signature stays pure contract; marker stays harness configuration; no new glyph, no grammar change.
options.technical: faults is a typed marker parameter (effect-root list) on the existing #Test registry row; unknown roots are a teaching error with a registered code and UI snapshot. The loop, injection points, and iteration verdict live in one Prelude harness part; engines marshal (I9). Iteration verdict: body returned (success or routed error), no panic, cleanup intact (deferred closes ran; sentry-clean when D-MEM-SENTRY1 is on). Parameterized #Test fn stays a property test; scratch space comes from the testing scratch API in the body.

options.name: Fault mark inside the effect row
options.detail: A per-effect question-mark suffix in the signature row: the harness fails the marked effects. The owner reviewed this shape and found it confusing. The deeper defect stands alone. Effect rows never carry failure information anywhere else in Jet, so the mark teaches a false lesson about rows. It also sits postfix while the deny mark sits prefix.
options.technical: Row grammar gains a test-only per-effect suffix; refused outside test signatures. Same Prelude harness loop as option A.

options.name: Harness flag only: jet test --faults
options.detail: Source stays exactly as today. The command line picks the roots: jet test --faults Fs.Write runs every selected test under the loop. Good for a broad sweep over an existing suite. The loss is truth in the source: a test that exists to prove fault recovery does not say so, and CI must carry the flag out-of-band forever.
options.technical: No syntax change. The same Prelude harness part; the flag selects roots globally.

options.name: A testing.faults library API
options.detail: A test calls testing.faults(.Fs.Write) { work } around the fallible section. Plans become ordinary values, reusable and composable. The loss is the shape the owner rejected first: the contract hides in a nested block inside the body, two levels deep, instead of standing at the declaration.
options.technical: Library function over the same Prelude harness part; closure re-runs per iteration.

comparisons.note: test is a first-class declaration, not an attribute; the allocator-failure harness (checkAllErrorPaths pattern) loops allocation failures exactly like this ballot's loop.
The reliability standard this card cites: run the test, fail malloc/io call N, verify recovery, N+1, until no new site.
#[test] attribute plus external crates (fail, loom) for injection; the contract lives outside the signature, which is the readability owners complain about.
Whole-process deterministic simulation; strongest results, but a platform commitment far past one test's contract.
comparisons.code: // simulation harness, not a per-test surface

recommendation.why: The fault plan is harness configuration, and the marker is the harness's one surface, so the contract lands where a reader already looks. The signature stays a pure contract, the body proves recovery on the ordinary error rail, and the common test gains nothing to learn. No new glyph enters the language.

whyNot.reason: Rows say what code touches; return types say what can fail. A failure mark inside the row teaches a false lesson, and the owner found it confusing on first read.
The fault contract vanishes from the source, and CI flags become load-bearing truth.
The contract hides in a nested block inside the body, and a second closure vocabulary arrives for something one marker argument can say.

recommendation.tradeoff: The marker line grows when faults are named, and marker arguments carry semantics rather than metadata alone. That is accepted because #Test already owns how the harness runs the body, and the argument only configures that run.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared marker arguments, a library API, a CLI flag, substitution declarations, and a scope member, and recommended the scope member.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added whole-process simulation (FoundationDB) and per-module fault manifests; both were folded away because the card's claim is per-test recovery, not a platform.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass merged the loop semantics with the owner's readability bar across three drafts: scope member, then row suffix, then marker argument. The marker argument kept the declaration-site contract while dropping the new glyph.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the CLI flag as the zero-source-change sweep and the library API as the reusable-plan story, and kept both as honest options. It also gave the row suffix its strongest reading before the owner review rejected it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: This pass killed the row suffix: rows carry no failure information anywhere else in Jet, the mark sat postfix against a prefix deny, and the owner could not read it. It confirmed deny is not reusable (deny proves absence; injection fails a present effect) and that the common test carries zero new ceremony.

decisions.title: Choose the expression fence glyph after the @ swap
decisions.gist: Choose the marks that open and close an expression fence.
decisions.lesson: A fence copies one statement for each entry. That meaning is settled. The old fence uses `$`, but `$` now belongs only to typed environment reads in config files. This choice repairs that conflict.
decisions.story: Mara updates eight account tasks after the compile-time mark changes to `@`. Her fence still contains `$`, so the source now teaches two conflicting rules for the same mark.
decisions.inWild:
use core.tasks as tasks

fn run() {
    from :: Shared.new(Account.{balance: 1000})
    to :: Shared.new(Account.{balance: 0})
    @[ t1..t8 ]@ :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
    @[ t1..t8 ]@.wait()
    from_bal :: from.read(a => a.balance)
    to_bal :: to.read(a => a.balance)
    print(@[ "from={from_bal}", "to={to_bal}", "total={from_bal + to_bal}" ]@)
}

// Output
from=200
to=800
total=1000

options.name: Symmetric @ fence
options.detail: Write `@[ entries ]@`. The fence uses the compile-time mark at both ends. The matching marks keep a wide or nested expression fence easy to scan.
options.technical: This amends only the spelling in D-VERDICT-1320-1. The one-copy and lock-step laws stay unchanged. `@[` and `]@` become longest-match tokens, and `]@` suppresses line termination. Sources: syntax-decisions.md:5826 and :5838 and :6636. Lexer digraphs: crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:241 and Terminators.rs:121. Parser: crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:122. Grammars: editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js:23 and editors/zed/languages/jet/highlights.scm:130.

options.name: Dollar fence carve-out
options.detail: Keep `$[ entries ]$`. A named exception says the two digraphs are fence tokens, not bare environment marks. Existing source stays unchanged, but ordinary Jet still shows `$` outside config files.
options.technical: This option amends D-ONCE-DOLLAR1 with one exception. The current lexer already gives `$[` and `]$` dedicated tokens at crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:242 and crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:254. The formatter reads the same constants at crates/jet-parser/src/Formatter/Statements.rs:74. The editor lists both digraphs at editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js:23.

options.name: @ plus normal brackets
options.detail: Write `@[ entries ]`. The opening `@` marks compile-time expansion, while normal brackets close the entry list. This form is viable, but its closing edge has no matching mark.
options.technical: This form is lexically viable. The lexer already emits `At`, `LBracket`, and `RBracket` at crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:241 and crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:252. The fence pass must match the outer bracket by depth because entries can contain lists and indexes. No new close token can suppress a line break. The parser must instead keep the bracketed fence segment open by context. Current pairing expects a dedicated close token at crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:124.

comparisons.note: Prefix `@` marks compile-time names and fact reads after D-ONCE-AT1. Option A makes statement expansion use the same visible mark.
Normal brackets already close lists and member spreads. Option C borrows that close, while option A keeps fences visibly distinct.
comparisons.code:
items :: [first, second]
use default.[cargo, ripgrep]
@[ first, second ]@ :: work()

recommendation.why: Option A follows the ratified mark law without an exception. A fence performs compile-time statement expansion, so `@` names its role. Matching edge marks also preserve the strong visual boundary chosen by D-VERDICT-1320-1.

whyNot.reason: It leaves `$` in ordinary source after D-ONCE-DOLLAR1 made that use a teaching error. Calling the digraph special weakens a simple language-wide rule.
It is viable, but the unmatched close makes fences look like marked lists. It also loses the dedicated close token that controls line termination.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each fence carries a closing `@` that normal bracketed forms do not need. The extra mark is accepted because it makes the expansion boundary explicit at both edges.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a symmetric `@` fence with a dollar carve-out. It recommended `@[ ]@` because the fence is compile-time expansion.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked words, braces, normal brackets, and the retired `<: :>` pair. Only `@[ ]` added a distinct viable design; the other forms either mint more syntax or revive a retired mark.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested `@` only at the opening edge. That form became option C, but it did not improve the symmetric recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the dollar option with its best case: digraphs are tokens, not bare `$`. It also confirmed that normal brackets can be matched by depth.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested editor support, nested brackets, line breaks, and the risk that `@` has too many roles. Dedicated symmetric tokens keep the parser boundary clear, so option A survives.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: Please reform the ballot using a2 & c beta (#context) as the baseline. Give me grammar options to pick from using those two choices. That is what I want to pick but need to ensure I like the syntax/grammar
questions.answer: Reformed and now RATIFIED. A2+Cβ fixed as the baseline; the grammar pick resolved to G2 — `#context(field: value) { … }`, reusing Jet's single `name: value` spelling (S61/S29), with `=` staying reassign-only. No single-field shorthand; bundle-spread deferred. Shipped as the c74 Smart Context feature.

questions.text: Option D but I dont want to defer the full implementation if avoidable. We are close to epoch 3 anyway, so what should we do to get this working? Propose a new approach in this decision.
questions.answer: Proposed Option D+ so nothing is deferred: an interpreter seam now (Phase 1) plus a Cranelift JIT this Epoch-3 (Phase 2, tiered — interpreter tier-0, Cranelift tier-1). I6 still holds because Cranelift is runtime-side, never in Source/. This needs your approval of the runtime-side Cranelift dependency (same posture as the regex dep). Recommendation: D+. Decision still open pending your call on the dep.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal
questions.answer: Not a blocker. `$` is plain ASCII and universal on physical keyboards; Jet already left the ISO-646-invariant subset behind by depending on `# @ { } [ ]`, so `$` adds nothing new. Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

questions.text: Please update this card so it isnt called "raw mode" AND we will have a separate library for TUI. This gives experts control but also provides batteries included TUI development features out of the box. Please update this question accordingly & give me alternatives to "raw mode"
questions.answer: Reformed the D-TERM1 card: dropped 'raw mode' (naming menu, rec `live { }`; alts direct_input/live_keys/keys/interactive/immediate/cockpit/takeover); confirmed a SEPARATE batteries-included `core.tui` library on top (old Option D is the library, not core), so experts get the low-level primitive and beginners get widgets out of the box; the card now decides only the primitive name + surface (A scoped block rec / B handle / C free fns).

questions.text: Break this into multiple cards, I cant choose multiple on one card
questions.answer: Split the old mega-card into three separate Focus Mode decisions: D-MIGRATE2A for migration operation vocabulary (`add`/`remove`/`change`/reorder), D-MIGRATE2B for where type-change converters come from (inline `via`, named `impl`, or both), and D-MIGRATE2C for `jet schema` CLI verbs (`status`, `squash --before`, and whether CI needs a separate `check`). c73 now links to all three IDs.

questions.text: I dont understand the downside. Please explain more precisely why we shouldn't just allow all core calls.
questions.answer: Updated D-CTCORE1 with the precise downside: allowing all Core at comptime turns pure compile-time evaluation into running a second runtime during compilation. That harms reproducibility, allows ambient side effects during builds (fs/env/process/net/secrets), forces the comptime interpreter to duplicate runtime behavior, complicates supply-chain policy, and creates machine-dependent compile failures. The recommendation stays B: deterministic pure whitelist now; explicit build-time IO/sandboxed recipe tier later.

questions.text: Please update the options to have a large number of sigils that include the = operator and are only two characters long. I want to see a wide array of options that may be more physically ergonomic & logical as an immutable operator before finalizing such a fundamental change
questions.answer: Expanded D-BIND2 with a broad two-character `=` candidate menu: `$=`, `::`, `::`, `!=`, `?=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `~=`, `.=` , `<=`, `>=`, `:=`, `=:`, `==`, `=>`, and `=<`. The shortlist is `$=`, `::`, `~=`, and `=:`; the card still recommends `$=` because it is unused, two characters, contains `=`, and is visually far from mutable `:=`.

questions.text: I like the three @, #, $ prefixes. Clean up the rest of the card to just have these options, then give a thorough analysis of logic, psychology, & the tradeoffs associated with each option
questions.answer: Updated D-BIND2 to only compare `::`, `::`, and `$=`. The card now focuses on what each prefix teaches: `::` reads anchored/address-like, `::` reads marked/metadata-like, and `$=` reads value-centric without borrowing meaning from another Jet sigil family. Recommendation remains `$=` because it keeps `=` in the binding family, stays visually far from `:=`, and does not overload Jet's existing `@` or `#` semantics.

questions.text: Break this into multiple questions, I cant choose multiple answers to one question
questions.answer: Done — the single card was split into four standalone, single-answer cards under board card c78: D-SOA2A (keyword name, rec `columnar`), D-SOA2B (whole-struct vs partial, rec A), D-SOA2C (reserve per-container spelling, rec A), D-SOA2D (serialization interaction, rec A). Each now takes one pick.

questions.text: I still have no idea what this looks like in practice between the two. I dont understand the difference. In general I want to keep the surface smaller & allow flags for experts to specify the behavior they want but out of the box it should be magic. Please update the ballot accordingly
questions.answer: Done — the card was reformed around the steer (small surface, magic default, expert flags) and now shows the actual terminal session under each option for both a script and a server: A = one verb `jet dev` that auto-detects (rerun a run-to-completion program, hot-swap a resident one) with `--restart`/`--swap`/`--watch=off` overrides; B = two verbs where the wrong one silently full-restarts a server. Rec flipped to A; Q2 (dev↔release output-diff = release blocker) kept as a hard rule. (Since submitted as D-DEVMODE1=A.)

questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. Card reformed with the Owner Q answer, the third option, and an updated tradeoff table.

questions.text: This seems broken, there are no options to choose from
questions.answer: Real bug, now fixed. The card's nine candidate keywords were written as a code block plus a table, not as `- **Option X — …**` bullets, and Tower only builds selectable choices from those bullets — so the card rendered with nothing to pick. Reformed the card into nine proper options A–I, one per keyword (A `soa`, B `lane`, C `columnar`, D `striped`, E `slipstream`, F `parallel`, G `split`, H `fieldwise`, I `wingspan`), each with its own example; the comparison table is kept as Tradeoffs. Recommendation is C (`columnar`) — self-defining from the column-store picture, strong prior art (Arrow/Parquet), no collision with concurrency vocabulary. The card is now pickable.

questions.text: How is this handled in Jai & Odin?
questions.answer: Answered in the D-CAP10 card. Odin: no implicit overloading; explicit overload GROUPS only (proc{a,b}). Jai: has overloading but dispatches on argument TYPE. Neither treats capability/mutability as an overload axis, so process(Data)/process(~Data) has no prior-art equivalent. Reinforces Option A; Odin's explicit-group model is the escape hatch if grouping is ever wanted.

questions.text: How is this handled in odin & jai?
questions.answer: Answered in the D-CAP9 card. Odin: ^T ptr type, &x address-of (prefix), p^ deref (POSTFIX). Jai: *T ptr type, *x address-of (prefix, = the doc's raw-of), deref moved from prefix <

questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

questions.text: What is the interplay with out idea for switft style unified protocol for both server & client to prevent drift?
questions.answer: The Swift insight is the `Responder` (or `Handler`) protocol pattern used by Vapor/Hummingbird/NIO: a single trait `trait Handler { fn handle(req: Request) -> Response }` becomes the composition unit for both the server's routing stack and the client's interceptor stack. Because both sides speak the same `Request`/`Response` types, they can never drift — any middleware that works on the server (auth, logging, retry) is structurally identical to a client-side interceptor. The plan for c164 already captures this: D-HTTPLIB2=B (split client/server modules) shares core types, and D-HTTPLIB1=A (function-first mux) is the routing side. The missing piece to make it Swift-unified is an explicit `Handler` trait in `core.http` that both the client and server implement. Concretely: the client IS a handler (wraps the network connection); the mux IS a handler (dispatches to route handlers); middleware wraps one handler with another. Testing then becomes free — inject a `MockHandler` anywhere in the chain. This should be a first-class design constraint in the c164 plan, not a separate decision. Agents writing the HTTP library plan should define `core.http.Handler` as the primary abstraction before splitting into client vs. server API docs.

Both should be baseline functional out of the box BUT ALSO have EVERYTHING fully defined in the  config.jet file so that everything is visible/auditable/modifyable. Experts need to know EXACTLY what is on their system & have COMPLETE control, allowing them to break their config by swapping low level components around if they choose, but then they are responsible for making sure it works. Terminal stays lean but modern: full boot, storage, user, network, firewall, logging, certificate, package, and compatibility substrate plus fish, Helix, Git, OpenSSH client, curl, rsync, ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, fzf, zoxide, jq, and btop; no remote server enabled by default. Experts may remove or replace kernel, bootloader, init, networking, desktop, apps, or any other layer; JetOS reports unmet obligations and proof failures but never heals their source behind their back. questions.text: Practically speaking what is the difference in performance between these options? I like the sound of universal in option a and run/dev commands already use cranelift, so what is the real benefit list at the end of the day in plain language?
questions.answer:
Measured today on this machine, one shell, warm toolchain, examples/features/basics/fizzbuzz.jet:

- `jet check` (all of Jet's own checking: parse, types, ownership): 0.007s.
- `jet build` (today's path: generate Rust text, rustc compiles it, link): about 12s cold, 11s warm.
- Even hello.jet pays about 11.7s through that path.

So nearly all of the wait for a binary is rustc re-checking code the Jet front end already proved, plus LLVM work a debug artifact does not need. The wait grows with program size roughly the way cargo build waits do.

One measured correction to the premise: the resident Cranelift engine currently serves `jet dev` and `jet serve` hot-swaps. Plain `jet run` still rides the rustc path today. That is why hello.jet takes 11.7 seconds to run once.

What each option means in practice:

Option A (rustc opt-level 0). The debug binary keeps the full current path with optimization turned off. That saves some LLVM time. It still pays Rust text generation, rustc parsing, type-checking, borrow-checking, codegen, and linking. Expect waits like cargo's debug builds, forever.

Option B (Cranelift). The same checked program lowers straight from Jet's internal form (TIR) to object code, then links. No Rust text, no rustc. Cranelift is built for exactly this; it recompiles programs between dev hot-swaps in well under a second. A debug binary lands at roughly check time plus link time. The 12 seconds above collapses to about a second, and the gap widens as programs grow.

Reference point: Rust's own Cranelift backend (rustc_codegen_cranelift) cuts debug build times by about a third while still paying Rust's full front end every build. Jet under B skips that front end entirely, so Jet's saving is much larger than Rust's third.

On "universal": option B keeps it. A target Cranelift cannot emit for automatically uses option A's exact path, and `jet explain build` names which backend ran and why. Behavior is identical either way: same checked TIR, same R12 differential tests, same diagnostics. Only the wait changes.

Bottom line. A means one backend everywhere, and every debug build waits on rustc. B means the dev-loop engine also produces your debug binaries on mainstream targets (x86-64 and aarch64 Linux, macOS, Windows), with A's exact path as the automatic, named fallback everywhere else.

What it decides: a profile merges several packages into one file tree (same engine for `jet profile`, JetOS systems, and user environments). questions.text:
1) Since we have the "build" method that lets us run code at build time, is there still a reason to keep comptime? What is the boundary & what is the value? 
2) I'm not entirely clear on what this question means. What are the real tradeoffs, where would people get the most value regardless of safety, how can we mitigate issues with safety? It's up to us to do more work on the backend to give the best end result and experience for the user
questions.answer:
Q1 — comptime vs fn build: the boundary and the value.

Keep both. The docs make them different tools. comptime (S26, D-CTEFFECT1) is pure value evaluation. A fuel-limited sema interpreter runs type-checked Core code and lowers the result to constant data. It has no authority and can never create or select a type (S26). Its only external reads are Tier-1 locked operations — `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, `find`, `fetch(url, sha256:)` — each recorded in `.jet/lock`. Tier-2 ambient reads need `#Impure` plus `--allow-impure`. comptime values feed constants, marker values, and module fields.

`fn build(b: BuildContext)` (D-BUILDENTRY1, D-BUILDACTION1) is a build-time action runner. It registers targets (`b.add_executable`, `b.add_library`), declares cached capability-gated actions (`b.action(name, inputs, outputs, run, caps)`), selects toolchains, and runs processes. It emits artifacts and generated source under `.jet/generated/`, with input and output hashes in the lock. Tier 1 is pure+locked by default; Tier 2 needs `#Impure` plus explicit permission plus provenance.

Why both exist: comptime is a calculator over declared values, available in every expression position with no ceremony. `fn build` is an authorized effect runner, invoked only by `jet build` and gated by granted capabilities. Merging them breaks safe-by-default (I1). Either every constant expression gains filesystem and process authority, or every build action loses its capability gate. A beginner would need a `BuildContext` just to write `label: "ledger " + release`.

Examples:
- comptime: `comptime release = "1.4.0"` then `label: "ledger " + release`. Pure, no lock entry.
- build: `b.action("gen-proto", inputs, outputs, run: protoc, caps: [.exec])`. Runs `protoc`, records provenance, emits generated source.
- comptime moving to build: `banner: embed_file("./banner.txt")` is a Tier-1 locked comptime read. Producing that banner by running `git describe` is a process effect, so it moves to a capability-gated `fn build` action. The ballot's own option-C error says the same for ambient reads: `env_var("TOKEN")` is Tier-2 and must move to an authorized `fn build` action.

Q2 — what the ballot decides and the real tradeoffs.

Plain restatement: this ballot decides whether one module field may reference another field in the same module, and whether a field may directly read a hash-locked external input such as an embedded file or pinned fetch.

Option A, pure dependency graph. A field can name a sibling. Cycles fail before any plan runs and print the full chain. A field cannot spell a Tier-1 read inline.

    module env.dev {
      label: "ledger " + release
      prompt: label + " > "
    }

Option B, independent fields. A field cannot name a sibling. Any shared value lifts to a top-level `comptime` binding. No graph, most ceremony for reuse.

Option C, graph plus locked reads. Everything in A, and a field may spell a Tier-1 read inline. The input is recorded in `.jet/lock` and reproduced offline.

    module env.dev {
      banner: embed_file("./banner.txt")
      prompt: banner + " > "
    }

Where users get the most value. Shared computed values across fields is the common case; A and C both cover it, B does not. Embedding a file or a version string is the next case. C spells it inside a field. A reaches the same value through a top-level comptime binding, which is already law (D-CTIO1):

    comptime banner = embed_file("./banner.txt")
    module env.dev {
      banner: banner
      prompt: banner + " > "
    }

The only delta between A and C is one binding line and where the read is written.

Safety, honestly. C is not unsafe. Tier-1 reads are hash-pinned, recorded in `.jet/lock`, and fail closed under `--locked` and offline. The safety story is fully engineerable, and effort is never a deterrent in this project. C does not lose on safety and must not be rejected for costing more backend work.

The real argument for A over C is I8, one way to mean it. External input already has one home: top-level `comptime` bindings and the `fn build` input surface. C adds a second home — every module field — where a locked read may appear. Provenance review then scans every field instead of one binding list. That is a legibility cost the reviewer pays on every module, not a safety cost.

Which option the analysis supports: A. The one concrete reason: a field under A can already reference a top-level `comptime banner = embed_file(...)` binding, so C buys one line of convenience while scattering external-input provenance across every field, which I8 rules against. If inline field reads later prove real value beyond that one line, C reopens on its own merits, not on a safety argument.

questions.text:

Updated ballot adds recommended D: reject ordinary mutable captures, add ordered par_partition for common splits, and replace the serial par_fold prototype with a truly parallel seed, step, and merge reducer. This covers beginner and expert cases without races, silent serialization, or guessed merges. Custom reducers stay explicit; diagnostics can show the equivalent reducer shape. questions.text: We are ALWAYS looking to spend more time and effort up front to have a better long term experience, both from a dx perspective, but also to get better performance and ergonomics at the end of the day. What kind of benefits do we get from option C? Since it sounds like it costs more up front but doesnt seem to have other negatives listed does that mean performance is better?
questions.answer:
No. Option C does not make runtime branches faster than option B.

B and C can feed the same middle-end arm-table IR. After that, D-BRANCH-CODEGEN1 (already ratified as B) picks select, match, data table, jump table, or ordered compares. That classifier is where bare-metal wins live.

What C buys instead:

1. One IR from the parser onward. No classic If tree beside Switch arms.
2. No desugar pass that can drift from parse or forget a path.
3. Every future lint, IDE walk, and lowering sees one shape.
4. Long-term simpler compiler DX, at higher up-front parser, formatter, and IDE cost.

What C does not buy:

- Faster user programs than a correct early desugar (B)
- Different user syntax (still one if)

So: spend more up front on C for a cleaner long-term compiler. Spend the performance effort on the classifier and subject binding, which you already locked in CODEGEN1.

I updated D-BRANCH-AST1: option C detail is clearer, and the recommendation now points to C given your up-front investment rule. You can still pick B if you want the smaller first patch with a desugar bridge.

questions.text: for a game loop, wouldnt you just put the loop inside the fn run() {...}? Or fn dev() {...}?
questions.answer: You do — your game code lives in fn run(), and on desktop you could hand-write loop { ... } there today. The loop itself sits behind game.run because the parts that vary per platform belong to the backend: the stop condition (window close vs headless frame budget), frame pacing (vsync / FPS cap), and the input/event pump. And on the web target you cannot write the loop at all — the browser forbids blocking the main thread, so frames must be scheduled as callbacks (requestAnimationFrame). The callback body inside game.run is the only shape that works on desktop, headless CI, and browser alike — the same write-once argument as apps. Option A adds no new mechanism; it fixes the stop condition so the loop game.run already owns runs until the player quits instead of exactly three frames. fn dev() is orthogonal here: it is an alternate entry for dev tooling, not a different loop.

questions.text: Ok now in this case I am starting to fail to see value in tags at all... What are the use cases? Why would you use a tag over a taint other than just for documentation?
questions.answer: Honest answer: today you are seeing it right — a plain value tag checks nothing, so over a taint it buys only documentation. The two also answer opposite questions. Taint is negative provenance, on by default: this value may be dangerous, tracked through the whole program, blocked at sinks, with #Sanitizer as the audited exit door. A tag is positive provenance, opt-in: this value passed X — reviewed, normalized, validated, escaped, canonical. You cannot get positive facts out of taint without inverting the world: every value would have to start tainted for every fact, with sanitizers everywhere. Taint tracks the dangerous minority; positive facts mark the verified minority. The real use cases only appear with option A, where the fact becomes checked: an untagged String cannot reach a #Reviewed String parameter, and the #Blesses fn is the greppable, audited door in — still zero runtime cost, and no wrapping tax, because the value stays a String and works with every String API. That last part is the whole case for a strict tag over distinct: distinct mints a new identity you must unwrap at every boundary; a strict tag is the same type carrying a verified property. TypeScript branded types are this exact pattern hand-rolled at massive scale — the demand proof. If checked positive facts do not earn their place for you, the honest pick is C (retire value tags from type position; distinct carries enforcement). B is the weakest of the three: it keeps signatures that look like checks and are not, which is exactly the trap in the story.

questions.text: Ok, based on your response, it sounds like tags and taints are two sides of the same coin. Why not just call all of them tags, then taints and tags are unified under one banner & users can choose which behavior they want in the definition or at call sites, etc? create a new proposal ballot with this idea, it probably supersedes this but you can decide that
questions.answer: Done — new ballot D-TAG-UNIFY1 on this card, and I agree it supersedes D-TAG-STRICT1, which I deleted (strict is now just one mode of the unified mechanism). The shape: every tag declares its checking behavior — plain (documentation, today's default), strict (positive fact: values must pass through a #Blesses door to enter tagged positions), taint (negative fact: spreads by dataflow, blocked at declared sinks, cleared only through a #Sanitizer door). The built-in taint kinds (Input, PII, Secret, Credential) become prelude tag declarations in taint mode, so #Tainted stops being a special case and taints join the tag namespace users can extend. Two notes. First, this builds on D-FACTMODEL1=A, which you ratified today: one fact registry behind tags, states, taint kinds, and effect leaves, with tree facts declared as enums — the modes here attach to that same model, so nothing is relitigated. Second, on choosing behavior at call sites: I worked it out as option C so you can see it honestly, but it breaks the guarantee — the same signature would be checked at one site and decorative at another, and a security property that holds only where someone remembered to ask is the property that fails. The declaration is the honest home for the mode; call sites interact through the doors. Recommendation is A.

questions.text: Shouldnt we make literals like this as small as possible so that they can auto widen with no loss?
questions.answer:
Half of it works, half of it backfires, and the good half is bigger than literals. I added both readings to the ballot as options E and F.

Option E is your idea taken literally: give the numeral its narrowest type, then widen it losslessly. Two problems, both found by probing the current binary.

1. "Narrowest" cannot be decided without looking at the other side. The narrowest type for 1 is an unsigned byte, and an unsigned byte does not fit in an I8. So `fn tick(x: I8) => I8 { return x + 1 }` gets refused. Once you consult the other side to avoid that, you have written option A.

2. The out-of-range case gets worse, not better. `U8.{200} + 300` would make 300 a 16-bit number, widen the U8 to meet it, and hand back a 16-bit sum. The mistake is accepted and the expression silently changes width. The error lands later, at the store, instead of on the 300 where you typed it. Today `U8.{ 300 }` is caught on the spot as E1003, and option A keeps that.

Option F is the bigger idea inside your question, and I think it is the real one. Lossless widening implicit everywhere, not just for numerals. `I32 + I16` is refused today (probed) even though every I16 value fits an I32 with nothing lost. F fixes that whole family, not just the literal case, and narrowing stays explicit.

F costs two things. It ends the deliberate separation of named widths in S42. And it splits the numeric menu: D-FLOATW1 keeps F32-with-Float as a compile error with a convert fix-it, so whole numbers would auto-widen while floats would not. If you want F, that float rule should be reopened in the same breath so both halves follow one law.

So: A if you want the argument-versus-operand inconsistency closed and nothing else moved. F if you want the general "no ceremony for a conversion that cannot lose anything" rule, knowing it amends S42 and pulls D-FLOATW1 with it. E is the one I would not take, because it refuses the I8 case and it accepts the 300.

questions.text: Conceptually I think I like A the most, but it isnt clear to me how this would work with different types of units. Like if we wanted to use measurements that compared pounds force to newtons or speed, but then if you dont have all the conversions directly and precisely then values could be off. We want extreme precision where possible while keeping exceptional speed. REMEMBER, BY DEFAULT WE NEED TO SUPPORT EVERY SINGLE UNIT OF MEASURE THAT IS STANDARD, including support for things like electronics with voltage, amperage, inductance, impedence, resistance, force, pressure, etc. EVERYTHING that would be a standard tool in the domain of ANY scientist, researcher, engineer, mathemetiian, or analyst
questions.answer: A handles mixed units through one coherent anchor, never pairwise conversion tables. A derived family's base member is pinned coherent: exactly 1 of the product of its base dimensions' base units, so 1 newton = 1 kg*m/s/s by construction. Every other unit of that dimension — kilonewton, pound-force, psi — is an exact arbitrary-precision rational scale from that anchor. Pound-force is exact, not approximate: the pound (0.45359237 kg) and standard gravity (9.80665 m/s^2) are exact by international definition, so 1 lbf = 4.4482216152605 N exactly. Nearly every standard unit has such an exact SI definition. PRECISION: any conversion is one ratio of two exact rationals, folded at compile time (already ratified in D-QUANTITY-DECL1); implicit conversion happens only when exact, and lossy conversion requires the explicit rounded form (D-UNIT-CONV1) — so a value rounds at most once, and only when you ask. SPEED: units erase after sema; a conversion is one runtime multiply (plus one add for affine units like celsius) against a compile-time constant, and same-unit math costs zero. COVERAGE: the ratified D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D prelude ships every standard unit by default — all 7 SI base dimensions; all 22 SI named derived units (hertz, newton, pascal, joule, watt, coulomb, volt, farad, ohm, siemens, weber, tesla, henry, lumen, lux, becquerel, gray, sievert, katal, radian, steradian, degree Celsius); the SI prefix ladder; accepted non-SI units (litre, tonne, minute/hour/day, degree, electronvolt, dalton, astronomical unit, bar, mmHg); and customary units with exact defined scales (inch, foot, yard, mile, ounce, pound, pound-force, psi, gallon, mph). Electronics is fully covered: ampere is a base dimension, and volt/ohm/farad/henry/siemens/weber/tesla/coulomb are coherent derived families. Ballot updated: option A now states the coherent-anchor rule and shows pound-force as an exact scaled member; the explainer carries the precision/speed/coverage model; the card plan enumerates the full default battery.

What about swift style where an unlabeled value is the logical default and a labeled value can choose either
questions.answer:
Ballot updated: option E now carries this idea, and it is the recommendation.

Half of the idea works, and it is the half that matters. Under D-APILABEL1=A, ratified today, a label-only zone lets one name carry both meanings: fn remove(*, at: Int = ..., value: T = ...). So remove(at: 3) and remove(value: 3) both read right, with no new names and no overloading.

The other half reopens the bug. If an unlabeled value keeps a logical default, then scores.remove(3) still compiles and still means one of the two. That line is Maya's whole story. Position as the default leaves the Python author wrong. Value as the default leaves every current Jet reader wrong, which is why option C loses. An explicit default is still an invisible one.

Swift does not do it either. Array has no unlabeled remove. remove(at:) is the only spelling and the label is required, so Swift's real answer is mandatory label, no default.

Two methods named remove, told apart by their labels, would need overloading. The breadth review of D-APILABEL1 tested overloads and turned them down as a second mechanism, in the version you ratified.

So option E keeps your shape, drops the default, and stops a bare remove(3) with a report naming both spellings. Its one cost: the signature says two optional labels while the real rule is exactly one, so sema needs one written check for a bare call or a doubled call.
