questions.text: I dont entirely understand the point of this. We should reunify meta things vs markers. Markers are # and "comptime" stuff/macros use $ for slices and $[...]$ for expansion macros. Maybe we use something like that instead of a regular marker? Need discussion.
questions.answer: The #! line is not Jet syntax and not a marker, so there is nothing to unify with the # / $ planes. It is an operating-system handshake: when you type ./backup.jet, the kernel — not Jet — reads the first two bytes of the file. If they are '#!', the kernel starts the named program (/usr/bin/env jet) and hands it the file. Jet only skips that first line; it produces no token and has no meaning inside the language. No Jet-owned spelling can do this job: a marker or $[...]$ form would run only after Jet is already running, but the whole point of this line is to start Jet when it is not running yet. The kernel accepts exactly one spelling, '#!', fixed since 1980 — Python, Ruby, shell, and Deno all accept the same line unchanged for the same reason; the resemblance to Jet's # marker sigil is coincidence. So the ballot adds no meta mechanism. The choice is only: A) tolerate the OS's line at byte zero so chmod +x works; B) generate a separate launcher file instead; C) do nothing, always type 'jet file.jet'.

questions.text: The point of this ballot and functionality is not at a;; c;ear to me. Would these not be markers/meta tags/traits/policies? I dont get it, need discussion
questions.answer: You are right that these shapes overlap — that overlap is exactly what this ballot decides. The job: wrap a function with behavior around each call (retry, cache, trace) without changing how callers call it. Python spells this @retry(3) above the def. The ballot picks where Jet spells it. Option B is literally a marker: #Policy(retry(3), trace(...)) on the declaration — the marker-plane answer. Option C spells it where the wrapped value is made: load_user_traced :: apply(retry(3), load_user). Option A is no new mechanism: you hand-write a wrapper function that repeats the whole signature, and the copy drifts when the original changes. Option D is a registry far from the code. Traits do not cover this job: a trait says what a type can do; a policy is a runtime value that wraps one specific function. So the live choice is B vs C. B: policy named once on the declaration — concise, but it changes the function for every caller and is invisible at call sites. C: policy named where the value is formed — the command tool and the web worker can wrap the same function differently, and a reader sees the wrapping where it happens. The rec is C for that locality; if you prefer all meta to stay on the # plane, B is the coherent pick and the ballot supports it. If the whole feature feels unnecessary, A ships nothing new.

questions.text: What about suiting beginner magic expert control by having both b and c? B is the default when something is called but maybe c can be an intentional override so you can enforce a SPECIFIC policy at a callsite but otherwise have localized control of a policy at the definition?
questions.answer: Yes — that combination works, and it is now option E on the ballot with the recommendation moved to it. It stays one mechanism: the marker and the application attach the same typed policy values, just at two points. The declaration marker is the beginner default: a library author writes #Policy(retry(3), trace(...)) once, and every plain call gets safe behavior with zero ceremony. The application is the expert override: apply(retry(1), load_user) at a call site enforces exactly that chain — the declared default does not stack under it, so what you read at the override is the whole truth. One rule had to be pinned for 'enforce a SPECIFIC policy' to mean something: apply replaces the declared chain rather than wrapping around it, and apply with no policies yields the bare function. The accepted cost: a plain call's default is visible at the declaration, not the call site — the same tradeoff Python decorators make — and any call site that cares can override locally.

questions.text: Conceptually I think I’m ok with A but the syntax seems to have no precedent and to be foreign. Please justify or provide more conventional cohesive Jet syntax
questions.answer:
Option A adds no new syntax at all. Jet already has function values: you can bind a function to a name and call that name, and you can call a function stored in a struct field. The example examples/features/basics/callbacks.jet already does both. The parser already treats a parenthesis after any expression as a call of that value (postfix.rs, Expr::CallValue), so compute.grad(loss)(w, x, y) parses today with zero grammar changes. The foreign look comes only from squeezing two ordinary steps into one line.

The conventional Jet spelling, and the one the docs and examples will teach, is bind first, then call:

  dloss :: compute.grad(loss)
  gw :: dloss(w, x, y)

That reads like every other function value in Jet, and it is what a training loop wants anyway: build the gradient function once before the loop, call it every step. A second derivative is the same idiom again: ddloss :: compute.grad(dloss). The one-line double call stays legal because the grammar is uniform and banning it would need a special-case rule, but it is the contraction, not the idiom. If ratified as A, the ballot examples, docs, and goldens will use the bind-then-call spelling.

questions.text:
1) What is the / separator in the examples? That doesnt look like syntax we have already and I dont think i like it. I might be ok with like a plus operator to concat strings together easily then a more advanced concat function to enable delimiters and stuff. I dont know the details of how a - operator would work or any others though. 
2) What if we need to ensure we have an ACTUAL path type, not just a string, for safety or other compatibility issues? Is that a legitimate concern or not? If it is, then how can experts enable path only input mode?
questions.answer:
1) The / in the ballot examples is not Jet syntax today. It was copied from Python pathlib as a sketch. / in Jet is still division. You are right to reject it here.

Path joining should use methods we already lean on (and that D-PATHFS1 started): path.join("logs"), path.parent(), and so on. No new operator is required for this ballot.

About +:
- String + String stays ordinary text glue. Writing base + "/" + name is still the bug Path exists to stop.
- Path + String (or Path + Path) can later mean “join as a path,” with the right OS separator. That is a separate, small syntax choice. It is not required to pick Path as a type.
- A richer join helper (custom delimiters, many parts) belongs on Path or strings as a named function, not as -, /, or other arithmetic operators. Those names fight math.

I will change the ballot examples to .join, not /.

2) Yes, wanting a real Path sometimes is a fair concern. A Path means “this value was built or checked as a filesystem path,” not “any text.” That matters for untrusted input, FFI, and APIs where a random String would be the wrong kind of value.

It is not a good default for every call. fs.read("notes.txt") is clear. Forcing Path.from on every literal is beginner tax (ballot option C).

Default Core stays String | Path (option A): beginners pass strings; experts pass Path when they have one.

Experts who need Path-only can use:
- APIs or overloads that take only Path (expert surfaces, FFI bridges, validators that return Path)
- A boundary convert once: raw text -> Path (check/normalize), then pass Path downstream
- Optional later: a project lint or policy that forbids bare String at filesystem calls

So: Path type yes; String still welcome at Core doors; Path-only where the API truly needs it, not everywhere.

questions.text:
What about all task keywords but nested so you have task, task.group, task.race, task.all, task.any

Any issue with this?
questions.answer: No blocking issue — nesting is strictly better. questions.text: This misses the philosophies of jet. Minimizes friction proportionally to frequency of use (most common things should be easiest/fastest) and beginner friendliness with magic and ergonomics out of the box but allow full expert control
questions.answer: Agreed, and the ballot is revised. Every name is now weighed by the usage-frequency report (docs/research/corelib-api-usage-frequency-2026-08-06.md), not by a flat rule. New recommended option C ships the high-traffic names directly on String: to_int and to_float (parse-to-number is a dominant string operation, and they chain: line.trim().to_int()) plus match and matches for regex. Each is a spelling of the one existing mechanism (Int.parse, Float.parse, core.regex), so beginners get the zero-ceremony call and experts keep one engine. The rest stay routed: mutation verbs clash with immutable String, and char-level sequence work sits below the frequency line, where one chars() call is proportional friction.

questions.text: This misses the philosophies of jet. Minimizes friction proportionally to frequency of use (most common things should be easiest/fastest) and beginner friendliness with magic and ergonomics out of the box but allow full expert control
questions.answer: Agreed, and the ballot is revised. New recommended option C ships Set.sort() and Set.shuffle(), each returning a List. Sorting is a top-tier operation in the usage-frequency report, and dedupe-then-sort is an everyday idiom, so the most common Set step becomes one call. Both are spellings of the existing List mechanism, so no second engine appears. indexof and indexed stay declined for meaning, not purity: a hash Set has no positions, and the number they return silently changes after any add or remove — a beginner trap, not a friction cut. Positions stay on List, where they are real.

questions.text: This misses the philosophies of jet. Minimizes friction proportionally to frequency of use (most common things should be easiest/fastest) and beginner friendliness with magic and ergonomics out of the box but allow full expert control
questions.answer: Applied the frequency lens; the decline survives it, so the ballot now argues from friction, not rule-citing. Five of the six names (fill, cycle_n, duplicate, tostring, clip/iterator, compact) are synonyms of repeat, join, to_list, and filter. The canonical call is already the same length, so shipping them cuts zero friction and only grows what a beginner must learn. next would add a second, stateful consumption model beside loops and adapters, and its workflows already have one-call routes: chunk for pairwise reads, take and skip for bounded steps. If a real stepping workflow ever appears without a route, the answer is a new adapter, not a cursor.

questions.text: This misses the philosophies of jet. Minimizes friction proportionally to frequency of use (most common things should be easiest/fastest) and beginner friendliness with magic and ergonomics out of the box but allow full expert control. We want the BEST APIs/surfaces/methods/etc of any language. If we can improve our APIs, then we should do so even if it means updating the existing one
questions.answer: Applied both lenses; ballot revised. Frequency: every one of the 75 already reaches its result in equal or fewer keystrokes under Jet's canonical name, so declining taxes no frequent path — the cost is one docs lookup, and the reference names the route beside each declined name. Best-API: the ballot now commits to your rule — when a competitor's spelling beats ours, we replace ours outright (greenfield), never alias. This sweep's head-to-heads all came out win-or-tie for the current names (v4 vs uuid4, query_one vs first, next vs read, float_range vs uniform). The four real gaps found ship with the card, and the two real TLS gaps have a follow-up card. Locks and reflect writes stay out by the safety design: concurrency routes through core.tasks, and reflection stays read-only.

questions.text: I want to use if but have a nicer native  syntax like option a’s select.
questions.answer: Done: the ballot now has option D, and it is the recommendation. The wait is a subjectless if table with option A's exact arms: if { job, jobs -> handle(job)  msg, control -> obey(msg)  after 100ms -> retry() }. No new keyword and no S68 amendment. A comma head can never be a Bool expression, so the parser knows the table waits, and the whole table compiles to one atomic wait. select stays a free name everywhere.

questions.text: I like the idea of a leading . for elementwise, but consider all of jet syntax (current and planned changes), then repropose a new perfect system that incorporates the current recommendation with the .* and * syntaxes
questions.answer:
Reproposed as option F, now on the ballot, and it is my new recommendation.

F = the type says which, and the dot asks for cells where the plain operator would compose. Matrix composes under *. Grid and lane vectors multiply cells under *. A leading dot is legal only on a Matrix, where it means cells: pose .* spin. Where * is already cell by cell, the dot is refused — so no meaning ever gets two spellings.

Three findings from the syntax sweep that shaped it:

1. The dot is already Jet's word for distribute across members. D-SPREAD1=A gives prefix.[a, b, c] as member spread, and D-ENUMDOT1 gives .Variant. Applying an operator across cells is the same idea one level down, so .* costs no new concept.

2. Do not take option E whole. Its call half, f.(x), reintroduces call fan-out, which your own ratified D-VERDICT-1324-1 removed. F takes E's operator dot and leaves the call dot retired.

3. Cell-by-cell * is already law. D-VECARITH1 ratified element-wise + - * / for lane vectors. So Grid multiplying cells under plain * is not a new rule to learn — it is the rule the language already has, and Matrix is the one type that composes instead.

What F fixes about D, your current recommendation: under D a person porting a formula writes .cells() at the crossing point, so a line that reads the same in every other language does not read the same here. Under F they write .* on the value they already hold.

Honest costs: five new infix tokens (.*, ./, .^, .+, .-) plus compound forms. A porter who writes .* on a Grid gets an error rather than a result — that error is the teaching moment and needs registered what/why/fix text under I4. One lexing risk to check: ^ is take in prefix position under D-MEM1=A and power in infix position, so .^ must be lexed against both.

An e4 agent set CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/jet-e4-target (15GB) plus 5GB scratchpad targets/logs; this filled 24GB swap and caused kernel OOM kills on the owner's machine. Never put cargo target dirs or multi-GB logs in /tmp; use a disk path and clean up session outputs.
papercuts.resolution: Fixed: jet-env rejects /tmp CARGO_TARGET_DIR, AGENTS.md documents the tmpfs trap, scripts/agent/tmp-guard.sh auto-cleans and blocks under memory pressure

papercuts.text: tests/comptime_diff.rs numbered rustc artifacts by per-test case index, so two tests both using index 0 raced for one output path and failed as a fake I2 miscompile; fixed on bd3/reader

CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<main>/target shared across worktrees caused a real build break (E0599: no variant ComptimeSplice for jet::AST::Expr in Source/CmdProve.rs) even though the variant exists in my worktree's own crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/expressions.rs — reproducible on retry, not transient. Likely stale rlib reuse across worktrees with divergent AST enum shapes. Fell back to the worktree-local target dir to unblock.

Shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR across worktrees poisons builds: concurrent cargo from worktrees/dollar and worktrees/profile made my build fail with 'no variant ComptimeSplice in jet_foundation::AST::Expr' on unmodified code. Different sources, one target dir, whoever writes last wins. Agents need per-worktree target dirs.

Sharing CARGO_TARGET_DIR across git worktrees lets another worktree's build replace target/debug/jet and shared dep artifacts mid-session: a stale binary made a working sema fix look broken, and a lib test failed with 'no variant named ComptimeName in jet_lexer::AST::Expr' from another branch's artifacts. Build and run in one command, or verify the binary is yours.

git stash push -- <one-file> with no local changes to that file reports 'No local changes to save' but a following git stash pop still pops whatever is on TOP of the stash stack (an unrelated old stash from a prior session) and can conflict — hit this in the main repo's stash list (foreign-eval-builtins, foreign-wip-during-1478-abi-fix, cleanup-session entries pre-date this session). Resolved safely by restoring the one conflicted file to HEAD; stash entries left untouched. Avoid stash push/pop entirely when just wanting a scoped before/after diff — use git show HEAD:<path> instead.

tower CLI resolves .tower from cwd, so running it from a worktree silently reads the worktree's stale tracked copy instead of the canonical main board; agents in worktrees must export TOWER_DATA=<main>/plugins/tower/.tower

A worktree whose branch predates the canonical-board redirect ships a vendored plugins/tower/app/paths.mjs without canonicalDataDir, so tower card add run from that worktree writes to the stale worktree .tower and mints a card number that already exists on the real board, with no warning. Run the main checkout's plugins/tower/tower.mjs for every board write from a worktree.
tower card criteria <ref> --list errors with 'unknown flag for card: --list' although the CLI help documents it; workaround is card show <ref>, which prints the same checklist
tower help advertises 'card criteria --unmeet n' but cli.mjs has no unmeet flag — falsely-met criteria cannot be reopened via CLI

Same binary passes cleanly under jet-env. Hit repeatedly on card #1763 (bd14/bd15/bd16/orchestrator probes); always reproduce FFI/lowlevel examples via jet-env, never a bare shell.

Worktree-isolated agents (spawned already sandboxed to .claude/worktrees/agent-*) cannot do git ops in the shared builder worktree: any bash command that cd's to .claude/worktrees/builder and runs git is hard-refused by the sandbox ('git operations must target its own worktree'), even for builder-sync.sh --release itself if cd'd there first. builder-sync.sh succeeds (claims the lock) but is then unusable for git in that session. Card #1850: fell back to the agent's own isolated worktree per the exit-75 contingency, and released the builder lock via the script's bare 'rm -f' path (no cd needed) so it didn't sit claimed.

tower card add/update --blocked-by accepts '#N' and the lane renders 'Blocked by #N', but lint's orphan-blockers rule only resolves internal card ids, so every '#N' blocker reads as dangling; pass the card id from 'card show --json'.

codex workers launched in a linked worktree under .claude/worktrees cannot reach the nix daemon socket (EPERM on /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket) so every scripts/agent/jet-env command dies before cargo starts, and git metadata is read-only so the required commit fails. Hit three workers in one session (cards 1801, 1864, 1650/1775/1844). Workers then report fallback-toolchain greens the orchestrator cannot trust, or leave work staged and uncommitted. The sandbox writable_roots entry for the main .git does not cover a linked worktree's own git dir.

Adding /nix/var/nix to a codex worker's sandbox_workspace_write.writable_roots breaks bwrap outright: every shell launch dies with 'bwrap: Cant mkdir /nix/var/nix/.git: Permission denied', including pwd. One worker burned 55k tokens and ran nothing. It was an attempted fix for the daemon-socket EPERM that blocks jet-env in worker sandboxes; it makes things strictly worse. Known-good roots are the repo .git plus ~/.cache/nix, which still hit the socket EPERM intermittently but recover.
